text:
Haley Stevens’ decision to put country over party may be resonating far beyond Michigan.

If Republicans retain control of the House and Senate, it will be because a majority of voters still love this country and are willing to put it first. It will not be because of Donald Trump’s endless self-congratulatory speeches at rallies. 
His closing remarks at the Reflecting Pool offered little more than another poorly delivered recitation of his own achievements and past victories. Rather than focusing on the high stakes of the moment, he returned to a familiar narrative of personal success that many Americans outside the MAGA base have grown tired of hearing.

Trump has delivered real accomplishments in less than two years, yet he refuses to accept that his personal popularity remains limited beyond his core supporters. His ego has repeatedly stepped on those successes. 
The constant demand for praise from staff, combined with the instant attack on anyone who offers even measured criticism, strikes many voters as abhorrent. It turns policy wins into personality contests and alienates people who might otherwise support the results.

Doug Burgum’s speech that followed only compounded the problem. What should have been a focused closing argument instead became an extended exercise in flattery. The repeated congratulations were so frequent they became embarrassing, reinforcing the impression that loyalty to the man matters more than the message.

Voters closing out months of hard-fought campaigns across the country are not looking for more rallies centered on Trump’s self-regard. 
They are rejecting the alternative. 
They are voting to stop what they see as damage, not to cheer another round of self-congratulation. 

Stevens’ willingness to break with her party on principle offers a clear contrast: a decision framed around the 'COUNTRY'S INTERESTS'  rather than personal or partisan loyalty. That kind of choice, repeated elsewhere, may be speaking to a broader electorate that wants results and accountability more than rallies and applause.

text:
Since yesterday I have written some 20 answers to communication engineers and analysts on @LinkedIn. 

A series asked what would happen if network capacity followed people. Others offered dishes on stadium roofs, parked Teslas as moving towers, and a hybrid of leased towers and satellites. 

This morning came news that SpaceX is in talks to buy Boost Mobile or use its network.

Every one of these arguments tries, in its own way, to write a new law of physics. Scratch the surface and the old laws are still there.

Musk stated them himself. In March 2020 he said Starlink was not a threat to telcos, that it would serve the 3 or 4% hardest to reach, and that it could not take many customers in Los Angeles because the bandwidth per cell was not high enough. The physics has not changed since. The ambition has.

There are three rules. Spectrum: SpaceX holds about 80 MHz, each of the big three American carriers 280 to 380. The beam: everyone under it shares it, and more dishes only divide the same sky more thinly. Distance: a phone’s signal reaching a satellite 550 km up is about 10,000 times weaker than at a tower 5 km away.

Then the money. The cash is in the cities, where about 98% of Verizon’s revenue comes from. The 300 million people outside coverage are mostly rural and poor. Musk himself sized that market at about $30 billion a year. It is a noble market, and Starlink serves it well. It cannot carry a $2 trillion valuation.

So SpaceX is coming down to the ground: Boost, which runs largely on AT&T’s network, and talks to lease up to 80,000 towers. Verizon puts a full network at $300 billion to $500 billion. The market prices the sky today at $10 a month, as an add-on. And the segment SpaceX calls AI is rent from a building in Memphis: a landlord and a tenant, not space and not AI.

I take on the strongest case against me, Jio, and show why it proves the point: Jio won on price, with a ground network.

SpaceX rewrote the rules of the reusable rocket. It cannot rewrite the laws of communication physics. Physics writes the rules, not SpaceX.

SOUTH AFRICA IS NOT A COLONY OF THE US: NO CAPITULATION TO US IMPERIALIST BULLYING, BUT STRATEGIC COMPOSURE TO PROTECT OUR SOVEREIGNTY
By Dr Zamani Saul, NC ANC Provincial Chairperson
03 November 2026

Introduction

Trading with the US or any other country does not reduce South Africa into a colony but a trading partner. The Trump administration's distorted view that small and middle power countries that trade with the US are their colonies must be openly challenges. This US empire predatory attitude and instinct must be rejected and countries must uncompromisingly defend their sovereignty.

On 2 November 2026, the US announced its intention to terminate South Africa’s eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective from 1 January 2027. Triggered by an annual interagency review led by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, US cited practices "inconsistent with AGOA's eligibility criteria", explicitly pointing to alleged trade barriers and threats to US foreign policy and national security.

The economic impact on South Africa

To accurately assess the economic impact, it is essential to untangle the actual data from confusing headlines. Since its enactment in 2000, AGOA has granted qualifying sub-Saharan countries duty-free access to US markets for over 1,800 products. South Africa historically stood as its primary beneficiary, facilitating substantial automotive and agricultural trade.

However, the real value of this trade agreement has faced aggressive erosion over the last two years under the Trump administration. The economic impact of the definitive 1 January 2027 ejection can be measured across several clear vectors:

First, ejection from AGOA has minimal impact on the South African export economy. According to Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau, AGOA exports were valued at approximately $1.7 billion in 2025, down significantly from $4 billion in 2024. Crucially, AGOA trade represented only about 1% of South Africa’s total global exports. Nearly 90% of South Africa’s total trade outbound to the US already bypasses the AGOA framework entirely.

Secondly, ejection from AGOA does not equal a trade ban. South African products will simply revert to standard Most Favoured Nation (MFN) tariff rates. Economists note that the average tariff benefit previously offered by AGOA was a modest 3.5%. Presidential Envoy on Agriculture and Land, Wandile Sihlobo, calculated that losing AGOA adds a 3.4% tariff bump onto the 12.5% foundational tariffs currently imposed by the US administration. A combined 15.9% tariff is challenging, but nowhere near the crippling 30% Trump "liberation day" tariffs that the agricultural sector successfully bypassed and competed against in 2025.

Thirdly, specific economic sectors will bear the brunt of the ejection from AGOA. While macro-economically stable, the micro-economic fallout will harshly hit specific localised businesses. The domestic automotive sector, which has already seen vehicle export earnings to the US contract from R17.7 billion in 2024 to R8 billion in 2025 due to punitive US Section 232 steel and aluminium tariffs, faces a distinct loss of edge.

Fourthly, the impact will be felt by the agricultural sector. High-value agricultural products like citrus fruits, macadamia nuts and wine will immediately feel the negative impact. Organised labour bodies, including the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), anticipate that the sudden removal could threaten up to 10,000 jobs across agricultural supply chains and specialised assembly plants.

Lastly, South Africa’s primary exports to the US, which include critical mineral resources such as platinum group metals, gold and diamonds, will remain entirely unaffected. They enter the US market duty-free under separate global tariff codes due to the US economy’s structural dependence on South African mineral inputs.

Tesla FSD: The Problem Isn't the Driving AI. It's the Terrible User Interface 

I recently got the latest FSD update on my Tesla and decided to try it on a routine ten-mile drive into town.

My car is a 2017 Model S with HW3, running software version 2026.38.5.11 and FSD v14.3 Lite.

During that one short drive, I had to disengage FSD numerous times. Not because the car was swerving into traffic, failing to recognize traffic lights, or doing anything particularly dangerous. It was because the car kept making decisions I didn't want it to make, and I couldn't find any reasonable way to tell it otherwise.

At first, I thought this might be user error. Perhaps I simply didn't understand how the new interface worked.

After researching it extensively, however, I've come to a rather different conclusion.

Tesla has made some truly awful user-interface decisions with FSD. And these aren't problems specific to my older HW3 vehicle. The same fundamental controls and design philosophy apply to HW4 vehicles running the full version of FSD.

That's an important distinction. People are quick to dismiss complaints from owners of older Teslas by saying that HW3 doesn't have enough computing power to run the latest driving AI.

But that's not what I'm complaining about.

I'm complaining about the deliberate decisions Tesla has made regarding how the driver interacts with FSD.

Let me explain.

My Experience on One Ten-Mile Drive

Right off the bat, I discovered that FSD doesn't behave the way I expect when I'm not navigating to a specific destination.

If I enable FSD without navigation turned on, the car still independently decides which lane it wants to occupy and which path it wants to follow.

Why?

If I haven't given the car a destination, why would it assume it should make lane changes without my telling it to?

I just want it to stay in my lane, maintain my desired speed, and let me tell it when to do something different.

You might respond, "What's the problem? Just enable navigation since, obviously, you're going somewhere."

But here's the rub.

Tesla's navigation is terrible.

Normally, that's not an issue. When I'm driving manually, I simply ignore the navigation system when it tells me to take a stupid turn that makes no sense.

But with FSD enabled, the car actually acts on those stupid navigation decisions.

And I couldn't find a reliable way to tell it not to.

Here's what happened.

Problem #1: It Wouldn't Change Lanes When I Told It To

Shortly after starting my drive, the highway I was on went from one lane to two lanes.

The car stayed in the left lane.

I suppose that's fine. Perhaps it decided there was some reason to prefer the left lane.

But I didn't want to be in the left lane, so I hit the right turn signal to tell it to move over.

The blinker blinked.

The car didn't budge.

In previous versions of Tesla's driving-assistance software, hitting the turn signal was how you told the car you wanted to change lanes.

Now, apparently, the turn signal is merely a suggestion that FSD may or may not honor.

Why?

What exactly is the point of having a human supervising the vehicle if the vehicle ignores the human's instructions?

And before someone asks why I cared so much about getting into the right lane, here's why.

I try to drive the speed limit.

In fact, just two weeks ago, I got a speeding ticket on this very section of road because I wasn't paying attention. Now I'm particularly careful about my speed.

The drivers in the left lane frequently travel 15 to 20 mph over the limit.

That's not where I want to be.

So, because the car ignored my turn signal, I had to disengage FSD, manually move into the right lane, and then re-engage it.

One disengagement, and I was barely into my drive.

Problem #2: I Can No Longer Set My Desired Speed

After re-engaging FSD, I noticed the car was still traveling considerably faster than the speed limit.

So I used the stalk to adjust the speed.

Except I couldn't.

Apparently, Tesla has removed the ability to specify an exact desired speed while using the new FSD system.

Instead, you select one of several driving profiles: Sloth, Chill, Standard, Hurry, or Mad Max.

Seriously?

I don't want a personality profile. I want to tell the car what speed to drive.

If the speed limit is 55 mph and I want to go 57 mph, I should be able to specify 57 mph.

This is not some wildly complicated user-interface concept. Cruise controls have worked this way for decades.

Instead, I found myself cycling through driving profiles until the car announced that I was a "Sloth" and finally slowed down to the speed limit.

I couldn't even see an exact target speed that I had selected.

This is an actual, intentional change Tesla made to the user interface. And it applies to HW4 vehicles as well.

This isn't a deficiency in HW3's processing power. It's a deliberate removal of useful functionality.

Why would Tesla think this is an improvement?

Problem #3: It Wanted to Make an Idiotic Left Turn

The remaining problems were almost entirely related to navigation.

At one point, during rush-hour traffic, FSD decided that the best route was to make an unprotected left-hand turn across two lanes of oncoming traffic.

No traffic light.

Just wait for an opening and navigate across two lanes of traffic.

Meanwhile, about a quarter mile farther down the road was an intersection with a traffic light and a dedicated left-turn signal.

I live here. I know these streets. I know which intersections are easy to navigate and which ones are a pain in the ass.

I would never take the turn FSD was planning.

Now, here's the important part.

I'm not complaining that FSD was incapable of making the unprotected left turn. Maybe it could have done it flawlessly.

I'm complaining that I didn't want to make that turn, and I couldn't find a simple way to tell the car to continue to the next intersection instead.

I tried to figure out how to override the navigation decision without disengaging.

I couldn't.

So I disengaged again.

Problem #4: It Wanted to Take the Wrong Street

A little farther down the road, the car decided to make a right-hand turn onto a street that I know is always backed up at that time of day.

I always take the next street instead.

Again, this is local knowledge. I know the traffic patterns here because I've been driving these streets for years.

All I wanted to communicate was:

"Don't turn here. Go one more block."

That shouldn't be a difficult instruction to convey to a supposedly sophisticated self-driving system.

But once again, I couldn't find a reliable way to communicate it.

So I disengaged again.

And again, the problem wasn't that FSD couldn't make the turn. The problem was that it was trying to make a turn I didn't want it to make.

Problem #5: Turning Off Navigation Didn't Solve Anything

Eventually, I realized that most of my problems were caused by FSD following a navigation route that I considered idiotic.

So I thought, fine, I'll just turn navigation off.

Surely, without a route to follow, FSD would simply maintain my current lane until I used the turn signal to tell it where I wanted to go.

Nope.

Without navigation enabled, FSD still makes its own lane and path decisions.

And my turn signals still weren't reliably getting it to do what I wanted.

So I was right back where I started.

This Is a User-Interface Problem, Not an HW3 Problem

Now, here's where I think the discussion about FSD frequently goes completely off the rails.

People will immediately point out that my car is a nine-year-old Model S running HW3, and that HW4 runs a significantly more capable neural network.

Fine.

I understand that.

I have a background in software development. I understand that more capable hardware can run larger neural networks and make better decisions.

But none of that addresses my primary complaints.

The inability to specify an exact target speed isn't a neural-network limitation.

That's a user-interface decision.

Replacing precise driver control with Sloth, Chill, Standard, Hurry, and Mad Max is a user-interface decision.

Treating a turn signal as an expression of preference rather than a command that the driver expects the system to execute when safe is a user-interface decision. Whether the inconsistent responses are an additional software bug is another question.

And failing to provide an obvious, reliable way to override an unwanted navigation turn is a user-interface design problem.

These are not things that require a more powerful GPU to solve.

HW4 uses the same fundamental FSD speed-profile system and the same general philosophy of allowing the software to make driving decisions.

It also uses Tesla's navigation and routing system. The driving model may execute routes differently, and a more capable model might make better decisions at intersections, but newer AI hardware does not magically give the driver a different navigation interface or a precise way to command an alternate turn.

In fact, owners of HW4 vehicles have reported the same kinds of difficulties overriding navigation decisions and requesting lane changes.

So please don't dismiss this as an HW3 issue.

A more powerful neural network doesn't fix a bad user interface.

I Actually Preferred Enhanced Autopilot

I've owned this Tesla for nine years and have experienced every generation of its driving-assistance software during that time.

For years, Tesla offered Enhanced Autopilot, or EAP.

And for what I wanted, it worked remarkably well.

It maintained my lane.

It maintained the precise speed I selected.

It performed lane changes when I requested them, and only when I requested them, using the turn signal, provided they could be completed safely.

I made the high-level driving decisions, and the car handled the tedious mechanics of executing them.

That's an incredibly useful system.

Now, with FSD, Tesla seems determined to eliminate as much driver input as possible.

I understand the long-term vision. The car is eventually supposed to be able to drive itself without human intervention.

But that's not the product we have today.

Today we have Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

And if I'm supervising it, shouldn't I be able to tell it what I want it to do?

I shouldn't have to completely disengage FSD because I want to take a different street.

I shouldn't have to disengage because I want to move from the left lane into the right lane.

And I certainly shouldn't need to choose between being a "Sloth" and being in a "Hurry" when all I want to do is drive two miles per hour over the speed limit.

These were solved problems.

Tesla has taken useful driver controls and replaced them with a system that increasingly insists on making decisions for me.

And, quite frequently, they're decisions I disagree with.

So When People Say FSD Works Great, I Call Bullshit

This is the part that's really beginning to frustrate me.

I constantly see people online claiming that FSD is amazing.

That they drive hundreds of miles without an intervention.

That it's practically solved self-driving.

And maybe those people really are having those experiences. I'm not claiming they're lying about their own drives.

But when those experiences are presented as proof that FSD has essentially solved the problem of everyday driving, I'm going to call bullshit.

I couldn't even drive ten miles into town without disengaging numerous times!

And again, those disengagements weren't because FSD was about to crash. It was mostly because the navigation sucked or the lane choices were idiotic.

They happened because the car made decisions I didn't agree with, and I couldn't find a reasonable way to correct them without taking over.

That's a critical distinction.

Someone might drive 100 miles on a highway with no interventions and declare FSD nearly perfect.

That's great.

But how does it handle a driver who knows that the next left turn is a terrible idea?

How does it handle a driver who wants to stay in a specific lane?

How does it handle someone who simply wants to set an exact speed?

What happens when the car's preferred route isn't the driver's preferred route?

These aren't obscure edge cases.

These are completely ordinary driving situations.

I don't measure the usefulness of a driving-assistance system solely by how many miles it can travel without disengaging.

I measure it by how effectively it helps me get where I want to go, the way I want to get there.

By that standard, the current version of FSD is, for me, effectively useless.

I'm not interested in constantly fighting the software over which lane to occupy, which intersection to use, or what speed to travel.

At that point, I might as well just drive the damn car myself. Or, better yet, bring back EAP!!!

The Bottom Line

I think Tesla has confused two very different goals.

One is making the car better at driving.

The other is making the car better at helping its owner drive.

Those aren't necessarily the same thing.

Tesla may be making tremendous progress on the first goal while actually moving backward on the second.

And the really frustrating thing is that none of my primary complaints require breakthroughs in artificial intelligence.

Give me the ability to specify an exact speed.

Make turn-signal requests reliable.

Give me a simple way to override an unwanted navigation turn.

And let me tell the car which lane I want to be in.

That's it.

Until Tesla addresses those basic user-interface problems, I don't particularly care how sophisticated the underlying neural network becomes.

A car that drives brilliantly but won't reliably let me tell it what to do is not a useful driving-assistance system.

ChatGPT Fact-Check: Are These Complaints Supported by the Evidence?

After describing my experience, I asked ChatGPT to research the current Tesla documentation, software release notes, and reports from other owners.

I specifically wanted to determine whether these problems were unique to my older HW3 vehicle or whether HW4 owners were experiencing the same things.

Here is what the research established.

1. Precise Speed Control Was Deliberately Removed on HW3 and HW4

Confirmed by Tesla's software release notes.

Tesla introduced speed profiles on HW4 and subsequently brought the same approach to HW3.

The release notes explicitly explain that FSD now determines vehicle speed based on the selected driving profile, speed limit, and traffic conditions rather than allowing the driver to adjust a precise maximum-speed offset.

The same basic design applies to both hardware generations.

HW3: Software 2026.38.5.11 release notes

HW4: Software 2025.45.5 release notes

This is definitively a design decision, not a hardware limitation.

2. Turn Signals Being Ignored Has Been Reported on Both HW3 and HW4

Confirmed as a recurring owner-reported problem, though not universal.

A 2019 Model S owner running v14 Lite reported that requesting a lane change caused the turn signal to blink three times and then cancel without the car changing lanes.

2019 Model S — Turn signal ignored

A 2018 Model S owner testing v14.3 Lite reported apparently losing the ability to request lane changes through the turn-signal stalk.

2018 Model S — v14.3 Lite test drive

And this isn't limited to HW3.

A 2026 Model 3 owner running full FSD v14.3.2 on HW4 reported that turn-signal requests frequently resulted in the signal canceling without a lane change.

2026 Model 3 — HW4 lane-change problems

Tesla's documentation still says that turn signals can indicate a lane-change preference. Other owners report that the functionality works for them.

So the evidence doesn't establish that Tesla intentionally removed turn-signal lane changes. It does establish that owners of both hardware generations are reporting similar failures.

The underlying design also makes the turn signal a preference rather than an unconditional command, although the car must still judge whether a maneuver is safe.

3. Overriding Navigation Decisions Is a Reported Problem on HW4

Corroborated by HW4 owner reports.

A particularly relevant report comes from the owner of a 2023 Model X with HW4 running FSD v14.3.2.

The owner specifically complained that the software no longer reliably allowed them to use a turn signal to select an alternate street and change the navigation route.

Interestingly, the same owner explained that ordinary lane-change requests still worked. It was the ability to override an upcoming navigation turn that had stopped working.

HW4 Model X — Lost ability to change route with turn signal

That distinction is remarkably similar to my own frustration.

The system may be quite capable of executing its chosen navigation route, but that doesn't necessarily mean the driver can easily tell it to take a different one.

Tesla provides route-editing tools, but I couldn't find a documented, guaranteed command that allows a driver to reject an upcoming turn and choose the next intersection without taking over.

4. FSD Making Driving Decisions Without Navigation Is Intentional

Confirmed by Tesla's owner's manual.

Tesla explicitly states that when FSD is activated without a navigation destination, it chooses what it considers the most probable driving path or suggests a destination.

Source: Tesla Model S Owner's Manual — Full Self-Driving

This is not an HW3-specific behavior.

It's part of Tesla's fundamental FSD operating philosophy.

So disabling navigation does not transform FSD into a conventional lane-maintaining cruise-control system that waits for the driver to direct each turn.

5. HW4 Has a More Capable Driving Model, Not a Fundamentally Different Driver-Control Philosophy

Confirmed in broad terms by the release notes and owner documentation.

Tesla explicitly describes v14.3 Lite as a version that distills capabilities from the larger HW4 FSD model so that it can run on HW3 hardware.

That means HW4 and HW3 can differ substantially in how they recognize and respond to driving situations.

It does not mean that an HW4 owner has restored precise FSD speed control or a fundamentally different set of commands for directing lane and route choices.

The speed-profile design is shared, the general navigation approach is shared, and owners of both generations have reported difficulty influencing the system through turn signals.

There are interface differences between vehicle models and software versions, so it would be inaccurate to say every screen and control is literally identical. But the fundamental driver-control limitations discussed here are not unique to HW3.

Source: Tesla FSD v14.3 Lite and HW4 release notes

Final Assessment

The research supports the central criticism.

Tesla has deliberately replaced precise speed control with driving profiles. It has designed FSD to make lane and navigation decisions autonomously, even when no destination is specified. Turn-signal requests remain officially supported, but both HW3 and HW4 owners report inconsistent responses. And there is no clearly documented, guaranteed method of commanding FSD to skip an unwanted navigation turn while remaining engaged.

That doesn't prove every owner will encounter these problems, nor does it establish that every undesirable navigation decision is identical across hardware generations.

But it does establish that this isn't simply a case of an old HW3 Tesla being unable to keep up with newer software.

The central problem is the way Tesla has chosen to let drivers interact with FSD.

And that problem doesn't disappear just because the car has a more powerful computer.

text:
Everyone's already got Quinn Hughes signing in New Jersey next summer. The brothers reunite, Jack and Luke and Quinn all on one blue line and one power play, and the Devils become a superteam overnight. I get it. It's the best storyline in hockey. But the more I look at it, the less I think it actually happens. I'll lay out why.

Start with last year. The Canucks and Devils reportedly touched base on a Hughes trade, and New Jersey never pushed it across the finish line. Their cap and a couple of no-trade/no-move contracts made it messy, and they let it go. My personal read is that Quinn wanted Jersey. When the team with both his brothers on it had the chance and passed, I think that stuck with him. Players remember who came for them and who didn't.

The bigger problem is money, and it's not close. The Devils are projected to have about $16.8M in cap space next season, and that's with only 16 roster spots filled. They still need to fill out the rest of the lineup with that same money. Quinn hits UFA as a Norris-caliber defenseman, and his max next summer is roughly $22.7M a year. Jersey can't even fit the max, let alone build a roster around it.

So what would it actually take? Quinn would have to come in well under market just to fit, and even then there'd be almost nothing left for depth. That means a hometown discount on the biggest contract of his career, which also sets the market for every elite defenseman after him. Guys don't do that, and their agents definitely don't let them. A small discount is possible. The discount Jersey needs isn't happening.

Meanwhile, look at what he already has in Minnesota. The Wild are first in the Central and #2 in the NHL's power rankings, and they're doing it while missing Faber, Gustavsson, both Folignos, and Spurgeon. That's a big chunk of their core on the shelf, and they're still near the top of the league. When those guys come back, this is a real Cup team. Why leave a contender to start over somewhere that can't afford you?

Then there's Brock Faber, and this is the part people sleep on. When he's healthy, Quinn isn't finding a better partner anywhere in the league. Faber can jump into the play and drive offense right alongside him, but he's also a legit shutdown defender. That combination lets Quinn take every risk he wants, because he knows Faber has the back end covered. Players love that kind of pairing, and you don't find it twice.

Put it all together. New Jersey passed on him once. They can't afford him without gutting the roster. And they can't offer him a better team or a better partner than what he has right now. The brothers thing is a great story, and I'd watch every second of it. But Quinn Hughes is staying in Minnesota.

Tell me I'm wrong

One of the unexplained mysteries in the scanty documentation of the early life of the 44th President of the United States is the appearance of the name Soebarkah as his last name on an official document filled out by his mother.

text:
Actually, likely everyone would be alive if she were the captain. There was nothing she could do to override her 35 year senior pilot.
The plane crashed because the 55 year old experienced white dude pilot (who i wouldn't worry about on sight) made a risky and fatal decision. The captain makes all final decisions.
He was warned by ATC of the "pretty nasty" weather and "moderate to extreme precipitation" 10 mins prior and made a risky decision for only a slight deviation that turned out to be fatal. 
It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. The captain made a slight deviation because it wasn't serious and they were above the storm until that cell ballooned up from 33000 ft to 48000 ft ceiling in a few minutes and by then it was too late for them to climb out of it.
From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (captain’s voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions.

ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (captain’s voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions.

text:
Brad Pitt bought his elderly neighbor’s house — then reportedly let him continue living there rent-free for the rest of his life. ❤️

The unusual arrangement came to light through actress Cassandra Peterson, better known as Elvira, who once owned the Los Feliz property that became the center of Pitt’s sprawling Los Angeles estate.

Over the years, Pitt purchased several neighboring properties to expand the compound. One belonged to an elderly widower named John, who was around 90 at the time.

Rather than require John to leave his longtime home after purchasing it, Pitt reportedly made him an offer:

Stay as long as you live. No rent required.

It turned into a considerably longer commitment than anyone may have expected.

John lived to 105 years old, meaning the arrangement appears to have lasted roughly 15 years. Peterson later joked that John “just kept living forever,” adding that Pitt was probably thinking, “Well, you know, he can live there till he dies, which might be any minute now.”

But John kept going.

An important distinction often lost when the story is retold is that Pitt was already buying surrounding properties for his estate. The generous part wasn’t simply purchasing John’s house — it was allowing an elderly man to remain in his home afterward without paying rent.

Peterson also remembered Pitt as consistently kind and respectful during the years they were neighbors.

For John, a property sale therefore didn't mean losing the place he had called home.

He sold his house at around 90 — and was reportedly allowed to keep calling it home until 105. ❤️

Would you make the same arrangement if you bought a home from someone who had lived there for decades?

Sources: Cassandra Peterson’s People interview; Fox News; NZ Herald; Tribune India; La Vanguardia.

🇮🇷|The Letter Exists. The Signature Is on It. The Boast Is Dead.

The office of the Leader published a handwritten letter bearing his signature. The text is a personal reply to a 10-year-old student, Alireza Bakhshi. The letter carries the Leader's own hand, his own words, and a footnote in his own voice: "You have legible handwriting."

The enemy camp had been boasting that no handwritten letter from him had appeared. That boast is now a sheet of paper with a signature on it, released by the office that holds his correspondence.

The forensic anchor is the point. Read why a child's letter was chosen.

A political statement can be drafted by a committee, typed by a staffer, and released as a "message from the Leader." It proves nothing about the man's hand or his presence. A reply to a 10-year-old cannot be manufactured the same way. It contains specific, personal, unscripted details: the month of his birth, a gift offered in return, a greeting to the child's family, and a teacher's note about handwriting.

The specificity is the authentication. The footnote about legible handwriting is the detail that no propaganda office invents. It is the mark of a man who read the child's letter closely enough to comment on the penmanship. That is the most credible proof of an active, present, reading mind that a state can publish without turning it into a political broadcast.

The signature is the file the intelligence services will run.

Handwriting is forensic. Graphologists, intelligence agencies, and hostile media will compare the signature and the script against known samples. The office knows this. It published the letter anyway. That is the confidence signal: the signature will survive the comparison, because the hand that wrote it is the hand that signs the state's decisions.

The timing is not sentimental. It is operational.

The letter was released as Iranian negotiators sat in Doha for the third day with Qatari mediators, as Bagheri Kani met Wang Yi in Beijing and the Sultan of Oman arrived in the same city, as Rezaei spoke with Putin, and as the judiciary pursued 159 indictments over the assassination of the Leader and his family.

The enemy camp's claim that the Leader is absent, incapacitated, or gone is not a gossip item. It is a psychological operation aimed at the Doha table and the Beijing architecture. If the decision-maker is gone, the negotiators have no authority. If the system is headless, the guarantees are worthless. The letter answers both: the authority is present, and the hand that signs is the hand that decides.

The release is an archive operation, not a news event.

The letter is dated 19 October 2021. The office held it for years and chose this week to publish it. That is not a spontaneous act of transparency. It is a strategic release from the archive, timed to a specific information environment. The office selected a personal letter, not a policy document, because a personal letter cannot be dismissed as a press release.

The decision chain is the buried confirmation.

Prior reports established the chain: the Supreme Leader authorizes, the Supreme National Security Council runs the file, Qalibaf negotiates, Araghchi executes the public face, Rezaei sets the conditions. The letter confirms the top of that chain is engaged. The man who signs the state's decisions is in his office, reading correspondence, and answering it in his own hand.

The contradiction the enemy camp cannot survive.

The same outlets that claimed no handwritten letter existed are the outlets that have spent months publishing claims about his health, his withdrawal from decision-making, and a succession struggle. They built a narrative of a system in collapse. The office has now produced a signed document, a personal reply, and a handwriting sample that will be examined forensically by the very services that promoted the narrative.

The claim was made in public. The refutation is made in public. The signature is the receipt.

The bill.

A 10-year-old wrote a letter. The Leader answered it in his own hand. The office held the answer and released it when the enemy's boast needed to be buried. The signature is on the page. The footnote is in his voice. The decision-maker is in the office. The Doha talks have authority behind them. The Beijing architecture has a guarantor with a hand that signs.

The boast is dead. The letter is the proof.

text:
🚨 NOMURA: THE MARKET MAY BE MISREADING THE ENTIRE AI DATA CENTER BOOM.

Big Tech is spending hundreds of billions on AI infrastructure. Free cash flow is under pressure. Investors are worried the AI boom isn't profitable.

But Nomura argues something very different:

AI infrastructure is already highly profitable. The cash flows simply haven't caught up with the investment cycle.

Here's the breakdown 🧵👇

1/ The profitability numbers tell a different story.

According to Nomura's November 2 report:

• AWS revenue: $46B, +39% YoY
• AWS operating margin: 38.7%
• Google Cloud revenue: $30.7B, +103% YoY
• Google Cloud operating margin: 36.2%
• Azure growth: +48%

These are not the numbers of an industry struggling to generate operating profits.

2/ The real issue is timing, not necessarily profitability.

Big Tech pays for data centers, GPUs, networking and memory upfront.

Revenue and cash generation arrive over subsequent years.

That creates a classic free-cash-flow J-curve:

CAPEX accelerates → FCF deteriorates → Infrastructure generates revenue → Investment growth moderates → FCF recovers.

3/ Nomura expects operating income to surge before free cash flow.

Its illustrative forecasts suggest operating-income growth could peak around 2029, while FCF growth accelerates later.

That distinction matters enormously for investors valuing AI infrastructure businesses.

4/ Why can't hyperscalers simply stop spending?

Because AI increasingly threatens their existing businesses.

Search, advertising, shopping, software and cloud services are being reshaped by AI agents.

Companies that underinvest today risk surrendering customers, data and market share tomorrow.

5/ Demand may not be the primary constraint. Capacity is.

Nomura cites enormous contracted cloud backlogs:

• Google Cloud: $560.8B
• AWS: ~$496B
• Microsoft commercial RPO: $677B

These figures have different reporting definitions, but collectively illustrate substantial contracted demand.

6/ Big Tech has financing alternatives to cutting CAPEX.

Nomura identifies four paths:

① Accelerate investment
② Freeze CAPEX
③ Use joint ventures and operating leases
④ Monetize contracted future cash flows
Its preferred expectation is continued investment supported by increasingly sophisticated financing structures.

7/ Oracle offers a real-world example.

Nomura highlights Oracle's combination of long-term leases, project financing, customer prepayments and customer-provided hardware.

The broader message: hyperscalers can restructure who finances infrastructure without necessarily reducing how much infrastructure gets built.

8/ This distinction is critical for semiconductors and memory.

Negative hyperscaler FCF does not automatically imply collapsing demand for GPUs, DRAM, HBM or other data-center components.

If spending continues through financing structures, semiconductor demand can remain resilient even while hyperscalers optimize their balance sheets.

9/ What could invalidate the thesis?

A genuine compute oversupply.

Watch:

• Cloud revenue growth
• GPU rental pricing
• Contracted backlog growth
• Data-center utilization
• Memory supply commitments
• Hyperscaler investment guidance

These are more useful indicators than negative FCF alone.

10/ The investment takeaway:

The key question is not simply:

"Why is Big Tech burning so much cash?"

It is:

"Will the infrastructure being built today generate enough durable cash flow to justify its cost of capital?"

Nomura is optimistic.

But the answer ultimately depends on pricing, utilization, investment discipline and the durability of AI demand.

The AI infrastructure cycle may be a cash-flow timing problem rather than a profitability crisis.

text:
Recap for the last 7 days - C2C Actors 

Bottom line: Iran is the main flashpoint of the week, a coercive bargaining standoff with the US and Israel, with Hormuz as the lever. The rest is attrition (Russia–Ukraine), proxy escalation (Saudi–Houthi) and managed rivalry (US–China). Data: Radarwire, 27 Oct–3 Nov.

1. US/Israel vs Iran: coercion on both sides

• Conflict-coded flows were heavy in all directions: US→Iran 476, Iran→US 404, Israel→Iran 324, Iran→Israel 242.

• Trump threatened strikes. Khamenei warned any attack gets an immediate response "without geographic limits". AP reports Netanyahu is pushing for new strikes.

• Rubio at the G20: no decision yet, and the US prefers diplomacy.

• Iran offered to reopen Hormuz within 48 hours if the US meets its demands (outlets cite four to seven terms). It also reported four tankers hitting mines there on 30 Oct.

• Motive: Iran is using the strait as its bargaining chip. Israel wants to degrade Iran's nuclear and military capability before any deal. Washington is weighing force against a deal, with midterms on the day itself. Russia voiced "deep concern".

• Caveat: the claims of an imminent US nuclear strike come from commentators (Tucker Carlson) and are thinly corroborated. Treat them as signalling, not fact.

2. Saudi Arabia vs the Houthis: proxy war widening

• Yemen has the world's highest escalation score this week.

• Riyadh reported intercepting a Houthi drone aimed at Mecca, and the Houthis deny targeting it. They reportedly hit Aden's government HQ and airport, and the coalition says it struck Houthi launch sources. Over 300,000 people are reported displaced.

• Saudi Arabia signed a formal agreement with Pakistan, and another African military power reportedly pledged support to Riyadh. Motive: Saudi Arabia is building a backing coalition and protecting Mecca's religious legitimacy and its energy infrastructure. Iran-aligned pressure on the Saudi flank is the likely read, though the data doesn't confirm it.

3. Russia vs Ukraine: attrition plus cyber, with small humanitarian openings

• About 1,160 conflict events each way.

• Ukraine is hitting Russian refineries, with reported fuel-shortage risk. Both sides reported fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks.

• Washington approved a $2.1bn Ukraine missile deal, funded by allies. 500 Patriots are slated for the 2030s.

• A rare truce let a humanitarian mission reach a devastated city, and Oleshky evacuees left via Belarus.

• The US embassy warned Moscow of a possible terror attack at a museum. Montenegro dropped visa-free entry for Russians and Moscow retaliated.

• Motive: Ukraine is squeezing Russia's energy revenue and logistics. Russia is trying to outlast Western supply, and the West is locking in long-term support.

4. US vs China: friction, not force

• China's activity is normal against its two-year baseline, with a cooperative tone.

• Rejections and legal actions run both ways at 80–90 events each. The Intel chip rout and Merz's warning to Brussels on protectionism show the fight is over tech and trade.

• Motive: securing supply chains and technology advantage while avoiding escalation.

5. Smaller power plays

• Israel opened a diplomatic mission in Somaliland after recognising it, raising Horn of Africa stakes. Uganda is pulling troops from Somalia after 19 years.

• The Intercept reports the CIA is openly recruiting Cuban assets online.

• Pakistan→Afghanistan threats ran at 90 events, but the sample I checked was about US deportations, so I wouldn't read it as a military signal.

Noise to ignore: the "most hostile" dyads (police vs US, France, Germany) are domestic policing and protest. France, Germany and Italy look unusual against their norms, but mostly for that reason.

Watch next: the Iran decision window (a Greek outlet cites 7 Nov, which I couldn't verify), the Hormuz reopening offer, and Houthi strikes toward Mecca.

text:
Two AI stories on one Monday. One lesson about how big bets are paid for. 🤖💰
Story 1: Marvell to buy Lumentum for about $115B
▪️ All-stock deal, with $115B as the enterprise value including debt
▪️ 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share
▪️ Aim: pair Marvell's chips with Lumentum's lasers and optical tech, the links inside AI data centers
▪️ Expected close: first half of 2028, subject to shareholder approval
▪️ Lumentum holders would own about a third of the combined company
Story 2: Oracle
▪️ Sold $10B in bonds and filed for $10B in stock, its entire fundraising plan through fiscal 2030, in a single day
▪️ Shares fell nearly 9%, its worst day since June
▪️ Over the past 12 months, Oracle has lost more than half its value, while Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta are all within about 5% of where they started (Yahoo Finance)
Same theme: AI. Same Monday. Very different reactions. 🤔
Think about this. 👇
A story. Two neighbours decide to build bigger houses. Ngozi pays mostly from savings. Femi borrows heavily and asks friends to chip in. Both houses will be impressive. But when interest rates rise or costs climb, which neighbour sleeps better?
AI infrastructure is the house. The balance sheet is how you pay for it.
What the deals teach us:
1️⃣ "All-stock" means a moving price. Lumentum holders get a fixed number of Marvell shares, not a fixed dollar amount. On Monday, Marvell fell about 13% and Lumentum nearly 19%. And the deal doesn't close until 2028. A lot can change in that time.
2️⃣ A premium isn't a guarantee. The offer carried a premium of about 24% to the pre-rumour price, yet the shares still fell. The market weighs the price paid, the integration risk and the dilution.
3️⃣ How you fund growth matters as much as the growth. Oracle's debt is judged far riskier than Microsoft's by credit markets, because it's financing the build-out with more borrowing and new shares.
4️⃣ Same sector, different outcomes. "AI stocks" aren't one trade. Revenue, cash flow, debt and dilution decide who wins.
What a leading professional does: start with the primary documents, such as Marvell's merger filing, Oracle's bond prospectus and its balance sheet. Then check the thesis against an independent test: do free cash flow and debt costs support the capex?
So ask yourself:
🤔 Do I know how the companies I own pay for growth?
🤔 What happens to my thesis if their share price falls 20%?
🤔 Am I buying the story, or the cash flows?
FQVDM determines what you buy, while the crash framework determines when the risk/reward becomes attractive.

text:
Scientists use sound waves to deliver genetic treatment into brain tumours
What if sound waves could help deliver cancer-fighting genetic molecules directly into the brain?

Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed an experimental approach that could help overcome one of the biggest obstacles in treating brain cancer.

The disease they are targeting is glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.

One major problem is the blood-brain barrier.

This natural protective system prevents many harmful substances from entering the brain. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous potentially useful cancer treatments.

The researchers combined three technologies:

Focused ultrasound, which directs sound waves towards a specific brain region.

Microscopic bubbles, which help temporarily open the blood-brain barrier.

Nanoparticles carrying microRNAs, small genetic molecules capable of regulating multiple cancer-related genes.

Once the ultrasound is directed at the target area, the microbubbles help create a temporary opening in the blood-brain barrier.

This gives the nanoparticles an opportunity to deliver their genetic cargo into the brain.

Why use microRNAs?

Unlike conventional approaches that may target one cancer-driving protein at a time, these molecules can influence several gene pathways involved in tumour growth.

In laboratory experiments and animal models, the treatment slowed glioblastoma growth and extended survival in mice.

This is particularly interesting because glioblastoma cells can activate multiple pathways to survive and escape treatment.

The ability to target several of these pathways simultaneously could offer a different therapeutic strategy.

However, there is a major caveat.

The results are preclinical. The approach has not yet demonstrated effectiveness in human patients, and further research is needed before clinical trials.

Still, combining focused ultrasound, nanotechnology and RNA-based therapeutics is an exciting direction for brain cancer research.

[Saha S et al. Therapeutic delivery of microRNAs discovered to target deregulated glioblastoma pathways inhibits tumor growth in mice. Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2026. DOI: 10.1172/JCI195639]

text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM

MY FATHER’S EXAMPLE, AND THE RESPONSIBILITY I NOW ACCEPT

By Kio Amachree
President, Worldview International

There comes a time when a man must ask himself what his education, his opportunities and his years of experience have done for anyone beyond himself.

I have reached that time.

My late father, Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree QC, understood that professional achievement carried obligations. A lawyer’s knowledge could protect someone whose freedom was threatened. Money could support a struggling community. Influence could open a door for someone who had nobody powerful to speak for them.

His example has become the standard against which I judge my own life.

Consider Isaac Adaka Boro.

When Boro and his fellow Niger Delta campaigners faced treason proceedings following their 1966 uprising, my father undertook their defence. Ella Prest’s published account of the struggle for Rivers State identifies him as their counsel. Here were men confronting the Nigerian state, and here was a lawyer prepared to insist that they receive a defence. (https://t.co/U8K27kcHki⁠￼)

That principle matters beyond any argument about Boro’s methods or politics. An accused person’s rights cannot depend on whether the government approves of his cause. The moment we make justice conditional on political obedience, every citizen becomes less secure.

Our family also remembers my father’s assistance to Ken Saro-Wiwa, whose struggle brought the suffering of the Ogoni people before the world. I preserve that recollection as part of the example he left us: the duty to take seriously the grievances of communities whose voices power would prefer to ignore.

Then there was General Yakubu Gowon.

Following the assassination of General Murtala Muhammed in February 1976, Gowon was accused of involvement in the attempted coup, an allegation he denied. Historical accounts record that in 1980 my father and Solomon Asemota made legal representations on his behalf to President Shehu Shagari. In October 1981, Shagari rescinded the order declaring Gowon a fugitive. Gowon had never been convicted. (https://t.co/VwS6EWGR9X⁠￼)

My father’s involvement extended to the effort to bring him home. Contemporary reporting in Talking Drums in December 1983 records Chief Amachree explaining the purpose of a committee working towards Gowon’s return with his dignity recognised. (https://t.co/rgs7OMjGkQ⁠￼)

As I remember it, my father undertook his legal work for Gowon without charging him. He helped a man living under accusation pursue the restoration of his name and the possibility of returning to his own country.

There is a lesson here for Nigeria.

The same lawyer could defend Boro, who challenged the federation, and later assist Gowon, who had led it. A commitment to justice required him to look beyond the political position of the person seeking help.

The law must protect the dissenter and the former ruler alike. It must restrain those who hold power and provide a fair hearing to those who have lost it.

Love of country requires that discipline.

Too much of our public life is consumed by the question: what will I gain? What appointment, contract, payment or personal advantage will come my way?

We must recover the habit of asking what we can contribute.

There is nothing shameful about earning money honestly or providing well for one’s family. But money cannot become the sole purpose of an educated life. A society suffers when people with knowledge, resources and influence see every human difficulty as somebody else’s problem.

The neighbour who cannot afford treatment matters. The child whose schooling has stopped matters. The widow facing intimidation matters. The young person who needs guidance matters.

Nigeria will move forward when helping such people becomes an ordinary expectation of citizenship.

Respect for the law must stand at the centre of that effort. We cannot demand justice for ourselves while accepting its denial to someone from another community. We cannot condemn corruption in our opponents and excuse it among our friends. We cannot build a secure country while treating another person’s rights as disposable.

I also have responsibilities to face.

My father spent heavily on my education. Eton, the University of Pennsylvania and my legal education gave me opportunities that millions of Nigerians never receive. I now understand more fully the obligation that accompanied that privilege.

I must use what I have learned to speak clearly, challenge injustice and help people less fortunate than myself wherever I can.

It has taken me a long time to wake up to the full weight of that responsibility. I say that honestly. A distinguished father’s name does not perform the work his children must do for themselves.

I endeavour to follow his footsteps through my writing, my advocacy and whatever practical assistance I can offer. I want my remaining years to contribute something useful to the country that formed me and to people who need support.

My father’s example continues to ask something of me.

I can assure you that I am now wide awake.

text:
The Catholic Church issued repeated proclamations, particularly in the early Middle Ages, condemning brigandage in the strongest possible terms, mostly to no avail. At the time of the First Crusade, the Vatican had a brilliant idea: offer absolution — and thus a shortcut to Heaven — to anyone who went to fight in the Holy Land. This was effective, for even murderers at that time were religious and sought to get around the divine reckoning. Europe was thereby able to unload a massive number of miscreants (most of whom got wiped out by the Turks near Antioch), but the improvement was ultimately marginal. As long as gold and goods kept flowing along those unguarded roads and footpaths, they continued to be a magnet for violent crime. And, needless to say, because the punishment for robbery was the same as the one for murder, most robbery victims ended up murdered.

A typical medieval country inn was like a mini-fortress: a rectangular structure with an inner courtyard where guests’ horses and carts were locked up for the night, and massive doors which, when slammed shut, seemed sturdy enough to repel whatever came from nearby woods.
Yet the structural safety was often an illusion. Inn-keepers were notoriously shady characters who were often in cahoots with local gangs and would tip them off about their guests and what they carried them. A traveler would rise in the morning, happy to have survived the night, and fortify himself with a breakfast of ale, bread and cheese, served by the friendly inn-keeper, then set off through the misty forest. The trees would sometimes tremble and whisper to the soft neighing of his horse. And sometimes, in the eerie crystal silence he would hear a haunting bird call, not knowing if it was a golden oriole reassuring his mate, or a savage bandit signaling his mates to pounce on their prey.

There are many, many accounts from medieval, Renaissance and early modern Europe attesting to how dangerous travel was at that time (at least for anyone not traveling at the head of an army), but perhaps my favorite comes from the writings of Felix Platter, a 16th-century Swiss physician and diarist. Platter was born in Basel. His father, Thomas Platter, came from poverty, but was lucky to receive an education and became a scholar and a publisher. By the time Felix was in his teens, his father had sufficient means to send him to study medicine at the University of Montpellier, which was then Europe’s foremost school in the field. While passing through Jurthen Forest along their journey, 16-year-old Felix and another teenage boy, accompanied by their French guide, were caught in a terrible rainstorm and were compelled to seek shelter at an inn in a hamlet called Meziers (good luck finding it on Google Maps). The place and its occupants had an attitude so suspicious that the group barricaded themselves in their room and kept vigil through the night. They slipped out early in the morning, and good thing too, for their guide had overheard the regular patrons plotting with the inn-keeper to rob and kill them.

Setting aside the physical dangers, travel was very uncomfortable in other ways as well. For instance, as well as dangerous, inns did little more than offer travelers some calories and shelter from the elements. It was not until the mid-eighteenth century that nice hotels would come into existence. Most inns were rough, with guests sleeping on benches, on straw, or, if they were fancy, sharing dank beds. People of high aristocratic or princely rank — especially women — tried to stay as guests in the castles of local nobility, as those were the only places that were, relatively speaking, comfortable and safe.

text:
*Indian Army Internship Program (IAIP) 2026-27*

An invitation to young India.  Intern with the Indian Army…

The Indian Army has opened the second edition of the Indian Army Internship Programme (IAIP) 2026-27 on the *AICTE National Internship Portal*.  

Students with an interest in technology, management or strategic communication are invited to look at this opportunity seriously.

*Interns work on live projects for 75 days, sixty of them on site and fifteen from home, under the mentorship of serving officers and domain experts. Those who complete it can earn a stipend of up to ₹75,000, up to 15 AICTE academic credits, and a certificate from the Indian Army.* 

The problems these projects address are real and consequential.

*Finding the right internship*

The programme spans Artificial Intelligence, Quantum Computing, Cyber Security, 
Financial Technology, Human Resource Management, 
Operational Logistics, Advanced Warfare Systems, 
Strategic Communications.

Students of computer science, IT and data science will find the closest fit in the AI, data and software projects. 

Those in electronics and communication should look at cyber security and advanced warfare systems, 

Physics or mathematics students with programming experience may find quantum computing worth a look. 

Management and commerce students can look at FinTech, HR and logistics. 

Students of mass communication and journalism should look at strategic communications. 

Each listing states its own eligibility, so read it fully before deciding.

Apply to two or three projects where your record genuinely matches, and avoid scattering applications across many. 

Shortlisting rests on your portal profile, academic record and stated skills. A GitHub link, a project report or a relevant certificate will carry more weight than a long list of interests. 

You may apply to several projects but can accept only one offer, so rank your choices before you begin.

*How to apply*

Register at https://t.co/qCmwxNIk51, complete your profile with care, and open the Indian Army dashboard to see the live listings. 

Registration is free, and you should deal only through the official portal and ignore anyone who asks for payment. 

After applying, check your portal dashboard and email regularly for shortlisting and interview slots.

*Before you commit*

Most positions are in Delhi-NCR and accommodation is not provided, so plan your stay in advance. 

You must be available for the full 75 days. 

Only basic phones are permitted inside the office complex, where dedicated workstations are provided. 

The internship carries no placement or employment commitment. 

Listings close on different dates, so please do not wait.

Teachers and parents, kindly share this with the students in your circle.

text:
The plane crashed because the 55 year old experienced pilot (who i wouldn't worry about on sight) made a risky and fatal decision. Yes even experienced pilots can make poor decisions. 
There is a captain and a first officer.
The captain makes all final decisions.
He was warned by ATC of the "pretty nasty" weather and "moderate to extreme precipitation" 10 mins prior and made a risky decision for only a slight deviation that turned out to be fatal. 
It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. The captain made a slight deviation because it wasn't serious and they were above the storm until that cell ballooned up from 33000 ft to 48000 ft ceiling in a few minutes and by then it was too late for them to climb out of it.
From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (captain’s voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions.
---

https://t.co/F9GDVLJlzr
