From Bergman's Proto-Periodic Chemical Architectures and Symbolic Reaction Calculus to the Resonant Retina, the Sonorous Labyrinth, the Nervous Economy, and the Extraordinary Boundaries of Medical Experience
Scholarly Abstract

A remarkable mathematical and experimental intelligence manifests itself in the engraved chemical architectures accompanying John Elliot's Elements of the Branches of Natural Philosophy Connected with Medicine (1782).

 Across an immense field of subdivided columns, numbered chemical substances appear in systematic correspondence with numerous other materials, their relations expressed through densely arranged symbolic characters, comparative positions, and distinctions between reactions accomplished in humid and dry conditions. 

A second monumental engraving transforms these relationships into sixty-five numbered chemical configurations, each representing an operation involving one or more substances, the possible decomposition of existing compounds, the formation of new combinations, and the relative powers by which one constituent may displace another. These historical illustrations preserve a rare form of graphical natural philosophy in which the properties of matter become legible through the disposition, direction, and interaction of symbols. Their significance extends into the history of scientific notation, diagrammatic chemistry, experimental classification, and the intellectual ancestry of modern representations of chemical reactions. [1]

The first engraving, entitled Bergman's Table of Simple Elective Attractions, with Improvements, possesses the character of an extraordinary proto-periodic chemical atlas. Its approximately fifty numbered columns organize substances according to their comparative attractions, with distinct regions for the humid and dry methods of chemical combination. Acids, alkaline substances, metallic bodies, mineral earths, salts, and other agents acquire their positions through historically proposed chemical relationships. The arrangement deserves the designation proto-periodic in the limited retrospective sense of a systematic chemical classification preceding the modern periodic table.

 Its operating principle is chemical affinity rather than atomic number or the recurrence of electronic properties. Nevertheless, its immense visual density, repeated comparative structure, and attempt to express the relative behaviour of numerous substances within one comprehensive matrix make it an exceptional monument of pre-Lavoisierian chemical architecture.

The companion engraving, Bergman's Second Table, is even more intriguing. 

Sixty-five numbered configurations employ brackets, curved signs, chemical characters, arrows, and altered orientations to express the progress of reactions. 

An upright bracket represents the composition of an existing compound; a horizontal bracket signifies a newly formed combination; directed marks indicate the comparative powers of attraction; and the downward inclination of a bracket denotes precipitation or material separation. 

Certain figures represent an apparent absence of reaction, while others display competing attractions through which previously united substances may be redistributed.

 The diagrammatic arrangement constitutes a historical precursor to dynamic reaction mapping, chemical network notation, and graphical accounts of material transformation. Its figures invite a renewed investigation into the possibility of constructing a modern, experimentally annotated Atlas of Dynamic Affinity, preserving the eighteenth-century character system while rendering its operations intelligible through contemporary chemical formulae and measurable conditions. [2]

The intellectual importance of this graphical apparatus becomes more apparent when examined alongside the two volumes of Johann Georg Zimmermann's A Treatise on Experience in Physic (1782).

 Zimmermann investigates the underlying conditions through which observations may disclose the causes of bodily events, distinguishing disciplined experience from the misleading authority of repeated familiarity. His examples repeatedly expose the intricate relationships among perception, interpretation, memory, causal inference, and the physical circumstances surrounding an event. A bodily manifestation may have several possible causes; an observed result may be influenced by the method of examination; a symptom may retain the same appearance while arising from a different internal condition; and an intervention may be followed by recovery without having produced it. These considerations give Zimmermann's medicine an unusually sophisticated epistemological character. His conception of genuine experience places the disciplined interpretation of phenomena at the foundation of the healing arts.

Bergman's chemical diagrams and Zimmermann's philosophy of observation therefore furnish two unusually complementary historical approaches to hidden causation. In the chemical figures, the investigator identifies material constituents, determines their relative affinities, and follows their rearrangement through a prescribed operation. In clinical investigation, the physician identifies bodily signs, distinguishes accompanying circumstances, and reconstructs the probable sequence through which an internal disorder became manifest. These operations create a profound historical correspondence between the classification of physical substances and the interpretation of physiological signs. They further invite comparison with mathematical reasoning, logic, experimental medicine, and the construction of scientific languages capable of representing processes ordinarily beyond immediate sensory comprehension.

The natural-philosophical investigations of Elliot subsequently introduce an exceptional theory of sensory organization. In his account of vision, colour is associated with the vibrations of light and the corresponding excitability of retinal structures. The retina is conceived as possessing an extensive variety of possible internal responses, capable of excitation through the arrival of differently coloured rays or through direct mechanical irritation. Elliot develops this theory through the analogy of musical strings, one vibrating body possessing the capacity to excite another whose natural period corresponds to its own. The eye consequently becomes an organ of selective harmonic responsiveness, in which material vibration and physiological sensation participate in an ordered relationship. His explanation of the visible spectrum connects the velocity of oscillatory movement, the recognition of colour, and the response of the nervous apparatus within one speculative physical system. [3]

The auditory investigations carry this analogy considerably further. Elliot describes the production of ringing and musical sensations through irritation of the ear, the transmission of sound through the tympanum into the internal labyrinth, and the supposition that the auditory organ contains numerous possible vibrations capable of being excited by external acoustic movements. The extraordinary significance of these passages is their treatment of sensation as a response generated through the organization of the receiving apparatus. Sound may therefore be considered both as a physical disturbance propagated through the air and as an internally excited auditory condition. The association of retinal colour and labyrinthine sound opens an unusually productive historical avenue into physiological acoustics, harmonic resonance, nervous excitability, the mathematics of sensory response, and the formation of perceptible experience from otherwise invisible motions.

The same physiological chapters disclose other neglected subjects: the dependence of muscular activity upon nerve influence, distinctions between voluntary and internally sustained bodily motion, the possible function of ganglionic unions in the sympathetic activity of different organs, the movement of blood through vascular circuits, and the perpetual replacement of corporeal material. Elliot considers the circulation of lymph, the formation of chyle, the organized composition of blood, the activity of secreting structures, and the sensitivity of the skin to different modes of contact. His explanation of tickling through an undulating mechanical stimulus and his account of pain as a protective manifestation of unusually intense sensation extend the vibratory interpretation of nature into the bodily surface itself. The resulting intellectual range reaches from the measurable oscillations of musical strings to the movements of fluids, the contraction of fibres, and the emergence of feeling within organized matter.

An additional and particularly extraordinary argument appears in Elliot's concluding postscript, where the colour of venous blood is compared with optical phenomena displayed by soap bubbles. Through this analogy, he attempts to investigate whether the changing appearance of blood reveals alterations in the constitution or relative dimensions of its material particles. His discussion proceeds to the chemical activity of respiration, the acquisition of atmospheric constituents, the production of animal heat, and the relation between the susceptibility of muscular fibres and the presence of an appropriate stimulus. The analysis eventually expands into a conjectural relationship among light, heat, electricity, respiration, and bodily motion. Here the chemical, optical, pneumatic, and physiological departments of his work attain a remarkable point of convergence. His original explanations employ the phlogiston vocabulary of the period, while the observations themselves constitute valuable evidence for the historical development of physiological chemistry and the study of interacting physical forces. [4]

Zimmermann's wider medical investigations introduce an equally substantial history of extraordinary corporeal phenomena.

 The effects of strong emotional impressions, recurrent convulsive conditions, altered states of consciousness, nervous debility, sudden bodily collapse, changes in sensation, and the interaction of mental and physical activity appear throughout his discussion of the remote causes of disease.

 He records historical accounts of apparitions, supposed supernatural visitations, extraordinary recoveries, inherited medical interpretations, and the disputes surrounding sorcery and other unusual testimony. 

These passages preserve an intricate eighteenth-century encounter between religious understanding, the operations of imagination, learned medicine, and the interpretation of events whose causes remained uncertain. Particularly important is the distinction between the reported occurrence, its subsequent explanation, and the philosophical principles employed by different witnesses to establish its meaning. [5]

The larger questions of vitality and corporeal organization are accompanied by an explicit theological vocabulary. Zimmermann reproduces discussions of the body's natural powers in which circulation, respiration, nourishment, and the elimination of injurious substances are attributed to an ordered constitution established by the Creator. 

The organism appears as an immense economy of dependent operations, in which the heart, lungs, nervous system, digestive apparatus, and secreting structures participate in the preservation of the whole.

 This conception offers important material for a comparison with older doctrines of natural agency, the vis medicatrix naturae, the historical physiology of the vital principle, and the philosophical question of how organized matter sustains activity through the cooperation of distinct parts.

The combined collection also contains an unusual experimental inventory of optical apparatus, exhausted vessels, atmospheric pressure, electric machines, Leyden jars, vibrating strings, refracting lenses, saline reactions, metallic preparations, mineral earths, and the chemical agencies of acids and alkaline materials.

 These instruments and substances illuminate the practical circumstances under which eighteenth-century investigators attempted to convert imperceptible operations into observable effects. 

A suspended feather may move under electrical influence; a sounding bell becomes faint within an evacuated receiver; a candle forms an inverted image through a convex lens; an electrical discharge produces a sudden mechanical and sensory event; and a substance subjected to a chemical reagent reveals properties that were previously concealed beneath its external appearance. 

The experimental instrument thus becomes an extension of the bodily senses and an indispensable means of recovering otherwise inaccessible causal relationships.

Across these investigations emerges a particularly fruitful opportunity for the restoration of neglected eighteenth-century(late 1700a(80s) sciences. 

The engraved affinity systems offer the materials for a comprehensive reconstruction of early chemical classifications and transformation diagrams. 

Elliot's theories of sensory response provide a rare conceptual passage between physical vibration, resonance, colour, sound, and nervous organization. 

Zimmermann's accounts of clinical observation and extraordinary testimony disclose the historical difficulties inherent in determining causes from their visible consequences. Together, these works preserve an immense collection of obscure experimental processes, unusual medical observations, chemical symbols, anatomical explanations, and philosophical problems whose importance extends far beyond the circumstances of their original publication.

Their distinctive contribution to the present scholarly undertaking resides in the possibility of restoring each investigation to its historical and material particularity: the individual engraved symbol, the named chemical substance, the apparatus through which an operation was demonstrated, the actual observation reported by the physician, the original source of a remarkable medical case, and the philosophical assumptions under which a result received its explanation. 

Such a reconstruction could develop into a substantial modern research apparatus encompassing historical chemistry, the mathematics of chemical relationships, experimental psychology, sensory physiology, medical hermeneutics, sacred natural philosophy, and the comparative history of invisible agency. The resulting work would recover an exceptionally rich intellectual inheritance through the close examination of sources that deserve a far more prominent position in the history of science. [6]

🔑📜 Principal scholarly notes & source locations 🔑📜 

[1] Chemical engravings. John Elliot, Elements of the Branches of Natural Philosophy Connected with Medicine (London: J. Johnson, 1782), printed pp. 139–144 and accompanying folded plates. In the combined facsimile, the two principal affinity illustrations appear near PDF pages 15–16. The large matrix is headed Bergman's Table of Simple Elective Attractions, with Improvements; the second engraving presents a numbered series of reactions.

[2] Graphic conventions. Elliot, Elements, pp. 141–144. The author explains upright and horizontal brackets, the directions of attracting powers, the marks used for precipitates, and the distinction between representations of simple and double elective attractions. See particularly his explanation of Figure 21.

[3] Sensory vibration. Elliot, Elements, pp. 185–193 and 264–269. The physical treatment of musical intervals and acoustic propagation precedes the physiological argument concerning retinal vibrations, auditory sensation, and the internal excitation of tones.

[4] Physiological chemistry. Elliot, Elements, Postscript, approximately pp. 290–302. The principal passages concern heat in different conditions, alterations in blood colour, respiration, and the proposed relationship between nervous activity and the maintenance of animal heat.

[5] Extraordinary observations. Zimmermann, A Treatise on Experience in Physic, 2 vols. (London: G. Wilkie, 1782), especially vol. I, Books III–IV, and vol. II, Book V. The historical reports of unusual states of mind, apparent supernatural visitations, convulsive manifestations, and disturbances of bodily function occur within broader arguments concerning the reliability of observation and the causes of disease.

[6] Vital powers and natural organization. Zimmermann, vol. I, approximately pp. 104–107; Elliot, Elements, pp. 212–289. Particularly valuable comparisons involve the body's organizing functions, nervous action, circulation, nutrition, respiration, and the preservation of living tissues.

[7] Comparative source literature. For later study, particularly relevant historical works include William Harvey's De motu cordis (1628), Francis Bacon's Sylva Sylvarum (1627), Ralph Cudworth's The True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678), Albrecht von Haller's Elementa physiologiae corporis humani (1757–1766), Joseph Priestley's The History and Present State of Electricity (1767), and John Elliot's earlier Philosophical Observations on the Senses of Vision and Hearing (1780). These are comparative authorities, not additional volumes physically contained in the uploaded collection.

📊 THE MARKET IS MOVING. BUT ARE INVESTORS THINKING?

Today's U.S. market snapshot offers an important lesson about investing.

Look at some of the stocks making headlines:

🔹 SLB: +1.91%
🔹 Pfizer (PFE): +1.47%
🔹 Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX): +1.24%
🔹 Applied Materials (AMAT): +1.10%
🔹 Texas Instruments (TXN): +1.00%

On the other side:

🔻 Apple (AAPL): -3.44%
🔻 Stryker (SYK): -0.92%
🔻 Elevance Health (ELV): -0.87%
🔻 UPS: -0.62%

Meanwhile, analysts maintained bullish ratings on companies like NVIDIA, JPMorgan and Alphabet, while Oracle received an upgrade.

But don't rush to conclusions.

HERE ARE 4 LESSONS EVERY INVESTOR SHOULD UNDERSTAND:

1. A rising stock is not necessarily an undervalued stock.

Price movement tells you what buyers and sellers are doing.

Fundamental analysis helps you understand what you're actually buying.

2. Analyst ratings are opinions, not guarantees.

A Buy rating and an attractive price target do not eliminate investment risk.

Check the assumptions behind the valuation.

3. Earnings beats deserve investigation.

Apple and Vertex both exceeded the EPS estimates shown in today's earnings snapshot.

Yet their stock prices can respond differently.

Why?

Because markets consider expectations, guidance, margins, future growth and valuation—not just whether a company beat estimates.

4. Unusual options activity is not automatically smart money buying.

Large options transactions can represent hedging, speculation or complex strategies.

Without understanding the position and its purpose, copying the activity can be dangerous.

THE UZEE INVEST APPROACH

Before buying any stock, apply FQVDM:

F — Fundamentals: Is the business financially sound?

Q — Quality: Does it have a competitive advantage?

V — Valuation: Is the price reasonable?

D — Dividend: Is the distribution sustainable?

M — Momentum: Does market behaviour support the investment thesis?

Remember:

The market rewards preparation, not excitement.

You don't need to own every stock that is moving.

You need to understand the businesses you own and the prices you pay.

WE LOOK BEFORE WE LEAP. FUNDAMENTALS FIRST. ALWAYS.

Which do you pay more attention to when selecting a stock: earnings growth, valuation or price momentum?

AI expansion is hitting power and grid constraints on Earth. Suitable orbits offer near-continuous sunlight without a grid connection queue. Musk says space will become the cheapest place for AI computing within two to three years. Test satellites are already flying.

But sunlight does not solve heat. Spacecraft can circulate coolant internally, but the heat must ultimately escape through radiation. That requires panels whose area grows with the heat load. Rejecting a gigawatt of waste heat at room temperature needs on the order of two and a half square kilometres of ideal radiating surface. Every kilogram adds manufacturing and launch costs.

Google's energy chief puts the cost of building space data centres at up to 100 times that of terrestrial facilities. SpaceX's own IPO filing warns that its orbital computing ambitions may never achieve commercial viability. That does not establish failure. It exposes the unresolved economics behind the "no-brainer" claim.

The missing calculation is lifetime cost per useful computation. Launches, solar arrays, radiators, communications, failures and replacement hardware must all be paid for. Chips must earn back their deployed cost before they fail or become uncompetitive. For large AI training workloads, thousands of processors must also exchange data fast enough to avoid sitting idle.

Cheaper rockets alone do not settle that arithmetic. Nor must Earth solve every grid problem to win. Terrestrial operators need only deliver the competing capacity more cheaply or sooner. Equally, an orbital operator could sell premium capacity into an acute shortage without ever being the cheapest provider.

Computing in orbit works. Becoming the cheapest location for AI at scale is a much harder proposition. A working test satellite does not prove the business case.

And sovereignty follows the hardware into orbit. Private space activities require state authorisation and continuing supervision. The registry state retains jurisdiction over the spacecraft. Launch permissions, communications infrastructure and applicable export controls add further constraints.

Whoever runs computers in orbit will still answer to somebody on the ground.

text:
Building in the open means showing consistent proof of work whether the market is loud or silent. 

True conviction is never measured when timelines are full of easy excitement. 

It is revealed when the spotlight moves away and only real utility remains on the table.

Many people get pulled off course by cyclical hype because chasing trends brings quick applause. 

The best builders operate differently. 

They ignore market noise and focus entirely on sovereign systems, decentralised infrastructure, and solving real user friction. 

Technology means very little if ordinary people cannot use it simply and safely.

Think of this like laying the stone foundation of a tall building during the dry season. 

Passersby rarely stop to clap for workers pouring concrete into a deep trench, because there is nothing flashy to see from the street yet. 

When heavy storms arrive, structures built purely for show collapse, while that quiet foundation holds all the weight without shifting an inch.

Quiet seasons are never a signal to slow down or wait for validation. 

They offer the cleanest window to test ideas, sharpen your craft in public, and build things that last. 

Keep your head down, stay curious, and let daily execution speak for itself.

text:
US, Russia and China edge toward a trilateral Trump-Putin-Xi meeting on the margins of APEC

Financial Times reports that Washington, Moscow and Beijing are discussing a possible three-way summit between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. The talks center on whether the leaders can meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November.⁠

The idea originated with Putin. He floated it during a 9 October phone call with Trump, the same conversation that produced an agreement for the US to buy Russian diesel. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov has said preparations are underway and that all three sides are in principle ready.

Putin’s goal is clear. He wants the meeting to address Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow, without Zelensky or European leaders at the table. Russian sources describe it as a new Yalta-style division of influence. Trump has said he is open, but only if the focus is nuclear denuclearization rather than Ukraine. He has also left the door open for trade talks.⁠

China remains the most cautious. Beijing has not publicly confirmed participation. Xi has long preferred to manage Washington and Moscow separately and has previously rejected trilateral nuclear talks. Hosting the meeting would give him a symbolic win, but it risks locking China into a format it does not control and spotlighting a European war at an Asian summit.⁠

The geopolitical stakes are high. A successful meeting could legitimize a three-power format that sidelines Europe and Ukraine. It would strengthen Putin’s claim to equal standing with Trump and Xi while he remains dependent on Chinese economic support. Failure or cancellation would leave the Ukraine track fragmented and nuclear arms-control talks still stalled.⁠

Geostrategically, the summit would test whether the three powers can set rules on spheres of influence, nuclear limits and regional security without wider participation. For the US it offers a channel to constrain both Russian and Chinese nuclear expansion. For China it risks tying its hands on Taiwan-related issues if the agenda broadens. For Russia it is an opportunity to freeze the Ukraine conflict on current lines.⁠

Geoeconomically, the meeting sits against recent US-Russia energy deals and ongoing US-China trade friction. Any agreement on Ukraine could ease pressure on Russian oil and diesel exports. Nuclear or trade side deals would affect defense budgets, technology controls and energy prices. Markets would price the outcome as either reduced geopolitical risk or confirmation that major powers are carving up influence without smaller states.⁠

European and Ukrainian officials have warned that a meeting without them would undermine any durable settlement. Chinese state media have already noted the lack of an agreed agenda as a practical obstacle. With APEC less than three weeks away, the next days will show whether Beijing is willing to host, whether Trump prioritizes nuclear talks, and whether Putin can force Ukraine onto the table.

text:
United States President Donald Trump's administration officially notified congress of its intention to terminate South Africa (and Rwanda) from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa), effective 1 January 2027.
Zimbabwe has never been eligible for Agoa since the trade program's inception in 2000 due to US targeted sanctions and financial restrictions.
When Agoa was signed into law in May 2000, Zimbabwe was excluded from the start due to US legislative restrictions, political governance concerns, and human rights issues, subsequently reinforced under the Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act (Zidera), whose active framework has shifted to
Magnitsky-related designations on select individuals and entities.
Zimbabwe remains ineligible for Agoa trade preferences, and its exclusion has repeatedly been noted during periodic US reviews and extensions of the framework.
Rwanda is targeted due to the US sanctions on it over the eastern Congo conflict.
The decision on South Africa deals a heavy diplomatic and economic blow to Pretoria following years of worsening relations with Washington DC.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said South Africa's current practices fail to meet Agoas strict eligibility criteria. 
The primary drivers behind the US decision include trade barriers, foreign policy clashes and national security issues and domestic policy differences.
Washington cited unfair trade and investment barriers, highlighting South Africa's high tariffs on US poultry, wine, and spirits, and unjustified restrictions on its pork.
The US government said Pretoria's actions pose threats to US national security interests. 
This follows deep-seated geopolitical clashes over South Africa's legal case against Israel at the International Court of Justice and its strong diplomatic ties with Russia, China, and Iran.
The Israel issue sits at the heart of US's aggression towards South Africa.
It is also now part of internal destabilisation tactics fronted by some anti-immigration groups.
Tensions have been amplified by friction surrounding South Africa’s land reform and black economic empowerment policies, alongside specific claims by Trump regarding the treatment of white farmers.
White conservative and right-wing elements, fronted by Afriforum and Solidarity, have been lying to the world that Afrikaner farmers are subjected to genocide in South Africa.
Removal from Agoa does not block South Africa from trading with the US. 
Instead, South African goods will lose duty-free status and be forced to clear the US market under standard tariff regimes.
•Economists estimate the loss of Agoa will add an immediate 3.4% tariff hike onto the standard 12.5% duties already faced by several local exports.
Analysts project up to 10 000 job losses overall, with the agriculture and manufacturing sectors taking the hardest hit.
Farmers who planted orchards specifically tailored to American consumer preferences face a severe blow, as they must now compete directly against lower-tariff, shorter-route South American competitors like Chile and Peru.
Vehicle and component exports — which already suffered a drop from R17.7 billion in 2024 to R8 billion in 2025 due to separate US reciprocal tariffs — will face even steeper financial strain.
Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau said South Africa has 60 days to formally appeal the decision before the suspension officially kicks in.
While the government continues to offer support to affected local companies, it is aggressively pushing an export diversification strategy. 
President Cyril Ramaphosa has sais South Africa must prepare for life outside the agreement by accelerating trade agreements and securing alternative markets across the African continent, the European Union, India, and China.

🚨Univerity of Michigan Board of Regents Election

ATTENTION MICHIGAN VOTERS!
The University of Michigan Board of Regents election is today - November 3, 2026. Voters elect two members to eight-year terms (at-large seats). 

It is a plurality block vote: 
Voters may select up to two candidates, and the top two vote-getters win the seats. There are not separate individual “seats” with dedicated candidates—all six candidates compete for the two open positions.

Democrats currently hold a majority on the eight-member board. The two seats up are those of incumbent Paul Brown (D) and Jordan Acker (D); Acker lost renomination at the Democratic convention. The winners will help oversee a university with a multi-billion-dollar budget, set policies on tuition/aid, hire the president, and address issues including free speech, campus funding (Ann Arbor/Dearborn/Flint), Michigan Medicine, and major projects.

Candidates (General Election Ballot)

✴️Paul Brown (Democrat, incumbent)
✴️Amir Makled (Democrat)
✴️Lena Epstein (Republican)
✴️Michael Schostak (Republican)
✴️Andrew Chadderdon (Libertarian)
✴️Kyle Maas (U.S. Taxpayers Party of Michigan)

A side by side comparison chart of the candidates is provided below.

Here is the DIRT on each candidate:

✨Michael Schostak (Republican)
Limited personal dirt identified. He has criticized the university’s handling of the $12 million athletics review (lack of a full public report) and other transparency issues, as well as the approach to the Ypsilanti Township project. No major personal allegations, investigations, or scandals appear in the available public reporting.

✨Kyle Maas (U.S. Taxpayers Party)
No significant public allegations, investigations, or scandals were found in searches related to this candidate. Coverage focuses on his unusual educational timeline (graduated high school at 10, started college at 12) and policy positions on fiscal responsibility, AI, and civil discourse. He participated in a Faculty Senate forum.

✨Andrew Chadderdon (Libertarian)
Party leadership disputes: As a former chair of the Libertarian Party of Michigan, he was involved in internal factional fights around 2022–2023, including a “vote of no confidence,” Judicial Committee appeals, competing claims to the chairmanship, and related lawsuits/motions over party control, finances, and records. These are internal party matters rather than criminal investigations. He has limited public campaign activity in this race and did not respond to some university/media requests for statements. No personal scandals or criminal allegations were identified.

🥵Paul Brown (Democrat, incumbent)
Athletics investigation transparency: 
Brown, as a sitting regent, has been involved in board oversight of a roughly $12 million external review of the athletic department (related to issues including the Sherrone Moore firing and broader culture). Critics, including the Republican candidates, faulted the university for not releasing a full written report (only a summary and video). Brown said he was largely satisfied with the process and findings, noted frustration at the cost, and called for as much release as possible while protecting privacy. He has described some athletic leadership lapses as unacceptable.

Gender-affirming care: 
Brown publicly stated he was “embarrassed” by Michigan Medicine’s decision to end gender-affirming care for minors amid federal pressure, calling it a dangerous precedent of politicizing medical decisions. He has a family member who is transgender and has spoken against the policy at board meetings.

Other: 
Activist groups have criticized him (along with other regents) for not delivering on earlier campaign promises related to endowment ethics/transparency and for support of certain projects (e.g., later criticism of the Ypsilanti Township computing center as “environmental racism”). No personal scandals or investigations targeting Brown himself were identified in major reporting.

🥵Amir Makled (Democrat)
Social media posts (main controversy):
 In 2025, Makled reposted (and later deleted) content praising Hezbollah leaders Hassan Nasrallah and Abu Ali Khalil as “martyrs,” referring to Iranian figure Qasem Soleimani with an honorific, and sharing posts from figures including Candace Owens that called Israelis “demons” or used other language widely described as antisemitic. The Detroit News and others reported on archived posts. Makled has stated he “disavow[s] antisemitism completely,” argued that criticism of Israeli government policies is not antisemitism, and said deleting the posts was his only mistake. The posts drew criticism from figures including U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin and former Michigan Democratic Party chair Brandon Dillon; SEIU Michigan rescinded an endorsement. He defeated incumbent Jordan Acker at the Democratic convention despite the controversy.

Legal work: 
He provided representation to some students charged in connection with pro-Palestinian encampments (charges later dropped). This is presented by supporters as civil rights advocacy and by critics as alignment with controversial protests.

🥵Lena Epstein (Republican)
2021 arrest: 
Michigan State Police arrested Epstein on September 2, 2021, at the Grand Hotel on Mackinac Island on suspicion of domestic assault involving her then-boyfriend (in the presence of her young daughter). Reports based on police records and bodycam footage describe alcohol involvement, physical signs such as broken nails and apparent blood, and pills found in her belongings. She spent a night in jail. The Mackinac County prosecutor (a Republican) declined to file charges after consulting the alleged victim. The incident surfaced in a later custody-related court filing by her ex-husband. Epstein has denied the allegations, called the matter a “nothing burger,” and attributed it to the trooper targeting her. Details received renewed coverage in 2026 during the campaign.

Past political controversies: 
In 2018, while running for Congress, she invited a Messianic rabbi to offer a prayer after the Tree of Life synagogue shooting, drawing criticism. text:
Ancient Hawaiian Petroglyphs (kīʻi pōhaku) carved into coastal rock and algae at Pōkaʻī Bay in Waiʻanae on the island of Oʻahu, Hawaii, with cultural practitioner Glen Kila standing nearby...

At least 26 human-shaped stick figure petroglyphs etched into the basalt and sandstone rock shelf. Estimated to be at least 500 to over 1,000 years old, representing some of the early Native Hawaiian inhabitants and voyagers to the islands.

. . . 

For centuries, they were hidden beneath the sand. Then the wind uncovered a thousand-year-old gallery.

On a beach near Waianae on the Hawaiian island of Oahu, at least 26 petroglyphs emerged unexpectedly in 2022 as shifting sands briefly revealed the ancient artwork. Some of the carvings are believed to be over 1,000 years old. The figures, etched into stone, depict human forms known as kī‘i pōhaku, created by Native Hawaiians long before European contact.

Petroglyphs are among the oldest surviving cultural expressions in Hawaii. Scholars believe they may have marked trails, told stories, or signaled sacred areas. Their exact meanings remain partially mysterious, but they offer a direct link to the lives and beliefs of early Hawaiians.

The reemergence of these carvings was short-lived. Just days after they were exposed, the tides buried them again. Local officials and cultural organizations now work to preserve and document these glimpses of Hawaii's past before they vanish once more beneath the sand.

text:
The Next AI Moat Is a Map, Not a Model

Why Context Graphs, Data Relationships, and Execution History Could Determine Who Captures the Value of the Agent Economy

I have been following the development of AI agents, enterprise software, and financial infrastructure.

One thing is becoming increasingly clear to me.

The next major competitive battle in AI may not be decided by which company has the smartest model.

It may be decided by which company understands the environment in which that model operates.

Consider a simple example.

Imagine asking an AI agent:

Should my company extend another $100,000 in credit to this customer?

A conventional AI system might retrieve the customer's financial statements, summarize payment history, and produce a recommendation.

But a genuinely useful business agent needs much more.

It needs to understand:

Whether the financial information is current.
Whether the customer has outstanding obligations elsewhere.
Whether existing credit agreements contain restrictions.
Whether guarantees or collateral arrangements exist.
Whether recent payments have actually settled.
Whether the person requesting the decision has the authority to approve it.
Which original documents support the recommendation.

The difference between these two systems is enormous.

One retrieves information.

The other understands relationships, business rules, authority, and the current state of the business.

I believe this distinction could become one of the most important economic opportunities in the AI agent era.

1. The Model Is Becoming More Accessible. The Business Context Is Not.

The AI industry has spent enormous resources competing on model intelligence.

Larger models, better reasoning, longer context windows, lower inference costs, and more sophisticated multimodal capabilities.

These developments remain important.

But there is another transition taking place.

Businesses are moving from asking AI questions to delegating actual work to AI agents.

McKinsey's August 2026 global survey found that 40% of respondents at large enterprises reported scaling AI agents, compared with 27% the previous year.

Interestingly, nearly one-third of respondents said their organizations had decided against purchasing at least one software product or feature because they could build it internally using agentic coding tools.

This suggests that AI is beginning to change not only how software is used, but also how software is purchased and developed.

However, the same survey found that only 37% of respondents attributed at least some EBIT impact to AI, while the proportion of high performers remained around 6%.

There is a substantial gap between deploying AI and capturing its economic value.

I think part of the explanation lies in something that receives less attention than model performance:

An intelligent system cannot make consistently valuable business decisions if it does not understand the business itself.

The model provides reasoning capability.

The business environment provides meaning.

And the ability to connect the two may become increasingly valuable.

2. Data Is Not the Same Thing as Context

This is perhaps the most important distinction in this research.

Imagine an enterprise with ten years of customer records.

It has contracts, invoices, emails, payment histories, internal reports, financial statements, and operational databases.

An AI agent can potentially retrieve all of these records.

But retrieving information does not automatically mean understanding it.

Consider three statements:

A customer owes $50,000.
The customer paid $20,000 yesterday.
The payment has not yet been confirmed as settled.

A system that simply retrieves these records may produce an incorrect conclusion about the customer's remaining exposure.

A context-aware system needs to understand the relationships between the records, their timestamps, their authority, and the underlying business rules.

This is the difference between information retrieval and contextual understanding.

IBM's September 2026 analysis makes a similar distinction.

It argues that enterprise AI needs more than access to documents and databases. It needs metadata, data lineage, ownership, governance, business definitions, and relationships.

IBM also estimates that less than 1% of enterprise data is currently being leveraged by generative AI.

That number should be understood as IBM's reported estimate, rather than a universal measurement across every organization.

Nevertheless, the underlying problem is significant.

Businesses possess enormous amounts of information.

But much of that information remains disconnected from the decisions that could create economic value.

3. The Rise of the Context Graph

I want to introduce a concept that I believe investors and technology researchers should pay closer attention to:

The Context Graph.

A traditional database stores information.

A search engine retrieves information.

A knowledge graph connects entities and relationships.

A context graph, as I use the term here, goes further by connecting business entities, events, decisions, permissions, time, and evidence in a way that an AI agent can use during an actual workflow.

For example:

A company owns a subsidiary.

The subsidiary signed a financing agreement.

The agreement contains a guarantee.

The guarantee references another legal entity.

That entity owns an infrastructure asset.

The asset depends on a specific utility connection.

A change in the financing agreement may therefore affect the risk profile of an entirely different part of the business.

A conventional document search might find every relevant file.

A context-aware system should be able to reconstruct the relationships and explain why they matter.

This is particularly important in:

Financial research.
Corporate credit analysis.
Supply-chain management.
Insurance underwriting.
Healthcare administration.
Regulatory compliance.
Enterprise procurement.

JPMorganChase's 2026 Emerging Technology Trends report explicitly identifies context-driven architectures as a major technology direction.

It highlights knowledge graphs, semantic layers, context engineering, agentic identity management, and data-centric security.

Forrester's October 2026 research also identifies context engineering and ContextOps as emerging disciplines for making agentic AI reliable across fragmented enterprise systems.

These are important signals.

They suggest that the industry is beginning to recognize that better models alone will not solve the operational problems of agentic AI.

4. Why Context Could Become an Economic Moat

Now comes the more interesting business question.

If context becomes important, who actually captures the value?

I see four potential sources of competitive advantage.

A. Proprietary and permissioned data

A company with access to reliable, frequently updated, legally usable information may have an advantage over competitors relying on public or outdated records.

But merely collecting more data is insufficient.

The information must be accurate, relevant, and permitted for the intended use.

B. Relationship intelligence

The ability to connect entities, transactions, obligations, ownership structures, and historical events can be much harder to reproduce than a simple search interface.

The value is not necessarily in possessing individual records.

It is in understanding how those records interact.

C. Workflow integration

An agent embedded in a company's financial, operational, or customer-management workflows may become more valuable over time.

It understands the company's processes, receives feedback from completed tasks, and can increasingly perform work within established controls.

Replacing it may require more than changing software.

It may require reconstructing an entire operational system.

D. Verified execution history

This may be the most overlooked advantage.

A system that can record what it recommended, what action was taken, what actually happened, and whether the outcome was successful can gradually develop a valuable feedback loop.

It is no longer simply retrieving information.

It is accumulating evidence about how the business operates.

However, I would not automatically classify context as a durable moat.

Generic connectors, vector databases, and memory features can become commodities.

A genuine moat requires some combination of differentiated data rights, difficult-to-replicate relationships, embedded workflows, reliable feedback, and measurable customer value.

Without those characteristics, context engineering may simply become another infrastructure feature bundled by a much larger platform.

5. The Hidden Battle: Who Controls the Agent's Permissions?

There is another issue that could determine which companies become important in this market.

Identity and authorization.

Imagine an AI agent that can access your company's financial system.

It can read invoices, inspect contracts, update customer records, and initiate payments.

The technical question is whether it can perform those actions.

The more important question is whether it should be allowed to perform them.

Under whose authority?

With what permissions?

For which customer?

At what financial limit?

Can the action be reversed?

Can an auditor reconstruct exactly what happened?

NIST published an August 2026 analysis emphasizing the need for stronger identity foundations for agentic AI.

Microsoft's agent identity guidance similarly emphasizes dedicated agent identities, narrowly scoped permissions, approval gates, and auditable actions.

This introduces another layer of the emerging agent economy:

The control plane.

I see several essential components:

Agent identity — identifying which agent is acting.
Authorization — defining what it is allowed to access.
Policy enforcement — determining which actions are permitted.
Provenance — recording where information originated.
Auditability — reconstructing what the agent actually did.
Revocation — immediately removing access when necessary.

This infrastructure may not look as exciting as a new frontier model.

But enterprises may be unwilling to delegate meaningful financial or operational authority without it.

And that creates a potentially important market.

6. Where Will the Money Actually Flow?

I would divide the emerging agent economy into five layers.

Layer 1: Intelligence

Foundation models and reasoning engines.

They provide the underlying cognitive capabilities.

Layer 2: Infrastructure

Compute, inference, databases, storage, networking, and data pipelines.

They make intelligence economically deployable.

Layer 3: Context and control

Memory, knowledge graphs, identity, authorization, provenance, and policy enforcement.

They connect intelligence to the actual business environment.

Layer 4: Applications and execution

Vertical agents that perform financial analysis, procurement, customer service, research, compliance, and other specialized tasks.

They turn intelligence into operational results.

Layer 5: Distribution and customer relationships

The interfaces, platforms, marketplaces, and trusted relationships through which businesses and consumers access these agents.

They influence who owns the customer relationship and who captures recurring revenue.

The important question is whether these layers will remain independent businesses or become increasingly integrated into a small number of platforms.

I would not assume that the context layer automatically becomes the most profitable.

Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, AWS, and other established platforms already control important enterprise relationships and data environments.

They have substantial advantages in distribution and integration.

Meanwhile, specialized companies may be able to build better solutions for particular industries.

The opportunity for independent providers will depend on whether they can offer something that large platforms cannot easily reproduce or bundle.

That is where I would look for differentiated businesses.

7. An Unexpected Opportunity: Financial Information Infrastructure

There is one application I find particularly interesting.

Financial research.

The financial world produces enormous amounts of information.

SEC filings.

Credit agreements.

Debt indentures.

Corporate ownership records.

Regulatory documents.

Utility filings.

Permits.

Institutional holdings.

Company announcements.

The problem is not simply finding these documents.

It is understanding how they connect.

Consider an AI system researching a large infrastructure company.

A headline might report a new data-center investment.

But the actual economic exposure could involve several separate entities, financing agreements, leases, guarantees, utility commitments, and future obligations.

A superficial AI summary might capture the investment announcement.

A more sophisticated research system would attempt to reconstruct the underlying economic relationships.

This is where information advantage could emerge.

Not because the information is necessarily secret.

But because the ability to connect fragmented public information into a reliable, time-sensitive picture is difficult.

I see an important distinction:

Information is public. Understanding its economic consequences is not equally accessible to everyone.

This is particularly relevant to our TERALIQ INFORMATION EDGE research direction.

We are interested in the gap between publicly available information, market expectations, and actual asset prices.

Context engineering could eventually make that research more systematic.

For example:

Detect a new corporate financing arrangement.
Connect it to historical debt obligations.
Identify related entities and guarantees.
Compare the latest filing with previous disclosures.
Determine which economic exposures have changed.
Examine whether market prices have incorporated the new information.

The objective is not to generate more summaries.

It is to identify meaningful information that has not yet been correctly interpreted or priced.

Of course, that final step requires independent market testing.

A better information system does not automatically produce investment alpha.

But it can improve the quality, speed, and reproducibility of the research process.

8. What Investors Should Measure

If I were evaluating companies competing in this market, I would avoid relying on impressive demonstrations.

Instead, I would examine several measurable characteristics.
MetricWhat it revealsContext freshnessHow quickly important information is updatedSource provenanceWhether conclusions can be traced to original evidenceRelationship coverageHow well the system connects relevant entities and eventsPermission accuracyWhether agents access only authorized informationTask completionWhether agents actually complete useful workflowsError and override ratesHow frequently human intervention is necessaryCost per verified outcomeWhether the economics improve with scaleCustomer retentionWhether the product becomes operationally important
One particularly important metric is cost per verified outcome.
A company may have extremely high AI usage but poor economics.
Another company may use fewer tokens while completing valuable workflows with fewer errors.
The second may have a much stronger business model.
The distinction matters because the agent economy will ultimately be judged by completed outcomes, not impressive demonstrations.
9. My Final Thesis: The Next AI Giants May Own the Relationships Between Things
I don't believe the next generation of valuable AI companies will necessarily be the ones with the largest models.
Some may own the infrastructure.
Some may own the customer relationship.
Some may own the most valuable industry-specific information.
Others may control the systems that connect data, authority, and execution.
But I think one principle deserves particular attention:
As intelligence becomes more widely accessible, the economic value of understanding a specific environment may increase.
A model can generate an answer.
A context system can explain why the answer matters.
A control system can determine whether an action is permitted.
An execution system can turn that action into a measurable result.
And a feedback system can establish whether the result was actually successful.
These are different economic functions.

They may be captured by different companies.

Or they may eventually converge into a few powerful platforms.

We don't know yet.

That uncertainty is precisely why this market deserves deeper research.

The AI industry has spent years competing to build machines that can think.

The next phase may be about building machines that understand the world they are operating in — and can act within it responsibly.

**The next AI moat may not be the intelligence itself.

It may be the map connecting intelligence to reality.**

— Le Wang
Teraliq Quant
Independent Research | AI · Markets · Risk

Evidence over hype.

SOUTH AFRICA IS NOT A COLONY OF THE US: NO CAPITULATION TO US IMPERIALIST BULLYING, BUT STRATEGIC COMPOSURE TO PROTECT OUR SOVEREIGNTY
By Dr Zamani Saul, NC ANC Provincial Chairperson
03 November 2026

Introduction

Trading with the US or any other country does not reduce South Africa into a colony but a trading partner. The Trump administration's distorted view that small and middle power countries that trade with the US are their colonies must be openly challenges. This US empire predatory attitude and instinct must be rejected and countries must uncompromisingly defend their sovereignty.

On 2 November 2026, the US announced its intention to terminate South Africa’s eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective from 1 January 2027. Triggered by an annual interagency review led by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, US cited practices "inconsistent with AGOA's eligibility criteria", explicitly pointing to alleged trade barriers and threats to US foreign policy and national security.

The economic impact on South Africa

To accurately assess the economic impact, it is essential to untangle the actual data from confusing headlines. Since its enactment in 2000, AGOA has granted qualifying sub-Saharan countries duty-free access to US markets for over 1,800 products. South Africa historically stood as its primary beneficiary, facilitating substantial automotive and agricultural trade.

However, the real value of this trade agreement has faced aggressive erosion over the last two years under the Trump administration. The economic impact of the definitive 1 January 2027 ejection can be measured across several clear vectors:

First, ejection from AGOA has minimal impact on the South African export economy. According to Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau, AGOA exports were valued at approximately $1.7 billion in 2025, down significantly from $4 billion in 2024. Crucially, AGOA trade represented only about 1% of South Africa’s total global exports. Nearly 90% of South Africa’s total trade outbound to the US already bypasses the AGOA framework entirely.

Secondly, ejection from AGOA does not equal a trade ban. South African products will simply revert to standard Most Favoured Nation (MFN) tariff rates. Economists note that the average tariff benefit previously offered by AGOA was a modest 3.5%. Presidential Envoy on Agriculture and Land, Wandile Sihlobo, calculated that losing AGOA adds a 3.4% tariff bump onto the 12.5% foundational tariffs currently imposed by the US administration. A combined 15.9% tariff is challenging, but nowhere near the crippling 30% Trump "liberation day" tariffs that the agricultural sector successfully bypassed and competed against in 2025.

Thirdly, specific economic sectors will bear the brunt of the ejection from AGOA. While macro-economically stable, the micro-economic fallout will harshly hit specific localised businesses. The domestic automotive sector, which has already seen vehicle export earnings to the US contract from R17.7 billion in 2024 to R8 billion in 2025 due to punitive US Section 232 steel and aluminium tariffs, faces a distinct loss of edge.

Fourthly, the impact will be felt by the agricultural sector. High-value agricultural products like citrus fruits, macadamia nuts and wine will immediately feel the negative impact. Organised labour bodies, including the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), anticipate that the sudden removal could threaten up to 10,000 jobs across agricultural supply chains and specialised assembly plants.

Lastly, South Africa’s primary exports to the US, which include critical mineral resources such as platinum group metals, gold and diamonds, will remain entirely unaffected. They enter the US market duty-free under separate global tariff codes due to the US economy’s structural dependence on South African mineral inputs.

text:
The Armenian Archives and the 1915 Debate: What Remains Unexamined?

The historical record concerning the events of 1915 is not confined to Ottoman state archives. Armenian political, revolutionary, ecclesiastical and diaspora archives also hold important documentation. Yet several major Armenian collections have historically operated under restricted access.

1. The Boston–Dashnak Archives

In his 2012 UCLA doctoral dissertation, historian Garabet K. Moumdjian documented that the Armenian Revolutionary Federation (ARF/Dashnak) archives were accessible only by special permission. He also identified the archives of the Armenian Patriarchates of Constantinople and Jerusalem as closed to the general public at that time.

2. The Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem

In a May 4, 2017 interview with The Armenian Weekly, historian Taner Akçam confirmed that he had repeatedly been denied access to the Jerusalem Patriarchate archives.

Akçam stated:

“Yes, scholars do not have access. I was declined over the years several times.”

He explained that cataloguing was repeatedly given as the reason, although he did not know why access had been refused.

3. The Patriarch Zaven Archives (1912–1922)

On November 21, 2017, the Armenian Genocide Museum-Institute itself acknowledged that the majority of documents from Archbishop Zaven Eghiayan’s archives had not yet entered scholarly circulation.

These collections contain significant correspondence and records relating to the Armenian question, wartime developments and the immediate postwar period.

4. Turkish Archives and the Missing Telegrams

Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence maintains an official application procedure for Turkish and foreign researchers wishing to consult military archives, subject to specified documentary restrictions.

Historical claims of restricted access must be distinguished from the absence of particular documents.

Akçam himself acknowledged in a 2016 interview that original documents associated with Aram Andonian and the purported Talat Pasha telegrams had disappeared after being deposited at the Boghos Nubar Pasha Library in Paris.

Missing documents, restricted collections and rejected research applications are three different archival problems. They should not be presented as interchangeable evidence.

5. The Rejected Joint Historical Commission of 2005

On April 13, 2005, then-Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan proposed a joint commission of Turkish and Armenian historians and experts to examine the events of 1915 using Turkish, Armenian and relevant third-country archives.

Armenian President Robert Kocharian declined that particular proposal in his April 26 response, arguing instead for diplomatic normalisation, open borders and an intergovernmental commission.

The proposed joint historical investigation was therefore not established on the terms offered.

The Central Question

If historical conclusions are to rest upon comprehensive archival research, scrutiny cannot be confined to Ottoman records while Armenian revolutionary and ecclesiastical collections escape equivalent examination.

The documented restrictions of 2012 and 2017 do not, by themselves, establish the present accessibility of every collection. That requires updated, independently verifiable access records.

Nevertheless, the historical questions remain:

Why were independent historians denied access to certain Armenian archives? On what grounds were these restrictions imposed? Have the relevant collections since been fully catalogued and made accessible to independent researchers?

Historical transparency requires equal scrutiny of all relevant archives.

text:
On December 20, 1943, U.S. 2nd Lt. Charles "Charlie" Brown was piloting his heavily damaged B-17F Flying Fortress, named "Ye Olde Pub", back from a bombing mission over Bremen, Germany...

The bomber was shredded by flak and fighter attacks, leaving it with a dead engine, a destroyed tail gunner station (killing the tail gunner), and multiple wounded crew members. German Luftwaffe ace Franz Stigler, flying a Messerschmitt Bf 109, caught up to the crippled aircraft. Instead of shooting down the defenseless bomber—which he later noted would be like "shooting at a parachute"—Stigler saw the bleeding crew and chose to spare them. Stigler flew alongside the bomber to shield it from German anti-aircraft fire and tried to signal Brown to land or fly toward neutral Sweden. When Brown continued toward England, Stigler gave a salute and turned away. Brown managed to cross the North Sea and land safely in England, where military authorities ordered the crew to keep the encounter secret so other airmen wouldn't expect mercy from German pilots.

. . . 

A German fighter pilot caught a crippled American bomber and chose not to shoot. On December 20, 1943, Luftwaffe pilot Franz Stigler approached a badly damaged B-17 Flying Fortress returning from a bombing mission over Germany. The American aircraft had lost its place in formation, its fuselage was torn open, and several crew members were wounded. One had already been killed. Stigler could have fired at the defenseless bomber and claimed another victory. Instead, after examining its condition, he flew alongside it and helped guide it toward safety. Nearly five decades passed before the two pilots met again.

The American bomber, nicknamed Ye Olde Pub, was commanded by twenty-one-year-old Second Lieutenant Charles Brown. His crew belonged to the US Eighth Air Force and had been assigned to attack an aircraft factory at Bremen. It was Brown's first combat mission as an aircraft commander. During the approach, German anti-aircraft fire damaged the aircraft, destroying the Plexiglas nose and disabling one engine while seriously damaging another. Enemy fighters then attacked the bomber as it became separated from the formation. Machine-gun fire tore through the aircraft, damaged its systems and inflicted casualties among the ten crew members.

The situation became increasingly desperate. The tail gunner had been killed, other crew members were wounded, and the aircraft's oxygen system was damaged. Brown temporarily lost consciousness as the bomber descended, but the surviving crew managed to regain control. With the aircraft struggling to remain airborne, they continued toward the North Sea rather than abandon men who were too badly injured to parachute safely. Their chances were uncertain. The B-17 was flying over enemy territory with extensive damage and without the protection of its original formation. A single additional fighter attack could have destroyed it.

Franz Stigler was an experienced German fighter pilot serving with Jagdgeschwader 27. He had already accumulated numerous combat victories and had been operating against American bombers attacking Germany. When he spotted Brown's damaged aircraft, he took off in his Messerschmitt Bf 109 to intercept it. He approached expecting an ordinary combat opportunity, but what he saw changed his decision. Through the holes in the bomber's fuselage, Stigler could see wounded and incapacitated crewmen. The aircraft's guns offered little effective resistance, and its condition suggested that it was barely capable of continuing flight. Stigler later recalled regarding the men aboard as being in a situation comparable to parachutists who could no longer defend themselves.

text:
THE SUBSTITUTE

In 1862 during our Civil War an 18-year-old named Willie Leer lived near the town of Palmyra Missouri. Like most of those in his neighborhood he sympathized with the south. Eventually Union soldiers occupied Palmyra and gained control of the district. Outrages were committed on both sides, and many lawless deeds are recorded in the local histories of that era. Union soldiers were shot down behind hedges and Union families driven from their homes and sometimes treated cruelly. To avenge these deeds and put a stop to them, the Union commander arrested a large number of civilians including Wille Leer.

They were all charged with being "Guerillas" and after a trial by court-martial, were all sentenced to be shot. Next, the commander decided to select ten of those condemned for immediate execution and reserve the remainder under hope of pardon if the outrages ceased or for future punishment if they did not.

Willie Leer wasn't among the ten to be executed but a neighbor of his was and was terribly shaken at the thought of his situation. He was the father of a very large and poor family and was destressed at the thought of his helpless condition in which he would leave his loved ones. Willie saw all of this and it deeply moved him. He stepped forward to the commanding officer and offered to take his neighbor's place. The officer had no objection and agreed. The neighbor with the deepest of gratitude accepted Leer as his substitute. Willie Leer took the place of his friend in line with the other nine men drawn up before the firing squad. At the command, "Fire" Willie fell with the others riddled with bullets, his blood soaking the earth.

With the fall of man in the Garden of Eden, sin entered the world, and death came through sin, and so death spread to all men, for the wages of sin is death. So, all have sinned and have come short of the glory of God. But God demonstrated His love toward us by providing a sinless substitute, His only begotten Son, Jesus Christ.

Jesus was sent into the world to take our place, to take our sin, to take our lawless deeds upon Himself, for by His wounds we are healed. It was His blood that soaked the ground beneath the cross so that all who believe in Him will be pardoned and given a free gift; the gift of eternal life. We are guaranteed of this because after His death, He was buried and raised on the third day according to the Scriptures and is presently in heaven at the right hand of God the Father acting as our Great High Priest making intercession for us. 

Just as Willie Leer's neighbor never tired of telling how he saved him, let us never forget the price that was paid for you and me by our Lord Jesus Christ.

I took this story from a Bible tract from the 1860's and modernized it with our current lingo.❤️
