text:
How big can a wolf actually get?

Bigger than most people think. Smaller than most photos claim. Both statements are true at the same time, and the space between them is one of the strangest corners of the internet.

I have watched people argue about this for years. Grown adults in comment sections, swearing a wolf they saw was the size of a pony, while someone else swears no wolf has ever topped a Great Dane. Each side has a photo. Each side is certain. Most of them are wrong in at least one direction.

So let's do this properly. Real numbers first. Then the tricks. Then the part that nobody expects.

And there is a short clip, under twenty seconds, that goes straight at this question. I will tell you why it is worth your time before the end of this post. But first you need the numbers, because without them the video is just a series of impressive animals. With them, it becomes an argument you can judge for yourself.

THE NUMBER YOU PROBABLY HAVE WRONG

Start with the baseline. A typical adult gray wolf weighs somewhere between 40 and 80 pounds, depending on where it lives. That is roughly 18 to 36 kilograms. A fit Labrador. A big husky. A medium dog with a very different job description.

If that sounds disappointing, hold on. That figure is an average across the entire species, and the species is spread across most of the northern hemisphere. A wolf in the Arabian desert and a wolf in the Yukon share a Latin name and almost nothing else about their bodies.

The smallest wolves, the Arabian ones, can weigh around 40 to 45 pounds. A long-legged, lean animal built to waste nothing, in a landscape that punishes anything extra. Mexican gray wolves are also on the small end, commonly in the 60 to 80 pound range.

Go north, and the scale shifts. Wolves in Alaska and northwestern Canada regularly reach 100 to 130 pounds for males, and some individuals go well past that. This is not folklore. Wildlife biologists have weighed them.

Now we hit the part where the internet loses its mind.

THE RECORD, AND WHY IT IS COMPLICATED

The most widely cited heavyweight in the literature is a wolf reported in Alaska in 1939 at 175 pounds. About 79 kilograms. It is the number that shows up again and again in serious references, and it is a genuinely enormous wolf. Almost twice the weight of a typical northern male.

Then there are the larger claims. You have seen them. 200 pounds. 230. Sometimes more. A few of them come with a story, a hunter, a scale, and a date.

Here is the problem with those. Weights without verification are just stories with numbers attached. A scale at a remote lodge, a wolf weighed after a big meal, an estimate by someone who was not there for the weighing, a typo that was repeated until it became a fact. Researchers tend to treat anything over about 175 pounds with serious caution, and I think that caution is correct.

Here is a detail most people never think about. A wolf can eat an enormous amount in a single sitting. Estimates commonly put the stomach capacity of a wolf at around 20 pounds of meat. So a wolf weighed right after a successful hunt can read differently from the same animal two days later. Same wolf. Different number on the scale.

That does not make the giants fake. It means the honest answer to "how big can they get" has to carry an asterisk, and anyone who tells you otherwise with total confidence is selling something.

HEIGHT IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE STORY

Weight is not what makes people gasp. Height is.

A big northern wolf can stand around 30 to 32 inches at the shoulder, and some run a little taller. That is the height of a large dog. But the proportions are different, and proportions are what the eye actually reads.

Wolves have long legs, narrow chests, and large feet. Their paws can print tracks around five inches long. A wolf is built like a long-distance runner, not like a bodybuilder. The legs lift the body far off the ground, so the animal looks taller than a dog of the same weight.

Take a 110 pound wolf and a 110 pound mastiff. The mastiff is thick, low, and heavy through the chest. The wolf is tall, tight, and long in the leg. If you stood both in a field and asked a stranger which one was bigger, many people would point at the wolf. It simply occupies more vertical space.

This is the first reason wolves look larger than they are. The second reason is stranger.

THE SECOND REASON: FUR, FEAR, AND THE HUMAN BRAIN

A winter wolf coat is a piece of engineering. The outer guard hairs are long and coarse. Underneath sits a dense layer of insulation. In deep cold, a wolf can look 30 percent heavier than it is, because a good portion of that silhouette is air trapped in fur.

Strip the coat away and you find a lean animal with a deep, narrow ribcage. The silhouette lies. The scale does not.

Now add the part that has nothing to do with biology. Humans are terrible at judging the size of things that scare us. Threat makes memory swell. A person who meets a wolf at dusk, at fifty yards, with their pulse in their ears, will often describe an animal twice the size of the one the biologist later measures. This is not dishonesty. It is how fear edits a memory.

There is a reason fairy tales have giant wolves. Nobody wrote a story about a medium-sized predator that behaved reasonably.

THE PHOTO PROBLEM

And then there are the photographs. This is where the real chaos lives.

Every few months a picture of a monstrous wolf takes over social media. Usually someone is holding it, or standing behind it, or hanging it from a pole. The caption says something like: record-breaking, 200 plus pounds, taller than a man.

Look at how these images are made, and you will start to see the tricks.

Forced perspective. If the animal is closer to the camera than the person, it looks bigger relative to that person. A wolf held out toward the lens will fill the frame. The human, a few feet behind, shrinks. The same trick makes tourists appear to hold up the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

Lifting. A wolf held upright by its front legs, with the hunter standing behind, can look like it is the same height as a grown man. But the lifting is doing the work. A big male wolf stretched to full length can be around six feet from nose to tail tip. Hold it vertically at the right angle, and it appears to tower.

Camera angle. Shoot upward at an animal and you add mass. Shoot downward at a person and you subtract it. Crop the frame so there is no reference object, no tree, no fence post, no vehicle, and your eye loses all scale.

Wide-angle lenses. Phone cameras exaggerate whatever is nearest the lens. A wolf's head at the front edge of the frame becomes a boulder.

Wolfdogs and large dogs mislabeled as wolves. This one gets ignored too often. Breeds like the Tamaskan, the Czechoslovakian Wolfdog, and various crosses can be big, lean, and wolfish to look at, and they are routinely passed around as wolves. A husky next to a true wolf tells you a lot about what the difference really looks like, and we will come to that.

Captive animals. A wolf living in a sanctuary, fed regularly and exercising less than its wild cousins, can carry more weight than a wild animal would. Fair comparison is difficult.

None of that means the biggest wolves are small. It means that when a picture looks too dramatic, you should be a little skeptical, and a little curious. Both reactions are healthy.

THE COYOTE QUESTION

Here is the comparison that rearranges how people see wolves.

A coyote typically weighs around 20 to 50 pounds. That is a lean, fox-faced canine, often mistaken for a small wolf and sometimes mistaken for a stray dog. Put an adult coyote next to a large northern wolf and the gap is not subtle. The wolf can outweigh the coyote by two, three, even four times.

People assume the species are close in size because they look alike in pictures. They do not. A coyote is a mid-sized predator. A big wolf is a different category of animal.

This is also why the two behave so differently around each other. In places where both live, wolves tend to dominate coyotes, and coyotes tend to learn the geography of wolf territory and steer around it. Size is an argument. In the animal world it is often the one that ends the debate before it starts.

THE HUSKY QUESTION

Now the comparison people most want to make: wolf versus dog.

The first thing to know is that dogs are not a different branch of the tree. They are descended from wolves, from an ancient population that no longer exists in the form it did. Domestic dogs and gray wolves can still produce offspring. They are close relatives with very different lives.

A typical husky weighs somewhere around 35 to 60 pounds. A big northern wolf can be double that. So when you see them side by side, the husky can look like it belongs to a smaller, softer chapter of the same book.

But weight is not the only thing that changes. Look at the proportions.

The wolf's head is broader, with a longer muzzle and a heavier jaw. The legs are longer for the body. The chest is narrower. The feet are enormous. The eyes sit slightly slanted, and they are usually amber or yellow rather than the icy blue that people associate with huskies.

A husky looks like a dog dressed as a wolf. A wolf looks like it has no interest in pleasing anyone.

That difference lives in the skull, the gait, the whole way the animal carries attention. Wolves watch the world as if it were a problem to be solved. Dogs, after thousands of years of living beside us, watch us.

THE REAL MEANING OF "BIG"

So far I have talked about pounds and inches, because that is what people search for. But size in a wolf was never really about the scale.

Here is the fact that changed how I think about this.

A wolf pack routinely hunts animals many times larger than any single member. Elk. Bison. Moose that can weigh a thousand pounds or more. A pack of wolves weighing a total of maybe 500 pounds takes on an animal heavier than all of them combined, with hooves and antlers, in deep snow, in the dark.

That is the actual scale of the wolf. Not what a single animal weighs, but what a coordinated group can do.

And it gets stranger when you look at the cost. A hunt like that can fail again and again. Many pursuits end without a kill, because a healthy moose is a dangerous thing to attack. A wolf that breaks a leg or takes a hoof to the head may starve. The animal that looks so powerful is operating very close to the edge of its own survival.

Which brings me to the question I keep returning to.

WHY DOES SIZE VARY SO MUCH?

If one species can range from a 40 pound desert wanderer to a 130 pound northern giant, something is driving it. Something is.

Biologists have a name for one part of the pattern: Bergmann's rule. In general, animals of the same species tend to be larger in colder climates. A bigger body loses heat more slowly relative to its volume. In the Arctic that is a survival advantage. In a hot desert it is a liability, because you need to shed heat, not store it.

Wolves follow this pattern reasonably well. The cold north produces the heavy ones. The warm south and the desert produce the slim ones.

But climate is only half the explanation. The other half is food.

Wolves are shaped by what they hunt. Where the prey is large, such as moose, elk, and bison, wolves tend to be large too, because a bigger body and bigger jaws help when the target is a ton of muscle. Where the prey is small, such as rodents, hares, and scavenged scraps, a smaller wolf is more efficient. The animal is a negotiation between the climate and the menu.

This is why the largest wolves on record come from places with cold winters and huge prey. The Mackenzie Valley region and Alaska are names that keep appearing in the heavyweight literature for exactly this reason. Everything lines up: the cold, the prey, the space.

Does that mean a 200 pound wolf is impossible? I will not claim certainty on a number nobody has verified. But the biology gives you a ceiling that points somewhere in the neighborhood of the documented records, not far beyond them. Extraordinary claims need extraordinary scales.

WHAT A WOLF CAN DO WITH THAT BODY

Let's leave the bathroom scale behind for a moment, because the size of a wolf shows up in other numbers.

Distance. Wolves routinely travel many miles a day while searching for prey, and can cover something like 30 miles in a day when they need to. They do it at a trot, a gait they can hold for hours.

Speed. In a chase, a wolf can reach somewhere around 35 to 40 miles per hour for short bursts. Not the fastest predator on earth, but fast enough to make every second of a pursuit matter.

Senses. A wolf's sense of smell is far beyond ours, built to read the history of a place from a single patch of ground: who walked here, how recently, whether they were healthy. A howl can carry for miles in open terrain. Hearing and scent give the animal a map of the world that we cannot see.

Bite. The canines can reach roughly two inches long. The jaw is built for gripping and holding. Researchers have debated the exact bite force for decades, and the most widely repeated numbers deserve skepticism. What is certain is that it is strong enough to break the bones of large prey.

None of those numbers fits in a photograph. That is the problem with judging a wolf by a picture. A picture holds a single second. A wolf is a long, patient process.

THE PART WHERE THE ANIMAL STOPS BEING A NUMBER

Here is a fact that tends to quiet a room.

A newborn wolf pup weighs about a pound. Blind. Deaf. Helpless. It cannot regulate its own temperature. Born in a den, in the dark, dependent entirely on its mother for the first weeks.

The animal that eventually weighs 100 pounds and crosses mountains starts out weighing about as much as a loaf of bread.

I find that more astonishing than any record. It reframes the whole question. "How big can they get" is really "how far can something that small travel."

And the answer depends on things that have nothing to do with the animal. It depends on the winter. It depends on whether the pack finds food in the first year. It depends on humans: roads, hunting seasons, the line where protected land ends. A pup that makes it to adulthood has beaten odds that look bad on paper. In the wild, a wolf's lifespan is often only around six to eight years.

So when you see a giant, you are looking at a survivor. A very specific, very rare outcome. Not a typical wolf. The one that made it.

THE YELLOWSTONE FACT

Many people know the story of Yellowstone. Wolves were gone from the park for roughly seventy years, wiped out by predator control. In 1995 and 1996, wolves captured in Canada were released there, 14 in the first group and 17 the following year.

What happened next is argued about by ecologists to this day. The popular version says wolves transformed rivers, changed where elk grazed, brought back willows and beavers. The careful version says the effects were real but more complicated than the viral retelling, and that other factors mattered too.

I mention it not to settle the debate, but because it shows something about scale. Thirty-one animals. Thirty-one bodies, none larger than a good-sized dog, changed the conversation about a landscape the size of a small country.

If you want a definition of big that does not appear on a scale, that is a candidate.

WHY WE KEEP OVERSTATING THEM

Let me say something slightly uncomfortable.

We exaggerate wolves because we have to. For most of history, the wolf has been the animal we use to hold our fears. In stories, they are the thing at the edge of the village. In politics, they are the thing at the edge of the pasture. In art, the thing in the forest.

An animal that carries that much symbolism cannot be allowed to be an ordinary canine. So we enlarge it. We pass around the 230 pound claim. We share the photograph at the wide angle. We choose the version that fits the feeling.

And the opposite also happens. People who love wolves can shrink the animal the other way, smoothing it into a misunderstood teddy bear. Neither version is honest. The truth is that a wolf is a wild predator that is smaller than the myth and more capable than the apologists admit.

The second part of that sentence is the part I think people should sit with. Smaller than the myth. More capable than the comfort.

THE GIANT THAT REALLY WAS BIGGER

If you want a creature that makes even the heaviest gray wolf look modest, look to the past.

The dire wolf, Aenocyon dirus, roamed North America until roughly ten thousand years ago. Estimates put it at around 150 pounds, with a sturdier build, a heavier skull, and stronger teeth than a modern gray wolf. It lived alongside mammoths and sabertooth cats, and it hunted in a world of enormous prey.

Here is the twist that surprised many people. DNA research published in 2021 suggested the dire wolf was not a close cousin of the gray wolf at all. It belonged to a separate and much older lineage. The two looked alike because similar lifestyles shape similar bodies, not because they were closely related.

The lesson holds for the modern animal too. Body shape follows the job. Give a canine a harsh climate, big prey, and open ground, and evolution produces a long-legged, heavy-jawed hunter, again and again.

It also means the question "how big can a wolf get" never has a single answer. It has an answer for each landscape, each era, each menu.

HOW TO READ A WOLF PHOTO LIKE A SKEPTIC

Here is a short field guide to the next viral picture, because you will see one this week.

Find the reference object. A fence post, a truck tire, a human hand, a boot. Anything with a known size. If there is none, treat the image as unmeasurable.

Check the distance between animal and reference. If the wolf is nearer the lens than the person, discount the size. If they stand at the same distance, trust it more.

Look at the legs. A wolf's real size shows in the length of the leg, not the width of the chest. If the animal is posed so the legs are hidden or bent, you are being shown a shape, not a size.

Ask about the weighing. Who weighed it, with what, and when? A number without that chain is a rumor.

Notice the claim. "Biggest wolf ever" is a sentence that should make you more suspicious, not less. Real records come with documentation. Fake ones come with enthusiasm.

And keep the opposite check in mind. Do not dismiss a photo just because it looks impressive. Some of the most striking animals are real. The goal is not cynicism. The goal is calibration.

WHAT THIS QUESTION SAYS ABOUT US

I want to step back for a second, because I think the size argument is secretly about something else.

When people ask how big a wolf can get, they are rarely asking for a number. They are asking how afraid they should be. They are asking whether the thing in the story is real. They are asking how much space the wild still takes up in a world that has paved so much of it.

There is a certain comfort in a large number. If wolves are enormous, then the wild is enormous too, and we are small in front of it. If wolves are just big dogs, the wild is manageable, and we can relax.

The truth sits between those. A wolf is a wild animal that has survived thousands of years of our efforts to erase it, and it did so without growing to any mythical size. It did so with patience, social intelligence, and the ability to cover ground that we cannot.

I find that more impressive than any record weight.

WHY THE QUESTION SHOWS UP IN A SHORT CLIP

I came across a short video that asks the question directly. Under twenty seconds. No long lecture, no soundtrack of dramatic strings. Just the question, and a handful of animals offered as the answer.

I will not tell you what it shows. That would ruin the one thing a clip like this does well, which is to let your own eyes revise your own guess.

What I will say is this. After everything above, you now know the baseline weights, the northern extremes, the tricks cameras play, the difference between a coyote, a husky, and a wolf, and the reason body size follows climate and prey. You are no longer the person who first scrolled to this post.

That makes the video a different experience. You will look at the animals and notice the proportions. You will glance for a reference object. You will have an opinion about the scale, and you will be able to test it.

Maybe you will think a few of those animals are bigger than the numbers allow. Maybe you will think the numbers are right and the instincts are wrong. Maybe you will disagree with me completely, which is fine, and the comments are open.

But watch it with the question still in your head. How big can a wolf get? And how much of what you feel when you look at one is the animal, and how much is the story we gave it?

ONE MORE THING ABOUT SIZE, AND THEN I'LL STOP

There is a myth about wolf packs that refuses to die: the idea of the alpha, a brutal champion who fights his way to the top and rules by force. It came from early studies of captive wolves, unrelated animals thrown together in an enclosure. The biologist whose work popularized the term spent years trying to retire it.

In the wild, a pack is mostly a family. A breeding pair and their offspring from the past few years. The "leaders" are the parents. The younger ones help raise the pups, carry food back to the den, and learn the territory by following. When young wolves reach maturity, many leave to find a mate and start a pack of their own.

That changes what a big wolf means. The largest animal in a pack is not a king. It is one member of a household, and the household is what survives the winter.

So the next time you picture the biggest wolf in the world, picture it with a family. Picture it sharing, tolerating, waiting for pups to eat first. The giant of the photograph is a parent, a sibling, a student, a survivor.

Size, in the end, is a poor measure of what a wolf is. It tells you how heavy the animal is. It does not tell you what it carries.

WHAT I WOULD ASK YOU TO TAKE FROM THIS

If you remember nothing else, remember five things.

A typical wolf weighs 40 to 80 pounds. The northern giants can pass 130, and the most famous record sits at about 175. Anything bigger needs proof, not volume.

Fur, posture, and camera angles can add the equivalent of fifty pounds to a photograph without adding a single ounce to the animal.

Coyotes, huskies, and wolves look related in pictures and are not interchangeable in life.

Size follows cold and prey. Where winters are hard and meals are enormous, bodies grow to match.

And the most extraordinary thing about a wolf is not its weight. It is how far it gets from a starting point of about one pound.

HOW SCIENTISTS WEIGH A WILD WOLF

It is worth knowing what a trustworthy number looks like.

Researchers who study wolves often capture animals briefly in order to fit tracking collars. The wolf is sedated, and the team works fast. They weigh the animal with a field scale, measure length and shoulder height, check teeth for age, take a blood sample, and note the condition of the coat and body. Then the collar goes on, and the wolf is released to recover.

That is a very different chain from a photograph taken beside a truck. The animal is measured by people who record the date, the location, the sex, the age, and the weight, and who are trained to check each other's numbers. Over decades, those records build the averages and ranges I quoted above.

It is slow, careful, unglamorous work. It rarely produces a viral image. But it is the reason we can say with confidence that a typical wolf is not a pony, and that the true heavyweights, while remarkable, live inside a documented ceiling.

If you want to trust a number, ask who handled the scale.

THE LAST QUESTION

I keep coming back to the pup.

A pound of blind, helpless animal in a hole in the ground. A winter that does not care. A forest full of things that kill. A species that humans spent centuries trying to remove from the map.

And yet there are wolves in the snow right now. Some of them are slender. Some are enormous. Some will be photographed, measured, argued over, and turned into a headline with a number that is wrong.

Think about what that implies for the biggest wolf anyone has ever seen. Somewhere, right now, a young animal is walking through snow that will decide whether it ever reaches that size. No camera is pointed at it. No caption has been written. The only audience is the weather.

No record, no myth, and no photograph will ever capture that part. The scale can only measure the survivor, never the odds. No scale has ever measured that kind of luck.

Watch the clip. Make your own guess before you read anyone else's.

Then ask yourself why the animal in front of you looks the way you expected, or why it does not.

Whatever you decide, the wolf will not care about the number. It has somewhere to be.

text:
Gay Mexican Trap House:

Where was a Chicano couple: short man with a pencil moustache and 49ers hat; girl in a corset style blouse, her tetas exposed: she talked, he listened, solemnly. There was a frizzy haired, chunky Mexicana who asked if she could drink with us and offered to buy shots. It was Sunday night — we were good enough company. A Samoan, Bob, joined us. He locked himself out of his car and was waiting for AAA.

Soon, it was 1:30 am and they kicked us out — California law. We huddled outside, finishing the beers we had snuck out the bar. Bob took a bump of coca off his credit card. Back in Australia, he was in a biker gang: “when I wanted out, I need to go on one last run, across the country. If I had gotten caught, that would be it. I left my family behind man — I’m a shift supervisor at a Home Depot now.” Another bump.

The AAA worker who showed up to open Bob’s car was dressed in a turban, a tunic ornamented in the design of my childhood pajamas and sturdy sandals.

I asked if he’s Afghani; he cautiously confirmed. I could tell he was nervous (with my slicked back hair, I’m skinhead-passing). He calmed when I tried to speak with him in my limited Farsi.

Bob told us there’s an after party in San Jose. We didn’t believe him — Silicon Valley is a stupid village. A dull ethnic lasagna of “people in tech.” “But listen,” Bob continued “this place is a bit special. It’s a private party at my friend’s house with some… unique guests, if you know what I mean.”

None of us knew what he meant. We still got into his Dodge Charger as he hauled arse down to one of San Jose’s many ethnic favellas (Filipino, Mexican, Vietnamese, Tongan). We parked the car in a residential area and approached the front door of a vanilla-colored house. Inside, there were so many Mexicans you couldn’t freely walk around without rubbing your dickbone with the collective la gente.

We found a corner in the back and order a basket of beers. Aside from our chubby Latina friend, the only woman at the party had scorpion tattoos on her chest — she attempted to seduce me but I lo siento, pero tengo esposa’ed her advances. Ten minutes later, the front door opened and half a dozen Latino trans amigos->mujeres waddle into the house: heels, fluffy 80s hair, one was in a purple quinceañera dress, another dressed like Lady Gaga.

With them, was a man in a ranchero outfit — black cowhide sombrero, gilded belt buckle, Saddam moustache — their wrangler?! This was our cue to leave. I contemplated calling I.C.E. but the host was welcoming, and I got to practice my Spanish. And really, who were they harming?

text:
A greyhound named Sarabi spends most of her day doing absolutely nothing.

Then one sound switches her on, and for about a minute she stops being a dog and becomes a physics problem.

I keep coming back to that gap. The distance between the animal who will sleep through an entire afternoon and the animal who, given the right trigger, produces a noise that has no business coming out of a creature that was snoring ten minutes earlier. Same body. Same collar. Same quiet house. Two completely different beings.

Most people only ever meet the first one. This is about the second.

And I'm going to be careful, because the second one is easy to ruin by over-explaining. So I'll tell you everything about her except the part you actually need to see.

Start with the engineering, because it's ridiculous.

The greyhound is the fastest dog on earth. The number usually quoted is around 45 miles per hour, roughly 70 kilometers per hour. That is faster than the speed limit on plenty of city streets. It is faster than any human sprinter has ever run, by a margin that isn't remotely close.

But top speed is the least interesting part. The interesting part is how the body pulls it off.

A greyhound at full stretch uses what biomechanics people call a rotary gallop. The spine works like a spring: it folds the whole animal up beneath itself, then snaps open again, and that flex adds enormous reach to every stride. In each cycle there are two separate moments when not one paw is touching the ground. At speed, a greyhound spends a surprising share of her time in the air.

Then there's the hardware underneath. The heart is large for the frame. The lungs are deep, the chest is shaped like the hull of a boat, the legs are long and light, and body fat is close to nonexistent. Greyhounds also carry an unusually high concentration of red blood cells, which means more oxygen delivered with every beat. It is one reason retired greyhounds so often make excellent blood donors for other dogs, saving lives long after their running days.

Thousands of years of selection shaped every one of those details, and the instruction never changed: faster.

So when you hear that Sarabi is a greyhound, understand what that really says. She is not a dog who happens to run quickly. She is a living answer to an old question: how fast can a medium-sized mammal go if you strip away everything that doesn't serve speed?

And the answer, apparently, naps.

There is a nickname in the greyhound world that every adopter learns within the first week: the 45-mph couch potato.

It's affectionate, and it's also a precise description of a strange biological bargain. Greyhounds are sprinters. They are built to burn everything they have in a short, violent burst and then shut down. Adoption groups will tell you a greyhound can sleep sixteen, even eighteen hours a day. Many of them would rather fold themselves into a single square foot of sofa than walk around the block.

This confuses people. They see the long legs and the muscle and expect an athlete who needs hours of exercise. What they get is a dog who treats movement like a luxury item: rare, expensive, and not to be wasted on errands.

But here's what I find fascinating. That laziness isn't a lack of drive. It's the opposite. It's a savings account. A body engineered for explosive effort has to be frugal the rest of the time, so that when the moment comes, there is something to spend.

Which raises the question I can't shake. What happens to a dog like that if the moment never comes?

A sprinter without a track. An engine that never leaves the garage. Some animals are quiet because they are content. Others are quiet because the thing they were built for has never been offered. From the outside, the two look exactly the same.

Greyhound owners also keep a private vocabulary that outsiders find hard to believe.

There's roaching: a dog sprawled on her back with all four legs pointing at the ceiling, completely unconscious, looking like an overturned insect. There's the famous lean, where a greyhound presses her entire body weight against your leg as a form of affection. There's the soft, wordless chatter of teeth that happens when they're happy. And there are the zoomies, what behaviorists call frenetic random activity periods: sudden bursts where a dog hurtles around for no reason anyone can identify.

Almost every dog does zoomies. But watching a greyhound do them is a different experience, the way a casual jogger and a professional sprinter are both technically doing the same verb. The scale changes. The sound changes. A living room stops being a room and becomes a very short track.

The reasons for these bursts are still debated, but the leading ideas involve releasing stored energy and regulating excitement. Which is another way of saying that a dog's body occasionally needs to run for no reason except that it can.

What interests me is what zoomies reveal about the unplanned version of joy. They happen in hallways, between pieces of furniture, after baths. They are a dog improvising happiness with whatever space she happens to have.

Now imagine what happens when the space is no longer improvised.

The greyhound has been a status symbol for longer than most countries have existed.

Dogs of this unmistakable shape appear in art from the ancient Mediterranean and Middle East, in carvings and paintings thousands of years old. In medieval Europe the breed was tied so tightly to the aristocracy that a law attributed to King Canute in the eleventh century is often cited as forbidding anyone below the rank of gentleman from keeping one. Whether the legal details are exactly as the legend tells them, the message survives: this dog was too valuable, too fast, and too beautiful to belong to ordinary people.

Think about what that means. For a very long time, the fastest dog in the world was the possession of the powerful. It lived in castles. It was bred for a single high-stakes sprint after a hare, where the whole point was to close a gap that no other dog could close.

I bring up the history because it explains something about the weight of watching one of these animals do what she was designed for. This isn't a trick. It isn't a talent. It is the continuation of a job description older than the English language, carried out by a dog who is almost certainly unaware that she is inheriting any of it.

She isn't performing history. She's just going.

And that is what makes it hard to look away from.

The sound.

The person who posted this clip used one word for what comes out of Sarabi when the moment arrives: a scream. And honestly, that isn't an exaggeration of dog behavior. Sighthounds are famously dramatic. Greyhounds yodel, they roo, they hold full conversations with the ceiling, and at the peak of excitement some of them produce noises that make visitors check whether someone is hurt.

The question worth asking isn't why she's loud. It's what is happening inside a brain that goes from sleep to that in a matter of seconds.

Part of the answer is old and simple. Pavlov showed more than a century ago that animals learn to treat a signal as the beginning of the reward. The bell becomes the meal. In Sarabi's case the signal is a sound she knows, and somewhere along the way her brain wired it to the best thing in her world. Which means the explosion doesn't begin when the fun begins. It begins the instant she hears the sound that promises the fun.

And that's the part neuroscientists find genuinely interesting. The late Jaak Panksepp, who spent a career mapping emotion in mammal brains, described a circuit he called SEEKING: a dopamine-driven system that pushes animals to anticipate, to reach, to want. Researchers who study motivation separate two things that feel identical from the inside. Liking is the pleasure of having the thing. Wanting is the electric, vibrating, can't-stand-still pull toward it.

What you hear in a scream like that is probably wanting at maximum volume.

Think about how rare that is. Most of us feel something like it a handful of times a year. The night before a trip. A phone about to light up with exactly the right name. A dog like this gets there with the turn of a key.

We don't know what it's like inside that skull. We never will. But we know the circuitry is real, we know it's shared across mammals, and we know it sounds like that.

There's a state psychologists call flow. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi spent decades studying it: the condition of total absorption where effort and enjoyment fuse, self-consciousness drops away, and time stops behaving normally. Climbers describe it. Surgeons describe it. Musicians, chess players, and long-distance runners all report some version of it.

The common ingredients are a clear goal, immediate feedback, and a challenge that matches your ability so precisely that you're stretched but not broken.

Now ask yourself what, in the entire life of a dog, comes closer to that recipe than a full sprint. The goal is unmistakable. The feedback is instant, in every muscle. And the challenge sits at the very edge of what her body can do.

I'm careful with the word, because flow was defined from human reports and we can't interview a dog. But the behavioral picture is hard to ignore: total attention, no hesitation, no scanning for threats, nothing held back for later. Whatever is going on in her head during those seconds, it looks like an animal with every system pointed at one thing and no part of her arguing.

Most humans spend their days in the opposite state. Split attention, constant self-monitoring, one eye always on the exit. We pay good money and travel long distances for a few minutes of what a greyhound gets by hearing a familiar sound.

Maybe that's the quiet reason we envy her. Not the speed. The undivided mind.

Here's the uncomfortable thing about every animal who lives in a human home.

We selected them, shaped them, and then asked them to be quiet in rooms. For a retriever we carved out a yard and a ball. For a terrier, a squeaky toy. For a border collie, an occasional frantic attempt to simulate sheep. But for a dog whose entire body is a monument to one extreme behavior, one that needs space, a straight line, and permission, the modern home is almost an architectural insult.

Apartments have corners. Yards have fences. Sidewalks have leashes. The very environments we think of as safe and loving are, for a sprinter, small.

This is the real tension inside greyhound ownership, and it's why the people who love them tend to talk about it with a particular seriousness. You can give a greyhound a soft bed, good food, and every kind of tenderness, and still be withholding the single thing her body is begging to do.

So what is at stake in a moment like this is not fun. Fun is a trivial word. What is at stake is whether a living creature gets to be fully what she is, even briefly, even a few times a month.

It's a strange standard for love, isn't it? We usually measure it in comfort. How warm, how safe, how fed. We rarely measure it by asking: did you let her be the thing she is?

I don't have a clean answer. But I've noticed that once people ask the question, they never look at their animals quite the same way again.

The tag on this clip says rescue dog. So let's talk about what that word often carries with it for greyhounds, while being honest about the limits of what I know.

I don't know where Sarabi's story began, and I'm not going to invent it for you. But I can describe the world she belongs to.

A great many greyhounds who end up in adoption programs come out of racing, an industry that produces more dogs than it keeps. The transition into home life, as adoption groups describe it, is startling. Many of these dogs have lived in kennels and on tracks and have never encountered the ordinary furniture of a house. Stairs can be terrifying. Glass doors can look like open air. A mirror can look like another dog. Toys can be a mystery, because nobody ever showed them what play with a person looks like.

Then there's the quiet part. A greyhound with a racing past has to work out, from scratch, what running is for when it belongs to her.

That's the thing I can't stop turning over. For any rescued animal, freedom is a negotiation with a past you can't see. You can offer a couch, and she'll learn the couch. You can offer a walk, and she'll learn the walk. But there is a different category of gift: the one where she discovers that the thing her body does best is no longer work. It is no longer duty. It is just hers.

What does that moment look like for a dog who has known running only as a job? I'm not going to tell you. That's the part I'd rather you see than read.

Let's address the claim at the top of the clip, because it's a big one: the favorite thing in the whole world.

A skeptic would say dogs don't rank their experiences. They don't keep a mental list with a number one at the top. And that's fair. None of us can open a dog's head and check.

But animal behavior scientists have found ways around the problem, and the methods are surprisingly elegant. One is preference testing: give an animal repeated choices and watch what she picks. Another is more revealing: measure how hard an animal will work for something. How many times will she press the lever? How heavy a door will she push? How long will she wait? Welfare scientists such as Marian Dawkins built a whole body of work on the idea that what an animal is willing to pay tells you what it needs.

By that standard, "favorite" is not a sentimental word. It's a measurement. A dog who erupts at a single sound before anything has happened, who vibrates with it, who can't hold it in, is paying the maximum price in the only currency she has: her whole body, her whole voice, her whole attention.

Is that the favorite thing in the whole world? Maybe not in the way a person would say it. But if you wanted to design an experiment to find out what a dog values most, you'd be looking for exactly this behavior.

And here's the part that gets me: most of us have never run that experiment on our own animals. We assume we know. We buy the toy we think is best, plan the walk we think is right. We rarely let the dog vote.

A fair warning before I go further, because trust matters more than drama.

I'm not going to tell you what Sarabi is thinking. Nobody can. When we say a dog is living for something, or dreaming of something, or knows exactly what's coming, we're interpreting. Sometimes well, sometimes poorly. Anthropomorphism is a real trap, and the loudest animal content is often the most guilty of it.

What we can say is narrower, and in my view stronger. A particular dog responds to a particular sound with an intense, repeatable pattern of behavior. That pattern matches what we know about anticipation in mammal brains. It is consistent with a strong preference. It doesn't require us to claim she has a bucket list or a philosophy of speed.

The honest version of the story is better than the sentimental one. It doesn't ask you to believe a dog has a human inner monologue. It asks you only to accept that a nonhuman animal can want something intensely, and that when she gets it, the evidence of her wellbeing is written all over her body, in a language that doesn't need translation.

That's enough. You don't have to inflate it.

There's a framework in animal welfare called the Five Freedoms, developed in the UK in the 1960s and 1970s and still influential. Freedom from hunger and thirst. From discomfort. From pain, injury, and disease. From fear and distress. And the one that quietly changes everything: freedom to express normal behavior.

Read that last one again. It doesn't say freedom from harm. It says freedom to express what you are.

For decades, welfare science mostly asked what we should prevent. Lately the question has shifted toward what we should provide: the positive experiences. Newer models talk about animals having good lives rather than merely not-bad ones, and treat exploring, playing, chasing, and anticipating as real components of wellbeing, not optional extras.

Seen through that lens, the difference between a safe dog and a thriving dog is the difference between the first four freedoms and the fifth. A greyhound can have all four and still go years without once being allowed to be a greyhound.

I think this is why clips like this one hit people harder than they expect. We recognize something we rarely see named. We don't just see a happy dog. We see a fifth freedom being cashed in, in real time.

And we start to wonder how many animals around us, and maybe how many people, are living with the first four and still waiting for the fifth.

Scientists have even found a way to test whether an animal is in a good mood, and the result is one of the quietly moving ideas in modern animal research.

It's called a cognitive bias test. The setup is simple: an animal learns that one location means something good and another means something bad. Then you place a bowl somewhere in between, in an ambiguous spot, and watch. Does she approach hopefully, or hesitate? Animals in a better emotional state tend to give the ambiguous spot the benefit of the doubt. Animals in worse states don't. In studies with dogs, rats, sheep, and other species, optimism turns out to be measurable.

Now think about what a trigger like the one in this clip does to that. A dog who has learned that a sound means joy isn't just anticipating one event. For that instant, she is living in a world where good things happen when the right noise starts. It is the bias test run live, by life.

Studies in several species suggest that richer environments, with more chances to explore and play, shift animals toward a more optimistic outlook. So the sprint may not be one minute of happiness. It may be the thing that colors the rest of the day.

Which would mean the couch, the nap, the soft, slow, sleepy hours that look so lazy from the outside, are shaped by what she gets to do in the short stretch when she isn't lazy at all.

There is a clock inside every one of these stories, and it's worth saying out loud.

Greyhounds often live a decade or more, a good run by dog standards. But the window in which a body can do what Sarabi's body does, at the level it does it, is narrower than the lifespan. Sprinters age in a particular way. Joints, muscles, and tendons are the first to remind them of what they used to be. The speed is the first thing to fade and the last thing they stop wanting.

Nobody tells you this when you fall in love with a young animal. You think of the years as a smooth, unbroken stretch. But some capabilities have an expiration date that arrives long before the animal does. The dog will still be there. The exact version of her that can do this, in this exact body, will not be there forever.

I say it because it changes what the clip means. This is not footage of a dog being cute. It's a record of a particular body on a particular day, as fast as it will ever be today, and a little faster than it will be someday.

There's a word for moments like that in people. We call them a prime. We rarely have a word for them in animals, mostly because we rarely notice.

There's a practical truth underneath all this, and it deserves honesty.

Greyhounds are sighthounds, which means they hunt by sight and react to movement at a speed their owners can't match. Adoption organizations are nearly unanimous: these dogs generally aren't safe off leash in unfenced places. The prey drive is real. The recall, in the middle of a chase, is often nonexistent. And a body capable of 45 miles per hour doesn't need much distance to be completely beyond a person's control.

So the places where a greyhound can truly open up are rare, and the people who find them tend to treasure them. A securely fenced field. A large enclosed space. A trusted area with nothing she can run into, run past, or run after. It isn't about risking something for a thrill. It's the opposite. It's an unusual amount of planning in the service of unusual freedom.

That's why I'd push back on the idea that freedom and care are opposites. For animals like this, they're partners. The more serious the safety, the bigger the freedom you can afford to give. A leash isn't the opposite of love. For a dog like this, a leash is sometimes what makes the greatest gift possible somewhere else.

One more thing, and it's easy to miss.

Behind every moment like this is a decision that someone made. At some point, a person noticed that a sound set off something extraordinary in their dog, and instead of treating it as a nuisance, they made room for it. They learned what the trigger was. They arranged life so it could happen again.

That's a quieter kind of love than the dramatic rescue stories get credit for. It isn't the single heroic act. It's the repeated, patient, slightly inconvenient habit of paying attention, and then acting on what you notice.

Rescue doesn't end at the moment an animal is saved. That's where it starts. The saving gets the headlines. The work that follows is the discovery, over months and years, of what this particular animal needs in order to feel like herself. Sometimes it's medicine. Sometimes it's patience. And sometimes it's something so simple and so loud that the neighbors know about it.

I don't know the details of Sarabi's household, and I won't pretend to. But I know this: a dog doesn't develop a favorite thing in a vacuum. Somebody had to offer it.

Why do clips like this travel?

Not because they're cute. The internet has plenty of cute. They travel because of something more specific, and psychologists have been circling it for years: emotional contagion. Humans are wired to catch feelings from one another and, it turns out, from other species. We see an expression of unguarded joy and some part of our nervous system quietly mirrors it. Our mood lifts a few degrees before we've even decided whether we feel anything.

And pure joy is strangely scarce online. The feed is optimized for conflict. It rewards the outraged, the anxious, the argumentative, the afraid. A creature with no agenda, no audience in mind, no opinion about anything except one overwhelming desire, is almost an anomaly. She isn't selling. She isn't arguing. She isn't aware of being watched.

That's the secret ingredient. Unselfconscious joy is the one emotion you can't perform. Humans have tried. We stage it, filter it, caption it. It never quite carries. But an animal in the grip of the real thing has nothing to hide behind, and we can tell instantly, in a fraction of a second, the difference between a performance and the genuine article.

When people share a clip like this, I think they're doing something small and generous. They're handing someone else a minute of their own nervous system's best behavior. Here. Feel this. I did.

That's the whole mechanism. It isn't content. It's a transfusion.

So here's the question I'd actually like you to answer, in your own head or in the replies.

What is your animal's version of this?

Not the thing you think they love. The thing that, when it begins, rearranges their entire nervous system before anything has even happened. The sound of the leash coming off the hook. The rustle of one specific bag. The jingle of keys that means the car, which means the lake. The cat who comes out of a dead sleep at the sound of a can opener at the other end of the house.

If you can name it, you know your animal. If you can't, that's an opening, not a failure. It might be something you've been doing every day without noticing it was the highlight of someone else's day.

And if you've noticed one, and you have a story, I'd love to read it. Because I suspect that if you collected a thousand of them, you'd have something close to a map of what animals actually want, written by the people who live closest to them.

Sarabi will never read any of this. She doesn't know there's a clip. She doesn't know it has been watched. She doesn't know that a sound most of us wouldn't notice has become the center of a long argument about what animals are for and what we owe them.

She only knows what it does.

And that might be the most honest thing about her. There is no gap between what she wants and what she shows. No strategy. No restraint. When the sound comes, the whole animal says yes, in a language everyone on earth can read.

Most of us spend our lives trying to feel that unambiguously about anything.

So watch it. Sound on. Not for the speed, though the speed is the reason this body exists. Watch it for what happens before you've had time to understand what you're looking at.

I won't tell you what that is.

I'll only say that a greyhound spends most of her life asleep, and a good life, for an animal like that, might be measured by what is waiting for her when she wakes.

Sarabi knows exactly what it is.

Go see.

The Captain was warned about the weather and made a bad decision. Stay in school, retard. Its not too late to delete this.
The plane crashed because the 55 year old experienced pilot made a risky and fatal decision. Yes even experienced pilots can make poor decisions. 
There is a captain and a first officer.
The captain makes all final decisions.
He was warned by ATC of the "pretty nasty" weather and "moderate to extreme precipitation" 10 mins prior and made a risky decision for only a slight deviation that turned out to be fatal. 
It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. The captain made a slight deviation because it wasn't serious and they were above the storm until that cell ballooned up from 33000 ft to 48000 ft ceiling in a few minutes and by then it was too late for them to climb out of it.
From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (CAPTAIN’S voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions.

SpaceX

SpaceX in talks to buy Boost Mobile or access its network

The Washington Post reported on November 2 that SpaceX is negotiating with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to the network it leases from AT&T and T-Mobile. Elon Musk reportedly discussed the idea directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen last month after major carriers declined to offer SpaceX a direct MVNO arrangement for Starlink Mobile. The potential deal is unconfirmed by the companies involved and would likely require consent from AT&T and T-Mobile, whose agreements are typically non-transferable; analysts have expressed skepticism that the contracts would simply transfer. EchoStar had roughly 7.4 million wireless subscribers as of mid-2026. Source: @WatcherGuru (citing Washington Post); also reported by The Verge and Reuters

No major new official announcements or high-engagement company posts specifically tied to SpaceXSI branding or core infrastructure appeared in the past 24 hours. Tesla

Robotaxi service expands to Fort Worth with unsupervised rides

Tesla’s official @robotaxi account announced late November 1 that unsupervised Robotaxi rides would open in Fort Worth starting at 6 a.m. local time on November 2. The launch geofence covers roughly 143 square miles centered on downtown and extending toward Saginaw, White Settlement, Benbrook, and nearby areas, making it Tesla’s third-largest unsupervised zone after Austin and Houston. Fort Worth is the seventh city overall with unsupervised rides (joining Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa) and the first new city in about three months. On November 1 Elon Musk replied on X that “the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” confirming the tighter allowances were intentional rather than a glitch. The agent has seen rapid paid-user growth—reports cite roughly 800,000 paid weekly users by late October—but Musk has not published the exact new limits or future pricing changes. Visa Officer: “Why do you want to travel to the United States?”
Applicant: “My elder brother has invited me to attend his wedding. He wants the whole family to be there.”

Visa Officer: “Your brother lives in America?”
Applicant: “Yes. He's been living there for almost fifteen years.”

Visa Officer: “And you've never visited him?”
Applicant: “No, sir. I've never had the opportunity.”

Visa Officer: “What does your brother do?”
Applicant: “He's an engineer. He works for a construction company in Texas.”

Visa Officer: “Who is sponsoring your trip?”
Applicant: “I'm paying for everything myself. I've been saving for this trip for almost two years.”
Visa Officer: “How long do you intend to stay?”
Applicant: “Three weeks. I have a business to return to.”

The officer looked through the applicant's documents before asking another question.
Visa Officer: “Your brother has offered you accommodation at his house?”
Applicant: “Yes, sir.”

Visa Officer: “I noticed something interesting. Your brother's invitation letter says this wedding is particularly important to him. Why?”
The applicant went quiet for a moment.
Applicant: “Because he almost didn't invite me.”
Visa Officer: “What do you mean?”

text:
You wake up on a hot, humid morning, slip into your jeans, and wonder: Do you really need underwear? With the Philippine heat making sweating almost unavoidable, skipping that extra layer sounds tempting.

But is going commando actually healthier?

The answer depends on your clothing, activities, anatomy, and hygiene habits. Neither option is automatically better.

THE CASE FOR UNDERWEAR

Underwear protects sensitive skin from rough fabrics, reducing friction and chafing, especially when wearing jeans or fitted trousers.

It also absorbs some sweat, oils, and bodily discharge, keeping outer garments cleaner.

During exercise, supportive, moisture-wicking underwear can reduce uncomfortable movement and irritation.

However, tight underwear made from poorly breathable fabrics can trap heat and moisture.

For men, some studies associate tighter underwear with higher scrotal temperatures and poorer sperm quality, although evidence of a direct effect on fertility remains inconclusive.

THE CASE FOR GOING COMMANDO

Skipping underwear improves airflow around the groin and may reduce heat and moisture buildup.

This can be particularly comfortable when sleeping or lounging in loose cotton shorts.

For people prone to heat rashes or jock itch, avoiding tight clothing may help reduce irritation.

But going commando also has disadvantages.

Without a protective layer, trouser seams can rub directly against sensitive skin, causing chafing.

Sweat and bodily discharge transfer directly onto clothing, requiring more frequent washing.

And yes, zipper accidents become a greater concern.

WHEN SHOULD YOU WEAR UNDERWEAR?

Underwear is generally preferable when wearing jeans, tight trousers, or rough fabrics.

It is also useful during workouts, particularly when additional support and friction protection are needed.

WHEN SHOULD YOU GO COMMANDO?

Sleeping without underwear is generally fine, especially with loose, breathable sleepwear.

Going commando at home in cotton shorts or a malong may also improve comfort.

However, persistent itching or fungal infections require proper treatment.

THE HEALTHIEST COMPROMISE

Loose cotton boxers offer a practical middle ground, providing airflow while protecting sensitive skin from clothing.

Ultimately, breathable fabrics, proper fit, regular changing, and good hygiene matter more than whether you wear underwear.

Your body does not necessarily need underwear every day. But depending on what you wear over it, your private parts might appreciate the protection.

text:
There are things you don't fully understand the value of until they're gone. Not necessarily because you failed to appreciate them while they were there, but because you didn't know what to do with them. You didn't know how to hold them, how to care for them, or how to keep yourself from destroying something that was good to you.
I learned a great deal from someone who was once part of my life. And perhaps what hurts the most is realizing that I never quite learned how to give back even a fraction of what I was given.
I tried forgetting, replacing, turning everything upside down, convincing myself that life moves forward and eventually everything becomes a memory. And all of that is true. Life does move forward. But some things don't disappear simply because you've decided.
Even now, there are mornings when I wake up and cry. And the strange thing is, I don't entirely know why. I don't need anyone to come back. I don't believe I'm incomplete without them. I genuinely believe the ending was right, perhaps even the best possible outcome for both of us. And yet, there's something that still lives in my chest, something I haven't figured out what to do with.
I was young, and I hated myself. I hated myself enough that I couldn't believe I deserved the good things that happened to me. When someone treated me with tenderness, I became afraid. Afraid of losing it, afraid they'd eventually discover I wasn't the person they thought I was. And at the same time, I was greedy. I wanted certainty, permanence, reassurance. I wanted someone to stay, even when I didn't know how to treat them well enough to make staying something they would want.
It's remarkable how contradictory a person can be. You fear losing someone and behave in ways that push them away. You love someone and hurt them. You desperately want tenderness, yet find yourself rejecting it. None of that is an excuse. Being young, being afraid, hating yourself. These things might explain your behavior, but they don't erase its consequences for other people.
Perhaps the hardest part of regret isn't wishing you could go back and change the past. It's becoming the person you should have been, long after the opportunity to be that person has passed.
And I think that's what I've been experiencing lately.
This past year has changed me in ways I never expected. I have a job now, responsibilities, things I build that other people depend on. I've started putting myself out there more, sharing my work, discussing ideas, allowing myself to be opinionated and occasionally ridiculous. I've become more comfortable with who I am, more positive, and perhaps most importantly, kinder to myself.
I've also discovered that I'm lonely, which is something I never expected to admit. For most of my life, I considered myself someone who could be alone indefinitely. I enjoyed my own company and rarely felt the need for anyone else. But loneliness found its way to me, too. Not as some overwhelming sadness, but as a quiet reminder that no matter how independent you become, you're still human. You still want to be heard, understood, and occasionally share your life with someone.
Something else has changed. I've started noticing people. My family, my colleagues, the small kindnesses that happen throughout an ordinary day. Even goodbyes have started to mean more. When someone leaves your daily life, there's a strange mixture of happiness for them and sadness that they won't be part of your ordinary days anymore.
I've started apologizing more, paying closer attention to my words, trying to understand people before judging them. And every time I apologize, a part of me remembers an apology I never managed to give with the sincerity and understanding it deserved. Not because it would bring anything back, but because I wish I could have offered that much maturity when it mattered.
I used to imagine growing up as some dramatic transformation. That one morning I'd wake up confident, successful, certain of my direction, and completely different from the person I used to be. But change doesn't work that way. From a distance, I still feel like the same person. Yet when I look closely at how I thought a year ago and how I think today, I realize something fundamental has changed.
Sometimes I wonder whether I've actually moved on from the past, or simply learned how to live alongside it. Perhaps moving on means acknowledging that something was beautiful, that you made mistakes, and that it ended, without trying to change any of those truths.
I don't write any of this to present myself as someone who learned his lesson and emerged a better man. I don't even know if I'm better. And I certainly don't want to turn the pain I caused someone else into some beautiful story about my personal development. There was a real person on the other side of my immaturity, someone with feelings and a life beyond whatever role they played in mine. I can appreciate what the experience taught me without pretending its consequences were necessary or deserved.
I think that's something I've finally started to understand. Even regret can become selfish if you're not paying attention. Sometimes we become so absorbed in how terrible we feel about what we've done that we forget the person who actually had to live with it. I don't want my remorse to become another demand for someone's attention, forgiveness, or understanding. They don't owe me any of those things, and that's all right.
For years, whenever I came across an old conversation or a reminder of the past, my instinct was to erase it. Delete it, close the door, and move forward, as though forgetting were a decision I could make rather than something that might happen naturally with time.
Today, for once, I wanted to leave something behind. Not because I expect anything to come from it, and certainly not because I want to reopen an old door. I just wanted to give these thoughts a place outside my head.
I don't have a conclusion, and I guess that's appropriate. I'm still discovering who I am, still making mistakes, still learning how to appreciate the people around me, and still trying to forgive the person I used to be.
Maybe some feelings don't need to be solved. Maybe you can be grateful and heartbroken, believe an ending was right and still mourn it, forgive yourself and still wish you'd never hurt someone.
Maybe growing up is simply learning to carry all of that without letting it stop you from living.
I suppose I just needed somewhere to say what's in my chest, and leave it to the wind.
