text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM
MR PRESIDENT, NIGERIA IS NOT YOUR PERSONAL POSSESSION
An Open Letter to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu
Mr President,

On Sunday you stood inside the Holy Ka'abah and thanked Almighty Allah for the privilege of leading Nigeria. You called that privilege an extraordinary blessing that must be matched with dedicated service.

I do not question your prayers. That is between you and your Creator. I question what you have done with the blessing. The Nigerians you left behind when you flew to Saudi Arabia have every right to ask: where is the service?

I have studied your leadership closely, and the more I study it, the angrier I become. In your approach to power I see the opposite of everything I was raised to respect. I keep asking: what did Nigeria do to deserve this?

When I misbehaved as a boy, my father gave me what his generation called "six of the best", or reprimanded me so firmly that I thought twice before repeating the offence. I resented it then. I understand it now. There is a difference between right and wrong, and a man is responsible for knowing it. Cleverness does not excuse dishonesty. Success does not erase misconduct. Money can buy comfort and influence, but it cannot buy a conscience.

Mr President, where is that discipline in your public life? Where is the restraint? Where is the willingness to accept responsibility? Where is the recognition that other people's suffering matters more than your political survival?

I will not explain your character through a childhood I did not witness, and I reject the lie that poverty makes people dishonest. Millions of poor Nigerians live honourably under pressures that powerful men could not endure for a week. It is your conduct in power that I challenge. So let us talk about your record.

THE ARITHMETIC OF SUFFERING
The World Bank says 63 per cent of Nigerians were living in poverty in 2025. That is about 140 million people. Your officials celebrated when inflation fell from 34.8 per cent to about 15 per cent. Poverty rose anyway. Prices rising more slowly does not mean prices have fallen. A mother cannot feed her children with a percentage. She cannot feed them with your reputation as a strategist either.

An unemployed graduate cannot build a future from another speech praising your political machinery. A pensioner cannot buy medicine with the applause of your supporters. Nigerians are told, again and again, to be patient. Patient for what? Patient for whom?

THE DEBT YOU ARE SIGNING IN OUR NAMES
When you took office, Nigeria's public debt stood at about 87 trillion naira. By June this year it was nearly 167 trillion. You have almost doubled it in three years. Last year alone about 16 trillion naira went on servicing debt. That is money that did not go to hospitals, schools or roads.

And on 27 October, with fewer than 110 days to the election, you asked the Senate for another 20.5 billion dollars and over a billion euros. Who will repay it? Not you. Not your family. The child in Kano who has never seen a functioning classroom will repay it. Nigeria is not a credit card for one man's ambition.

THE DEAD WHO DESERVED BETTER
Amnesty International counted at least 10,217 Nigerians killed in your first two years, more than 6,800 of them in Benue alone. On a single day in February this year, gunmen killed over 200 people in Kwara and Katsina. Last week, at least 62 more were killed in the northeast.

These are not statistics. They were farmers, children, wives, grandfathers. Every one of them was promised security by a man who campaigned on his competence. What has that competence delivered to the graves of Benue and Zamfara?

THE PRESIDENT WHO IS NOT THERE
By May this year you had made 51 foreign trips and spent about 261 days outside Nigeria. Records compiled by GovSpend show the Presidency spent more than 37 billion naira on travel in under three years. Campaigning for the presidency opened on 19 August. Eleven days later you left for a three-week leave in London and Paris. Now you have gone to Saudi Arabia.

Nigeria needs a president who is present. A captain who keeps leaving the ship cannot complain when the passengers stop trusting him.

THE PROTESTERS YOU SILENCED
In August 2024, young Nigerians marched against hunger. Amnesty International says police killed at least 24 of them, including children, and detained more than 1,200. The police denied it. A year later, Amnesty reported that not one victim had received justice.

Journalists are still being detained under the Cybercrimes Act. Your own Vice-President claimed that no journalist has been harassed since you took office. The Committee to Protect Journalists has documented case after case proving otherwise.

And this very week, police in Kaduna arrested a supporter of Nasir El-Rufai after he posted images of low turnout at your rally. Is that what Nigeria has become? Arrested for photographing empty chairs?
You cannot arrest a country into loving you. You cannot intimidate citizens into believing their lives have improved. Fear may produce silence. It cannot produce legitimacy. Today, young people in Zamfara blocked a major road shouting "Tinubu Must Go." You should listen to them, not send men with guns after them.

RIVERS STATE IS NOT A PLAYTHING
In March 2025 you suspended an elected governor, his deputy and an entire House of Assembly. You handed the state to a retired admiral for six months. No elected state government had been removed like that since 1962. Nyesom Wike later said openly that he had wanted the governor impeached.

My father helped to build Rivers State. Its people did not vote for a sole administrator. They voted for a government, and you took it away from them.

YOUR CIRCLE IS NOT ABOVE THE LAW
Your wife and your son must understand that public influence brings public scrutiny. The First Lady holds no elected office, yet she tours the country promising "fresh empowerment" in exchange for votes. With whose money? Records published by Daily Trust show more than half a million dollars in foreign exchange released for her foreign trips in 2023 and 2024. 

Nigerians have every right to question access, influence and the line between family interests and government business. Being related to the president does not place anyone above accountability.

And Nyesom Wike, especially Wike, must understand that power does not cancel the obligation to answer for one's record. The same applies to David Umahi and every other influential member of your circle. Where credible evidence of wrongdoing exists, let independent investigators examine it. Where charges are justified, let prosecutors bring them. Let courts decide guilt. I want accountability strong enough to reach powerful people, including those who believe their usefulness to you will protect them forever.

THE CHICAGO FILES
In 1993, a United States court ordered the forfeiture of 460,000 dollars in a civil case connected to accounts linked to you. In April 2025, Judge Beryl Howell found that the FBI and DEA had officially confirmed investigations of you relating to a drug trafficking ring, and ordered them to process the records. Your lawyers have since fought to keep the redactions in place.

On 30 October, the judge rejected some of Aaron Greenspan's requests, and your spokesman celebrated on social media. But the case is not over.

Your Presidency says the files contain nothing new. Then release them. If there is nothing to hide, stop hiding it. Every month you spend fighting transparency in a Washington courtroom tells Nigerians more than any document could.

THE SECURITY SERVICES BELONG TO NIGERIA
The DSS, the police and the armed forces must understand their duty. They serve Nigeria and the law, not a man. They must never become instruments for keeping anyone in office against the freely expressed will of the people.

History should give you pause. Samuel Doe's Liberia and Mobutu's Zaire are grim warnings about personal rule, repression and the belief that a ruler's survival matters more than his country's future. Those histories ended in suffering that Nigeria must never repeat.

I want no such catastrophe. I want peaceful change, constitutional government and the protection of every human life, including yours and your family's. So I say plainly: do not let your ambition, or the ambition of those around you, endanger Nigeria's peace.

Nigerians vote on 16 January 2027. Do not permit anyone to rig that election in your name. Do not let state institutions be turned against lawful opposition. Tell your supporters there is no justification for intimidation or violence.

If Nigerians vote you out, pack your bags and leave peacefully. There is dignity in accepting the people's judgment. There is none in making a nation suffer because a leader cannot imagine life outside office.

YOUR HEALTH AND YOUR DUTY
I will not diagnose your health from photographs, speculate about medication, or pretend to know the purpose of a journey abroad. My question is simpler. Can you carry the full weight of this office every day? Nigerians deserve the truth about anything that affects your ability to govern. When you leave the country, transmit the Section 145 letter, as the Constitution requires. Your welfare matters. So does the country's. Neither should be hidden behind political theatre.

THE KIO SOLUTION: FIVE DEMANDS
One. Publish your Code of Conduct asset declaration, and require every minister and adviser to publish theirs.
Two. Instruct your lawyers to stop opposing the release of the FBI and DEA records, and ask the United States government to release them in full.

Three. No new foreign loans before the 16 January election without an independent public audit of every loan taken since May 2023.

Four. Set up an independent judicial inquiry into the August 2024 protest killings. Free everyone detained for speech, and end the use of the Cybercrimes Act against journalists and critics.

Five. Commit in writing to accept the result of the election. Order the DSS, police and military to remain strictly neutral.

A NOTE ON FAIRNESS
The 1993 Chicago matter was a civil forfeiture, not a criminal conviction, and President Tinubu has never been charged with a crime in the United States. The Presidency denies wrongdoing and says the records contain nothing new. Allegations referred to in this letter are allegations, not findings of guilt. Everyone named is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

My father spent heavily on my education because he expected me to do something useful with my life. It took me a long time to wake up to the full weight of that responsibility. I can assure you that I am now wide awake.

I have made mistakes. I have wasted opportunities. I claim no perfection. But I know that a life devoted only to money, influence and personal advancement leaves something essential undone. We owe something to our neighbours and to those less fortunate than ourselves. Those entrusted with public power owe more still. That is why I write, and why I will keep writing.

Mr President, your leadership is doing grave damage to public trust. Repairing it will take far more than speeches, loyal crowds and prayers abroad. It will take accountability that reaches your own circle, and humility that begins with you.

Listen to the people who have nothing to gain by flattering you. Fear the adviser who never disagrees with you. Answer the people. Respect them. Accept their right to reject you.

You have had your chance to exercise power. You have no right to demand that Nigeria surrender its future to preserve it.

This is nothing personal. It is politics.

Nigeria belongs to Nigerians.

Sincerely yours,
Kio Amachree�
President, Worldview International�Stockholm, Sweden

text:
Oh I would say those Israelites had more than second chances.  Don’t be disingenuous:

At the Red Sea (Exodus 14:10–12). With Pharaoh's army closing in, they turned on Moses: "Were there no graves in Egypt?" They said it would have been better to stay slaves than die in the desert.

Bitter water at Marah (15:22–24). After three days without water they found only bitter water and grumbled, "What shall we drink?" God made it sweet.

No food in the Wilderness of Sin (16:2–3). The whole community longed for Egypt's "pots of meat" and bread, and accused Moses and Aaron of bringing them out to starve. God sent quail and manna.

Breaking the manna rules (16:19–20, 27–28). Some kept manna overnight against instructions, and it bred worms. Others went out to gather on the Sabbath when told not to. God asked, "How long will you refuse to keep my commands?"

No water at Rephidim (17:1–7). They quarreled with Moses so fiercely he feared they would stone him. They tested God by asking, "Is the Lord among us or not?" Water came from the rock, and the place was named Massah ("testing") and Meribah ("quarreling").

Fear at Sinai (20:18–21). At the thunder and smoke of the mountain, they stood at a distance and asked Moses to speak to them instead of God. This was fear more than open rebellion, but it showed they kept God at arm's length.

And finally -
The golden calf (Exodus 32). While Moses was on the mountain for 40 days, they lost patience and told Aaron, "Make us gods." They worshiped a calf made from their gold earrings, offered sacrifices, and "rose up to play." All of this came just weeks after promising, "All that the Lord has spoken we will do" (24:3, 7).

The same pattern runs through all of these. They forgot past deliverance at each new hardship, longed for Egypt, blamed Moses, and tested God. That's why later passages like Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3 point back to this stretch as a warning.

It wasn’t murder, it was God’s righteous judgement.  Don’t like it, start your own universe and creation, and you can make the rules.  Otherwise, I would heed the warnings read in His inspired word and be careful when questioning His righteousness.  

Asking questions is one thing, asking attempted indicting God questions is quite another.

P.S. there are some terrible replies to your post. Goal post movers when absolutely none is needed.  They should read more and respond with their erroneous “takes” less.

text:
For those who prefer reading to watching, here’s a written version of my comments on @RT_com about Syria’s potential entry into the Mecca Pact, its implications for Israel and Iran, Turkey's role, and the complexities surrounding NATO’s collective-defense commitments:
There is still considerable ambiguity surrounding Syria’s potential entry into the Mecca Pact. We do not know whether the existing members invited Syria or whether Damascus itself expressed an interest in joining. Personally, I do not think any formal invitations have been issued yet.

Many mistakenly regard Syria as a Turkish vassal. However, Ankara has two main objectives. First, to keep Syria united, with strong law enforcement institutions, while protecting it against potential external aggressors, not only Israel, but also ISIS and Iranian militia networks. The Mecca Pact could be a useful mechanism for achieving these objectives.

Second, Turkey wants to reintegrate Syria into the regional system. Syria has been fragmented for more than a decade. Instead of functioning as an important component of the regional security network, it was consumed by civil war and remained largely absent from regional diplomacy. Ankara now seeks to bring Syria back into this network and perhaps revive the famous saying: “There can be no war in the Middle East without Egypt, and no peace in the Middle East without Syria.”

This also explains the Syrian foreign minister’s emphasis on the interconnected nature of regional security. Any power vacuum in the Middle East inevitably affects other countries. A security gap in Anbar or along the Abu Kamal–Deir ez-Zor line could quickly facilitate the resurgence of ISIS. Similarly, the collapse of Iran and its possible ethnic fragmentation could open Pandora’s box, triggering interethnic conflicts that spill across borders and draw numerous regional states into the turmoil.

This is not quite the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe, where regime preservation and stabilization were paramount. Nevertheless, contemporary Middle Eastern states increasingly prioritize stability above almost everything else, even when this means tolerating or contributing to oppressive domestic regimes.

For Syria, joining the Mecca Pact could offer several advantages. It would align with Ahmed al-Sharaa’s efforts to reestablish Syria as a regional actor. On its own, Damascus has very limited leverage against Israel. As part of a regional organization, however, it could exercise considerably greater political influence.

Membership would also help Syria distance itself from the Iranian axis and avoid relying on Hezbollah or Hamas if retaliation against Israel became necessary. In a broader historical sense, this would represent Syria’s return to its traditional Sunni Arab alliance network, which existed before Iran established its so-called Shiite Crescent.

There are also military and institutional benefits. Syria currently depends heavily on Turkish training and support, but membership could diversify that assistance by combining Saudi resources, Turkish military experience and defense industry capabilities, and Pakistan’s military capacity.

Such cooperation could also help suppress potential rebel groups during the difficult process of integrating Syria’s fragmented armed factions into a unified national army, replacing the existing landscape of small chieftains and warlords with a single military structure.

But what could Syria offer the other members? Syria is still recovering from the devastation of its civil war, and the reorganization of its armed forces is progressing slowly. Nevertheless, yesterday’s rebel commanders and fighters are today’s experienced officers and soldiers. They are battle-hardened, and that experience represents a significant military asset.

While other members might hesitate to risk their own soldiers in ground operations, Syrian units could potentially undertake such missions. This could even draw Syria into Yemen. Yet such a development might be turned into an advantage. Non-Syrian former rebels who helped Sharaa to topple Assad find themselves with very limited room to maneuver. They are not Syrian citizens, despite having made substantial contributions to the victory. These battle-hardened fighters could be deployed to Yemen, where their combat experience could be useful while their numbers could gradually be reduced.

Egypt’s exclusion from the Mecca Pact is another important issue. Tom Barrack has pointed to Egypt’s existing peace treaty with Israel and its security agreement with Greece. However, Egypt’s absence is also understandable in light of the longstanding geographical rivalry between the civilizations of Anatolia and the Nile Valley. The Turkey–Egypt rivalry is frequently underestimated, despite having deep historical, economic, and geopolitical foundations.

As for the pact itself, Israel is indeed one of its principal concerns. A major purpose is to deter Israeli military attacks. Syrian Foreign Minister al-Shaibani has complained about more than 1,000 Israeli attacks over two years. Article 2 covers “an externally originating armed attack” against any member. Israeli strikes on Syrian territory would fall within this description. This is precisely why Syria would be interested in such a provision and why Syrian membership would put the agreement to a serious test.

However, the pact is not directed exclusively against Israel. Iran is another major consideration. The participating countries generally regard Iranian regional involvement and its network of proxies as major causes of the Middle East’s current security problems. Consequently, they are also attempting to construct a barrier against Iranian influence, even if they avoid explicitly identifying Tehran as a target.

There is, nevertheless, a fundamental contradiction regarding Israel. Al-Sharaa has consistently attempted to reduce tensions with Israel. Yet once Syria becomes part of the Mecca Pact, maintaining this restrained approach could become considerably more difficult.

The agreement does contain important limitations. Assistance is based on “an objective assessment of the assistance required” and remains “within the limits of their available resources.” Each member ultimately determines what these provisions mean in practice. Nevertheless, participation in such an alliance creates potentially serious complications for the other signatories.

Israel is only about 20 kilometers from Damascus. Under a broad interpretation of collective defense, even a single bullet fired across the border could technically trigger expectations of retaliation from the other members, potentially transforming a limited confrontation into a regional war.

Turkey's NATO membership makes the situation even more complicated and raises the same questions of overlapping military commitments that have been invoked regarding Egypt. Consider a scenario in which Syria joins the Mecca Pact and is attacked by Israel. Turkey intervenes to defend Syria, and Israel retaliates by striking Turkish forces on Turkish territory.

In that situation, NATO’s collective-defense obligations could become relevant. Other NATO members would face the prospect of defending Turkey in a conflict in which they had not originally participated. The obvious question is whether the United States and European NATO members would defend Turkey against Israeli attacks or even find themselves drawn into a direct confrontation with Israel.

This is precisely where the distinction between diplomatic deterrence and actual military commitments becomes critical. None of this necessarily means that the Mecca Pact is a stillborn alliance. However, its formation appears to have been excessively rushed, with numerous possible scenarios and contradictions either overlooked or left deliberately unresolved.

Alternatively, the pact may have been conceived primarily as an instrument of diplomatic deterrence rather than as a fully operational military alliance. That distinction will ultimately determine whether the Mecca Pact becomes a meaningful regional security architecture or remains a political declaration whose collective-defense commitments are far more difficult to implement than to announce.

text:
RUSSIA AFTER UKRAINE: HOW LONG TO REBUILD?

Russia has recovered from military defeats before. But history offers no guarantee of a quick recovery from this war.

The human cost is already enormous. By 23 October 2026, Mediazona and BBC Russian had identified approximately 283,000 Russian military dead by name, including more than 7,900 officers. These are documented minimums; the full toll is higher. (https://t.co/BN8RvGosxr)

A separate statistical study by Meduza and Mediazona estimated approximately 352,000 Russian military deaths through the end of 2025. This estimate and the named list use different methods and reference dates; they must not be added together. (https://t.co/0lOM4ftivv)

Recruiting replacements is only one part of rebuilding an army.

Experienced officers, trained specialists and cohesive formations take years to develop. The US Congressional Research Service reports that replacement recruits receive less training than the personnel they replace. Russia’s defence industry also faces shortages of components, manufacturing equipment and workers, even as military production has expanded. (https://t.co/NCxC49xXEd)

There is no single recovery clock. Ammunition stocks, combat units, command structures and industrial capacity recover at different speeds. Some capabilities can expand while others remain depleted.

Demographic pressures make that burden heavier. They do not establish that another major war is impossible.

European warnings therefore deserve serious attention. Danish defence intelligence assesses that an end or freeze to the fighting could release substantial Russian resources for military expansion. The danger also depends on Western rearmament, NATO cohesion and US involvement. (https://t.co/Vhw4AmfSbO)

My assessment: rebuilding an effective, balanced military would take years, with lasting consequences from lost experience and industrial constraints. But Russia could regain enough capability for another attack before that process is complete.

Ukraine has imposed costs Moscow will carry long after the fighting ends.

Europe must use the time Ukraine has bought to strengthen its defences. Russian exhaustion alone cannot guarantee lasting security.

The pig was never banned for the worm. The worm was found in London in 1835. Sit on the throne of a small kingdom in the hills of the Near East around 900 BC and you will find the pig was banned for something you could see from the palace roof.

Your treasury is counted in sheep. The temple's ledgers count them by the ten thousand, and every one of them is a tax you can see walking. A sheep grows a fleece you shear every spring. A sheep gives milk, a sheep gives a lamb, and a sheep goes where the shepherd drives it, in a flock, to the altar, to the army, to the tithe barn, over the hills to the market you own. A sheep needs pasture, and pasture has an owner, and the owner answers to you.

The cow is better still. The ox pulls the plough that grows the grain you tax. The cow gives milk every day and a calf every year, and a bull on the altar is the prestige of the house that offered it. Cattle need land, wide land, the kind only a great house holds, so a man with cattle is a man with a landlord, and his landlord has you.

And then there is the thing in the yard behind every hovel in your kingdom.

It has no wool. It gives no milk you would drink. It will not pull anything. You cannot drive it to the temple in a flock, because it will not be driven, and nobody in your army wants to march to war behind it. It needs no pasture at all. It lives on the household's peelings, the acorns in the wood, the waste behind the house, and it turns the lot into fat. A sow throws ten piglets, twice a year, and they are bacon in six months. A family with a pig behind the house has meat and lard through the winter and has asked nothing of you, your priests, your pasture or your landlords to get it.

That is the problem. The pig is a democratic animal. It is the one source of meat in your kingdom that the ledger cannot see, and a man who can feed himself can afford to be rude.

So you want it gone, and you cannot simply take it, because there are thousands of them and they are in every yard. You need the people to give it up themselves, gladly, and look down on the neighbours who do not.

Which brings you to the second thing you can see from the roof. Down on the coast are the Philistines, the richer people, the ones with the iron and the ports, and they eat pork like Greeks. Their rubbish is a fifth pig bone. Yours is almost none. You did not plan that; the hills were always sheep and goat country. But it is a gift, because the easiest way to make a people is to tell them what they do not eat. Draw the line at the pig and every man in your hills is on your side of it and every man on the coast is on the other. Identity is cheaper than a garrison and it never mutinies.

You still need a reason, because people like a reason. Do not say the pig makes a poor man independent. Say it is unclean. Say the god finds it filthy. Do not explain why the cow, which stands in its own dung and carries a tapeworm of its own, is clean; nobody will ask, because the cow belongs to their betters and they already know better things are cleaner. Write it into the law with the hoof and the cud so it sounds like zoology. Your priests will enforce it for free, because it enlarges them, and in three generations nobody will remember it was ever a decision.

That is how the thing is done, and it was done again and again. In Egypt the swineherds were the one class in the country barred from every temple, and the workmen's villages behind the great building sites are knee-deep in pig bone, because the ledger never fed the men who cut the stone and the pig did. Every state that wanted its people dependent has found the same animal in the same yard and reached the same verdict.

The reason the modern reader has been given is the worm. Trichinella was first seen by a medical student with a microscope at St Bartholomew's Hospital in 1835, two and a half thousand years after the law was written. It is killed by cooking. Beef carries its own worm and was never banned. Goat carries brucellosis and sat on every altar. The hygiene story is a Victorian explanation bolted onto a Bronze Age tax policy, and it has lasted because it is flattering: it makes the ancient lawgiver a sanitary inspector rather than a man who had counted the sheep and could not count the pigs.

From the roof it was never about what the pig carried. It was about what the pig gave, to whom, without asking you first.

text:
I think the problem with Rice and Bruno playing together is that they offer almost the same qualities in certain phases of the game. When we are looking to attack, both of them can be effective because they are progressive players, they like to move the ball forward, take risks and get the team into attacking positions. But football is not always about attacking. There are moments when the opposition presses aggressively, closes down spaces and forces you to play under pressure. That is where I think the partnership starts to struggle.

When teams press us, we need midfielders who can stay calm, receive the ball in tight spaces, turn under pressure, retain possession and give us an alternative way of progressing the ball. Unfortunately, I don't think Rice and Bruno offer enough variety in that department when they play together. They can both be effective going forward, but when the game becomes about controlling possession, resisting pressure and dictating the tempo, we sometimes lack that midfielder who can slow things down, take responsibility for the ball and connect the different phases of play.

That is exactly where Myles Lewis-Skelly comes in. MLS is a different profile of player compared to Bruno. He brings something different to the midfield. He is comfortable receiving the ball in tight areas, has the composure to play through pressure, can carry the ball into spaces and, most importantly, gives us another option when the opposition tries to suffocate our midfield. He doesn't necessarily have to do what Bruno does; that's the whole point. We need different profiles in midfield, not three players trying to influence the game in similar ways.

His introduction against Liverpool showed how important that balance can be. It wasn't just about making a substitution; it was about bringing in a player who could help us establish control, retain possession and give the midfield a different dimension. Sometimes, what a team needs isn't another player who wants to force the game forward, but someone who knows when to hold the ball, when to turn, when to carry it and when to release it.

For me, the issue isn't that Rice or Bruno are bad players. They are both quality footballers, and there are games where playing them together makes perfect sense. But we cannot expect that combination to solve every midfield problem, especially against teams that press aggressively. We need balance, composure and variety. MLS offers a different solution, and that's why keeping him was so important. I would hate to see us develop a player with those qualities only for him to end up at Manchester United or Chelsea because we failed to recognise what he brings to our midfield.

Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 driver, Arvid Lindblad, is celebrating Diwali - the “Festival of Lights” - by unveiling a special Indian-inspired helmet ahead of the São Paulo Grand Prix, with the festival falling on race day, Sunday, November 8.

Diwali, India’s most significant and widely celebrated festival, holds a special place in Arvid’s life, having celebrated it with his maternal grandparents, Nani and Nana, from a young age. The celebration symbolises hope, joy, triumph and the victory of light over darkness, with homes and communities traditionally illuminated by lamps, diyas and candles. The helmet offers a personal celebration of Arvid’s Indian heritage while bringing his family’s traditions to the Formula One stage.

Arvid played a key role in shaping the design; combining contemporary elements with references to Diwali, his Punjabi heritage and the experiences that have shaped his journey. The result is a creative, modern and deeply personal expression of his Indian roots and his belief in having the power to shape your own path.

The helmet design draws inspiration from the rangoli patterns Arvid has created over the past few years, including one he made during last year’s Diwali. The intricate pattern on top of the helmet forms the foundation of the overall design, with elements flowing down the sides to build on the same visual theme.

Subtly integrated into the design is one of the most recognisable symbols of Diwali, the diya, representing light, hope and joy. At the front and rear of the helmet, the design comes to life with two further elements closely associated with the festival: the lotus and traditional fireworks. The lotus symbolises purity, resilience and the ability to rise above adversity. This resonates with Arvid's belief that your circumstances do not define you and that, through determination and hard work, you have the power to shape your own path. The fireworks reflect celebrations enjoyed by families around the world and Arvid’s family memories of lighting diyas together with his Nana.

The base of the helmet is a Phulkari-inspired pattern, a tribute to Arvid’s Nani and her Punjabi heritage.

 Visa Cash App Racing Bulls is supporting Arvid’s initiative to celebrate Diwali by bringing the spirit of the Festival of Lights to his side of the garage during the São Paulo GP. A dedicated “Happy Diwali” sticker will feature on the halo of Arvid’s car, while the garage floor will feature an intricate rangoli pattern alongside a lotus flower and diya positioned above his surname. The garage panels behind the car will also carry complementary rangoli-inspired designs, creating a visual connection between the helmet and the wider garage environment.

Arvid Lindblad, Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Driver, said: “Celebrating Diwali with my family, especially my Nani and Nana, has always been a very important part of my upbringing. Bringing this special helmet to life is a meaningful moment, as it celebrates my Indian heritage and family roots that are such an important part of who I am. I was really involved in the creative process because I wanted to create something that felt cool, while staying true to the meaning and traditions of Diwali. The design brings together elements like rangoli, the lotus flower, diyas and fireworks in a way that feels personal to me. I can’t wait to get back in the car in Brazil wearing this helmet. I know it will be an emotional moment, and I hope the helmet helps share the spirit of Diwali with people celebrating around the world. Happy Diwali.”

“Then Peter said, ‘Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.’” — Acts 3:6

Sunrise through Mesa Arch, Canyonlands National Park, Utah.

One afternoon Peter and John were heading up to the temple for prayer. At the gate called Beautiful sat a man who had been unable to walk since the day he was born. Every day someone carried him there so he could ask passersby for a few coins. When he saw the two friends coming, he held out his hand and hoped for a little money.

Peter stopped, looked him in the eye, and offered something far greater than coins. He spoke the name of Jesus, took the man by the right hand, and helped him up. Strength flooded into his feet and ankles. He sprang up, stood, and walked, then went into the temple courts with them, walking and leaping and praising God, while the whole crowd stared in wonder.

Some days we feel like we have little to offer. Our wallets are thin, our energy is low, and the needs around us look bigger than our resources. But Peter shows us that the best gifts are rarely about silver or gold. A kind word, a steady hand, a prayer, or simply seeing someone others walk past can open a door to grace.

Like the morning sun pouring through the stone frame of Mesa Arch, hope has a way of shining through the gateways where we least expect it. Whatever you carry today, give it freely. A small kindness offered in His name can help someone stand up and walk into a brighter morning.

Religion has been an integral part of human existence almost since the dawn of consciousness. It has shaped societies, inspired art and architecture, motivated philosophical inquiry, triggered conflicts, and comforted billions through life’s uncertainties. This article offers a high-level overview of how religion has evolved across time and geography.

📜 Prehistoric and Ancient Roots
In prehistoric times, humans likely practiced animism and ancestor worship, seeing spirits in nature and venerating those who came before. The earliest archaeological evidence—such as burial rituals, cave paintings, and figurines—suggests ritualistic behavior as far back as 40,000 years ago.

By the Bronze and Iron Ages (circa 3000 BCE onward), organized polytheistic systems emerged in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, and China. These traditions included pantheons of gods, mythologies, temple worship, and priestly classes.

✡️ Birth of Major Monotheisms
Around the first millennium BCE, a shift toward ethical monotheism appears in the world’s spiritual narrative:

Judaism: One of the earliest religions to emphasize a single, universal God, Judaism consolidated during exile periods in Israel and Babylon.
Zoroastrianism: In ancient Persia, Zoroaster preached a dualistic cosmology (Ahura Mazda vs. Angra Mainyu) and an ethical path toward truth and righteousness.
Hinduism and Upanishads: In Vedic India, religious thought began evolving into more philosophically rich traditions, spawning ideas of Brahman (cosmic principle) and Atman (self).
Buddhism & Jainism: Reacting to ritualism, reform movements in India like Jainism and Buddhism emphasized nonviolence, meditation, and liberation from suffering (nirvana or moksha).
✝️ The Spread of Christianity & Islam
Christianity, emerging in the 1st century CE from Jewish tradition, became a dominant force in the Roman Empire and beyond through missionary activity, councils, and state patronage. Over time it fractured into multiple branches (Catholicism, Orthodoxy, Protestantism).

Islam, founded in the 7th century CE by the Prophet Muhammad, introduced a direct, scriptural monotheism with the Qur’an as the revealed text. It expanded rapidly across the Arabian Peninsula, North Africa, Iberia, Persia, South Asia, and beyond, blending universalism with vernacular cultures.

🌍 Religion in Late Antiquity & the Middle Ages
During the Middle Ages, religion was deeply entwined with governance, education, and social order. In Europe, the Catholic Church controlled moral, legal, and intellectual life. In the Islamic Golden Age, scholars flourished in science, philosophy, and theology under faith-based patronage. In Asia, Buddhist, Hindu, Confucian, and Taoist traditions coexisted, competed, and syncretized.

⚖️ Reformation, Enlightenment & Modernity
The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century challenged Catholic doctrine, ushering in new Christian denominations and ideas of individual conscience and religious freedom. During the Enlightenment, thinkers like Voltaire, Kant, and Hume critiqued religion, advocating reason, skepticism, and secular governance.

The 19th and 20th centuries saw the rise of secularism, scientific materialism, and new movements such as modernism, liberal theology, and nonreligious philosophies (e.g., existentialism, humanism). At the same time, religion remained powerful in global politics, identity, and resistance movements.

🧩 Contemporary Landscape & Challenges
Today, religion is as diverse as ever — with Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, new religious movements, Indigenous faiths, and nonreligious identities (agnostic, atheist) coexisting. Globalization, digital media, migration, and scientific advance create both opportunity and tension.

Key modern challenges include secularization, interfaith dialogue, extremism, religious pluralism, and the role of faith in public life — especially in an age of increasing polarization.

From ritual fires of ancient tribes to digital apps of modern believers, religion’s story is woven into humanity’s story. Understanding our spiritual heritage helps us navigate the future with insight, empathy, and critical reflection.

The History of Religion: From Early Rituals to Global FaithsReligion has shaped human societies for tens of thousands of years, influencing art, law, philosophy, politics, and personal meaning. It has united communities, justified power, sparked conflict, and offered explanations for life, death, and the natural world. This overview traces major developments from prehistoric practices to the present, noting where evidence is limited or interpretations debated.Prehistoric and Early Practices

Archaeological traces suggest ritual behavior long before writing. Intentional burials, red ochre, and grave goods appear in some Neanderthal and early Homo sapiens sites (tens to hundreds of thousands of years ago), though whether these indicate belief in an afterlife remains uncertain. Upper Paleolithic cave paintings, figurines (such as the Venus figures), and portable art from roughly 40,000 years ago onward are often interpreted as linked to ritual or symbolic systems, possibly involving animals, fertility, or ancestors. Animism—the idea that spirits inhabit animals, plants, landscapes, and objects—and ancestor veneration are widely inferred for hunter-gatherer groups from ethnographic parallels, but direct evidence is sparse. Monumental sites like Göbekli Tepe (southeastern Turkey, ~9600–8000 BCE) show organized construction and possible ritual activity before widespread farming, challenging older assumptions that complex religion required settled agriculture.Ancient Civilizations and Polytheism

Around the first millennium BCE, a shift toward ethical monotheism appears in the world’s spiritual narrative:

Judaism: One of the earliest religions to emphasize a single, universal God, Judaism consolidated during exile periods in Israel and Babylon.
Zoroastrianism: In ancient Persia, Zoroaster preached a dualistic cosmology (Ahura Mazda vs. Angra Mainyu) and an ethical path toward truth and righteousness.
Hinduism and Upanishads: In Vedic India, religious thought began evolving into more philosophically rich traditions, spawning ideas of Brahman (cosmic principle) and Atman (self).
Buddhism & Jainism: Reacting to ritualism, reform movements in India like Jainism and Buddhism emphasized nonviolence, meditation, and liberation from suffering (nirvana or moksha).
✝️ The Spread of Christianity & Islam
Christianity, emerging in the 1st century CE from Jewish tradition, became a dominant force in the Roman Empire and beyond through missionary activity, councils, and state patronage. Over time it fractured into multiple branches (Catholicism, Orthodoxy, Protestantism).

Islam, founded in the 7th century CE by the Prophet Muhammad, introduced a direct, scriptural monotheism with the Qur’an as the revealed text. It expanded rapidly across the Arabian Peninsula, North Africa, Iberia, Persia, South Asia, and beyond, blending universalism with vernacular cultures.

🌍 Religion in Late Antiquity & the Middle Ages
During the Middle Ages, religion was deeply entwined with governance, education, and social order. In Europe, the Catholic Church controlled moral, legal, and intellectual life. In the Islamic Golden Age, scholars flourished in science, philosophy, and theology under faith-based patronage. In Asia, Buddhist, Hindu, Confucian, and Taoist traditions coexisted, competed, and syncretized.

⚖️ Reformation, Enlightenment & Modernity
The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century challenged Catholic doctrine, ushering in new Christian denominations and ideas of individual conscience and religious freedom. During the Enlightenment, thinkers like Voltaire, Kant, and Hume critiqued religion, advocating reason, skepticism, and secular governance.

The 19th and 20th centuries saw the rise of secularism, scientific materialism, and new movements such as modernism, liberal theology, and nonreligious philosophies (e.g., existentialism, humanism). At the same time, religion remained powerful in global politics, identity, and resistance movements.

🧩 Contemporary Landscape & Challenges
Today, religion is as diverse as ever — with Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, new religious movements, Indigenous faiths, and nonreligious identities (agnostic, atheist) coexisting. Globalization, digital media, migration, and scientific advance create both opportunity and tension.

Key modern challenges include secularization, interfaith dialogue, extremism, religious pluralism, and the role of faith in public life — especially in an age of increasing polarization.

From ritual fires of ancient tribes to digital apps of modern believers, religion’s story is woven into humanity’s story. Understanding our spiritual heritage helps us navigate the future with insight, empathy, and critical reflection.

The History of Religion: From Early Rituals to Global FaithsReligion has shaped human societies for tens of thousands of years, influencing art, law, philosophy, politics, and personal meaning. It has united communities, justified power, sparked conflict, and offered explanations for life, death, and the natural world. This overview traces major developments from prehistoric practices to the present, noting where evidence is limited or interpretations debated.Prehistoric and Early Practices

Archaeological traces suggest ritual behavior long before writing. Intentional burials, red ochre, and grave goods appear in some Neanderthal and early Homo sapiens sites (tens to hundreds of thousands of years ago), though whether these indicate belief in an afterlife remains uncertain. Upper Paleolithic cave paintings, figurines (such as the Venus figures), and portable art from roughly 40,000 years ago onward are often interpreted as linked to ritual or symbolic systems, possibly involving animals, fertility, or ancestors. Animism—the idea that spirits inhabit animals, plants, landscapes, and objects—and ancestor veneration are widely inferred for hunter-gatherer groups from ethnographic parallels, but direct evidence is sparse. Monumental sites like Göbekli Tepe (southeastern Turkey, ~9600–8000 BCE) show organized construction and possible ritual activity before widespread farming, challenging older assumptions that complex religion required settled agriculture.Ancient Civilizations and Polytheism

#SinonDiary

https://t.co/G3dbb9k8xc

When I turned on the stream, Sinny was munching on something.  
So right as it started, I asked if it was an apple, and I nailed it, lol.  

But it wasn't just any apple—she said it was a yellow golden apple.  
At first, I thought it was some kind of metaphor, but holy cow, it actually exists.  
I'm pretty sure I've only seen that in Greek mythology.  
Was it selectively bred or something?  

Anyway, every time I watch Sinny's stream, I feel like I learn all sorts of things about food.  
Oh, and dirty jokes too.  

Anyway, while saying that, she hilariously explained that she stole the apple from her aunt's place, lol.  
Her aunt gets her side dishes, plates, and all kinds of daily necessities.  
If it weren't for her aunt, I honestly think life would be tough for her.  
She really feels like a second mother.

After that, as always, she went into all kinds of zatsu.  
Things like how she sleeps diagonally,  
or how she uses six pillows, but only has five if you include the tomato-shaped cushion, and so on.

Oh, and lol,  
she started the stream earlier than scheduled today, and the reason was, lol,  
she was too lazy to answer her DMs, so she wanted to use streaming as an excuse, lol.  

Dang it, Sinny is always using us like this  
(though to be honest, I'm actually happy about it).  

What's even crazier is that Panko senpai did the exact same thing before, lol.  
The Phase girls are truly unstoppable, lol.

Then she introduced a stomach medicine called Pepto-Bismol,  
but wait, why is the volume a massive 480 ml?  
Do Americans actually drink stuff like this?  
I was honestly pretty shocked.  

After that, totally out of nowhere,  
she tried an experiment to see how long she could go without talking,  
and she couldn't even last 30 seconds, lol.  
No joke, she might actually have ADHD...

Oh, right, and speaking of ADHD,  
she told a story about when she did a temple stay in Korea.  

She saw a young monk's shaved head and said she wanted to do it too,  
so she chopped off half of her long hair at the time,  
which totally terrified her mom.  

And did she say she still has the picture from back then?  
While giggling with a "teehee"?  

Dang, just hearing that story makes it feel so Little Sinny, lol.  

Not only that, but the temple food was bland and didn't taste good,  
and back then, she was an even pickier eater than she is now  
and had a habit of spitting out food she didn't like.  
Her mom made her eat it anyway,  
and every time, Sinny would chew it and keep spitting it back out...  

Dang, I don't really like using this word, but it was so cute.  
Still, even though Sinny is a bit reckless,  
she actually listens to her parents pretty well,  
which makes her likeable.

After that, she said while watching Malice's meme stream,  
she felt like her English might be the worst among the SAGA members...  

But honestly... speaking as a foreigner...  
Your English is the easiest to understand.  
Thanks to You, I'm learning easily.  
Thank You.

After a few more random chats, she played Metal Slug 3.  

She said Papa Siren recommended the game itself,  
but every time I see the games Papa Siren recommends,  
I feel this strange inner closeness to Him for some reason  
(though I'm overwhelmingly younger than Papa Siren, I bet).  

And as usual, She shamelessly tried to play while introducing Herself as a pro gamer...  
but this time, it was really not easy.  

As the game went on, it was harder than expected,  
so She died over 20 times just in the first mission.  

Then a viewer made an offer where She could get a Super Chat,  
with the condition that She had to clear it before dying a total of 167 times.  

After that, She played with sweaty hands, focusing on the game.  
Every time it seemed like She might fail a mission, Her energy would drop,  
but She pulled Her energy back up each time.  

How did it end? Check it out for yourself.  
It'll be especially fun to watch if you count how many times She dies while watching the stream.  

The whole time, I was focusing on whether She'd be able to succeed or not.  
I'm sure not just me, but other viewers felt that way too.

Anyway, after the game finished like that,  
She told us that the 3D show on Chzzk is being prepared soon.  
Seeing how She said it'll probably happen anytime soon,  
I'm thinking we'll hear definite news around next week.  

Aren't You guys excited too?  
It's definitely going to be fun.  

And She brought up wanting to move to Suwon again.  
It seems the main reason is that the rent is cheaper than Seoul.  
There were other candidates before,  
but it seems She's settling Her mind toward that direction.  

Honestly, in my personal opinion,  
VTubers don't necessarily need to be close to the capital area to work.  
In that sense, I think moving to an area with relatively cheaper rent definitely has its merits.  

Whatever decision She makes,  
I sincerely hope good luck follows Her.

text:
WARRIORS FINAL SQUAD: GO WARRIORS GO, BUT WHO IS READY FOR THE HARD WORK?

The final Warriors squad is out. We say Go Warriors Go! Although, if we are honest, quite a few in our admin team are currently more excited about the U23s. New prospects, new possibilities and slightly fewer arguments we have already had seventeen times.

Still, this is the senior team. These are the players who must deliver against Equatorial Guinea. Chipezeze is out, Navaya has not made the cut and the coaches have backed some familiar faces whose club football has been rather less familiar lately. Team yemasupporter haidyiwe, but the supporters are certainly allowed to inspect the ingredients.

Who is protecting the back post?

Martin Mapisa, Future Sibanda, Nelson Chadya and Aaron Ngwenya are the goalkeeping options. The bigger concern remains: where are the imposing keepers with convincing international and continental-club experience coming through our system? Chadya offers some of that exposure, but his struggles with crosses against the Angolan club in the CAF Champions League did not inspire confidence in our camp. Equatorial Guinea have forwards who can attack the box and the ball in the air. We should expect the crossing examination, not act surprised when the first delivery arrives.

This is a grassroots problem for the technical director, not something a goalkeeper coach can fix with three training sessions and a motivational speech.

This defence still lacks convincing international quality. Kelvin Moyo and Peter Muduhwa, bless them, are not suddenly going to become world beaters. Hopefully they can do a job at centre-back. Corbin Mthunzi has the ball-playing potential we need, but he is young, has grown up in a different football system and could do with a quality, experienced head beside him. Talent does not automatically organise the defensive line.

Shane Maroodza offers another possibility, especially on the left of a back three. He has just completed Sarajevo’s 1-1 draw at BSK Banja Luka, giving him a useful 90 in the legs. A club back-three role and an international back-four role are not the same job, but at least this option comes with recent football rather than hope alone.

Emmanuel Jalai and Sean Fusire can give us pace going forward on the right. Our concern is the other end, where far-post headers have become far too comfortable a route to goal. Height and the aerial match-up are part of our worry with those right-back options. Fusire’s three senior Wednesday appearances this season are also a thin preparation diet, even with his full EFL Trophy outing. Jordan Zemura has a stronger rhythm on the left: 681 Championship minutes and a 75-minute start at Norwich after returning from injury. Tinotenda Muringai understudies from league-leading Hardrock. We remain rather excited by the U23 left-back options too.

Fabisch has the call-up. Where are the minutes?

Jonah Fabisch is the selection that raises an eyebrow. No questions about the footballer when fit, but Golden Arrows still record no competitive debut. He has been rehabilitating after a training injury, with the club match minutes still at zero. The KZN photo with Thando is cheerful enough; unfortunately, catching derby vibes is not the same as catching match rhythm.

That selection says plenty about our midfield options beyond Marshall Munetsi, Marvelous Nakamba and Andy Rinomhota. We need Andy’s balance in midfield, not another emergency right-back assignment. Nakamba attracts plenty of criticism, but in our view he remains the only genuine international-level defensive midfielder in this group. His eight Greek league appearances and 362 minutes are at least real preparation. He was unused against OFI on Sunday; that is a bench fact, not a reason to invent a new injury.

Mthokozisi Msebe and Abubakar Moffat must be ready to prove themselves in training. Away conditions and the likely heat will make changes important. The bench cannot just be a collection of people waiting to applaud the substitutions.

Navaya out, Msendami in, and Tino keeping us guessing

The selectors are clearly still not buying what Washington Navaya is selling. His name is absent, while Daniel Msendami remains despite having no verified competitive minutes for Gallants since returning on loan. He did play for Pirates earlier in the season; the concern is the Gallants spell, where the promised fresh start has not produced fresh football. We already saw the rust in the last Warriors games. International camp cannot keep doubling as a preseason programme.

Tino Kadewere is in again, and we will still hold our breath until he actually arrives. His injury history has earned that nervousness. But there is a more encouraging recent line: a cup goal against Panathinaikos followed by a full 90 at Levadiakos, 122 minutes across the two matches. He is not arriving in this discussion with no football at all. If he reports fit, his link-up play gives us a proper forward option even when the goal numbers are not making headlines.

Tino and Thando Ngwenya are our clearest number-nine options. Maswanhise has played centrally too, but his biggest danger is cutting in from either flank. We need that AFCON fire in the belly, not a polite jog through proceedings. Bill Antonio supplies explosive pace, while Chirewa is gradually earning trust at Wolves. His coach has praised his work, patience and willingness to learn different positions; the match-winning Burnley cameo and another appearance against Cardiff give that praise some substance.

The opponents are not bringing a buffet of passengers

Equatorial Guinea’s circulated squad has professionals spread across Europe and Asia, and the standout names deserve attention. Torino’s Saúl Coco brings Serie A experience; FotMob rates his league season at 6.87, although his club and live-data workload totals are not yet aligned. Luis Asué has eight goals and five assists in 14 Chinese Super League starts for Shanghai Shenhua. Viborg’s Dorian Hanza has six goals from 13 Danish league starts and scored the winner on Sunday. Midfielder Pablo Ganet arrives off a Persita hat-trick, with four goals and two assists in seven Indonesian league games. Álex Balboa is playing senior Spanish second-tier football at Valladolid, and Manuel Sapunga brings substantial South African club experience in goal. This is a team with actual performers, not just impressive addresses.

Zimbabwe’s list has ten locally based players and fourteen abroad. Our Greek, Championship and Belgian connections are useful, but there is no serious argument that every one of our club environments outranks theirs. Coco plays in Serie A; Balboa’s Valladolid is in Spain’s second division, not LaLiga. Compare the actual players and levels, not the postcode on the graphic.

The response should be clear: stop easy crosses, track the far-post runner and make the midfield protect our centre-backs. When we attack, use Antonio’s pace, Chirewa’s combinations and Maswanhise’s runs to get behind them and deliver cutbacks. Endless hopeful high balls into Coco’s neighbourhood would be doing his warm-up for him.

Go Warriors Go. We can argue about the list all week. Now give us a team that makes the argument worth having.

The final 24

Goalkeepers: Martin Mapisa (Hardrock), Future Sibanda (ZPC Kariba), Nelson Chadya (Scottland), Aaron Ngwenya (Highlanders).

Defenders: Jordan Zemura (Watford), Corbin Mthunzi (Ipswich Town), Tinotenda Muringai (Hardrock), Kelvin Moyo (Scottland), Peter Muduhwa (Scottland), Emmanuel Jalai (Scottland), Sean Fusire (Sheffield Wednesday), Shane Maroodza (Sarajevo).

Midfielders: Abubakar Moffat (Scottland), Mthokozisi Msebe (Scottland), Marshall Munetsi (Wolves), Andy Rinomhota (Reading), Jonah Fabisch (Golden Arrows), Marvelous Nakamba (Panetolikos).

Forwards: Tawanda Chirewa (Wolves), Tawanda Maswanhise (Motherwell), Bill Antonio (KV Mechelen), Daniel Msendami (Marumo Gallants), Tinotenda Kadewere (Aris), Thando Ngwenya (AmaZulu).

Head coach: Ramon Catala. Names and club labels transcribed from the supplied final ZIFA squad graphic; ZIFA’s 3 November announcement confirms the final-squad release.

text:
🇮🇷| From the parliamentary podium, Ghalibaf laid out three issues simultaneously: the objectives of the United States, Iran’s missiles, and the trucks that have been stuck in queues at the border for over a week.

November 3, 2026, Tehran. Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly, delivered a speech before the parliament. On the surface, the occasion was the commemoration of the "Day of Fighting Against Global Arrogance." In reality, it served as a comprehensive status report for a wartime cabinet, addressing military, diplomatic, economic, and logistical fronts all at once.

💥 The U.S. Objective: To Devour Iran, From Day One

Ghalibaf spoke with blunt directness, leaving no room for diplomatic niceties:

"From the very day the United States first wielded power, and continuing to this day, and for as long as it remains capable of doing so, it has sought to devour Iran, and it will continue to do so in the future."

"In the past, it pursued this goal by compelling puppet rulers to surrender. Today, faced with the resistance of a united and independent Iranian nation, it employs the tools of military, economic, and cognitive warfare."

He did not characterize U.S. actions as mere "policy disagreements" or "strategic competition." Instead, he described them as part of an annexation agenda spanning nearly seven decades, from the 1953 coup and the support for Saddam Hussein during the Iran-Iraq War to sanctions, assassinations, and eight months of relentless bombardment. It is all part of the same trajectory, driven by the same objective.

"The resistance of our nation has transformed this goal into the aspiration of free peoples across the globe." This statement is not merely rhetorical. It asserts that Iran is not fighting solely for its own sake. It is fighting for a broader principle, a principle that is now being recognized by other nations.

🎯 Military: The Terms of Engagement Are No Longer Defined by Washington

Speaking from the podium, Ghalibaf delivered a message that serves as one variation of a unified stance, echoed by the Supreme Leader’s directives, the Defense Minister’s statements, and the remarks of the Revolutionary Guard’s spokesperson:

“Through two imposed wars, the United States and its regional proxies have learned that the era of arrogance has come to an end. The Commander-in-Chief has clearly defined our military strategy for countering any potential enemy aggression. Consequently, our military and strategic response to any miscalculation by the enemy will be ‘unpredictable,’ transcending geographical constraints and ensuring that the consequences of their misjudgment engulf not only their actions, but all of their tangible and intangible assets.”

“Unpredictable.” Not merely “stronger” or “more lethal,” but *unpredictable*. This term is designed to render an adversary’s defensive planning obsolete. You may know the range of our missiles; you may know our list of potential targets, but “unpredictable” means you no longer know where the next missile will land.

“Transcending geographical constraints.” This is the core of the statement. Previously, Iran’s operational reach was bounded by specific parameters, Israel, U.S. military bases, or facilities within Gulf states. Now, those boundaries have been removed; the geographical limitations on our target database have been erased.

“Engulfing their miscalculation along with all their tangible and intangible assets.” By “intangible assets,” we refer not to oil, bases, or aircraft carriers, but to credibility, deterrence, alliance structures, and domestic political stability, all of which are now potential targets.

📜 Diplomacy: Whose Court Is the Ball In?

Ghalibaf offered a remark that, within the context of Tehran’s strategic discourse, is highly precise:

“Iran has provided the U.S. side with an authoritative and rational response. Now, the ball is in Washington’s court.”

“The ball is in Washington’s court.” This signifies: We have done what was required of us. We have presented you with a proposal, a timeline, and a formal response. Now, it is your turn to act.

“Countries in the region should be aware that the Islamic Republic of Iran, even as it stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, has also provided the American side with an authoritative and rational response. The ball is now in Washington’s court; it is up to them to prevent war.”

“Preventing war” is Washington’s responsibility, not Tehran’s. Tehran has already put forward a plan, set out conditions, and provided a timeline. Ghalibaf has made it perfectly clear who will bear the responsibility should war break out.

“If Washington commits another strategic error, it should know that this time it will face an entirely new battlefield and will find itself searching for an escape route even more desperately than it might today.”

⚔️ The Economy: The People on the Front Lines, the Market in the Rear

Another part of Ghalibaf’s address from the podium was directed at a domestic audience within Iran. While perhaps less resounding than his military declarations, its weight is no less significant than that of any missile.

“Reports from the ground and legitimate grievances from citizens indicate that recent price hikes and volatility have placed a heavy burden on households. Unfortunately, a critical issue within the market is the fragmentation of prices and a lack of effective, standardized regulation, conditions that have allowed speculators and middlemen to exploit the current wartime environment.”

“Our people, through their heroic resistance, have stood with honor and dignity amidst one of the greatest conflicts in history; they deserve the very best service and support.”

“The Parliament expects the government, regulatory bodies, and in particular the Judiciary and the State Discretionary Punishments Organization, which bear direct responsibility here, to immediately implement rigorous and effective oversight of the distribution and pricing systems for goods.”

“Price fragmentation” and a “lack of effective regulation” are not merely “market volatility.” It is a situation where speculators and middlemen are taking advantage of the chaos to profit at the expense of the people. From the parliamentary podium, Ghalibaf has explicitly named the responsible parties: the Judiciary and the State Discretionary Punishments Organization. For these institutions, the expectation is not merely to “pay attention,” but to “take action.”

📜 The Border: Trucks Queued for Days on End

Ghalibaf brought another issue to the table:

“Another critical matter that must be immediately placed on the Parliament’s oversight agenda is the severe congestion and the long queues of trucks and transport convoys at several of the country’s border crossings, including key transit points in the northwest and southeast.”

“Trailers carrying exports and imports are left waiting in line for days, or even weeks. This not only damages our export markets and the nation’s commercial reputation but also places immense pressure on economic actors and our hardworking drivers.”

“I am directing the Commission on Industries and Mines, the Economic Commission, and the Special Committee for the Protection of Production to conduct on-site inspections. In coordination with relevant authorities, including the Ministry of Roads and Urban Development, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Economic Affairs, and the Customs Administration, they must immediately investigate this situation from both legal and administrative perspectives and submit an expert report to the Parliament.”

“Days, or even weeks.” This is not merely a “logistical delay.” It is the physical manifestation of a war playing out at border checkpoints. Pakistan has closed its borders; Iraq has shut the Al-Sheeb crossing; [Marco] Rubio is visiting India and Uzbekistan; and Iran Air has been denied cargo permits. Every channel is being constricted, and the queues of trucks are the price being paid for this tightening.

Ghalibaf’s point is this: military victories cannot mask logistical bottlenecks. Missiles may land in Riyadh, but if export trailers are stuck in line at the border for three weeks, it means the arteries of the economy are being blocked elsewhere.

🔻 Four Points from Ghalibaf’s Podium: A Comprehensive Wartime Report

The U.S. Objective: Unchanged from 1953 to 2026, to swallow Iran.

Military Response: Unpredictable, without geographical limits, and involving all available assets.

Diplomatic Response: Already extended; the ball is now in Washington’s court. Preventing war is Washington’s responsibility.

Economic Front: Speculators are exploiting the war. The Judiciary and regulatory bodies must take action.

Border Logistics: Trucks have been lined up for days, even weeks. The committee must conduct an on-site investigation.

This is no mere "speech." It is a "status report." Military, diplomatic, economic, and logistical fronts are all laid out on the table simultaneously. Each front is being tracked by a specific agency, under a designated official, with a clear, defined deadline.

The remark made by Ghalibaf from the parliamentary podium encapsulates the entire war: "A finger on the trigger, while simultaneously offering the adversary a rational response."

The trigger and the response are not in conflict; they belong to the same hand. And that hand is not in Washington.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.
