text:
Something is walking through the tall grass of an African savanna, and every snake in that grass has a problem.

It is not a lion. It is not a honey badger. It stands about as tall as a seven-year-old child and weighs about as much as a large house cat. It has no venom. It has no claws built for tearing. It does not even have the hooked, curved talons that make an eagle an eagle.

By every rule we are taught about predators, the advantage belongs to the animal in the grass. The one with fangs. The one with a venom system refined over tens of millions of years for a single purpose. The one whose entire body is an argument that you should step back.

The advantage does not belong to the animal in the grass.

There is one number attached to this bird that I have read maybe fifty times and still cannot feel properly. Fifteen milliseconds. I will tell you what it measures, but not yet. A number like that means nothing until you understand what it is up against. So first, let me introduce you to the secretary bird.

Almost nobody knows this animal exists, and that is strange, because it may be the most improbable thing evolution ever built on two legs.

Start with the family tree, because that is where the weirdness begins. The secretary bird is a raptor. A bird of prey. Its relatives are hawks, kites and eagles, animals that spend their lives in the air, dropping out of the sky onto things that cannot see them coming. And somewhere in the deep past, one branch of that family looked at the sky and decided it would rather walk.

Not walk as in "forgot how to fly." It can fly, and it does, and at night it roosts at the top of a thorny tree like any self-respecting raptor. But the way it makes its living is on foot, across open grassland, in a landscape that rewards patience and punishes the clumsy. It covers an extraordinary amount of ground doing it. By most accounts, a single bird will cover somewhere around twenty to thirty kilometers in a day, pacing through the grass at the speed of a person on a long, purposeful hike, head level, eyes working, legs doing something no other bird of prey has ever managed.

Those legs deserve their own paragraph. They are the longest of any raptor on Earth. They make the bird look like it is standing on stilts it borrowed from a much larger animal, topped with a body that seems almost too small to belong to them. Black feathers wrap the upper legs like a pair of trousers. Below that, thin, scaled lower legs that look, frankly, a little fragile.

They are not fragile.

Here is the first thing I want you to hold onto, because it will matter later. Everything about this bird is built backwards from what you expect. A normal raptor catches its prey with its feet, closing the talons like a vise. The secretary bird's talons are short and blunt. They are not made for gripping. They are made for something else entirely, and that something else is the reason this post exists.

Its scientific name is Sagittarius serpentarius.

Sagittarius. Latin for archer. Serpentarius. The one associated with serpents. Put together, it reads like a job title: the archer who hunts snakes. Somebody, centuries ago, watched this animal work and decided that the only fitting description was a weapon.

I want you to sit with that, because the name was not given by a poet. It was given by naturalists, people trained to be dry and precise, and they could not resist. They looked at a bird and thought of a bowman.

Why?

To answer that, you have to understand what a snake actually is. Not the cartoon version. The engineering version.

A venomous snake is a machine for a single decision. It spends most of its life doing almost nothing. It waits. It does not chase, it does not tire, it does not waste energy on bluffing. It spends its calories on stillness and then spends them all at once, in a strike that, in the fastest vipers, is over in a time most of us would struggle to even perceive. We are talking about a fraction of a second to cross the gap and deliver venom. The whole design philosophy is: be so fast that the fight is finished before the other animal has realized it began.

This is why so many animals simply give snakes room. A lion does not need to prove anything to a puff adder. An antelope does not negotiate. The snake's reputation is not an exaggeration. It is the result of a very real, very old, very effective weapon.

Which makes the next fact feel like a glitch in the rules.

There are a handful of animals on Earth that have learned to beat that weapon. The famous one is the mongoose. You have heard the legend: the small, quick, fearless animal that squares up to a cobra and walks away. And the legend has a real core. Mongooses move with tremendous speed, and some of them carry something even stranger, a change at the molecular level in the very receptors that snake neurotoxins attack. In plain terms, part of the mongoose's defense is chemical. The venom that would stop a different animal has a much harder time doing its job. Add reflexes, add nerve, and you have a creature that treats the most feared animals in its environment as lunch.

Honey badgers have a version of this reputation. Some hedgehogs and opossums carry a resistance of their own.

Notice the pattern, though. Every one of those animals is, in some way, cheating the venom. They beat the weapon by making it matter less. They get bitten, they survive it, they win anyway. It is a strategy of absorbing the hit.

The secretary bird plays a completely different game.

It does not appear to rely on being bitten and surviving. It relies on not being bitten at all. And to do that, it has to solve a problem that sounds almost impossible when you say it out loud: how do you beat a creature built to strike faster than you can react, when you are not faster than it, not immune to it, and not even armed with the right kind of claws?

You do it with physics.

And this is where I have to be careful, because the temptation here is to hype it. People love to hype this bird. There is a lot of folklore, a lot of confident claims that circulate with no source attached, and a lot of videos that simply say it is the world's deadliest bird and leave it at that. I do not want to do that. The truth is more interesting than the hype, and that is not a figure of speech. The real story has a plot twist that the legend does not even know about.

So here is what we actually know.

In 2016, a team of researchers in the United Kingdom did something nobody had done properly before. They stopped relying on stories and put a measuring instrument in front of the bird. They worked with captive secretary birds and a stand-in for a snake, and they measured what happened when the bird did the thing it is famous for.

What came back reorganized how I think about this animal.

Two numbers.

The first is force. When a secretary bird delivers its kick, the impact comes in at roughly five times the bird's own body weight. Read that again with the animal in mind: a bird that weighs a few kilograms, standing on one leg, delivering a blow with the force of an animal several times its mass. Most of us imagine kicks as something that happens at the end of a big, swinging motion. This one does not need a wind-up that long. It is compact, and it is violent.

The second number is the one I promised you. Fifteen milliseconds. That is roughly how long the contact lasts. A human blink takes something like a hundred milliseconds, often more. The whole event, from the foot meeting the target to the foot leaving it, is over several times faster than you can close and open your eyes.

Think about what that does to the logic of the encounter.

The snake's entire strategy depends on speed. The bird's response to a speed-based weapon is a speed-based weapon of its own, delivered through a limb that is built, not to hold or to tear, but to hit. When contact is that short, and that forceful, there is almost no window in which anything can happen back. That is my inference rather than a claim from the study, but it is hard to read those figures and arrive at a different feeling.

Now, the second plot twist. You might expect, after reading all that, that this bird is a bundle of reckless aggression. A brawler. A kicker with a death wish.

Nothing about the way it is built suggests that. A fight like this is not survivable on bravery. It is survivable on geometry. Those absurdly long legs, which look so ridiculous in a photograph, put the part of the animal that matters, the body, the head, the part that cannot be replaced, as far from the danger as the shape of a bird allows. The distance is part of the defense. The kick is the answer.

And there is a third piece that rarely makes it into the legend. The wings. Observers have described secretary birds fanning them wide during an encounter, in a way that looks like a display and may work more like a tool. A snake has to commit to a target, and a large, shifting, feathered surface is a worse target than a bird standing still. Whether you call it a shield or a distraction, it buys the leg a moment.

A moment is all the leg needs.

I keep returning to that idea, because it points at something deeper than a clever hunting technique. The secretary bird does not beat snakes by being stronger than them. It beats them by having refined, over a very long time, the art of making a single moment decisive. The legs, the posture, the height, the patience, the wings: all of it exists to deliver one moment on terms the bird controls.

There is a lesson about competence in there. When something is truly good at what it does, it does not look like rage. It does not look like noise. It looks like calm, and then it looks like it was always going to go that way.

And there is a question I cannot answer, which is how much of this is learned and how much is simply written into the animal. Young birds grow up in a landscape that offers them plenty of chances to practice on lesser targets, and the physical skill involved is so exacting that I would not want to guess where instinct stops and experience starts. I would rather tell you I do not know than invent a neat answer. That uncertainty is part of why the animal is worth watching.

Now let me complicate the legend, because I promised you the truth is better.

If you only know this bird from the viral clips, you would assume it spends its days hunting cobras. That is the brand. That is the image on the poster. But when researchers look at what secretary birds actually eat, the picture gets quieter and more interesting. Snakes are on the menu, including venomous ones, but analyses of the diet suggest they make up a smaller share than the legend implies. A lot of the daily menu is smaller and less cinematic: insects, rodents, lizards, small mammals, the occasional egg.

At first that sounds like a deflation. It is the opposite.

It means the snake-killing is not a stunt. It is not a party trick the bird performs because it is bored. It is one expression of a much larger skill: the ability to turn an entire landscape into a hunting ground by walking it, listening to it and reading it. The bird that can end an encounter with a venomous snake in a few thousandths of a second is the same bird that, an hour earlier, was stamping through grass to flush out a rodent. The same legs. The same blunt feet. The same stubborn rhythm.

That is another thing the legend misses. The bird does not wait for a snake to appear. It goes looking. It walks with a steady, deliberate gait, scanning ahead, sometimes stomping at the grass to startle hidden animals into moving. Sometimes a pair will work the same ground together. The vegetation that hides the small and the shy is, for this bird, a kind of menu board.

And think about the confidence that takes. Walking into tall grass in Africa, deliberately, on foot, day after day, in a place where the creatures you might meet include some of the most dangerous snakes on the continent, is not what most of us would call a relaxed way to make a living. The bird does it because it has an answer to the question that makes the rest of us hesitate.

Small prey gets swallowed whole. Larger prey is dispatched first and dealt with afterward. Everything about the feeding habit says the same thing: this animal has found a role in the ecosystem that nobody else is quite filling. Not a vulture, not an eagle, not a fox. Something in between that has its own rules.

I want to point out how rare that is. The usual story in nature is convergence: similar problems lead to similar solutions, and animals in similar jobs end up looking alike. The secretary bird breaks that pattern so thoroughly that when scientists classify it, they do not put it in a group with other species at all. It sits in a family of its own. One family. One genus. One species.

Think about what that means. Somewhere in the history of life on Earth, a branch split off and kept going alone. Not a few cousins sharing a habit. Just one lineage, one design, still standing, still walking across the grass.

Every other raptor you can name belongs to a crowd. This one does not.

And it does not look like it minds.

It looks, if anything, like it has somewhere to be. Take a moment with its face, the one feature you will notice when you see it up close. The bare skin around the eyes is a deep, flushed orange-red. The eyes themselves are framed by long, dark lashes, so long that they have become one of the first things people mention when they see the bird in person. It is difficult to feel afraid of a face like that. It is difficult to believe, looking at it, that this is the animal that other animals fear.

Which is exactly the kind of contrast that makes the whole story work. The softness of the face, the length of the lashes, the almost comic stilt-walk, the crest of feathers that looks like someone left a handful of pens in a hat. And behind it, a mechanism that turns that gentle-looking walker into one of the most precise answers to a snake that the natural world has ever come up with.

Speaking of that crest.

The crest is the reason for the name, or at least that is one of the explanations, and the argument about it has gone on long enough to become a small piece of natural history in its own right.

One version says the long quills sticking out from behind the head reminded early European observers of the pens that clerks used to tuck behind their ears. Secretary, in the old sense of a person who writes things down. A bird dressed for the office.

The other version is stranger and, to me, more appealing. It holds that the name began as an Arabic phrase meaning something like hunter-bird, and that over time, through the usual wear and tear of travel and translation, a foreign word for a hunter became an English word for a desk job. If that is true, then the most dangerous-sounding description of the animal was lost, and the most office-friendly one survived.

Nobody has settled it conclusively, and I do not think anyone needs to. Either way, the story has the same shape as the bird: a name that sounds harmless, attached to an animal that is not.

And the name tells you something else. People have been looking at this bird, and arguing about what to call it, for a very long time. It was never invisible. It was part of the landscape and the imagination of the people who lived beside it. Which brings me to a detail I find quietly remarkable.

Two countries put it on their national symbols.

The secretary bird appears in the emblem of Sudan. It also appears on the coat of arms of South Africa, wings raised above the national flower. When a nation looks for an image to stand for itself, it chooses a bird that stands for vigilance, for protection, for the clearing of danger from the ground we live on. An animal that goes into the grass so that others do not have to.

I find it hard to think of a more fitting symbol, and I find it harder to think of what it means that the symbol is now in trouble.

Here is the part of the story that does not get a dramatic soundtrack.

In 2020, the conservation status of the secretary bird was raised from Vulnerable to Endangered. Read that sentence slowly. Not a rare, obscure animal tucked away in a single valley. A bird with a continental range across the open country south of the Sahara, an animal that makes a living across thousands of kilometers of grassland, and the people who assess these things looked at the trend lines and concluded that it was in serious decline.

Why would an animal that handles cobras struggle?

Because the things that threaten it are not the things it was built to defeat.

The grasslands it depends on are being converted, broken up and built over. Open ground that supported a walking hunter becomes farmland, fenced and fragmented. Fires, grazing pressure and changing land use all reshape the vegetation the bird needs. Infrastructure adds new hazards that evolution never prepared it for, from power lines to roads. And because the bird is big, visible and slow to breed, every loss counts for more than it would in a species that produces dozens of young at a time.

There is something almost unbearable about that mismatch. Here is an animal that has solved one of the hardest problems in nature, how to meet the fastest strike in the grass and answer it first. And the thing that is wearing it down is not fast at all. It is slow. It is patient. It is the gradual erosion of the world it knows how to walk through.

No kick, however precise, answers that.

I think this is why I find the bird so hard to stop thinking about. Its genius is local. It is perfectly tuned to a specific kind of landscape, a specific kind of encounter, a specific kind of danger. Take away the landscape and the genius has nowhere to go.

Let me tell you about the other end of the life cycle, because it changes how you see the adult.

Secretary birds build nests at the top of trees, and not small ones. The structure is a broad platform of sticks, often placed in the flat crown of a thorny acacia, wide enough that a person could not wrap their arms around it. Pairs tend to come back to the same site and add to it, season after season, until the nest becomes a kind of landmark in the landscape. A permanent address for an animal that otherwise spends most of its time moving.

The eggs are few. One to three, usually. The chicks that hatch are helpless, and they are raised in a nest far above the ground, in a tree whose branches are armed with thorns. Falls from those heights are a recognized cause of chick loss, which means that a young bird's first great danger has nothing to do with snakes. It is gravity.

Sit with that for a moment. The animal that will grow up to meet the fastest strike in the grass begins its life as a small, downy thing at the edge of a platform of sticks, many meters above hard ground, with nothing standing between it and a long drop except the instincts of its parents and a little luck.

That is the real arc of this animal. It is easy to look at the grown bird and see only a weapon. But every adult you will ever see made it through a period of total vulnerability first. The calm, upright, stilt-legged hunter was once a creature that could not stand.

I think that is what lingers when the technical details fade. The contrast. Fragility at the beginning and mastery in the middle, and now, again, fragility at the scale of the whole species.

So let me say something about the people on the other side of this story.

Humans have always had a complicated relationship with predators that handle danger. Where a snake is a threat to a farmer's child, a bird that kills snakes looks like a friend. Where a bird of prey is a rumored thief of chickens, it looks like an enemy. The secretary bird has benefited from the first kind of thinking in many places and has been caught by the second in others. Its reputation is its best protection and its worst liability: a bird so famous for one thing that people forget it does a hundred others.

And then there is the question I find myself asking whenever I see an animal like this.

Why does it grip us so much?

Part of it is obviously the contest. We are built to pay attention when something small meets something dangerous. We have been watching that story for as long as there have been stories. The hero and the serpent. The archer and the beast. Our oldest myths are full of it.

But I do not think it is only that. I think it is the reversal. We are used to the idea that danger belongs to the one with the weapon. We are used to the idea that the quick and the venomous rule the grass. When an animal turns that around, not through brute size but through the discipline of a perfectly rehearsed move, something in us recalibrates. We see a thing that should not be possible, done so cleanly that it looks routine.

Competence is moving to watch. Not talent displayed for an audience, but skill applied to a real problem with real consequences, in real time, by an animal that has no idea anyone is looking.

And that is the other thing I want to say about this bird. It does not perform. Nothing about its behavior is for us. The bird in the grass is not aware that it is magnificent. It is simply getting through a Tuesday. It is looking for lunch, in the only way it knows how, in the only place it has ever lived.

That ordinariness, to the bird, is what makes the whole thing extraordinary to us.

There is a reason people share clips of this animal with the caption "how is this real." The honest answer is that it is real because an enormous number of small decisions, made across an enormous number of generations, by an enormous number of birds that never knew they were part of a long argument about speed, accumulated into a body that can win it.

Every kick that ever worked was inherited from every kick that came before.

I have thought a lot about what it means to look at that and feel nothing but amusement at the stilt legs, or nothing but surprise at the speed. I think the better response is a kind of respect. The bird does not need our admiration. But the grassland that made it does need our attention, and the two are linked more tightly than they seem.

One more thing, and it is the thing that makes the margin feel so thin.

For a hunter that lives on foot, the legs are the whole business. A hawk that is injured can still, in principle, drop from a perch. An owl can still wait. But an animal that makes its living by walking twenty or thirty kilometers a day, and whose signature weapon is a leg, has no backup plan built into its body. I cannot tell you how often a bird gets hurt, and I will not pretend to. But the logic is hard to avoid. Every encounter is a trade between a payoff and a risk, and the bird has to keep winning that trade for years.

Which means the calm is not casual. It is the visible side of an enormous amount of discipline. The animal is not fearless in any foolish sense. It is selective. It commits when the geometry is right and it gives the situation what it needs. The skill is not only the kick. It is the judgment about when the kick is allowed to happen.

That, to me, is the most human thing about it. Not the courage. The restraint.

So here is where I leave you.

You now know the things the clip will not tell you in so many words. You know the bird is a raptor that chose the ground. You know its talons are blunt on purpose, its legs are the longest of any bird of prey, and its name is an argument that nobody has finished. You know the number: fifteen milliseconds. You know the force: about five times its own weight. You know it was lifted to Endangered in 2020, and you know why that should bother us more than any record-breaking kick ever could.

What you do not have yet is the thing a paragraph cannot give you. The sense of how it looks when a theory about speed and geometry turns into an animal doing the work in front of you, with no explanation and no apology.

A last thought before the clip. Most animal videos ask you to feel something about the animal. This one asks for something slightly different: to notice how much skill can hide inside a creature that looks, at a glance, like it was assembled from spare parts. Tall, thin, crested, lashed, a little absurd. Nobody designs a legend that way. Nature just did, and then left the proof in a few seconds of footage.

That part cannot be written. It can only be watched.

It is short. Short enough to watch twice. The second time, stop looking at the snake. Look at the bird. Look at how little it seems to be worrying. Then look at those legs once again, and try to hold the number fifteen in your head while you do it.

Then ask yourself the question that I could not stop asking while writing this: if an animal can be this good at something this dangerous, what exactly are we losing when the grass it walks through disappears?

Watch it.

text:
Good morning, Sunrisers. Today is Election Day, and I'm voting RED.

Many of you have already voted, but Alabama is one of three states that requires a qualifying excuse for absentee voting and does not provide early in-person voting.

I grew up in this system so it seems perfectly normal to me. Indeed, the idea of polls being open for days or weeks in advance seems antiquated, a relic of the 18th Century when travel was slow and difficult, even to one's county seat.

Congress standardized a single national Election Day in 1845 — the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November. For most of our history, voting was overwhelmingly an in-person, Election Day event.

The first non-Election Day voting was absentee balloting for soldiers. Pennsylvania allowed limited absentee voting for soldiers during the War of 1812. During the Civil War, 19 Union states allowed soldiers to vote from the field in the 1864 presidential election. Similar provisions were extended for subsequent wars.

By World War II, every state allowed military absentee voting. Civilian absentee voting (for illness, travel, etc.) began spreading state-by-state in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as the population grew more mobile.

For decades this remained limited and excuse-based. California was the first to allow any registered voter to request a mail ballot, in 1978, the year I graduated from high school. 

By 2000, about 24 states offered early in-person voting to all voters and roughly 14% of ballots were cast before Election Day. The 2020 pandemic produced a temporary spike (about 69% of ballots cast early or by mail); the share settled around 50% in 2022.

I've never lived in an early-voting state, so the traditional way seems normal to me while the weeks of early voting seems antiquated, something that belongs in horse-and-buggy days.

And I can't help but wonder if the convenience of early voting is worth the trade-offs. Employers used to be required to let employees have sufficient time to go vote. Now, they don't.

Newspapers wouldn't publish any new allegations against a candidate on the Monday before Election Day because there was no time for them to be proved false before voters went to the polls. With early voting, there is no such cutoff and, in fact, early voters have missed breaking news that might have influenced their votes.

I sense, too, that voting has become less important where one has many opportunities to cast a ballot instead of just one. We tend to value things more when they are more difficult.

Voting is a privilege. If you haven't already, cast your ballot today. I hope you will vote RED because I believe our futures depend on it.

Meanwhile, coffee (even with some caffeine withheld), prayer, and exercise await me. And trauma therapy. God bless all here. 💛

text:
Good morning, Sunrisers! Today is the first day of Carole412 without caffeine. 

I apologize in advance.

I don't have to go cold turkey, but I do have to replace 1/4 of my coffee with decaf, then 1/2, then 3/4 until I am caffeine free by mid-December when I will undergo surgery to repair the damage I suffered in a car wreck 10 months ago.

The bang-bang impact of a slightly offset head-on collision followed by the Jeep flipping around and hitting the door behind me caused two injuries to my cervical spine.

I've tried physical therapy (snd have 2 more weeks) and nerve blocks. PT has helped tremendously with the muscle damage caused by the force of the impact and has improved my range of motion. But it can't do anything to resolve the nauseating pain that results when I tilt my head back.

I drink out of straws to avoid that motion. I avoid looking up when I reach for something above eye level. But in my sleep, I push my head back just a little, just enough to cause me to wake up throughout the night with pain.

And the only way to stop this is surgery. The surgery involves taking bone from my hip to create wedges that will be inserted between each pair of vertebrae, along with some hardware to hold everything in place.

Last week, the surgeon informed me that 3 things inhibit healing: smoking, steroids and NSAIds, and caffeine. I was shocked. I don't smoke, and I had already decided that nothing short of severe pneumonia will make me take oral steroids again. NSAIDS (ibuprofen, naproxyn sodium) give me bleeding ulcers in about a week. But I am addicted to caffeine.

I've tried cutting it out. I'm grumpy without caffeine — hence the need to apologize in advance — but I suffered severe caffeine withdrawal headaches. For a month. And then I surrendered to the addiction.

I was tempted to, for once, not be the most compliant patient ever, especially as my friends @21memaw and @SuzanneMartis weren't required to go caffeine-free before their surgeries.

But of course I looked it up. And discovered that while many surgeons don't tell their patients to give up caffeine, caffeine does slow bone formation. And with all the things I can't control, giving up caffeine is one thing I can. So, I will.

And that starts today. No more Ninja Coffee Machine grinding beans fresh for each cup it brews. Back to Mr. Coffee and the cannister of decaf that sits in the freezer between visits from my husband's 99-year-old aunt.

And hello to another type of headache.

On the bright side? This time I do have some pain medication for the other headaches. Maybe it will work on both.

Time to find out. Three-quarter-caf, here I come. God have mercy on me and bless all here. 💛

Belgium: PM De Wever offers resignation amid 10-billion-euro budget deadlock
BRUSSELS — Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has offered his government’s resignation to King Philippe after the five-party governing coalition failed to agree on the 2027 federal budget. The Royal Palace said the monarch has postponed a decision and will consult the leaders of the coalition parties.
The crisis stems from a fiscal gap of about €10 billion that the government aims to close by 2029. De Wever’s N-VA and the liberal MR favour spending cuts, including in healthcare, while socialist Vooruit, CD&V and Les Engagés want higher taxes on the wealthy.
The five-party alliance is known as the “Arizona coalition.” King Philippe has urged the parties to seek a compromise; if the resignation is ultimately accepted, Belgium could face new coalition talks or early elections.

text:
🇺🇸 The Arab-American and Muslim vote in the 2026 midterms

The Arab-American and Muslim vote is once again attracting attention in this year’s midterm elections. These are two distinct but overlapping constituencies: not all Arab Americans are Muslim, and most American Muslims are not Arab. Both, however, have become increasingly visible in the country’s political landscape.

Recent polling suggests that Arab-American voters are moving back toward Democratic candidates after the significant shift toward Donald Trump among some voters in 2024. One Arab American Institute @AAIUSA survey found that 59% intended to vote Democratic for Congress, compared with 26% supporting Republicans. Among Muslim voters, a @CAIRNational survey found that 72% intended to vote Democratic and just 6% Republican.

That doesn’t mean these communities have become a reliable Democratic voting bloc. Independent identification remains substantial, and political preferences vary considerably by generation, national origin, religious identity, socioeconomic circumstances and geography.

The issues driving their choices are also broader than the Middle East. Economic pressures, inflation, healthcare, civil rights and immigration all matter. At the same time, Gaza, US military involvement in the region and relations with Israel have become major considerations in how many voters assess political candidates.

Michigan is perhaps the most closely watched example. The Senate race involving Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian-American Muslim Democrat, and Republican Mike Rogers has brought these issues into sharper focus. El-Sayed’s candidacy also raises the possibility of electing the first Muslim senator in American history. The controversy surrounding Israel and Gaza has exposed divisions within the Democratic Party, particularly following Representative Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers after losing the Democratic primary to El-Sayed.

But the significance of this electorate extends well beyond Michigan. Muslim and Arab-American candidates are increasingly running for office at different levels of government, while established politicians are having to pay closer attention to communities that were once too often treated as peripheral to national electoral politics.

The broader takeaway is that the political realignment of 2024 may not have been permanent. Some Arab-American voters who supported Trump have since become disillusioned with his administration, while Democratic support appears to have recovered. Yet neither party can take these voters for granted.

The central electoral significance of Arab-American and Muslim voters is not that they constitute a large share of the national electorate, but that their votes are concentrated in places where elections can be decided by narrow margins. Michigan is the clearest example, but the same dynamic applies to competitive congressional districts and local races elsewhere. In these contests, shifts in turnout, party allegiance or support for individual candidates can have consequences far beyond the communities’ numerical size.

Their electoral influence is therefore disproportionately tied to geography: a relatively small but politically engaged constituency can become pivotal in a closely contested race. Just as importantly, their growing willingness to withhold support from candidates and parties they believe have disregarded their concerns challenges the assumption that their votes can be taken for granted.

For Democrats and Republicans alike, the lesson is that Arab-American and Muslim voters are no longer simply constituencies to be courted. They are increasingly organised political actors whose participation, preferences and mobilisation can affect electoral outcomes. The 2026 midterms will offer an important test of whether that influence can translate into sustained political leverage and greater representation at the national level.

text:
MICHIGAN: A TEST OF AMERICA’S CONSCIENCE

I have been following the US midterm elections with particular interest in Michigan’s Senate race. What should be a contest of ideas and leadership has become something more consequential: a test of America’s commitment to equality, pluralism and its own democratic ideals.

At the centre is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an American born to Egyptian immigrant parents, a Muslim, and an exceptionally accomplished public servant.

Educated at Columbia and Oxford, with an impressive record in public health, El-Sayed possesses the intellectual credentials, eloquence and leadership qualities that any democracy should value.

Yet his path has been anything but straightforward.

Proud of his Muslim identity and outspoken against the devastation in Gaza and what he regards as genocide against Palestinians, El-Sayed has faced formidable opposition from powerful political interests, pro-Israel lobbying organisations and wealthy donors. More disturbingly, elements of the opposition have exploited religious prejudice and Islamophobia.

The extraordinary decision of Haley Stevens, whom he defeated in the Democratic primary, to endorse Republican Mike Rogers underscores the bitter divisions surrounding this election.

Political opposition is legitimate. Disagreement over policies is fundamental to democracy. But when a candidate’s faith or ancestry becomes a weapon against him, it is democracy itself that is diminished.

A leader should be judged by competence, character and commitment to the public good, not by the God he worships or the origins of his parents.

What gives me hope is the response from ordinary Americans.

Across Michigan, Christians, Muslims, Jews and people of diverse backgrounds are rallying around El-Sayed. The surge in grassroots contributions suggests that many refuse to let wealth, prejudice and political manipulation dictate their choices.

Having listened to El-Sayed speak, I see an exceptionally articulate, thoughtful and courageous young leader who combines intellectual depth with conviction and genuine concern for public welfare. He represents the kind of new-generation leadership America needs.

Whether he wins remains uncertain. But the significance of this election extends far beyond Michigan.

If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim in the US Senate, affirming that the American dream belongs to every citizen, regardless of race, religion or ancestry.

For millions of young Americans from minority and immigrant communities, it would demonstrate that they need not conceal their identity or compromise their convictions to aspire to national leadership.

At a time when fear and division increasingly shape politics, America has an opportunity to offer the world a different example.

The real question is not whether America is ready for a Muslim senator. It is whether America is ready to honour its promise of equal opportunity and belonging for every citizen.

I hope Michigan chooses merit over prejudice and principle over political expediency.

For democracy is not truly tested when the majority prevails, but when someone from a minority seeks to lead.

Michigan’s choice will speak far beyond its borders. Will America allow prejudice to define who can lead, or prove that its ideals are greater than its divisions?

text:
Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, 3 November 2026 - Jon Rahm has given Yas Links a glowing first review ahead of his Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship debut, as the Spaniard sets about securing his place in next week’s DP World Tour Championship.

It is Rahm’s first trip to Abu Dhabi and it comes just weeks after he and his wife, Kelley, welcomed their fourth child, Begoña. He touched down in the capital on Monday after a long day of travel and wasted little time getting to know the front nine. 

“It’s in about as good shape as you can expect a golf course to be,” said Rahm, a two-time Major Champion, after his first practice round at Yas Links. 

“That was absolutely fantastic. Not a blade of grass out of place. Firm, but reactive in a consistent way. It was truly enjoyable. The one thing everybody has told me coming to this golf course is that it’s always in great shape and there’s a lot of movement to the greens.”

Rahm starts the opening event of the DP World Tour Play-Offs as the man on the bubble. He sits 51st in the Race to Dubai Rankings Delivered by DP World with only the top 50 going through to the season finale at Jumeirah Golf Estates. 

But he isn’t losing sleep over it.

“The good thing about this week is that we are all guaranteed points, right. So I know I need to play well but I don’t think I need a stellar effort to make it to next week.

“I would say if I just play solid, I know the way that I can play golf, I should play next week. But yes, it’s an unusual thought to have. It’s a little bit added to just the tournament itself.”

The wind was already up on Yas Island on Monday, and Rahm’s record suggests the conditions should suit him. Both of his Irish Open titles came on exposed coastal links, at Portstewart in 2017 and Lahinch in 2019, where the breeze is rarely far away. He has also shown he can win in the UAE, triumphing at the DP World Tour Championship three times, in 2017, 2019 and 2022.

Still, Rahm believes it’s up to the player to adapt to the course, not the other way round.

“I think nowadays, we get very caught up on a golf course fitting a player, where I think as players, it’s our duty to adjust to the golf course and the conditions,” said the World Number 15.

“I think the players that can do that the best are the ones that can win consistently. If you only play where you think you can play good, it’s going to be a very short career, at least as far as I’m concerned.”

Away from the course, Rahm hopes to see more of Yas Island once his Pro-Am duties are done.

“Obviously I’m aware that the F1 track is right there, Ferrari World is right here. I just haven’t been able to go out and explore,” he said. 

“Tomorrow after the Pro-Am when I have a free afternoon, maybe I get to do a little bit of that.”

The Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, staged by the DP World Tour and Abu Dhabi Sports Council, runs from 5–8 November at Yas Links Abu Dhabi. The top 70 available players on the Race to Dubai Rankings are competing for the 50 places in the DP World Tour Championship the following week.

Away from the golf, the tournament will offer a full programme of family entertainment and live music. In celebration of the UAE Year of the Family, this year’s Family Weekend takes place across both Saturday and Sunday, while children aged 17 and under go free throughout tournament week.

Every ticket includes access to the Future Falcons Kids’ Zone, which features a bouncy castle, face painting, bubble shows, giant games and interactive activities. Young golfers can enjoy free golf lessons, and fans of all ages can watch live trick-shot shows just steps away from some of the world’s best players.pic credit DPW tour ⛳️

text:
rebellion, false religious assurances, and refusal to hear His word. It should not be carelessly transferred into the present Church as though Israel's national covenant circumstances and the believer's spiritual position were identical. Nevertheless, the moral condition described is unmistakable. People had become so accustomed to disobedience that shame no longer restrained their conduct. What once should have produced repentance was now practiced without embarrassment. This is the dreadful danger of becoming past feeling. The problem is not that every person must experience the same emotional reaction to sin. The problem is that conduct clearly condemned by God is no longer recognized as requiring correction. When a people lose the ability to acknowledge wrongdoing, they have not progressed beyond morality. They have learned to make rebellion appear respectable.

Isaiah 5:20 supplies another warning: “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness.” Here the problem advances beyond merely practicing wickedness. Moral judgment itself becomes inverted. Sin is praised as virtue, restraint is condemned as oppression, and obedience to divine truth is presented as something shameful. The outward vocabulary changes, but the authority of Scripture does not. Human society may approve practices that God's word forbids, yet popularity cannot transform unrighteousness into holiness. Nor should Christians imagine that every cultural disagreement constitutes an attack upon Scripture; they must first establish clearly what the Bible actually teaches. But where God's commands are plain, public approval cannot overturn them. The Christian must not allow the shifting judgments of society to replace divine revelation. When men begin calling darkness light, the answer is not to repaint the lamp. The answer is to restore the distinction between what God has declared good and what He has condemned.
First Timothy 4:2 carries this warning directly into the realm of religious deception, describing false teachers as “Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron.” This is particularly serious because the men involved possess enough religious language to deceive others while their own consciences have become corrupted. A preacher may learn to defend wrongdoing with carefully selected verses, impressive theological terminology, and appeals to spiritual authority. He may become so practiced in concealing his motives that he no longer recognizes the seriousness of manipulating those who trust him. Yet no religious position gives a man permission to silence the Scriptures or treat his conscience as something to be overcome whenever it becomes inconvenient. False teaching is not merely a mistake in public communication when it is deliberately employed to excuse corruption. The most dangerous religious hypocrite is not necessarily the man who knows he is wearing a mask, but the man who has worn it so long that he begins mistaking it for his own face.
4. The Sinner Who Signs Himself Over To Bondage
Ephesians 4:19 contains an expression that places personal responsibility directly before the reader: “have given themselves over.” Paul does not describe individuals who merely stumbled into a difficult circumstance and immediately sought deliverance. He describes people surrendering themselves to lasciviousness and the practice of uncleanness. The language emphasizes yielding, and Romans 6:16 explains the seriousness of that action: “to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey.” Sin offers the appearance of independence while establishing another form of servitude. A person may claim that refusing moral restraints proves he is free, yet his conduct may reveal that his desires have become masters he feels compelled to satisfy. text:
DIHEXA isn’t a nootropic. It’s a synapse factory.

I’ve been running Dihexa for around a month now again, for the third time, and pairing it with tesofensine. It’s become one of the more interesting (to say the least) compounds in my stack for the cognitive side of everything I’m doing.

I have talked about it before, but after recently seeing more posts about it, would rather just cover the entire damn thing of what it is, what it could help with, and the real fucking risks that it carries. 

This, like most of my stuff, is what it offers for the enhanced biohacker, although it really applies to anyone who uses it in a time of preferred focus on a particular subject.

Dihexa is a synthetic compound derived from a fragment of angiotensin IV. It was originally developed at Washington State University as an orally active, brain-penetrating molecule aimed at Alzheimer’s-type cognitive issues. It’s not a normal peptide, it’s a modified version designed to last longer in the body and get into the brain.

The idea behind it is that it binds to hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and boosts signaling through the c-Met receptor. In the brain that pathway is involved in growing new connections between neurons (synaptogenesis) and increasing dendritic spines. Early lab work claimed extremely high potency compared to BDNF in cell assays for building those connections. That said, the main 2014 paper that laid out the HGF/c-Met mechanism was retracted in 2025 after an investigation found issues with some of the figures. A related 2012 paper was also retracted. The original 2013 paper that showed the behavioral effects in rats still has an expression of concern on it. There has been some independent work since then (including a 2025 rat study on working memory after repeated mild TBI), so the story isn’t completely dead, but the foundational mechanism paper is gone. c-Met is also involved in certain cancers, so long-term activation is a theoretical risk that hasn’t really been studied.

In animals it improved spatial learning in impaired and aged rats, helped in an Alzheimer’s mouse model, protected some hair cells in zebrafish, and showed benefits in a TBI working-memory model. There are zero published human trials on Dihexa itself. The closest related drug (fosgonimeton) failed its big Alzheimer’s trial, it looked a little better than placebo on some measures but didn’t hit statistical significance.

In theory, after you research Dihexa, it is absorbed into the bloodstream and, thanks to its chemical modifications, remains circulating for an unusually long time while readily crossing into the brain and concentrating there above blood levels. Once inside the brain it binds to hepatocyte growth factor and promotes its dimerization, which strongly amplifies signaling through the c-Met receptor. This heightened pathway activity is what drives the formation of new dendritic spines and synaptic connections, particularly in regions involved in memory, attention, and motor learning. Over time the increased synaptic density and plasticity can strengthen the neural networks responsible for encoding information, sustaining focus during long sessions, recovering mental clarity under fatigue or stress, and more efficiently learning or refining skills.

In rats it has a ridiculously long half-life (over a week depending on the route). No human pharmacokinetic data exists. People online usually run it in cycles of a few weeks on and then off, with doses commonly in the 5-20 mg range orally or sublingually, but that’s all anecdotal.

Potential theoretical benefits in humans (based on the proposed HGF/c-Met mechanism and animal data only, not proven in people):

-Increased formation of new synaptic connections: By potentiating HGF binding and c-Met signaling, it may promote spinogenesis and synaptogenesis in the hippocampus and other brain regions, which could support stronger neural networks for learning and memory.
-Improved memory acquisition and recall: Enhanced synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation pathways could make it easier to encode and retrieve information, similar to effects seen in rodent water-maze and working-memory models.
-Faster skill and motor learning:  More efficient synaptic remodeling in motor and prefrontal circuits might help with acquiring new physical skills, techniques, or coordinated movements.
-Greater mental stamina and sustained focus: Supporting neuronal connectivity and resilience could reduce cognitive fatigue during long sessions of work, training, or problem-solving.
-Reduced brain fog and clearer thinking:  Strengthening synaptic function and potentially lowering neuroinflammation markers (as observed in some animal models) may improve mental clarity.
-Better neuroprotection and recovery from stress: HGF/c-Met signaling is linked to neuronal survival; this could theoretically help protect against oxidative stress, mild inflammation, or recovery from intense training or cognitive load.
-Support for neuroplasticity over time: Ongoing promotion of new connections might help maintain or rebuild cognitive flexibility with consistent use, based on the synaptogenic effects reported in cell and animal work.

These remain speculative extrapolations from preclinical findings. Human effects, optimal dosing, and long-term safety are unknown.

Dihexa’s main risk comes from strongly amplifying HGF/c-Met signaling, a pathway controlled by a proto-oncogene that drives cell growth, survival, and movement. In humans this overstimulation could promote the growth, invasion, or spread of existing or undiagnosed tumors, accelerate pre-cancerous changes, or disrupt normal tissue and neural remodeling over time, potentially leading to cancer progression or unpredictable long-term changes in brain connectivity, all without any human safety data to show how likely or severe those effects would be.

For me personally, I don’t use it for direct muscle-building. There’s no real evidence it does anything anabolic or improves recovery in the traditional sense. What I’ve noticed when I pair it with tesofensine is better mental endurance, cleaner focus for long work sessions (especially content, research, and strategy), less brain fog, and an easier time staying locked in on training and learning movements. It feels like it supports the cognitive side of progress, research skills, content creation, staying consistent with biohacking experiments, and keeping my head clear while pushing physique goals. Results aren’t dramatic for everyone and some people feel almost nothing, but for me the combination has been worth keeping around.

Safety is completely unknown in humans. No real long-term data. Theoretical cancer concern because of the pathway, plus the usual risks of research chemicals. It’s not FDA-approved and banned in sport under non-approved substance rules. This is just my experience with it as a research compound. 

To me, it’s the real limitless compound.

text:
The Blockchain Revolution Is Moving Into Your Bank Account — Not Your Wallet

Stablecoins, Wall Street and the Battle to Control the Next Generation of Money

Imagine running a small business in the United States.

You need to pay an overseas supplier. You send an international wire, wait for banking hours, deal with intermediary institutions and reconcile the payment.

The money may be digital, but the financial infrastructure behind it still operates around traditional banking systems.

Now imagine being able to move dollar-denominated value across borders, at almost any hour, with settlement recorded on a blockchain.

No complicated crypto trading interface. No need to speculate on Bitcoin. Just a different way to move money.

This is the opportunity behind stablecoins.

And something important is happening in the United States right now.

The blockchain industry is gradually moving away from its original identity as a speculative cryptocurrency market and toward something much more consequential:

Financial infrastructure.

But I don't think the most important question is whether blockchain will replace banks.

I think the real question is:

Who will own the infrastructure, distribution and customer relationships when money starts moving on-chain?

1. The Regulatory Turning Point Has Arrived

On October 21, 2026, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced its final rule implementing the GENIUS Act.

The rule establishes requirements for payment stablecoin issuers under OCC jurisdiction, covering:

Reserve assets.
Redemption requirements.
Risk management.
Audits and reporting.
Supervision and custody.
Capital and operational safeguards.

The final rule becomes effective January 18, 2027.

This is an important development because stablecoins are no longer operating entirely in an environment defined by regulatory uncertainty.

The Federal Reserve is also developing its own implementation framework, including proposed requirements for reserve backing, capital and risk management. Its current comment deadline is November 30, 2026.

However, the regulatory framework is not completely finished. Anti-money-laundering and sanctions requirements are still being addressed through separate rulemaking.

The distinction matters.

Regulatory clarity can make it easier for banks, payment companies and institutional investors to participate.

But regulation does not automatically create customers.

That is the next challenge.

Sources: OCC final rule | Federal Reserve proposal
2. Visa Is Already Testing the New Financial Infrastructure

One of the most interesting developments came on September 30.

Visa and Lloyds Banking Group announced a live stablecoin settlement pilot.

During a seven-day trial, Lloyds used USDC to settle $750,000 in payment obligations with Visa.

The funds reached Visa in under an hour, including over the weekend.

There is an important technical detail here.

This was not a demonstration of consumers buying groceries with cryptocurrency.

It was a test of institutional settlement: the process through which financial institutions exchange funds and complete payment obligations.

Lloyds used its own node on the Canton network, while Visa supported settlement on a separate public blockchain.

The experiment therefore also tested interoperability between private and public blockchain environments.

Why does this matter?

Traditional payment networks already have enormous distribution.

They do not necessarily need to replace their existing systems to benefit from blockchain.

They can integrate blockchain settlement into the infrastructure they already operate.

That is a very different competitive strategy from trying to replace Visa entirely.

Source: Visa and Lloyds stablecoin settlement pilot

3. Coinbase and Citi Are Building the Bridge Between Two Financial Systems

Another development deserves attention.

On September 28, Coinbase announced an expanded collaboration with Citi.

The arrangement connects Coinbase's stablecoin infrastructure with Citi's regulated banking infrastructure.

Coinbase Virtual Accounts allow businesses to receive traditional fiat payments and automatically convert incoming funds into stablecoins.

Meanwhile, Citi's institutional merchant clients can accept stablecoin payments through its Spring platform.

Coinbase handles conversion back into fiat, while Citi settles the funds as the bank of record.

Think about the implications.

A merchant may be able to accept a stablecoin payment without ever having to manage stablecoins directly.

This is potentially a much more powerful adoption model than expecting millions of ordinary consumers to download crypto wallets and understand blockchain networks.

The technology becomes invisible.

The customer simply sees a payment system that works.

This is how infrastructure often wins: not by demanding that everyone understand it, but by removing friction from something people already do.

Source: Coinbase and Citi partnership

4. But There Is a Problem: Blockchain Transaction Volume Is Not the Same as Real Economic Adoption

Here is where I would challenge the industry's enthusiasm.

Stablecoin transaction volumes are frequently reported in the trillions of dollars.

That sounds enormous.

But how much of this activity represents actual payments for goods and services?

McKinsey and Artemis Analytics examined this issue in February 2026.

Their analysis estimated annualized actual stablecoin payment activity at approximately $390 billion, representing around 0.02% of global payment volumes.

The authors explained that much of the much larger headline transaction volume consists of cryptocurrency trading, internal fund movements and automated blockchain activity.

The Kansas City Federal Reserve reached a similarly important conclusion in its April 2026 analysis.

Using estimates based largely on November 2025 data, it calculated that:

Approximately 48.8% of stablecoins were being used as trading assets within crypto finance.

Approximately 29.3% were associated with transfers.
Approximately 21.2% were idle.
Only approximately 0.7% were estimated to be used for payments.
These figures are estimates, not a complete direct measurement of every stablecoin transaction. The underlying data remain incomplete.

But the message is important.

A blockchain can process enormous amounts of financial activity without becoming a major part of the real economy.

We should distinguish between three things:

Money moving between cryptocurrency exchanges.

Money moving between wallets and financial protocols.
Money actually being used by businesses and consumers to pay for something.
Only the third category directly demonstrates the payment use case that the industry frequently promotes.

Sources: McKinsey | Kansas City Fed

5. The Biggest Obstacle May Not Be Technology. It May Be Customer Demand.
This is perhaps the most revealing piece of research I found.

The Cleveland Federal Reserve published a September 2026 study examining stablecoin adoption among 148 businesses in its Fourth District.

The findings were surprisingly weak.

Only one company reported already using stablecoins.

Seven additional companies said they planned to use them.

The remaining respondents generally had no plans, had never heard of stablecoins or did not know whether they would adopt them.

The businesses cited several reasons:

Existing payment methods already worked.

Customers and suppliers were not demanding stablecoin payments.

Employees lacked familiarity with the technology.
Regulatory and operational risks remained concerns.
This was a regional survey conducted in September 2025, not a nationally representative survey of every U.S. business in November 2026.
Nevertheless, it exposes a fundamental commercial problem.

A technology can be faster, more programmable and potentially cheaper without being sufficiently valuable to convince customers to change their existing behavior.

If a small business can already receive money through its bank, why should it introduce another financial system?

The answer must be measurable.

Lower total costs. Faster access to funds. Better international liquidity. Easier reconciliation. More reliable settlement.

Without these benefits, blockchain adoption becomes a technology project looking for a business problem.

Source: Cleveland Fed — Will US Firms Adopt Stablecoins?

6. Who Actually Captures the Economic Value?

This is the investment question I find most interesting.

Imagine that stablecoin payment activity grows tenfold.

Does that automatically mean every blockchain token becomes ten times more valuable?

Of course not.

The economic value created by a financial network can be distributed across several layers.

Layer 1: Stablecoin issuers

Issuers manage the dollar-backed tokens and the reserves supporting them.

Their competitive advantages can include trust, liquidity, redemption access, regulatory permissions and distribution.

The economics of reserve management are important, particularly as the regulatory framework evolves.

Layer 2: Banks and custodians

Banks can provide reserve custody, fiat conversion, institutional accounts and regulatory infrastructure.

Rather than being eliminated by blockchain, some banks may become essential participants in the new system.

Layer 3: Payment networks and distribution

Visa, Mastercard, Coinbase and Stripe are particularly interesting because they already have relationships with businesses and consumers.

They do not necessarily need to convince everyone to adopt a new financial interface.

They can integrate blockchain into existing products.

This creates a significant distribution advantage.

Layer 4: Blockchain infrastructure

Networks provide transaction execution, settlement and security.

Different chains compete on transaction costs, reliability, throughput, liquidity and developer ecosystems.

But there is an important distinction between network adoption and token value capture.

More transactions do not automatically translate into higher token prices.

The economic value must flow through actual network fees, security incentives, token utility and sustainable demand.

Layer 5: Application and integration businesses

This is a layer I think investors sometimes overlook.

Businesses need:

Wallet infrastructure.

Payment APIs.

Compliance monitoring.
Transaction reconciliation.
Cross-chain interoperability.
Fraud prevention.
Accounting integration.
Institutional custody.
The most valuable companies may not be the ones building the most visible blockchain.
They may be the ones making blockchain usable for businesses that do not want to understand blockchain.

7. The Risks That Could Stop This Transition

I do not think the transition is guaranteed.

There are several structural risks.

First: Reserve and redemption risk.

A dollar-pegged token is not automatically equivalent to a dollar deposited in an FDIC-insured bank account.

The FDIC does not insure crypto assets. The GENIUS Act does not turn payment stablecoins into government-guaranteed bank deposits.

The quality of reserves, custody arrangements and redemption mechanisms remains fundamental.

Second: Smart contract and bridge vulnerabilities.

The Kansas City Fed highlighted the lack of interoperability across blockchain networks.

Moving assets between networks introduces additional infrastructure and security dependencies.

Third: Regulatory and compliance risk.

A blockchain transaction may settle quickly, but financial institutions still need to comply with applicable identity verification, anti-money-laundering and sanctions requirements.

Fourth: Liquidity and conversion risk.

A payment is only useful if the recipient can reliably convert or spend the received value.

A cheap blockchain transaction does not guarantee a cheap end-to-end financial transaction.

Fifth: Competition from traditional finance.

Banks are not standing still.

If traditional payment networks modernize their settlement infrastructure and offer similar speed, reliability and pricing, stablecoins will have to compete on more than technological novelty.

Source: FDIC Deposit Insurance

8. What I Would Monitor Over the Next 12 Months

I would focus on evidence of commercial adoption rather than token prices.

My research dashboard would track:

IndicatorWhat it tells usAdjusted payment volumeWhether real economic usage is growingActive business usersWhether companies are adopting the infrastructureRepeat transactionsWhether customers find lasting valueRedemption performanceWhether the dollar peg is operationally credibleCross-chain settlementWhether interoperability is improvingOn/off-ramp costsWhether the system is genuinely cheaperNetwork fee revenueWhether infrastructure captures economic valueInstitutional partnershipsWhether traditional finance is integrating the technology

I would also monitor the competitive positioning of USDC, USDT, RLUSD, PYUSD and newer institutional payment stablecoins.
Importantly, market capitalization alone is not enough.
A token can grow substantially because investors hold it as crypto-market liquidity without becoming a widely used payment instrument.
The two activities should never be confused.
9. My Conclusion: Blockchain May Win by Becoming Invisible
I used to think the blockchain revolution would be defined by people adopting cryptocurrencies.
I increasingly think that is the wrong way to measure its long-term success.
Imagine a future in which:
A small American business pays an overseas supplier in seconds.
A freelancer receives international payments without waiting for traditional banking windows.
Financial institutions settle obligations around the clock.
Merchants accept digital dollar payments without managing crypto wallets.
Businesses automate parts of their treasury operations through programmable financial infrastructure.
The customer may never know which blockchain processed the transaction.
And that may be precisely the point.
The biggest infrastructure transformations do not always require consumers to adopt a completely new behavior.
They often happen underneath familiar products.
But I would not declare victory yet.
The regulatory framework is advancing. Major financial institutions are experimenting. Payment infrastructure companies are integrating stablecoins.
However, independent evidence of broad commercial adoption is still developing.
The next phase will be decided by actual customer demand, repeat usage, reliable settlement and sustainable economics.

My thesis is that the biggest winners in blockchain may not be the companies selling the most tokens. They may be the companies controlling the trusted infrastructure and distribution through which digital dollars move.

The blockchain industry spent years trying to convince the world to enter its ecosystem.

Now its biggest opportunity may be to enter the world's existing financial ecosystem.

And that is a much bigger commercial challenge.

— Le Wang
Founder, Teraliq Quant

Independent Research | AI · Markets · Risk · Financial Infrastructure

Evidence over hype.

Sources & Further Reading

OCC — GENIUS Act Final Rule, October 21, 2026
Reuters — Coinbase Adds Ripple's RLUSD, October 28, 2026
Visa — Stablecoins Gain Traction in Business Payments, October 1, 2026
Visa and Lloyds — Cross-Border Stablecoin Settlement Pilot, September 30, 2026
Coinbase and Citi — Institutional Stablecoin Infrastructure, September 28, 2026

Cleveland Federal Reserve — Will US Firms Adopt Stablecoins?, September 28, 2026

McKinsey — Stablecoins in Payments: What the Raw Transaction Numbers Miss, February 18, 2026

It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (CAPTAIN’S voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.

text:
Tutor Intelligence rents out its Cassie palletizing robot for $14 to $18 an hour. Its own job ads offer the remote operators who guide those robots $20 to $23.

The Watertown, Massachusetts startup just closed a $75M Series B led by a16z, bringing total funding to $117M. Customers pay per robot-hour or per pick, Tutor keeps the hardware, and remote “tutors” steer the fleet through real shifts in US factories and warehouses. So the math only works if one tutor covers several robots at once, and more of them every quarter. Strip away the headline and this round is a bet on how fast humans-per-robot falls.

If you run end-of-line palletizing, that’s good news for your ROI sheet, because the rate is all-in with maintenance and model updates included. The supervision cost is the vendor’s problem now. Best-paid worker in the building, and he’s never on the floor.

The shell isn't attached to this hermit crab. Its soft, curved abdomen fits inside the old snail shell, and tiny appendages called uropods help grip the inner spiral. That hidden anchor lets the crab carry its shelter—but the shell can't grow with it. Would a roomier shell still be worth moving into if its balance felt wrong?
