WHAT GLOBAL PALESTINE MASS HYSTERIA ? (And what bloodlust fervor that defies rationality in the Free Palestine movement that in a few years has swept and infected the world like a latter-day Covid-like pandemic ?)  

“Free Palestine”—the slogan, the fantasy, and the policy—has always consciously implied the mass murder of Jews in their towns, streets, shops, and living rooms. Few are willing to say so openly, but in many intellectual, professional, and popular circles in the Middle East and the West, the idea of Palestinian national liberation has long been framed in terms that condone or necessitate the indiscriminate killing of Jews. For more unambiguous actors such as Hamas and the Islamic Republic of Iran, freeing Palestine simply means the total eradication of Israel without qualification. This is not a polemical point, but a basic reality and fact of our lives that demands scrutiny.  

Consider the ideological milieu in which many Arabs and Muslims have been raised, including me. Growing up as a Muslim in Egypt, the concept of Palestine was never a geopolitical issue; it was a deeply ingrained part of our collective moral identity, the unifying element of both our religious and secular Arab nationalism. It was, and remains, a cause that resonated with us politically, socially, and spiritually, often approaching a fervor that defies rationality. This emotional charge, embedded in the political and religious narratives of much of the Arab Muslim world, has made rubbish of the idea that the Palestinian cause is merely based on anti-Zionism rather than antisemitism.  

This milieu, however, is not in any way essential to what it means to be Arab or Muslim—it is a thoroughly modern phenomenon shaped largely by the influence of European revolutionary ideologies on Arab intellectuals and political activists. Among these imported systems of thought is a strain of revolutionary antisemitism that casts Jews as the eternal enemy not just of Arabs but of all human beings. Not every Arab or Muslim subscribes to these views, of course, but when fused with preexisting religious and cultural biases, they have infected almost every institution, pattern of thought, and aspect of life in the Arab Muslim world. Modern Arab political and religious literature is filled with the claim that Jews are hostis humani generis, the enemies of mankind—a classical European libel, and a French revolutionary cry.  

The problems of this poisonous strain of thought are compounded by the concept that “freeing Palestine” is a species of resistance against foreign settler colonialists, a Fanonian revolution in which violence against civilians is defended as a legitimate means of achieving racial justice. The wholesale labeling of Israeli Jews—the vast majority of whom are refugees or descendants of refugees from Arab Muslim dictatorships and Soviet totalitarianism—as colonizers, settlers, and imperialists is in fact a type of collective ethnic punishment, nonsensical even on its own twisted terms, which recalls the medieval Christian denunciation of Jews as moral abominations, as a group and as individuals. You might have noticed in the last few days that those committed to liberating Palestine can’t seem to avoid the abject dehumanization of the Jews as a people—and that their aim is not for Palestinians to simply live in peace, dignity, and freedom alongside Israelis, but a state that is necessarily established upon the ruins of Israel. Hamas is explicit in its intention to murder the Jewish population of Israel and enslave any survivors; its partisans in the Middle East and the West are coyer on this point.  

Islamists articulate the fantasy of Jewish eradication in the language of jihad, framed in eschatological terms, and imbued with a sense of divine justice and cosmic warfare—what Westerners would ordinarily recognize as a type of religious fascism. But while the Islamist version of this idea is potent for the purposes of mobilizing the impoverished and uneducated masses, the “left-wing” or secular version—couched in the language of Fanon and Karl Marx, of human emancipation, equality, anti-capitalism, and social justice—is the more effective means of mobilizing opinion among the Western intelligentsia. The point is that they are two sides of the same coin, the value of which is set in Jewish blood.  

For those who are shaped by such a worldview—whether the “right-wing” or the “left-wing” version, the religious or the atheistic—celebrating the murder of innocent Israeli civilians, including children, women, and the elderly, is an expression of the partial fulfillment of a moral vision. As a teenager in Egypt, I recall nearly all the adults around me expressing such feelings when following the news of suicide bombings targeting Israeli civilians during the Second Intifada. Egypt’s most prominent religious authorities declared the perpetrators to be martyrs and saints. In a way, it was not unlike the valorization and even canonization of those who destroyed livelihoods, burned property, and targeted police officers during the protests in America in the summer of 2020. I do not mean to inject American domestic politics where they do not belong, or to suggest a perfect moral equivalence, but there is a reason that leaders of Hamas and the Islamic Republic of Iran themselves insist that they are engaged in the same struggle against racism.  

Almost every Arab Muslim knows that what I’m describing is not a personal opinion but objective reality. We may try to belittle these facts, or dismiss them as the delusional daydreams of uneducated know-nothings under the influence of religious and populist fanatics. But we should not deny that they are true.  

My fear is that the impulse to dismiss and belittle is the byproduct not of sincere belief but of a deep sense of helplessness. After many recent conversations with the rising generation of young, intelligent, Westernized, and highly educated Arab professionals and diplomats, I have witnessed a strong urge not to confront this reality. Even among those who genuinely accept the legitimacy of Israel in a way their parents would have never been capable of, I almost always hear them describe the deaths of innocent Israelis as somehow being their own fault, or at least the fault of the Israeli government for not unilaterally making peace and ending the conflict. There is nothing more depressing than the surrender of the young to a problem they see as too big to solve.  

Those of us who belong to the cosmopolitan professional class of Arabs, who jump from country to country and from one lifestyle to another, benefiting from foreign cultures that live on the moral currency of liberalism and tolerance, are in many cases secretly ashamed. We see the antisemitism, the bloodlust, the insanity, and we cringe—but we hope it goes away. It’s easier for us to look forward to a hypothetical future where things are otherwise. It’s easier to ingratiate ourselves to the new social world where we want to belong, rather than grapple with the failures of the one we’ve left behind. We dismiss, we belitte, we explain away, we say, “What about Shireen Abu Akleh?”—and we go on pretending.  

But even we are not as fresh or youthful as we like to think. We are walking in the footsteps of previous generations of modernizing, secular, intellectual Arabs. They too wanted nothing to do with their native lands, which they saw as having none of the power, prestige, or respect they craved. In their egotism and intellectual narcissism, they didn’t want to belong to “backward” societies. So they sought in foreign, mostly Western ideologies a refuge and a hiding place from backwardness. They joined the progressive secular movements and trendy revolutions because they offered an escape hatch from the drudgery of slow, marginal, local change. They became revolutionaries because they were afraid and insecure. Like Edward Said, they were anti-Zionist and anti-American “humanists” because they did not want to be, or could not be, “Arabs.” Their obvious cultural chauvinism was simply an urge to self-annihilate, to disappear into universalism. Their lives were a hopeless quest to shed their own skin.  

To the Arabs of my own generation, I say we need a truly different approach. I’m not asking you to love Israel or Zionism, or to hang a poster of hipster Herzl in your bedroom. If you are critical of Israel and think there should be a Palestine, continue to do so. All I ask is for you to be authentically courageous, to admit that the murder we all witnessed in the last few days is an accurate representation and logical consequence of a catastrophic moral system, the one we all know intimately. This is a moment for collective introspection. It’s time to confront the darker corners of our ideological heritage, and question the ideas and beliefs we may have uncritically absorbed. Only by doing so can we hope to contribute to a more constructive and humane world for ourselves.  

Hussein Aboubakr Mansour (October 10, 2023)

Think about it. Same coin. Two sides.

Could it be that prosecuting Smith would bring investigators dangerously close to the very evidence surrounding January 6 and Mar-a-Lago that Trump and his allies have spent years trying to discredit?

His thesis about chemical crutches for people sustaining a system they know is hollow lands hard.

 In the US the parallel is not primarily cocaine among the political class. It is marijuana, the default anesthetic for the broad left since the mid-1990s and especially after legalization.

Recreational marijuana is now legal for adults in 24 states plus Washington, D.C. Medical programs cover most of the rest. That formalization followed decades of cultural work that began with the 1960s hippie counterculture, where pot was both sacrament and political signal of rejection of the “system,” and accelerated from the mid-1990s. 

The “just a plant, basically harmless” framing won in media, entertainment, and large parts of academia. Risk perception collapsed. Use rebounded from its early 90s low and never stopped climbing.

 Average THC rose from around 4% then  to double digits now, with commercial weed THC concentrates routinely 60–80%+. This is not the weak Mexican brick the original hippies smoked, Dave man

Monthly adult use roughly doubled in many tracking series between the 2010s and 2020s. Daily use exploded even faster. By the early 2020s the United States had more daily cannabis users than daily drinkers. That pattern holds among parents and across age groups that previously stayed away from it.

On the American left this is the signature drug. Support for legalization and reported use have long skewed heavily liberal. In practice it often functions as a form of ID or membership card. Someone offers it at a gathering, a campaign event, or a local party meeting. 

Once they know you partake, "the dude imbibes" the barrier drops. You move more easily into the inner circle. Shared use becomes a quiet signal of cultural alignment and trust.

A politics that requires constant defense of outcomes that are visibly fraying benefits from a substance that reliably blunts urgency, dampens anxiety about contradictions, and replaces “this isn’t working” with a diffuse, doper low nergy tolerance.

Unlike cocaine, which supplies manic forward momentum, marijuana supplies the softer version: the ability to keep participating in, or simply not actively resisting, a system while treating its accumulating failures as background noise rather than a prompt to exit or reform.

The hippie lineage makes the political valence explicit. The original 1960s association was antiestablishment, antiwar, and left of center. After the 1990s rebranding as medicine or harmless recreation, the same substance migrated into mainstream progressive culture while retaining its role as social lubricant and mild disengagement tool. 

Once legalization locked in the supply, heavy cannabis use became a normalized background condition in exactly the political and cultural strata most committed to defending the current American administrative and cultural order.

A functional order does not require millions of people to anesthetize their perception of it on a daily basis. As noted,the false one does. In the United States the preferred fuel, after three decades of normalization and a decades  of legalization, is marijuana.

Je me suis toujours posé la question : comment font les gens qui savent que tout le système est un mensonge pour tenir ?

Je crois avoir trouvé la réponse.

Récemment, je discutais avec un mec qui a traversé une période de sa vie sous cocaïne. Beaucoup de cocaïne. À l'époque, il bossait sur un projet financier qui était du vide intégral. Il le savait. Tout le monde autour de lui le savait. Mais ça rapportait énormément d'argent.

Pendant un an et demi, croissance délirante. Sauf que c'était de la croissance fictive. Ils se vendaient comme le « nouveau Wall Street », et toute l'équipe était sous coke. C'est ce qui leur permettait de tenir.

La drogue ne leur servait pas à faire la fête. Elle leur servait à rester branchés sur quelque chose que leur cerveau savait être faux.

Et là, j'ai fait le lien avec une question qui me travaille depuis dix ans.

Notre système. Un État qui prélève plus de la moitié de la richesse produite, qui planifie, redistribue, régule tout, jusqu'à ta façon de parler. Appelons-le par son nom : un système communiste qui ne dit pas son nom. Et ceux qui le pilotent ne sont pas des idiots. Ils ont fait les grandes écoles. Ils ont lu l'histoire. Ils savent comment ça finit, à chaque fois.

Et pourtant ils continuent. Chaque jour. Avec une énergie folle.

Comment ?

Ma thèse : une grande partie des gens qui font tenir un système profondément dysfonctionnel ont besoin d'une béquille chimique pour le faire. La cocaïne fait exactement ça. Elle te permet de rester couplé à un système complètement illégitime. Elle anesthésie le doute et remplace le sens par de l'énergie brute. Tu n'as plus besoin d'y croire. Tu as juste besoin d'avancer.

Ce n'est pas une théorie de comptoir. C'est le Premier ministre lui-même qui l'a mise sur la table.

Le 16 juin, Sébastien Lecornu signe une circulaire : tests antidrogue obligatoires et inopinés dans les ministères. Ministres, membres de cabinet, hauts fonctionnaires. Tests salivaires. Sanctions possibles jusqu'au renvoi.

Réfléchissez deux secondes à ce que ça veut dire. Le chef du gouvernement juge nécessaire de dépister le cœur de l'État. On ne dépiste pas un problème qui n'existe pas.

En juillet, dans Paris Match, Lecornu confirme : les tests ont eu lieu, et des collaborateurs ont été écartés. Il ajoute qu'environ un million de Français consomment régulièrement de la cocaïne, et que ça touche tous les milieux. Y compris celui qui gravite autour du pouvoir.

Et les noms ? Secrets. Matignon refuse de les rendre publics. Un député a même dû poser une question écrite à l'Assemblée pour réclamer les résultats.

La transparence s'est arrêtée pile au moment où ça devenait intéressant.

Pourquoi protéger le résultat si le système est sain ?

L'histoire a déjà vu ce film. Le Troisième Reich a littéralement tenu sur la méthamphétamine. La Pervitine était distribuée par millions de comprimés aux soldats de la Wehrmacht. Hitler lui-même recevait des injections de son médecin personnel, Theodor Morell, presque tous les jours. Un régime bâti sur un mensonge total a eu besoin de chimie pour que ses hommes restent debout.

Ce n'est pas un hasard. Un humain sain d'esprit ne peut pas porter un mensonge pendant des années sans se fissurer. Soit il décroche. Soit il se drogue.

Alors la prochaine fois que vous voyez quelqu'un défendre avec une énergie surhumaine un système qu'il sait condamné, posez-vous une seule question : d'où vient cette énergie ?

Le vrai tient tout seul. Le faux a besoin de carburant.

**The US decision is based on its assessment of the ANC-led South African government’s policies and actions (or inactions), not AfriForum as the primary actor.**[](<https://t.co/QnW0KHqGcW>)

### Official US reasons
President Trump notified President Ramaphosa in a 28 October 2026 letter (with the formal announcement by USTR Jamieson Greer on 2 November) of the intention to terminate South Africa’s AGOA eligibility from 1 January 2027. The stated grounds under AGOA Section 104 include:

- Failure to establish or make continual progress on systems to combat corruption and bribery.
- Significant tariff and non-tariff barriers to US trade and investment (agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections, intellectual property).
- Actions on international security and cooperation with governments of concern to the US that risk undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.[](<https://t.co/Rn8Mc2LSRX>)

US Ambassador Brent Bozell described the outcome as “predictable and preventable” due to the South African government’s rejection of concerns raised by Washington. Broader reporting links the tensions to SA policies on land/expropriation, Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (BEE), foreign policy (including the ICJ case against Israel and ties with Russia, China, and others), and related issues. These are policy choices of the ANC-led government.[](<https://t.co/QLT8NiyqvN>)

AGOA is a unilateral US preference program. The US President determines eligibility annually against the statutory criteria; the decision-maker is the US executive.

### AfriForum’s role
AfriForum and Solidarity have long lobbied in the US on property rights, the Expropriation Act (which allows for expropriation without compensation), farm security/crime, and what they describe as race-based discrimination under BEE and related laws. They have met US officials and raised these issues, which align with some of the concerns the Trump administration has voiced.[](<https://t.co/3rdnbOBIzO>)

AfriForum publicly blames President Ramaphosa and ANC leaders for the policies that triggered the outcome, noting they had warned about risks (including from the Expropriation Act) and that ordinary South Africans will bear the costs. Critics, including COSATU, counter that AfriForum’s lobbying and framing of issues (including around farm murders and “persecution” narratives, which the SA government rejects) damaged bilateral relations and contributed to the political climate that led to the termination.[](<https://t.co/4cvMwPp7bv>)

AfriForum has stated it does not support measures that punish ordinary citizens and previously argued against a full AGOA exit while acknowledging that SA government policies conflicted with the eligibility criteria.

### Bottom line
- **Primary responsibility for the policies cited by the US** rests with the ANC government, which sets trade, anti-corruption, land, transformation, and foreign policy.
- **AfriForum** is a private advocacy group whose lobbying amplified certain domestic concerns in Washington and helped shape perceptions (especially under an administration already critical of SA). It did not enact the policies or make the US decision.
- The SA government says it offered concessions in negotiations and that the US raised new issues; it is preparing support for affected sectors. AGOA covered a relatively small share of SA’s total exports (around 10% of exports to the US and ~1% of global exports in 2025).

Nuclear Versus Conventional Strikes on Iran: Military Feasibility, Fallout and Strategic Escalation Through 2028 - Principal judgment — High confidence: The existence of an American nuclear earth-penetrating weapon does not establish that nuclear employment against a deeply buried Iranian facility would reliably eliminate the target or produce an acceptable strategic outcome. The principal distinction is between physical destruction, verified elimination of nuclear capabilities and the political consequences of crossing the nuclear threshold.

The B61-11 is an established strategic nuclear gravity-bomb modification, whereas the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator has documented conventional employment against Iranian nuclear-related infrastructure during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025. These capabilities have fundamentally different radiological consequences, command requirements and strategic implications.

The operational baseline has changed materially since June 2025. U.S. Central Command officially records the commencement of Operation Epic Fury on 28 February 2026 and reported more than 9,000 targets struck, 9,000 combat flights and 140 Iranian vessels damaged or destroyed by 23 March 2026. These are command-reported cumulative figures, not an independently established assessment of the Iranian nuclear programme’s destruction.

High confidence: Nuclear detonation at or below ground level can create severe radioactive contamination when surrounding material is entrained into the radioactive cloud. A buried nuclear facility cannot therefore be evaluated solely by the amount of structural damage inflicted.

High confidence: The U.S. President holds sole nuclear-use authorisation authority under the established American command system, subject to the requirement that military orders comply with applicable law. That authority does not establish the legality of any particular first-use decision.

Medium confidence: Nuclear employment against a non-nuclear-weapon state would create exceptionally consequential risks for alliance cohesion, international nuclear restraint, regional escalation and the credibility of non-proliferation commitments, even where a geographically limited military objective were achieved.

Decisive uncertainty — Low confidence in facility-specific claims: The available official record does not establish the complete internal arrangement, operational status, material inventory or actual vulnerability of the Pickaxe Mountain/Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La complex. No defensible public assessment can guarantee its destruction through either nuclear or conventional attack.

Decision implication: The controlling policy question is not whether nuclear explosive power exceeds conventional explosive power. It is whether any additional, demonstrable and durable military effect could justify the distinct legal, humanitarian, alliance and proliferation consequences of nuclear first use.

Iran’s Nuclear Facilities: Why Greater Destructive Power Cannot Deliver Strategic Certainty
The United States has demonstrated its ability to strike Iran’s hardened nuclear infrastructure, but the decisive problem remains unresolved: military destruction has not restored independent knowledge of Iran’s nuclear-material inventory. On 27 October 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) still could not verify approximately 440 kilograms of previously declared highly enriched uranium, despite the American conventional operations of 2025 and 2026. This discrepancy exposes the central weakness of arguments favouring nuclear earth-penetrating weapons against underground installations such as Pickaxe Mountain. Greater explosive power could increase physical destruction without guaranteeing the elimination of nuclear capabilities, while introducing radioactive contamination, international legal controversy and a historic precedent of nuclear first use. For Washington, the immediate question is whether additional military force can produce verifiable strategic results without increasing the security and economic costs already borne by its allies.

The 440-Kilogram Verification Gap Is More Consequential Than the Destruction of Another Facility
The nuclear confrontation has entered a phase in which the condition of Iranian infrastructure and the status of Iranian nuclear material can no longer be treated as equivalent measures of success. During the United Nations Security Council proceedings of 27 October 2026, IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi identified the continuing inability of the Agency to verify previously declared nuclear material, including approximately 440 kilograms of highly enriched uranium. Normal inspections had not resumed, although monitoring arrangements differed among facilities. The Agency also reported no identified reconstruction activity at installations damaged during the 2025–2026 attacks. These findings establish two different realities: observable physical damage has persisted at certain locations, while the accounting of strategically relevant nuclear material remains incomplete.

The distinction matters because an enrichment programme is not reducible to an underground chamber. Nuclear material, centrifuge manufacturing, specialised engineering knowledge and industrial reconstruction capacity represent different elements of capability. Destroying a facility can interrupt production without determining where previously declared uranium is located or whether equivalent manufacturing capacity remains available elsewhere. Conversely, the absence of observed reconstruction does not establish that Iran has abandoned nuclear-related activities. The IAEA’s October assessment therefore reveals a fundamental limitation of military coercion: physical destruction can be documented without resolving the proliferation uncertainty that originally justified the attack.

The approximately 440-kilogram figure is not an independently measured November 2026 inventory, nor does it establish that Iran possesses operational nuclear weapons. It represents previously declared material whose status has not been adequately verified. That qualification is decisive. Transforming an unresolved safeguards figure into a claim about an existing arsenal would distort the evidence; interpreting the lack of verification as evidence that the material has been destroyed would produce an equally unsupported conclusion.

The B61-11 Can Deliver Nuclear Destruction, but Not Guaranteed Programme Elimination
The technical debate surrounding Iran’s deeply buried infrastructure is frequently distorted by an inadequate comparison between conventional penetration and nuclear explosive yield. The United States maintains the B61-11 as a strategic nuclear gravity-bomb modification, while the GBU-57/B Massive Ordnance Penetrator represents a specialised conventional capability with documented combat employment during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025. The American Air Force’s published technical characteristics describe the GBU-57/B as a weapon weighing approximately 30,000 pounds, or 13.6 metric tonnes, with more than 5,300 pounds of explosive material in the historical configuration documented by the service.

The B61-11 operates through fundamentally different physics. Nuclear detonation can produce substantial subsurface destructive effects beyond those associated with conventional explosive energy, but this does not establish the elimination of every protected chamber or industrial function. The National Research Council’s 2005 study, Effects of Nuclear Earth-Penetrator and Other Weapons, concluded that nuclear earth-penetrating weapons could threaten categories of underground targets inaccessible to conventional penetrators. It also established that available earth-penetration technology could not achieve the burial necessary to contain radioactive consequences reliably. Nuclear explosive power therefore creates both an additional destructive capability and a distinct environmental liability.

The engineering uncertainty is particularly important at Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, known as Pickaxe Mountain, approximately two kilometres south of Natanz. Construction activity documented from 2020 and intensified during 2026 indicates sustained investment in protected infrastructure. Published estimates place parts of the complex approximately 80–100 metres underground, but those estimates are not verified chamber measurements. The actual internal configuration, industrial equipment and nuclear-material inventory remain insufficiently established. Consequently, neither the B61-11 nor the GBU-57/B can be assigned a credible probability of complete destruction using the available public evidence.

The strategic issue is not whether a nuclear explosion would merely damage the mountain’s surface. The relevant distinction is between substantial underground destruction and demonstrable, irreversible elimination of Iran’s wider nuclear capability. The former is physically possible; the latter requires evidence that explosive yield cannot supply.

Nuclear Fallout Would Transform a Military Operation Into a Persistent Liability
Nuclear employment against an underground installation would introduce consequences fundamentally different from those of a conventional strike. The National Research Council’s 2005 assessment found that shallow underground nuclear detonations could release substantial radioactive material into the atmosphere, generating fallout hazards extending beyond the immediate area of physical destruction. In one historical modelling exercise, fallout accounted for approximately 75% of casualties associated with a modelled 10-kiloton earth-penetrator explosion. That result is not a prediction for Iran or the B61-11, but it demonstrates why underground nuclear employment cannot be assessed exclusively through local structural damage.

The resulting problem would extend into nuclear verification itself. A contaminated installation could become difficult for inspectors and technical personnel to enter, while radioactive products generated by the explosion could complicate the identification and accounting of materials previously present. Military destruction might therefore increase the physical inaccessibility of a facility without increasing certainty about the nuclear material it contained. This is a particularly important consideration when the IAEA has already identified substantial unresolved material-accounting gaps.

The international legal consequences would be equally distinct. The International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion of 8 July 1996, Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons, established that nuclear threats and employment remain subject to the United Nations Charter and international humanitarian law. The Court did not grant general permission for nuclear attacks against suspected proliferation-related infrastructure. A decision to employ nuclear weapons against Iran would therefore require legal scrutiny concerning the justification for force, civilian protection, expected radiological consequences and military proportionality, independently of the political importance assigned to the target.

The consequence for American decision-making is structural: nuclear force could increase the magnitude of physical destruction while making the verification, humanitarian and diplomatic dimensions of the confrontation more difficult to resolve.

Hormuz Demonstrates That Military Escalation Already Has a Measurable Economic Price
The economic consequences of the Iranian confrontation are no longer hypothetical. According to the United States Energy Information Administration, oil and petroleum-liquids transit through the Strait of Hormuz declined from 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, a contraction of approximately 77.3%. Over the same comparison period, liquefied natural gas transit fell from 10.5 billion to 0.8 billion cubic feet per day, a decline of approximately 92.4%. These figures measure maritime flows rather than global production losses, but they establish the exceptional scale of the disruption affecting a critical international energy corridor.

The EIA’s October 2026 outlook projected average Brent crude prices of $96 per barrel in 2026 and $84 in 2027, compared with the September outlook’s respective forecasts of $91 and $74. The October revision reflects the continuing vulnerability of Middle Eastern exports and infrastructure. Brent had averaged $114 per barrel during September 2026 and reached a reported daily price of $131 on 15 September following attacks affecting Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline. That pipeline had carried more than five million barrels per day through Yanbu, demonstrating that alternative export routes reduce dependence on Hormuz without eliminating infrastructure exposure.

The industrial transmission mechanism extends well beyond oil producers. Restricted tanker movements, insurance uncertainty and higher delivered energy costs affect refineries, manufacturers, shipping operators and energy-importing economies. For Europe, this creates an additional security-policy constraint: continued military escalation can increase industrial costs while governments remain dependent on transatlantic security cooperation. A nuclear event would introduce further uncertainty into an energy market already operating under disrupted maritime conditions, although no defensible model permits assigning a precise oil price to nuclear first use.

Washington’s Military Authority Does Not Resolve the Alliance Problem
The American nuclear command system gives the President sole authority to authorise nuclear employment, subject to the requirement that military orders comply with applicable law. This institutional concentration does not eliminate the international consequences of the decision. Nuclear first use against Iran would establish a precedent affecting the strategic calculations of Russia, China, NATO allies and states considering whether nuclear deterrence provides protection against coercion.

The European position is particularly differentiated. On 15 June 2026, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer welcomed the United States–Iran memorandum of understanding and emphasised verifiable nuclear commitments and freedom of navigation through Hormuz. Their joint declaration demonstrated common opposition to Iranian nuclear-weapons acquisition, but it did not establish support for nuclear military action.

France and the United Kingdom possess independent nuclear deterrents and would have to assess the implications of American first use for their own doctrines. Germany would confront the consequences for NATO nuclear arrangements and domestic legal-political commitments, while Italy would face the combined exposure of Mediterranean security, alliance consultation and energy dependence. The European Union would have to coordinate diplomatic and economic measures among governments with different military responsibilities.

Russia and China would confront a separate strategic problem. Nuclear employment against a non-nuclear adversary could alter their interpretation of American escalation doctrine without necessarily producing direct military intervention. The more consequential medium-term effect might concern future nuclear crises and proliferation incentives. States observing the event could reassess whether nuclear acquisition or stronger external security guarantees offered greater protection against coercion. Such responses are not predetermined, but their possibility demonstrates why a geographically limited attack could produce consequences extending well beyond Iran.

The Next 24 Months Will Be Determined by Verification, Not Explosive Yield
Three pathways frame the confrontation through December 2028. Under continued nuclear restraint, the principal question would be whether diplomacy and safeguards can restore reliable knowledge of Iranian nuclear material while maritime security stabilises. Under further conventional escalation, additional infrastructure damage could occur without resolving nuclear-material accounting, potentially prolonging the cycle of military disruption and reconstruction. Under nuclear first use, significant physical destruction could coexist with radioactive contamination, uncertain programme-wide effects and a lasting change in the international nuclear non-use precedent established since 1945.

The immediate institutional constraint is already visible. On 27 October 2026, the IAEA still lacked the access required to verify the previously declared highly enriched uranium. The United States and its European partners therefore confront a problem that additional explosive force cannot independently settle: verifying the location and status of nuclear material after extensive military operations. The June diplomatic framework demonstrated that negotiations remain possible, but the September regional hostilities showed that an announced agreement does not necessarily produce durable security.

Over the next 12–24 months, the costs of continued uncertainty will fall on several constituencies. Iranian civilians face the consequences of infrastructure damage, economic pressure and possible renewed hostilities. Gulf governments and commercial operators face the costs of maritime insecurity. European manufacturers and energy importers remain exposed to disruptions transmitted through petroleum, gas, insurance and freight markets. Washington bears the diplomatic and strategic costs of sustaining military pressure without independently verified nuclear restraint.

The governing contradiction is therefore measurable: the United States possesses the ability to inflict extensive physical destruction, but the October 2026 safeguards record shows that this has not produced verified programme-wide nuclear elimination. Nuclear first use would increase the destructive and radiological consequences while crossing a historical threshold whose implications would persist beyond the immediate conflict. By December 2028, the relevant measure of success will not be the number of facilities damaged or the explosive power employed, but whether nuclear-material accounting, industrial restrictions and regional security have become independently verifiable and politically sustainable. -

If Nero is remembered for playing his lyre as Rome burned, Trump seems to have taken the metaphor into the modern age: fires are spreading across the world, while he sits in the White House playing his guitar.

Few elections anywhere in the world like the American elections - both presidential and midterm -, have the power to trigger a butterfly effect across the globe. The ballot box in Washington can sometimes resemble Pandora's box where its consequences reach far beyond America's borders.

Consider Harry Truman's presidency and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, among the greatest human tragedies of modern history. Consider George W. Bush and the invasion of Iraq, followed by years of devastating human and strategic consequences. And now Trump, whose policies have set fires across multiple regions of the world, while his rhetoric has fueled racial hostility, polarization, and divisions among peoples.

Perhaps John F. Kennedy's presidency offered a brief glimpse of light amid a much darker political landscape. His tenure lasted less than three years before his assassination in Dallas brought it to an abrupt end.

Yet history is not condemned to repeat itself, and elections do not determine the future alone. Institutions, public awareness, accountability, and international cooperation can all help restrain power and redirect political trajectories.

If American elections can change the course of the world, the collective awareness and responsibility of its peoples can help change that course too.

A new Islamic defense axis? Why India is watching the Badr accord closely
The new pact between Türkiye, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia brings money and military technology together in ways New Delhi will have to track carefully
Published 3 Nov, 2026 
https://t.co/GZhjDE3KPu
By Air Marshal Anil Chopra (Retired), an Indian Air Force veteran fighter test pilot and is the former Director-General of the Center for Air Power Studies in New Delhi.
-------
Türkiye, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia signed the ‘Badr’ defense cooperation accord in the Qatari capital, Doha, on October 21. It is intended to deepen their defense industry cooperation, reflecting a broader effort by countries in the region to widen their network of security partners amid the prolonged US-Israel war on Iran.
The four countries are planning to build on existing military projects through joint production, technology transfers, and more closely integrated supply chains. The initiative is a result of the failure of the US and Iran to reach a concrete peace agreement, which pushes countries in the region to diversify their defense partnerships and look beyond overreliance on Washington for their security.
The four countries clarified, however, that closer cooperation does not mean abandoning long-standing alliances. Instead, the ambition is to gain greater control over their own security while strengthening pre-existing partnerships.
The implications could extend well beyond the four participants. It will impact both the Gulf Region and South East Asia. India, for instance, has been watching the Mecca Accord which earlier brought Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia together. Now, Badr brings in Indonesia, a country with the largest Muslim population, and with which New Delhi is involved in practical cooperation, including in the defense sector.
Inside the military pacts
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement (also known as the Mecca Pact), is a trilateral security pact concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan and covering collective defense, military and intelligence cooperation, defense-industrial development, logistical support, and institutional coordination. The Mutual Defense Clause in the document is modelled similarly to NATO’s Article 5, stipulating that an armed attack against any one of the three member states is regarded as an attack against them all.
The Mecca Pact builds directly upon the bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) signed between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in September 2025. Now, the trilateral alliance combines Saudi capital and energy influence, Turkish defense and drone technology, and Pakistani military manpower and strategic (nuclear) capabilities. Pakistan approved the pact, and the Turkish government officially submitted the 16-article text of the pact to the Turkish Parliament for ratification. Senior foreign and defense officials from all three nations have held committee meetings (including sessions in Istanbul and Riyadh) to coordinate implementation timelines, intelligence-sharing frameworks, and rapid-deployment logistics amid ongoing regional security tensions.
The Badr Accord (officially the Badr Memorandum of Understanding) is a joint defense cooperation agreement with a core goal to deepen military and defense industrial collaboration, move past simple “off-the-shelf” arms purchases, and build shared domestic manufacturing and technological capabilities. Focus areas include joint production of military hardware (including drones and precision missiles, airborne radars, air defense systems, and rockets).
Unlike the Mecca Accord’s mutual defense focus, the Badr Accord focuses primarily on defense-industrial cooperation rather than an automatic collective-defense trigger. The pact is designed to reduce the nations’ reliance on external Western or foreign arms suppliers and pool their complementary manufacturing strengths. Each country will bring its own resources or set of skills to the table. Türkiye contributes technological expertise, systems integration, and a mature defense industry; Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces, and sizeable domestic markets; and Qatar provides investment potential and demand.
Such arrangements could give buyers a larger role in producing and supporting their own equipment, while providing manufacturers with longer-term orders and investment. This could bring down costs for Turkish companies and bring jobs to Pakistan and Indonesia, while tapping into Qatari financial muscle.
Pakistan’s existing naval manufacturing project with Türkiye is an example of how weapons purchases can support domestic manufacturing. Of the four ships announced under the project, two are to be built in Istanbul and two at Karachi Shipyard. Türkiye and Indonesia are meanwhile jointly building a tank.
Islamic symbolism
While the Badr Accord functions strictly as an industrial framework for joint weapons production, its nomenclature is deeply rooted in Islamic religious and historical symbolism. The accord derives its name directly from the Battle of Badr (624 CE), the most consequential and spiritually significant early military engagement in Islamic history. In Islamic tradition, the Battle of Badr represents a foundational victory where a small, under-equipped group of early Muslims (around 313 men) defeated a much larger, well-armed Meccan Quraysh army (around 1,000 men) through steadfast faith and divine intervention. By choosing the name for the pact, the signatory nations explicitly invoke themes of resilience, unity, and overcoming asymmetric structural disadvantages.
The accord mirrors the civilizational alignment and focuses heavily on the practical pan-Islamic integration of defense manufacturing. The timing and religious framing of the Badr Accord reflect a collective push among these prominent Islamic republics and monarchies to build an autonomous “Islamic security layer.”
The word “Badr,” which literally translates to “full moon” in Arabic, was chosen to symbolize how the four distinct nations complement one another. The agreement aims to promote cooperation in military production, strengthen military capabilities, and support collaboration in technical military training and research and development, the Turkish Defense Ministry said.
Türkiye, under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, has actively staked a claim to leadership in the Islamic world by presenting itself as the modern heir to the Ottoman Empire and the defender of global Muslim causes. Erdogan frequently champions the Palestinian cause, opposes Western policies in the Middle East, and speaks out on issues affecting minority Muslim populations such as the Uyghurs and Rohingya, and supports Pakistan on Kashmir. As a part of NATO, Türkiye has the most developed military industry while it faces heavy competition and deep-seated political rivalry from nations like Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran, and the UAE.
Saudi Arabia is not only a significant petro-dollar economy and one of the world’s top three largest defense importers, the King of Saudi Arabia also holds the title of Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, which represents the monarch’s official responsibility for protecting and maintaining the two holiest sites in Islam.
Indonesia has the world’s largest Muslim population, with approximately 251.25 million Muslims. Pakistan follows it with a Muslim population of 231 to 234 million people. Pakistan also has the seventh largest military and possesses the so called “Islamic bomb” (nuclear weapons)...link to read full article

Trump to strip South Africa and Rwanda of US trade benefits
Washington has cited concerns over Pretoria’s handling of corruption and Kigali’s human rights record as grounds for their exclusion from AGOA
Published 3 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/1u8gfU6h5W
The US plans to strip South Africa and Rwanda of preferential access to its market next year, accusing both countries of undermining American trade and foreign policy interests.
Pretoria has pushed back, saying it would accelerate efforts to diversify export markets by pursuing opportunities elsewhere in Africa, India, the European Union, and China to protect jobs.
President Donald Trump has notified Congress and both governments of his intention to terminate their participation in the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from January 1, 2027, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced on Monday. Greer said an annual review identified “barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region.”
Washington cited corruption and trade barriers in South Africa, while its concerns about Rwanda also included human rights, workers’ rights, political pluralism, and the rule of law.
South Africa’s Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC) said it had offered additional concessions to address US concerns during negotiations that began in 2025. It accused Washington of raising “new issues that have not been the basis for discussions.”
Established in 2000, AGOA grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access for thousands of products. Trump signed an extension through December 2028 in September, but individual countries remain subject to eligibility reviews.
South Africa exported about $1.7 billion in goods under AGOA in 2025, accounting for roughly 10% of its exports to the US and 1% of its worldwide exports, according to the DTIC. The department stressed that it would accelerate efforts to diversify markets. President Cyril Ramaphosa warned last month that exclusion could have a “devastating” impact on jobs, particularly in vehicle manufacturing and agriculture.
US-South African relations have deteriorated since Trump returned to office in January 2025, with Washington halting aid and expelling Pretoria’s ambassador. Trump accused South Africa of permitting “white genocide,” which it rejects, while US lawmakers targeted its Russia and Iran ties and genocide case against Israel. Richard Neal, the senior Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, called the removal “yet another trade decision grounded in grievance” and demanded clarity on reinstatement.
Trump previously suspended Rwanda’s apparel benefits in 2018 over tariffs on imported secondhand clothing and footwear, following complaints from the American used-clothing industry.
There was no immediate response from Rwanda’s authorities to the latest move, which follows US sanctions on its Defense Ministry on October 28 over alleged support for rebels in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kigali denies backing the fighters.
Washington has repeatedly withdrawn AGOA benefits over governance and human rights concerns. Ethiopia, Guinea, and Mali lost eligibility in 2022, followed by Burkina Faso in 2023. The Central African Republic, Gabon, Niger, and Uganda were removed in January 2024. Gabon was reinstated under a proclamation issued in May 2026.

When Good News No Longer Fixes Anything: The Market Asks Who Will Pay for AI
Market analysis, 3 November 2026

Picture a day when oil loses almost eight percent, American manufacturing shows more strength than expected, and political tension between Washington and Tehran eases slightly, yet the stock market still falls. That is exactly what happened on Monday. The Nasdaq 100 lost 1.4% and, according to morning market reports, slid into correction territory. The conventional S&P 500 fell 0.5%, while the Dow Jones rose 0.4%.
This is not a contradiction. It is a message: the market regime is changing.

A Falling Index, a Rising Majority
The biggest story of Monday was not the Nasdaq’s decline but what was happening beneath the surface. Roughly twice as many S&P 500 stocks finished the day in the green as in the red. The equal-weighted index gained a good three quarters of a percent, while the conventional index, in which the technology giants carry the most weight, lost half a percent.

Investors, then, were not fleeing every risky asset. They were reallocating capital. They bought consumer, industrial, financial and materials stocks and sold the more expensive parts of the technology sector. Trading volume exceeded its twenty-day average, so the move was no accident.

Still, one day of positive breadth does not make a healthy market. Several warning indicators in the supporting material paint a different picture. Goldman’s risk appetite indicator entered the week well below its long-term average. The high-yield bond market, measured by advancing versus declining issues, remains weak, and the share of stocks in a long-term uptrend is shrinking quickly. At the same time, optimism in the options market has cooled sharply: there are far fewer stocks with strongly bullish positioning than a month ago.

Equally telling is a figure published by one market commentator: hedge funds are estimated to have cut their equity positions on a scale said to be the largest in recorded history. Even the most experienced players are reducing their exposure.

Oil Falls, Inflation Stays
Brent fell by more than seven percent on Monday, to about $105 a barrel, after US-Iran talks mediated by Qatar. In normal circumstances, that would bring relief to equities. This time it did not, for three reasons.

First, the price is still not low. Brent remains markedly more expensive than at the start of the year. The drop reflects a smaller geopolitical premium, not a solved supply problem. On Tuesday, reports of limited American defensive strikes on Iran’s island of Qeshm pushed prices up again. The market is not paying for peace; it is paying for the probability of peace.

Second, the domestic economy is not helping. The October ISM manufacturing index rose from 54.5 to 55.5, and output is strong, but the prices-paid index stayed at 75.2 despite easing. Activity is solid, yet costs are high. That leaves central banks little room for quick easing, so good economic news can be bad news for the most expensive stocks.

Third, the bond market said something that may prove crucial. The nominal yield on 10-year US Treasuries fell to about 4.91%, while the real yield rose slightly. Inflation expectations therefore fell by more than the nominal yield did, and companies did not get an equivalent relief in their real cost of capital. Meanwhile, high-yield credit spreads remain close to multi-month highs. The two-year yield barely reacted to the oil drop, and its chart still shows a pattern that technical analysts read as a possible move higher.

Add public finances and the picture is complete. By several sources, US interest costs as a share of GDP are at their highest level since 1985, and corporate bond supply in November is expected, by one of the largest banks, to be above average. Governments and companies are competing for the same capital.

Oracle, Marvell, Lumentum: Strategy Versus Market Value
Three stories from Monday best illustrate how the question investors ask AI companies is changing.

$ORCL  (−8.8%) set the terms for a combined $20 billion of financing: about $10 billion in new shares at $116 and $10 billion in bonds with coupons from 7.00% to 8.65%. The interest on the new issue alone comes to roughly $777 million a year. The company is thus paying twice: creditors through interest, shareholders through dilution. If the data centers generate a sufficient return, this can make perfect sense. But the time lag between investment and profit is a risk the market is now pricing in.

$MRVL  (−12.7%) and $LITE  (−18.6%)announced an all-stock acquisition worth about $115 billion, with more than a billion dollars of promised annual cost synergies. The strategic logic is clear, since optical interconnects are becoming a bottleneck for AI clusters. But the market does not value strategy alone. It also values the price, the exchange ratio, dilution and integration risk. Being right about the technology is not the same as being right about the investment.

$PLTR  may be the purest example. Revenue grew 96% to $2.31 billion, US commercial revenue grew 148%, and free cash flow exceeded a billion dollars. The result is outstanding. Yet the stock fell in extended trading after the release. The reason was the growth in the total value of new commercial contracts, which was only about 11%. When a company grows this fast, the market no longer asks whether it is growing but whether the growth can hold up on a much larger base.

The common thread is the same: a year ago, it was enough to show how much was being invested. Today the market demands to know how much cash flow it produces, how much additional capital will still be needed, and how much value will remain for shareholders.

Safety Has Become Expensive
The simple reaction to such an environment would be to flee into defensive stocks. But the supporting data show that this too is more expensive than it looks.Low-volatility S&P 500 stocks trade at about 19 times forward earnings, near their highs for the year, and the dividend-yield and value factors sit in historically high percentiles. Growth and momentum stocks, by the same measures, have become relatively cheap. We are already paying a premium for the feeling of safety, while some quality growth has become cheaper.

The Elections: A Catalyst, Not a Thesis
The US midterm elections are taking place today amid very low presidential approval and signs that voters are worried about tariffs, prices and the cost of living. Betting markets and prediction models see a Democratic sweep of both chambers as the most likely outcome, a divided Congress as less likely, and a full Republican sweep as very unlikely. Results will arrive overnight Slovenian time, and nobody knows them in advance.

History offers some encouragement, but it should not be trusted too far. In the seven cases when a Republican president lost Congress, the S&P 500’s average return over the following six and twelve months was positive. The sample is small. Returns also depend on starting valuations, economic cycles, interest rates and earnings. Elections are therefore not an investment thesis.

What matters more is whether they change expectations for the deficit, the supply of government bonds and the cost of capital. The most reliable sign of improvement would not be a one-day jump in the index but stocks rising while real yields fall and credit spreads calm. The calendar for the rest of the week is full: Wednesday brings the US Treasury’s refinancing plan, Thursday the Bank of England and Norges Bank decisions, and Friday the US jobs report.

The World Is Not Calm: Australia and Asia
Australia’s central bank raised its rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, the highest level in about 18 years. The vote was six to three, and growth forecasts were lowered. Inflation is forcing tightening even as the economy cools. This combination warns that the classic script of cooling, lower rates and rising valuations may not follow the textbook.

In Asia, South Korea’s KOSPI fell more than 3% in early trading, and Samsung and $SKHY dropped about 5%, even though South Korean exports jumped by almost 94% in October. Real activity confirms the investment cycle, while the stock market tests its financial sustainability. It is worth noting that holiday calendar effects also flattered the comparison.

Metals and crypto point the same way. Gold met resistance around $3,970, copper is near the $6.30–6.40 zone, and bitcoin stabilized around $76,800, though bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows. Structural demand is not the same as short-term price gains.

Three Scenarios for the Coming Days
Base case: selective rotation. Oil stays volatile, credit spreads do not narrow meaningfully, and technology sees sharp but brief rebounds. Capital moves according to valuation and cash flow.

Positive case: a relief rally with confirmation. Talks with Iran become more credible, oil settles at a lower level, and credit spreads tighten. Confirmation would be market breadth and improving credit, not the index alone.

Negative case: a spreading sell-off.A geopolitical shock pushes oil up again, spreads widen, and the sell-off spreads from AI to financials, industrials and the defensive part of the market.
Current signals most support the second path, a prolonged selective correction in which companies still grow but share prices stagnate because multiples compress.This is an assessment, not a forecast.

What to Watch
-   High-yield credit spread (around 339 basis points): whether it narrows or breaks above recent highs.
-   10-year yield (around 4.91%): whether the oil drop genuinely lowers required yields.
-   Brent (around $105–107): lasting calm or a new geopolitical spike.
-   VIX (around 21): calming after the election or spreading volatility.
-   Copper (around $6.38): defense of the $6.30–6.40 zone.
-   ISM prices-paid index (75.2): whether input costs ease.
-   Corporate earnings: AMD, Arista, Shopify, Pfizer and      Eaton. Management comments on the pace of data-center orders, financing and margins will say the most.

Return Is the New Capital
The story of this week is not the oil drop, the election or any single earnings report. It is a change in the yardstick by which the market judges growth. First, investors paid for the promise of technology, then for rapid market capture. Now they pay for what is left to the owners after the chips, electricity, networks and creditors have been paid.

Two lessons follow for the long-term investor. Market disappointment must not be confused with business failure. And business success must not be confused with a guaranteed good investment. An excellent company can be a poor investment if the price is too high. So tie new purchases to a combination of valuation, business metrics and an improving market regime, not merely to a price drop.

This text is an analytical assessment, not investment advice, and is not intended as personal financial advice. Please verify the data and facts yourself before making your own decision.

Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi stated: "We do not link our foreign policy, principles, or priorities to the elections of other nations. Naturally, U.S. elections are a matter for the American people, who will make their own decisions based on the policies of their government. However, we will not wait for the U.S. elections to adjust our own policies. Whenever we deem it necessary to make a decision that aligns with our country's interests and national security, we will do so, uninfluenced by any external factors."

The venue is the message.

Gharibabadi spoke at a meeting held to review annual reports on human rights violations in the United States and the United Kingdom. The Iranian Foreign Ministry produces these reports. They are not diplomatic courtesy documents. They are legal dossiers, the same category of document as the 159 indictments against US and Israeli officials, the $290 billion in judicial verdicts, and the $48 billion execution order for the Soleimani assassination.

Gharibabadi is the official who carried the nuclear legal file at the IAEA in Vienna, who handled the safeguards negotiations, and who is now in Doha facilitating the message exchange with Washington. He is not a spokesperson. He is the legal architect of Iran's case against the United States. When he says Iran will not wait for US elections, he is speaking as the official who writes the documents that will be enforced regardless of who sits in the White House.

The election file is the hidden target.

The US midterm elections are on 3 November 2026. US officials told Arab Gulf governments to prepare for a "short and intense" military campaign after the elections. The timing was not accidental. The Pentagon wanted the campaign framed as a post-election decision, insulated from electoral consequences.

Gharibabadi has now stated, from Tehran, that Iran does not care about the American political calendar. If Iran decides to act, on the naval siege, on the nuclear file, on the response to any new attack, it will act on its own schedule, not Washington's.

That removes the one variable the Pentagon was counting on: the assumption that Iran would wait out the American election cycle before making any major move. Gharibabadi says that assumption is wrong.

The military column of the same page.

Major General Ali Abdollahi, Chief of the General Staff, said the response would be "immediate, impactful, and without geographical limitations."

Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, IRGC spokesperson, said "new targets and new geographical areas" are on the agenda.

Sardar Radan, Faraja commander, said "geography will no longer have meaning" and cited "the order of the Supreme Leader."

Gharibabadi now says Iran will not wait for US elections to adjust its policies.

Four officials. Three military chains plus the diplomatic-legal channel. One doctrine: the decision calendar is Tehran's, not Washington's. The election is not a pause button. It is not a deadline. It is not a factor.

The contradiction Washington cannot answer.

The United States has built its Iran policy for decades on the assumption that Tehran can be timed. Sanctions pressure builds until the Iranian system cracks. Negotiations are offered when the American political calendar permits. Military action is calibrated to the election cycle.

Gharibabadi has now stated that the assumption is false. Iran will not wait for the American election. Iran will not adjust its policies to accommodate the American political season. Iran will decide when Iran decides.

The bill.

The Doha talks are on day three. Gharibabadi is in the room. The human rights reports on the US and UK are being reviewed. The 159 indictments are on the books. The $290 billion in verdicts is being enforced. The naval siege is the condition. The nuclear doctrine is under review. The NPT exit bill is in Qalibaf's briefcase.

Gharibabadi's statement is the diplomatic form of the military doctrine. The decision calendar belongs to Tehran. The election is Washington's problem, not Iran's.

I’m sat by the pool on holiday thinking about St.Mirren. Cos that’s what we do innit.

Some random thoughts and questions for you all…….

THE GOGIC QUESTION
Dropping Gogic would be a massive call, a guy that took home every POTY trophy last season but he’s been poor at the back this season, and it seems generally accepted that if he’s playing there we need to play a three which makes us more solid but costs us a player in the middle.

Would you consider moving Gogic into the middle of the park, at the base of a diamond, playing in front  of the back four?

Or would you actually be happy to see Gogic dropped??

THE RICHARD KING QUESTION
Would you consider giving Richard King some game time? He’s so far out of the picture it’s unbelievable but is he really THAT bad? He has certainly made mistakes but he does offer better use of the ball than most if not all of our other central defensive options.

THE SAMMY RAMOS QUESTION
Earlier in the season Sammy looked fabulous and looked like the creative spark we were so lacking last season. He’s dropped off a cliff the last few weeks though, getting a few minutes here and there. Would you like to see him getting more starts, maybe playing at the top of that midfield diamond as a ten???

THE MARCUS FRASER QUESTION
Everyone loves and appreciates what Marcus Fraser has done for this club. Last season alone, goal in a cup final and a goal that kept us in the division.

But all good things come to an end. 

Would you consider dropping Marcus Fraser and perhaps giving Louis Jackson a shot? Would it make us too inexperienced at the back? Would Donnelly deserve game time at the back????

THE LOUIS JACKSON QUESTION
Maybe he’s young and raw but he was trusted to start at Ibrox and did very well and yet he’s not been seen since. Would you give him more game time???

THE FRAZ TAYLOR QUESTION
Is there a formation that better suits what Fraz can bring to the table or are we simply flogging a dead horse with him and should we give up?

I could go on all day to be honest. There’s so many conundrums with our squad right now and I don’t have all the answers.

Interested to hear your thoughts.

Long before European colonial rule, one of the most remarkable kingdoms in Igbo history rose in what is now Anambra State. From the 10th to the 19th century, the Nri Kingdom spread across Igboland without a standing army. Its ruler, the Eze Nri, was as much a spiritual leader as a king, and his authority rested on belief rather than force.

Nri's priests offered ritual purification, cleansing communities and restoring them to good standing with the divine order. Alongside this was Aso Nri, a code of religious taboos that gave surrounding settlements a shared moral framework. Through this spiritual diplomacy, neighbouring communities were drawn into a peaceful confederation held together by trade and faith.

Nri reminds us that history is not only a record of wars. For centuries, shared beliefs and trusted institutions bound people together across a wide region of Igboland.

text:
Today in History 
November 3rd 
1926
Died On This Day
Annie Oakley, the legendary American sharpshooter and one of the most celebrated women of the Wild West, died at the age of 66 in Greenville, Ohio. Known around the world as “Little Sure Shot,” Oakley had captivated audiences with her extraordinary marksmanship, remarkable precision, and fearless determination. Her death marked the end of an extraordinary life that had challenged traditional expectations of women and established her as an enduring symbol of American frontier history.

Born Phoebe Ann Mosey on August 13, 1860, in Darke County, Ohio, Annie grew up in poverty. Her father died when she was young, leaving her family struggling to survive. By the age of eight, she had begun hunting with her father’s rifle, developing the shooting skills that would eventually make her famous. She sold game to local businesses and restaurants, helping support her family financially.

In 1875, Annie entered a shooting competition against Frank E. Butler, an accomplished professional marksman. Despite Butler’s experience, the teenage Annie defeated him. Their meeting blossomed into romance, and they married in 1876. Butler became her devoted partner and manager, supporting her career rather than competing against her growing fame.

Annie adopted the stage name Oakley and began performing professionally alongside her husband. Her astonishing ability to hit moving targets, shoot objects from great distances, and perform seemingly impossible tricks quickly attracted attention.

In 1885, she joined Buffalo Bill Cody’s famous Wild West Show, becoming one of its greatest attractions. Despite standing only five feet tall, her talent was enormous. She could split playing cards edgewise with bullets, shoot cigarettes from her husband’s lips, and hit targets while looking into a mirror. Her performances earned her international fame and the admiration of audiences across America and Europe.

During European tours, Annie performed before royalty, including Queen Victoria of Britain. The legendary Lakota leader Sitting Bull admired her abilities and reportedly gave her the nickname “Little Sure Shot,” which became forever associated with her.

Beyond her performances, Annie was a pioneer for women’s independence. At a time when shooting was considered a man’s pursuit, she demonstrated that women could achieve extraordinary success through skill, discipline, and determination. She encouraged women to learn firearms safety and marksmanship, believing these abilities could provide confidence and independence.

In 1901, Annie suffered injuries in a train accident, forcing her to reduce her performances. In 1903, she successfully fought false newspaper accusations that threatened her reputation, pursuing numerous libel lawsuits to defend her name.

During World War I, she offered to organize a regiment of female sharpshooters for the United States military, although the proposal was rejected. She continued supporting charitable causes and helping wounded veterans.

A serious automobile accident in 1922 left her with further injuries, but her determination remained unshaken. She continued demonstrating her shooting abilities whenever her health permitted.

By 1925, Annie’s health had deteriorated significantly. She returned to Ohio, where she spent her final months near family. Her husband, Frank Butler, died just 18 days after her death, ending a remarkable marriage of 50 years. They were buried beside one another in Greenville, Ohio.

Annie Oakley’s legacy extends far beyond her astonishing marksmanship. She became an international celebrity, inspired generations of women, and helped redefine what women could accomplish in a male-dominated world. Her life later inspired the celebrated Broadway musical Annie Get Your Gun.

More than a century after her greatest performances, Annie Oakley remains an unforgettable American legend #OTD

text:
I was leaving a grocery store in Ohio when I noticed a young boy standing beside a parked car, holding two bags of groceries.

He looked about ten years old.

As I walked past him, I heard him asking people if they could help him carry the bags across the parking lot.

Most people ignored him.

I stopped and asked where his parents were.

He pointed toward an old apartment building across the street.

“My mom is home. She’s sick, and I don’t want her walking all the way here.”

I looked at the bags and noticed they contained bread, milk, eggs, vegetables, and a few cans of soup.

I asked him if he had come shopping alone.

He nodded.

“She gave me a list and the money. I promised her I wouldn’t forget anything.”

I offered to carry the bags for him.

As we crossed the street, I asked if his mother was feeling better.

He went quiet for a moment.

Then he said, “I hope so. She hasn’t been able to work this week, and she keeps telling me everything will be okay.”

Something about the way he said it stayed with me.

When we reached the apartment, I helped him carry the groceries upstairs.

His mother opened the door slowly.
