text:
The most dangerous-looking animal in your home can be the safest one.

The brightest blue frog isn't hiding from anything.
It's doing the opposite, on purpose.

And the tiny specks at the bottom of that cup are the reason.

---

I did not want the frog.

I want that on the record before anything else, because by the end of this story I will be the kind of person who sets an alarm for a fruit fly delivery, and I would like you to remember that it started with fear.

My uncle Teodor died in March. He was seventy-one, a retired ferry mechanic who lived alone in a third-floor flat with a view of a car park, and he left me three things: a toolbox, a bicycle with a bent wheel, and a glass tank on the sideboard with a blue frog in it.

The lawyer read the line aloud as if it were a joke. "To my niece Maren, the frog. He has a name, but he will not answer to it."

The name, I found out later, was Captain. Teodor had spent thirty years watching ferries come and go from engine rooms, and he liked anything that held its post.

I drove the tank home on the back seat with the seatbelt across it.

Here is what I knew about blue frogs with black spots: they are poison dart frogs, and poison dart frogs kill people. I knew it the way you know shark facts. Nobody had ever taught me. It was just in the air, like the idea that spiders crawl into your mouth at night.

That first evening I put a towel over the tank and slept with the bedroom door shut. At two in the morning I got up, opened my laptop, and typed the worst possible question into a search bar: how many people can one poison frog kill.

The internet was happy to help. There was a frog in Colombia, a yellow one, the golden poison frog, and the commonly cited estimate was that a single animal carries enough toxin to be lethal to several adults. There were photographs of blowgun darts. There was a paragraph about how some Indigenous hunters in western Colombia had traditionally wiped dart tips across the backs of these frogs, which is where the whole family got its name.

I closed the laptop and sat in the dark with my heart going.

In the morning I found the notebook. It was tucked under the tank, a green accounting ledger with a rubber band around it. On the first page, in Teodor's square engineer's capitals, he had written seven headings, each numbered, each followed by blank space. At the bottom he had written one more line:

FILL THESE IN YOURSELF. IT WORKS BETTER THAT WAY. DO NOT LET THE COLOUR FOOL YOU. IT IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK.

I read the last sentence about six times. Then I put on the yellow rubber gloves from under the sink, lifted the towel, and looked at my inheritance for the first time.

He was about the length of a paperclip, a little under four centimetres. His skin was a blue so saturated it looked wet, like a gemstone under a lamp, covered in black spots of different sizes. He sat on a dry brown leaf at the front of the tank, in plain view, with his throat pulsing in tiny sips of air.

He was not hiding. He was looking straight at me.

---

RULE ONE: A WARNING LABEL IS NOT A WEAPON.

The first person I called was a vet. Not a normal one. I found an exotics clinic across the city, and a receptionist with a calm voice booked me in for Thursday and told me not to bring the tank, only photographs, and above all not to panic.

Dr. Hanne Alder was a tall woman with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair. She looked at my phone for ten seconds and said, "Oh, he's lovely. Dendrobates tinctorius, one of the blue forms, the ones people call azureus. How old?"

"I don't know. My uncle had him a long time."

"Then he's probably well past ten. They can live that long, sometimes into their mid-teens, if they are kept properly. Your uncle did something right."

"Sit down. Let me explain the colour, because it's the most misunderstood thing about these animals. In the wild, a bright frog in the open in daylight is making a statement. Biologists call it aposematism. It means warning colouration. The colour is a label. It tells snakes, spiders and birds: I taste terrible, I might hurt you, learn from this and leave me alone. That's why he can sit on a leaf in plain sight while every other frog in the forest hides under logs."

"So he is poisonous."

"Where does a wild frog get its poison?" she asked.

I had no idea.

"From its food. The leading explanation among researchers is the dietary hypothesis. The frogs eat certain ants, mites and tiny beetles in the leaf litter, and they pick up alkaloid compounds from those prey animals and store them in their skin glands. They do not make the toxins themselves. Raise a frog on a diet of fruit flies for generations in a clean tank and it never gets the ingredients. A captive-bred poison frog is, as far as anyone can tell, essentially without the toxins of its wild cousins."

I stared at her. "Then why is he blue?"

"Because the blue is inherited, and nobody told his genes that the forest is a long way off. He is wearing a warning label for a weapon he doesn't carry." She tapped the table. "The golden poison frog you read about is a different animal, in a different genus, from a very different forest. Those frogs are the real danger. Yours is a small, shy, harmless pet with a ferocious wardrobe."

I wrote the first rule into the ledger that night, in my own handwriting, under Teodor's heading:

1. A warning label is not a weapon. The colour is inherited, the toxin comes from wild food, and a captive-bred frog on a captive diet has none. The only animal at risk in this flat is him.

I took off the yellow gloves and put them back under the sink. I made one amendment that Dr. Alder insisted on, which I will repeat here because it matters: you still do not let children or other pets handle him, and you still wash your hands. Not because he can hurt you. Because you can hurt him. I did not understand that yet.

---

RULE TWO: FEED THE FOOD BEFORE YOU FEED THE FROG.

The second heading in the ledger said only FOOD, and beneath it Teodor had drawn a small diagram of a cup with dots in it.

I found the cup on a shelf in the hall cupboard, a deli container with a foam plug and a pinch of what looked like fine grey dust at the bottom. I held it up to the window. The dust moved.

I almost dropped it. The container was alive with specks, hundreds of them, each smaller than a grain of rice, crawling over a lump of fermented-smelling mash.

I took it to the shop Dr. Alder had recommended, a narrow place called Reed & Root, run by a man named Oskar who wore the same grey apron every day. He turned the cup in his big fingers and said, "Your uncle's. I know this culture. Flightless fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster, the wingless strain. Good stock. It's old now. These are about to crash."

"Crash?"

"A culture of fruit flies is a short little world. Eggs, maggots, pupae, adults, about ten days at room temperature if it's warm enough. Then the medium runs out and the whole thing collapses. You have to start new cultures every week, so there is always a fresh one coming up behind the old one. Think of it as a bakery. You never bake just one loaf."

He sold me two new cultures, a bag of medium, and a small tub of white powder.

"What is this?"

"Calcium. Sometimes with vitamin D3, sometimes without. And a multivitamin, a different tub, on a rotation. You dust the flies before you feed. Put a few in a little cup, add a pinch, give it a shake like salt on chips. Then tip them in. It's the single most important thing you will do."

I nodded and did not do it.

Not at first. It felt fussy. Captain ate the flies without the dust perfectly well; I watched him flick out his tongue and snap one off the leaf. It seemed like extra work for a cosmetic benefit. I did it twice, then skipped it for most of three weeks, because he looked fine and I was tired and the whole thing felt like a ritual.

Then I noticed that he was sitting oddly. One of his back legs lay out at a slightly awkward angle, and when he hopped, it didn't push the way it should.

Dr. Alder looked at the photograph and her face changed. "How have you been feeding him?"

I told her. Honestly. I'd like to say it was difficult. It wasn't. I just said it.

"Okay," she said, quite gently. "This is metabolic bone disease. It's one of the most common problems in captive amphibians and almost all of it is preventable. A frog eating plain fruit flies is eating a diet that is very low in calcium, because a fruit fly's body has far too little for a growing or even an adult amphibian. Without supplements, the skeleton goes soft. You caught it early. That matters."

She showed me how to dust. She showed me how to feed a gut-loaded culture, meaning flies raised on nutritious medium so they are nutritious in turn. She showed me what a good feeding session looks like: a handful of flies, watch the frog hunt, stop when he stops. Adults often eat daily or every other day, in small amounts, and they respond to movement, which is why their food has to be alive.

2. Feed the food before you feed the frog. Fruit flies are nearly empty calories for an amphibian. Dust them with calcium (sometimes with D3) and rotate a multivitamin, start a fresh culture every week, and offer small, regular meals.

---

RULE THREE: BUILD A WORLD, NOT A BOX.

By the summer I had graduated from fearing the frog to being slightly obsessed with the tank.

Teodor had left the substrate and the plants and a scatter of dried leaves across the floor, and I assumed they were decoration. Brown leaves seemed untidy. So on a Sunday I did what any sensible person would do: I took out the leaves and put in a layer of smooth grey pebbles.

Captain stopped coming out.

For four days he sat in the corner behind a plant and did not hunt. I kept shaking flies at him, and he kept ignoring them. On the fifth day I called Oskar in a mild panic.

"You took the leaves," he said, immediately.

"They looked dirty."

"They are the floor of a forest," he said. "In the wild, a poison dart frog lives in the leaf litter. That layer is shelter, humidity, nursery, hunting ground and supermarket. The frog hides under it, feels safe under it, and lays eggs near it. The litter is also home to the tiny animals that eat the mould and keep everything clean. Take it away and you have taken the walls off his house."

I put the leaves back that evening. Oskar had told me to use dried oak or magnolia leaves, rinsed and either boiled or baked to kill pests, from somewhere away from roads and pesticides. Within an hour Captain walked out from behind the plant and sat on the nearest leaf, looking at me the way an ex looks at you after an apology.

The tiny animals Oskar was talking about came in a small tub, a tangle of damp bark and white flecks. Springtails. They are not insects exactly, though they are six-legged relatives, and they live in soil all over the world. A culture of them in the substrate eats mould and waste and keeps the tank from turning slimy. They are the unpaid cleanup crew. Captain also eats them, which solves the question of who supervises the crew.

The third heading, in my handwriting now:

3. Build a world, not a box. Dead leaves are not mess; they are shelter, humidity and a food chain. Add leaf litter, hiding places, live plants, a cleanup crew of springtails, and keep humidity high with airflow.

---

RULE FOUR: HIS SKIN IS A LUNG AND A SPONGE.

I had the most ordinary accident of my life in August.

I'd been applying hand cream all week because the office air-conditioning cracked my knuckles. One morning, before breakfast, I reached into the tank to straighten a leaf, a small thing, and Captain, who usually sat still when I worked, leapt backward as if I'd touched a hot pan. He hid for two days.

I didn't connect it. I thought I'd frightened him. On the third day, I used hand sanitiser at the sink, opened the tank to drop in flies, and he did the same thing, only faster.

"What did you put on your hands?" Dr. Alder asked on the phone when I called. She didn't sound surprised.

"Hand cream. And sanitiser."

"Oh, Maren. Okay. I'm going to teach you the thing that all new keepers should be taught on day one. A frog's skin is not like ours. It is thin and permeable, and it does several jobs. He breathes partly through it. He takes in water through it; frogs don't generally drink the way we do, they absorb moisture through patches of skin on the belly and legs. Anything on your hands, lotion, soap residue, sanitiser, sunscreen, insect repellent, goes straight to a very sensitive surface. A thin film of something harmless to you can irritate him or worse."

"But I wasn't even touching him."

"You were touching his leaves and his water. Same thing."

The rules she gave me were simple. Wash hands before and after going into the tank, in plain water, with no soap or at the least a thorough rinse until nothing slippery remains. No lotions or sanitiser beforehand. Handle the frog as little as possible, ideally never; a poison frog is a look-don't-touch pet, and picking him up stresses him. When you must move one, use clean wet hands or a damp container.

Then she asked about the water.

"Tap," I said. "I mist him from the tap."

"Which, in most cities, has chlorine or chloramine to keep it safe for humans. Both are bad for amphibians. Use dechlorinated water, or water from a reverse-osmosis system, or use a conditioner made for amphibians. It sounds fussy. His whole body drinks it."

I spent the weekend buying a reverse-osmosis jug and a pump sprayer and a bottle of conditioner for the dish he drank from, and on Monday I stood at the sink and washed my hands for the first time in my life the way a surgeon does, thoroughly, with the water running over my wrists.

Captain came out onto the leaf while I did it. Then he sat there while I fed him, bold as brass.

4. His skin is a lung and a sponge. Wash hands with plain water before and after, no lotions or sanitiser, use dechlorinated or reverse-osmosis water, and handle him as little as possible.

---

RULE FIVE: HEAT KILLS QUIETLY.

July came to our city like a bill. Thirty-one degrees on the thermometer, thirty-two the next day, a heatwave that fed on itself while the whole country sweated and read about it.

I had put the tank on the sideboard because it was the nicest place in the flat. It sat two metres from a south-facing window. It had never been a problem before because the summers had been mild.

I came home from work on the third day of the heat and my first thought was that the flat felt strangely quiet. My second was that Captain was not on his leaf.

He was on the floor of the tank, flat against the damp substrate, legs splayed out, eyes half closed. His blue looked dull. I touched the glass and it was warm as a hand.

I did not own a phone number I trusted more than Oskar's. He picked up on the second ring, listened to about two sentences, and said in the voice of a man who has done this before:

"Get him out of the sun. Right now. Turn off any light on the tank. Put a fan in the room, not pointing at the glass but circulating the air. Fill a bottle with cold water, not ice, and stand it near the tank, not inside it. Mist him with cool dechlorinated water. Cool, not cold. Don't shock him."

I moved the tank to the hallway, the coolest part of the flat. I turned on the fan, I misted, I stood with a thermometer in my hand and watched the number inside the glass drop from thirty to twenty-eight to twenty-six over an hour. I did not take my eyes off him.

At about the fifty-minute mark, Captain lifted his head. He walked, slowly, to the nearest leaf, and sat on it.

The next morning Dr. Alder said what I had half known. "Glass tanks are greenhouses. Amphibians don't sweat; they lose water through the skin and they can't regulate their temperature the way mammals do. Most keepers aim for something like twenty-two to twenty-seven degrees Celsius, roughly seventy-two to eighty Fahrenheit, and sustained temperatures much above that are dangerous. These animals come from shaded forest floors, remember. The understory is cooler than the open air."

She gave me a list. Keep the tank out of direct sun, always. Don't sit it on a windowsill, don't put it near a radiator. Use a digital thermometer with a probe and read it daily. In a heatwave, cool the room, add airflow, lower or turn off lights, and have a plan before the weekend, not during it.

I wrote down the temperature range on a sticky note and put it on the side of the tank where I'd see it every morning.

5. Heat kills quietly. A glass tank is a greenhouse. Keep it out of the sun, aim for roughly 22 to 27 degrees Celsius, read a thermometer every day, and have a cooling plan before the heatwave arrives.

---

RULE SIX: WATCH BEFORE YOU ACT.

By autumn I had a ritual. At seven every evening I sat on the floor in front of the tank for ten minutes and did nothing at all.

It started as penance. After the heatwave I wanted to be sure I'd never miss a warning sign again. It turned into the best part of my day.

I learned his habits. He was most active in the morning and early evening, patrolling the leaves in a loop that took him past the plant, along the bark, and around the water dish. He stopped to hunt with a kind of freeze-and-lunge that I could have set my watch by. He had favourite spots. He liked the underside of a particular leaf at dusk.

I'm telling you all this because one evening in October, the pattern broke. He sat on the same leaf for three days and didn't hunt. His body looked narrower. The bones of his hips showed in a way they hadn't.

Because I had watched him every day for months, I knew it wasn't a bad mood. A healthy poison frog is bold. He sits out in the open, hunts, explores, and walks with a firm, deliberate tread. A frog that hides constantly, stops eating, looks thin or has sunken hips, a swollen belly, cloudy eyes or odd skin, is telling you something is wrong, and the earlier you notice, the better.

I booked him an appointment the same morning. Dr. Alder ran a gentle faecal test and found a parasite load, a common problem, that had been simmering under the surface. One course of treatment later he was back in his loop.

"If you hadn't been watching," she said, "I'd have seen him two weeks later. In an animal that small, two weeks is a very long time."

6. Watch before you act. Spend ten quiet minutes every day, photograph him monthly, and learn what healthy looks like: bold, active, round, bright. When it changes, call an exotics vet early.

---

RULE SEVEN: NEVER BUY THE WILD ONE.

The message arrived in November, in a group chat for local hobbyists I'd joined partly out of loneliness. Someone going by Rook posted a photograph of a frog much like Captain, a vivid blue on a brown leaf, and underneath: WILD CAUGHT, HALF PRICE, NO PAPERS NEEDED. CASH ONLY. Pick up tonight.

A year earlier I wouldn't have understood what was wrong. I'd have seen a bargain. I'd have thought about how nice it would be for Captain to have a friend.

I understood now.

Wild-caught frogs are a bad idea for the animal, the keeper and the species, in roughly that order. They arrive stressed from capture and transport and often carry parasites, and many die within weeks of arriving in a home tank. Because wild frogs have eaten wild prey, they may carry the skin toxins that captive-bred ones lack. And they move disease. Chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, has been linked to declines in hundreds of amphibian species around the world, and traded animals are one of the ways it spreads.

There's also the matter of law. The entire family of poison dart frogs, Dendrobatidae, is listed in Appendix II of CITES, the international convention that regulates trade in wildlife. In plain terms, moving them across borders legally requires permits. "No papers needed" is not a selling point. It is a confession.

And there is the simplest truth. Captive-bred poison frogs are widely available from responsible breeders. They are healthier, used to captivity, used to the food, and often much longer lived. You don't have to take a single animal from a forest to enjoy one in your living room.

I closed the app and sat looking at Captain. He was walking in his loop, bold and bright and entirely without a warning sign he needed.

I opened the ledger to the final heading, and wrote:

7. Never buy the wild one. Choose captive-bred animals from a breeder who can tell you where they came from. Wild capture spreads disease, kills animals and is often illegal. Also ask yourself honestly: can I feed this animal for fifteen years?

---

The next spring there was a knock on my door. A boy of about nine stood in the corridor with his mother just behind him, apologising before she'd spoken.

"He saw your tank through the window when the curtain was open," she said. "He's been talking about it for a week. We won't stay."

The boy looked at the tank on the sideboard. He didn't look at me. He had the same expression I'd had on the first day, except in reverse: all hunger, no fear.

"Is it a poison frog?" he asked.

"He's a poison dart frog, yes."

"Can he kill me?"

"No," I said. "He can't hurt you. But you could hurt him by accident, very easily, if you didn't know how. Do you want me to show you?"

His mother nodded slowly. The boy came in and sat on the floor where I always sat. I handed him a small cup. At the bottom, tiny, alive, grey as dust, were a hundred wingless fruit flies.

"This is the important bit," I told him. "Everyone thinks the exciting part is the frog. It isn't. The frog is only the label. The food is the secret."

I showed him how to dust them with the white powder. I showed him how to tip the cup. We watched Captain's head turn, the sudden lunge, a fleck of grey vanishing from a leaf.

"That's it?" the boy whispered.

"That's it. That's the whole thing. You feed the specks, and the specks feed the frog, and the frog stays blue."

I thought about the paradox as I watched them, and it finally clicked into place.

The most dangerous-looking animal in my home was the safest one, because its danger was only ever a message, a colour inherited from a forest it would never see, a warning for predators that did not exist in my flat. The only real hazards in that room were the ones I brought in myself: dry hands that weren't dry, tap water, a sunny windowsill, a missing pinch of calcium, a tidy-minded urge to throw out dead leaves. The brightest frog on the shelf wasn't hiding from anything. It was telling the truth in the loudest colour it had. It was the humans who had to learn to listen.

My uncle's last line in the ledger, I understood at last, had been a joke and a gift in one. DO NOT LET THE COLOUR FOOL YOU. IT IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK.

It wasn't danger. It was an invitation to pay attention.

---

THE SEVEN RULES (SAVE THIS)

1. A warning label is not a weapon. Captive-bred frogs don't carry the toxins their wild cousins get from wild prey. Treat him as fragile, not fierce.

2. Feed the food before you feed the frog. Dust flightless fruit flies with calcium (sometimes with D3), rotate a multivitamin, and start a fresh culture every week.

3. Build a world, not a box. Leaf litter, hiding places, live plants and springtails create shelter, humidity and a working food chain.

4. His skin is a lung and a sponge. Wash hands with plain water, skip lotion and sanitiser, use dechlorinated or reverse-osmosis water, and handle him as little as possible.

5. Heat kills quietly. Keep the tank out of the sun, aim for roughly 22 to 27 degrees Celsius, and read a thermometer every day.

6. Watch before you act. Ten quiet minutes a day teaches you what healthy looks like. If he hides, stops eating or looks thin, call an exotics vet early.

7. Never buy the wild one. Captive-bred only, from a breeder who can tell you where he came from. Dendrobatidae are listed under CITES Appendix II, and wild trade spreads disease.

If this was useful, bookmark it for the day you or a friend brings home a small, loud, beautiful animal. And tell me in the replies: what is the one thing about the animals you keep that nobody warned you about?

(The characters in this story are fictional. The facts about poison dart frogs and their care are real and widely documented, but every animal and every home is different, so confirm the details for your own with an exotics vet.)

text:
While fretting that her son hadn’t eaten breakfast that morning, worrying whether the slap she had given the little one for losing his pencil for the tenth time the day before had been too hard, thinking that the newly bought rice might have been overcooked, wondering whether she would get leave to go with her mother-in-law for the medical check-up on Tuesday, and glancing at her watch from time to time—have you ever seen a woman riding a scooter like that?

Have you ever seen a woman who doesn’t go out to work, but as a homemaker, fights without pause for her own family and children?

Have you seen her running around, throwing her own routines off balance so that her husband’s routines stay intact?

Have you noticed her trying to remember and recite her husband’s net-banking password, keep track of the last date for filing the tax return, correctly state the children’s class and division, and not forget the final date for paying the school fees?

When the husband who never turns to look in the kitchen points at the rotting vegetables in the fridge and picks a fight; when, without meaning to, the milk boils over once in a while; when she forgets where she kept the receipt from the gold loan; when the dosa batter turns out too watery; when she doesn’t manage to clean the washbasin before the guests arrive—have you heard her mutter to herself, “Ayyo! Oh no!”?

I’m asking you! Have you heard it? Have you seen it? Have you noticed it?

Somewhere in the midst of all this, she is living her life.

Now and then she makes herself a cup of coffee and drinks it; sits quietly in one or two WhatsApp groups, reading everything and smiling; replies in a single line to the private “Hello! How are you?” messages from some people in those same groups that no one else sees; runs off at some point and gets her hair cut; casually browses Amazon and Myntra, looking at this and that with longing; laughs with the children; waters the plant on the balcony; answers the landline calls from relatives; half-watches the movies that come on TV; lights the lamp before the gods in the house—and thus she lives her life in silence.

How much time does she really have for herself?

When women stand up for themselves, and we see some people’s desire to defeat them, it becomes impossible not to say these things, impossible not to remind. Whether they are fans of film stars or people waving party flags of various colours, they cannot bear it when women who understand their own sexuality, who have individuality, who value life, speak up about certain things. If this continues, our land will become a place where people who lack the ability to enter the heart of a woman who reads four books will rule.

We need to understand! When she stands up courageously in front of society, fighting for justice, and we defeat her through cyber-attacks and silence her by questioning her character at every turn, we are only defeating ourselves! Children growing up in homes where women do not speak will grow up to be mute.

We need to understand! Just like a man, a woman too can have opinions on everything in the world; she can travel wherever she likes when she likes; she can ride a motorcycle; she can walk in the rain; she can make decisions about her own body! She may do all these things, or she may choose not to. There are those who want to, and those who don’t.

That is her wish. Her wish alone. But when she does these things, there exists a method of attacking and subduing her mentally and physically—that is what is frightening. Every misogynistic statement and every celebration of such things is our contribution to her silent sacrifices.

We must remember. After everyone has gone to bed, it is only after wrestling with the kitchen sink and switching off the light, wiping her hands on the towel, that she reaches the bed as a wife. It is the goodness she offers by getting up in the morning before her sleep is complete, tying up her hair, and switching on the kitchen light that makes up all our days. A day begins with the first spark when the gas stove is lit.

Our lives are an event that unfolds between the switches a woman turns on in the morning and turns off at night.

Have you ever noticed that?

text:
THE ROCK THAT LOOKED BACK

I was sure I was watching a rock for 10 seconds.
Then the "rock" turned its head and looked straight at me.
I'd been filming an animal that had been studying me the whole time.
And that's when its arm began to

move.

Not fast. That is the first thing I want you to understand, because everyone who has never met a giant Pacific octopus imagines something out of an old sailor's nightmare: a lunge, a grab, a cloud of ink. What I got instead was the slowest, most deliberate gesture I have ever seen from a living creature. One arm, thick as my forearm at its base, lifted off the boulder it had been draped over, hung in the green water for what felt like a full minute, and then began to unroll toward the lens of my camera like a question being asked politely.

I am getting ahead of myself. I tell stories badly when I start in the middle, and my editor, who has read every draft of this one, says the middle is the only part anyone will remember. So let me go back to the morning, to the cold, to the mistake that put me in front of that animal in the first place.

CHAPTER ONE: THE MISTAKE

My name is Mara Voss, and for eleven years I have filmed things that live under cold water. Kelp forests, wolf eels, schools of herring so dense they turn the light silver. I am not a scientist. I am the person scientists call when they need footage that proves something they already know.

That autumn, the person who called was a marine biologist named Dr. Ines Okafor, who ran a small monitoring program off the northern end of Vancouver Island. None of these people are real, by the way, and neither is the reef. I have changed everything except the animal and what it taught me. Dr. Okafor's program tracked the local population of giant Pacific octopus, Enteroctopus dofleini, by counting dens along a two-kilometer stretch of rocky slope. She needed video of den activity to compare with her field notes. Simple work. Boring, in the best sense.

My dive buddy was Teo Alder, a quiet man who had once spent a season as a commercial urchin diver and still checked his gauges every ninety seconds out of what I can only call love. We had done forty-odd dives together. He was the reason I was alive to tell this, and I will come back to that.

The mistake was mine, and it was a small one, which is how the best mistakes begin. We had a plan: descend at the north marker, follow the slope down to fourteen meters, film three known dens, and ascend by the planned time. The plan was written on a slate strapped to my wrist. The water that morning was nine degrees Celsius, green as bottle glass, and the visibility was perhaps eight meters, which on that coast counts as generous.

At the second den, I stopped following the plan.

There was a rock I did not recognize. It sat on the slope above the den site, a rounded mass the color of old brick, crusted with the same barnacles and sponges as everything around it. I almost swam past it. But something about the surface bothered me. Real rocks do not have texture that looks like it is thinking about itself. I raised the camera, told myself I would give it ten seconds, and started recording.

I counted those ten seconds in my head, bubbles rising past the housing, my breathing loud in my own ears. For nine of them it was a rock. On the tenth, a ridge on the top of the rock, a small horn-like bump, swiveled. A slit opened beneath it. And a copper-colored eye, with a pupil like a thin horizontal bar, looked directly into my lens.

I did not know it yet, but I had been in that animal's view for at least four minutes. It had watched me descend. It had watched Teo's light sweep the slope. It had waited, perfectly still, until I committed to staying, and then it had decided to let me see it.

That was the first lesson of the dive, and I will give it to you as a rule, because rules are what you came for. I will give you seven of them. Each one cost me something to learn, and each one is true.

RULE 1: BE STILL BEFORE YOU DECIDE WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING AT

The octopus I was filming was, I later estimated, about two meters from arm tip to arm tip, which is middling for the species. Giant Pacific octopuses are the largest octopus species on Earth. The biggest reliably measured specimens weigh around seventy kilograms, roughly 150 pounds, with arm spans of a few meters. You will read claims of much larger animals, six hundred pounds and thirty feet across, and I will save you the search: those numbers have never been verified. The documented record is impressive enough.

What matters here is not the size. It is what the animal did with its skin.

An octopus carries millions of pigment sacs in its skin called chromatophores, each one wired to muscles that stretch or squeeze it open, controlled directly by the nervous system. Beneath those sit reflective cells that bounce light around. Together they let the animal change color and pattern in a fraction of a second. But the part that stunned me, when Dr. Okafor explained it afterward, is that the skin also changes texture. Small muscles raise fleshy bumps called papillae, so an octopus can turn smooth skin into something spiky and barnacle-like. That is why I thought I was looking at a rock. It was not only the color. It was the surface. The animal had built a rock out of its own body, bump by bump.

CHAPTER TWO: THE ARM

Now. The arm.

It came toward the camera in a long, slow curve, the tip curling and uncurling. I want to describe the suckers, because they are the reason I am writing this at all. Along the underside of each arm, in a double row, sit the suckers, and a giant Pacific octopus has somewhere around two thousand of them across its eight arms. They are not simple suction cups. Each one is a muscular, flexible organ, and each one is lined with chemoreceptors, which means the animal can taste whatever it touches. An octopus does not so much feel the world as sample it, with every sucker, all at once.

I had been taught, years before, never to touch wildlife. I had written it on slates. I had said it aloud to student divers. I had a professional reputation for keeping my hands tucked against my chest. So I kept them there, and I let the animal do the touching, and that turned out to be the correct decision for reasons that took me a long time to articulate.

RULE 2: LET THE CURIOUS ONE COME TO YOU

Here is the rule, and then the reason.

Never initiate contact with wild animals. If contact is going to happen, let the animal begin it, and let it end it. There are practical reasons: your skin carries oils, sunscreen, and bacteria that can harm marine creatures, and an octopus's skin is a delicate, living interface with its world. There are ethical reasons: you are a guest in a place where the animal is the resident. But there is a deeper reason, and it is about information.

The giant Pacific octopus is, as far as anyone can tell, a curious animal. Aquarium keepers have documented individuals that recognize particular human faces, and that squirt water at people they dislike while greeting people they like. I cannot prove the film I made supports any grand claim about octopus minds, and I will not pretend it does. But I can tell you that the arm held on my camera light for almost forty seconds, exploring, before it let go and drew back, and that the let-go was as gentle as the reach.

When it withdrew, it did something else. It retracted the arm along the rock, and the skin of the arm shifted from brick red to a deep, mottled purple-brown, and then, within two seconds, to nearly white. A flash. Then back to red.

CHAPTER THREE: THE EYE

Look at an octopus's eye, and you will see something that looks eerily familiar. It has a lens, an iris, a retina. It is a camera eye like ours, and yet it evolved completely independently. Our last common ancestor with the octopus was a small, worm-like creature that lived more than five hundred million years ago and had, at most, a patch of light-sensitive cells. We got our eyes one way. The octopus got its eyes another way. The result looks nearly identical.

But the pupil is different. Ours is round. Theirs is a horizontal slit, and the slit stays horizontal. This is one of those facts that sounds made up. A small organ near the octopus's brain, called a statocyst, works like an inner ear and senses the direction of gravity. As the animal rolls and tumbles, the eyes rotate in their sockets to keep the pupil level with the horizon. You can flip an octopus over and its pupils will compensate. A horizontal slit gives a wide panoramic view along the seafloor, which is where both its dinner and its predators come from, and the eye makes sure the slit never tilts.

And here is the paradox that kept me awake. Most octopuses, as far as researchers can determine, have only one type of photoreceptor in their eyes. By the standard definition, that makes them colorblind. They cannot compare signals from different receptors the way we do to perceive hue. And yet these animals match the color of their surroundings with astonishing accuracy.

How? Nobody knows for certain. There are several hypotheses, and this is where I want to be careful, because careful is the only way to treat a puzzle that is genuinely unsolved. One hypothesis is that the skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins, opsins, similar to those found in eyes, so the skin might sense light directly. Researchers have found these proteins in octopus skin. Another proposal is that the odd shape of the pupil, with its off-axis openings, lets the animal exploit a property of lenses called chromatic aberration, in which different wavelengths come into focus at different depths, to infer color from blur. That one is a clever idea, published in a respectable journal, and still debated. A third possibility is that much of the matching is not about color at all, but about contrast, brightness, and texture, and that the animal's skin cells and reflective layers produce the right hues almost automatically.

RULE 3: READ THE EYE, THEN CHECK WHAT YOU THINK YOU KNOW

This rule has two halves.

The first half is practical: when you meet any animal, look at its eyes and body orientation before you look at anything else. In an octopus, a pupil that is wide and relaxed, a body that is smooth and low, and arms that move with unhurried purpose usually describe a calm animal. Darkening skin, a raised mantle, flattened posture, and sudden jets of water may mean stress. In general, any wild animal that is watching you steadily has already made decisions about you. Your job is to find out what they are before you do something that changes them.

The second half is intellectual, and it matters even if you never get wet. The octopus is a living reminder that our explanations are often more confident than our evidence. For decades the standard line was: octopuses are colorblind, therefore they cannot be matching color by sight. The line was tidy and the animals ignored it. The correct response to a paradox is not to deny the observation or to defend the theory. It is to say, I do not understand this yet, and to keep looking. Write down what you actually saw, separately from what you think it means. Then go back and look again.

CHAPTER FOUR: THE DEN

By the time the arm had withdrawn, my air check was due. Teo had been tapping his gauge against his light, a signal we used when it was time to talk numbers. I glanced at my console and my stomach did a small, cold turn.

I had been on the plan for twenty-two minutes. I had been off the plan for eleven.

I had burned through a third and a half. I had done it on a rock.

Teo's hand came into view, two fingers pointing from his eyes to my console, then a thumb up with a questioning tilt. How much gas? I showed him the number. He held his own gauge next to mine so I could compare. His was lower than I expected, because he had also been holding position in the cold. Then he made the signal for ascending, a flat palm lifted slowly, and he waited.

This is the part I promised to return to. Teo did not criticize me. He did not wave his arms or tap his watch or give me the cutting look of a man who has watched a colleague drift from the plan. He simply put the situation in front of me, and let me make the right decision on my own.

RULE 4: THE PLAN IS A PROMISE TO YOUR FUTURE SELF. KEEP IT WHEN THE WORLD GETS INTERESTING

The most dangerous moment in any adventure is not the moment of fear. It is the moment of fascination. When you are afraid, you are careful. When you are fascinated, you are generous with your attention and stingy with your caution, and the numbers on your wrist stop feeling real.

Before every dive, I write the turnaround rules on a slate: the depth I will not exceed, the gas pressure at which I will head up, the time I will end the dive. These are not limits I set in the moment. They are rules I set when I was calm, rested, and thinking clearly, for the version of me who would be cold, tired, and entranced later. That later me cannot be trusted with the decision. That is why the earlier me made it.

I looked at the octopus one last time. It had settled back onto the rock, its skin turning once more to the color and texture of the surrounding stone. Within a few seconds I could no longer tell where the animal ended and the reef began. I raised my hand in a small wave, which is ridiculous, and then I turned and began the slow climb up the slope with Teo beside me.

CHAPTER FIVE: WHAT THE BIOLOGIST SAID

Back on the boat, over bad coffee, Dr. Okafor watched the footage on a laptop shielded from the glare with a tarp. She did not say anything for almost four minutes. Then she paused the frame on the eye.

"That," she said, "is a female."

I asked her how she could tell. She smiled, with a tiredness I did not yet understand, and said that she could not, not with certainty, from the footage alone. But the location, the posture, and the way the animal had positioned itself near the den entrance all suggested to her something she had seen before. She believed this animal was preparing to brood.

I want to give you the facts here, because they are some of the most remarkable and most overlooked in all of natural history, and every one of them can be checked.

A giant Pacific octopus lives, on average, about three to five years. That is a short life for such a complex animal. It spends most of it feeding, growing quickly, and avoiding being eaten. Males mate and then enter a stage of decline, called senescence, that usually leads to death within weeks or months. Females lay tens of thousands of eggs, sometimes well over a hundred thousand, in strings that hang from the ceiling of a den like strands of pale rice. Then the mother stays.

She stays for months. For the giant Pacific octopus, brooding typically lasts around six to seven months, depending on water temperature. During that time she does not leave the den to hunt. She guards the eggs, cleans them with her suckers, and blows streams of water across them to keep them oxygenated. She generally does not eat. When the eggs hatch, she dies. A gland near the eye seems to trigger the whole sequence, and experiments in which that gland was removed produced females that resumed eating and lived longer. Which is to say, her death is not simply exhaustion. It is a program.

I thought about the eye that had looked into my lens. I thought about the arm that had tasted my camera with such patient precision. I looked at Dr. Okafor and I asked the only question I could think of.

"Does she know?"

She did not answer for a long time. "I do not know," she said at last. "Nobody does. But I will tell you what I tell my students. Do not decide too fast what an animal does or does not feel. We have been wrong about that for centuries."

RULE 5: LOG EVERYTHING. MEMORY IS A STORYTELLER, NOT A RECORDER

Dr. Okafor had asked me, before the dive, to keep a written log. Not just the video. A notebook, with times, depths, temperatures, and behaviors, written in plain language within an hour of surfacing. I had grumbled about it. I am a visual person; I trust my footage.

Here is what the notebook taught me. When I sat down on the boat to write what I had seen, my memory had already begun to improve the story. In my head, the octopus had looked at me for a long time before moving. In my notes, written from the timestamps in the video, it was nine seconds. In my head, the arm had been reaching for the camera. On the footage, it had reached for the red light. In my head, I had been calm. On my dive computer, my breathing rate had spiked at the moment the eye appeared.

The practical version is this: whenever you witness something that matters, write down what happened within an hour, before it hardens into an anecdote. Put down times, numbers, and what you literally saw, in one column, and what you think it meant in another. The two columns will not match, and the gap between them is where you learn. This is how scientists work, and it is also how people who want to make better decisions work. The brain is a wonderful storyteller and a poor archivist. Hire an archivist.

CHAPTER SIX: THE SECOND DIVE

I went back the next morning. Not to film. Dr. Okafor had asked me to return to the den and document it from a distance, no closer than three meters, with the lights off if possible, for the monitoring record. She wanted to know if the den was occupied, and if so, whether the occupant was brooding.

The water was colder. Nine degrees had become eight and a half, and the visibility had dropped to five meters because of a plankton bloom that turned the light a murky jade. Teo and I descended with a new slate and a revised plan, with turnaround numbers more conservative than before. I did not argue with them.

We found the den without trouble. The rock was where I remembered it, though the animal was nowhere in sight. A pile of discarded crab shells lay at the entrance, which is exactly what biologists look for: an octopus midden, the garbage heap of a resident. Octopuses carry their prey back to the den, eat the soft parts, and push the empty shells out the door, so the pile is a record of everything the animal has eaten. I counted shells of at least four species. Rock crab. Dungeness. Something smaller I could not identify. A scatter of clam halves, drilled neatly through with a tiny round hole.

That hole is a signature. An octopus drills through clam shells with its radula, a tongue-like ribbon of tiny teeth, and then injects saliva that contains enzymes and a paralytic. It is a remarkable method, and it leaves a mark that marine biologists can read like a handwritten note.

I settled onto the sand, three meters away, and turned my lights off. For a long time, I saw nothing. Then, slowly, my eyes adjusted to the green gloom, and I saw it: the same bump, the same slit, the same copper glint. She was at the den entrance, half-hidden, one arm curled across the opening like a door she did not intend to close.

RULE 6: OBSERVE WITHOUT TAKING

Here is a rule that sounds simple and is not. When you are in a place that belongs to something else, take only what the place offers freely, and leave everything else exactly as you found it.

I did not touch the den. I did not move a shell. I did not shine a light into the entrance, because bright light can stress brooding animals, and a stressed mother can abandon her eggs or abandon the den. I did not try to get closer for a better frame. I filmed at three meters, as asked, and I took my footage and went.

CHAPTER SEVEN: THE LAST ARM

I want to tell you about the last thing that happened, because it is the reason I opened this story the way I did, with an interrupted sentence.

On the second dive, as Teo and I finished our observation and prepared to ascend, the octopus came out. Not all the way. She extended one arm from the den, slowly, along the sand, until it lay across the ground about a meter from my fins. It lay there, perfectly still. The suckers faced up, pale and open.

I did not move. Teo, behind me, did not move. I could hear the soft rhythm of our breathing. A long time passed, perhaps a minute, and then the arm slowly turned over, so that the suckers pressed against the sand, and began to explore it, small movements, one sucker at a time, tasting the grains. She was not reaching for me. She was reading the seabed, the way you might run your fingers along a shelf to find a book in the dark.

And then, with no hurry, the arm retracted. It slid back along the sand, curled once at the entrance, and vanished into the shadow of the den.

I have never received a higher compliment.

RULE 7: LEAVE BEFORE YOU WANT TO

The final rule is the one I find hardest.

The best encounters end before you are ready. If you stay until you are satisfied, you have stayed too long. If you wait for the perfect shot, the perfect moment, the perfect fullness of experience, you will outstay your air, your warmth, your welcome, or your luck. Experts in many fields, from mountaineering to medicine, will tell you the same thing in different words: the decision to turn around is easiest when you are still enjoying yourself. It is nearly impossible once you are not.

I think about the octopus, and her six or seven months in the dark, and I understand something about how little she asked of the world. She wanted a hole in the rock, a steady supply of oxygen-rich water, and to be left alone with what she was guarding. I wanted a few minutes of footage. We both got what we needed, and the only reason we both did is that I left when the plan told me to leave, with something still unseen.

EPILOGUE: WHAT THE FOOTAGE SHOWED

I have given you what I know. Here is the short version, the one I wrote on a slate and taped inside the lid of my dive bag, so that I read it before every dive:

1. Be still before you decide what you are looking at. The first ten seconds belong to your assumptions.
2. Let the curious one come to you. Information that arrives honestly is worth more than information you force.
3. Read the eye, then check what you think you know. Report what you saw before what you believe it means.
4. The plan is a promise to your future self. Keep it when the world gets interesting, because fascination is when your numbers stop feeling real.
5. Log everything within the hour. Memory is a storyteller, not a recorder.
6. Observe without taking. Ask what your presence costs and who pays for it.
7. Leave before you want to. The best encounters end with something still unseen.

And here are the facts, in the same compressed form, so that you can check every one of them yourself:

Giant Pacific octopuses are the largest octopus species, with verified weights up to roughly seventy kilograms. They have around two thousand suckers lined with chemoreceptors, so they taste by touching. They have three hearts and blue, copper-based blood. Their nervous systems hold on the order of five hundred million neurons, with a majority located in the arms rather than the central brain. Their skin contains chromatophores and can change texture as well as color. Their pupils are horizontal slits that stay level thanks to organs called statocysts. Most octopuses appear to have a single photoreceptor type, and how they match colors so well is still debated. They live about three to five years. Females brood their eggs for months without eating and die soon after the eggs hatch.

That last fact is the one that stays with me.

I never went back to that reef. Dr. Okafor told me, months later, that the den was empty by spring, the shells swept away by winter storms, the strings of eggs gone, the rock only a rock. She said the program had recorded a dozen new dens that season, and that the next generation of octopuses, each one smaller than a grain of rice at hatching, had drifted out into the open water in a cloud, to eat and grow and find a place of their own in the cold green dark.

I like to think one of them found a rock that looked a lot like the one she had left behind.

If you ever find yourself in front of a rock that seems to be looking back, do me a favor. Hold still. Count ten seconds. Let the evidence take its turn.

And when the arm begins to move, be patient. It is only asking a question.

text:
Malachi 3

1 Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the LORD, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.

2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:

3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.

4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old, and as in former years.

5 And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts.

6 For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.

7 Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return?

8 Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.

9 Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation.

10 Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.

11 And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts.

12 And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts.

13 Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee?

14 Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts?

15 And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up; yea, they that tempt God are even delivered.

16 Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.

17 And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.

18 Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not.

Na bud. No kids are involved in worshipping anything during Halloween. It’s just a bit of ancient tradition. 

This however is pure pagan rite at the Kaaba in Mecca: a pilgrim kissing a Black Stone (a sacred baetyl).
The Kaaba is a major shrine housing idols (chiefly Hubal, a red agate statue with a golden hand used for arrow divination, plus goddesses Al-Lat, Al-Uzza, and Manat). Pagans circled it (tawaf), touched or kissed the Black Stone, offered sacrifices, and held seasonal pilgrimages. Stone veneration of this kind was widespread across pre-Islamic Arabia and carried on today. In fact the reason you all kiss it is because Muhammad did the exact same thing when it truly was a temple to pagan Gods.

Follow the southward expansion of the Wuyue Kingdom (907–978) on a three-day journey through Taizhou, Wenzhou, and Fuzhou, discovering ancient city walls, historic landmarks, and the enduring legacy of the Qian family. 

Begin in Taizhou, where Rongxing Hall, the ancient city wall, and Linhai Museum offer a glimpse into the Qian family's treasured heritage and Wuyue's military defences. Continue to Wenzhou to explore the historic Qiaolou Gate and the former prefectural government site, tracing how the kingdom strengthened its southern territories. Finally, head to Fuzhou, the southernmost part of Wuyue's territory, to discover the Five Dynasties stone carvings of the Wu Pagoda and Hualin Temple Hall, where Wuyue's cultural influence met local Fujian traditions.

text:
#RadioMoskva

Shock and awe vs the Command of the Reload

On paper Russia spends a fifth as much on defence as America does. On the battlefield, Russia would probably run rings around the US as it has the right weapons. Just counting the cash is not enough when judging which military is more powerful. 

Russia’s 2027 budget has military spending up and accounting for 41% of all spending with a nominal value of $210bn. That is a fifth of the US spending of just under a trillion dollars, (and Trump wants to hike to $1.5 trillion next year). However, obviously, you need to convert this to PPP adjusted spending as Russia literally gets more bang for its buck and then the total is $574bn – about 60% of what the US spends.

But if you dig into it even more deeply, even the PPP adjustment is flawed as it is an aggregate for the entire economy. If you look very specifically at what weapons a dollar can buy in Russia, then the multiple is even higher than the 2.7-times more that the PPP adjustment suggests.

So, I tried to calculate the spending not in terms of adjusted dollars, but in terms of like-for-like military production units. For example, in the US it costs $4,000 to make a standard 155mm artillery shell, but in Russia the same 152mm shell costs $1,000 a pop – four-time less, not 2.7-times less.

In artillery shell-units, Russia’s defence spending is about 90% of America’s so the gap is actually much smaller.

I went on to compare with other units: tank-units, jet fighter-units, etc, but the really interesting one was drone- and missile-units. Here the difference between the cost was not so big, but in both two other factors come into play: production capacity and technology.

On production you can’t compare as the US doesn’t make drones in the way that Russia does. It does have the MQ-9 Reaper drones, which cost about $30mn each, vs the new Russian Geran-5 which cost about $150,000 to make, so there is no real comparison there as the ratio is well over 200-times. The real comparison should be between the Geran-5 and the US’ new LUCAS (Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System) drone – a copy of Iran’s low-cost, one-way Shahed drones, which cost the same as their Russian equivalent – except the US doesn’t actually make them. There a few proto-types knocking about, but Russia is now making 7mn drones of all sorts a year. The production gap is mindboggling huge.

The same is true for missiles where again the costs are about the same in both countries, but not only is Russia massively outproducing the US it has a whole class of hypersonic missiles which can’t be stopped, even by the fabled Patriot PAC-3 interceptors (as has been amply demonstrated in the Iran war). The US version of this missile is also still on the drawing board. So, the ratio here is infinite as that is what you get if you divide anything by zero.

This production gap between Russia and the US radically skews the whole picture of the “defence spending”. It not just about how much you are spending, but what you are spending it on.

Explosives is another example. The Holston Army Ammunition Plant in Kingsport, Tennessee, operated by BAE Systems, is America’s sole domestic producer of RDX and HMX - two powerful explosives used in pretty much all its missiles. The (aptly named) Ministry of War invested over $1bn into modernising the factory but saw only a 3% gain in output. This failure could turn out to be a major bottleneck for any large-scale US war effort.

The details are understandably vague, but Russia appears to have substantially greater domestic production capacity for conventional military explosives than the US, although there is no reliable, directly comparable figures. The biggest differences are in TNT production, where the US has effectively lost its domestic manufacturing base, and the sheer scale of Russian production of explosives and artillery propellants.

Russia has substantially expanded its explosives and gunpowder industry since invading Ukraine in 2022, which have tripled from pre-war levels and continue to grow. Worryingly, the Kremlin just banned the export of four key chemicals needed to make explosives (toluene, orthoxylene, paraxylene and phenol), so it’s still going up in scale despite the talk of peace.

The chink in Russia’s armour is technology. A Russian artillery shell is so cheap as everything that goes into making it is Russian: labour, metal and gunpowder. That is not true of missiles: while China is steadily replacing western components, over 90% of the electronics in a Russian missile is still Western-made. The Integral chip factory in Belarus plays a surprisingly important role here, but all the chips it makes are made using Western technology too.

This is driving Zelenskiy potty as he keeps calling for the West to tighten its technology sanctions on Russia as that would cut Russian missile production off at the knees – and it’s just not happening. In the meantime, the residents of Kyiv are sitting under a hail of Russian missiles. Kyiv has already been blacked out after all four of its power stations have been destroyed in the tit-for-tat missile war and now Putin is systematically targeting power substations to cut off even the power from the NPPs.

Winston Churchill quipped that generals are always preparing for the last war. And that is the big difference: Putin isn’t preparing for anything; he is in the middle of a real war. That is what he is spending his money on: things he needs yesterday to beat his opponent. The speed of his innovations is extraordinary. Just the increase in speed of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones since the summer has doubled, according to my reconning. Both sides seem to have got the design-to-production cycle down to a few months. Hitler did this too, throwing cash at a Wunderwaffen, and failed. Amazingly, Zelenskiy is investing billions into his Wunderwaffen and some of them actually work. From here, Trump looks like he is in the same boat as Hitler and has refused Zelenskiy’s mega drones-for-weapons deal which could have solved his problems.

Which brings me to my last point. The US has been, and still is, following the “Command of the Commons” doctrine - the deployment of powerful ‘bunker-buster-bombs” or “smart missiles” to bases scattered around the world so it can respond to any crisis quickly with overwhelming force – better known as “shock & awe.”

But hat tip to Zelenskiy, who out of necessity, has changed the nature of war out of all recognition to the  Command of the Reload: it is now the side that can build more cheap, "good-enough," weapons wins. Whatever happens to him politically (it doesn’t look good), the history books are going to name him as the man who revolutionised modern warfare, (with Azerbaijan as an important footnote for demonstrating the overwhelming power of offensive drones in its short war with Armenia in 2020).

Zelenskiy had no choice. He was hoping for those “awesome” weapons from the West. I recommend you watch his “close the skies” appeal, recorded in the first week of the current conflict. He looked terrified, as you would if Russia had just invaded your country, and he appealed to his allies for exactly this: the Western treasure trove of powerful weapons. They didn’t come. What was offered after the first Ramstein meeting a few months later was always “some, but not enough” as we have been complaining about for four years.

What is so amazing is that Zelenskiy has pioneered a technique where, as former commander-in-chief General Valerii Zaluzhnyi said, a smaller country (and Ukraine was also the most dysfunctional of all 15 former Soviet Republics in 2021 to boot) can take on a much larger military power and drag it into a protracted war of attrition for years.

The difference between shock & awe and the asymmetrical war now being fought, is the death toll. The whole point of overwhelming force is to bring the conflict to an end really fast to minimise the casualty count. In the Yugoslav war the US pulled their punches flying US sorties over enemy territory as President Bill Clinton was not prepared to lose a single US soldier.

I made a table of the major wars since USSR-Afghanistan detailing the estimated dead. You’ll note in several – Bonia, Kosovo, Libya – not a single  Western soldier was killed and even in the US-Afghan and Iraq wars, the US death tolls were 3,500 and 4,800 respectively in campaigns that went on for 20 and 8 years respectively. That works out to be an average US death per day of 0.34 and 1.39 respectively.

The one war that is off the chart is – Russia-Ukraine. It is not clear at all how many people died in this war but on the estimates below it’s already somewhere between 500,000 and 600,000: that is an average daily death toll of 252–283 (Russians), 79–94 (Ukrainians) and 331–378 (combined). Only the two world wars are worse, but a lot more people were involved in those wars than this one.

And the real death toll is almost certainly higher; I have seen reports recently suggesting its over one million – by far the worst since WWI and WWII, which were both total wars, not like everything since which were campaigns rather than all-out war.

But I'm afraid this war is in its end game now. WWII showed that in the late stages it is industrial production that takes the buscuit. At the end of WWII the Allies were simply pumping out more materiel than the Nazis. In particular, once the Luffwaffer had been cleared from the skies and Bomber Harris began carpet bombing Germany there was little hope left.

That is where we are in Ukraine now: the air defence ammo has run out and Putin, who as we all know is a history buff, is carpet bombing Ukraine. The big difference between now and then is that neither Europe or the US has not ramped up its investment into defence – something else we have been complaining about for over four years.

On paper the US is spending more than Russia, but it’s spending on the wrong things. The EU is now trying to ramp up both its spending and improve what it spends it on, under the Danish model, but it is already almost bankrupt and has been unable to offset the departure of the US, as weapons supplies to Ukraine actully fell for the first time last year.

Low-fat diets do not prevent dementia deaths in older women | Karina Petrova, PsyPost

Adopting a diet low in fat and high in fruits, vegetables, and grains does not lower the risk of dying from dementia for most postmenopausal women. While earlier research hinted at potential cognitive benefits, a secondary look at a large clinical trial revealed that these dietary modifications did not prevent dementia related deaths over a twenty year period. The findings were published in the journal Menopause.

Dementia and cognitive impairment represent major health risks associated with aging. Women make up more than two thirds of people over the age of sixty five living with Alzheimer’s disease in the United States. Researchers want to understand whether modifying everyday habits like eating patterns can protect brain health and delay the onset of severe cognitive decline.

In the past, observational studies have linked diets lower in fat to better cognitive health. An observational study is one where researchers simply track people’s behaviors over time without asking them to change their habits. However, these studies can only show associations, rather than proving that a specific diet directly prevents cognitive decline. To find stronger evidence, scientists rely on randomized clinical trials, where participants are randomly assigned to follow a specific intervention or act as a control group.

A major project called the Women’s Health Initiative previously conducted one such trial. This large study tracked the health of tens of thousands of postmenopausal women, meaning women who had permanently stopped having menstrual periods. In previous reports from a subset of this trial, researchers noticed that women assigned to a low fat diet had lower rates of possible cognitive impairment, based on scores from a test of global cognitive functioning, compared to those eating their usual diet.

Based on those initial results, researchers wanted to test if this dietary pattern also translated to a lower risk of eventually dying from dementia. Rowan T. Chlebowski, a researcher at The Lundquist Institute in Torrance, California, led a team of investigators to examine this question. They looked at the long term survival data of the original trial participants. The goal was to see if the dietary intervention provided lasting protection against fatal neurodegenerative conditions.

The researchers analyzed data from a large randomized clinical trial that originally enrolled 48,835 postmenopausal women in the United States. The participants ranged in age from fifty to seventy nine years old. When they joined the study between 1993 and 1998, all of the women consumed diets where at least thirty two percent of their daily calories came from fat. Cognitive function was not a strict requirement for joining the study, but all participants had to be functionally independent.

The research team randomly assigned the women into two groups. Forty percent of the participants joined a dietary intervention group. Nutritionists guided this group to reduce their fat intake to twenty percent of their daily calories while increasing their consumption of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. The remaining sixty percent of the women served as a comparison group.

The women in the comparison group received standard health materials but did not receive ongoing counseling from study nutritionists. The intensive dietary intervention lasted for a median of eight and a half years. During this time, women in the intervention group successfully reduced their fat intake and increased their consumption of plant based foods. The differences in fat intake between the two groups remained measurable for up to thirteen years.

To determine how this dietary shift affected dementia mortality, the researchers tracked the participants for a median of twenty years. They verified causes of death using medical records, death certificates, and the National Death Index, which is a centralized database of death record information in the United States. They looked specifically at deaths caused by Alzheimer’s disease and non-Alzheimer’s forms of dementia.

The results showed that the dietary intervention did not prevent deaths from dementia. Out of the original study population, 1,386 women eventually died from dementia related causes. The rates of dementia mortality were almost identical between the group that ate a low fat diet and the group that consumed their usual diet. The difference between the two groups was not statistically significant.

The researchers also looked at specific types of dementia to see if the diet had a targeted effect. They found that the low fat eating pattern did not change the rate of death from Alzheimer’s disease. It also did not change the rate of death from other types of dementia, such as vascular dementia or Lewy body dementia. The overall impact on severe cognitive decline resulting in death was effectively zero.

The research team did perform analyses on specific subgroups of women based on their age at the start of the study. In one of these subgroup analyses, they noticed a trend toward lower dementia mortality for younger women, particularly those in their fifties and sixties when the trial began. The researchers noted a gradual decrease in dementia deaths for these younger age brackets compared to older participants. However, this trend did not extend to women who were seventy or older when they altered their diets.

The researchers noted that the low fat diet did produce other measurable health benefits during the trial. The intervention positively influenced body weight, physical activity levels, and the risk of developing diabetes and high blood pressure. Medical professionals widely consider these factors to be potential contributors to dementia risk. Because the diet improved these health markers but failed to reduce dementia mortality, the study suggests that improving cardiovascular health in later life may not be enough to reverse existing neurodegenerative processes.

While the study tracked thousands of participants over two decades, readers should consider a few important caveats. The researchers evaluated dementia mortality, which means they only counted cases where dementia was recorded as a cause of death. They did not measure dementia incidence, which is the number of people who developed the condition but perhaps died of something else. This distinction means the diet might still influence the onset of mild cognitive issues without necessarily changing the ultimate cause of death.

Determining the exact cause of death in older adults can also be imprecise. As people age, they often develop multiple overlapping health conditions, making it difficult for doctors to pinpoint a single fatal disease on a death certificate. This inherent ambiguity in medical records could obscure subtle benefits of the dietary intervention. The reliance on death certificates is a standard practice in long term studies, but it is an imperfect measure of cognitive health.

The positive trend observed in women under the age of seventy also requires cautious interpretation. Because the researchers analyzed many different subgroups, this single positive finding could simply be a result of statistical chance. Alternatively, it might suggest that lifestyle changes need to start much earlier in life to effectively protect the brain. Future clinical trials will need to test dietary interventions specifically in younger age groups to confirm if early changes offer true protection against dementia.
