text:
Dem Senate candidate pushed church-backed private real estate venture that broke securities laws | Ashe Short, Just The News

Adam Hamilton is asking Kansas voters to trust him with a Senate seat, but the last time he used his pastoral influence to raise money, the church-backed venture he promoted admitted breaking state securities laws and ran out of cash.

In 2000, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, now the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Kansas, was the most visible advocate for a development company that raised millions from church members but failed to deliver on its promises.

Hamilton was the founding pastor of the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kansas, just outside Kansas City when the church used a for-profit company, COR Development, LLC, to buy 47 acres to develop commercially, with 15 acres to be set aside for the church.

The company registered a public offering with the SEC but only raised about $8.65 million, or roughly half of its $16 million goal, and offered units directly to the public. The company's filing added that "COR Development is an early-stage company with no operating history, and COR Development expects to encounter risks frequently faced by early-stage companies in real estate development in growing markets."

Hamilton claimed to be behind the land acquisition idea in Reuters interview

The religious angle was unheard of during the dot-com boom of the early 2000s. The SEC filings list the Church of the Resurrection as the only member with an interest in CORnerstone Development, which selected COR Development’s managers. While the church was heavily involved in COR, Hamilton is not listed as a manager or leader in any documents regarding the company, but he appeared to be behind the land acquisition idea, according to an interview with Reuters in September 2000. Hamilton told the outlet that the decision to create a stock offering came after he realized the church needed more land – as it was one of the fastest growing churches in the nation at that time – but could not afford to pay $250,000 an acre for the land that was available in the area.

Hamilton reportedly told Reuters that the church began a massive fund-raising drive to build a new church by 2002, but that church members would not give large amounts of money to buy the land. A stock offering seemed like the best solution.

"When I went to seminary, I never dreamed of helping to design a commercial real-estate project," Hamilton told Reuters. "But this really is a means to another end.”

"We've said we want to be a 'whatever it takes kind of church.' The public offering is part of the whatever it takes."

Hamilton’s campaign did not respond to a Just the News inquiry prior to press time.

The plan for the 47 acres was to build shops and offices on about two-thirds of the land and donate 15 acres to the church, allowing investors to make charitable tax deductions. In COR’s SEC prospectus, the 15 acres were to be split into two donations: two acres to the church in the first year, and the remaining 13 acres in 2002. As of 2003, SEC filings still show the land donation as planned.

Hamilton does not appear as filing or being a signatory to the share offerings.

COR admits that the 2001 sale had not complied with exemptions from state securities laws

The entire development nearly collapsed in 2003. That year, COR admitted that it had violated Kansas and Missouri securities laws, stopped public SEC reporting in 2003, and disclosed that management had concerns the company might not be able to pay its debts or stay in business very long.

The company admitted that the 2001 sale had not complied with state exemptions from registration, so the units it sold “may be subject to rescission,” meaning that investors could demand their money back. COR also disclosed “substantial doubt about the Company's ability to continue as a going concern." On June 30, 2003, COR said it had zero dollars in cash, a $5.08 million banknote and a $610,000 bank overdraft. Its lender stated that it would not fund phase one of the development until a buyback offer to Kansas investors was completed. Because COR stopped public SEC reporting in 2003, Just the News was unable to find any results of the rescission or if any investors received their money back.

COR also made a $2 million loan to Market Foods for a grocery store in the development, but was only repaid $37,905 before Market Foods defaulted and eventually filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2005.

In the end, the development was completed as the Cornerstone of Leawood, which still exists today, and is, at least in part, still listed for sale or lease. The Church of the Resurrection eventually built a new church for $80 million, and Hamilton is still the church’s lead pastor.

Four new priests have been ordained in France after years of uncertainty and I wonder whether their story offers a glimpse of a more sensible way forward in the Church's increasingly bitter dispute over the Traditional Latin Mass.

On 31 October, Bishop François Touvet of Fréjus-Toulon ordained four members of the Society of the Missionaries of Divine Mercy at the Benedictine abbey of Notre-Dame de Triors: Clément Anouil, Henri Gilliot, Guillaume Le Gall and Thibaud Perruchot.

For any Catholic, four new priests should be cause for rejoicing, but these particular ordinations carry a significance that extends well beyond the four men involved. The community, founded in 2005 under Bishop Dominique Rey, has a particular attachment to the traditional Roman liturgy. Its priestly ordinations had been caught up in the restrictions imposed upon the diocese in 2022, leaving candidates waiting for years while questions surrounding their formation, liturgical identity and relationship with Rome were addressed. What makes the eventual resolution so interesting is that neither the community nor the bishop appears to have treated ecclesial communion and fidelity to liturgical tradition as mutually exclusive.

Bishop Touvet pursued sustained discussions with Rome, and an agreement was eventually reached. The ordinations took place in Latin, using the postconciliar liturgical books, accompanied by Gregorian chant from the Benedictine monks. The newly ordained priests retain permission to celebrate Mass according to the 1962 Missal. It was not an unqualified victory for those who wanted the ordinations celebrated according to the older rite and we should not pretend otherwise, but neither was it the extinction of the community's traditional liturgical identity.

There is something rather encouraging about that.

For too long, the debate surrounding Traditionis custodes has been characterised by an extraordinary degree of suspicion, as though attachment to the liturgical patrimony of the Church necessarily implies rejection of the Second Vatican Council or the authority of the Roman Pontiff. Equally, some traditionalists have responded to restrictions by treating legitimate ecclesiastical authority as an obstacle to be circumvented rather than an essential element of Catholic communion. Neither approach offers a satisfactory vision of the Church.

What happened at Triors suggests that another approach remains possible: one in which a bishop takes seriously both his responsibility for ecclesial unity and the legitimate spiritual aspirations of a community entrusted to his care. There is a particularly interesting detail in Bishop Touvet's homily. Rather than defining these men primarily by their liturgical preferences, he spoke of the priesthood as an ontological configuration to Christ, invoking Vatican II's Presbyterorum Ordinis and the priest's sacred responsibility to act in persona Christi Capitis.

That seems to me precisely the right starting point. The Church needs holy priests who offer the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass with reverence, preach the Catholic faith without compromise, administer the sacraments faithfully and bring souls to Christ. The question of which authorised form of the Roman liturgy nourishes their vocation should not eclipse that fundamental mission.

Of course, these ordinations do not constitute a reversal of Traditionis custodes, nor do they resolve the wider difficulties facing Catholics attached to the older liturgy. The community has accepted a compromise, and there are legitimate questions about why such a prolonged and painful interruption was necessary in the first place.

But four men who might otherwise still be waiting are now priests of Jesus Christ, serving the Church in communion with their bishop and the Successor of Peter.

Surely that is something worth celebrating?

I have long believed that the traditional liturgy is a treasure of the Church, not an embarrassing historical anomaly to be managed towards extinction. I also believe that communion with Peter and the bishops is constitutive of Catholic life, not an optional extra dependent upon whether we happen to approve of every ecclesiastical decision.

The experience of Fréjus-Toulon suggests that these convictions need not be irreconcilable.

Perhaps the most encouraging thing about these four ordinations is not that one side has won, but that, for once, the Church has found a way to move forward without demanding that fidelity to tradition and fidelity to ecclesial communion be treated as enemies.

"He was history.
.285 average, 3,419 hits, Hall of Fame history.
He had driven into that parking lot at Fenway for the first time with a sixth-place team being asked to replace Ted Williams, and he left with a six-place team under a cloud of the John Updike goodbye of Williams."
Peter Gammons. "Boston Globe."
"Red Sox scout Frank "Bots" Nekola had had his eye on Carl since he was a sophomore in high school.
But he wasn’t coming up with $100,000, either, and so Carl’s father sent his son off to college.
They’d fielded full scholarship offers from a number of colleges, but chose Notre Dame, where he played on a scholarship that was half baseball and half basketball.
Yaz completed his freshman year, without playing on the varsity team, but then the offers got more serious, even exceeding $100,000.
The Red Sox didn’t make the largest offer, but the admiration of the local parish priest for Tom Yawkey counted for a lot, and Yaz’s father wanted him to play for an East Coast team, not too far from home.
Yaz signed with the Red Sox on November 29, 1958 for a $108,000 bonus, and their agreement to cover the rest of his college education. 
Sox GM Joe Cronin then met Yaz for the first time;
And saw a 5’11”, 160-pound kid.
Cronin couldn’t help himself, blurting out:
"We’re paying this kind of money for this guy?"
Carl went back to finish up the fall semester at Notre Dame;
After signing the six-figure contract, Yaz’s father increased his son’s weekly allowance from $5 to $7.50 a week."
Carl Yastrzemski's father was Karol Yastrzemski, who anglicized his name to Carl Yastrzemski.

text:
The afterlife. Arrivals, 2026. A man of forty-four comes through the gate and finds his ancestors waiting for him.

Grandad: "You're early, lad."

Vegan: "Early? People used to die at thirty-five."

Grandad: "I was eighty-one. She was ninety. He's the youngest of us and he had the Black Death and a landlord. So. What was it?"

Vegan: "Heart, apparently. Which is mad, because I was plant-based for twelve years. No meat, no dairy. Lentils, oats, beans. I ate the way humans ate for most of history."

Grandad: "Did you hear that? He ate like us. On purpose."

Medieval peasant: "What was in your pot?"

Vegan: "Lentils. Beans. Oats in the morning."

Medieval peasant: "Peas, beans and oats, one pot, every day of my life. We called it pottage and it killed me at forty. Who's your lord?"

Vegan: "I don't have a lord."

Medieval peasant: "Then who was eating the deer?"

Vegan: "Nobody. Beef was in every shop. I chose not to."

Medieval peasant: "A free deer, and he ate the pottage. Four hundred years of this family dreaming of the lord's table and the first one who gets to sit at it orders the peas."

Vegan: "Red meat is linked to heart disease and cancer. The science is pretty clear."

Medieval peasant: "Whose science?"

Vegan: "The government's. There's an official plate."

Medieval peasant: "The lord had an official plate. It had a swan on it."

Highland crofter: "Milk?"

Vegan: "Oat milk."

Highland crofter: "What in God's name is an oat milk?"

Vegan: "Oats soaked in water and strained. Dairy's inflammatory and it's cruel to the cows."

Highland crofter: "That's thin porridge. I had porridge three times a day while the laird's cattle were driven past my door to market. Was there a cow where you lived?"

Vegan: "Thousands."

Highland crofter: "Thousands of cows, and my descendant is standing here telling me he drank the oats. On the cow's behalf."

Irish tenant's wife: "What happened when the lentils ran out?"

Vegan: "They never did. The shops are full."

Irish tenant's wife: "I watched the beef go up the gangplank for England with soldiers on either side while my children ate grass. You had the beef in a shop, with no soldiers, and you left it there."

Vegan: "Cattle are destroying the planet. Methane. There was a whole UN conference on it."

Grandad: "What did they eat at the conference?"

Vegan: "I didn't check."

Grandad: "We did. We get the telly up here. Beef."

Vegan: "I covered my nutrition with supplements. B12, iron, vitamin D, zinc, omega-3."

Grandad: "That's a Sunday roast in tablet form. Who sold you the tablets?"

Vegan: "A plant-based company."

Grandad: "Course they did."

Vegan: "Look, the point is I chose this. None of you had a choice. That's the difference."

Medieval peasant: "That's the exact bit none of us can get past, boy. Every soul in this family ate the plants because the man above him kept the animal. You had the animal put in front of you and you handed it back."

Vegan: "Plant-based is actually more expensive now. I paid more for the lentils than beef costs."

Irish tenant's wife: "You paid extra. For the famine."

Vegan: "It's ethical."

Highland crofter: "So said the laird, every rent day."

Vegan: "I'm sorry, but none of you understand modern nutrition."

Grandad: "You're forty-four and the whole family's come down to the gate. Which of us is it that doesn't understand?"

Grandad: "Come on. Your nan's done a joint."

Vegan: "I don't eat beef."

Grandad: "Every one of us ate what you ate, and every one of us would have swapped it for what you were offered. Sit down. It's what your ancestors ate, the one day they were allowed."

text:
B.C. Safer Supply — Independent Evidence

The questions are who owns the equipment, who receives public money, who lobbies government, who profits, and whether the programs work.

The evidence needs to distinguish documented financial relationships from allegations of improper influence.

Established facts:

* Mark Tyndall: Former senior B.C. public-health official; founded MySafe, which operated automated hydromorphone-dispensing machines.
* MySafe: Received $3.4 million in federal funding in 2019.
* Perry Kendall: Former B.C. provincial health officer; co-founded Fair Price Pharma.
* Martin Schechter: Fair Price Pharma co-founder; reported as a registered B.C. government lobbyist.
* Machine ownership: MySafe operated the dispensing machines. That does not establish who legally owned the hardware or received manufacturing profits.

Machine manufacturer and financial connections

6. Dispension Industries Inc. — Dartmouth, Nova Scotia

* Manufactured and supplied the MySafe machines.
* Corey Yantha: Identified as company president in 2020.
* Machines were offered on a lease basis.
* Company provided data-management services.
* Received a $500,000 federal government loan in 2020.
* Current shareholders, beneficial ownership and total government payments remain unverified. CityNews Ottawa +1

7. FP Pharma Inc. — Government lobbying records

* Martin Schechter: Listed as president and CEO.
* Registered lobbying activity in 2020–2022.
* Government contacts included senior B.C. health officials and Vancouver Coastal Health board chair Penny Ballem.
* The registry listed no government funding for the organization in those registrations. Lobbyists Registrar

What independent research found

8. 2024 — JAMA Internal Medicine

* B.C. opioid prescribing increased.
* Opioid-poisoning hospitalizations increased.
* No statistically significant change in overdose deaths was identified.
* Observational findings; causation not established. PubMed

9. 2025 — JAMA Network Open

* Hospitalizations associated with B.C.‘s safer supply policy increased an estimated 33% compared with the study’s counterfactual.
* Following decriminalization, the combined increase was estimated at 58%.
* Researchers could not conclusively attribute increased overdose deaths to the policies.
* The study could not establish that safer supply itself caused the hospitalization increase. PMC

10. 2024 — Vancouver observational research

* 50 safer supply recipients studied.
* 20% reported selling or trading some prescribed hydromorphone.
* Two reported selling or trading their entire prescription.
* Small sample; not representative of all B.C. recipients. INHSU

The financial trail established so far: Dispension manufactured the machines, MySafe operated them, federal funding supported both organizations, and FP Pharma registered lobbying activity.

Still requiring independent verification: Dispension’s actual shareholders, machine lease payments, individual financial interests, government procurement contracts and any financial relationships between these organizations and public officials.

The strongest independent evidence currently supports concerns about diversion and hospitalization outcomes. It does not establish corruption or improper personal profit.

text:
I just can’t get my head behind this indulgent nanny statism. 

From 6 Nov 2026, new provisions of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 will criminalise possession of certain types of porn in England & Wales, with offenders facing up to THREE YEARS in prison. THREE YEARS

This has been gnawing at me for DAYS. 

It is quite a crude subject so i can understand why people might not want to discuss it over tea. BUT the implications for individual liberty are worth examining

I don’t particularly like porn or sex work. Neither appeals to me. In fact i find both degenerate & exploitative. 

But the Govt isn’t seeking to ban either outright. Instead it’s selectively criminalising certain depictions, including some involving adults roleplaying sexual acts that aren’t necessarily unlawful in themselves…

I have no difficulty supporting prohibitions on child sexual abuse material. In fact i welcome it

BUT I do question criminalising depictions of oral sex for example, “face sitting”, involving consenting adults.

Is there sufficient evidence that watching something causes someone to commit sexual violence? And even if exposure influences behaviour, does that justify criminalising private possession?

At what point does the state stop preventing sexual violence and start policing private sexual fantasy?

Feminism has fought for women’s bodily autonomy, sexual freedom & protection from coercion. But doesn’t protecting women risk becoming paternalistic when the state starts determining which consensual sexual expressions are acceptable?

John Stuart Mill’s harm principle seems particularly relevant here… the exercise of power over an individual against their will requires justification by reference to harm to others not merely moral disapproval

We ought to be able to distinguish between what is immoral, what is distasteful, what is dangerous and what ought to be CRIMINAL . . . 

And if we’re going to start sending people to prison for what they privately watch, I’d rather hope we can offer a more convincing justification than an article about throat cancer 😂

text:
GST Officer Relies on AI Prompts to Draft Show Cause Notice: High Court Quashes Notice for Lack of Independent Application of Mind!

Issue:
Whether a Show Cause Notice (Form GST DRC-01A) issued by the Department primarily relying upon an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool, without independent application of mind by the proper officer, has legal validity under the Central/State Goods and Services Tax Act.

Rule:
Under the provisions of the Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, the issuance of a statutory show cause notice requires the competent authority to personally examine the factual matrix and independently apply its mind. The statute mandates that quasi-judicial powers cannot be delegated to automated mechanisms, and the deployment of AI tools for drafting or initiating adverse penal proceedings lacks statutory sanction unless expressly permitted by law.

Application:
In the present case, the Department issued a Show Cause Notice dated 02.02.2025 (in Form GST DRC-01A) against the Assessee. Along with the notice, an unedited document was uploaded on the GST portal containing clear output prompts from an AI tool. The AI text blatantly offered suggestions to the officer such as: tightening the allegations with paragraph-wise citations, converting notes into Order-in-Original reasoning, inserting specific clauses of inferring knowledge and connivance, and drafting a “defence-proof rebuttal” against the Assessee's anticipated defences by offering commands like “make it lethal”.

Conclusion:
Holding that the preparation of a show cause notice through an AI tool lacks statutory sanction and establishes a patent non-application of mind, the High Court quashed the impugned Show Cause Notice dated 02.02.2025 along with all consequential proceedings, reserving liberty to the Department to issue a fresh notice strictly in accordance with law upon independent examination of facts.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling establishes a crucial precedent in Indian tax jurisprudence that statutory and quasi-judicial functions cannot be outsourced to AI tools, reaffirming that administrative convenience cannot replace the statutory mandate of a tax officer’s independent application of mind.

Title: SRO INDIA vs. STATE OF PUNJAB
Court: THE HIGH COURT OF PUNJAB AND HARYANA
Citation: CWP-11494-2026 (O&M)
Dated:  07-07-2026

2 — But for us as Christians, the bottom line goes even deeper than politics or constitutional language.

✝️ God says, “You shall not murder.”

Scripture repeatedly condemns the shedding of innocent blood and calls us to defend those who cannot defend themselves.

If the child in the womb is every bit as human as the child outside the womb, we cannot find a biblical reason why that child’s right to life should change because of how he or she was conceived, because of a disability or fetal anomaly, or because of age, size, location, developmental stage, or dependency.

None of those things changes what that child is.

That is where Amendment 3 becomes a matter of conscience for us.

We understand the argument that if we cannot presently save every baby, we should save the ones we can. We have wrestled with that argument.

But we keep coming back to the difference between being unable to save everyone and affirmatively voting for constitutional language that gives legal permission to intentionally take the lives of some innocent children.

For us, those are not the same thing.

We desperately want to save every baby we possibly can. But we do not believe we can accomplish that good objective by giving our affirmative vote to something that permits what we believe God has clearly forbidden.

We keep coming back to two biblical examples that have challenged us as we’ve wrestled with this decision.

In 1 Samuel 15, King Saul obeyed much of what God commanded but made exceptions based on his own judgement. He even offered a religious justification for his actions. Yet Samuel reminded him that “to obey is better than sacrifice.” Saul’s intentions and explanations did not excuse his disobedience, and God rejected him as king.

Contrast that with Daniel in chapter 1. Daniel accepted a Babylonian education and a new name, accommodating where God had not clearly forbidden it. But he resolved not to eat the king’s food because he understood that doing so would defile him before God, who had given the Israelites specific dietary laws. Daniel did not reject every accommodation; he drew the line where God had drawn the line. And Scripture tells us that God blessed Daniel and his companions, giving them favor, wisdom, and understanding.

These accounts have caused us to ask ourselves a difficult question:

Does a desirable outcome justify an exception to a divine command?

We understand why some Christians believe Amendment 3 is the best available way to save more unborn children. But for us, the question is whether we can affirmatively support constitutional language that permits the taking of innocent human life, even while hoping that other lives will be saved.

We cannot reconcile that with what we believe God has commanded.

🙏 That is why, with deep conviction and much prayer, we will be voting NO on Amendment 3.

We say this without questioning the faith, sincerity, or motives of our brothers and sisters in Christ who have also prayed deeply about this and reached a different conclusion. This is a fallen world, and we believe the choice placed before Missouri voters is a terrible one.

We aren’t sharing this to argue with our Christian friends or divide from people we love. We are sharing it because this issue is too important for us to remain silent, and because we know many of you are still praying and wrestling with the same questions we have been wrestling with.

Our prayer is that someday very soon we will stop being asked which unborn children we are willing to protect and instead recognize that every human being, from the moment of conception, deserves equal protection under the law.

And perhaps the most important question for each of us as Christians is not simply:

“What is politically achievable?”

But rather:

✝️ “Where has God drawn the line—and am I willing to draw mine in the same place?”

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📊 KEY NUMBERS

🔹 Revenue: ₹645.4 Cr ↑12.5% YoY | ↑2.7% QoQ
🔹 USD revenue: $67.4 mn ↑3.6% YoY
🔹 Constant currency growth: ↑6.8% YoY
🔹 Operating profit: ₹119.1 Cr ↑22.4% YoY
🔹 Operating margin: 18.5% (17.5% last quarter, 17.0% a year ago)
🔹 Reported PAT: ₹62.2 Cr ↑15.1% YoY | ↓8.0% QoQ
🔹 Adjusted PAT: ₹79.1 Cr ↑20.7% YoY
🔹 Interim dividend: ₹3.05/share (record date 6 Nov)

PAT fell QoQ because of a ₹4 Cr one-time charge, lower other income and higher interest costs.

🚀 GROWTH ENGINES

▪️ Infra & Security (IMSS): ↑24% YoY at a 31.7% margin
▪️ GenAI Business Services: more than doubled YoY
▪️ Revenue from its own AI platforms (IP-led) rose to 10.5% of the total from 9.3%, led by SecAIGenie and ELLIPSE
▪️ BFSI is now 27.7% of revenue, up from 10.9% in FY24
▪️ Attrition fell to 14.3%; utilisation rose to 81.8%

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎙️ MANAGEMENT COMMENTARY & GUIDANCE

▪️ FY27 growth guidance of 12.5% reconfirmed; H1 is running at 13.4%
▪️ The operating margin band is 17.5–18.5%, and Q2 landed at the top
▪️ The US (56% of revenue) grew only 0.9% QoQ, hit by EdTech pressure and project completions at hi-tech clients. Management says bookings have improved.
▪️ Part of IMSS's QoQ jump came from revenue that slipped from Q1 into Q2
▪️ AI productivity is letting the company bid more aggressively on fixed-price deals
▪️ Collection days rose to 101 from 92 on billing and system migration delays. Management expects recovery in H2.
▪️ Next focus areas: AI-first Global Capability Centres (GCCs), the private equity ecosystem, and industry-specific solutions

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🤝 ITC INFOTECH MERGER: THE REAL STORY

▪️ Shareholders get 25 ITC Infotech shares for every 81 Happiest Minds shares, which values Happiest Minds at ₹405/share
▪️ The promoter is selling 22.1% to ITC Infotech for cash at ₹390–400. There is no open offer for public shareholders.
▪️ ITC will own 73.4% of a combined company targeting $1 bn revenue by FY28
▪️ The merger needs regulatory approvals, then NCLT approval. Completion is expected by Oct–Nov 2027, after which the merged company lists.

At ₹306, the stock trades 24% below the swap value. That gap is the price of a ~12-month wait plus approval risk.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💰 VALUATION SNAPSHOT (@ ₹306)

🔹 Market cap: ₹4,658 Cr
🔹 P/E (TTM): 19.9x | On adjusted EPS: 15.2x
🔹 Forward P/E FY27E: ~17.5x
🔹 EV/EBITDA: ~11x (the swap deal valued it at 15.1x)
🔹 P/B: 2.8x | P/Sales: 1.9x | PEG: ~1.2
🔹 Dividend yield: ~2.1% | ROE: ~13%

📈 P/E: history vs no
🔹 3-year average: ~48x
🔹 Now: 19.9x, about 63% below the 5-year average

A re-rating back to 50x is unlikely: growth has halved and ROE has fallen from ~21% to ~13%.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 @SharesNservices VIEW :

✅ Positives: The best margins in several quarters, AI platforms gaining share, and BFSI diversifying revenue.
⚠️ Watch: Currency did almost half the growth work, the US is stagnant, and H1 cash flow was only 0.63x profit.
💡 Valuation: The stock is cheap against its own history, but the swap ratio now sets the price. Adjusted for the wait, the ₹405 swap value is worth about ₹355 today.

Our View: POSITIVE ✅

📉 TECHNICAL LEVELS

🟢 Support: ₹290–300
🔴 Resistance: ₹340, then ₹370, then ₹410

₹410 sits close to the ₹405 swap value, which makes it a natural ceiling.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧾 BOTTOM LINE

The business is improving, but the stock is now a merger story.

💬 Would you hold for ITC Infotech shares or exit before the merger?
💬 Can AI-led services keep margins above 18%?

Drop your view below 👇

Happy Election Day! Here's what to expect throughout the day, along with a rough timeline of how election night will unfold. All times Eastern.

8 a.m. - 6 p.m.
No results yet, but we'll be tracking turnout and other updates throughout the day. More than 30 million Americans are expected to vote across the country today. Much of what we'll hear won't be particularly informative, and I'm sure there will be plenty of reports about long lines somewhere, for example. But we will also get some hard data that can offer decent insights into the electorate. We shouldn't expect these numbers to tell us very much about the eventual outcome, but some will be more informative than others, particularly in Florida, where we receive regular updates on turnout by party registration throughout the day.

6 p.m.
The first polls close in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. IN-05 and KY-06 offer early tests of Democrats' ability to compete in Republican-held districts, while Indiana's secretary of state race is also worth watching. However, we expect much of the first hour's vote to come from early ballots, which are likely to be more Democratic than the final results. They also won't tell us much about who turned out on Election Day itself.

7 p.m.
We should begin receiving some informative results very quickly. Florida's House races will provide an important early benchmark. Democrats winning more than two of FL-07, 09, 14, 22, 25, and 27 would be an encouraging sign for the party, while Republicans would hope to carry at least five of the six. Still, Florida's recent shift toward Republicans limits how much we can extrapolate from these results to the national political environment. Georgia and suburban Virginia should offer additional clues, while races in New Hampshire and South Carolina will help establish how broad the battleground is tonight.

7:30 p.m.
Ohio and North Carolina bring the Senate fight into focus as Democrats hope to flip both seats. Roy Cooper is favored in North Carolina; a close race would be encouraging for Republicans. Sherrod Brown’s Ohio comeback bid is a more demanding test of Democrats’ path to a majority. Early and mail ballots may give Democrats an initial advantage that narrows as Election Day votes arrive.

8 p.m.
Most Texas polls close, with James Talarico challenging Ken Paxton. Large early returns should offer a useful first read. Maine and Michigan also begin entering the picture, but their Senate races may require considerably more patience. A competitive Kansas Senate race would suggest Democrats are reaching well beyond the usual battlegrounds. Results will start reporting in tons of competitive U.S. House races.

9–10 p.m.
The Senate battlefield extends to Iowa and Nebraska. Wisconsin’s governor race, House contests in Arizona and Colorado, and later Nevada and Montana broaden the picture. Poll closings won’t always mean immediate results.

11 p.m. onward
The West Coast adds many safe Democratic seats, so a rising Democratic seat count alone won’t signal a change in the national trend. Hawaii and most of Alaska close at midnight. Alaska’s first results are scheduled after 1 a.m., bringing Mary Peltola’s challenge to Dan Sullivan into focus.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the third day of November in 1941, in the quiet rooms of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo, Admiral Osami Nagano stood before Emperor Hirohito and laid before him the completed plan for an attack on the American fleet at Pearl Harbor.

Nagano, then sixty-one and newly installed as Chief of the Naval General Staff, was no stranger to the United States. Years earlier he had studied at Harvard and served as naval attaché in Washington; he knew the size of the American industrial base and the strength of its navy as well as any officer in the Japanese service. Yet on this day he presented a scheme born of calculated risk and narrowing options: a carrier task force would cross the Pacific in silence, launch its aircraft before dawn on a Sunday morning, and strike the ships lying at anchor in Hawaii. The object was to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet in a single blow, buying time for Japan to seize the oil and resources of Southeast Asia while negotiations in Washington still appeared to offer a faint chance of settlement.

The plan itself had been shaped largely by Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto and the staff of the Combined Fleet, refined through months of study and argument. Nagano, after earlier reservations, had come to accept it. In the audience with the Emperor he described the operational outline—the routes, the timing, the element of surprise—knowing that final authority rested with the sovereign. Two days later, on November 5, an Imperial Conference endorsed the decision that war would begin in early December if diplomacy failed. The machinery of the attack was already in motion; the fleet would sail for its staging area in the Kuriles later that month.

What Nagano presented that November morning was more than a naval plan. It was the moment when Japan’s leadership committed itself to a course whose outcome no one could fully foresee, a gamble that would bring the United States into the war and reshape the balance of the Pacific. The quiet of the palace that day stood in sharp contrast to the violence that would follow on the morning of December 7.

text:
Starbase Louisiana Week in Review, Issue 2

Another busy week, and BIG NEWS. The State's contract with SpaceX is finally public, and there's a new job opening too. 🎉

STATE CONTRACT RELEASED
After a public records request by Vermilion United, Louisiana Economic Development released the State's signed agreement with SpaceX, dated Aug 25, 2026.

• New jobs must pay at least 150% of the statewide average wage
• At least $25M to the Community Foundation of Acadiana by Dec. 31, 2030
• Reasonable efforts to prefer Louisiana suppliers and contractors when they're competitive on price, quality and delivery
• LED will offer FastStart workforce training and the High Impact Jobs Program
• Approved uses: a rocket launch spaceport plus related manufacturing, compute, power generation and storage, and employee housing and amenities
• The State will set up long-term funding for the agencies that handle the project's permits
• Permit and FAA licensing delays pause deadlines on both sides
• SpaceX files budgets, twice-yearly progress reports, quarterly payroll reports and a sworn yearly compliance certification with LED
• The $100M land payment goes into LED's Site Investment and Infrastructure Improvement Fund
• The State can buy the land back only in narrow cases, by refunding the full $100M
• Rebates of state and local sales and use taxes on aerospace equipment and materials for 20 years, renewable for 10 more if SpaceX creates 200 jobs and invests $1B
• The contract runs through Aug. 25, 2037

JOBS
• SpaceX now has 9 openings in Pecan Island, including a second Communications Lead role posted Nov 2.

BIG NUMBER: 70%
• SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell says about 70% of the Starbase, Texas workforce is local to the Rio Grande Valley, and SpaceX aims for a similar share in Louisiana.

SCHOOLS
• The Vermilion Parish School Board is having about 4,000 acres of school land near White Lake appraised ahead of possible land-swap talks with SpaceX. Superintendent Tommy Byler says the land brings in only $20K to $30K a year from hunting leases, and he'd like land closer to "where they're building two hotels and a restaurant."

COMMUNITY
• At the Police Jury committee meeting on Wed, Nov 4 at 5:30 PM in Abbeville, the Vermilion Council on Aging will request SpaceX-related funding.

PERMITS
• Day 39 for @SpaceX's big coastal permit for the road, bridge, and wharf. It's still marked incomplete after the state asked for more information on Oct 1. No new SpaceX filings this week.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT
• Starbase Louisiana is getting international attention. Canada's Globe and Mail visited Pecan Island for a long feature on what the project means for rural Cajun country.

• LED's official SpaceX FAQ says SpaceX will pay for its own new power generation and lines.

• DOTD selected Royal Engineers & Consultants of New Orleans for work tied to the SpaceX site, under a contract running through 2031, as the State studies roads and possible LA 82 improvements.

text:
Kidnapped: In 1988, Nigeria kidnapped a Jamaican who had made Nigeria his home for 18 years...

He lectured Sociology at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria from 1970-1988

He was married to a Nigerian woman named Makki Sakaba.

I was still in secondary school at FGC Portharcourt (SS2), but I remember this case cos I read a lot of newspapers and listened to news a lot too.

His name is Dr Patrick Wilmot.

He was born in Jamaica in 1942, studied at Yale and Vanderbilt, and arrived in Nigeria in 1970.

He was brought in by people such as Aminu Kano and MD Yusuf, the former Inspector General of Police, who introduced him to ABU Zaria. It was MD Yusuf who sent him a flight ticket to come and see him in Nigeria, then MD Yusuf sent me to Ishaya Audu who was the vice chancellor and he offered me employment at ABU.

For 18 years he taught Political Sociology at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.

He became one of the most popular foreign lecturers in Nigeria. He was radical, vocal, close to the Marxist group in ABU that included Yusuf Bala Usman, Jibrin Ibrahim, Raufu Mustapha. Students adored him.

Then Babangida happened.

In February 1988, security operatives picked him up close to his house in Zaria. They pushed him into a vehicle without his shoes, without his passport, without his personal items. He was flown out.

Government claimed he was a security risk, a foreign agent, teaching what he was not paid to teach.

He was married to a Nigerian. He had lived here for 18 years. His children knew Nigeria as home. It did not matter.

They said he would be removed to Jamaica through London.

When he arrived in London under escort of Lagos immigration officers, British immigration contacted the Home Secretary and Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher herself said, “You better do whatever he wants. If he wants to stay in this country, let him stay because if we do something to him the repercussions will not just be in Nigeria but all over the world and British interest will be damaged.”

He remained in London.

Students at ABU protested. Academics protested. But the man was gone.

More than 35 years later, Wilmot still cannot live in Nigeria again. He says so himself.

Picture residing in a nation for 18 years, marrying from there, teaching its children, and one morning they carry you like a criminal without your shoes and say leave.

That was Nigeria in 1988.

Democrat Agenda: Pack the Supreme Court, Kill the Filibuster, Add New States, and Let Illegals Vote | Antonio Graceffo, The Gateway Pundit

Democrats have proposed a series of strategic moves that, taken together, would lock in Democratic control of the federal government: expanding the Supreme Court, eliminating the Senate filibuster, abolishing the Electoral College, admitting Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico as states, extending voting rights to illegal aliens, and federalizing election rules.

The push to expand the Supreme Court began in earnest in April 2021, when Senator Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Representatives Jerrold Nadler, Hank Johnson, and Mondaire Jones introduced the Judiciary Act. The bill would add four seats, creating a 13-justice Supreme Court. Democrats controlled both chambers of Congress, and Joe Biden was three months into his presidency. Passage would have given Biden four appointments, turning the Court’s 6–3 conservative majority into a 7–6 majority of Democratic appointees.

The legislation was reintroduced in May 2023, with support from Senator Tina Smith and Representatives Adam Schiff and Cori Bush. Speaking outside the Court in July 2024, Markey said, “We must expand the court.” Smith explicitly linked expansion to eliminating the filibuster, calling on Congress to “reform and expand the Court” and urging Democrats to abolish the filibuster so they could pass the legislation.

Support for expansion has widened in 2026. On a podcast released October 14, former Vice President Kamala Harris said, “I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court,” as Newsweek reported.

House Minority Whip Jim Clyburn has endorsed adding four seats, while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has said Court reform will be a priority if Democrats win both chambers in the midterms. Representative Jamie Raskin, the likely Judiciary Committee chairman if Democrats retake the House, has also backed expansion.

On September 2, House Republicans forced a vote on a constitutional amendment that would fix the Court at nine justices. The measure received 212 votes in favor and 206 against, falling short of the two-thirds majority required for passage. All but one Democrat voted against it. Representative Don Davis of North Carolina was the only Democrat to vote with Republicans.

Ending the legislative filibuster would allow a simple Senate majority to pass ordinary legislation, including Court expansion and statehood bills.

In January 2022, President Joe Biden told an Atlanta audience that if voting bills remained blocked, Democrats had no option but to change Senate rules, “including getting rid of the filibuster for this,” as NPR reported. Days later, Senators Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema joined Republicans to defeat the change, 52–48.

Other prominent Democrats have called for eliminating the filibuster or creating exceptions for specific legislation. In his 2020 eulogy for John Lewis, former President Barack Obama called the filibuster “another Jim Crow relic” and urged its elimination if necessary to pass his proposed voting reforms. He also voiced support for statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C.

As the 2024 Democratic nominee, Harris said, “I think we should eliminate the filibuster for Roe,” in a radio interview. Schumer likewise said Democrats would prioritize circumventing the filibuster to pass voting legislation if they controlled the White House and both chambers of Congress. Senator Angela Alsobrooks campaigned on the pledge, “I will vote to abolish the filibuster.”

Democrats have also sought to replace the Electoral College with direct election of the president. In 2019, Senators Brian Schatz, Dick Durbin, Dianne Feinstein, and Kirsten Gillibrand introduced an amendment to do so. “In an election, the person who gets the most votes should win,” Schatz said at the time.

Schatz, Durbin, and Senator Peter Welch reintroduced the proposal on December 12, 2024, weeks after Trump won both the popular vote and the Electoral College. Durbin described the Electoral College as “this 18th-century invention that disenfranchises millions of Americans,” according to his press release. In an October podcast interview, Harris said: “The popular vote has to matter.”

Because a constitutional amendment requires approval from two-thirds of both chambers of Congress and ratification by 38 states, Democratic-led states have pursued another route: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. Under the agreement, participating states would award their electoral votes to the nationwide popular-vote winner once jurisdictions holding at least 270 electoral votes have joined.

Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger signed legislation adding her state in April 2026. That brought the compact to 19 jurisdictions holding 222 electoral votes, leaving it 48 short of taking effect.

Statehood for D.C. and Puerto Rico would add four senators, along with additional House seats and electoral votes. The Washington, D.C. Admission Act, H.R. 51, passed the House on April 22, 2021, but died in the Senate. Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton reintroduced the bill on January 3, 2025, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries among its 207 cosponsors.

The House passed the Puerto Rico Status Act on December 15, 2022, by a 233–191 vote, with all 217 voting Democrats and 16 Republicans in favor. The bill called for a binding vote on Puerto Rico’s political status, including statehood as an option. Then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the House had voted “to tear down the vestiges of colonialism.”

Democratic strategist James Carville urged Democrats to act immediately if they regained the White House and both chambers of Congress: “on day one, they should make Puerto Rico [and] D.C. a state.” Harris also supported statehood for both if their residents wanted it.

The Democratic-controlled D.C. Council passed the Local Resident Voting Rights Amendment Act on November 21, 2022, allowing noncitizens, including those in the country illegally, to vote in local elections only. The law extends eligibility to residents aged 18 or older who have lived in the District for at least 30 days, regardless of immigration status. Democratic Mayor Muriel Bowser allowed it to become law without her signature. Councilmember Charles Allen, a cosponsor, said the council wanted to focus on “removing barriers to voting.”

The House voted to block the law in February 2023, but the Democratic-majority Senate never took up the resolution, allowing the law to take effect, according to the House committee report. On May 23, 2024, the House voted to repeal it, with 143 Democrats opposing repeal and 52 supporting it. The House passed another repeal bill, H.R. 884, on June 10, 2025, by a 266–148 vote.

In New York City, the City Council passed a law in late 2021 that would have allowed roughly 800,000 noncitizens with green cards or work authorization to vote in city elections, according to Malliotakis’s office. New York’s Court of Appeals struck down the law in a 6–1 ruling on March 20, 2025, finding that the state constitution limits voting to citizens.

The final element is federal control over election rules through the For the People Act. H.R. 1 passed the House in March 2021, with 220 Democrats supporting it and one Democrat joining 209 Republicans in opposition. Among other provisions, the bill would require states to offer same-day voter registration for federal elections. The 2019 House-passed version also contained extensive findings supporting D.C. statehood, linking federal election legislation to the push for new states.

This week’s midterms will determine whether Democrats gain the congressional power to advance these proposals, which could reshape the rules of political competition for years to come.

text:
Compliance that starts after the rejection email is damage control.

The audit belongs inside creative development, while the ad is still cheap to change.

Here's what I run before an ad goes anywhere near Meta.

Eight checks, in this order, because each one changes what the next one looks for.

First, I classify the industry and the product.

A sleep gummy, a weight loss program and a telehealth offer live under different rules. Get this one wrong and every check after it runs on the wrong rulebook.

Then I pull out every claim, including the ones the copy only implies.

"Wake up rested" is a claim.

A before photo sitting next to a price is one too.

Personal attributes come next, and this is the check that catches good writers.

Meta's own policy bans copy that asserts or implies something about the reader's health, age or financial status.

"Struggling with your weight?" tells the reader something about her own body, which is the implication the policy names.

Point the line at the product instead of at her and the idea can stay.

After that I read the language and the headline line by line, hunting for outcome words.

"Melts belly fat" promises an outcome, but "two gummies after dinner" only describes an experience.

The visuals get their own pass, because an image says things the copy never wrote.

A tape measure, a pinched waist and a split screen all make claims without a single word.

If you could not write it as a sentence, you cannot show it as a picture.

Proof is the sixth check.

Every claim still standing needs a study, a review count or a test result behind it.

If nothing is on file, the claim comes out.

Then I open the landing page beside the ad and read the two as one piece.

Say the ad promises gentle support for sleep and the page says knocked out in ten minutes.

The reviewer is reading the PAGE.

Last come the disclosures the offer needs.

A free trial that rolls into a monthly charge has to say so before anyone clicks.

This is why the headline alone was never the test.

The ad you approved and the ad Meta reviews are different sizes.

Meta's Advertising Standards say review can include the images, video, text, targeting and the ad's landing page. Your headline is one line in a file the reviewer reads front to back.

Checking only the headline is folding the top layer of a suitcase for a customs officer who empties all of it.

Category, claims, attributes, language, visuals, proof, landing page, disclosures.

Run all eight before the creative is locked.

After the rejection, the same fix costs a reshoot.

P.S. On the last ad you had rejected, where did the problem live: the headline, the image or the page it sent people to?

text:
Your lowest point shouldn’t come with an audience.

Cut off anyone who treats your hard season like content for gossip.

We're living in strange times when people pretend to be coming to comfort you when they're coming to turn your situation into content.

A family is going through the saddest moment of burying their loved one, and someone else is filming them to trend online.

Someone comes to see you at the hospital, and before you know it, your images are uploaded online in your most vulnerable and disturbing form.

They try to cover their savagery and digital cruelty with 'Let's keep him in prayers' or 'We visited her at the hospital, and here's the updates.'

If you visit a sick person and they're grateful for your gesture, why do you need to take photos with them at the same time? For whom?

If someone has suffered an accident and they're covered in blood, what are you thinking when you're filming them in such a state?

Other people are so shameless they've been seen bringing cameras to body-viewing processions.

It's not humane to try and shine with people's struggles. When you find people crying or fighting with life, offer them empathy. Not exposure.

And when you hold events that matter to you and your family, remember to include digital security guards. Their work is to remind people that they've been invited as guests, not reporters.

They also monitor TikTok intruders who sit among the people but are just paparazzi.

You don't want your distinguished guests feeling so uneasy that they can't enjoy the moment or half of the audience being constantly distracted by their phones.

Boundaries are not just needed for your personal life. They're also needed for your personal events and important days.

[So unnecessary. Completely preventable.]

➡️ New York state reports first measles-linked child death in over 30 years amid outbreak

- The New York State Department of Health said on Monday that a child in Lewis County had died in connection with an ongoing ‌measles outbreak, marking the state's first known measles-associated death in more than 30 ‌years.

- Last month, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas ​of New York and neighboring states.

- "The Department has offered resources to Lewis County to assist with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts – both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak," the ‌state department said.

- The death comes ⁠as the US experiences its worst measles resurgence in decades.

- Hochul told Reuters in October that the state would seek federal assistance to help contain ⁠the outbreak, but did not confirm whether it had submitted a formal request for a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Epidemic Intelligence Service, or Epi-Aid, response.

- ➡️. As of October 24, New York ​had ​reported 178 measles cases this year, including 170 ​cases outside New York City and ‌8 cases in New York City.

- State ➡️ health officials said they were working with county health departments and local partners to provide measles, mumps and rubella vaccinations to unvaccinated individuals who request them and to investigate reported cases.

- "At New York's request, CDC has deployed epidemiologists and other experts to work alongside state health officials on the ground, providing surveillance, data analysis, strategic ‌planning, and other outbreak response support," the US Department ​of Health and Human Services told Reuters in an ​emailed statement.

- ➡️ The CDC has recorded three ​measles-related deaths this year, but did not name the states where they ‌occurred.

- Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of the ​outbreak this year, reporting ​1,433 confirmed cases and five measles-associated deaths so far this year.

- ➡️ The gap in numbers follows a policy shift under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., with ​the CDC switching to the ‌National Center for Health Statistics' mortality data to track measles deaths, replacing its earlier ​reliance on state health departments' figures.

text:
Learjet-60 “Mach Tuck” | An F/A-18 pilot offered a possible explanation —

A friend sent me this. Former Navy pilot and friends with the man who posted this below. 

Here is how AI explains it — Icing and turbulence could have disrupted the aircraft, sending it into a dive where increasing speed made recovery progressively harder and with weather conditions impossible.  

At sufficiently high Mach numbers, shock waves change airflow over the wings and shift the center of pressure rearward, creating a nose-down tendency called “Mach tuck.”

That can become a dangerous feedback loop: nose drops, speed increases, and the nose-down tendency worsens—potentially exceeding the aircraft’s ability to pull out.

Icing could compound the problem by disrupting airflow and reducing lift capability.

This provides a logical explanation of what happened and what was observed. It’s tragic. 

As more information comes forth we will know what happened. My thoughts and prayers go out to the family of those who lost their lives.

Losing Kelly Oubre Jr. is the textbook cost of the new CBA: trapped against the luxury tax and second apron, the Sixers simply couldn’t afford to match Indiana's 2-year, $17M deal without triggering brutal compounding penalties and frozen draft assets. Punishing roster math at work.  I hate the buisness side of sports that revolves around money! We lost Jared McCain the same way but a little differently.
With Oubre, the Sixers were backed into a corner in July free agency—matching Indiana’s offer would have pushed payroll across the second apron and triggered compounding tax bills alongside frozen draft assets.
​With McCain, the front office moved first:
​The Tax Motive: In February 2026, the Sixers shipped McCain to Oklahoma City specifically to dump his ~$4.2M rookie scale hit, dodge the luxury tax line entirely, and reset the clock on repeater penalties.  
​The Roster Cost: Instead of keeping an ascending young guard on cost-controlled rookie money, Philadelphia took back draft capital (Houston’s 2026 first-rounder and second-rounders) simply to clear salary off the books and avoid being penalized by the new CBA's tax structure.  
​Both departures came down to the same underlying reality: shedding talent to survive the financial restrictions of the current CBA.

With the risks of renewed war and the prospects for diplomacy both hanging in the balance, it's important to pay attention to what influential voices in Tehran are saying and how they're interpreting developments.

In his latest update, Mahdi Mohammadi (@mmohammadii61), an adviser to Iranian Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf, who has led Iran's negotiations with the US since April, offers several noteworthy assessments of the rapidly evolving military and diplomatic situation:

-US strikes on Qeshm and Sirik (Iranian islands in the Persian Gulf): Mohammadi confirms recent US attacks on Iranian positions in the Persian Gulf, placing them in the context of ongoing Iranian attacks on vessels attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz. 

He claims the US strikes have failed to degrade Iran's operational capabilities in the area, with Iranian attacks on tankers continuing and intensifying. He points to continued Iranian strikes on vessels and the downing or capture of US aircraft and drones today.

-Preparations for a larger war? He does say that US attacks have recently shifted from coastal anti-ship missile launchers toward Iranian air defenses on Qeshm and Sirik. 

He interprets this as a possible precursor to a much larger offensive.

-Diplomacy and the US midterms: He considers a diplomatic breakthrough highly unlikely, arguing that Washington is unwilling to make the concessions Iran demands. 

Nevertheless, he defends continued exchanges through intermediaries, saying it's important to clarify both sides' final positions before any renewed major war. 

He also dismisses concerns that diplomacy temporarily lowers oil prices ahead of the US elections, arguing that the electoral impact will be negligible at this point and prices will rebound.

-Nuclear escalation: He dismisses speculation about a potential US or Israeli nuclear strike on Iran as psychological warfare aimed at frightening Iranian society. 

He argues that such an attack is improbable for strategic reasons, while claiming that Iran would respond with a nuclear strike against Israel if it occurred.

Taken together, his remarks suggest that some influential figures in Tehran either view the current diplomatic exchanges as potentially the final maneuvering before another major round of fighting, rather than a breakthrough toward a deal, or at least see strategic value in publicly framing them that way.

🚨 ECONOMIST STEVE HANKE ARGUES IRAN HOLDS STRONGER HAND IN POST-CONFLICT TALKS

WASHINGTON, UNITED STATES - Iranian officials continuing to negotiate from a position of confidence matters more than the debate over who can claim victory. Military exchanges often end without a clear battlefield verdict, yet bargaining power becomes visible in the demands each side feels comfortable making afterward. Hanke's argument rests on that distinction.

If Tehran believes it absorbed pressure without conceding core interests, it has less incentive to offer compromises simply to restart talks. That changes the negotiating environment for Washington because pressure tools lose some of their value when the targeted side concludes they failed. The problem then shifts from securing leverage to persuading an opponent that compromise is worth more than endurance.

text:
Europe Is Aflame, and It’s Not Going to Stop https://t.co/Gq3jUhUEdv 

Europe’s Perfect Storm: Ukraine War, Civil Unrest and U.S. Withdrawal Threaten Its Prosperity

Europe, once a prosperous and powerful continent that rebuilt itself after World War II, is now facing an unprecedented crisis. Civil unrest, anti-immigration protests, economic stagnation and the seemingly endless Ukraine war are threatening its stability. Adding to the turmoil is America’s declining commitment to European security. A continent that once stood shoulder to shoulder with the United States is struggling to confront its problems.

Europe’s diversity is both its strength and its weakness. Every few hundred miles brings a different country, language, culture and religious tradition, predominantly Catholic or Protestant. In recent decades, this complexity has been compounded by large-scale immigration from North Africa, the Middle East and Pakistan. Integration has proved difficult, creating tensions over cultural values, public services and political representation.

The growing anti-immigration movement has become a vehicle for wider public discontent. Rising living costs, excessive welfare spending, mounting government deficits and economic stagnation have all fuelled resentment. Immigration is only one part of a much larger problem.

The Ukraine war has made matters worse. What began as a continuation of the Cold War confrontation with Russia, initially backed heavily by America, has become an increasingly costly European burden. With no clear end in sight and Washington less willing to carry the financial and military responsibility, European governments face the prospect of spending even more on a war with no guaranteed victory.
President Trump has offered his own diagnosis and proposed solutions. He identifies mass Muslim immigration as a major source of Europe’s social turmoil. Cultural differences and failures of integration have undoubtedly created serious challenges, although blaming an entire religious community oversimplifies the problem. 

Europe once welcomed immigrant labour to fill shortages; it must now confront the consequences of inadequate integration policies.

Trump has also called for a political settlement in Ukraine, including a change in leadership in Kyiv. Whatever the merits of that proposal, the central issue is undeniable: the war must eventually end through negotiation. War-weary Ukrainians and financially exhausted Europeans have much to gain from a settlement.

Europe’s excessive public expenditure is another major weakness. Borrowing to sustain expansive welfare systems increases debt-servicing costs, leaving less money for investment, infrastructure and economic growth. Meanwhile, trade restrictions and weakening external markets are adding to the pressure.

Europe’s present crisis is therefore not the result of one problem but several that have converged. It needs fresh leadership, realistic immigration policies, fiscal discipline, economic revival and, above all, an end to its confrontation with Russia.

The damage will not be repaired overnight. Even with decisive changes, Europe may need five to ten years to restore its economic strength, social cohesion and political confidence. Its prosperity is not beyond recovery, but its leaders must first acknowledge how seriously it has been compromised.

text:
with the US debt already above $40 trillion and the debt ceiling getting closer, i’d be more concerned about how far trump might push things if congress refuses to cooperate.

he could turn the threat of default into a political game of chicken, betting that the other side blinks first. and if neither side backs down? washington has spent years entertaining some pretty wild ways around the debt ceiling.

1. the trillion-dollar platinum coin

mint a coin with a $1 trillion face value and deposit it at the Fed. a trillion dollars in Treasury cash without selling a single bond, provided the Fed accepts it. yes, this has actually been discussed.

2. gold revaluation

america still carries its gold reserves at $42.22 an ounce. reprice those holdings at market value and the paper gain runs into the trillions. getting that money into the Treasury’s account is legally complicated, but the temptation is hard to ignore.

bessent dismissed gold revaluation in 2025, saying, “that’s not what I had in mind.” whether he’d stick to that position during a full-blown debt ceiling crisis is worth considering.

3. premium bonds

can’t borrow more because of the debt ceiling? offer investors higher coupons so they’ll pay $150 for a bond with a $100 face value. the idea is to raise $150 while counting only $100 against the ceiling, assuming that interpretation holds up legally. the extra interest payments are tomorrow’s problem.

4. perpetual bonds

the British were issuing consols centuries ago, paying interest indefinitely without ever having to repay the principal. washington could explore something similar, although whether such bonds could legally escape the debt ceiling is another question for the lawyers.

5. the 14th Amendment

Section 4 says the validity of US public debt shall not be questioned. trump could argue that this allows continued borrowing despite the statutory ceiling, leaving the courts to decide whether the president actually has that authority.

6. change the rules

trump has already called for abolishing the debt ceiling. why negotiate over the limit if you can pressure congress to get rid of it altogether? of course, that still requires legislation.

none of these is a confirmed administration plan. several face serious legal obstacles, but the Treasury’s financing needs aren’t going away.

while washington fights over borrowing authority, the Treasury could be drawing down its TGA balance, releasing liquidity into financial markets. traders might enjoy that for a while, until a deal is reached and the Treasury starts borrowing again to rebuild its cash reserves.

and if trump decides to push the confrontation to the brink, markets may end up pricing in something far worse than a temporary liquidity squeeze: the risk of US Treasuries themselves becoming bargaining chips in washington’s political fight..

**The US decision is based on its assessment of the ANC-led South African government’s policies and actions (or inactions), not AfriForum as the primary actor.**[](<https://t.co/QnW0KHqGcW>)

### Official US reasons
President Trump notified President Ramaphosa in a 28 October 2026 letter (with the formal announcement by USTR Jamieson Greer on 2 November) of the intention to terminate South Africa’s AGOA eligibility from 1 January 2027. The stated grounds under AGOA Section 104 include:

- Failure to establish or make continual progress on systems to combat corruption and bribery.
- Significant tariff and non-tariff barriers to US trade and investment (agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections, intellectual property).
- Actions on international security and cooperation with governments of concern to the US that risk undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.[](<https://t.co/Rn8Mc2LSRX>)

US Ambassador Brent Bozell described the outcome as “predictable and preventable” due to the South African government’s rejection of concerns raised by Washington. Broader reporting links the tensions to SA policies on land/expropriation, Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (BEE), foreign policy (including the ICJ case against Israel and ties with Russia, China, and others), and related issues. These are policy choices of the ANC-led government.[](<https://t.co/QLT8NiyqvN>)

AGOA is a unilateral US preference program. The US President determines eligibility annually against the statutory criteria; the decision-maker is the US executive.

### AfriForum’s role
AfriForum and Solidarity have long lobbied in the US on property rights, the Expropriation Act (which allows for expropriation without compensation), farm security/crime, and what they describe as race-based discrimination under BEE and related laws. They have met US officials and raised these issues, which align with some of the concerns the Trump administration has voiced.[](<https://t.co/3rdnbOBIzO>)

AfriForum publicly blames President Ramaphosa and ANC leaders for the policies that triggered the outcome, noting they had warned about risks (including from the Expropriation Act) and that ordinary South Africans will bear the costs. Critics, including COSATU, counter that AfriForum’s lobbying and framing of issues (including around farm murders and “persecution” narratives, which the SA government rejects) damaged bilateral relations and contributed to the political climate that led to the termination.[](<https://t.co/4cvMwPp7bv>)

AfriForum has stated it does not support measures that punish ordinary citizens and previously argued against a full AGOA exit while acknowledging that SA government policies conflicted with the eligibility criteria.

### Bottom line
- **Primary responsibility for the policies cited by the US** rests with the ANC government, which sets trade, anti-corruption, land, transformation, and foreign policy.
- **AfriForum** is a private advocacy group whose lobbying amplified certain domestic concerns in Washington and helped shape perceptions (especially under an administration already critical of SA). It did not enact the policies or make the US decision.
- The SA government says it offered concessions in negotiations and that the US raised new issues; it is preparing support for affected sectors. AGOA covered a relatively small share of SA’s total exports (around 10% of exports to the US and ~1% of global exports in 2025).

text:
Who gets to switch off an ally's battlefield communications in the middle of a war? A new CSIS analysis by Clayton Swope, Lauryn Williams and Alexei Hoffman, published Nov 2, argues Congress should write the answer down.

The trigger was the October episode in Ukraine. On Oct 14, Ukrainian officials reported that SpaceX had imposed speed restrictions on Starshield service without warning, so terminals moving faster than 100 miles per hour lost connectivity. That hindered Ukrainian interceptor drones chasing Russia's jet-powered Shaheds, which can fly nearly four times that speed. Ukrainian officials said service was back to normal by Oct 24. Who ordered the cap is still disputed, according to CSIS: some reporting points to the White House, President Trump denied direct involvement, Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed it to SpaceX, and Elon Musk said SpaceX restricted commercial Starlink over terms-of-service violations while saying the US government controls Starshield access.

The authors place the episode in a longer record of decisions with geopolitical weight: Musk declining to extend coverage near Crimea in 2022, a reported shutdown around Kherson that September, terminals the State Department reportedly bought and had covertly delivered into Iran, as reported by the Wall Street Journal, and free service Musk offered Venezuelans after the January 2026 US strikes.

Allies are drawing conclusions. The European Union is building its IRIS 2 constellation. Ukraine signed a letter of intent with ICEYE and Nokia to explore sovereign satellite communications. Poland says it wants its own Starlink-style system. CSIS cites a recent poll, which it does not name, finding only 11 percent of Europeans view the United States as an ally.

In Congress, Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Thom Tillis asked the Pentagon inspector general to investigate; the inspector general declined, calling it a "contractual matter" for the Air Force and Space Force. Senator Richard Blumenthal opened a separate inquiry.

The CSIS proposal is the news. The authors suggest a Government Accountability Office review, contract clauses requiring continuity plans and crisis performance, and a rule modeled on arms-sale notification: before a provider withdraws or materially changes a "critical national security service" to an ally, a designated agency approves it, the State Department reviews it with the Defense Department and Congress is notified, with service maintained pending approval except in narrow emergencies.

The argument for Americans is commercial as much as strategic. Washington wants allies buying US space, imagery and AI services, and that requires trust that the service will still be there when it is needed most.

text:
🇷🇺 🇮🇷 As Washington weighs new strikes on Iran, Tehran is leaning harder on Moscow. On Monday, Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei and Vladimir Putin held a phone call on the regional situation, with a focus on West Asia, according to Iranian outlets Mehr and Fars and Russia's RIA Novosti. Both sides stressed continued strategic cooperation under a roadmap set by the two countries' leaders, per Mehr. We found no Kremlin readout of the call.

The call fits a pattern traced by Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, an associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, in an expert comment published on Nov 2. In October alone, Iranian and Russian leaders met three times. President Masoud Pezeshkian met Putin in Turkmenistan on Oct 8. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov visited Tehran on Oct 19, his first trip since the war began on Feb 28, and met Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Rezaei. Pezeshkian then went to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum on Oct 27. Afterward Araghchi said: "never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now."

That marks a shift. For years, influential voices in Tehran saw Russia as a partner that took Iranian drones for its war in Ukraine and gave little back. Leaked contract documents indicate Russia agreed to pay about $290,000 per drone for 2,000 Shahed-136s. Tehran felt Moscow did little during the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, and Russia failed to deliver weapons Iran said it had bought, such as Su-35 fighter jets.

The war has changed that calculation, Bassiri Tabrizi argues. According to several reports she cites, Russia gave Iran intelligence on US military positions, satellite imagery for targeting and weapons components. She cautions that the real battlefield impact of that support is hard to assess, and these reports have not been independently verified. She adds that the evidence contradicts President Trump's statement that Moscow and Beijing have not been helping Tehran. Putin says bilateral trade rose 10.4 percent in the first eight months of 2026, and Rosatom says it will raise its construction workforce at the Bushehr nuclear plant to 200 after evacuating staff when the war began.

The limits are real. Russia's own war in Ukraine constrains what it can spare, and there is no binding security guarantee. In her assessment, Russian help is "unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Iran's favour." What Moscow can offer is selective: replacement components for the S-300 air defense system, electronic warfare technology and expertise to rebuild air defenses, drones and missiles.

For Americans, the stake is durability. Bassiri Tabrizi expects military cooperation between the two to become institutionalized, which would make it harder to reverse no matter who is in power in Tehran. That ties the Gulf war more tightly to the war in Ukraine, a link Europeans will feel too. Separately, the Critical Threats Project reported that Iran's deputy security chief Ali Bagheri Kani met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing the same day, and it assesses that Russia "almost certainly cannot provide Iran with significant material or financial support."
