⚡ SNF PULSE™ | U.S. ENERGY — MARATHON'S $4.2B REFINERY SALE REVEALS A MAJOR CAPITAL SHIFT

The U.S. energy industry is revealing an important distinction between exceptional refining profitability and the long-term ownership of energy infrastructure.

Marathon Petroleum ($MPC) announced an agreement to sell two refineries and related midstream assets to CVR Energy ($CVI) for approximately $4.2 billion.

The transaction comes alongside third-quarter earnings demonstrating how significantly disruptions to global energy supplies have improved refining economics.

But the most important development is not simply the size of the transaction.

It is what the buyer and seller are choosing to do with capital during an unusually profitable period for refining.

🟨 WHAT CHANGED

🟢 Marathon agreed to sell its St. Paul Park, Minnesota, and Mandan, North Dakota, refineries to CVR Energy.

🟢 The transaction carries a purchase price of approximately $4.2 billion, plus inventory value and customary adjustments.

🟢 Marathon will receive $3.45 billion for refining assets, while MPLX will receive $750 million for related infrastructure.

🟢 The facilities represent 177,000 barrels per day of combined refining capacity.

🟢 CVR's total refining capacity would increase from approximately 207,000 to 384,000 barrels per day.

🟢 Trafigura will invest $800 million in CVR and establish long-term crude-supply and product-offtake arrangements.

🟢 Marathon's third-quarter refining and marketing margin reached $45.70 per barrel, compared with $17.60 a year earlier.

🟢 Refinery utilization reached 100%, supporting approximately 3.2 million barrels per day of throughput.

The acquisition is expected to close by year-end, subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions.

🟨 WHY IT MATTERS

Global oil disruptions have created unusually favorable conditions for portions of the refining industry.

When refined fuel prices rise faster than crude acquisition costs, refiners can experience substantial margin expansion.

Marathon's latest results demonstrate that dynamic.

Its refining and marketing margin increased more than two-and-a-half times from the previous year.

That improvement reflects a period of unusually strong economics across refining operations.

But exceptionally favorable margins also create strategic choices.

Companies can reinvest in additional capacity, return capital to shareholders, acquire competitors or monetize existing infrastructure.

Marathon and CVR are choosing different approaches.

Marathon is selling two regional refineries while directing future investment toward Gulf Coast operations and its midstream business.

CVR is expanding its physical refining footprint and entering new regional markets.

Both decisions reflect expectations about where future returns can be generated.

Neither guarantees those returns.

🟨 THE CAPITAL REALLOCATION

Marathon's transaction demonstrates how an established energy company can reshape its portfolio without necessarily reducing its broader financial exposure to energy infrastructure.

The company intends to reinvest proceeds primarily along the Gulf Coast.

MPLX plans to direct capital toward growth opportunities in the Permian and Marcellus basins.

This creates a distinction between ownership changes and changes in actual energy supply.

The announced transaction transfers existing refinery capacity.

It does not, by itself, add 177,000 barrels per day of new processing capability to the U.S. market.

For Marathon, the decision represents an opportunity to monetize assets and redirect capital toward areas management believes offer more attractive long-term returns.

For CVR, it represents a substantial expansion in scale, geographic reach and marketing capabilities.

🟨 THE REFINING MARGIN TEST

CVR estimates that the acquired business generated approximately $1.16 billion in EBITDA over the twelve months ended September 2026.

But the same operations generated approximately $506 million during calendar 2025, using CVR's accounting treatment.

That difference is critical.

The assets' recent profitability reflects exceptionally favorable refining conditions.

It should not automatically be interpreted as a permanent earnings baseline.

CVR expects the transaction to strengthen earnings and cash flow while generating approximately $70 million in annual operating and commercial synergies.

Those benefits remain management expectations rather than realized results.

The investment case depends on integrating the acquired facilities, maintaining operational performance and generating acceptable returns when refining margins normalize.

The price being paid matters.

The durability of the cash flows supporting that price matters more.

🟨 THE TRAFIGURA CONNECTION

The transaction also introduces a significant commodity-trading component.

Trafigura has agreed to provide $800 million in equity financing and establish commercial arrangements supporting the acquired facilities.

Following closing, Trafigura would become the exclusive crude supplier and trading intermediary for the refineries, alongside certain refined-product offtake agreements.

That structure connects refining assets more directly with a global commodity-trading network.

It could improve access to crude supply, logistics capabilities and marketing channels.

But commercial integration does not eliminate commodity-price exposure or execution risk.

The economic value of these arrangements will depend on their operation under changing market conditions.

🟨 THE BROADER ENERGY SIGNAL

Today's announcement arrives while crude markets continue evaluating the possibility of improved diplomatic conditions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.

The distinction between crude prices and refining margins remains important.

Lower crude prices do not automatically translate into weaker refinery profitability.

Refining earnings depend on the relationship between crude input costs, refined-product prices, utilization and operating expenses.

If disrupted international fuel supplies normalize, the unusually strong margins currently benefiting refiners could face pressure.

But normalization is not yet confirmed.

Marathon's transaction provides evidence of how companies are positioning capital while that uncertainty remains unresolved.

🟨 WHAT SNF IS WATCHING

The regulatory approval and closing of the $4.2 billion transaction.

Whether refining margins remain elevated as Middle Eastern supply conditions evolve.

Marathon's reinvestment strategy and Gulf Coast capital commitments.

CVR's integration of the acquired refineries and marketing operations.

Trafigura's financing, supply and product-offtake arrangements.

The impact of acquisition financing on CVR's leverage and financial flexibility.

Changes in regional fuel inventories, refining utilization and product spreads.

And whether exceptional refining earnings translate into sustainable long-term returns.

🟨 SNF LENS™

🟢 SIGNAL: Marathon is monetizing $4.2 billion of refining and midstream assets while reporting materially stronger margins, and CVR is using the transaction to nearly double its refining capacity.

⚪ NOISE: Treating the ownership transfer as new U.S. refining capacity or assuming today's exceptionally strong margins represent permanent profitability.

🟡 CONFIRMATION: Transaction completion, disciplined capital reinvestment, successful integration and durable cash generation under normalized refining conditions.

🔴 RISK: Refining-margin compression, acquisition financing costs, integration challenges, regulatory delays and weaker returns if current earnings conditions prove temporary.

🟨 THE BOTTOM LINE

Marathon's refinery sale demonstrates that strong energy markets can produce more than higher earnings.

They can accelerate the redistribution of capital and physical infrastructure across an industry.

Marathon is choosing to monetize regional assets and reinvest elsewhere.

CVR is choosing to expand its refining footprint.

Trafigura is providing capital and commercial infrastructure to support that expansion.

The transaction reveals three different approaches to participating in the same energy market.

The next test is whether those decisions generate attractive returns after the current period of exceptional refining profitability begins to normalize.

Strong margins create opportunities.

Capital allocation determines how much of that value endures.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Trump’s Energy Crisis Causes Food Shortages, Skyrocketing Prices, and Global Suffering. What’s Next?

Overview

Modern civilization still runs almost entirely on hydrocarbons, and the West has spent decades pretending otherwise. Roughly 90% of global energy comes from oil, natural gas, and coal, a share unchanged for 50 years, yet policy in Europe and parts of the US has treated solar and wind as replacements rather than additions. The consequences are now compounding: electricity several times more expensive than in the US, fertilizer and food supply exposed to natural gas disruptions, and a sanctions regime that has handed China discounted crude and a strategic reserve possibly aimed at a Taiwan contingency. The argument runs that energy blindness, not scarcity, is driving the crisis, and that the diesel shock from the Middle East conflict will reach food prices with a lag into 2027.

Key Themes
- Hydrocarbons remain roughly 90% of world energy and have not been displaced; added renewables have met new demand, not replaced oil, gas, or coal.
- Natural gas is both a fuel and the base of most fertilizer, so gas disruptions translate directly into food shortages and price spikes.
- Western policy is framed as energy blind: banning gas production and pipelines while depending on gas-fired electricity is self-defeating.
- Europe’s ideological shift away from coal, nuclear, and Russian gas has produced electricity roughly 10 times the US price and suppressed economic growth.
- Fracking and private mineral rights made the US the world’s largest energy producer; government ownership and taxation elsewhere discourage drilling.
- Sanctions on Russia, Iran, and Venezuela have failed to cut exports and instead delivered discounted crude to China, which has built a strategic reserve far larger than the US SPR.
- The Iran conflict knocked out Gulf refining and LNG capacity, blowing out the diesel crack spread from about $10 to $100 with global food consequences.

Detailed Summary

The starting point is arithmetic. Oil, coal, and natural gas each supply roughly one-third of world energy, with the remaining tenth split between nuclear and small solar and wind. That ratio has held for half a century and is projected to hold for another. China draws about 60% of its energy from coal and India about 80%, which is why coal remains the base-load answer for the world’s fastest-growing economies. Solar and wind sit at roughly 5–6% of global energy, and the speaker argues that new renewable capacity has been additional rather than displacing hydrocarbons, while population and demand growth have been met by oil and gas.

Natural gas is the hinge of the food system. Roughly 80% of the world’s food depends on gas-derived fertilizer, produced through the ammonia and urea process discovered in Europe around 1910, which raised crop yields by 500–600%. Without it, the speaker claims, the world could feed only about 2 billion of its 8 billion people. A Middle East and Iran-related disruption this year is expected to hit fertilizer production, with lagged effects on food into 2027 because of crop cycles. Shutting down global gas production, in this framing, is not an environmental measure but a starvation policy.

The policy critique follows. New York State sits atop the Marcellus and Utica fields yet bans gas drilling and new pipelines, while Manhattan power stations run on natural gas. The same pattern appears in Washington, New England, Maine, and California, described as sharing Europe’s energy blindness. Government subsidies such as $100 electricity checks in New York increase dependence on the government that restricts supply. Environmentalism is framed as having shifted from legitimate pollution cleanup, the 1960s California smog fight that produced CARB, sulfur cuts, lead removal, and catalytic converters, into an ideological control agenda, federally institutionalized through the EPA and captured over 50 years.

Europe is the cautionary case. Shutting down coal, nuclear, and much of its gas system for ideological reasons left electricity roughly 10 times more expensive than in the US. Gasoline runs about $3.85 a gallon in Maine versus about $12 in Denmark, with roughly $8 of the European price going to government and $4 to industry, so taxation rather than scarcity drives the gap. Europe’s shift from Russian gas to US gas, with purchases at least doubled versus a decade ago, has increased dependence on the US while benefiting US producers greatly. Nord Stream is discussed, including one line never activated and one destroyed, with the conversation weighing claims about who was responsible.

The US story is fracking. Production declined from the early 1970s until 2005, when roughly one well in 100 was fracked. Horizontal drilling and fracking then became the default method, and the US now produces roughly a quarter of the world’s oil and a quarter of its natural gas, up from under 10%. Private ownership of subsurface minerals encourages risk-taking, while government ownership elsewhere discourages it. The UK illustrates the opposite: windfall taxes and crown ownership of the resource removed the profit incentive, so North Sea drilling no longer pays despite shared geology with Norway, which deliberately stayed out of the EU and structured its oil and gas sector around profit incentives.

Ireland is offered as the tax case. Joining the EU in 1973 with about 3% unemployment, it saw unemployment reach roughly 22–23% by the late 1980s after tariffs were dropped. Cutting corporate tax toward zero and slashing income tax produced growth the following year. Per-capita oil consumption, meanwhile, has stayed near four barrels globally for about a century, with the US at roughly 20 barrels per person per year and Europe at about 10, suggesting taxation has not reduced hydrocarbon use. Europe’s lower driving rates are attributed to population density, not virtue.

Sanctions are the next failure. Russian crude was capped at $60 per barrel; the price went to $70, Europe starved itself of crude, and Russian production barely changed. China reportedly bought about 2 million barrels a day each of sanctioned Venezuelan, Iranian, and Russian crude at $10–$20 discounts. China consumes 16 million barrels a day and imports 12 million, and its strategic storage is estimated at 1.5 billion barrels against roughly 300 million in the US SPR, built over four or five years largely on sanctioned oil and reportedly tied to a 2027 Taiwan contingency. Coal-to-liquids via Fischer-Tropsch is technically possible but uneconomic at roughly $200 a barrel, so it does not explain China’s behavior. China behaves like a trader, buying below roughly $70 and drawing down reserves above roughly $100.

Natural gas is framed as the only fuel that can deliver true US energy independence, because it is difficult and expensive to ship and therefore largely trapped domestically. US gas at about $3 per MMBtu against roughly $31 in Europe and Asia keeps American electricity and manufacturing costs low. Cheap gas, not environmental lobbying, destroyed US coal by undercutting it on price in the early 2000s. The speaker argues that increasing gas production is the path to lowering costs across the economy and reshoring some manufacturing.

The Middle East conflict is where the analysis turns urgent. The oil market first priced the Iran war as a short event, then repriced when Iran retaliated with drones and hit Gulf production facilities. About 2 million barrels a day of Persian Gulf refining capacity was knocked out, and Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries removed another 2 million, against roughly 100 million barrels a day of global production. Qatar’s LNG plant was hit, with half its production reportedly out for three to five years, and Qatar supplies about 20% of world LNG.

Because refineries can shift only 2–3% of the barrel between diesel and gasoline, and because Asia and Europe consume more diesel than the US, diesel tightened far more than gasoline. The diesel crack spread blew out from about $10 above crude to $100 and stayed there. With crude at $100, diesel reached roughly $200 a barrel and gasoline about $160. Shipping became the second chokepoint: VLCC day rates rose from $50,000–$100,000 to about $1.5 million, insurance climbed, and Saudi and Emirati tankers began speedrunning the Strait of Hormuz along Oman’s coast and doing ship-to-ship transfers outside the Gulf of Oman. The East-West pipeline was ramped from 2–3 million to 7 million barrels a day, with another pipeline adding about a million.

Iran is described as hitting one to two tankers a day with cheap drones, targeting engine rooms and killing civilian crews, which the speaker calls the most urgent problem because the physical tanker market cannot wait for diplomacy. The proposal is tit-for-tat escalation: for every tanker hit, knock out two Iranian power stations, starting with Tehran’s five major ones. Iran has 150 power generation stations and five refineries, and its economy is described as vulnerable enough that knocking out the refineries could halt the country within about 20 days. The killing of Iran’s religious leader during what the speakers call a fake peace negotiation is framed as a strategic and moral failure, and the argument is that the conflict must be resolved within three to six months because effects are already flowing into food and fertilizer.

text:
The History of Hipshot: From the 1939 Electraharp to Modern Guitar Hardware, 1939-2026

Hipshot’s mechanical ancestry begins with early pedal-steel guitar engineering, when inventors developed mechanisms to change individual string pitches without interrupting performance.

1939 - Alvino Rey and machinist John Moore were involved in developing the Gibson Electraharp, an electric steel guitar employing pedals and mechanical linkages to change string tension.

August 23, 1940 - Moore filed the patent application for its pitch-changing mechanism.

March 11, 1941 - U.S. Patent 2,234,874 was issued to Moore, describing a six-pedal system capable of producing multiple chord combinations. Gibson commercially introduced the Electraharp in 1941.

February 1948 - Paul Bigsby completed a four-pedal steel guitar for Speedy West, contributing to the development of modern pedal-steel mechanisms.

1954 - Webb Pierce’s recording of “Slowly,” featuring Bud Isaacs on pedal steel, became a major country hit. Isaacs demonstrated moving pitch changes during sustained notes, helping popularize the modern pedal-steel sound.

1982 - Guitarist, pedal-steel player and machinist Dave Borisoff founded Hipshot Products in California.

His first invention was the Hipshot String Bender, a hip-actuated mechanism that raised an electric guitar’s B string, generally by one whole step, reproducing a characteristic pedal-steel technique.

Mid-1980s - Borisoff developed the Hipshot Xtender, initially for bass guitar. Its lever-operated tuning mechanism permitted immediate switching between two predetermined pitches, commonly E and D.

The tuning key establishes the upper pitch, while an adjustable mechanical stop determines the lower pitch. No electronics are required.

1989 - The bass Xtender was outselling Hipshot’s original String Bender.

1990s - Guitar Xtenders expanded alternate-tuning capabilities on conventional six-string instruments. The Trilogy bridge, documented by 1994, offered three selectable pitches per string, providing 729 theoretical combinations.

1994 - Hipshot relocated from California to Interlaken, New York.

2000s-2026 - Hipshot expanded its range of Grip-Lock locking tuners, Ultralite bass tuners, precision bridges and specialized hardware.

The underlying principle remains: mechanical control of string tension, connecting early pedal-steel inventions with modern electric guitar and bass engineering.

TWO DETECTIVES CAME TO MY HOUSE WITH A PHOTOGRAPH OF ME ENTERING ANOTHER WOMAN’S APARTMENT. MY WIFE SWORE I HAD SPENT THE NIGHT BESIDE HER. THEN THEY ASKED ABOUT HER TWIN SISTER.

At 11:06 the next morning, two detectives stood on my porch holding a photograph that would turn my marriage upside down.

The man in the picture looked exactly like me.

Same face. Same beard. Same haircut. Even the dark jacket I had worn the previous evening.

But according to my wife, I had never left our bedroom.

And according to the detectives, that man had entered an apartment at 10:47 p.m. and left forty-nine minutes later.

The woman who lived there was now in hospital, unconscious.

My name is Michael Carter. I am 34, married to Rachel, and until that Saturday morning, I thought I knew everything important about the woman I had shared my life with for five years.

Apparently, I didn't.

The previous evening had been ordinary.

Rachel and I had ordered pizza, watched a few episodes of a crime series and spent some time together in the bedroom. Around nine, I told her I was going downstairs to get food because we had run out of snacks.

She laughed and told me to bring back ice cream.

I remember putting on my jacket, picking up my car keys and heading out.

I also remember coming home later, putting the food on the kitchen counter and going to bed.

Nothing unusual. Nothing worth remembering.

Until the detectives arrived.

"Mr. Carter?" the taller one asked.

"Yes."

"I'm Detective Harris. This is Detective Lewis. We need to ask you a few questions about last night."

I invited them inside.

Rachel appeared from the kitchen, still wearing her oversized sweatshirt. She offered them coffee, but Harris politely declined.

"Where were you between ten p.m. and midnight?" he asked.

"At home."

Rachel answered before I could.

"He was with me."

Harris looked at her.

"All evening?"

"Yes. He never left the bedroom."

I glanced at her.

I was about to correct her when Lewis opened a folder and placed a photograph on the coffee table.

It showed a man entering an apartment building.

I leaned forward.

My stomach tightened.

"That's me."

"You're certain?" Harris asked.

"Of course I'm certain. Look at the picture."

"Then perhaps you can explain why you entered the building at 10:47 last night."

"I didn't."

Lewis placed another photograph beside the first. It showed the same man leaving at 11:36 p.m.

"Someone has used your identity," Harris said. "The woman who lives in that apartment was found unconscious shortly before midnight."

Rachel's expression changed.

"Who is she?"

"Vanessa Reed."

The coffee cup in her hand stopped halfway to her mouth.

I noticed.

"Rachel?"

She slowly put it down.

Harris watched her carefully.

"Do you know Vanessa?"

Rachel swallowed.

"She's my twin sister."

I turned towards her.

"Your twin sister? The one you told me moved to California?"

"She came back."

"When?"

"Three months ago."

I stared at her.

"You've known she was back for three months and never told me?"

Rachel began crying.

"Michael, I can explain."

"Then explain why detectives have a photograph of me entering her apartment."

Harris interrupted.

"Mrs. Carter, Vanessa identified the man in the photograph as her sister's husband."

I shook my head.

"That's impossible. I've never even met her since she returned."

Rachel looked at the floor.

Then Harris asked the question that changed the conversation.

"Mr. Carter, did you leave your house last night?"

I looked at Rachel.

"Yes. I went to get food. Why?"

She suddenly grabbed my hand.

"Don't."

I pulled away.

"What are you talking about?"

She looked at the detectives.

"I lied earlier. He did leave."

Harris sat forward.

"Why did you tell us he hadn't?"

"Because I didn't want you asking where he went."

I stared at her.

"Rachel, I went to get food. What are you hiding?"

text:
Five Neighbors, Three States, One Continuing Conversation

The following story is fictional.

On the first Saturday, five people in three states opened five cardboard boxes.

Inside each box were 100 door hangers ordered from an online printer. No campaign headquarters. No paid staff. Just five neighbors who believed that citizenship should continue between elections.

James and another volunteer lived in Kansas. Two teammates lived in Missouri. The fifth lived in Oklahoma. They met online, compared their proofs, and paid for their own batches.

Across the front of every hanger were six words:

THE ELECTION ENDS. TAXPAYER OVERSIGHT DOESN’T.

Below that were two issues: protecting property rights and making government spending visible. The reverse carried QR codes linking to public GitHub essays, supporting documents, and a voluntary invitation to participate in Runtime Republic.

The essays were proposals open to examination. Readers could see the reasoning, question assumptions, and follow revisions.

That mattered to the team. They wanted a conversation they could defend with evidence.

On weekends, they walked their respective neighborhoods. Some residents wanted to talk. Others accepted the material and closed the door. Some disagreed.

One renter asked whether eliminating a landlord’s property tax would actually reduce rent.

“We shouldn’t promise that it automatically would,” the volunteer replied. “That question belongs in the public discussion.”

Another resident liked the spending-transparency proposal but questioned its cost. The team recorded the question without attaching the resident’s name.

They distributed the same information without screening households by party or registration status. Anyone could read, challenge, or join.

After several weekends, each volunteer prepared a report for the elected officials serving that area.

The team had initially discussed reporting which registered voters received a hanger. They settled on something more accurate and respectful: a delivery report could establish where materials were distributed; it could not establish who read them, agreed with them, or intended to vote a particular way.

Their reports listed quantities delivered, dates, general areas covered, recurring questions, and links to the exact materials. Names appeared only when residents explicitly asked to join a signed statement or receive a response.

Each report included a direct request:

“Please review these proposals and provide a written response we can share publicly, including your objections and suggested changes.”

Some offices acknowledged receipt. One sent a substantive answer. Another offered a meeting. Several remained silent.

The team recorded those outcomes accurately. An acknowledgment was an acknowledgment. A meeting was a meeting. Silence was listed as no response received by the report date.

At their next online meeting, they reviewed what they had learned. They shortened confusing language, corrected an overstatement, and added the renter’s question to the public essay.

That was their working rhythm: Plan. Do. Check. Act.

Five people had started with 500 door hangers across three states. Their larger contribution was a continuing public record—what they proposed, what neighbors questioned, what officials answered, and what needed improvement.

The message to officeholders was steady:

We will keep participating. We will keep checking the evidence. And we will keep asking you to answer publicly.

text:
No she's not, retard. 
The plane crashed because the 55 year old experienced pilot (who i wouldn't worry about on sight) made a risky and fatal decision. Yes even experienced pilots can make poor decisions. 
There is a captain and a first officer.
The captain makes all final decisions.
He was warned by ATC of the "pretty nasty" weather and "moderate to extreme precipitation" 10 mins prior and made a risky decision for only a slight deviation that turned out to be fatal. 
It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. The captain made a slight deviation because it wasn't serious and they were above the storm until that cell ballooned up from 33000 ft to 48000 ft ceiling in a few minutes and by then it was too late for them to climb out of it.
From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (captain’s voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmE8tv archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions.

TUSLA UNDER FIRE: CHILDREN FACE SEXUAL EXPLOITATION AND DRUG-RELATED DEATH WHILE SPECIAL CARE BEDS LIE CLOSED

A report in today’s Irish Times by Kitty Holland reveals that a 16-year-old boy who vomited up approximately 40 bags of crack cocaine remains without a special care bed, despite a High Court order requiring his detention in a secure facility.
The boy, who is using fentanyl and is described as being at serious risk of death, is one of several extremely vulnerable children for whom Tusla has been unable to secure appropriate special care placements.

The High Court heard that three children are currently being held in highly dangerous circumstances, with Tusla failing to comply with court orders directing that they receive specialist care.

One of the most disturbing cases involves a 14-year-old girl who is being sexually abused by multiple men while continuing to use drugs. The court heard that she had been offered cocaine in exchange for sexual activity and had little memory of events when brought to hospital.
Barrister Sarah McKechnie told the court that the boy who swallowed the crack cocaine had been warned that he would be handed over to the Gardaí if the drugs were mentioned. He subsequently became distressed and cried when Gardaí arrived.

Mr Justice John Jordan expressed serious frustration at the continuing failure to provide special care placements, describing the situation as one in which children were being left in danger while the authorities failed to take effective action.

The court also heard that staffing shortages are preventing Tusla from operating its full complement of special care beds. HIQA has restricted admissions because of concerns about staffing levels and the safety of children already accommodated.

Only 13 of Tusla's 26 designated special care beds are currently operational, leaving half the national capacity unavailable despite High Court orders requiring vulnerable children to be detained for their protection.

The court was told that HIQA has prohibited further admissions to Crannóg Nua, the largest special care unit, because of continuing staffing and safety concerns.

In an extraordinary intervention, Mr Justice Jordan lifted the in-camera rule in the three children's cases to allow contempt proceedings to be pursued against Tusla for its alleged failure to comply with court orders.

The judge said the obvious solution was improved pay and working conditions for special care staff. He criticised the continued failure of Tusla and Government to resolve the crisis, insisting that the children needed someone to speak for them.

The report exposes a deeply troubling failure of the State's child protection system: three children facing extreme risks of drug-related death, sexual exploitation and serious harm remain without the secure care ordered by the High Court.

The judge's intervention raises urgent questions about Tusla's compliance with court orders, Government accountability and the continuing failure to provide adequate special care capacity for some of Ireland's most vulnerable children.

The boy, who is using fentanyl and is described as being at serious risk of death, is one of several extremely vulnerable children for whom Tusla has been unable to secure appropriate special care placements.

The High Court heard that three children are currently being held in highly dangerous circumstances, with Tusla failing to comply with court orders directing that they receive specialist care.

One of the most disturbing cases involves a 14-year-old girl who is being sexually abused by multiple men while continuing to use drugs. The court heard that she had been offered cocaine in exchange for sexual activity and had little memory of events when brought to hospital.
Barrister Sarah McKechnie told the court that the boy who swallowed the crack cocaine had been warned that he would be handed over to the Gardaí if the drugs were mentioned. He subsequently became distressed and cried when Gardaí arrived.

Mr Justice John Jordan expressed serious frustration at the continuing failure to provide special care placements, describing the situation as one in which children were being left in danger while the authorities failed to take effective action.

The court also heard that staffing shortages are preventing Tusla from operating its full complement of special care beds. HIQA has restricted admissions because of concerns about staffing levels and the safety of children already accommodated.

Only 13 of Tusla's 26 designated special care beds are currently operational, leaving half the national capacity unavailable despite High Court orders requiring vulnerable children to be detained for their protection.

The court was told that HIQA has prohibited further admissions to Crannóg Nua, the largest special care unit, because of continuing staffing and safety concerns.

In an extraordinary intervention, Mr Justice Jordan lifted the in-camera rule in the three children's cases to allow contempt proceedings to be pursued against Tusla for its alleged failure to comply with court orders.

The judge said the obvious solution was improved pay and working conditions for special care staff. He criticised the continued failure of Tusla and Government to resolve the crisis, insisting that the children needed someone to speak for them.

The report exposes a deeply troubling failure of the State's child protection system: three children facing extreme risks of drug-related death, sexual exploitation and serious harm remain without the secure care ordered by the High Court.

The judge's intervention raises urgent questions about Tusla's compliance with court orders, Government accountability and the continuing failure to provide adequate special care capacity for some of Ireland's most vulnerable children.

text: In global cities like London, Paris, or Berlin, the entire region is divided into unified rings or zones. A single Zone 1–3 ticket covers the subway, regional rail, and local buses interchangeably. New York lacks this because the MTA's funding and political jurisdictions are deeply fractured. Metro-North stretches into Connecticut and is partially funded by the Connecticut Department of Transportation (CTDOT), while the subway and LIRR operate under distinct New York state and city funding mandates. Merging these entities into a single regional zone system would require complex inter-state political negotiations, massive capital to overhaul fare collection systems, and a complete restructuring of how tax revenue is distributed between NYC and its suburban counties. The closest the MTA has come to a common urban zone is the CityTicket program, which offers a discounted flat rate ($7.25 peak / $5.25 off-peak) for any LIRR or Metro-North ride that begins and ends inside New York City limits.

text:
𝐈𝐍𝐃𝐈𝐀𝐍𝐀 𝐒𝐂𝐇𝐎𝐎𝐋 𝐅𝐎𝐑𝐂𝐄𝐃 𝐎𝐔𝐓 𝐀 𝐂𝐇𝐑𝐈𝐒𝐓𝐈𝐀𝐍 𝐓𝐄𝐀𝐂𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐅𝐎𝐑 𝐇𝐈𝐒 𝐅𝐀𝐈𝐓𝐇 — 𝐒𝐈𝐗 𝐘𝐄𝐀𝐑𝐒 𝐋𝐀𝐓𝐄𝐑, 𝐇𝐄 𝐖𝐎𝐍

Brownsburg Community School Corporation gave orchestra teacher John Kluge an ultimatum in 2018: call students by names and pronouns that clashed with his faith, or lose the classroom he’d spent four years building. 𝘈𝘴 𝘢 𝘊𝘩𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘯, 𝘐 𝘣𝘦𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘷𝘦 𝘎𝘰𝘥 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘶𝘴 𝘮𝘢𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘦𝘮𝘢𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘵 𝘮𝘺 𝘊𝘩𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘮, Kluge said at the time. The district pushed him out anyway.

Kluge hadn’t refused to teach his students. He’d offered a compromise — calling every student only by last name, the way some coaches already did — and the district accepted it for months. Then administrators 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 anyway, giving him a choice between compliance, quitting, or getting fired. He sued in 2019.

For years, Brownsburg won. A federal judge sided with the district, and Kluge’s case looked finished — until the Seventh Circuit reversed course, citing the Supreme Court’s Groff v. DeJoy ruling, and sent the case to a jury. That precedent requires employers to accommodate an employee’s religious beliefs unless doing so is a genuine hardship. Facing a jury instead of a friendly judge, the district did what districts do when the facts turn against them: it reached for the checkbook.

Brownsburg still won’t admit it did anything wrong — it says it settled for financial reasons, not fault — but it agreed to pay Kluge $𝟔𝟓𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 and train its own senior staff on how federal law protects employees from religious discrimination. 𝘈𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘢𝘭𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘧𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢 𝘩𝘢𝘭𝘧 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴, 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘮𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘦𝘯𝘴𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘵 𝘉𝘳𝘰𝘸𝘯𝘴𝘣𝘶𝘳𝘨, said David Cortman, senior counsel for Alliance Defending Freedom, which represented Kluge throughout the fight.

The same administrators who decided a Christian teacher’s convictions didn’t belong in their building are now the ones cutting the check — out of a budget your property taxes help fund, whether you live in Brownsburg or not. Kluge never got his old job back, and he’s no longer in public education at all. But the district that spent six and a half years and $650,000 of other people’s money fighting him ended up exactly where his faith told him to stand in the first place.

𝐇𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐦 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐡. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐰𝐨𝐧’𝐭 𝐚𝐝𝐦𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐰𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 — 𝐛𝐮𝐭 $𝟔𝟓𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐬𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐲.

text:
Elizabeth Holmes fooled the whole world. She was 30, the youngest self-made female billionaire on the planet, and her company was worth $9 billion. Under oath, she said “I don’t know” more than 600 times.

In the video below, Holmes explains the technology she said would change medicine: hundreds of blood tests from a single drop of blood.

She dropped out of Stanford in her 2nd year and founded Theranos in 2003. No more needles, no more vials. A finger prick and a small machine would do it all.

She fooled the investors. The Walmart family put in $150 million. Rupert Murdoch put in $125 million.

She fooled the most powerful men in America. Henry Kissinger, George Shultz and James Mattis sat on her board.

She fooled the businesses. Walgreens signed a $140 million deal to put her tests in its stores. Real patients got real results.

Inside the company, employees say the machines didn’t work. A former employee said only 7 tests ran on Theranos devices. Most were run on other companies’ machines. One breast cancer survivor got a hormone result that a later test showed was badly wrong.

In 2015 a Wall Street Journal reporter published the first story. Within 2 weeks Walgreens froze its plans. Within a year Forbes cut her net worth from $4.5 billion to $0.

In 2017 the SEC sat her down for 3 days of questioning. Asked about tests that didn’t work, she said, “I know that we made mistakes.” Shown a 2014 claim that Theranos offered over 200 tests, she said, “Reading it now, I don’t think it is.”

In 2022 a jury found her guilty of defrauding investors. She was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months and ordered, together with her ex-partner Sunny Balwani, to pay $452 million back.

Her defense said she never stopped believing the technology was close to working. She blamed Balwani, Theranos’s former COO and her ex-boyfriend, for the lab’s problems, and testified that he abused and controlled her for years. He denied it.

The jury also acquitted her on every count involving patients.

She’s now in a federal prison camp in Texas, with a release date at the end of 2031. She has asked for her sentence to be commuted.

1 drop of blood. $9 billion. 11 years.

Did Elizabeth Holmes set out to fool the world, or did she fool herself first?

text:
OpenAI uses Opus 5.5 to code promo films

It's Tuesday morning, and we've got some exciting news from Yipeng Gao, a CS PhD student at USC and researcher at Google DeepMind. He shared some fascinating insights on X about how OpenAI is now creating its promo films entirely through code rather than traditional video production methods.

So, what does this mean for the future of AI-generated content? How will it impact developers and designers? And why should anyone care beyond just being curious?
The Tech Behind It

Gao’s revelation centers around Opus 5.5, a tool that generates films using three.js—a JavaScript library for creating interactive 3D graphics in browsers—and GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language). These tools are combined with an SDF (Signed Distance Field) heroine to define complex shapes and animations through mathematical functions rather than pixel-by-pixel rendering.

Three.js allows developers to create stunning visual effects directly within web browsers, making it a powerful tool for interactive content. GLSL is used to write shaders that control the appearance of graphics in real-time, enabling dynamic and responsive visuals. The SDF heroine adds an extra layer of complexity by defining shapes through mathematical distances rather than traditional pixel-based methods.
What’s the Big Deal?

The real question is, why now? Why shift from traditional video production methods to code-based generation? One reason could be efficiency. Traditional video production can be resource-intensive, especially for high-resolution content. By moving to a coding approach, OpenAI aims to reduce costs and speed up content creation.

Another factor might be the flexibility offered by code-based generation. With three.js and GLSL, developers have more control over every aspect of the visuals, from lighting to texture mapping. This level of detail can lead to highly customized and unique visual experiences that traditional video production methods struggle to match.
The Creative Angle

Beyond the practical benefits, this move opens new avenues for artistic expression. Imagine tweaking an equation in real-time and seeing how it affects 1D models or animations instantly. It’s like having a digital paintbrush that can draw anything, limited only by your imagination.

Developers and designers can experiment with different mathematical functions to create intricate shapes and dynamic scenes. This approach allows for rapid prototyping and iteration, making the creative process more fluid and responsive. The ability to manipulate visuals through code also opens up possibilities for interactive content, where users can influence the visual output in real-time.
Who Cares?

If you’re in tech, particularly those involved with AI-generated content, this could be significant for future projects. For developers and designers, learning these new tools is crucial to stay ahead of the curve. But even casual observers find it fascinating as a testament to digital creativity’s evolution.

For instance, imagine creating an interactive promotional video where users can customize elements like lighting or camera angles. This level of interactivity could make content more engaging and personalized for each viewer. Additionally, the ability to generate high-quality visuals quickly and efficiently means that projects can move from concept to execution faster than ever before.
The Limitations

While powerful for certain types of content, code-based generation might not be as flexible or intuitive for traditional video production tasks. Plus, mastering three.js and GLSL could present a steep learning curve for those without programming backgrounds in 3D graphics.

Traditional video editing tools offer a more user-friendly interface with drag-and-drop functionality and pre-built templates that make it easier to create polished content quickly. Code-based generation requires a deeper understanding of mathematical functions and graphical algorithms, which might be daunting for non-technical users.
Open Source and Beyond

Gao has open-sourced the full code and agent logs on GitHub, inviting others to explore and contribute. This democratization of technology means anyone interested can dive into this world of digital creativity now.

The GitHub repository provides a wealth of resources, including detailed documentation, sample projects, and community discussions. By making the tools available for free, Gao is fostering a collaborative environment where developers from all backgrounds can experiment with new ideas and share their findings.
The Artistic Choices

It’s worth noting that while the technical aspects are impressive, the hardest part isn’t always the visuals but the art style and video direction/script choices. These creative decisions still play a crucial role in making compelling content.

Earnings season AI and cost pressures drive layoffs; investor reactions depend on corporate motivation

As CEOs respond to the rise of artificial intelligence while trying to cut costs, several companies announced thousands of job cuts during this earnings season.

Analysis shows that mentions of layoffs and dismissals in news reports have risen again, reaching the highest level since May in October. In Europe, even governments are joining the ranks of downsizing.

The latest news shows that previously reported Disney (112.645-0.47, -0.41%, ) is preparing to cut thousands of jobs, and the entertainment giant will announce its earnings later this month. German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it will cut 3,460 jobs in Europe, after which its stock price subsequently dipped slightly.

The market's reaction to layoffs seems to depend on how investors view corporate motivations: whether to proactively adjust workforce structures to adapt to environmental changes in advance, or to take urgent action when threatened. PayPal and Microsoft (509.452.33, 0.46%, ) saw slight increases in their stock prices after announcing related plans. In contrast, Volvo Cars stated that due to the sharp contraction in the Chinese market, further layoffs would occur, causing its stock price to plunge.

Berenberg equity strategist Chris Armstrong said, "The stock price reaction largely depends on whether the market believes the company acted when it is strong, or, like Volvo, forced under tremendous pressure." ”

Many companies have seen significant layoffs this time. Microsoft offers voluntary resignation plans to 60,000 employees, equivalent to a quarter of its total workforce; Netflix (62.590.25, 0.40%, ) will lay off 6%; Barclays plans to use AI to reduce costs by cutting 5,000 jobs; Further layoffs at Volvo Cars will affect 2,500 people.

Violeta Todorova, Senior Research Analyst at Leverage Shares, said investors should ask one question: "Is this company laying off employees for growth, or just to survive?" "She said that a profitable company streamlining management and investing the saved funds into technology could be good news in the long run; But if layoffs are merely to fill the gap left by declining demand, that's a warning signal, not a solution.

The government has also begun envisioning streamlining the civil service workforce through greater use of AI. The Netherlands plans to cut 25,000 civil service positions in the coming years, hoping to save 3.5 billion euros annually through AI-driven efficiency improvements.

Joachim Klement, strategist at Panmure Liberum, believes that corporate layoffs are one of the signs indicating the COVID-19 pandemic and Qualcomm's 2022 (162.460.38, 0.23%, )The rapid growth cycle of revenue and profits following the inflation phase is nearing its end. Profit growth in 2027 and 2028 may be more moderate.

"The easy fruit has already been harvested, and further cost cuts will become more difficult in the future," Klement said. "The market hopes that productivity gains brought by AI will help companies increase profits even when revenue growth slows." But so far, we have no evidence that AI has already increased productivity outside the tech industry. ”

PayPal stated that its total workforce has been reduced by more than 2,000 people, with management positions cut by more than a quarter, and its stock price rose after the announcement. In contrast, French auto parts supplier OPmobility lowered its full-year profit forecast and announced plans to lay off 770 employees, causing its stock to drop its largest drop in three years.

Aggregated data shows that the number of S&P 500 constituents announcing broader restructuring measures this earnings season is expected to increase by about 20% compared to the same period last year; The pace of related announcements by European companies was roughly the same as last year.

With about 70% of S&P 500 constituents already reporting earnings, 147 companies announced restructuring charges, compared to 178 companies for the entire Q3 2025 earnings season. Among MSCI Europe Index constituents, the number of companies disclosing restructuring expenses is expected to be roughly equivalent to the 60 companies disclosed in the same period last year.

Rajeev De Mello, Chief Investment Officer at Gama Asset Management, said: "In most cases, layoffs mean companies are becoming leaner and more productive. However, some industries are under pressure for various reasons, such as competition in the automotive sector and interest rate-sensitive sectors. Investors are carefully examining companies, looking for those that can improve productivity through the application of AI. ”

text:
Revolut Switches Engineers to In-House GLM

They’ve made the bold decision to transition around two thousand of their engineers from external AI services like Claude Code and Codex to an in-house self-hosted GLM model. This shift has not only slashed costs but also boosted productivity across the board.
What Changed: The Numbers Behind the Move

According to Guillermo Flor’s tweet, Revolut moved approximately 2,000 engineers onto a self-hosted GLM for coding and pushed Claude Code and Codex to an exception list. David Abitbol, who leads AI operations at Revolut, revealed that they set up 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs for their new system. These GPUs now cost them only $0.30 per million tokens—about one-tenth of what they were paying Anthropic and OpenAI previously.
How It Works: The Impact on Development Lead Times

One of the most striking outcomes of this transition is the 70% improvement in development lead times. By eliminating token rationing, Revolut engineers can now use AI more freely across all tasks rather than reserving it for complex issues alone. This shift has unlocked a new level of productivity within their teams.
What Is Stored: Cost Savings and Efficiency Gains

Revolut’s move highlights the growing trend towards self-hosted AI solutions for large-scale operations. By cutting costs so drastically, they’ve made AI more accessible to all engineers, not just those working on high-priority projects. This democratization of AI tools has led to significant efficiency gains in development cycles.
What Is Excluded: The Challenge for Smaller Teams

But here’s the awkward bit: why would other companies follow suit? For startups and smaller teams without their own DevOps and GPU hardware, this move might seem irrelevant. They still rely on external APIs like Anthropic and OpenAI because setting up an in-house solution is not feasible or cost-effective for them.
How It Works: The Performance Gap

Another key factor to consider is the performance gap between top-tier models and in-house solutions. While Revolut’s GLM model offers substantial savings, it may not be as powerful as the frontier models they used before. As one commenter noted, “the difference is negligible for seasoned engineers,” suggesting that while the price drop is significant, the performance gap might not matter much to experienced developers.
User Controls: Maintenance Overhead

Running 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs requires a dedicated team of experts to keep everything running smoothly. While the upfront cost savings are substantial, ongoing operational costs and manpower requirements must also be factored into the equation. This maintenance overhead can eat into some of the initial savings Revolut has achieved.
What This Does Not Prove: The Question for Larger Organizations

For big companies like Revolut, it’s clearly worth it. But smaller teams might find that sticking with existing APIs remains more practical and cost-effective for now. Would you move your team off frontier APIs if the bill dropped 90%? This is a question many tech leaders are grappling with.
Practical Takeaway: The Broader Implications

Revolut’s approach offers a compelling path forward for larger organizations with the resources to manage complex AI infrastructures. However, it remains a challenging proposition for smaller teams without the necessary infrastructure and expertise. As more companies look to leverage AI in their operations, this shift towards self-hosted models could become increasingly common.
What Do You Think?

Is this shift towards self-hosted AI models a game-changer or just another tech trend that won’t stick around? Share your thoughts in the comments below!

text:
Chamath Flags a Hidden Risk Building Under the AI Boom
For years, America’s largest technology companies operated under a simple and powerful assumption: they could do nearly everything at once. Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META), Alphabet (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) generated so much cash that they could build vast data centers, repurchase tens of billions of dollars in stock, and still maintain some of the strongest balance sheets in corporate America. Conventional wisdom held that these firms were uniquely insulated from the financing constraints that limit almost every other industry.
Artificial intelligence is now testing that paradigm. On the October 30 episode of the All-In Podcast, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya argued that the current AI spending boom carries a less obvious but significant risk. Technology companies may increasingly need outside capital to finance the massive infrastructure required for AI, placing them in direct competition with the U.S. government—another enormous borrower—in the capital markets.
Palihapitiya estimates that the broader AI industry already owes roughly $340 billion to $400 billion to capital markets. Even with strong demand for AI products and services, that scale of borrowing is consequential. Big Tech is already returning less cash to shareholders while pouring more into infrastructure. Investors, he suggests, may need to focus far more closely on borrowing costs and free cash flow than they have in the recent past.
The numbers illustrate the shift clearly. According to Reuters, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle generated a combined $542.9 billion in operating cash flow during the first nine months of 2026. Their capital spending, however, doubled to $556.9 billion—exceeding the cash flow these five companies produced for the first time in data going back to 2011.
Shareholders are already feeling the impact. The group’s total stock buybacks dropped 83% to just $13.6 billion. Microsoft accounted for the majority of the remaining repurchases, while Alphabet and Meta made none. For years, buybacks provided a reliable boost to earnings per share by reducing the share count. That long-standing financial windfall is now largely disappearing.
“The entire United States economy is levered to the AI complex,” Palihapitiya said. The enormous expenditure does not automatically make AI a poor investment. If the new infrastructure eventually generates sufficient revenue and profit, stockholders could still benefit. Yet the barrier is rising. The same five companies swung from $143.5 billion of free cash flow a year earlier to a $14 billion deficit in the first nine months of 2026. In short, investors are forgoing cash returns today in exchange for the possibility of higher AI-driven earnings tomorrow.
The financing pressure extends beyond individual balance sheets. Palihapitiya projects that the funding requirements of these companies through the end of 2027 may account for almost 30% of the anticipated issuance of new U.S. Treasury notes and bonds over the same period. While this is his estimate rather than an official government figure and should be treated with caution, the underlying idea is straightforward: many of the same large investors fund both corporations and the federal government. Increased corporate borrowing can crowd out demand for Treasuries, potentially forcing companies to offer higher returns to attract capital. That, in turn, raises the hurdle rate for AI investments themselves.
The AI race is no longer solely about developing the best technology. Financing has become the central challenge. The companies once viewed as cash-rich engines of the economy are now testing how far their balance sheets—and the broader capital markets—can stretch to fund the infrastructure of the next technological era.

✈️ Why Michael @Saylor Stopped Flying His Own Airplane

Before becoming one of Bitcoin’s most influential advocates, Michael Saylor studied aerospace engineering at MIT and learned to fly in the Air Force.

In an interview with physicist @Briankeating 

Dr. Brian Keating on “Into the Impossible”Saylor revealed something fascinating about his personal life and approach to risk.

Brian Keating: “What’s your dream plane in your hangar?”

Michael Saylor: “I have a Global Express. I like it. I’m going to keep it.”

Keating: “Are you type rated in it?”

Saylor: “No, I don’t fly it. I used to fly. I mean, I learned to fly when I was in the Air Force.”

✈️ Why He Stopped Flying

Saylor explained:

“It takes a lot of time and energy to keep up with that and it’s not safe to be a hobbyist in that.”

“A lot of wealthy people died crashing their own airplane. So, I don’t really wish to emulate that model.”

Despite his engineering background, aviation experience, and financial resources, Saylor prefers leaving the flying to professionals.

The lesson? Knowing your limitations is just as important as knowing your capabilities.

⚙️ From Aviation to Bitcoin

Throughout the interview, Saylor repeatedly connects aerospace engineering principles to Bitcoin.

He asks:

“Would you put your children into an airplane designed by an engineer that … bragged to you that he ignored the laws of thermodynamics and he broke all the rules in the airplane?”

His argument is simple.

We wouldn’t trust an airplane designed without respect for engineering principles.

So why trust a monetary system where a small group of people can arbitrarily change the rules governing the money supply?

For Saylor, Bitcoin represents an alternative: a monetary network with transparent, mathematically enforced rules and a fixed maximum supply of 21 million coins.

🫁 “Bitcoin Is Oxygen”

When Keating questioned Bitcoin’s risks, Saylor offered another aviation analogy.

Imagine an airplane depressurizing at altitude. Oxygen masks drop from the ceiling.

Do you spend two hours debating whether the oxygen is safe?

Or do you put the mask on?

Saylor concludes:

“Because Bitcoin is oxygen and it’s new.”

His point isn’t that Bitcoin is risk-free.

It’s that people often focus entirely on the risks of adopting something new while ignoring the risks of doing nothing.

🧠 The Bigger Lesson

What fascinates me is the contrast.

Saylor stopped piloting aircraft because he recognized the risks of flying without maintaining professional-level proficiency.

Yet he embraced Bitcoin despite the financial establishment viewing it as extraordinarily risky.

The common thread?

Risk isn’t simply about doing something unfamiliar. It’s about understanding the system, evaluating the alternatives, and recognizing the consequences of inaction.

The more I study Saylor, the more I appreciate how deeply his aerospace engineering background influences his philosophy of money.

Know the system. Respect the risks. Understand your limitations. Never confuse familiarity with safety.

🟠

text:
From Rizal to the Maritime Silk Road: Keeping the Philippines-Fujian link alive

QUANZHOU, China – Around 1,300 years ago, the first batch of Chinese merchants - faced with an upsurge of private business and instability of society - left their homeland through the shores of Jinjiang County in the southeastern Chinese coastal province of Fujian in search of new means of livelihood in foreign lands and eventually settled across more than 50 countries worldwide. 

Since then, estimates place the total number of these then new breed of “migrants,” so-called overseas Chinese workers or OCW, from this county at around 5 million - some 1 million of them ended up in the Philippines.

One such migrant went by the name Ke Nan, born in Fujian’s Shangguo Village in Jinjiang in this city in 1662, who later migrated to the Philippines as Domingo Lamco and gave rise to probably one of the most important bloodlines in Philippine history. His great-great-grandson? Dr. Jose Rizal.

Rizal’s storied and heroic revolutionary journey - already well-known the world over - made so much impact in Fujian that an almost identical replica of the Luneta Park was built across a 5.7-hectare patch of land in Shangguo in 2006 to honor his Chinese ancestry.

Standing on an 18.61-meter monument (in honor of his birth year), the 3.3-meter bronze statue of Rizal looks over the sprawling park, the largest of its kind outside Manila and serving as a reminder of “the friendship between China and the Philippines and promotes communication between the two countries,” Shangguo Village Vice Captain Ke Jingang told a group of visiting journalists from the Philippines’ Integrated State Media last week.

Jingang said locals are very well-aware of Rizal and his contribution to Philippine independence. “The story of Jose Rizal is really famous in the village [that is why] they offered this place, which belonged to the village, [as a site] to build this park.”

Since then, important Filipino officials, like former President Joseph Estrada who attended its opening ceremony, as well as Filipino organizations and student groups have paid the park a visit.

Just a short distance from the square sits the Jinjiang Museum, where a special section is fully devoted to the Philippine martyr, featuring statues, images, and paintings - all crafted by Filipino artists and donated by the museum’s Filipino friends, including the Philippine consul general in neighboring Xiamen.

The museum, one of the largest county-level museums in China, has devised a clever way to make Rizal even more relatable and bring his story closer to visitors, especially the youth, both local and foreign ones.

“We use famous Chinese people who have a similar experience as reference to introduce Jose Rizal’s stories to teenagers because they are important persons in Chinese history just like Jose Rizal,” said Jinjiang Museum curator Lin Qianhai, citing as an example Sun Yat Sen, the revered Chinese revolutionary who overthrew the Qing Dynasty and founded the Republic of China.

“We would introduce them to Jose Rizal’s story and tell them he is regarded as a national hero of the Philippines,” he added.

While the museum has a vast collection tracing the steps of the overseas Chinese across Southeast Asia, around half of it is exclusively about the Philippines. Apart from Rizal, also featured at the museum are images of former Philippine presidents like Estrada and Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, as well as prominent Filipino tycoons with Chinese roots including Henry Sy and Lucio Tan, both born in Fujian.

“We put this content at this museum to show what the Jinjiang people did in Southeast Asia… so this is also about our Chinese ancestors’ contribution, to some degree,” he said.

Another of these eventual overseas Chinese tycoons also left his mark on Fujian soil and built the famous Yang Family Mansion at the Houganbing Village in Yonging Town, Sishi City, also in Quanzhou.

Yang Bangsuo, a Chinese trader who settled and made a living in the Philippines with his brothers at the height of the Jinjiang migration, returned to China in the 1920s to build the rear section of the mansion, completed in 1933 and blends Chinese and western architectural styles.

Regarded as one of the largest residences built by an overseas Chinese in Quanzhou, the mansion, also called the “Ninety-Nine Room Historic Residence,” houses more than 100 rooms, accommodating 300 families at its peak.

Apart from Quanzhou, the city of Zhangzhou, still in Fujian, also traces its role and links to other countries, including the Philippines, via the Maritime Silk Road, a vast ancient network of sea trade routes connecting Southeast Asia, East Asia, the Indian subcontinent, the Arabian Peninsula, eastern Africa, and Europe.

Home to more than 11,000 cultural relics from the ancient maritime trade route, the Zhangzhou Museum features Pan Zhencheng, a Chinese merchant whose family hails from Zhangzhou, was able to travel to Luzon three times selling silk and tea.

Visitors of this museum are greeted at the entrance with a passage that says the cultural exchange that came with the maritime trade “unveiled a magnificent landscape of early modern globalization with a far-reaching impact on human culture. We are supposed to follow the example of our forefathers by benefitting from cooperation and joint contribution to an ideal world.”

Be it Rizal’s ancestor, merchant Bangsuo, or these ancient maritime trade routes taken by many overseas Chinese, who came before and after them, all of them - in one way or another - played a central role in this cooperation and joint contribution to a shared history and a two-way cultural exchange between the Philippines and China, something kept alive to this day. (PNA)

RIZAL PARK IN CHINA. Tourists wander around the 5.73-hectare Jose Rizal Square in Jinjiang City in Fujian, China on Oct. 26, 2026. The biggest of its kind outside the Philippines, the park – located along Shangguo intersection – features a 3-meter bronze statue of Rizal similar to the one at the Luneta Park in Manila and highlights the Chinese ancestry of the Philippine martyr, whose great-great-grandfather was born in Shangguo Village in Fujian and later migrated to the Philippines. (PNA photo)

text:
Starbase Louisiana Week in Review, Issue 2

Another busy week, and BIG NEWS. The State's contract with SpaceX is finally public, and there's a new job opening too. 🎉

STATE CONTRACT RELEASED
After a public records request by Vermilion United, Louisiana Economic Development released the State's signed agreement with SpaceX, dated Aug 25, 2026.
• New jobs must pay at least 150% of the statewide average wage
• At least $25M to the Community Foundation of Acadiana by Dec. 31, 2030
• Reasonable efforts to prefer Louisiana suppliers and contractors when they're competitive on price, quality and delivery
• LED will offer FastStart workforce training and the High Impact Jobs Program
• Approved uses: a rocket launch spaceport plus related manufacturing, compute, power generation and storage, and employee housing and amenities
• The State will set up long-term funding for the agencies that handle the project's permits
• Permit and FAA licensing delays pause deadlines on both sides
• SpaceX files budgets, twice-yearly progress reports, quarterly payroll reports and a sworn yearly compliance certification with LED
• The $100M land payment goes into LED's Site Investment and Infrastructure Improvement Fund
• The State can buy the land back only in narrow cases, by refunding the full $100M
• Rebates of state and local sales and use taxes on aerospace equipment and materials for 20 years, renewable for 10 more if SpaceX creates 200 jobs and invests $1B
• The contract runs through Aug. 25, 2037

JOBS
• SpaceX now has 9 openings in Pecan Island, including a second Communications Lead role posted Nov 2.

BIG NUMBER: 70%
• SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell says about 70% of the Starbase, Texas workforce is local to the Rio Grande Valley, and SpaceX aims for a similar share in Louisiana.

SCHOOLS
• The Vermilion Parish School Board is having about 4,000 acres of school land near White Lake appraised ahead of possible land-swap talks with SpaceX. Superintendent Tommy Byler says the land brings in only $20K to $30K a year from hunting leases, and he'd like land closer to "where they're building two hotels and a restaurant."

COMMUNITY
• At the Police Jury committee meeting on Wed, Nov 4 at 5:30 PM in Abbeville, the Vermilion Council on Aging will request SpaceX-related funding.

PERMITS
• Day 39 for @SpaceX's big coastal permit for the road, bridge, and wharf. It's still marked incomplete after the state asked for more information on Oct 1. No new SpaceX filings this week.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT
• Starbase Louisiana is getting international attention. Canada's Globe and Mail visited Pecan Island for a long feature on what the project means for rural Cajun country.
• LED's official SpaceX FAQ says SpaceX will pay for its own new power generation and lines.
• DOTD selected Royal Engineers & Consultants of New Orleans for work tied to the SpaceX site, under a contract running through 2031, as the State studies roads and possible LA 82 improvements.

STARBASE LA MERCH
• If you're interested, check out the Starbase, LA gear from @SERobinsonJr and the Occupy Gumbo shirt from @JoshWest247. Links below.

This week's video with Luke and Lena is linked below. Thank you to everyone following along. ❤️

text:
The Twelve Months Sanctified by Prayer: November, Month of the Souls in Purgatory by M. L'ABBE A. RICARD, D.S.G. Translated from the French. 1877 November 22 FASTING.
.
Prelude.
.
Let us represent to ourselves the fearful austerities which are practised by so many religious orders, both men and women. throughout the whole Church. From them spring a treasure of merit in which the merciful justice of God is pleased to make the souls in Purgatory participate.
.
Meditation.
.
We read in the First Book of Kings that, "when the inhabitants of Jabes Galaad bad heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the most valiant men arose and walked all the night, and took the body of Saul, and the bodies of his sons, from the wall of Bethsan: and they came to Jabes Galaad, and burnt them there; and they took their bones. and buried them in the wood of Jabes, and fasted seven days."
.
This example shows us how for ages the faithful have fasted for the dead, and we see with lively admiration that this practice has at all times been approved and followed in the, Catholic Church. Besides, under the name of­ fasts all other mortifications and austerities are comprehended, as disciplines, hair-cloth, lying on the ground, etc.
O my Jesus, Thou Who hast said that, "As long as you did it to one of these My least brethren, you did it to Me," what pretext then in my cowardice find to dispense me from helping the souls in Purgatory, knowing that the good which I should do them would not be less agreeable to Thee, than if I had done it to, Thyself? I offer Thee then for them all the· mortifications which I resolve to practice for their intention.
.
Resolution.
.
Shake off our cowardice, so as to embrace courageously the practices of voluntary penance, in favour of the poor souls in Purgatory.
.
Aspiration.
.
And they took their bones and buried them in the wood of Jabes, and fasted seven days." (1 Kings xxxi. 13.)
.
EXAMPLE: CONTINUAL PRESENCE OF A SOUL.
.
We read the following incident in the annals of the Visitation of Dijon: Sister Mary Bernard Chicolier, who attained to great sanctity, was prevented by special, graces from her earliest years.  She formed, when quite young, the design of consecrating herself to God, and was clothed, and made her profession under the government of our mother, Anne Lidwine Boulier. The Mere Chahu, who was her successor, helped this dear sister, amidst the great trials through which it pleased God to make her pass, and Who imprinted in her heart a most lively horror of the smallest imperfections by permitting a soul in Purgatory to appear to her, and to be in a manner continually present to her. Our mother, to whom this dear sister disclosed all that she suffered, caused her to be examined by M. Chaudot, our superior, and by the Rev. Father Jacquinot) Provincial of the Society of Jesus, who after a serious examination, judged that there was in this neither illu­sion nor imagination. It was, therefore, decided that the community should have masses celebrated, and recite every day a De profundis for the repose of this soul, and that Sister Chicolier should be at liberty to make particular penances for this intention. This dear sister practiced great austerities, offering besides for this soul, all her good works, which were very numerous, and never allowing herself a single inclination of nature, or the slightest satisfaction. The priest, who was charged with celebrating the Masses, was a Capuchin monk of great holiness, and who entirely ignored everything that had happened. He came one day to find Mere Chahu, and assured her that the soul whom she had caused to be prayed so much for, had entered into possession of the glory of God.

to the maid, “bring the princess her gray dress, and you’ll see,
