The AM Brief, Tuesday November 2, 2026 Part 1

Good morning, 

It’s 9am in Miami and here is a recap of market related events that caught my eye. Part 1

     Historical market performance indicates that November is consistently the strongest month of the calendar year for equity markets. Over the past century, the S&P 500 has averaged a 2.3% gain during the month of November. The seasonal rally becomes even more pronounced during political election cycles, with historical data showing that November average stock gains rise to 2.7% in midterm election years. This longstanding Wall Street trend offers a compelling historical backdrop for institutional and retail equity investors alike.

     Financial firm Glenmede highlights a remarkable historical market trend: the S&P 500 index has delivered positive 12 month returns following every single midterm election since 1942. Historical data further reveals distinct economic performance patterns based on Washington's political alignment. Post election periods featuring "weak sweeps", where one political party captures both the presidency and Congress generated average annual real returns of 9.3%, whereas periods characterized by a divided federal government yielded average real returns of 7.7%.

     Wall Street consensus projects S&P 500 EPS to expand 16.1% to $425 next year and 16.2% to $494 in 2028, with forward earnings reaching all time highs across the S&P 500, MidCap 400, and SmallCap 600 last week. The S&P 500 forward P/E ratio contracted to 18.2, marking its lowest valuation multiple since the April 2025 "Liberation Day" low point. Meanwhile, S&P 500 forward earnings have surged 49.1% over the exact same period, underscoring robust underlying corporate profit expansion despite recent stock market valuation compression.

     In the year's largest M&A transaction on an equity basis, Marvell has reached a definitive agreement to acquire Lumentum in an all stock deal valuing the optical technology firm at $115 billion in enterprise value. Under the terms of the transaction, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell stock for each share they own. The mega merger significantly consolidates market leadership across optical networking and chip technologies, with final transaction closing anticipated to take place in the first half of 2028.

Sources : Morning Brew (11-2), Barron's (11-2), Yardeni (10-31), 

Thank you for reading
Live your best life,
AL Maulini

🏆 INTRODUCING THE POWER 15: COMPANIES SHAPING TOMORROW

THE CHAMBER GUY® PRESENTS A NEW SIGNATURE EDITORIAL FEATURE

⚡ 15 Companies. Transformative Innovations. One Changing World.

THE FUTURE OF BUSINESS ISN'T WAITING FOR TOMORROW. IT'S BEING BUILT TODAY!

Somewhere right now, engineers are developing robots that could transform manufacturing. Scientists are advancing treatments that could revolutionize healthcare. Artificial intelligence is changing how companies operate, how consumers make purchasing decisions and how businesses compete.

Meanwhile, other innovators are rethinking energy, transportation, cybersecurity, financial services and even access to outer space.

As business owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs, we cannot afford to ignore these developments.

That's why I'm excited to introduce something new to The Chamber Guy® LinkedIn Newsletter.

🏆 THE POWER 15 — THE COMPANIES SHAPING TOMORROW

A recurring editorial feature examining 15 companies whose innovations, technologies and potential economic influence deserve the attention of business leaders everywhere.

This is not a list of stocks to buy.

It's a look at the businesses helping build the world in which all of us will operate.

And today, I'm proud to introduce our inaugural POWER 15.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔬 HOW DID WE SELECT THE POWER 15?

Our goal wasn't to find the 15 largest corporations, the most popular stocks or the companies with the highest share prices.

We wanted to identify businesses helping drive meaningful change.

Our selection process considers:

🚀 INNOVATION — Are they developing technologies, products or business models capable of changing industries?

🧠 RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT — Are they investing in discoveries and capabilities that could create lasting economic influence?

🌎 INDUSTRY IMPACT — Could their work influence how businesses operate over the next five to ten years?

🏗️ EXECUTION — Are they demonstrating the ability to develop, manufacture, distribute or commercialize important technologies?

🛡️ COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGES — What capabilities, intellectual property, infrastructure or expertise distinguish them?

⚠️ RISKS & CHALLENGES — What obstacles could limit their success?

No company receives a permanent place on THE POWER 15.

And no company can purchase inclusion.

Our mission is to follow meaningful business innovation, not promote particular securities.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌟 MEET THE INAUGURAL POWER 15

The numbers identify our selections. They are not rankings of investment merit or expected stock performance.

🍎 1. APPLE (AAPL)

THE FUTURE OF PERSONAL TECHNOLOGY

Apple's connected ecosystem of devices, software and services influences how people communicate, work, shop and interact with technology.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: AI-powered devices, connected services and healthcare technologies could create new ways for businesses to serve customers.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Maintaining innovation and customer loyalty in an intensely competitive global market.

💻 2. MICROSOFT (MSFT)

THE FUTURE OF ENTERPRISE COMPUTING AND WORKPLACE AI

Microsoft operates at the intersection of business software, cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: AI-assisted productivity, automation and cloud computing could fundamentally change how organizations operate and manage their resources.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Turning enormous AI infrastructure investments into sustainable business value while managing security and competition.

🔎 3. ALPHABET / GOOGLE (GOOGL)

THE FUTURE OF INFORMATION AND INTELLIGENT DISCOVERY

Google helped define how people search for information and how customers discover businesses. Alphabet also develops artificial intelligence, cloud computing and autonomous-driving technologies.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: AI-powered search and discovery could fundamentally reshape advertising, marketing and customer acquisition.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Adapting its established search business as AI changes how people find answers.

📦 4. AMAZON (AMZN)

THE FUTURE OF COMMERCE, LOGISTICS AND CLOUD INFRASTRUCTURE

Amazon's influence extends from online retail and distribution to cloud computing, automation and AI infrastructure.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Its innovations are changing how products are sold, delivered and supported, while cloud technology gives businesses access to sophisticated computing capabilities.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Managing enormous infrastructure investments, competitive pressures and regulatory scrutiny.

🧠 5. NVIDIA (NVDA)

THE COMPUTING FOUNDATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Nvidia develops accelerated-computing technologies used in AI development, data centers, scientific research and advanced automation.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: The capabilities and economics of AI depend heavily on the computing infrastructure behind increasingly sophisticated systems.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Competition, export restrictions and the possibility that demand or spending patterns could change.

🌐 6. META PLATFORMS (META)

THE FUTURE OF DIGITAL COMMUNICATION AND AI-POWERED MARKETING

Through Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and its advertising technologies, Meta influences how businesses connect with customers.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: AI-powered advertising, digital communication and emerging computing interfaces could change how companies build relationships and reach buyers.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Balancing innovation with privacy, regulation and the costs of developing new technologies.

🚗 7. TESLA (TSLA)

THE CONVERGENCE OF TRANSPORTATION, ENERGY AND ROBOTICS

Tesla's ambitions extend beyond electric vehicles into energy storage, autonomous-driving technology and humanoid robotics.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: These initiatives could influence transportation, manufacturing and industrial automation.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Competition, execution and proving that ambitious technologies can become commercially sustainable businesses.

🛡️ 8. PALO ALTO NETWORKS (PANW)

PROTECTING THE DIGITAL ECONOMY

As businesses become increasingly dependent on AI, cloud computing and connected systems, cybersecurity becomes essential to business continuity.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Protecting digital operations, intelligent systems and critical infrastructure will remain an important challenge for businesses and governments.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Staying ahead of constantly evolving cyber threats and intense industry competition.

🧬 9. ELI LILLY (LLY)

TRANSFORMING HEALTHCARE AND METABOLIC MEDICINE

Eli Lilly's research and treatments for diabetes, obesity and other serious diseases could influence medical care, healthcare spending and workforce health.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Advances in medicine can affect patients, employers, healthcare systems and the broader economy.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Maintaining clinical innovation while addressing affordability, manufacturing capacity and competition.

🚀 10. SPACEX (SPCX)

TRANSFORMING ACCESS TO SPACE AND GLOBAL CONNECTIVITY

SpaceX became publicly traded in June 2026, with its shares beginning trading on Nasdaq under SPCX on June 12.

Its reusable launch systems, satellite communications and space infrastructure are changing the economics of accessing space and connecting people around the world.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: SpaceX's technologies could influence telecommunications, national security, commercial space activity and industries beyond Earth.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Launch execution, infrastructure costs, regulation and the enormous complexity of commercial space operations.

🛩️ 11. AEROVIRONMENT (AVAV)

THE FUTURE OF AUTONOMOUS DEFENSE TECHNOLOGY

AeroVironment develops unmanned aircraft, autonomous systems and related defense technologies.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Robotics, software and intelligent systems are changing military capabilities and defense procurement.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Government procurement cycles, evolving requirements, competition and execution risks.

💳 12. ROBINHOOD MARKETS (HOOD)

THE MODERNIZATION OF FINANCIAL SERVICES

Robinhood illustrates how mobile-first financial platforms can challenge established institutions and change how customers access financial products.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Digital financial services are influencing customer expectations for convenience, accessibility and technology-driven experiences.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Regulatory requirements, customer trust, competition and sensitivity to financial-market activity.

⚡ 13. GE VERNOVA (GEV)

POWERING THE NEXT GENERATION OF INDUSTRY

Artificial intelligence, data centers, advanced manufacturing and electrification are increasing the importance of reliable electricity and modern power infrastructure.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Power generation and electrical-grid technologies will play essential roles in supporting future economic development.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Large industrial projects involve complex supply chains, substantial investment and execution risk.

🤖 14. ANTHROPIC — PROPOSED TICKER: ANT

THE FUTURE OF ENTERPRISE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Anthropic develops Claude AI models and related technologies designed for business, research and other applications.

The company filed for an initial public offering on October 26, 2026, and updated its SEC registration statement on November 2, 2026.

Anthropic intends to list on Nasdaq under ANT, but its shares are not yet publicly trading as of this edition.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Anthropic's technology could transform business operations, software development, research and decision-making.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Intense competition, enormous computing costs, financial losses and the responsible deployment of increasingly capable AI systems.

🏥 15. INTUITIVE SURGICAL (ISRG)

THE FUTURE OF ROBOTIC-ASSISTED HEALTHCARE

Intuitive Surgical develops robotic-assisted surgical systems and supporting technologies for minimally invasive procedures.

🔍 WHY IT MATTERS: Medical robotics could continue influencing surgical capabilities, medical training, hospital investment and healthcare delivery.

⚠️ THE CHALLENGE: Healthcare affordability, clinical outcomes, competition and the economics of adopting advanced surgical technology.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌎 15 COMPANIES. ONE INTERCONNECTED FUTURE.

What makes THE POWER 15 especially interesting isn't simply what these companies do individually.

It's how their industries intersect.

🧠 Artificial intelligence needs computing power.

⚡ Computing power needs electricity.

🛡️ Connected infrastructure needs cybersecurity.

🤖 Robotics needs advanced software and engineering.

🧬 Healthcare needs scientific breakthroughs.

🌐 Businesses need effective ways to communicate, reach customers and manage financial transactions.

🚀 And advances in space technology could create opportunities that barely existed a generation ago.

Tomorrow's economy will not be shaped by one technology or one industry.

IT WILL BE SHAPED BY THE INTERACTION OF MANY.

That's why THE POWER 15 is more than a collection of company names.

It's an ongoing examination of the forces reshaping our economy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏢 WHAT DOES ALL THIS MEAN FOR YOUR BUSINESS?

You may be thinking that artificial intelligence, space exploration or robotic surgery has little to do with your own company.

But consider these examples.

🏪 THE LOCAL RETAILER

AI-powered search could change how customers discover your store, compare products and decide where to shop.

🏥 THE HEALTHCARE PROVIDER

Medical technology and AI-assisted administrative systems could influence patient services, operating costs and the delivery of care.

🏭 THE MANUFACTURER

Robotics and automation could change production efficiency, workforce requirements and competitive economics.

🏢 THE PROFESSIONAL SERVICES FIRM

AI tools could affect research, customer communications, document preparation and how services are delivered.

🔐 EVERY BUSINESS WITH CUSTOMER INFORMATION

Cybersecurity becomes more important as organizations store more information and depend on connected systems.

⚡ EVERY BUSINESS THAT USES ELECTRICITY

Power availability, reliability and infrastructure investment can affect operating expenses, expansion plans and business continuity.

You don't have to work in these industries to be affected by them.

And you don't need to predict the future perfectly to prepare intelligently.

The important thing is to recognize developments that could affect your customers, your employees, your expenses and your opportunities.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💰 ARE YOU BUILDING A SUCCESSFUL BUSINESS—AND A SUCCESSFUL FINANCIAL FUTURE?

Here's something I believe every business owner should think about.

We work incredibly hard building our companies.

We invest in employees, equipment, marketing, technology, inventory and growth.

But how much attention do we give to building our own financial futures?

Your business may be your greatest professional accomplishment.

But it shouldn't necessarily be your only plan for retirement.

Building wealth isn't simply about how much money you earn.

It's also about how much you preserve, how wisely you manage it and whether you're creating long-term financial security for yourself and your family.

That's another reason I'm introducing THE POWER 15.

Not to tell you which stocks to purchase, but to encourage business owners to become more informed about the companies, technologies and industries shaping tomorrow's economy.

Understanding business innovation is valuable in its own right.

Learning about saving, diversification, retirement planning and long-term investing is another important part of financial education.

Because after spending decades building your business, you deserve to have a thoughtful plan for your own future, too.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 THREE QUESTIONS EVERY BUSINESS OWNER SHOULD ASK

As you follow THE POWER 15, I encourage you to consider three important questions.

1️⃣ WHAT IS CHANGING?

Which technologies, products or business models are challenging the way things have always been done?

2️⃣ HOW COULD IT AFFECT MY BUSINESS?

Could these developments change how I attract customers, manage employees, deliver services or compete?

3️⃣ WHAT SHOULD I BE LEARNING TODAY?

What knowledge, skills or capabilities might help my company prepare for tomorrow?

You don't need to become an expert in artificial intelligence, robotics, medicine or aerospace.

But you should understand the developments that could influence your business.

THE GREATEST OPPORTUNITIES OFTEN BEGIN WITH RECOGNIZING CHANGE BEFORE EVERYONE ELSE DOES.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔄 THE POWER 15 IS JUST GETTING STARTED!

This is our inaugural edition, not a permanent list.

As technologies develop, companies execute—or fail to execute—and new businesses emerge, THE POWER 15 may change.

Some companies may remain for years.

Others may eventually be replaced by innovators we haven't even identified yet.

Each future edition will provide an opportunity to revisit important developments, evaluate new evidence and consider whether the list should change.

And here's where you come in.

I want readers to participate in the conversation.

If you discover a company developing extraordinary technology, challenging an established industry or creating a meaningful new market, tell me about it.

Your suggestion could become a candidate for a future POWER 15 review.

Companies cannot purchase inclusion.

And being an influential business does not necessarily mean its stock is attractively valued or appropriate for any particular investor.

OUR GUIDING QUESTION IS NOT WHICH STOCK WILL MAKE INVESTORS THE MOST MONEY.

IT'S WHICH COMPANIES ARE HELPING SHAPE THE BUSINESS WORLD OF TOMORROW?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💬 NOW IT'S YOUR TURN!

Which of these 15 companies do you believe will have the greatest influence on business over the next decade?

Which company did we overlook?

What emerging technology do you believe could have the biggest impact on YOUR business?

And which companies should we examine for future editions?

I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

🔁 PLEASE SHARE THIS ARTICLE with business owners, CEOs, entrepreneurs and executives who want to stay informed about tomorrow's economy.

Your perspective may help shape future editions of THE POWER 15.

text:
History sharpens @nxt888 Sony Thắng's challenge to the term "Third World", because "Third" is a rank. It sets most of the world's people beneath a First World and a Second, and ranking people in order to take from them is far older than the term. The number comes from pre-revolutionary France, where society was divided hierarchically into three estates: the clergy first, the nobility second, and everyone else, the commoners who made up the great majority, third. The commoners shouldered most of the tax burden, while the two estates above them were mostly exempt [1].

In 1788, France's finance minister, Jacques Necker, invited writers to say how the Estates-General, the country's assembly of those three estates, should be organised. Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès, a priest who took the commoners' side, answered for them in a pamphlet published in January 1789. It opened with three questions and answers: "What is the Third Estate? Everything." "What has it been hitherto in the political order? Nothing." "What does it desire? To become something." Within months, the commoners' deputies had declared themselves the National Assembly, and the French Revolution was under way [1]. The commoners of France had turned a rank into a demand.

The empires of Europe went on to rank whole peoples in the same way, and the rank was their licence to take land, labour, and resources. In 1919, after the First World War, Article 22 of the League of Nations Covenant described the peoples of territories taken from the German and Ottoman empires as "not yet able to stand by themselves". It placed them under the "tutelage" of "advanced nations", in practice the war's victors, and called that rule "a sacred trust of civilisation" [2]. When the United Nations was founded in 1945, Article 73 of its Charter kept that language, speaking of peoples who "have not yet attained a full measure of self-government", held as "a sacred trust" [3]. Some 750 million people, nearly a third of the world's population, then lived in territories "dependent on colonial Powers" [4]. As we read it, "not yet" had become the ranking: the rulers stood above, and the ruled were told to wait while their land and labour went on being taken.

After the Second World War, colonised peoples from Indonesia and Vietnam to Algeria rose against their rulers [5], and the powers above them reached for new language. In his 1949 inaugural address, US President Harry Truman offered help to what he called "underdeveloped areas", and said "The old imperialism--exploitation for foreign profit--has no place in our plans" [6]. As we read it, the rank stayed, and what had been taken dropped out of the picture. The fault was now a lack of development, to be fixed by the powers that had grown rich on the taking. A World Bank blog cites the historian William Dalrymple's figures for 1600: "Britain was producing 1.8 percent of global GDP, while India was producing 22.5 percent" [7].

In August 1952, more than 160 years after Sieyès, the French demographer Alfred Sauvy reached for his pamphlet. Writing about the impoverished nations caught between the Western and Soviet blocs of the Cold War, he closed by calling them a "Tiers Monde", or Third World: "ignored, exploited, despised" like the Third Estate, and one that "also wants to be something". By his own account, he was transposing Sieyès's famous phrase on what the Third Estate desired [8]. Eugenia Palieraki, a historian at Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, reads him as a conservative technocrat warning the French public about overpopulation, migration, and communist revolution [9].

The people he described made the term their own anyway. Through the 1960s and 70s, anticolonial voices such as Frantz Fanon, in The Wretched of the Earth, and leaders such as Chile's Salvador Allende filled it with revolutionary meaning. Like the commoners of France in 1789, they turned a rank into a demand [9]. The UN General Assembly gave "not yet" a direct answer. In December 1960, it declared in resolution 1514: "Inadequacy of political, economic, social or educational preparedness should never serve as a pretext for delaying independence" [10]. In 1964, 77 nations, most of them from Africa, Asia, and Latin America, joined as a bloc at the UN, the Group of 77, to press together for "a new and just world economic order" [11].

The powers at the top of the ranking moved against that demand. In September 1970, US President Richard Nixon told his CIA director, Richard Helms, to stop Allende taking office, and Helms's notes of the meeting read "make the economy scream" [12]. Allende died in the military coup of 11 September 1973 [13]. By the 1980s, the term "Third World" had been reduced to a byword for poverty and marginality [9]. We (SCRDI) read that as colonial appropriation of terminology (CAT): the powers above kept the term and emptied out what it stood for. The World Bank's own investment arm was already replacing it. In 1981, as the writer Afshin Molavi records, Antoine van Agtmael, a young investment officer at the International Finance Corporation, pitched a "Third World Equity Fund". He then told his boss that the name "does not inspire confidence", and proposed "emerging markets" instead [14]. The people Sauvy had written about were now a market.

The ranking carries on today under newer labels. The World Bank sorts 135 countries, with 84% of the world's population, into low- and middle-income bands [7]. Since July 2026, it has listed as institutionally fragile those of the countries it lends to most cheaply that score below 3.0 on the Bank's own assessment of their institutions [15]. That is a lender grading its own debtors. Those who refuse the ranking have a label of their own: "Global South", thought to have been coined in 1969 by the American activist Carl Oglesby to name the North's dominance [16].

Some of the language of 1919 and 1945 never left. Article 73 of the UN Charter stands as written, and the UN says "fewer than 2 million people live under colonial rule in the 17 remaining non-self-governing territories" [4]. Westminster rules ten of them [17]. The International Monetary Fund's top tier is "Advanced Economies" [18], the word Article 22 used in 1919 for the powers placed over the colonised.

Westminster has also renamed its own colonial institutions, keeping the body and changing the name. Hansard, House of Commons, 25 June 1947: the Colonial Secretary, Arthur Creech Jones, announced a Colonial Development Corporation that would "operate on commercial principles" and "stimulate the supply of products of which this country and the world at large stand in need" [19]. As colonies broke free of England's Empire, the body became the Commonwealth Development Corporation in 1963, then CDC Group in 1999, and British International Investment in 2022 [20]. Launching that last name at the London Stock Exchange, Westminster said the aim was to "bring more countries into the orbit of free-market economies" [21]. The word "Colonial" went and the institution stayed.

Scots, Irish, and Welsh know what a name can hide: the annexation of their nations by England, renamed "Union". So do those who suffered at the hands of England's Empire, which the classes who grew rich on its extraction renamed "Commonwealth".

On 30 October 2026, the struggle for control of a people's land and what lies in it reached the UN Security Council, with a terminology change added to disguise the impact on the Sahrawi people.

Western Sahara is one of the 17 non-self-governing territories, annexed by Morocco after Spain withdrew in 1975 [22]. Western Sahara Resource Watch, which tracks the trade ship by ship, estimates that about 2 million tonnes of phosphate rock left the territory in 2025, worth around 376.5 million US dollars [23].

In 1991, the UN set up the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, or MINURSO, to prepare a vote for the Sahrawi people on their future, and that vote has yet to be held [22].

Westminster joined the push against that vote. It had backed self-determination for Western Sahara until June 2025, when its Foreign Secretary, David Lammy, went to Rabat and called Morocco's autonomy plan the "most credible" solution, reversing that position [24].

That October, it voted for Security Council Resolution 2797, which made the plan a basis for talks, and its representative, Mr Kariuki, told the Council the text "provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara" [25, 22]. We read that as CAT at work: the term kept while what it stood for is emptied out.

In October 2026, the United States put forward a text that would have renamed the mission MINUSO, striking the word "Referendum", and made Morocco's autonomy plan "the only basis for negotiation" [26]. The United States held the pen, and the pattern keeps leading back to Westminster.

In plain terms, the world's top security body would have taken the Sahrawi people's vote off the table and named the outcome itself: their land stays under Morocco's sovereignty, with a measure of self-rule.

Eleven of the Council's 15 members backed the text, Westminster among them [22]. Any one of the five permanent members can block a text alone, and Russia did [22].

The US ambassador, Mike Waltz, complained that the veto had been used to "preserve the letter R" [22]. That letter stood for the people's vote.

The United States then voted against a Russian text to keep the mission running unchanged, Westminster declined to back it, and with no mandate left the mission ended on 31 October [22, 27].

Morocco still occupies the Western Sahara, 'territory' being the UN General Assembly's own word in 1979 [28], and its Rulers have welcomed the mission's end [22]. What the veto has denied is the UN's legal cover for the colonial act of annexation.

The Sahrawi people's right to choose stands, as UN Secretary-General António Guterres has said [29].

As we read it, this has bought time for every people still under colonial rule, and for the Global South, because a precedent set against one listed territory would have been there to use against the rest.

The UN General Assembly debates the veto on 10 November [30].

Refusing the terminology of colonialism is an act of decolonisation and anti colonialist action every one of us can undertake now.

"Third World."

Someone decided there was a first.

Someone decided there was a ranking.

Someone decided the measure was proximity to themselves.

And then that ranking, invented, imposed, self-serving, became the vocabulary everyone uses, including the people it was invented to subordinate.

That’s how soft power actually works.

Not by forcing you to accept their hierarchy.

By giving you no other language to describe yourself.

The first act of decolonization is refusing the name.

Not because the name is merely offensive.

Because the name is a map.

And the map was drawn by someone who put themselves at the center.

text:
Elon Musk lost a $56 billion pay package to a man who owned 9 Tesla shares. A judge voided the deal, then ordered Tesla to pay that man's lawyers $345 million, after they asked for $5.6 billion.

Then Delaware's Supreme Court gave it all back. By then the package was worth $139 billion. The man with 9 shares got $1.

In the video below, Musk walks on stage right after shareholders voted for his pay a second time: "Hot damn, I love you guys."

In 2018 Tesla's board offered Musk options on 304 million shares, about 9% of the company, if Tesla hit a set of huge targets. It hit every one.

Richard Tornetta, a former heavy metal drummer with 9 shares, sued that same year.

In January 2024 a Delaware judge struck the deal down and called it "unfathomable."

His lawyers asked for $5.6 billion in fees. The judge called that a windfall and gave them $345 million.

In June 2024 shareholders voted for the package again. In December the judge rejected it again.

Musk moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas.

On December 19, 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed it, unanimously. Throwing the deal out, it said, left Musk "uncompensated for his time and efforts over a period of six years." The lawyers' fee was cut by about 80%. Damages: $1.

Musk said he was "vindicated."

9 shares froze the biggest paycheck in history for 7 years. The final bill for the man who started it: $1.

Did the system protect shareholders, or did 9 shares nearly cost Musk $139 billion?

This is no ordinary midterm election; it is a battle that will determine the fate of the United States for the next hundred years.
Tomorrow, when you step into the polling station, the ballot you cast is no ordinary vote. It is a pledge to future generations, a defense of the original intent of the nation’s Constitution, and a final stand for the principle of "one person, one vote"—the bedrock of citizen sovereignty. 2026: The Key to 2028
Whoever holds the House of Representatives and key state legislatures in 2026 will control the path toward 2028. Whoever occupies the White House in 2028 will oversee the 2030 Census. The census is no mere statistical exercise; it is the foundational code for the distribution of power. It dictates the allocation of House seats, electoral votes, and the flow of federal funding for the decade to come.
The Left knows this well. For years, they have used the "headcount" of illegal immigrants to inflate the populations of "blue" states, effectively seizing congressional seats and electoral votes that rightfully belong to "red" states. While the Constitution mandates the counting of "persons," it never intended for individuals who owe no allegiance, lack legal residency, and possess no right to vote to serve as the basis for determining America’s destiny. By including illegal immigrants in the apportionment base, states like California, New York, and Illinois—which are already struggling with population outflows—continue to hold a disproportionate number of seats. This constitutes a systematic dilution of the influence of lawful citizens and a betrayal of our republican system.
A Fair Census: Restoring Authentic Representation
Through a fair census—by excluding illegal immigrants from the apportionment process—blue states will be forced to relinquish the power they have effectively stolen:
• California will lose a significant number of its excess seats, and its political hegemony will be reduced to its true, rightful scale. •  States like New York and Illinois—characterized by high taxes, heavy regulation, and high crime—will continue to bleed population.
•  "Red" states experiencing genuine growth—Texas, Florida, Arizona, North Carolina, Georgia, Idaho, and Utah—will gain congressional seats commensurate with their population growth.
The Sun Belt is expanding, while "blue" states are shrinking. This is not merely a slogan; it is an iron law of demographic migration. Americans are "voting with their feet"—fleeing the tax burdens and chaos of California, as well as the crime and over-regulation of New York, in favor of states that offer jobs, order, and freedom. This trend will become even more pronounced once the "inflated" population counts—driven by illegal immigration—are stripped away. Red states will secure more seats, and blue states will be forced to confront the real-world consequences of their own failed governance.
Meanwhile, the redistricting process will unfold. In states like Indiana, Missouri, North Carolina, and Georgia, maps that were once skewed to favor Democrats will be replaced by more equitable ones. There will be no more artificially drawn "minority-majority districts" designed to lock in a leftist advantage, nor will there be partisan gerrymandering that fragments rural and suburban communities. Fair maps will ensure that the true voice of the American people once again shapes the House of Representatives.
A Permanent Mathematical Advantage
As congressional seats shift from declining blue states to growing red states—and as redistricting further cements these gains—it will become mathematically nearly impossible for the Democrats to regain control of the House, let alone easily secure the Electoral College in presidential elections. The "Blue Wall" is crumbling,

🚨 HUGE news for every Ohio homeowner on Election Day! @VivekGRamaswamy is telling every single Ohio voter that he will deliver the BIGGEST PROPERTY TAX CUT in STATE HISTORY, and he plans to do it on top of PHASING OUT the state INCOME TAX.

This is pure common sense for Ohio families! 👏

The polls are open until 7:30 TONIGHT, and Amy Acton has no plan to deliver either one of those promises.

The person Ohioans choose today will have a direct hand in the size of their property tax bill, how much of their paycheck they keep, and whether the state finally gets serious about Medicaid fraud.

Ramaswamy's plan resets the property tax base to where it stood before the pandemic within the first six months of 2027, then caps how fast it can grow after that. He calls it "the biggest property tax cut in the history of the state of Ohio."

He told ABC 6 in Columbus that he hopes homeowners feel the relief by this time next year.

That promise means the most to the people who have been hit the hardest. Ramaswamy says he has met seniors all over Ohio who feel they have to move out of their homes because they can no longer keep up with the tax bill.

Those are people who paid off their mortgages years ago. 

They did everything right, and rising tax bills are pushing them out of the homes they own.

Ramaswamy also wants Ohio to join Florida, Tennessee, and Texas as a state with no income tax. "You get to keep what you earn," he says. Plenty of Ohio families know someone who now spends half the year in Florida for exactly that reason, and Ohio loses that tax money every time one of them changes their legal address.

Amy Acton's property tax plan is much smaller. She would raise the income limit on the homestead exemption from $41,000 to $50,000.

She would also offer a rebate of up to $1,000 when a property tax bill jumps more than 4% in a single year. To get that rebate, a household would have to earn less than $132,000 and own a home worth $350,000 or less.

A married couple who both work full time can easily earn too much to qualify.

Acton opposes Ramaswamy's plan to phase out the income tax. Republican leaders in the Statehouse have not been impressed with her alternative. Senate Finance Chairman Jerry Cirino said her plan is "a spending spree and a give-away."

Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman pointed out that a funding plan has two sides, revenue and spending, and that Acton only talks about the spending.

Ohio spent $27 billion on Medicaid ten years ago. Today it spends $47 billion, even though the number of people enrolled has barely moved, from about 2.9 million to about 3 million.

Reporting earlier this year found seven buildings in Ohio that housed 288 companies registered with Medicaid, and those companies billed taxpayers more than $250 million over six years.

Ramaswamy has a specific plan to go after that money.

Right now, when Ohio uncovers Medicaid fraud, the state keeps about 35 cents of every dollar it recovers. Ramaswamy wants Washington to let Ohio keep 65 cents instead. His campaign says the plan would return $3.1 billion to Ohio taxpayers through lower premiums, help with co-pays, and support for rural hospitals.

He has also promised to end sanctuary cities in Ohio. He made that pledge on stage with President Trump at a rally last week.

Every city in Ohio should follow the same law, and every Ohio family deserves to know that local officials will work with law enforcement instead of against it.

Lower property taxes, no income tax, and a real fight against the fraud draining the Medicaid budget add up to a clear agenda.

Ramaswamy summed it up on the campaign trail with a line every Ohio voter can measure him against: "Lower costs, bigger paychecks, better schools, safer streets." If he wins today, Ohioans will be able to check his work on their own tax bills by this time next year.

Go vote NOW and make sure 3 of your friends got to the polls today!!

text:
Caleb Wilson is a Bull, taken 4th overall by Chicago in June. He's 20.

Last night in Philly he scored 24 points on 9-17 shooting, 7 rebounds, 4 assists, 4 steals and 4 threes. Chicago lost the game by 19.

He's in the top three of the first rookie rankings the league released this season.

His most defining characteristic in fact has nothing to do with basketball.

Caleb Wilson reads Stoicism every morning. He's been doing that since high school.

It started in an ancient history class (on philosophy) back in Georgia and it's stayed with him.

I think it does make me go about the days in a different way to how I used to before.

He says the reading has changed the way he deals with people.

"You can't control what other people think."

He also builds Lego sets and his all time favourite is a Lamborghini. He listens to country music (mostly Zach Bryan and Tyler Childers). He runs on his own time.

"You can't put all your mental cards in one deck."

Those are the words of a 20 year old who's been in the profession for a matter of weeks.

The ball has always been there with it. At Holy Innocents' Episcopal School in Sandy Springs, GA he averaged 21.6 points, 11.1 rebounds and 5 assists as a senior and led that school to its first state title ever. He was a McDonald's All American and Mr. Georgia Basketball.

He committed to NC in January 2025 (over offers from Kentucky and Ohio State), played in all 24 games and averaged 19.8 points and 9.4 rebounds with a 57.8% field goal percentage. Scored 24 against Kansas and 23 in a three pointer win over Duke. Finished the year as a consensus 2nd team All American and 1st team All ACC.

Then on Feb 10 he broke his left hand and his college season was effectively over.

Chicago picked him 4th overall in the draft all the same.

In his very first summer league game he scored 35 points with seven three pointers. That's the most any rookie has ever scored in a pro debut.

The season ahead is going to be a real test of that philosophy as Chicago are going to lose games and the rookies on a losing team are going to be asked about losing for months on end. He's apparently already done the thinking.

'I've never worked as hard in my life as I did over the summer.'

His college coach was Hubert Davis and Davis described him thus:

"Everything he talks about is about the team."

Wilson put his own ambition down in quite different terms.

'I'm here to make myself a legend and win a bunch of games.'

He is 20 years old, he reads philosophy every morning, and last night he scored 24 points in a game his team lost by 19.

text:
Grading the Unannotated: Insights from the WorkRB Skill Extraction Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026 : https://t.co/6FwPvYbMvp

"arXiv:2611.03525v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 02 Nov 2026
Grading the Unannotated: Insights from the WorkRB Skill Extraction Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026
Warre VeysCorresponding author.TechWolf, 9000 Gent, BelgiumGhent University – imec, 9052 Gent, BelgiumLuis GascoAvature, Barcelona, SpainJens-Joris Decorteworkrb@techwolf.aiTechWolf, 9000 Gent, BelgiumAbstract
Skill extraction benchmarks score models against a small set of human-annotated positives and treat every other skill in the vocabulary as equally wrong. At the scale of ESCO (13,939 skills) this binary view can rewards models that rank the annotated positive high for the wrong reason, and hides predictions that are semantically nonsensical. The WorkRB Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026 replaces this binary protocol with graded relevance: every candidate skill in a model’s ranking window carries a 0 to 4 relevance grade, and the leaderboard scores nDCG@100 against these grades. Since ternary judgements already proved too coarse for objective annotation, relevance is decomposed into a cascade of four simple binary questions (same domain, activity mentioned, right granularity, replacement of a gold positive) that a smaller LLM judge can answer reliably, and the resulting labels are validated with blind human and frontier-model re-annotation. This paper documents the annotation methodology, the construction of the five benchmark datasets, four with vacancy sentences as queries and one with lexically distant skill surface forms, the validation of the LLM cascade, and the insights from the challenge submissions. The field converged on multi-stage retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, whose gains come from clearing nonsense out of the ranking window rather than from finding more positives: at the top of the leaderboard, the graded ordering is uncorrelated with what binary evaluation would have said. The graded labels expose substantially bigger gaps between the top submissions and the baselines than the binary protocol does, and show that the domain of semantic-understanding skill recommenders is still wide open. The clear direction after this challenge is bringing efficiency back: every submitted system we could size spends at least 42×, and typically several hundred times, more parameters than the baselines it beats.Keywords: skill extraction; graded relevance; LLM-as-a-judge; benchmark; skill normalisation; information retrieval
1Introduction
Skill recommenders decide who gets seen at work. The ranking a model returns for a vacancy sentence or a profile feeds crucial applications like hiring shortlists, internal mobility and project staffing, promotion and succession pools, and the learning paths an organisation offers. A skill placed in the top of such a ranking for the wrong reason does not simply cost a point of accuracy: it attaches a requirement to a role that the role does not have, or attaches a capability to a person who was never assessed on it, and both propagate into decisions about that person. Nonsense high in the window is therefore not only a quality problem but a fairness one, and it is precisely the failure that the prevailing evaluation protocol cannot see.Previous skill extraction evaluation frameworks share a blind spot: every unannotated skill is treated as equally wrong. With a vocabulary of 13,939 ESCO skills [8] and only a handful of human annotated positives per sentence, this assumption does not hold. Veys et al. [22] showed that the standard training setup for skill recommenders is prone to lexical shortcuts, potentially ranking skills by surface overlap with the input rather than by meaning, and that binary ranking metrics hide this completely: the annotated positive and the shortcut often coincide, so MAP stays high even when some of the other top predictions are nonsense from an unrelated domain.The remedy proposed there is graded evaluation: instead of positive versus everything-else, distinguish predictions that are perfect, merely plausible, and clearly wrong. Their ternary rubric (Positive, Acceptable, Nonsense) exposed the failure mode but proved too coarse as an annotation target: the Acceptable bucket collapses near-misses, broad umbrella skills, and genuinely additional correct skills into one class. Asking an annotator (human or LLM) for a direct 0 to 4 grade invites inconsistency: assessor agreement is known to degrade as relevance scales grow finer [23, 18], something Section 3.4 measures the same instability for our own judge.This challenge tries to close that gap with an automatic annotation framework built for objectivity. We decompose the graded judgement into a tree of four binary questions, each simple enough to optimise and answer reliably in isolation (Section 2). An LLM judge walks the cascade for every (sentence, skill) candidate pair, producing dense graded relevance labels over the top-2000 retrieval candidates per query.The challenge poses the task of ranking all of ESCO against a free-text query. It runs over five datasets that differ only in what that query is. Four are existing, binary annotated, skill extraction datasets whose queries are vacancy sentences, re-annotated with graded relevance. The fifth targets skill normalisation: its queries are lexically distant surface forms of individual ESCO skills, built from ESCO’s own alternative labels filtered to be lexically far but semantically equivalent (Section 5), and it is annotated for full-vocabulary recommendation in exactly the same way. All five are served through WorkRB, an open benchmark library that normalizes evaluation of AI in the work domain [5], and the challenge allows any technique that produces rankings.
Contributions.
We (1) introduce a binary-cascade annotation framework that turns graded relevance into a sequence of objective yes/no decisions, (2) release graded validation and test annotations for five benchmarks, four established skill extraction datasets and a new skill normalisation dataset, all annotated for the same full-vocabulary recommendation task, (3) validate the LLM-produced labels with blind human and frontier-model re-annotation, and (4) report what the challenge’s 154 valid submissions reveal: a field that converged on multi-stage retrieve-and-rerank pipelines at least 42× larger than the trained baselines, and a top of the leaderboard whose ordering binary evaluation cannot reproduce (Kendall τ=0.06 against binary MAP over the twelve best teams).Read together, these results say something the binary leaderboards of the last few years did not. Semantic skill understanding was not a solved problem going into this challenge: under graded evaluation the strongest, efficient, published skill extractor available off the shelf sits 0.24 nDCG@100 below what a field of motivated participants could reach, a gap the binary protocol reports as a third of that size. It is also not solved coming out of it. What closed the gap was scale and pipeline depth, not a better skill encoder, and the road to an open-source semantic-understanding skill recommender that an organisation could actually deploy, remains open.
2The graded relevance rubric
Figure 1:The annotation cascade, with a worked example on every exit. A pair descends the gates in order and the first “no” fixes its grade, while human gold positives bypass the cascade entirely. The six red skills are real ESCO entries judged against one real House query, and each is placed by its ESCO description rather than its label. design hair style (“design the styles of hair based on the preference of the customer”) shares only the word “design”, the kind of surface overlap a retriever scores highly and the domain gate exists to reject. test materials is engineering work, so it clears the domain gate, but its description covers testing the composition and characteristics of materials, never designing anything or using software. use ICT systems (“select and use ICT systems for a variety of complex tasks”) is true of the job and of thousands of others, an umbrella too broad to be core. design engineering components (“design engineering parts, assemblies, products, or systems”) is correct and genuinely additional, describing the design act itself rather than the drafting tool the gold names. The two grade-4 exits differ only in provenance: use CADD software is the human annotation, and use CAD software is the jury judging a near-paraphrase of it, the two differing only by the drafting suffix. Section 7 turns that last distinction into the submission screen.
Query “Use software for basic mechanical design”human-annotated gold?1. Domainsame domain?2. Activitymentioned or implied?3. Granularityright level to be core?4. Replacementequivalent to a gold?noyesyesyes0 nonsense design hair style1 plausible, not mentioned test materials2 recommendable, not core use ICT systems3 additional and correct design engineering components4 replacement of a gold use CAD software4 human gold use CADD softwarenonononoyesyesDirect graded annotation is unreliable: the difference between “somewhat relevant” and “relevant” is not something two annotators, or two LLM calls, resolve the same way, as Section 3.4 measures against the same judge and referee. Our rubric therefore asks four binary questions in a fixed order, the grade being determined by where the cascade stops (Figure 1):1.Domain. Is the skill in the same broad occupational domain as the sentence? A “no” yields grade 0 (nonsense): the pair will likely never appear in the same job description.
2.Activity. Is the specific activity described by the skill actually mentioned or directly implied? For example, “theoretical knowledge of mechanical equipment” does not imply “operate mechanical equipment”. A “no” yields grade 1 (plausible, but the activity is not there).
3.Granularity. Is the skill at the right granularity to be core to the sentence, neither a generic umbrella nor an incidental sub-step? A “no” yields grade 2 (could be recommended, but not core).
4.Replacement. Is the skill semantically equivalent to one of the existing gold positives? A “no” means the skill is genuinely additional and correct: grade 3. A “yes” means it is (close to) a paraphrase of what a human already annotated: grade 4.Human-annotated gold positives are grade 4 by definition and never reach the judge. Each gate assumes the previous passed, so every prompt operationalises exactly one decision. The judge always sees the skill’s ESCO description alongside its preferred label, since many labels are ambiguous alone (“monitor environment” could be system administration or forestry).The decomposition buys three things: objectivity, since each question has a defensible yes/no answer where a direct 0 to 4 grade does not, diagnosability, since a disagreement localises to a single gate, which is how we iterated on the prompts, and, measurably, accuracy, since on a judge of the size this workload requires walking the gates beats asking the same model for the grade outright (Section 3.4).
3Annotation pipeline

3.1Candidate generation
Judging all 13,939 ESCO skills against every sentence is wasteful, since the bulk of the label matrix is obviously unrelated. We prefilter to the top-2000 candidates per sentence with a BGE-M3 bi-encoder [4] over sentence-to-description similarity. Pooled over all datasets and splits this recovers 96.6% of the human-annotated gold positives (micro recall@2000). Per dataset: the normalisation dataset is fully covered (100% on both splits, trivially so: the prefilter query for these rows is the target concept’s own ESCO description, not the lexically-distant surface form, so the prefilter is never exercised on what makes the dataset hard), Tech reaches 96.2% (validation) and 97.6% (test), House 97.7% and 93.2%, SkillSkape 94.7% and 96.5%, and TechWolf (test only) 96.4%. The misses do not concentrate on one failure mode. Roughly a third come from long, multi-topic job-ad paragraphs carrying up to nine gold skills each, where a single pooled embedding cannot stay close to every skill mentioned. A further quarter fall on generic targets (communication, work independently) that collide with near-duplicate ESCO entries. The remainder are ordinary retrieval misses, some even where a lexical bridge exists: the query java reactjs web-services ranks Java (computer programming) only 3,681st. Skills outside the top-2000 default to grade 0, except should they be a human-annotated gold positive one. In the latter case the pair is released at grade 4.
3.2LLM-as-a-judge cascade
The four gates are answered by an open-weight LLM judge (Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct [15, 16], FP8) served locally on a single Nvidia DGX Spark. Each gate is one call emitting a single boolean, constrained to a one-field JSON object with no rationale, so every prompt operationalises exactly one decision and calibration stays gate-local.The validation release is single-juror. For the test release we hardened the two most subjective gates with a second juror from a different model family (Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it [10]), re-judging gate 3 and, for its survivors, gate 4, on only the pairs the first juror passed through gate 2. A gate passes only if both jurors agree, so the second can demote a grade 3 or 4 but never promote it, firming up the soft upper gates without touching the high-volume lower ones. This costs 46K extra calls (about 1% of first-pass volume) and demoted 6,449 of the 31,557 pairs it re-examined. The test cascade also ships a recalibrated gate-3 prompt, though Section 3.4 shows the resulting labels behave near-identically to the validation configuration under blind review.
3.3Prompt calibration
Prompts were calibrated iteratively against hand-graded pilot pairs. After a first full pass over the validation annotations, we used Claude Opus 4.7 to (1) cluster the most frequent failure cases per gate and (2) interactively probe the local judge to tune the corresponding prompt. After the validation release, a human iteration over the same judge-of-the-judge loop refined the prompts once more before the test set was annotated.Three recurring failure modes drove the concrete prompt changes. At the activity gate, the judge conflated qualified and unqualified activities, failing “manage ICT project” against a sentence mentioning generic “project management” even though the mismatch is one of granularity: the fix strips sector, method, audience and instance qualifiers to a bare verb-noun pair before checking presence, deferring the qualifier judgement to gate 3 where it belongs. The same gate needed a carve-out for job-description phrasings, where “experience with X” and “proficient in X” license the activity X. At the granularity gate, the validation-era prompt defaulted too far toward rejection, treating any skill phrased more generally than the sentence as too broad. The test-era recalibration reframes it as “a filter, not a hurdle” while hardening the opposite direction with an unnamed-specific-instance rule: a generic category mention (“a modern programming language”) never licenses one specific member (Python). Finally, the released cascades drop the one-sentence rationale an early variant asked for, after a pilot showed the boolean-only variant stays within one grade on 95.6% of pairs, the residual disagreements concentrating on 2 to 4 word “section header” inputs where human annotators also disagree.
3.4Human validation of the labels
To validate the released labels, a fixed, stratified manifest of pairs (280 test, 224 validation, per dataset 12 pairs of each grade 1 to 4 and 8 of grade 0) was blindly re-graded under the identical rubric: no cascade label shown, one independent judgement per pair. There are two reviewers: a frontier model from a different family than the cascade judge (Claude Opus 4.8 [2]), covering both splits, and a human expert, covering the 280-pair test manifest.Grades 3 and 4 are reported together throughout this section. The only thing separating them is gate 4, which asks whether the skill is a replacement for one the dataset already carries as a human gold positive: that is a property of the pre-existing annotation rather than of the (sentence, skill) pair, and a blind reviewer cannot see the gold list, so the distinction is not one they are positioned to confirm. Collapsing it leaves the three substantive gates (domain, activity, specificity) as what the validation measures. Gate 4 is not noise: the pairs it promotes draw a higher mean blind grade than the grade-3 pairs it rejects (2.63 versus 2.22 from the human expert, 2.48 versus 2.20 from Opus). It is simply not a distinction this validation can referee.Figure 2:Blind validation of the cascade labels, test manifest. Left: row-normalised confusion matrix (%) between the released cascade grade and the blind Opus reviewer. Middle: the same, against the blind human expert. Both show mass on the diagonal or one cell to its left with a nearly empty upper-right triangle: the disagreement is one-directional for both reviewers, human included. Right: mean blind grade per cascade grade, Opus (both splits) and the human expert (test only). All three curves sit below the identity line, and the human curve is markedly less extreme at grade 1 but has the same overall shape. Grades 3 and 4 are reported together throughout, since grade 4 is defined against the gold-positive list the blind reviewer cannot see.
📷📷Four findings (Figure 2). First, ordering is strongly preserved between the cascade and both reviewers. Quadratic-weighted kappa (QWK), which is chance-corrected agreement that charges a disagreement in proportion to its squared distance on the grade scale, is 0.73 (Opus) and 0.69 (human); Spearman rho, the rank correlation between the two gradings, is 0.82 and 0.69; 93% and 90% of pairs are within one grade and exact agreement is 51% and 59%. Plain Cohen’s kappa (0.36 and 0.43) is the wrong lens for an ordinal scale, punishing a 2-against-3 miss as harshly as a 0-against-3 one. Second, the disagreement is monotonic for both reviewers: the cascade is generous 47% of the time against Opus and 29% against the human, against only 2% and 12% too strict, and grade-0 negatives are highly reliable for both (98% and 85% confirmed). Third, the bias is stable across cascade versions, reproducing near-identically on both splits (kappa 0.73 test against 0.68 validation). Fourth, and this is what closes the validation, the human expert, sharing neither the reviewer’s model family nor its rubric prompt, reproduces the same one-directional generosity, so it is a property of the LLM-cascade approach rather than an artifact of one model grading another. Comparing human and Opus directly is consistent: the human grades higher on the same pair 34% of the time against the reverse 11%, sitting between Opus and the cascade rather than in an independent third direction. The one genuine disagreement, rather than added noise, is at grade 1 (“weak”), graded far less harshly by the human (mean blind grade 1.18 against Opus’s 0.37).What the labels are asked to do is order candidates within a query, not to fix an absolute grade, so an offset that is monotonic and the same for every system leaves that ordering intact and some noise in the exact grade is acceptable. We therefore document the offset rather than re-label. The challenge metric is graded nDCG, and for any binary relevant/irrelevant cut we recommend grade ≥2, where binary agreement with the blind reviewers peaks.The cascade spends up to four calls per pair to reach a grade a single call could be asked for directly, so it is fair to ask what the decomposition buys. We ran the same juror over the same 280-pair test manifest in one call, emitting the whole grade from a prompt that carries the calibrated content of gates 1 to 3 and states the decision order explicitly, and scored both arms against the blind human expert. Everything outside the decomposition is held fixed: same weights, same greedy decoding, same structured output, byte-identical user prompt. Neither arm sees the gold-positive list, so both are judged on the 0 to 3 scale used above.The cascade wins on every agreement measure (Table 1). Against the rationale variant it is +0.068 QWK and −0.125 in mean absolute error (MAE, the average distance in grades between judge and human), with 95% confidence intervals of [+0.006,+0.132] and [−0.204,−0.046] from a paired bootstrap over pairs (10,000 resamples, stratified by cascade grade), and a signed-rank test on the per-pair absolute errors at p=0.005. Against the grade-only variant the MAE gap holds at p=0.002 while the QWK gap is directionally the same but not significant. The one-shot arms also use the middle of the scale less consistently, and which intermediate grade thins out moves with the decoding format, where a cascade grade is a consequence of where a pair stops. The claim we draw is the narrow one: at the model scale this annotation workload requires, decomposing the grade into ordered binary gates produces labels closer to a human expert than asking the same model for the grade directly.Table 1:Cascade versus one-shot direct grading by the same judge, against the blind human expert on the 280-pair test manifest (grades 0 to 3). text:
Big Tech is buying its way into biotech, and a clear pattern is emerging - AI companies started with the promise of designing drugs. Now they're acquiring the infrastructure to actually develop them:
- Isomorphic Labs, spun out of DeepMind, targeted clinical trials in 2025. That slipped to 2026, with no confirmed clinical start date.
- Anthropic acquired Coefficient Bio for a reported $400M, bringing drug discovery expertise in house.
- OpenAI acquired Orchestra Bio to automate the operational complexity of drug development.
- Anthropic acquired Mithril Medicine, a one person biotech coordinating experiments across 11 external labs using Claude.

And the economics explain why. Orchestration offers immediate productivity gains and recurring revenue. Owning successful medicines offers a much bigger prize. Keytruda alone generated $31.7B in 2025.
My take: AI companies are building the operational capabilities of pharma before taking on its biggest financial risks.

That being said, today's AI infrastructure providers could become tomorrow's pharmaceutical companies and I wouldn't be surprised if in 10-15 years these companies have the majority of successful drugs globally

text:
The Wages of Loyalty
Louisiana wasn't supposed to be interesting tonight. No Democrat has won a Senate race here since 2008, Republicans hold every statewide office, and when Rep. Julia Letlow won the GOP runoff in June, the political class all but booked her flight to Washington. Instead she heads into Election Day in a real contest with Jamie Davis. He's a Tensas Parish farmer and one-term police juror, and if he wins he'd be the first Black Louisianan elected to the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction. A poll his campaign paid for last week had them tied at 45. Internal polls flatter whoever pays for them, and most analysts still favor Letlow. But a month ago nobody thought they'd need to hedge at all.
How a safe seat got shaky is no mystery. The answer is Donald Trump, who has spent this cycle grading Republicans on loyalty and sending the party the bill.
Start with the candidate. On June 29, 2024, Letlow signed a nondisclosure agreement with Laidley LLC, a Meta shell company. It gave her confidential details of what became a $50 billion data center in Richland Parish, inside her own district. Within months, her account was buying Meta stock, and Nvidia too, whose chips power Meta's data centers. She didn't report those trades until January, more than a year past the STOCK Act's 45-day deadline. They were among 210 trades she disclosed late. Her office says she didn't direct the trades and didn't know they were happening. Maybe so. But a congresswoman who signed a secrecy pact with a tech giant and never noticed her own portfolio buying that same tech giant leaves voters two explanations, and neither one helps her. She has also turned down a debate with Davis, which is one way to avoid being asked.
Then the map. In April the Supreme Court threw out Louisiana's map with two majority-Black districts in Louisiana v. Callais. Gov. Jeff Landry suspended the congressional primaries in the middle of early voting, and the Legislature rushed through a new map that erased Rep. Cleo Fields' district. Trump praised Landry for "moving so quickly." Black Louisianans, about a third of the state, noticed. They cast 34 percent of the more than 520,000 early ballots. In two decades of early voting here, their share has been higher only four times. Republicans redrew the lines to pick up a House seat, and they may have handed Davis a motivated electorate in the process.
Then the purge. Bill Cassidy voted to convict Trump in 2021, and the state party censured him for it. He spent the next five years trying to earn his way back. He voted to confirm Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pete Hegseth and backed most of the president's agenda. None of it counted. Trump called him "very disloyal" and endorsed Letlow in January over the objections of Senate GOP leadership. Cassidy finished third in May. The party swapped a two-term incumbent with a statewide brand for a first-time statewide candidate with a Meta problem, because the test was never whether she could win. The test was obedience.
South Carolina offers the same lesson in a different key. After Lindsey Graham died in July, Trump urged his sister Darline to run for a full term. She'd been appointed to the seat but had never been elected to anything. Trump carried her past Rep. Ralph Norman in the runoff, and last week a New York Times poll had her barely ahead of Democrat Annie Andrews. South Carolina hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate since the last century.
The pattern isn't subtle. Trump values personal loyalty above every other qualification, and when loyalty and electability collide, electability loses. The psalmist warned against putting your trust in princes. Republican primary voters have been asked to trust one prince's endorsements.

text:
Some interesting thoughts on why $TSLA in China might issue a golden share or carve-out to appease China in the event of a $TSLA $SPCX merger. I think either of these situations is quite likely to allow the merger to go through:

That's exactly why JPMorgan floated it. A carve-out is not an argument against the deal, it's the proposed price of the deal.

But "golden share" and "carve-out" are two very different payments, and the distinction decides whether it works. It also has to satisfy three buyers at once, not just Beijing.

1. Golden share in Tesla China only — cheap, plausible

Scope matters: a Chinese golden share in the merged global parent is a non-starter in Washington. A golden share in the onshore Chinese subsidiary is an established Chinese instrument.

The precedent is ByteDance: since ~2015-16 state-backed entities have taken "~1% 'special management shares'" in the China operating subsidiaries of major platforms, "typically with a board seat and content-veto rights" — in ByteDance's case, the China Internet Investment Fund took ~1% of Beijing ByteDance Technology in April 2021 and installed a director.

Translated to Tesla China, a workable version looks like:

State-linked fund takes 1-5% of Tesla China, 1 seat on a 5-7 person China board
Veto narrowly scoped to: data export out of China, mapping/geographic data, appointment of the China data-security chief, any future change of control of the China entity
Hard IT/data firewall: ChinaCo has its own servers, its own China-specific FSD stack trained on data that never leaves China, no SpaceX personnel, no shared systems with Starshield
Parallel undertakings: Starlink never operates in China, no China-sourced components/personnel in classified SpaceX work

Why it helps China: they get visibility and a kill-switch over the thing they actually fear — data flowing from a Chinese car fleet to a US spy-satellite parent — for essentially no money.

Why Tesla should happily pay it: it costs shareholders almost nothing. ~1% of the China entity, no loss of consolidation, no loss of that disproportionate China FCF.

Why it might still fail: the remedy for Beijing is the red flag for Washington. A CCP-linked director inside any part of a company merged with a classified defence contractor becomes the exhibit in US congressional hearings and a future NDAA fight. It only works if the veto is provably confined to China domestic/data matters, with US-side audit rights — a double firewall. That's negotiable, but it's drafting, not a handshake.

And note a problem with your premise, in China's favour: Beijing already gets most of the economic benefit of Giga Shanghai for free — jobs, tax, exports, 400+ local suppliers — under 100% Tesla ownership. A golden share doesn't add economics, it adds control. So their incentive is to demand the maximum control at the minimum price. They have no reason to be generous.

2. Majority carve-out — helps China a lot, and that's the problem

This is the actual JPMorgan proposal: Tesla's Chinese operations "placed under the majority control of a consortium based in China," holding "more than 50% of the local entity, while Tesla would continue receiving payments through licensing agreements" covering brand, a separated FSD technology, and possible future Optimus agreements — a structure JPMorgan itself compared to the TikTok arrangements, in reverse.

Yes, that genuinely helps China: majority economics and control of Tesla's most efficient plant, technology licensed locally, no US defence owner in charge.

But now price it. JPMorgan puts China at only ~10% of its ~$1.7T Tesla sum-of-the-parts — call it ~$170B. A majority stake is ~$85B+. Three things follow:

If the consortium pays full fair value in cash, shareholders aren't expropriated — Tesla gets ~$85B in, keeps a minority stake plus a high-margin royalty stream. The deal can absolutely be re-cut on that basis.
But then what is SpaceX buying? A Tesla stripped of control of its highest-FCF operation, its China robotaxi market, and its most likely Optimus scale-up site. SPCX holders will not pay the modelled 30-35% premium for that Tesla. The exchange ratio has to be renegotiated, the carve-out proceeds have to be allocated (cash distribution? retained? shares in ChinaCo for Tesla holders?), and a disposal that large likely needs its own shareholder approval on top of the merger vote.
If the consortium does not pay full value — control transferred at a political price — it becomes a forced sale of the crown-jewel plant, and the special committees can't accept it without inviting entire-fairness litigation.

Add execution frictions: Shanghai's land, incentives and tax commitments were granted to Tesla; change of control needs Shanghai's consent. And a Chinese-majority-owned Shanghai plant exporting to Europe and Canada invites exactly the anti-China EV tariff treatment Tesla currently partly avoids.

In other words, majority carve-out converts a merger negotiation into a merger negotiation plus an ~$170B asset sale to a buyer who knows you need their government's permission. That buyer does not bid against itself.

3. So, can a deal be made? Yes — with these odds

Conditional on the committees agreeing terms and, per your earlier assumption, the Tesla vote passing — China-path outcomes:

China outcomeEstimateClean approval, no material remedy~10%Golden share + behavioural/firewall undertakings suffice — deal closes essentially intact~30%Majority carve-out demanded and accepted — deal closes, restructured and repriced~25%Demands unacceptable (majority at a discount, FSD tech transfer, rights reaching beyond China) or slow-walked past the outside date~35%
That last row is not hypothetical behaviour. In Qualcomm/NXP, eight of nine regulators cleared the deal; SAMR repeatedly had Qualcomm withdraw and resubmit, resetting the clock, and when it "chose to remain silent even as the final deadline of July 2018 approached, Qualcomm exited the deal, paying NXP US$2 billion". Intel/Tower died the same way in 2023. Beijing's strongest move is rarely a formal "no" — it's silence a deal with a deadline can't survive, and this deal has a hard one: closing under Trump, before Jan 2029.
Bottom line: you're right that China can be paid — and a scoped golden share in Tesla China is a genuinely cheap, precedented payment that helps Beijing where it actually cares, over data and control, so expect the committees to offer something very like it early rather than wait to have a carve-out imposed. The deal fails on China only if Beijing insists on the expensive version (majority control) or Washington decides the cheap version (a state director inside the fence) is itself unacceptable. The risk isn't that no bargain exists — it's that the bargain has to clear two capitals whose conditions point in opposite directions, inside a two-year window.

text:
Apple tops expectations, gets sold anyway: At first glance, Apple seemed to offer bulls plenty of nutrition. Still, shares retreated 4% in a tech market where "sell first" seems dominant. Participants are worried about margin, which Apple said could narrow to 45% to 46% in the current quarter due to high memory chip prices. Analysts had expected 46.5%. Even beyond that, Apple had a high bar considering its historically lofty valuation. Results beat consensus across the board, with iPhone and services revenue of $57.6 billion and $31.6 billion surpassing estimates of $56.6 billion and $31.5 billion, respectively. Quarterly iPhone sales climbed 15% annually. Earnings per share of $2.10 beat consensus of $1.99. Revenue of $114.5 billion topped the $113.4 billion consensus from FactSet. More tech reports arrive later including Arm Holdings (ARM) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). Both are chip barometers, with AMD's results possibly providing clarity for competitor Nvidia (NVDA) before its earnings later this month. Arm competes with Intel (INTC), shares of which tumbled 29% Friday and another 9% Monday as guidance disappointed. Intel cited issues in the PC market, also served by Arm.
 
Jobs week underway: Besides tech earnings, this week is packed with jobs data. It starts at 10 a.m. ET today with the September Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS), expected to show 7.13 million openings, barely changed from August. The quit rate, also closely watched, is expected to be near 3.05 million, also near August's level. A drop in openings or quits might be seen as a sign of tightening labor conditions, possibly bearish for the economy. Tomorrow morning brings the ADP employment change report for October after September's strong 90,000 gain. Friday's October nonfarm payrolls consensus is moderate at 65,000, though it's the sort of number that might be in the "Goldilocks" range as far as the Federal Reserve is concerned, not showing jobs growth drying up but also not indicating potential wage-propelled inflation. September growth was lackluster at 29,000. The Fed gets October inflation data next week and another jobs report early next month before its December rate decision and several policymakers sounded hawkish recently. Odds of a December hike are 77% according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
 
Seasonals, post-election moves seen as tailwinds: Emerging from last week's sell-off, there are some positive signals for Wall Street assuming election results don't set off new fireworks. First, this is historically a solid time of year for stocks, and October's sell-off could fuel some buy-the-dip sentiment. "Seasonality is in the bulls' favor, as November and December are two of the most bullish months, historically," said Nathan Peterson, director of derivatives research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research (SCFR). "After we get past the midterm elections, there could be a 'buy on the news' response, regardless of the outcome." Also, it's hard to argue that corporate fundamentals aren't generally healthy with S&P 500 earnings per share growth above 29% year-over-year with around two-thirds of S&P firms reporting. And though personal spending remains a concern considering inflation outpacing wage growth in some recent months, the recent drop in borrowing costs might be a tailwind as consumers start their holiday shopping. It is hard to say how long it might take, however, for lower yields to be reflected in mortgages and costs for other big items like cars.

"Can you do it for less?"

Yes. Just not the same work.

Many pricing objections are really scope questions. So when a client pushes back, offer a smaller scope instead of a discount:

"I can work within that budget if we reduce the scope to five pages instead of ten and remove the follow-up call. The full audit with the review call would stay at the original price."

The client still hears yes. You keep your rate. And the trade-off is out in the open, so nobody's left guessing what they gave up.

You can offer fewer pages, fewer calls, a shorter report, no implementation, or a narrower review. A more flexible deadline may be another trade-off.

It's easier still when the smaller option already exists. The image shows a three-option menu for an SEO service. If the standard audit is over budget, the client can pick the starter review, and each option keeps its quoted price.
