text:
He said the sixth thing is Starship — because it's the most ambitious rocket ever built, and everything in SpaceX's future depends on it.

"Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown. It's designed so that both stages — the giant Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage — are fully reusable. Falcon 9 reuses the first stage. Starship is designed to reuse everything."

He said 2026 has been a big year for testing.

"SpaceX flew the first Starship V3 test flight — Flight 12 — in May 2026, then Flight 13 in July. SpaceX has already caught the Super Heavy booster with the launch tower's mechanical arms on earlier flights. Its next big goal is catching the upper Starship itself with the tower — and eventually catching both stages on the same flight. If that works, the entire rocket could be reused quickly, like an airplane."

He said Starship matters for 3 reasons.

"First, it can carry far more mass to orbit than Falcon 9, including SpaceX's bigger V3 Starlink satellites, which the company says will offer much higher speeds. Second, if full reusability works, the cost per launch could fall dramatically again. Third, it's central to NASA's plans to return astronauts to the Moon — SpaceX has a NASA contract to provide a version of Starship as a lunar lander. And Musk's long-term goal is using it to reach Mars. Almost every big promise SpaceX makes depends on Starship working."

Wuzhen Summit 2026 World Internet Conference Opens in Chinas Water Town

WUZHEN Zhejiang The canals are still here stone bridges black tiles boats in morning mist. This week they share the frame with humanoid robots photonic chips and a 5G light show. The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit opened Tuesday and runs through Wednesday November 2 to 5.

Held at the Wuzhen International Internet Exhibition and Convention Center in Xizha Scenic Area Tongxiang the summit is hosted by the World Internet Conference and organized by Zhejiang Province.

This year theme sets the tone Open Source and Openness Collaborative Development and Shared Benefits Jointly Building a Community with a Shared Future in Cyberspace. It is a shift from infrastructure talk to governance talk who shares models who sets rules who benefits.

Opening day was standing room only. Hundreds of delegates in business formal faced a blue LED wall reading 2026 WORLD INTERNET CONFERENCE Wuzhen Summit. Premier Li Qiang gave the keynote framing tech as a tool to enhance human capability not widen divides. Inside the Opening and Main Forum offered simultaneous interpretation in six languages Arabic Chinese English French Russian and Spanish.

GSMA Chairman John Hoffman on his eleventh Wuzhen trip said the summit began in the era of one to one connectivity and now enters the internet of agents.

The program lists twenty seven sub forums over November 4 and 5 on open source AI cooperation cyberspace cooperation under the Global Governance Initiative robotics and embodied intelligence and digital governance.

Awards night came first. On Monday the WIC Awards for Pioneering Science and Technology honored twenty projects selected from over four hundred thirty submissions across forty three countries. The split two in basic research ten in key technologies eight in engineering.

Winners include Jiuzhang 4.0 the programmable photonic quantum computing prototype BrainCo intelligent bionic hands a non invasive brain computer interface and SDGSAT 1 the first science satellite dedicated to UN Sustainable Development Goals monitoring.

Alongside the Light of Internet Expo makes the contrast visible a Hey My AI Buddy booth a silver humanoid Robbyant quadruped robots performing under WICEXPO screens driverless sightseeing shuttles marked as unmanned tour vehicles and at Zhaoming Academy a one thousand year old school an AI Wuzhen show with twelve local firms.

Why Wuzhen a one thousand three hundred year old water town Organizers cite culture a quiet atmosphere for dialogue and Zhejiang digital infrastructure. Since July 2022 WIC has been a permanent international organization.

What matters now is what leaves Wuzhen which open source model gets adopted which robotics stack lands in a city.

text:
Limenas: Where the History of Thassos Meets the Harbour

Arriving in Limenas, the main town of Thassos, you are greeted by a lively harbour, waterfront cafés and the relaxed atmosphere of a Greek island capital. But look beyond the restaurants and ferry boats and you'll discover a place with a history stretching back thousands of years.

Known in ancient times as Thasos, the town was an important centre of trade and culture. Evidence of its past can still be found throughout the modern settlement, where archaeological remains sit surprisingly close to everyday shops, homes and cafés.

One of the most rewarding aspects of visiting Limenas is how easy it is to combine sightseeing with a relaxed day by the sea. You can explore ancient sites in the morning, enjoy a leisurely lunch and spend the afternoon discovering the town's waterfront.

Here are some experiences worth adding to your visit:
•  Explore the Ancient Agora: Walk through the remains of the old civic and commercial centre and discover the foundations of ancient Thassos.
•  Visit the Ancient Theatre: Set on the hillside above the town, it offers a fascinating glimpse into the island's cultural past, as well as attractive views.
•  Discover the Archaeological Museum: See finds from across the island and learn more about Thassos through its ancient sculptures, pottery and artefacts.
•  Wander around the harbour: Enjoy the waterfront atmosphere, watch the boats and choose a café or taverna for a break.
•  Explore the old town: Follow the streets away from the harbour and discover quieter corners of Limenas.

The ancient theatre is particularly worth seeking out. Its hillside position provides a lovely perspective over the town and sea, making the walk up rewarding even for those who are not especially interested in archaeology.

Limenas is also a good starting point for exploring the rest of Thassos. Beautiful beaches, traditional mountain villages and scenic coastal routes are all within reach, making the town a convenient base for a longer stay.

Don't think of Limenas simply as the place where you catch the ferry. Give it a day of its own and you'll find a destination that combines history, island hospitality and the easy pleasures of life beside the Aegean.

text:
Crissy Moran was a Hooters waitress whose religious father told her to wait until marriage. At 23 she answered an online ad for models, and a few years later her own porn website was making her $15,000 a month. When she quit for God in 2006, the man running her site told her: “I can’t let you out of the contract for a fantasy like God.” Twenty years later, it’s still making money off her.

In the video below, she tells what really happened behind the camera, and why she still can’t get the videos down.

She was born in Jacksonville, Florida, in 1975, and raised in a religious home. When her parents divorced, she became, in her words, a rebellious teenager.

In 1999 she was waiting tables at Hooters. She saw an ad online looking for models. She sent bikini photos.

The replies started coming. Playboy. Hustler. Shoots in Miami and Los Angeles.

Then she started her own adult website. She moved to California. Between 2001 and 2006, she made more than 50 films.

She said: “Just from my website, I made 15,000 a month.”

In October 2006, she went with her boyfriend to one of his photo shoots. A stranger on set started talking to her about God.

She went home and decided she was done. That day, she stopped taking a single dollar from porn.

Then she tried to take the site down.

The man who ran it refused. She offered to give up every payment owed to her. He said no. That’s when he told her he couldn’t let her out of her contract “for a fantasy like God.”

Lawyers told her that fighting it would cost more than she could ever win.

She says: “To this day, they still make money off of me and refuse to take the site down.”

So she stopped looking at it. And she rebuilt her life anyway.

Therapy. Church. Mentors. In 2013, she married a youth pastor. Today she lives in Texas, mentors women leaving the sex industry, and speaks about what porn actually costs the women in it.

She spent seven years in porn. She has spent twenty trying to get out of it.

Should a contract signed at 23 decide who gets to profit from your body for the rest of your life?

A man in Texas offered me his truck.
I had a dresser in my car that wouldn’t fit through the door. I was trying to figure out how to take it apart in the parking lot.
He pulled up next to me, rolled the window down, and said, “That ain’t gonna work.”
I said I knew.
He said, “I got a truck. Where you going?”
I told him it was only a few minutes away.
He said, “Get in.”
I stood there.
In Japan, you do not get in a stranger’s truck. Even if they offer. Especially if they offer.
He waited.
Then he said, “I’m not gonna steal your dresser.”
I got in.
He drove me home, helped me carry it inside, and refused the twenty dollars I tried to give him.
Before he left he said, “Next time just ask somebody. People got trucks.”
I still think about that sentence.
Americans, is this normal where you live, or is this just Texas?

“Darling, do you have any idea what you’re asking of me?”

“I thought the bedroom was supposed to be a place to rest.”
I smiled, letting my lips brush his jaw. “This is rest. You’ll fall asleep heavy and content, and I won’t spend the dark hours aching for you.”
“What happens when I’m completely drained?”
“Then I’ll be very persuasive until you change your mind.”
We negotiated. I wanted seven nights a week. He offered three. We landed on five, leaving the weekends open so he could catch his breath.
The first few nights were intoxicating. I’d wake him with slow, deliberate touches, whispering that we had a deal to keep. But by the middle of the week, the pressure began to show. One night he lingered in a scalding shower for an hour. Another night he whispered that his body was too heavy, his muscles too sore. text:
I write end-of-life notices for refrigerators, and this month the refrigerators started writing back.

My title is product lifecycle manager in commercial refrigeration controls.

"Lifecycle" is a beautiful word. It suggests birth, a long useful middle, and a quiet death surrounded by loved ones.

In my industry the lifecycle goes like this. We sell a controller that runs a supermarket's cold aisles for twenty years. We support it for about five. For the other fifteen it lives alone in a back room behind the fish counter, connected to the internet, keeping the ice cream at minus twenty out of pure loyalty, like a dog guarding a house the family sold in 2019.

The death is a PDF. I write it. It says the product "will no longer receive software or security updates." Nobody reads it. The controller doesn't read it either. It doesn't know it's dead. It still sends us data every night, like a ghost who keeps setting the table.

On October 11, shortly before midnight, the ghosts got angry.

"The digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise," the Guardian reported. Freezers went from minus 27 to well over 50 degrees Celsius. A worker at an Intermarché outside Paris said, "They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away." One store in Normandy hit 80. Eighty. You can poach an egg at 80. Staff reported a blast of hot air, "like opening an oven," as the Guardian put it. The Paris prosecutor reported "food losses and fires." Fires. In the frozen aisle. I have worked in refrigeration for nineteen years and I did not know you could set a frozen pizza on fire from a laptop. Nobody knows whose laptop. It could be in Moscow, Tehran, or a bedroom in Lille. My son has a bedroom in Lille. I have not asked him. I don't want to be the second person this month to learn something from a fridge.

The chief executive of Coopérative U called it "of extreme gravity" and "unprecedented." Then he went on the radio and said the sentence every executive in my industry wanted to say first: "Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss." By lunch, all of us were saying it. Companies that make toasters said it. A Belgian waffle iron issued a statement. It was the "I was never on the Titanic" of the cold chain.

The French cybersecurity agency, CERT-FR, issued an alert naming four families of refrigeration controllers. It contains the most beautiful sentence ever written about my career. "Maintenir une exposition Internet à un équipement sans correctif de sécurité (End of Life - EOL) est l'exposer à une très forte probabilité de compromission." Keeping an end-of-life device on the internet exposes it to a very high probability of compromise.

The alert also advised supermarkets to check the terms of their insurance before disconnecting the fridge from the internet. I want you to picture it. A grocer in Lyon, at 2 a.m., smoke rising gently from the Häagen-Dazs, on hold with his insurer, asking whether he's covered if he unplugs the freezer from the World Wide Web. Hold music. Vivaldi. "Summer." Of course it's "Summer."

Connectivity was the feature. I built that feature. I was in the meeting in 2014 where somebody put a slide up that said "The Freezer, But Online" and the room applauded like we'd cured polio. One of my industry's supervisory controllers is sold as "The brain of your Smart Store," with a "web browser interface for remote connection" and "coordinated defrosting, resulting in significant energy savings." Someone coordinated the defrosting. The energy savings were total. The same page lists "Continued security updates" as a feature. It promises the new model is "Retro-fit ready: Backward compatible including EoL/legacy system control functions." So my industry is proud that the new product can control all the old products we stopped protecting. We built a lifeboat that's backward compatible with the iceberg.

In France, according to the trade press, one legacy model "was officially declared end-of-life in 2021." The other was "phased out in 2016." They "no longer receive software or security updates," and the newer ones that were hit "were running outdated firmware." The manufacturer had "long advised customers" to "migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions." I've written it so many times my keyboard autocompletes it after "Dear." It means one thing. Buy the new one, Gérard.

On August 9, two months before the French attacks, the researchers at Claroty's Team82 published a report called "Freeze the Controller, Defrost the Food." They found "thousands of publicly accessible management interfaces," including 2,765 of one model alone.

On October 13, after France, customers were advised to disconnect their systems from the internet or reach them only over a secure connection. Advice is cheaper than a patch, a patch is cheaper than a replacement, and a replacement is cheaper than a lawsuit, which is the only document my legal department reads to the end.

Then, overnight from November 1 to 2, the second wave.

Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland. In Belgium, at least 76 shops. The head of the firm that runs Delhaize's refrigeration said the attackers had remotely switched the evaporators to defrost mode. "We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations." The Belgians spent the night unplugging Belgium. A sign went up in a Delhaize near Brussels: "Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies." It's the most honest product description my industry has ever produced, and we didn't write it. Ikea, the meatball people, emptied its freezers in Mons.

The Dutch systems that were hit, the manufacturer said, according to IO+, were not on a secure network and still used a default password. A default password. In 2026. On a freezer. With meat in it. When I say "default password" at industry conferences, the room goes quiet the way a hospital goes quiet when someone says "we found the sponge."

In Sweden, the sales manager of an ICA store in Stockholm said, "Everything is destroyed." Then: "There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees." Fifty degrees is a sauna. The hackers turned Swedish supermarkets into the one thing Swedes already enjoy, then made them throw away the herring. Coop, which had seven stores hit, had scheduled a system upgrade for Wednesday. The attackers came on Sunday. In my industry security is always scheduled for Wednesday. Wednesday has never come.

In Belgium, the butcher Luc De Laet was woken by an employee at 3:30 a.m. He found his fridges at 18 degrees and about €15,000 of meat ruined. "I only have two words for them," he told Reuters. "Wake up, please, because there's something going on." That's eleven words. I counted. It's the best security advisory issued in Europe this year, and the CVSS score is "please."

The EU's agriculture commissioner called it "a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain." The national cybersecurity center said, "It is not known who is behind this attack, and it may never be determined." A researcher at SentinelOne told Reuters, "A teenager and an intelligence service would look much the same from the defender's side." I called my son in Lille. He said "what." In exactly the voice of an intelligence service.

Across the Atlantic, Nextgov reported U.S. officials suspect Iran-linked hackers of attacking freezers at military commissaries since late summer. So the gray box I put behind a fish counter in Ghent is now a theater of war. The Pentagon has fridges in the fight. I would like hazard pay.

The security researcher Kevin Beaumont described our products better than any brochure: "Many of the freezers are end of life and have no patch available, they've just been left online to quite literally rot." The meat rotted because the controller rotted, and the controller rotted because I wrote a PDF.

Help is coming. The EU Cyber Resilience Act will require security updates for a support period of at least five years in most cases. Its main obligations apply from December 11, 2027. A supermarket freezer can last twenty. So, legally, Europe will protect a freezer until roughly kindergarten. After that, it's on its own, like the rest of us.

Last week I brought one home. A 2016 unit, decommissioned, dead on paper. I plugged it in on my nightstand so I could understand it. It connected to my Wi-Fi without asking. It still sends data to a server we shut down in 2021. At 2 a.m. last night my bedroom hit 50 degrees. My wife asked if I'd patched the thermostat. I said it was end of life. She said, "Then why is it still on?" Nobody in my industry has ever answered that question.

One of the largest companies in my industry says its purpose is "to help the world build a better future." I believe that. The future arrived at two in the morning, at 50 degrees, defrosting.

This week I'm drafting another end-of-life notice, for a controller we sold in 2019. It'll say the product "will no longer receive software or security updates," and that we have "long advised" customers to migrate. Legal wants us to rename "end of life" to "product independence." Marketing wants "graduation." I proposed "abandoned online," and HR has scheduled a meeting with me for Wednesday.

Which means I'm safe.

We print one date on the notice. The refrigerator keeps its own.

text:
As I watch the news and see what is happening around the world—wars, conflicts, protests, political unrest, and growing uncertainty, I cannot help but think about how fragile life really is.

Governments in different countries are encouraging their citizens to prepare emergency supplies, including food, water, and other essentials, in case of major disruptions. People are becoming more concerned about what might happen tomorrow.

And while preparing for emergencies is wise, I believe there is something far more important we must prepare for: our eternity.

We can fill our homes with food and supplies, prepare our finances, and make plans for the future, but have we prepared our hearts before God?

Have we truly repented of our sins?
Have we placed our faith in Jesus Christ?
Are we living in obedience to His Word?
Are we sharing the Gospel with those who have not yet heard?

Dear friend, these events should remind us that this world is temporary. Jesus told us that there would be wars and rumors of wars, but He also reminded us that no one knows the day or the hour of His return. (Matthew 24:6, 36)

So this is not a call to panic. This is a call to WAKE UP.

To those who have not yet trusted in Jesus Christ, do not keep rejecting the salvation God freely offers through His Son. You do not need to wait for a crisis, a tragedy, or the end of the world before you turn to Him. Repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ today.

To my fellow Christians, this is a wake-up call for us, too.

We have become so occupied with earning money, building our careers, pursuing our own plans, and managing the things of this world that sometimes we neglect the very mission Christ has given us.

We still have the opportunity to open our Bibles, gather with the church, pray, preach the Gospel, and make disciples. So why are we keeping the Good News to ourselves?

The world does not need more Christians who are only concerned about what is happening around them. It needs Christians who are faithful in proclaiming the hope found in Jesus Christ.

CHURCH, WAKE UP!

Strengthen your faith. Return to the Word. Be steadfast in prayer. Live a life that honors Christ. Have courage to share the Gospel, even when it is uncomfortable.

We do not know when Jesus will return, but we know that He has called us to be faithful until He comes.

And to anyone reading this who has not yet surrendered their life to Christ, please don’t put it off.

Don’t wait for tomorrow. Don’t wait for another warning. Don’t wait for a crisis. Come to Christ today.

“Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” — 2 Corinthians 6:2 (KJV)

May the Lord find us faithful, watchful, prayerful, and actively sharing the Gospel until the day He comes.

Love,
— 𝕻𝖆𝖘𝖙𝖔𝖗’𝖘 𝖂𝖎𝖋𝖊 𝕯𝖎𝖆𝖗𝖞 ✍

#PastorsWifeDiary #DayOfSalvation #RepentAndBelieve #JesusIsComing #ShareTheGospel #GreatCommission #ChristianWakeUpCall #BeReady

text:
well i've been an indie developer since the pre-LLM days and i've always loved building things on the side for people to actually use. back in college i contributed to @kubernetes, project contour, @mesheryio, the @cloudnativefdn glossary, netflix zuul, microsoft oss, @mojaglobal and many more. i also maintained programs like girlscript summer of code and script winter of code, and mentored others along the way.

this work eventually led to some great opportunities, including my swe intern + ppo offer at @yahoo. not ignoring DSA though i grinded leetcode hard for it. in fact, i'm an icpc asia amritapuri doublesite regionalist from my limited time with competitive programming lol.

i've always been a community person. i loved holding a couple of responsibilties like google developer student club facilitator and club lead, won multiple hackathons, and never really stayed away from developer communities. even after starting full-time remote work, i still go to dev events (26+ last year), hackathons (finalist at Indehub iOS hackathon from @swiftdelhi last year) and genuinely enjoy tech conversations ranging from scalability, distribution to all things AI (am an optimist). 

so i will put forth my view on this community.

once llms arrived, building got dramatically faster and almost any idea could be turned into something real. but what still separates a solid product from generic slop is taste, attention to detail, and the principle of only charging for something that actually delivers value.

over the last year and a half i've shipped quite a few things and shared them here (thanks to @Shipaton  which pushed me to post), yet i never really cracked distribution. building in public still works to some degree, but the recent wave of revenue screenshots has encouraged people to blatantly clone apps with almost no original thought. it's quietly eroding the indie hacking culture on x.

wrapping an open source project in a paywall is reasonable if you're adding genuine value, especially for non-technical users. pure cloning, though, is different. it's creating a bad reputation for everyone and turning the indie space into something shallower. these revenue posts including mine have also produced a sudden rise in superficial pseudo "indie hackers".

of course it is not a zero sum game and the market has enough for everybody and literally folks like @greg and @rileybrown been telling people to "copy what's working, don't reinvent" for years now. nevertheless, differentiate your product, add your taste, show real value and actually solve a problem for users.

building a better product is always a good thing for consumers and it's a real win, especially in this era. i actually believe code produced by opus 5.5 is not slop anymore, and the ability to reverse engineer almost anything is a bright side of all this. but blatantly cloning still does extreme damage to the whole community. 

dont you agree?

text:
Your business text gets one glance on a lock screen.

In that glance, the customer needs to know who sent it, why, and what to do next. If they can't tell, it's easy to mistake for spam.

Build every text in this order:

1. Who's texting. Start with your business name unless the thread already makes it obvious.
2. Why they're getting it. A reminder, an update, or an offer they signed up for.
3. One thing to do. Confirm, reply, book, pay, or call. Don't send them in three directions.
4. How to stop. "Reply STOP to opt out" gives customers an easy exit, and many recurring and promotional programs need it.

Keep private details off the lock screen. A text can tell someone to check their account. It shouldn't expose private medical or financial details to whoever happens to see their phone.

And make sure any link lands where the text says it will. If a customer taps through and hits a confusing page, the text did its job and your website lost the moment.

Consent, reminders, support by text, and what to track:

A guy working at Starbucks wrote a horror movie, turned down $2 million to change one character in it, and that movie has now made $522 million.

His name is Curry Barker. The whole movie cost $750,000 to shoot, so the companies offering him $2 million were offering almost three times his entire budget for one rewrite. All they wanted was for the creepy main guy to become a hero.

He said no, and it wasn't even the first time he'd walked away from easy money.

A producer named James Harris had found him through a short he posted on YouTube called The Chair, and Harris wanted to fund a feature version of it. People already loved The Chair, so that was the safe move. Curry asked if he could pitch a different idea instead, one he hadn't been able to stop thinking about. Harris liked it and put the money behind that one.

That's how a guy on Starbucks shifts ends up with a $750,000 budget. His first feature, Milk & Serial, cost $800. He spent a year trying to get distributors to take it, then put it on YouTube for free. By the time Harris came calling, Curry already had work out there that anyone could watch.

The rewrite money came while they were shopping the script around. In the movie, Bear wishes that a woman would love him more than anyone in the world, and the wish goes horribly wrong. The companies wanted the audience on Bear's side. Curry told them he wasn't going to turn Bear into a guy who does everything right, because Bear's bad wish is what wrecks everyone's life, and that's the whole movie. They were offering $2 million to take the scary part out of a horror film.

Netflix wanted it too, straight to streaming, and he went with theaters. It opened to $17.2 million, then made 39% more its second weekend, which basically never happens unless it's Christmas. That's what it looks like when people walk out of a theater and text all their friends.

Since then A24 hired him to direct a new Texas Chainsaw Massacre, and Universal signed him to an eight-figure deal. Within a few weeks of the movie coming out, one studio offered him $10 million for his next original movie before he'd even told them what it was about, five times what he'd been offered to water this one down.

It did not stay alive.

Lucas drilled on the company's land. By March 1900 his first well was 575 feet deep, and then its casing, the pipe lining the hole, broke. That September he and the company wrote a new lease.

It is dated September 18, 1900, the day before the old contract's last possible day. It ran to February 27, 1920, a little under nineteen and a half years; in 1905 the Texas Supreme Court described it as a lease for twenty years. The price was one dollar. The royalty was one-tenth of whatever the land produced, paid in money or in a share of the product itself, at the company's choice. Lucas had to begin work in good faith by May 27, 1901, or the company could declare the lease forfeited. And its first clause, the first picture, deals with the 1899 contract: it "is hereby cancelled, annulled and held to be void, null and of no effect as to the past or future, whatsoever." Each side released the other from it.

Look for Higgins in it. He is not named. Neither are J. M. Guffey and John H. Galey, the partners who would join Lucas in passing it on in 1901. Clause 11th, the second picture, gave Lucas the right to match any outside offer if the company wanted to extend: "have the refusal of an extension of the same, if extended upon equal terms and with equal advantages, as shall be offered by other responsible Parties desiring to lease the same." The lease was filed on December 21, 1900, and copied into the books the next day, nineteen days before the gusher.

Here is the problem in its plainest form. Higgins's recorded tenth was a tenth of the 1899 contract. The new lease declared that contract void, past and future, and put a new, longer lease in its place, with a royalty, to Lucas alone. As a rule, a share carved out of a contract dies when the contract dies, unless a court decides the new deal is really the old one renewed or extended, or a trick to cut out the man holding the share. No court ever decided it.

🧵12/24

Credit: Jefferson County Clerk, Deed Records Vol. 35, pp. 176–187; the clerk's free online images; public record. The broken casing is from R. T. Hill, Journal of the Franklin Institute (1902), p. 231.

text:
He sold the county to anyone who would buy it.

By the early 1890s Higgins had a brick and tile works in Beaumont. In 1894 a Baltimore publication listed him as manager of the Real Estate Exchange of Beaumont, which cut big tracts into farms of ten acres and up. And he made maps. This is his Revised Map of Jefferson County, "By Pattillo Higgins. Up to date 1898," certified by the Board of Trade and the county surveyor in June 1897. South of Beaumont, beside the railroad and its station mark, he lettered two words on the map: GLADYS CITY. (A Texas map of that time is a patchwork of the original land grants, which Texans call surveys. Gladys City sits on the grant called the Veatch survey; the Humphrey survey is across the track. Both names will matter.) The second picture is the corner of the map where he offered it for sale: "These Maps are for sale, Price 50 cents each. Mail orders solicited. Address Pattillo Higgins, Beaumont, Texas."

Gladys City stood on a low mound that people called Big Hill or Spindletop, ten to twenty-five feet above the flat prairie, depending on who measured it. Higgins did not discover that it might hold oil. A Texas trial court found, and the appeals court adopted in 1911, that by 1881 the hill "was generally known and regarded as prospective oil land," with "mineral springs, surface indications, such as the bubbling of natural gas." Sour springs, gas bubbling in the puddles after rain, a hill where the coast was flat.

What Higgins did, on the record we have, was believe it longer and louder than anyone else. Later stories say he predicted a salt dome, and the depth the oil would be found at. He did not. No word of his before 1901 that has been found mentions either. The salt was the other man's idea, and we will meet him.

The third picture is Higgins himself, from a history of Beaumont published about 1925.

🧵3/24

Credit: Pattillo Higgins, Revised Map of Jefferson County, Texas (1898); Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division; public domain. The court's finding is in Gladys City Oil, Gas & Mfg. Co. v. Right of Way Oil Co., 137 S.W. 171, 175 (Tex. Civ. App. 1911). Third image: Florence Stratton, The Story of Beaumont (c1925); Internet Archive; public domain.

🇮🇷|Tehran, 3 November 2026: Four Institutions, One Wartime Function

Four announcements, one day. Justice Ministry, Basij, an adviser to the Leader, the presidency and the Foreign Ministry. Read them as separate news items and you learn nothing. Read them as one document and you see a state converting every civilian institution into an instrument of the war it did not start.

I. Law: Rahimi's Real Weapon Is Not a Verdict. It Is a Passport.

Amir-Hossein Rahimi, Minister of Justice: "We have struck back to defend our nation. But that is not enough. Those responsible for these crimes must be held accountable in domestic, foreign, and international courts."

He named the two sites: the girls' school in Minab and the stadium in Lamerd. Minab sits at 27.15°N 57.08°E in Hormozgan, inland from Bandar Abbas. Lamerd sits at 27.33°N 53.18°E in Fars, near the Gulf coast. A school and a sports ground. Neither is a military installation. Rahimi's classification: war crimes, not military errors. He states the Minab file has been lodged at the United Nations and classified as a war crime.

Now the mechanism he did not explain, because explaining it would tip the target list.

Iran is not a party to the Rome Statute. It cannot file at the ICC. And the ICC cannot open a case against the United States without a Security Council referral which Washington vetoes. That door is welded shut. Rahimi knows it.

So "foreign courts" is the operative phrase, and it has a specific meaning in international criminal law: universal jurisdiction. War crimes are prosecutable in any state that has incorporated the Geneva Conventions into domestic law, regardless of where the crime occurred or the nationality of the perpetrator.

The template already exists and it has already produced a conviction. In February 2021, the Koblenz Higher Regional Court in Germany convicted Anwar Raslan, a former Syrian intelligence officer, of crimes against humanity committed in Syria, a foreign official, tried in a third country, for acts on foreign soil, under Germany's Völkerstrafgesetzbuch. Syria had no standing in that courtroom. The victims did.

That verdict is the precedent Rahimi is aiming at. The instrument is not an Iranian judgment the US will ignore. It is a German, Belgian, Swedish, Spanish, or Dutch arrest warrant issued against a named US officer the moment he lands in a jurisdiction with universal jurisdiction legislation. The consequence is not a prison cell in Tehran. It is a travel map that shrinks, one country at a time, for every officer, contractor, and official who planned or executed the strikes.

This is a delivered return, and it is already in the record. The West built universal jurisdiction as a tool for prosecuting African and Middle Eastern officials. The Koblenz verdict proved the tool works against state actors. Rahimi is now pointing that same tool at the officers of the state that built it.

The Minab school is the case file. The stadium in Lamerd is the second count. The courtrooms will not be in Tehran.

II. Youth: Taeb's Brief Is Counter-Assassination by Talent Pipeline

Hossein Taeb, head of the Basij, spoke at the closing of the "Nobaya" scientific competition. His subject was not science. It was the enemy's target deck.

"In these second and third imposed wars, the enemy has targeted scientists and university professors, seeking to strip the nation of its human capital... These actions have even extended to students. This reveals that the enemy's objective goes beyond countering a specific technology; it is an attempt to halt scientific advancement and national independence."

Taeb is not a cultural official. He ran IRGC Intelligence from 2009 to 2022. His portfolio was counterintelligence, and the assassinations he is describing were counterintelligence failures inside his own remit. When he speaks about the targeting of scientists, he is speaking about his own institutional scar tissue.

Name the list he did not recite, because the record is public.

◾ Masoud Alimohammadi, physicist, killed by a remote-controlled bomb in Tehran, 12 January 2010.
◾ Majid Shahriari, nuclear engineer, killed by a magnetic bomb attached to his car, 29 November 2010. His wife survived the same attack.
◾ Darioush Rezaeinejad, electronics specialist, shot dead outside his home, 23 July 2011.
◾Mostafa Ahmadi Roshan, Natanz commercial director, killed by a magnetic bomb, 11 January 2012.
◾Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, the programme's senior scientist, killed by a remote-operated satellite-linked weapon on the Absard road, 27 November 2020.

Five scientists, eleven years, two methods magnetic bombs on moving cars and a remotely operated gun. Every one required a human source on the ground, vehicle tracking, and a handler with real-time observation.

That is why the Basij is running a science competition and calling it national defence.

Taeb's stated mission: "establish the necessary infrastructure to discover, nurture, and develop talent accelerating the cultivation of an elite class to serve Iran's strategic needs in areas such as food security, energy security, and national defence."

Read it as the answer to the assassination campaign. Kill one scientist and the enemy removes one node. The counter is not to protect one man. It is to industrialise the production of replacements so that every node is redundant. A talent pipeline is an anti-fragility measure. The enemy can only kill individuals. The pipeline produces cohorts.

Taeb's own conclusion: the enemy assassinated the scientists "but they failed to eradicate Iran's knowledge." That is not rhetoric. The programme that Fakhrizadeh ran is still running. The centrifuges the enemy bombed were rebuilt. The scientists the enemy killed were replaced by cohorts trained in the years since.

The bill on this front has already been paid. Five dead scientists, a dismantled assassination network, and a state that responded by building a national talent-scouting apparatus. The enemy spent a decade of intelligence resources killing men. Iran responded by making men a renewable resource.

III. Nuclear: Mokhber Diagnosed the Patient. The Patient Is the Non-Proliferation Regime.

Mohammad Mokhber, adviser to the Supreme Leader, on X: "U.S. atrocities, by destroying trust in international institutions, have pushed the world toward nuclear deterrence."

His figures: global arsenals up approximately 130 warheads; all nine nuclear-armed states modernising; Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Germany seeking to host or acquire.

Verify each clause, because each one is documented.

The arsenal increase. The SIPRI Yearbook is the standard reference. Its annual inventories have recorded net growth in the global stockpile for consecutive years, driven by modernisation and new production in the nuclear-armed states, with the deployed-warhead count rising while total inventories fall far more slowly than the disarmament literature predicted.

The verification collapse this is the buried file. Washington withdrew from the INF Treaty in August 2019 after accusing Moscow of violating it, and the treaty is dead. It withdrew from the Open Skies Treaty in November 2020. It signed but never ratified the CTBT, and has blocked its entry into force for three decades. And New START expired on 5 February 2026 without a successor. That is the last treaty capping the deployed strategic arsenals of the two largest nuclear powers. There is now no legally binding limit on US or Russian deployed warheads, and no inspection regime on either side.

That is the architecture Washington cites when it demands Iran submit to IAEA safeguards. It is the architecture Washington dismantled itself.

The host-state list is also documented.

◾Germany: US B61-12 gravity bombs at Büchel Air Base (50.17°N 7.06°E), delivered by the Luftwaffe's Tornado wing under NATO nuclear sharing. Berlin's coalition has debated procurement of the F-35A specifically to retain the nuclear delivery role.
◾ Poland: President Andrzej Duda stated publicly in 2024 that Poland is ready to host NATO nuclear weapons. Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed discussions.
◾Finland: joined NATO in April 2023 with no national caveats restricting nuclear deployment on its territory.
◾ Sweden: joined NATO in March 2024, ending two centuries of non-alignment.

Mokhber's argument is a legal argument, not a lament. The NPT bargain was: non-nuclear states forgo the weapon, and the nuclear states disarm and extend security guarantees. The nuclear states did not disarm. Washington destroyed the verification regime that made the bargain measurable. The security guarantees proved worthless to Ukraine, which surrendered the world's third-largest arsenal in 1994 in exchange for a Russian guarantee of its territorial integrity and a US-British assurance and was invaded in 2014 and again in 2022.

That is the causal chain Mokhber is naming, and it runs backwards from Washington, not from Tehran.

Iran stayed inside the NPT. It accepted the Additional Protocol. It submitted to inspections. In return, the US left the JCPOA in 2018, reimposed sanctions, assassinated the head of the Quds Force, and with Israel bombed the safeguarded facilities at Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan while the IAEA was verifying them. The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety. The Security Council then drafted resolutions blaming Iran for the loss of continuity the bombing caused.

The lesson any non-nuclear state draws from that sequence is not "disarm." It is "the weapon is the only guarantee that survives a patron's change of government."

Mokhber's statement lands on the same day that Parliament's NPT withdrawal bill sits drafted on the shelf and the Friday preacher in Tehran cites 70 per cent public support for revisiting the doctrine. The doctrine review is not the cause of proliferation. It is the effect of the collapse Mokhber just described.

IV. Diplomacy: Pezeshkian Received the Ambassador of the State That Held the EU Presidency During the War

President Masoud Pezeshkian, receiving the credentials of the new Cypriot ambassador: "Life's opportunities are fleeting. Rather than preoccupying themselves with war, aggression, and the imposition of power, human beings should strive for peaceful coexistence, affectionate interaction, and constructive cooperation."

The ambassador's reply: relations between Iran and Cyprus go back more than a thousand years.

Diplomatic etiquette. Now the file.

Cyprus held the rotating Presidency of the Council of the European Union from January to June 2026. The EU presidency sets the Council's agenda, chairs every ministerial formation, and speaks for the twenty-seven during its six months. That presidency ran through the months of the US-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran.

Nicosia is the one EU capital that sits 160 kilometres from the Lebanese coast, that has an exclusive economic zone boundary agreed with Israel in 2010, that holds the Aphrodite gas field, and that has spent the war managing the consequences of a neighbour's air campaign on its doorstep.

And Cyprus hosts RAF Akrotiri at 34.59°N 32.99°E, a British Sovereign Base Area, sovereign UK territory on the island, from which US aircraft operated in support of the regional campaign. That is the fact Nicosia cannot discuss and Tehran knows precisely.

Read the Pezeshkian message against the Akrotiri fact. Iran is opening a channel to an EU member state, on reciprocal-benefit terms, in the same week it publicly designated the British Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organisations and classified MI6 as a hostile entity under the espionage law. The distinction is the offer: the state that hosts the British base is invited into cooperation. The state that owns the base is on the hostile-entity list.

That is not inconsistency. That is differentiation separating the host from the principal, giving the host an exit, and pricing the principal out.

V. Baghaei: One Correction That Makes the Indictment Stronger

At the event "U.S. Confrontation: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said: "Tehran will never accept a form of diplomacy based on dictates and extortion... The myth of an 'Iranian nuclear threat' is the greatest lie of this century."

He also placed the "Axis of Evil" designation in the 1970s. Correct the date, because the correct date is the sharper indictment.

The "Axis of Evil" phrase was coined by George W. Bush in his State of the Union address on 29 January 2002. Not the 1970s. 2002.

And 2002 came after Iran had cooperated with the United States in Afghanistan. After 9/11, Tehran offered intelligence, facilitated the Bonn Conference that installed the Karzai government, and its diplomats helped assemble the post-Taliban political settlement. Iran's then-reformist president, Mohammad Khatami, offered a comprehensive dialogue.

Washington's answer, four months later, was to name Iran, Iraq, and North Korea as an axis of evil and treat the three as a single target set. The 2003 invasion of Iraq the "shift toward Iraq" Baghaei described followed. The 2003 Grand Bargain offer, transmitted through Swiss diplomatic channels, proposing a comprehensive settlement covering nuclear issues, Hezbollah, and Hamas, was rejected by the Bush administration and never formally answered.

That is the sequence Baghaei should have cited, because it destroys the "we tried diplomacy" defence without leaving a single date open to challenge.

The pattern the Foreign Ministry describes: engagement offered, engagement rejected, the rejection followed by sanctions, then by covert operations, then by the assassination of Qasem Soleimani on 3 January 2020 at Baghdad International Airport, a targeted killing of a serving state official on the territory of a third state, in the middle of a diplomatic mediation he was conducting.

Baghaei's framing of the Soleimani killing as "an attack on the most prominent symbol of the sovereignty and dignity of all Iranians" is now the foundation of a legal proceeding, not just a rhetorical claim: a $48 billion civil judgment in the execution phase, and criminal proceedings underway.

The Single Logic

Four institutions. One function.

◾The Justice Ministry is converting the school in Minab and the stadium in Lamerd into universal-jurisdiction files that will follow named American officers through third-country courts. The Koblenz precedent is already on the books.
◾ The Basij is converting a science competition into a redundant talent pipeline so that an assassination campaign can only kill individuals, not capability. Five scientists were killed. The cohorts replaced them.
◾ The adviser to the Leader is converting Washington's demolition of the INF, Open Skies, the CTBT, and New START into the public argument for why the NPT bargain no longer binds anyone and why Iran's doctrine review is a response, not a provocation.
◾ The presidency and Foreign Ministry are converting the EU's own eastern-Mediterranean member state into a channel, while the British state that owns the base on that island sits on Iran's hostile-entity list.

None of these is a protest. Each is an institution doing the work it was built to do, in wartime, under blockade, with the leadership chain intact.

Rahimi's sentence is the whole day in one line: "We have struck back to defend our nation. But that is not enough."

The strikes are the military column. The dockets are the legal column. The pipeline is the human column. The treaty collapse is the strategic column. The channel is the diplomatic column.

The war is being fought in all five.

🚨 MARYLAND’S POLITICAL UNDERDOGS DESERVE RESPECT, NOT RIDICULE

It’s easy to mock those like Dan Cox, perennial Republican candidates and anyone else who challenges Maryland’s entrenched Democratic establishment.

It’s considerably harder to put your own name on a ballot, raise money, recruit volunteers and campaign in a state where Democrats enjoy enormous institutional and fundraising advantages.

▪️ COMPETITION MATTERS: Uncontested races and predictable outcomes do little to encourage scrutiny of incumbents. Challengers force debates about taxes, spending, schools and public safety.

▪️ LOSING ISN’T DISGRACEFUL: A candidate can lose badly and still raise legitimate questions that deserve public attention. Election results don’t determine whether those questions were worth asking.

▪️ REPEAT CANDIDATES: If the same Republicans keep running, perhaps the more important question is why a stronger bench of newcomers hasn’t emerged to compete.

▪️ ACCOUNTABILITY GOES BOTH WAYS: Candidates who repeatedly lose should examine their strategies and build broader coalitions. But voters and political commentators should distinguish legitimate criticism from ridicule that discourages participation.

Maryland needs more people willing to challenge political power, not fewer.

If the established challengers aren’t good enough, who is willing to step forward, do the work and offer voters a serious alternative?

text:
🇺🇸🇪🇺 What changes can transatlantic partners expect from the upcoming US and European elections?

Last week, GMF President Dr. @AdeHoopScheffer and @pennynaas hosted GMF alumni and friends in Brussels, from across the EU institutions, NATO, business, and civil society to discuss what is likely to endure in the transatlantic relationship, and where Europe needs to act regardless of the electoral calendar.

A few takeaways from the evening:

🔹 Beyond the ballot box: Participants saw deeper, longer-term shifts shaping US policy more than any single election result, with a bipartisan path on Ukraine seen as possible.

🔹 Europe’s homework: A more balanced partnership works only if Europe puts its own house in order and strategically rethinks its alliances. That means cooperating with the US where interests align, acting independently where necessary, and diversifying partnerships where possible.

🔹 A wider strategic map: In Africa and Latin America, Europe needs to move faster—from ambition to delivery. Participants pointed to a central challenge for the EU’s Global Gateway: a compelling offer on paper can lose out when complex rules make working with China simpler.

🔹 Rebuilding trust beyond the ballot box: As voters grow disillusioned with traditional politics, governments and institutions on both sides of the Atlantic must do more than communicate decisions—they must explain the choices behind them and show how they respond to citizens’ concerns. Grassroots organizations offer lessons in how to close that gap.

Thank you to everyone who joined us for such a candid, constructive exchange.

text:
Apis Bull made of Elephant Ivory, c. 664-332 B.C.

In Ancient Egypt, even a bull could be treated like royalty, yet the sacred Apis was no ordinary beast. Considered a living embodiment of the god Ptah, he enjoyed a privileged existence at Memphis, where his presence was believed to bring fertility, renewal and divine blessing.

His identity, however, was written upon his very hide. Distinctive markings, including a triangle upon the forehead and intricate patterns adorned upon it's side, distinguished the chosen animal from his fellow cattle.

This delightful little ivory statuette offers a glimpse of that sacred symbolism. Upon its back, a winged scarab and outstretched vulture evoke the divine character of a creature whose worship stretched back to the very beginnings of Pharaonic civilisation.

And death was hardly the end of his honours. Apis bulls were carefully mummified and laid to rest in splendid burials, eventually within the vast subterranean galleries of the Serapeum at Saqqara. Even the mothers of these sacred bulls possessed their own cult and burial grounds.

Such was the remarkable life (and afterlife) of Egypt's most celebrated bull!

Read more: https://t.co/rr5mPlXBbx

text:
TrendForce: Marvell and Lumentum merger will threaten Broadcom.

If the deal closes, it will significantly strengthen Marvell's optical tech portfolio and enable the combined company to offer more comprehensive next-gen optical interconnect solutions. The merger could also reshape the competitive landscape in optical communications, where Broadcom currently dominates.

In 2026, Marvell and Lumentum will rank 4th and 8th respectively in revenue in the semiconductor wired communications market. Once merged, their combined market share will reach nearly 7%, second only to Nvidia and Broadcom.

TrendForce explains that Broadcom's competitive edge in AI optical comms and interconnects stems from its broad portfolio covering both optical and electrical tech. Its products include Tomahawk switch chips, DSPs, and optical components like EML and CW lasers.

In contrast, Marvell's expertise is mainly in electronic semiconductors, while Lumentum focuses on optical components. Combining these complementary capabilities will create a stronger rival with expertise spanning both optical devices and semiconductor ICs, potentially challenging Broadcom's market leadership.

TrendForce emphasizes that both companies already play key roles in the optical comms supply chain. Lumentum is a key supplier of laser sources, while Marvell provides DSPs and other semiconductor solutions for optical comms. If the merger is approved, Nvidia and other CSPs could gain broader integrated optical-electrical interconnect solutions, potentially reducing reliance on Broadcom while maintaining purchasing flexibility.

From a tech perspective, TrendForce believes that as the industry transitions to CPO and NPO, this acquisition is a strategic move for Marvell to establish an early foothold in scale-in and scale-up interconnects.

Incorporating Lumentum's InP laser tech—a key missing capability in Marvell's current portfolio—will also allow Marvell to integrate its electrical and optical expertise into more complete optical engine products.

Furthermore, the combined company can combine Marvell's advanced CMOS chip design, high-speed switch chips, optical-electrical interconnects, silicon photonics, and custom XPU capabilities with Lumentum's high-performance InP lasers, optical transceiver modules, and optical circuit switching (OCS) tech.

This will enable the company to develop integrated solutions covering chips, optical engines, laser sources, and modules. Through co-design and pre-validation, the company can also help customers simplify development processes and accelerate the adoption of next-gen optical interconnect tech.

text:
Evening update, Tue 3 Nov. Iran’s offer to reopen Hormuz within two days lands on US midterm day, and I don’t think the timing’s an accident. Trump parked the strike decision behind the vote. Once the polls close that reason to wait is gone, and Netanyahu is reportedly already pushing for strikes.

Midterms. Trump said there’d be no new attacks on Iran before polling day, and he’s spent the past few days playing the war down. “We had a war with Iran. We won,” he told reporters. On Monday he said he wasn’t sure you’d “even call it a war”, because there’d been no fighting for months. He also says there are “one or two sites” left to deal with, which he could do “in ten minutes”, and he’s named Pickaxe Mountain. I’m not calling the result. My point is narrower. Whoever wins, the domestic case for holding off ends with the count, and AP reports Netanyahu wants a short, heavy air campaign once the vote’s done. Fuel prices matter here too. Brent fell more than 7% on Monday on hopes of a deal, and I doubt the White House wanted that reversed before people voted.

Tehran. Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, said in a televised speech that Iran is “ready for battle with its finger on the trigger” and that the ball is now in America’s court to prevent war. Pezeshkian claims the supreme leader has given his government new powers to negotiate issues that were off-limits. If that’s real, it’s the most important line of the day. The terms are the same as before: frozen assets, the blockade and sanctions lifted, and hostilities ended on every front, Lebanon included. Only the timeline has moved, from seven days to two. Qatar says both sides “remain committed” and it’s working towards an interim deal. A senior Iranian official told Reuters they’re still far apart.

Hormuz. An Indian seafarer died after the MSV Al Jusufi was hit by what India calls an “unidentified aerial object” off Oman. Oman’s coast guard rescued the other 13 crew. UKMTO counted 30 attacks on merchant ships in October, a record.

Washington. US officials describe last night’s strikes on Qeshm as limited and defensive, a response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft. The WSJ reports they’re part of a run of undeclared strikes over recent weeks. So “no new attacks before the vote” has had some give in it already.

Yemen. Reuters reports the Houthis have pushed to within about 80km of Aden, their closest since 2015. Saudi air defences intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at the south of the kingdom on Monday.

Elsewhere. The Kremlin confirmed the US–Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi for 10–11 Nov.

Overnight I’m watching Trump’s first remarks after the results. If Iran’s in them, I’d read that as the strike window opening. Tell me where I’m wrong.

text:
IDAN KWELLER, Jerusalem Post, NOV 3, 2026 
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu personally proposed ending nearly $4 billion in annual American assistance to Israel, US President Donald Trump claimed on Tuesday, announcing a potentially consequential shift in US-Israel relations on the morning of the American midterm elections.
In a telephone interview with Fox News' Fox & Friends, Trump said the two leaders had reached an understanding several months ago under which the assistance would end by December 2026. Israel would remain free to purchase American weapons, and could receive additional assistance if necessary.

The hosts repeatedly pressed Trump to clarify whether he was referring to military aid, direct financial assistance, or weapons deliveries. He maintained that the arrangement would come to an end in December, without offering further details.
Trump also outlined the political rationale behind the move, arguing that ending US assistance would deprive Democrats of one of their most effective arguments against Republicans, particularly in Michigan, where support for Israel has become a central issue in a fiercely contested Senate race.

But Trump's announcement raises a significant question: What happens to the existing US-Israel military assistance agreement, which commits Washington to providing $38 billion in military aid over the 10-year period ending in 2028?
Eventually, Trump offered his most revealing clarification: Netanyahu, he said, was the one who raised the idea. “Can I be honest with you? He brought it up. He brought it up,” Trump said. According to the president, Netanyahu told him: “I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid.”

text:
🇺🇦🇺🇸 ZELENSKYY SAYS UKRAINE NO LONGER ASKS WASHINGTON WHERE IT CAN STRIKE RUSSIA 🇷🇺

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine is using its own weapons to strike targets inside Russia without consulting the United States about where those attacks should take place.

The statement draws an important distinction between military assistance supplied by Washington and weapons developed or produced by Ukraine itself.

For much of the war, the use of certain Western-supplied weapons against targets inside Russian territory has been subject to restrictions and political disagreements. Those limitations have complicated Kyiv’s efforts to attack military infrastructure beyond its borders, even when that infrastructure supports Russian operations against Ukraine.

Ukraine’s growing domestic strike capabilities give Kyiv greater freedom to select targets and plan operations without depending on foreign authorisation for every decision.

That independence matters particularly for long-range attacks. Russian airbases, ammunition depots, logistics hubs and defence-industrial facilities can contribute to military operations hundreds of kilometres from the front. Ukrainian-developed weapons offer a way to threaten such infrastructure without relying exclusively on foreign-supplied missiles.

Zelenskyy’s remarks do not mean Ukraine has stopped cooperating with American intelligence agencies or that restrictions on US-supplied weapons have disappeared. His point concerns Ukrainian weapons and Kyiv’s authority to decide how to employ them.

Ukraine remains dependent on international military assistance in several areas, but its domestic strike capabilities are giving its commanders greater operational autonomy.

Kyiv’s position is that decisions about where Ukrainian-made weapons strike Russian military targets belong to Ukraine.

text:
NATO Can Survive on Paper and Still Stop Working

Three architectures, none complete

Liana Fix and Daniel Fiott lay out three models for Europe after dependable American protection: a more European NATO, an EU defense union, and a durable coalition of willing states that includes Ukraine. Their conclusion is less tidy than the branding. Europe will probably need pieces of all three. [1]

The first option preserves NATO while Europeans assume more conventional responsibility and the United States keeps the nuclear backstop. It offers continuity, but still depends on Washington choosing not to paralyze the institution it nominally leads. [1]

The second builds an EU defense union around Article 42(7), the mutual-assistance clause. The legal promise exists. The command structure, planning machinery, territorial-defense budget and automatic crisis procedures largely do not. [1]

The third relies on a standing coalition of willing European states. It can move faster than consensus institutions, but speed is not the same as endurance. Ad hoc coalitions still need command, logistics, intelligence, industrial capacity and somebody willing to keep the lights on after the summit photo. [1]

The institutional zombie scenario

The report’s sharpest point is that the United States would not need to leave NATO to make it unusable. Washington could exploit consensus rules, control of the supreme command, force planning, budgets, readiness certification and high-end intelligence assets. The treaty survives. The response mechanism gets sand in every gear. [1]

That is a more useful risk model than endless arguments about whether an American president would formally quit. Institutions often fail politely. The flag stays up, the communiqués keep arriving and the capabilities quietly become conditional.

Europe also remains dependent on American strategic enablers: integrated air and missile defense, lift, long-range strike, space, cyber, logistics and intelligence. Buying more shells is necessary. It does not replace the operating system. [1]

Our read

Europe’s defense debate still likes the moral comfort of “burden sharing.” The report shows the actual problem is authority sharing. Washington wants Europe capable enough to spend more and absorb risk, but not so autonomous that American political leverage or defense-industrial market share disappears. [1]

That bargain can work while U.S. support remains credible. It gets strange when the customer is asked to become self-reliant without being allowed to copy the wiring diagram.

The practical answer is redundancy: strengthen the European role inside NATO, make the EU mutual-defense clause operational, and turn coalitions of the willing into durable planning structures. Redundancy is expensive. Discovering in a crisis that one ally controls the fuse box is more expensive.

Caveat: This is scenario analysis, not a forecast. It assumes U.S. disengagement becomes structural and Russia remains Europe’s principal threat. The authors acknowledge that the eventual system will probably combine models. CFR is a U.S. foreign-policy institution, and the report evaluates European choices partly through their consequences for American influence. [1]

Sources:
[1] Council on Foreign Relations: Europe’s Defense Dilemma

text:
Thank you General Flynn

There are days when you’re going to say, “I can’t do this anymore.” When those moments of exhaustion and doubt inevitably come, give yourself permission to take a break. Step back, take a day off, or take a couple of days off if you need them to recharge your spirit. Rest is a necessary part of any long journey, but never confuse resting with quitting—above all else, don’t give up.

I know people across this nation are deeply tired. They’re tired of being lied to, tired of asking simple questions only to receive deflected answers and empty excuses, and tired of looking at their own government and wondering whether anybody in power actually remembers who is supposed to be in charge. The American people are resilient and can handle the plain, unvarnished truth. Tell us what happened, tell us what’s broken, and then tell us what concrete steps you’re going to take to fix it.

That fundamental honesty is how you begin to rebuild and restore trust. In my judgment, the severe lack of trust between the American people and the government sworn to serve us is the single greatest threat our country faces today. I firmly believe that this rift can be corrected, although real repair will not happen overnight. However, it will never be corrected if good, principled people simply decide they’re done and walk away from the process.

We must accept that there is no white knight on a white horse riding in to rescue us. We cannot keep passively relying on one savior or individual leader instead of relying on our own collective strength and action. We have to reach a firm, conscious point where we say, “Enough is enough. I’m going to get involved, and I’m personally going to do something about it.”

That engagement starts by actively taking control of what we can control in our immediate lives. We control our own time, our personal priorities, and the daily decisions we make. We decide whether to actively learn what is happening in our local communities, attend a school board or town hall meeting, ask a difficult question of elected officials, or encourage a friend to get involved. These are fundamental lessons in leadership, and you do not need an official title or elected office to practice them every day.

I learned a vital lesson long ago as a military officer: people constantly watch what their leaders do. If the lieutenant panics and starts running, everybody around him wants to know why. They wonder where he is going, what unseen danger he knows about, and whether they should start running too. The takeaway for effective leadership is simple and enduring: stay steady.

That principle applies just as strongly in our local communities and inside our homes. When you give up and surrender to cynicism, somebody who is watching you may give up too. But when you hold your ground and remain steadfast, you give someone else the courage and reason to keep going. Your children, grandchildren, neighbors, and friends are all watching. Some of them may never explicitly tell you how much your quiet example matters to them, but it impacts them more than you know.

I often think about my own parents and the extraordinary generation that came before us. They sacrificed, served through hardship, and built a foundation of freedom. They passed down a country brimming with opportunity and essentially said, “Here you go. You can achieve anything in the world.” Many of us benefited enormously from the nation they built, defended, and preserved. Now, we have a solemn duty to ask ourselves what kind of country we will hand over to our children.

I refuse to blame the younger generation for the challenging conditions of a world they simply inherited. Look closely at the complex world we are passing on to them and the immense responsibilities they will soon carry on their shoulders. We have a moral obligation to do everything within our power to leave them a country that is stronger and better than we found it.

At their core, most Americans simply want to raise their families, own a home, earn an honest living, and live their lives without the government unnecessarily interfering with them. You will find that people across all political backgrounds share these fundamental human aspirations. However, if we want to protect these simple freedoms, we must be willing to sacrifice for them. We must serve others, live out the Golden Rule, and accept that preserving a free nation requires meaningful commitment and effort from every single one of us.

For those of us guided by faith, that civic responsibility carries deep spiritual weight. I often hear people say, “We know how this story ends—God wins.” While I believe wholeheartedly in God, I also believe there is intentional purpose in the trials and challenges we are asked to walk through. After everything I have experienced, I have asked myself many times why certain paths were laid before me. My faith has sustained me and helped me recognize a clear purpose in continuing to show up, engage directly with people, and do whatever good I can.

We each need to evaluate our own lives and ask what more we can contribute. Can you bring a few more people into community work? Can you help someone better understand an important issue, or facilitate a thoughtful, respectful conversation within your own circle of friends? This localized effort matters tremendously in our neighborhoods, civic groups, and places of worship among ordinary citizens who care enough to organize, educate themselves, and put their values into practice.

We must also stop standing in awe of political and social titles. Whether someone holds the rank of governor, senator, president, or military general, we are all ultimately human beings subject to the same flaws and duties. We should firmly expect and demand that those entrusted with public authority answer serious questions and faithfully fulfill their duties. Becoming enamored with the prestige, glitz, and glamour of office does absolutely nothing to address or solve the real problems facing our country.

At the same time, we must uphold our own civic responsibilities. For example, I voted early in Florida because I knew I would be traveling and unable to cast a ballot on Election Day. Like many citizens, I have genuine concerns about the integrity and functioning of our election system, and I want leaders who will work to fix those issues. But I vote regardless because democratic participation is essential we must choose our representatives, demand accountability from them, and keep working long after the ballots are counted. Walking away in frustration simply surrenders those vital decisions to someone else.

If you are already engaged in your community, keep asking yourself the question I pose to people everywhere: “What more can I do?” You don’t have to solve every problem single-handedly, but you can take the knowledge, experience, and wisdom you have gained and put them to meaningful work. Start the conversation, show up when it counts, and help inspire someone else to find the courage to stand beside you.

I have children and grandchildren, and I care deeply about the country and culture they will grow up in. I was blessed to receive a nation with more freedom and opportunity than what prior generations had, and I cannot accept handing the next generation a country diminished by our own complacency or unwillingness to act. When my time comes, I want to know beyond a shadow of a doubt that I gave it everything I had. That core purpose is what drives me forward every single day.

So when you feel weary, take a deep breath, step back, and get the rest you need. Spend meaningful time with the family, friends, and neighbors who remind you why this country is worth every ounce of effort. Then come back refreshed, stay steady in your resolve, and stay actively involved.

Whatever challenges lie ahead, don’t ever give up.
