text:
Vladimir Putin's Russia is once again at the centre of growing fears that the Kremlin is waging a calculated campaign of intimidation against Britain and its European allies, after a wave of bomb threats forced passenger aircraft into emergency landings across Europe. Two British flights were among those affected, with security experts warning that Moscow could be exploiting IRA-style terror tactics to spread fear, create chaos and deliberately undermine Western security. The message to Putin must be absolutely unmistakable: Britain will not bow to Russian intimidation, will not tolerate attacks on its infrastructure and will never allow a hostile foreign dictator to dictate how this country protects its national interests.

For far too long, Putin and his cronies have behaved as though Russia can threaten Western nations, interfere with their infrastructure and intimidate their populations without facing serious consequences. The Kremlin's contempt for international security has become increasingly difficult to ignore. From its invasion of Ukraine to its aggressive military provocations, cyber operations and suspected interference across Europe, Putin's regime has repeatedly demonstrated the danger it poses to the security of democratic nations.

Britain must stop treating Russian hostility as an inconvenience that can be brushed aside with carefully worded diplomatic statements. The Kremlin is not a trustworthy partner, and Putin is not interested in respecting the security of countries he regards as geopolitical rivals. His regime has repeatedly shown that it is prepared to exploit fear, instability and weakness whenever doing so serves its interests.

The latest incidents saw six passenger aircraft forced into emergency landings following reports of suspected explosive devices on board. Among them was a flight from London Heathrow which diverted to Warsaw Modlin Airport, while a Ryanair aircraft travelling from Manchester was forced to land in Murcia, Spain. Two further Ryanair aircraft, travelling from Lisbon and Dublin, were grounded at Rome's Fiumicino Airport following a double bomb threat.

Yesterday, a Wizz Air flight from London was also forced to make an emergency landing in Budapest after receiving a bomb threat. Although no explosives have so far been discovered, the consequences have been serious. Passengers have been frightened, airports have been thrown into confusion and emergency services have been forced to respond to potentially dangerous incidents.

If Moscow is responsible, this is precisely the sort of cowardly intimidation that demonstrates the lengths to which Putin's regime may be prepared to go. Rather than confronting its opponents openly, hostile actors can exploit civilian infrastructure and place ordinary families in danger while attempting to maintain plausible deniability. It is an ugly form of aggression, and Britain must not allow it to become normalised.

Security and intelligence expert Professor Anthony Glees believes Russia could be behind the latest campaign of disruption. He warned that Britain was facing an increasingly sophisticated shadow war involving physical intimidation and covert attempts to destabilise Western societies.

"There’s a kinetic shadow war going on against us, but there’s also a secret subversive war underway using disinformation which is what hoaxes are," he said.

Professor Glees warned that these tactics were designed to spread mayhem, create panic and test the resilience of Western countries. He also suggested that the present circumstances offered Putin an opportunity to challenge Britain and its allies while avoiding the immediate consequences of conventional military confrontation.

That should send a chilling message to every politician in Westminster. Putin does not need to send tanks across the English Channel to threaten Britain. Disrupting airports, attacking computer networks, targeting essential industries and spreading fear can all serve the Kremlin's interests. This is precisely why Britain must stop underestimating the Russian threat.

Experts have drawn comparisons between the latest bomb threats and tactics historically employed by the IRA during the Troubles. Bomb hoaxes were used to create widespread disruption, force evacuations, paralyse transport networks and spread fear among ordinary members of the public.

If the suspicions surrounding Moscow prove correct, Putin's regime is exploiting the same principle on an international scale. The Kremlin would effectively be using civilian fear as a weapon against Western societies. There is nothing sophisticated or respectable about deliberately putting innocent passengers through the terror of a suspected bomb threat. It is an attack on public confidence and a direct challenge to the security of European nations.

Defence expert and former Army Lieutenant Colonel Stuart Crawford suggested that the incidents could form part of a coordinated sub-threshold attack originating from Moscow. However, he also cautioned that further evidence would be necessary before Russia could formally be identified as responsible.

This is precisely why Britain's intelligence services must be properly funded, equipped and supported. The country cannot afford to sit around waiting for the next incident while hostile states potentially exploit weaknesses in our security. Those responsible must be identified, hostile networks exposed and every available measure taken to prevent further disruption. If the Kremlin is behind this campaign, Putin must understand that Britain will not simply shrug its shoulders and accept it.

The aviation disruption comes as another cyberattack has struck Britain's meatpacking industry, with similar incidents reported elsewhere in Europe. Paul Chichester, director of operations at the National Cyber Security Centre, confirmed that the industry had been targeted.

NCSC chief technology officer Ollie Whitehouse warned that hostile actors were increasingly seeking to produce consequences in the physical world through cyber operations.

Britain's food supply chains, transport networks, energy infrastructure and communications systems are essential to national security. Any hostile state attempting to undermine these systems is potentially threatening the livelihoods, safety and everyday lives of millions of people.

The Russian leadership must understand that Britain's infrastructure is not a playground for its intelligence operatives or cybercriminals. Our airports, factories, food supplies and essential services must be defended against foreign interference. The Government must urgently strengthen national resilience and ensure that the Kremlin cannot exploit years of political complacency.

Meanwhile, Poland has been forced to strengthen security along its border with Russia's Kaliningrad region after reports of suspicious movements during the night.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had received information about individuals carrying flashlights near the border shortly after midnight. Polish authorities rapidly mobilised additional security forces and resources to prevent potential provocations.

Although the precise intentions of those involved remain unconfirmed, the incident adds to the growing security concerns facing European nations bordering Russian territory. Poland knows only too well that living alongside Putin's Russia requires constant vigilance. Britain should pay attention to the determination with which its European allies are protecting their national security.

The latest developments also come as the Royal Navy has been forced to scramble combat jets from HMS Prince of Wales to intercept another Russian reconnaissance aircraft in the North Atlantic.

GB News revealed that fifth-generation F-35 stealth fighters were launched from Britain's flagship aircraft carrier after a Russian Tupolev reconnaissance aircraft, nicknamed the Bear, approached the carrier strike group.

It is yet another reminder that Putin's hostility towards the West extends well beyond the battlefield in Ukraine. Russian reconnaissance aircraft continue to operate near British and allied military formations, placing additional pressure on the Royal Navy and Nato forces.

In July, a Russian Bear repeatedly approached the British carrier strike group and reportedly dropped sonobuoys dangerously close to HMS Prince of Wales. Such behaviour is deeply provocative and demonstrates why Britain's armed forces must remain on constant alert.

The Kremlin should understand that Britain will not abandon its strategic interests simply because Moscow wishes to throw its weight around. British sailors, pilots and military personnel are not there to be used as props in Putin's military intimidation campaign. Their safety must be an absolute priority, and the Royal Navy must have every resource necessary to protect them.

The political left should be answering some deeply uncomfortable questions. Why has Britain allowed its critical infrastructure to face such serious vulnerabilities? Why have successive governments failed to provide our security services and armed forces with everything they need to confront an increasingly hostile Russia? And why should British taxpayers accept years of defence neglect while Putin continues to expand the pressure placed on European security?

Britain deserves better than political complacency, weakness and endless excuses. Our intelligence agencies, police forces and armed services should never have to question whether they have sufficient resources to protect the public. National security is not an optional extra that can be sacrificed whenever politicians decide that other spending priorities are more convenient.

There must also be a fundamental reassessment of Britain's relationship with Moscow. The days of pretending that Putin's Russia can be treated as a normal, reliable international partner should be firmly behind us. His invasion of Ukraine demonstrated the devastating consequences of allowing Kremlin aggression to go unchecked. Britain must never repeat the mistake of believing that Russian hostility can be overcome through empty diplomatic gestures and wishful thinking.

Donald Trump has repeatedly challenged Nato members to take greater responsibility for their own defence. Whatever politicians in Westminster think of his approach, the underlying point remains important. Britain cannot continue relying on others to shoulder the burden of European security. Our armed forces, intelligence services and critical infrastructure need serious and sustained investment.

There should be no confusion between preparing for conflict and seeking it. Britain does not need an unnecessary confrontation with Russia. What it needs is a military so capable, so well-equipped and so professionally prepared that Putin thinks twice before attempting to threaten British interests.

Weakness invites intimidation. Strength provides deterrence.

The Russian regime must understand that Britain will not surrender control of its security, abandon its allies or allow hostile foreign powers to terrorise its population. Any attempt to threaten British aviation, disrupt essential industries or interfere with national infrastructure must be investigated with the utmost seriousness. If Russian involvement is established, the response must be firm, meaningful and coordinated with our Nato allies.

Our intelligence officers, police personnel, aviation security teams and military forces deserve enormous respect. While politicians argue over budgets and priorities, these men and women are working around the clock to protect the country from threats that most ordinary people will never see. They deserve a Government that backs them without hesitation and gives them the resources to do their jobs.

Britain has a proud history of standing against those who threaten its national security. From the defeat of fascism in the Second World War to the long struggle against terrorism during the Troubles, our country has repeatedly demonstrated that it will not allow intimidation to determine its future.

That determination must never disappear through political cowardice or an unwillingness to confront uncomfortable realities. Putin's Russia must never be allowed to interpret Britain's desire for peace as an opportunity to attack its security.

Enough appeasing the Kremlin. Enough diplomatic hand-wringing. Enough excuses for years of defence neglect. And enough pretending that Putin's increasingly hostile Russia does not represent a serious threat to Britain and the wider Western world.

If Russia is found responsible for these bomb hoaxes, those behind the campaign must face serious consequences. Britain must work with Nato allies to expose hostile operations, strengthen aviation security and ensure that the Kremlin understands that attacks on civilian infrastructure will not go unanswered.

Putin can send his spy planes, threaten European security, exploit cyber vulnerabilities and attempt to spread fear across Britain. But he must never mistake our commitment to peace for weakness or an unwillingness to defend ourselves.

Britain is not Russia's playground. Our airports are not targets for Kremlin intimidation. Our infrastructure is not there for Russian operatives to sabotage. Our armed forces are not there to be bullied by Putin's military.

The British people deserve a Government that puts their safety first, a military capable of defending the nation and intelligence services equipped to confront hostile states.

Britain must stand firm, rebuild its national defences and make one thing absolutely clear to Vladimir Putin: this country will not be bullied, intimidated or brought to its knees by the Kremlin. Putin can keep testing the West, but he should never underestimate Britain's determination to defend itself.

text:
In this post I am going to take the Apocryphon of John seriously as our interpretive lens and build the strongest possible case that the God portrayed as the creator and lawgiver in the Hebrew scriptures is not the ultimate God, and that Jesus came to reveal a higher God.

In the Apocryphon of John, the creator figure is called Yaldabaoth, also known as Saklas and Samael.

The text describes him as an ignorant ruler who possesses power but does not understand where his power originated.

Then he declares:

"I am a jealous god; there is none beside me."

This is an extraordinary theological reversal.

Why?

Because this declaration echoes Isaiah 45:5 and 46:9, where the God of Israel declares that there is no other God.

The Gnostic author takes a declaration of divine supremacy and places it in the mouth of an ignorant, lesser creator.

The being who claims to be the only God may simply be a lower divine ruler who does not know that a higher God exists.

2. The names of the Hebrew God appear among the lower rulers

In the Apocryphon of John, Yaldabaoth creates subordinate authorities. Their names include:

See image below

These figures belong to the hierarchy of rulers associated with the lower cosmic order.
This is not a trivial coincidence.

The text takes names and titles associated with the God of Israel and places several of them within a system of subordinate cosmic powers.

It is effectively challenging the assumption that the deity worshipped under these names must be the supreme, ultimate God.

There is a qualification: the text does not simply say every biblical divine name represents an evil being. Its mythology is more complicated, and some figures within the hierarchy change allegiance.

But the overall theological challenge is unmistakable.

3. The Apocryphon of John repeatedly challenges the Genesis account as transmitted through Moses.

Consider three examples.

A. The creation of Eve

Genesis 2:21–22 describes God taking a rib from Adam and creating Eve.

The Apocryphon of John presents a different explanation.

It describes the creator as attempting to extract the spiritual power within Adam, while the divine Intelligence of Light cannot be controlled by him.

The author explicitly contrasts this with Moses' account.

B. Adam's sleep

Genesis describes Adam falling into a deep sleep.

The Apocryphon interprets this differently: the ruler covers Adam's perception and makes him unable to understand.

The underlying idea is that humanity is being kept ignorant.

C. The movement over the waters

Genesis 1:2 describes the Spirit of God moving over the waters.

The Apocryphon challenges Moses' description and gives the movement a different symbolic meaning, associating it with the Mother's distress over the defective creation.

These aren't minor disagreements over biblical details.

They represent a deliberate reinterpretation of the creation story.

The central argument is that the creator's version of events is not necessarily the truth.

4. The serpent becomes an instrument of enlightenment

This is another major reversal.

In the traditional Genesis narrative:

God prohibits eating from the tree of knowledge.

The serpent encourages Eve to eat.

The serpent is associated with deception and disobedience.

In the Apocryphon of John, the interpretation is dramatically different.

The serpent's intervention is connected with the awakening of humanity.

The spiritual Intelligence of Light helps Adam and Eve recognize something the lower creator does not want them to understand.

Knowledge becomes a path toward liberation.
This changes the moral structure of Eden.
The question is no longer simply whether humanity disobeyed God.

It becomes whether the authority prohibiting knowledge was actually protecting humanity or keeping it ignorant.

That is one of the most radical features of this Gnostic interpretation.

5. Jesus reveals a God above the creator

This is the foundation of the entire system.

In the Apocryphon of John, the risen Jesus reveals to John the existence of the Invisible Spirit.

The supreme God is described as:

Beyond the material universe.

Beyond ordinary human categories.

Uncreated.

Invisible.

Not dependent on anything.

The source of goodness, life, and light.

The creator Yaldabaoth is not this supreme God.
He is a subordinate being who mistakes his own authority for ultimate authority.

The distinction is crucial:
Supreme divine reality
The Invisible Spirit
The ultimate source of existence, light, knowledge, and goodness.

Lower cosmic authority

Yaldabaoth

The ignorant creator who believes himself to be the highest God.

Revealer

Jesus Christ

The messenger who reveals the existence of the higher divine reality and awakens humanity.

This hierarchy is explicitly described in the Apocryphon of John.

6. Now let's bring this back to Revelation

Revelation

Apocryphon of John

A beast claims authority over humanity
=
Yaldabaoth claims supreme divine authority

The beast demands allegiance
=
The lower rulers demand obedience

The beast controls economic participation
=
The lower cosmic authorities control the material order

The beast's followers receive a mark
=
Divine identity is expressed through spiritual belonging

The Lamb offers an alternative allegiance
=
Jesus reveals the higher divine reality

Babylon represents an oppressive world order
The material cosmic order is associated with ignorance and lower authority

There are thematic similarities, particularly around false authority, allegiance, deception, and liberation.

7. The historical problem: Were these actually the same John?

This is the most important historical qualification.
The Apocryphon of John presents its revelation as something Jesus gives to John, the brother of James, the son of Zebedee.
But that does not establish that the historical John of Patmos wrote it.

The development of this underlying Gnostic material can be placed before or around the late second century, with the later dialogue form developing subsequently. Revelation is generally dated to the late first century.

So we have at least three possibilities:

The later Gnostic author developed an entirely different theology and attributed it to John.

The author inherited earlier ideas that were circulating among some Christian communities.

Some traditions associated with Jesus and John were reinterpreted through a Gnostic understanding of the creator.

We cannot presently establish which historical influences came first.

The Gnostic interpretation of John presents a fundamental challenge to the identification of the creator with the ultimate God.

It suggests that the being who claims exclusive divine authority may actually be an inferior ruler, one who possesses power but lacks knowledge of the higher divine source.

Jesus' role is consequently not simply to establish another religious institution. It is to reveal the truth that liberates humanity from ignorance.

This gives us an entirely different way to examine the symbolism of Revelation:

Who claims authority?
Who demands allegiance?
Who controls access to life?

Who benefits from human ignorance?

Who is actually revealing truth?

Is the apparent divine authority really the ultimate source of goodness?

I would not yet claim that John of Patmos secretly believed Yahweh was Yaldabaoth. The surviving evidence cannot establish that. But the theology I am exploring is a genuine ancient Christian theological position

9. The next five texts I will examine

Isaiah 45:5–7: The God of Israel declares that there is no other God and claims responsibility for light and darkness.

Genesis 2–3: The creator prohibits knowledge, and the serpent challenges that prohibition.

John 8:44: Jesus speaks about the father of lies and the nature of those who follow him.

Revelation 13: The beast demands allegiance and controls economic participation.

The Apocryphon of John: Yaldabaoth claims to be the only God, while Jesus reveals the Invisible Spirit above him.

The particularly interesting comparison is Isaiah 45:7 alongside the Apocryphon of John.

The Gnostic author takes the very language of divine exclusivity from the Hebrew scriptures and turns it into evidence of the creator's ignorance.

That is the theological reversal we need to understand.

Now I will investigate whether Jesus' teachings in the Gospel of John distinguish his Father from the creator described in Genesis. That would help me  determine whether there are earlier textual foundations for the theology that later appears explicitly in the Apocryphon of John.

text:
South Africa: Farm torture: “The worst was when they started cutting my wife”

Les Brett (67) says the worst part was not what happened to him: “It was when they started cutting my wife’s nipples, just to cause pain. She’s a very, very strong woman. A good woman.”

He and his wife, Natasha (68), have lived for 13 years on a farm at Broederstroom, near Hartbeespoort Dam, where he is involved in wildlife conservation. That is why he has guns, including an AK-47 assault rifle.

“They put the AK-47’s barrel in my mouth and pulled the trigger, but it didn’t fire,” he says.

“It was God’s grace. There’s nothing wrong with my gun. But they didn’t know much about guns, to be honest.”

The attackers left with seven of Les’s guns and the couple’s cellphones.

Three attackers broke into the house and overpowered the couple. They tied their feet, blindfolded them and tied their arms behind their backs.

“But they kept us apart, so most of the time we could only hear what was happening to the other one,” says Natasha.

The motive for the attack? “There were only two reasons. They wanted to get into the safe, and they wanted cash,” says Les.

He says it was as if they knew he owned firearms. “That’s when they started assaulting my wife in front of me. But once they had the keys, they got it into their heads that we keep cash.”

The couple can’t remember exactly how long the torture lasted, but estimate it was between two and three hours. “It’s difficult, because you’re in so much pain that time passes more slowly,” says Natasha.

Photo caption: Les and Natasha Brett before the attack. (Supplied)

Les and Natasha are already back home, but their injuries are still serious.

“They slapped me and cut the clothes off my body. Exactly like in the movies, as if there’s a mafia above them giving them instructions,” she says.

She also believes that at times it felt as if they were simply taking out their frustrations in anger. “You could see the adrenaline and the rage in their eyes. They also acted as if they weren’t coordinated among themselves.”

In the middle of the attack, one of them told her: “We’re not here to steal cables.”

The couple’s bank cards were left untouched. “I even offered to drive to an ATM, but they didn’t want to,” she says.

Natasha also says she was nearly raped twice. “But they’re like children in a toy shop. When the safe opened, he forgot about me.”

Natasha suspects that if they had not handed over the keys to the safe, the attackers would have killed Les. “It was like a negotiation.”

Photo caption: One of Les’s wounds. (Supplied)

Her lips are now badly swollen, there are bruises behind her ears, and the attackers almost dislocated her shoulder.

“They tied my hands so tightly that the blood circulation was cut off, and then there were the rags they kept pushing into your mouth...” This later tore her frenulum (the tissue that attaches the tongue to the floor of the mouth).

Both of them were tortured with boiling water, but it is not yet clear how serious the burns are.

Les’s injuries are worse than his wife’s. “They hit him over the head with bolt cutters. His face was very swollen, the white of his eye was red and full of blood, and he can’t hear out of his left ear. His eardrum is burst,” she says.

Natasha remembers that it later went quiet where she was sitting alone. “I think they realised we had nothing. When I thought it was quiet enough, I struggled for 15 minutes to untie my feet,” she says.

There was a knife on the table, which they used to cut each other loose.

“The strangest thing is that they let our dogs out, and even threw their pellets in for them to eat,” she says. They have boerboel and Rhodesian ridgeback crosses, as well as a terrier, “and they didn’t even bark.”

Les thanked all the services that helped them after the attack. “We can’t complain at all,” he says.

Leilani Basson of Bush Babes Conservation Adventures has worked with Les for 14 years. “That something like this should happen to a man like him is tragic. That it should happen to someone so devoted to conservation.”

She describes him as “a man who is always ready, a real army man who stays out in the veld with the wild animals because he loves them.”

“He can tell you about anything, from history to facts about the soil and the grass. He’s a walking encyclopaedia of the veld!”

Les also runs the Dung Beetle Bush School, which aims to teach children and women more about the Bushveld. It is also part of an anti-poaching unit that Les runs together with several other organisations.

The police are investigating a case of house robbery. No one has been arrested yet, says police spokesperson Sergeant Kelebogile Morake.

Lieutenant General Arthur Peter Adams, the provincial police commissioner in North West, condemned the attack.

“It is concerning that criminals continue to target vulnerable members of our communities in the safety of their own homes. We condemn such acts of violence and intimidation in the strongest terms.”

Adams said the police would “intensify efforts” to make sure the attackers are arrested.

Anyone with information that can help the police investigation can contact the investigating officer, Warrant Officer Gregory Kwadi, on 082 373 9636.

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

ANNALS OF THE DAY 🪔

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A HISTORICAL CHRONICLE OF NOVEMBER 3RD EDITION

⏱️ READING TIME: APPROXIMATELY 13 MINUTES

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🪔 EPIGRAPH

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to light the road behind us, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” — Hodgepodgery, 2026

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📑 TABLE OF CONTENTS

🏛️ Major Historical Events — Turning points that shaped our world.

🔬 Scientific, Technological & Cultural Milestones — Discoveries, innovations, and cultural firsts.

🎂 Famous Birthdays — Remarkable lives born on this date.

🥀 Memoriam — Remembering lives and legacies.

🏟️ Sports Highlights — Moments that changed the history of sport.

❓ History Quiz — Test your knowledge of the day.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🔎 INTRO

November 3 is a date of extraordinary contrasts: the struggle for freedom, the cost of defiance, the consequences of ambition, and the courage to challenge accepted limits. Across centuries, people have confronted powerful institutions, fought for a voice, pushed into the unknown, and sometimes paid the ultimate price. From political upheaval and scientific milestones to remarkable lives remembered and celebrated, today's history reminds us that progress is rarely simple—and its consequences can last for generations. Turn the page and discover what November 3 has to tell us.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🧭 CALENDAR OVERVIEW  ♏️

November 3 is the 307th day of the year in the Gregorian calendar (≈84.11% of the year completed). There are 58 days remaining after this date, representing ≈15.89% of the year. The year 2026 is a common year of 365 days. Today is Tuesday, falling in ISO week 45. Observances associated with this date include Election Day in the United States, Culture Day in Japan, Independence Day in Dominica, and Separation Day in Panama, commemorating its 1903 separation from Colombia. Unofficial and lighthearted observances include Cliché Day.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

Across centuries, November 3 has witnessed political struggle, national independence, revolutionary upheaval, mass murder, and a scientific achievement that carried a living creature beyond Earth.

1793 — Olympe de Gouges Is Executed During the French Revolution ⚖️

The French Revolution proclaimed liberty, equality, and fraternity. Olympe de Gouges challenged its leaders over why those promises excluded women.

Born Marie Gouze, she became a playwright and political writer. In 1791, she published her Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, demanding equal political rights. She also opposed slavery and revolutionary violence.

Her criticism of powerful factions made her enemies. During the Reign of Terror, she was tried and guillotined in Paris on November 3, 1793.

The Revolution that proclaimed universal rights had executed a woman for demanding that they truly be universal.

🧩 TRIVIA: Her original name was Marie Gouze; she adopted the name Olympe de Gouges as she developed her literary and political career.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A revolution’s ideals are tested by the people it allows to claim them.

1903 — Panama Declares Independence from Colombia 🇵🇦

Panama declared independence from Colombia on November 3, 1903, amid an international struggle over a proposed canal across the isthmus.

After Colombia rejected a canal agreement, President Theodore Roosevelt supported the Panamanian separatist movement and dispatched American warships. Their presence helped prevent Colombian forces from suppressing the revolt.

The United States recognized Panama on November 6. A subsequent treaty granted America extensive rights over a ten-mile-wide Canal Zone. The canal opened in 1914, transforming global shipping.

Panama had gained independence, but its relationship with the powerful country that helped secure it remained contentious for generations.

🧩 TRIVIA: The United States recognized Panama three days after its declaration of independence.

⚠️ IRONY: The power that helped Panama break away from Colombia soon secured extraordinary control over strategically vital Panamanian territory.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Independence can be won in a day; negotiating the meaning of sovereignty can take generations.

1918 — The Kiel Uprising Helps Bring Down the German Empire ⚓

By autumn 1918, Germany’s military leaders knew the First World War was lost. Yet the Navy contemplated one final attack against the British fleet.

Sailors saw no reason to die in a battle that could not change the outcome. Resistance spread after sailors were arrested for refusing to participate.

On November 3, thousands gathered in Kiel to demand an end to the war. Workers and civilians joined them, and troops sent to suppress the demonstrations sided with the protesters.

The uprising spread across Germany. Workers’ and soldiers’ councils challenged the imperial government, and within days Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated. The German Empire collapsed, paving the way for the Weimar Republic.

🧩 TRIVIA: The revolt was triggered by a proposed final naval operation against Britain, despite Germany’s military leaders recognizing that the war was lost.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: When those ordered to enforce obedience refuse, the balance of power can change with astonishing speed.

1943 — Aktion Erntefest: The Nazi Massacre Known as “Operation Harvest Festival” 🕯️

At dawn on November 3, 1943, Nazi SS and police units began Aktion Erntefest—“Operation Harvest Festival”—in German-occupied Poland.

The operation targeted Jewish prisoners in forced-labor and concentration camps in the Lublin District, particularly Majdanek, Trawniki, and Poniatowa. Fearing further Jewish resistance, Heinrich Himmler ordered the murder of the remaining Jewish laborers in the region.

Prisoners were taken to prepared killing sites and shot. The operation continued into November 4, when the killings at Poniatowa were completed.

Approximately 42,000 Jewish people were murdered, making this the largest German-perpetrated massacre of the Holocaust.

🧩 TRIVIA: At Majdanek and Trawniki, loudspeakers played music to drown out the sounds of the mass shootings and victims’ screams.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Atrocity is not always committed in a frenzy. Sometimes it is organized, scheduled, and administered with chilling precision.

1957 — Laika Becomes the First Animal to Orbit Earth 🚀

On November 3, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, carrying Laika, a stray dog from Moscow, into orbit.

The mission demonstrated that a living creature could survive launch and enter orbit, advancing the prospect of human spaceflight. But Sputnik 2 had no recovery system. Laika was never expected to return alive.

NASA’s historical account indicates that she survived only a few hours. Later technical histories identify overheating as the cause of her death.

🧩 TRIVIA: Laika’s original name was Kudryavka, meaning “Little Curly.”

🏆 FIRST: Laika was the first animal to orbit Earth—not the first animal sent into space. Other animals had previously flown on suborbital missions.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Scientific progress can expand humanity’s horizons while forcing us to confront its ethical costs.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🔬 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL & CULTURAL MILESTONES

November 3 has witnessed the birth of international distress communication, constitutional transformation, iconic popular culture, and landmarks that changed the modern world.

1493 — Christopher Columbus Sights Dominica 🧭

During his second Atlantic voyage, Christopher Columbus sighted the Caribbean island now known as Dominica. He named it after the day of the week: Sunday, or dies Dominica in Latin.

The island was inhabited by Indigenous Kalinago people and later became a contested colonial possession before gaining independence from Britain in 1978.

🧩 TRIVIA: Dominica’s name derives from the Latin word for Sunday.

1534 — England’s Act of Supremacy Establishes Royal Supremacy over the Church 👑

Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, recognizing Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church of England and severing its institutional authority from the pope in Rome.

The law reshaped English religious and political life, strengthening royal control over the national church.

🧩 TRIVIA: The act declared the king the “only supreme head on earth” of the Church of England.

1848 — The Dutch Constitution Is Reformed 📜

Constitutional reforms associated with Johan Rudolf Thorbecke transformed the Netherlands into a parliamentary constitutional monarchy.

They strengthened elected representatives, made ministers politically responsible to Parliament, and reduced the monarch’s direct political authority. The revised constitution was promulgated on November 3.

🧩 TRIVIA: Thorbecke chaired the commission that drafted the reforms and later became the first prime minister under the new parliamentary system.

1906 — SOS Becomes an International Maritime Distress Signal 📡

The International Radiotelegraph Convention signed in Berlin established the familiar Morse-code distress signal:

··· — — — ···

Three dots, three dashes, three dots.

SOS became an internationally recognized call for help at sea. Despite popular explanations such as “Save Our Ship” and “Save Our Souls,” the signal was selected for its distinctive, easily transmitted pattern.

🧩 TRIVIA: The 1906 convention established SOS internationally, but the agreement did not enter into force until 1908.

🏆 FIRST: The Berlin convention established SOS as the international radiotelegraphic distress signal.

1946 — Japan Promulgates Its Postwar Constitution 🇯🇵

Japan promulgated its new constitution on November 3, 1946, establishing popular sovereignty, guaranteeing fundamental rights, and making the emperor a symbol of the state rather than its governing authority.

Article 9, renouncing war and the maintenance of war potential, became one of its most debated provisions. The constitution entered into force on May 3, 1947.

🧩 TRIVIA: Japan celebrates November 3 as Culture Day, commemorating the constitution’s promulgation.

1948 — “Dewey Defeats Truman” Becomes a Famous Journalistic Mistake 📰

The Chicago Daily Tribune published an early edition declaring Republican Thomas E. Dewey the winner of the presidential election. Its editors were so confident in the prediction that the headline appeared before the results were settled.

But Harry S. Truman had won. The next morning, photographers captured the victorious president holding up the newspaper and displaying its spectacularly wrong headline.

🧩 TRIVIA: Truman held up the newspaper for photographers during his post-election train journey.

⚠️ IRONY: A newspaper declared the winner before the voters had finished proving it wrong.

1954 — Godzilla Makes His First Appearance 🦖

On November 3, 1954, Godzilla premiered in Japan.

More than a cinematic monster, Godzilla reflected a nation still confronting nuclear warfare and the atomic bombings. The creature’s destructive power embodied anxieties about radiation, military technology, and forces humanity could not control.

The film launched one of cinema’s longest-running monster franchises.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Japanese title was Gojira, a name associated with the words for gorilla and whale.

1964 — Washington, D.C., Votes in a Presidential Election for the First Time Since 1800 🗳️

Residents of Washington, D.C., cast presidential ballots on November 3, 1964, following ratification of the Twenty-Third Amendment in 1961.

The amendment granted District residents Electoral College votes, although it did not provide voting representation in Congress.

🧩 TRIVIA: The District’s three Electoral College votes went to Lyndon B. Johnson, who won the 1964 election by a landslide.

2014 — One World Trade Center Opens in New York City 🏙️

One World Trade Center officially opened on November 3, 2014, becoming the centerpiece of the rebuilt World Trade Center site in Lower Manhattan.

Its opening marked a major milestone in the reconstruction following the September 11 attacks. The tower’s symbolic height of 1,776 feet evokes the year of American independence.

🧩 TRIVIA: Condé Nast employees were among the first to begin working in the building.

Human curiosity continues to carry us beyond the boundaries of what earlier generations believed possible. ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎂 FAMOUS BIRTHDAYS

Today we celebrate remarkable individuals whose lives have left lasting impressions through exploration, leadership, creativity, science, and achievement.

1793 — Stephen F. Austin 🏛️

American empresario known as the “Father of Texas.” Austin led the colonization of Anglo-American settlers in Mexican Texas and became central to the movement that established the Republic of Texas.

🧩 TRIVIA: Austin was born in southwestern Virginia, not Texas.

1921 — Charles Bronson 🎬

American actor whose tough, understated screen presence made him an international star. Known for The Magnificent Seven, The Great Escape, Once Upon a Time in the West, and Death Wish.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before becoming an actor, Bronson worked in a Pennsylvania coal mine.

1952 — Roseanne Barr (age 74) 🎭

American comedian and actress whose sitcom Roseanne challenged the polished conventions of television by portraying working-class family life.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Roseanne series premiered in 1988 and ran for nine seasons.

1957 — Dolph Lundgren (age 69) 🥋

Swedish actor, filmmaker, and martial artist known for Rocky IV, Universal Soldier, and The Expendables.

🧩 TRIVIA: Lundgren holds a master’s degree in chemical engineering from the University of Sydney.

1995 — Kendall Jenner (age 31) 📸

American model and media personality who became one of the most recognizable figures in contemporary fashion.

🧩 TRIVIA: Jenner made her runway debut during New York Fashion Week in 2011.

Happy birthday to them all! 🎉

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🥀 MEMORIAM

We pause with gratitude to remember those whose remarkable lives, contributions, and achievements remain part of our shared history.

1926 — Annie Oakley (aged 66) 🎯

American sharpshooter and performer whose extraordinary marksmanship made her one of the most famous stars of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West show. She became an international symbol of skill and independence. Oakley died on November 3, 1926, from pernicious anemia.

🧩 TRIVIA: During World War I, Oakley offered to fund and raise a regiment of women volunteers and to teach soldiers marksmanship. The government declined her offers.

1954 — Henri Matisse (aged 84) 🎨

French painter, sculptor, and printmaker whose bold use of color helped define modern art. Alongside Pablo Picasso, he became one of the most influential artists of the twentieth century.

🧩 TRIVIA: When illness made painting increasingly difficult, Matisse developed his celebrated cut-paper technique.

1990 — Mary Martin (aged 76) 🎭

American Broadway star remembered for South Pacific, The Sound of Music, and especially Peter Pan. Her warmth and musical talent made her one of the defining performers of the American musical stage. She died of cancer on November 3, 1990.

🧩 TRIVIA: Her portrayal of Peter Pan became iconic through a televised production.

2024 — Quincy Jones (aged 91) 🎼

American composer, arranger, and producer whose career crossed jazz, film, television, and popular music. He worked with Frank Sinatra and Ray Charles and produced Michael Jackson’s landmark albums Off the Wall, Thriller, and Bad. Jones died of pancreatic cancer on November 3, 2024.

🧩 TRIVIA: Jones won 28 Grammy Awards over his career.

2025 — Dick Cheney (aged 84) 🏛️

The 46th vice president of the United States, serving under George W. Bush from 2001 to 2009. A controversial figure in American politics, Cheney was central to the administration’s national security policy after September 11 and a leading advocate for the Iraq War. He died on November 3, 2025, from complications of pneumonia and cardiac and vascular disease.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before becoming vice president, Cheney served as U.S. secretary of defense during the Gulf War.

In fond remembrance of them all. 🕯️

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🏟️ SPORTS HIGHLIGHTS

November 3 has witnessed extraordinary individual performances, championship victories, and careers that helped define their sports.

1899 — James J. Jeffries Defeats Tom Sharkey 🥊

Heavyweight champion James J. Jeffries defeated Tom Sharkey by decision after 25 rounds at Coney Island, New York.

🧩 TRIVIA: The bout lasted all 25 scheduled rounds before the judges awarded Jeffries the decision.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Championship victory often belongs to the fighter who can endure as much as he can deliver.

1962 — Wilt Chamberlain Scores 72 Points 🏀

Wilt Chamberlain scored 72 points for the San Francisco Warriors against the Los Angeles Lakers. Despite his extraordinary performance, the Warriors lost 127–115.

🧩 TRIVIA: Chamberlain’s 72 points were the fourth-highest single-game total in NBA history at the time.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Even an astonishing individual performance cannot always overcome the collective strength of an opponent.

1968 — Graham Hill Wins the Mexican Grand Prix and the World Championship 🏎️

On November 3, 1968, Britain's Graham Hill won the Mexican Grand Prix and secured his second Formula One World Drivers' Championship.

Driving for Lotus, Hill finished ahead of Bruce McLaren and Jackie Oliver at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

The victory capped a season in which Hill's consistency and racecraft carried him to the championship.

🧩 TRIVIA: Hill had already won the Monaco Grand Prix earlier that season, one of his five victories at the famous circuit.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Championships are not always won by the fastest driver on a single afternoon; they are earned through performance across an entire season.

1996 — Kobe Bryant Makes His NBA Debut 🏀

An 18-year-old Kobe Bryant made his NBA debut for the Los Angeles Lakers against the Minnesota Timberwolves. He played six minutes and scored no points. He would go on to win five championships and earn 18 All-Star selections.

🧩 TRIVIA: At 18 years and 72 days old, Bryant became the youngest NBA player at the time; Andrew Bynum later broke the record.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A legendary career can begin with six quiet minutes.

2016 — The Chicago Cubs End a 108-Year World Series Drought ⚾

The Chicago Cubs defeated the Cleveland Indians 8–7 in ten innings in the early hours of November 3, ending a 108-year championship drought.

Game 7 had begun on November 2. After a rain delay following the ninth inning, play resumed in the tenth, and Ben Zobrist delivered the decisive RBI double.

🧩 TRIVIA: The Cubs had not won a World Series since 1908.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Some victories carry the hopes, disappointments, and memories of generations.

These sporting achievements remind us that talent, determination, innovation, and perseverance can transform individual performances into lasting history. 🏆

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

Today's question:

Which animal became the first to orbit Earth on November 3, 1957?

[A] Belka.

[B] Ham the chimpanzee.

[C] Laika.

[D] Strelka.

👇 (Scroll down to the bottom of today's issue for the answer!)

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🌎 CLOSING

And so November 3 takes its place in the history books—a day marked by courage and cruelty, independence and uncertainty, discovery and remembrance. Olympe de Gouges reminds us that the demand for equality can carry a terrible price. Panama's independence and the Kiel Uprising reveal how fiercely people struggle for self-determination. Aktion Erntefest stands as a devastating reminder of humanity's capacity for organized evil, while Laika's journey into orbit forces us to consider the price of scientific progress.

Beyond these defining events, the day's milestones, birthdays, memorials, and sporting achievements add their own chapters to the story. From constitutional change and cultural landmarks to unforgettable moments on the playing field, November 3 shows how history is shaped by both world-changing events and individual lives.

The past is never merely past. Its choices, sacrifices, triumphs, and warnings continue to shape the world we inherit.

History has had its turn. Now go make yours. ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [C] — Laika

Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth aboard the Soviet spacecraft Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. Unlike later Soviet space dogs Belka and Strelka, she was never brought home.

Her journey was a milestone in space exploration and a sobering reminder of the sacrifices made in the pursuit of scientific progress.

text:
A Speech by His Majesty King Charles III
Head of the Commonwealth @RoyalFamily 

CHOGM Opening Ceremony, St John’s Antigua
Tuesday, 3rd November 2026

"Prime Minister Browne, Secretary-General, Presidents, Prime Ministers, Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, The Queen and I are delighted to join you for this twenty-eighth Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.  

I must say it is rather sobering to think that I attended my first of these meetings almost thirty years ago. It is even more sobering to think that thirty years ago, most people had never bought anything online, many had never sent an email and connecting to the web involved a rather alarming series of screeches from a telephone line. In fact, in those days the internet was so new people referred to it as the ‘information superhighway’. I suspect that, thirty years later, many of those early users – some in this room perhaps – are still trying to remember their first passwords!  

I did want to begin by thanking the Government and people of Antigua and Barbuda for their remarkable hospitality and for making us so welcome. It was a particular pleasure to be able to celebrate on Sunday the 45th anniversary of your Independence, and to honour the achievements of Antiguans and Barbudans in so many fields. For one of the smallest nations on Earth, your impact in the world is tremendous. There is great truth in the saying: “Small Island, Big Vibes”!  Ladies and Gentlemen, that in four short years we should have met in Kigali, Apia and now St John’s, shows the extraordinary span of the Commonwealth and the diversity it represents. Our histories, circumstances and perspectives may differ, but together they inspire us in our shared endeavors and strengthen us in our common cause.  

Our Commonwealth family has mattered greatly to me for my whole life – and now, particularly, as King and Head of the Commonwealth– to which I have always tried to offer whatever service I can, especially in support of young people, of whom Commonwealth countries can count more than a billion, not to mention the protection of the uniquely important natural environments we each depend upon. I can only say how glad I am that The Queen shares my enthusiasm for our Commonwealth family and all that it represents, not least through The Queen’s Commonwealth Writing Competition.  

None of us, of course, would be here today were it not for our history, which has shaped us in myriad ways. History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know. Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs.  

History can be hard to compass, viewed as it is through the prism of time, which can be both clarifying and distorting, and yet its consequences resonate with contemporary force. Our history inspires us, can appall us, yet it can always teach us.  

We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past. The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other Members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.  And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.  

The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future. Through improving access to education, investing in jobs and opportunities, encouraging intra-Commonwealth trade, and inspiring vital climate resilience measures across the world, I have always felt that there is so much that can be done to help lift up those who struggle against hardship and disadvantage. I have always tried to play my part in doing just that. For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us – but we can choose how we set our sails.  

The Commonwealth of today is not merely a product of the past – it is a response to the world of today. Its vocation is more compelling than ever. In fact, in a desperately troubled world, the Commonwealth has welcomed new members who see the unique value of this organization and have chosen to be part of its future.  

All around us, trust between nations is under critical strain, as international norms and systems are tested to their limits. Brutal conflict stalks our world, destroying lives and casting long shadows across the globe. Technology is transforming our societies and our economies at dizzying speed, with little certainty about where it might lead us.  As I have consistently tried to emphasize, climate change is no longer just a terrifying prospect, but a catastrophic reality which threatens our very way of life. Nature is under constant attack and critical natural systems are collapsing. And in each of our countries, for too many people, the opportunity to fulfil their own potential lies far beyond their reach.  Each of these is a challenge of the highest order. Together, they comprise the crisis of our time. The Commonwealth cannot provide all of the solutions. It does, however, offer an unparalleled opportunity to work together – across our societies and our economies, through our businesses, our institutions and our communities. It allows us to draw on the collective ingenuity of a third of humanity to address the challenges confronting us all.  

This, it seems to me, is the vital essence of the Commonwealth. It lives in the people we serve. It courses through the dynamic connections between them. It flows through partnership and trade and in the solutions we find to shared challenges. It drives co-operation across borders and inspires our young people to imagine the future they can build. It provides Member States, today, here, now, with a unique opportunity: to forge common cause in the interests of our peoples.  And what unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values: of democracy and the rule of law; of respect, equal dignity and human rights; of sustainable development; of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts. And they guide us to action.  

That is why, Secretary General, the theme of this C.H.O.G.M. – Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth – represents such a vital opportunity for us all.  

To realize these opportunities, in the field of climate and Nature for example, transformative investment can drive real change, such as in renewable energy and resilient infrastructure, in sustainable, regenerative agriculture and agroforestry and food systems, in our oceans, our forests and in the natural systems upon which our economies and societies ultimately depend.  Here in the Caribbean, as in so many parts of our Commonwealth, climate change is not some distant prospect, it is an alarming reality. As we know, large Ocean States have contributed little to the causes of climate change and yet they are among those bearing the greatest cost.  

If we mobilize climate finance through the private sector, and with the leveraging capacity of the public sector, we can drive investment into climate resilience. Nature herself is an essential form of capital that sustains our prosperity and wellbeing and yet we have persisted for too long to live off Nature’s capital rather than her income. To restore Nature is therefore not to choose our environment over our economy – it is to invest in the very foundations of our economy, not to mention our security.  

The Secretary General has announced a series of Nature and climate proposals for consideration at this year’s Heads Meeting: a new Commonwealth Nature Initiative with funding to restore habitats; work with insurers on the proposal for a Commonwealth-backed mutual insurance mechanism to provide rapid payouts after disasters; and aspirations for a Commonwealth Net Zero Fund to provide access to credit for a renewable-energy revolution. I look forward to hearing how Commonwealth leaders, the private sector and civil society will work together on innovative proposals like these in support of all the citizens of the Commonwealth, especially in countries most vulnerable to the reality of climate change.  

Another area in which, it seems to me, there is such great potential for the Commonwealth to do more, is in international trade.  Our shared legal traditions, our institutions, the long-standing networks between us, as well as the English language, give us a remarkable common advantage. So much so, that the Commonwealth Enterprise and Investment Council reminds us that it is twenty-one per cent cheaper to do business across the Commonwealth.  

We can surely make far better use of this advantage – by reducing barriers to trade; improving our digital connectivity; helping small and medium-sized enterprises to find new markets; sharing the burden of insurance; and by encouraging investment across our borders.  

The potential is tremendous – and it goes far beyond trade in traditional goods. There are enormous opportunities in digital services, sustainable tourism, clean energy, the creative industries, the blue economy and in the technologies of tomorrow.  In light of all these opportunities, I was so pleased to learn of the initiatives you are pursuing, Secretary General, on intra-Commonwealth trade, including those involving the private sector, which aim at realizing that potential.  Ladies and Gentlemen, today I have had time to mention just some of the ways in which our Commonwealth can use its unique advantage to deliver real and tangible change. There are, I know, many other such opportunities which you will be discussing in the days ahead.  

As you do, I trust that you will take inspiration from the many remarkable leaders who came before you – the men and women from across the Commonwealth upon whose vision and determination, and unshakeable belief in the endless opportunity inherent in this unique family of nations, the modern Commonwealth was built.  Today the leadership of this unique institution is in your hands. Each of you has the opportunity to make the greatest possible difference. I pray that over these coming days you will embrace this opportunity and commit yourselves to action.  

I pray that you will renew your determination to build a Commonwealth in which prosperity and Nature flourish side by side; in which investment builds resilience as well as social and economic capital; and in which trade creates opportunity from which everyone can benefit – especially those people in Member States in most need of those benefits, both economic and environmental.  

Above all, Ladies and Gentlemen, I trust that each of you will recommit yourselves to a Commonwealth in which our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose. So that from this remarkable family of nations, our people can draw inspiration and hope – just as I, myself, have always done."

ENDS

text:
A Nebraska businessman sold his company for $500 MILLION and completely ruined his life. 

After his exit, he started gambling and in a single year lost $127 MILLION at one casino. 

They would get him to keep playing by giving him endless vodka and painkillers. 

He knew this was wrong and tried to sue the casino, but they were only fined $225,000.

Terrance Watanabe spent 25 years building Oriental Trading Company

His family's party favor import business in Omaha, Nebraska, turned into one of the largest mail order retailers in America.

In 2000 he sold the company. 

His net worth climbed to around $500 MILLION.

He got bored with so much time in his day now and had so much money he didn't know what to do with.

That's when Harrah's casino came into play.

It was across the river in Council Bluffs, Iowa, and he saw an ad for them on a billboard.

He then started going to pass the time.

By 2005 he was flying to Las Vegas regularly. In 2006, he was living there full-time.

Steve Wynn noticed him at the Wynn casino and called him into a private meeting.

He could see that Watanabe was a compulsive gambler and also an alcoholic.

He then was banned from the property not wanting to violate Nevada law, which prohibits casinos from letting visibly intoxicated people gamble.

Harrah's called him the same week. 

They offered $12,500 a month in airfare, Rolling Stones tickets, $500,000 in gift store credit, and 15% cash back on any table losses over $500,000.

An incredible deal for a degenerate gambler.

They had also givn him a free three bedroom suite at Caesars Palace and he obviously accepted.

2007 Terrance Watanabe bet $825 MILLION across Caesars Palace and The Rio.

Around 825,000x the average.

This was also the largest amount ever wagered by a single individual in Las Vegas history.

He lost $127 MILLION of it. 

One man generated 5.6% of Harrah's entire Las Vegas gambling revenue that year.

Casino staff kept him supplied with his preferred vodka at all times of his degeneracy.

When he became addicted to prescription painkillers, staff delivered Lortabs to him at the table hidden inside boxes of candy.

This was going too far.

He even sometimes played for 24 hours straight, one day he even lost $5 MILLION in a single day.

There was one instance where he was playing blackjack for $50,000 per hand.

You don't normally see this type of gambling.

His sister showed up at Thanksgiving 2007 and had no idea what had happened. 

She took him back to Nebraska and sent him to rehab.

The lawyers then looked closer at the actual losses, which weren't even $127 million.

text:
Iowa's vapor products directory is now expected to publish Monday, Nov 16, per the Iowa Department of Revenue. Once it's published, only listed products may be sold or offered for sale in Iowa, with penalties expected to start Dec 17.

Dates from the Department:
• Nov 16: directory expected to publish and take effect (earlier expected Oct 15)
• First 21 business days: Department says it will focus on education
• Dec 17: Department expects to begin enforcing penalties
The Department calls the timeline an estimate that may change.

Key facts:
• Applies to retailers, delivery sellers, distributors, subjobbers and manufacturers
• Eligibility (Iowa Code 453A.52): an FDA marketing order, or a product marketed as of Aug 8, 2016 with a PMTA submitted by Sept 9, 2020 that is still pending
• Certification fee: $100 per product, renewed each Aug 1
• Parts sold separately (empty tanks, batteries, coils, cases) need no listing; bundles sold at one price do

For Iowa sellers, this means the directory is in effect once it publishes, even while the Department focuses on education.

text:
Expedient acquires phoenixNAP’s U.S. managed VMware business; sales grew more than 40%

Expedient announced that it has acquired phoenixNAP’s managed VMware cloud business in the United States, expanding Expedient’s VMware Cloud Foundation business. The transaction also covers phoenixNAP’s Veeam-based backup and disaster-recovery-as-a-service operation, alongside the managed VMware services. The companies have not provided the transaction’s financial terms, so the announcement does not establish a purchase price or other deal value. The stated scope is limited to the U.S. managed VMware business, rather than phoenixNAP’s full range of operations. The clients served by the acquired services are in the United States, with service delivery from facilities in Phoenix, Arizona, and Ashburn, Virginia. Because the deal is confined to managed VMware services in the United States, it should not be read as a transfer of phoenixNAP’s entire operation.

For clients, the immediate arrangement at closing is continuity in their existing environments, service levels, consoles, and support engineers. Expedient CEO Bryan Smith said clients would not have to alter the way their businesses function on the first day of the deal. Smith also said customers would retain their VMware environments and the engineers familiar with them, supported by a team with more than 20 years of VMware management experience. Expedient says its Pinnacle-tier VMware Cloud Service Provider standing means clients’ VMware Cloud Foundation environments can stay licensed and supported without client action. These statements describe the conditions at close and the support Expedient says it can provide; the announcement does not disclose a count of affected clients. That distinction matters to organizations using the acquired service: continuity at closing is the immediate assurance, while it does not mean that future arrangements will never change.

The acquired services are delivered from two named U.S. locations: phoenixNAP facilities in Phoenix and Ashburn. The scope is defined by the business and its U.S. clients, not by a reported number of customers, workloads, or servers. Expedient says it will work with each organization over the coming months to form a longer-term plan for moving its environment onto Expedient Cloud. The company says each client will set the pace of that work, rather than having a single migration timetable imposed across the acquired business. Expedient also says no workloads, networks, or IP addresses will be moved unless a plan has first been agreed with the relevant client. The approach places the timing of a possible move with each organization, while the commitment to agree a plan first is intended to prevent unplanned transfers.

The announcement places the deal against a change in Broadcom’s VMware Cloud Service Provider program, which Broadcom is consolidating. Contracts for providers that are not renewing under that program, including phoenixNAP, are due to end in March 2027. That date describes the stated contract end for non-renewing providers; the release does not give a separate schedule for each client’s eventual move. Expedient says organizations may continue growing on VMware Cloud Foundation, seek cost optimization, or add cloud and AI services after moving to its platform. Those are options identified by Expedient for clients on its platform, not announced requirements or a fixed sequence of changes. The scheduled contract end makes planning relevant for affected clients, but the company says the pace of any later migration will be set with each organization.

phoenixNAP President Ian McClarty said the transaction would allow phoenixNAP to concentrate on its Bare Metal Cloud platform and global network while giving managed VMware clients a long-term home. phoenixNAP says its Bare Metal Cloud offering, dedicated-server services, global network, and infrastructure operations will remain in operation. That continuing activity helps define the boundary of the announced transaction: the acquired operation is the U.S. managed VMware business, while those other services remain with phoenixNAP. The deal announcement therefore describes a change in responsibility for the specified managed VMware services, without identifying a sale of phoenixNAP’s other listed operations. The parties have not disclosed deal terms, and the release gives no monetary measure for the business being transferred. For phoenixNAP, the stated effect is a chance to focus on its other platforms and services while its managed VMware clients are served by Expedient.

Expedient reports that its sales increased by more than 40% over the past 12 months, a company-wide figure rather than a disclosed value for this acquisition. The release presents that sales growth as part of strong momentum for Expedient, but does not attribute the increase to the phoenixNAP transaction. Expedient describes its Cloud platform as running on infrastructure it owns across 14 U.S. data centers. It also says the platform includes engineering support based in the United States, available 24/7/365. Those figures describe Expedient’s stated platform footprint and support availability; they are not a count of the phoenixNAP sites or clients involved in the deal. The reported sales growth provides context for Expedient’s business, while the release does not give a separate sales figure for the acquired operation.

Expedient says it is one of 14 Broadcom Pinnacle-tier VMware Cloud Service Providers in the United States. The company identifies its Pinnacle standing as the basis for keeping clients’ VMware Cloud Foundation environments fully licensed and supported without action from those clients. Broadcom’s Private Cloud Outlook 2026 found that 83% of enterprises were considering returning workloads to private cloud, compared with 69% in 2025. The later reported share is higher than the earlier one, and the figures measure enterprise consideration of private-cloud moves, not completed migrations. The outlook provides broader context about enterprise interest in private cloud, while the acquisition announcement concerns a particular managed VMware business and its clients. The survey figures indicate more enterprises were considering private-cloud returns in the later survey than in the earlier one, but they do not show how many actually moved workloads.

The release says general support for vSphere 8 ends in October 2027, after the stated March 2027 end for contracts of providers that are not renewing. These are two distinct dates in the announcement: one concerns specified provider contracts, and the other concerns general vSphere 8 support. Expedient offers a no-cost VMware Health Check that uses an RVTools export to report whether systems remain supported, their VCF 9 readiness, and compliance exposure in about a minute. The company says the Health Check workbook stays on the user’s own machine. Organizations with a VMware provider that is not renewing can also begin a 15-minute Bridge Fit Check without cost or obligation. These tools are presented as ways for organizations to review their position, with the Health Check focused on support and readiness and the Bridge Fit Check available to clients of non-renewing providers.

Together, the announcement describes an immediate continuation of current client setups and a later process in which each organization can plan its path to Expedient Cloud. Expedient says clients retain their current service levels and engineers at close, while later migration planning is to be conducted with each organization. The company’s stated migration safeguards include client control of pace and prior agreement before any workloads, networks, or IP addresses move. The broader transaction remains limited to phoenixNAP’s U.S. managed VMware cloud business, with its other named services continuing under phoenixNAP. No purchase terms were released, so the announcement establishes the businesses and services involved but not a financial measure of the acquisition. Taken together, the stated commitments address both continuity now and client participation in possible later changes, while leaving the deal’s financial value undisclosed.

text:
🌾 Update on Monette Farms

Monette Farms has asked the court to extend its creditor protection from Nov 13 to Nov 25, 2026. The hearing is Tuesday, Nov 10 at 2:00 PM, before Justice D.R. Mah on Webex. 

The company says it needs the time to finish harvest, close the Arizona sale and finish the sale process.

The details are in Darrel Monette's fifth affidavit:

Harvest: The group seeded about 385,000 acres and harvested about 500,000 tonnes. About 3,000 acres are still out, mostly in northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Yields and quality came in a bit below expectations because of a wet September.

Sale process: Bids were due Nov 3 and are still under review, and the process ends Dec 4. The company aims to close deals by year end.

Arizona: The US court approved the sale on Sept 30, but it hasn't closed yet. It's waiting on the transfer of some state-granted leases. The updated service list names Byner Cattle Company as the buyer.

Aircraft: The company is cancelling the USD 1,050,000 sale of its Beechcraft Premier 1 (C-GYPV) to Industrial Measuring Systems because windshield parts can't be sourced. The cancellation takes effect Nov 15. A letter filed with the affidavit says another buyer has offered USD 985,000 as-is.

Assuming a typical prairie mix of cereals, oilseeds and pulses Monette’s harvest would be around 52 bu/ac which is far from paying off $1.1 billion they owe.

Outside Lonoke, Arkansas, student pilots learned to fly in planes they called "flying coffins."

And the town cemetery sat right across the road from the airfield. The instructors made sure the cadets noticed.

This was Eberts Field, a World War I flight school almost nobody remembers.

In 1917, Lonoke County outbid Pulaski County for the Army's aviation school. Lonoke offered 960 acres rent-free and a new railroad spur to the Rock Island line. The government said yes on November 19, 1917. Construction started a month later.

By spring 1918, cadets were arriving. Before barracks were finished, enlisted men slept in the Lonoke school gym.

The field was named for Melchior McEwen Eberts, a Little Rock native and West Point man, class of 1915. He became one of the Army's early aviators. On May 15, 1917, the day he was promoted to captain, he took off from Columbus, New Mexico, for an exhibition flight. His plane went down and he was killed. He was 27.

About 1,000 cadets trained at the field that bore his name, with around 1,500 officers and enlisted men stationed there.

They learned in the Curtiss JN-4D "Jenny." Wood, wire, fabric, open cockpit. Hence the nickname.

The Arkansas Gazette reported it wasn't unusual to see several hundred planes flying in formation over the field.

At the northeast end stood a dirt mound about 20 feet high. Cadets fired thousands of machine gun rounds into it, learning to shoot from a moving airplane. Local kids later dug bullets out of it.

Then the war ended on November 11, 1918, shortly before the first class graduated.

The field kept flying a while longer. On June 18, 1919, Lt. C. E. Johnson of Eberts Field flew 300 copies of the Arkansas Gazette to Lonoke. It was the first newspaper delivered by airplane in Arkansas.

That November, stunt fliers swooped under the Little Rock bridges over the Arkansas River while thousands watched from the banks.

Today, a few concrete foundations, a historical marker, and an old flying field are about all that's left.

How many times have you driven past a spot like this without knowing what happened there?

#Arkansas #WW1

text:
Lean hog futures have been under steady pressure since early September, and the selloff picked up speed last week. December lean hogs (/HEZ26) fell $2.65 on October 27 to settle at $62.025 per hundredweight, the lowest close for a nearby contract since December 2020. The cash market has led the way lower, with USDA’s national base hog price dropping to $57.94 and the CME Lean Hog Index slipping to $70.06.

Weak wholesale pork demand is the main reason. USDA’s pork carcass cutout value fell to $73.09, also the lowest since December 2020, and is down nearly 25% from its summer peak, with bellies and hams leading the decline. Consumers have not shifted to pork despite high beef prices, and larger chicken supplies are adding competition at the meat case. Pork in cold storage totaled 427.8 million pounds at the end of September, nearly 9% above a year ago. With slaughter entering its seasonal peak and most holiday ham buying already done, packers have little reason to chase hogs.

Supplies are less of a concern. USDA’s September Quarterly Hogs and Pigs report put the U.S. herd at 74.3 million head, down 2% from last year, and the breeding herd at 5.875 million, the smallest September total since 2013. However, record litter sizes and heavier slaughter weights have kept pork production slightly above last year. USDA’s October supply and demand report cut 2026 pork production by 150 million pounds to 27.6 billion, trimmed exports to 7.05 billion pounds on weaker shipments to Western Hemisphere markets and lowered its 2026 hog price forecast by about $1 to $63.79 per hundredweight. Trade remains a headwind, as U.S. pork still faces retaliatory duties in China and demand growth from Mexico, the top export market, has slowed.

The lean hog futures price curve suggests traders expect conditions to improve next year. June 2027 lean hogs settled at $85.00, more than $20 above December, reflecting tighter hog supplies expected through mid-2027 and stronger summer grilling demand. Fund positioning could also matter, as managed money held a large net short position of about 41,100 contracts as of October 20, which could fuel a short-covering rally if cash prices stabilize. Seasonal patterns may limit any near-term rebound, though, as the pork cutout has often posted its fourth-quarter low in early December.

In the near term, traders will be watching daily cash hog and cutout values for signs of a bottom, along with weekly export sales and slaughter weights. USDA’s next supply and demand report on November 10 and the December 23 Quarterly Hogs and Pigs report will offer fresh reads on production and prices heading into 2027.
