EARLY VOTING IS UP FOR THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS COMPARED TO 2022 AND MORE DEMOCRATS THAN REPUBLICANS VOTED EARLY  

As a general rule turnout for midterm elections is normally lower than for general elections.

Political observers are marveling at those numbers and note how they surged in places with more competitive Senate contests, such as Ohio, Maine and Michigan.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton have locked horns in arguably the most watched race of this year's cycle. The early totals show more than 7.7 million people have cast early ballots, which surpasses the Lone Star State's high mark of 40% turnout during the 2018 midterms.

"Their record for a midterm election is 8.3 million total. So they're just over about 600,000 or so ballots away from their highest turnout ever... Election Day hasn't even happened yet. That's remarkable," David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said during CBS' Face the Nation on Nov. 1.

The pattern of early voting is also happening in other key states: 

++ Georgia, where more than 2.8 million voters have showed up already representing a 13% increase compared to 2022; 

++ Michigan with more than 2.3 million marking a 26% increase; 

++ South Carolina where about 1.1 million have shown up compared to approximately 620,000 four years ago which is a whomping 75% increase.

What early voting does and doesn’t tell us about the 2026 midterms
Turnout is surging, especially in states with key races and the increasingly diverse electorate has skewed Democratic.

Early voting data for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections indicates a surge in turnout characterized by a younger, more diverse, and more politically independent electorate. Preliminary figures show higher engagement among Democrats and voters of color, while Republican turnout appears lower in comparison.

On the eve of Election Day a record number of Americans have already passed judgement on President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress.

Roughly 57 million voters cast their early ballots over this past weekend ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.

The deluge offers a glimpse into a forecasted wave election that many experts believe could sweep Democrats in power for the president's final two years in the White House.

Every state has different rules on compiling voters' age, race or party affiliation with some providing no demographic statistics at all. But it does reveal important voter behavior and some demographics that paint a clearer picture about who is more motivated in the 2026 midterms.

Michael McDonald, a political science professor who runs the Election Lab, said the initial outlook indicates a younger, more diverse and politically independent electorate is showing up.

"I can confidently say that the 2026 election will be the most diverse midterm electorate in U.S. history," in an Oct. 28 post on X.

But the data alone, much like the various polls, cannot predict the outcome of who will be in charge of the House and Senate next year, McDonald and others have warned.

Here's a look at the big takeaways from the early voting totals.

A lot more people are showing up than in 2022
Early voting in Tallahassee, Florida, on Oct. 19, 2026.
For starters, 8 million more people took advantage of the early in-person and mail-in ballot options over the weekend than during the last 2022 midterms, which gave Republicans control of the House during former President Joe Biden's term.

Political observers are marveling at those numbers and note how they surged in places with more competitive Senate contests, such as Ohio, Maine and Michigan.

text:
The Data Center Wants Credit for Turning Itself Down

OpenAI’s first detailed Grid Protectors example is a proposed Georgia compute campus with a planned electric load of roughly 3,200 megawatts. Its utility contract includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response when the grid is under strain. [1][3]

That is the practical consequence behind the launch language. A future data center designed to consume power on the scale of several large generating stations would sometimes be able to cut roughly a third of its planned draw. An enormous new customer wants credit for briefly becoming a smaller customer.

The contract is more specific than the national program

Georgia Power says the proposed Effingham County project will pay the full cost of the infrastructure and electric service required to serve it. The utility places the contract inside a wider portfolio of large-load agreements that it projects will reduce customer costs by $950 million a year beginning in 2029, including at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours. [2][3]

Those are meaningful commitments if the campus is built, the load arrives and the demand-response system performs. They are also projections issued by the utility and the prospective customer. They are not observed household bills, an operating record or an independent stress test.

The distinction matters because “flexible load” is becoming the preferred answer to a basic infrastructure problem: AI developers want enormous amounts of electricity faster than grids can add generation and transmission. Curtailment can help during tight periods. It does not create the missing power lines, substations or generation needed during all the other hours.

A framework with site-specific blanks

OpenAI describes Grid Protectors as a national program for future compute campuses. It says each arrangement will reflect local conditions and that additional commitments will be announced as sites move forward. That makes the Georgia contract evidence of one negotiated structure, not proof that every OpenAI campus will offer the same flexibility, customer protections or cost allocation. [1]

The Georgia project is still in development. “Up to 1,000 megawatts” is a contractual ceiling, not a meter reading. The utility’s savings estimate begins years from now. None of that makes the agreement imaginary. It sets the proper evidentiary level: a real contract around a proposed campus, with performance and consumer effects still to be demonstrated.

The useful test is not whether a press release says the grid will be protected. It is whether the campus pays every attributable cost, curtails when called, publishes enough operating evidence to check the claim, and leaves ordinary customers better off after the forecasts meet an actual bill.

Sources:
[1] OpenAI: Introducing the Grid Protectors Program — November 2, 2026

[2] Georgia Power: Georgia PSC approves OpenAI contract as part of large-load portfolio — August 26, 2026

text:
My father and I shared a mentor/student relationship for the whole of my life. It was he who taught each of us to measure twice and cut once – and anytime I measured once and screwed up the cut, I always thought back to those backyard lessons in the early ‘70s at our rambling two-story house in a formerly genteel part of town. I first learned by watching, and then by doing under his supervision.
 
 A summer storm blew down our rows of sweet corn one summer night, and in the morning, Dad asked me to try and set up as many of the plants as I was able; it took most of the morning, but I straightened each stalk, tamped dirt around them, and they once again stood tall. Perhaps he had been watching through the kitchen window, because as I walked over to the old pump to wash the dirt off my hands, he came out of the back door and warmly thanked me.  And then he handed me two or three dollars – a gesture I sure hadn't even been dreaming about.
 
 When he opened his own print shop in 1976, I was there – helping in any way that I could without getting underfoot.  I was just barely thirteen, and so began my life in printing as his printer's devil . . . once the shop was set up and work began, Dad first taught me how to use the Ludlow Typograph to set lines of larger type, and the Vandercook proof press to make sure everything was spelled correctly.  Soon, I was setting much of the Ludlow type needed in the shop and rarely made a mistake.  I even learned where all the characters were located in the case and could gather the individual brass matrices quickly and with ease . . . to the point that he trusted me, a thirteen-year-old, to set and proof type that he could then deliver without worry.

Soon enough, he had taught me how to smelt the type metal, to clean it, and to pour pigs of lead alloy that I then needed to carry up from the basement. This wasn’t normally boy’s work – and yet, even on something as dangerous as melting metal at 550°F, he taught me what he had first learned thirty-five years earlier and taught me to do so safely. He initially had concerns when I told him – at age seventeen – that I’d asked Grace to marry me . . . but he and mom had taught each of us what a good marriage consisted of. Even as a child in Michigan when Dad would come home for lunch each day, he always kissed Mom goodbye (and me, too – I still remember his scratchy whiskers), and their love for the other was always on display.

After high school, I worked with him in a different print shop, and the training continued; the day came when an expensive order of business cards was printed with a 3 instead of an 8 – Dad’s mistake – and I suggested cutting another 8 in half and trying to match up the left half of that one character with the 3 already on the sheet by running them through the press again; he was genuinely impressed and grateful that my suggestion worked – and so was I, since I wanted my dad to be proud of me. He offered advice when I began to collect letterpress equipment for my own print shop, and then would often show up to help, to talk, or perhaps to set and print type for his own needs. (I still have some of the type he composed.)

If I had an issue with my Linotype machines, Dad, who had been running these beasts since he was fifteen, was always ready to help me fix whatever had gone wrong. There were times when I didn’t have the time to set my own type, and he would always agree to help – and even into his eighties was still faster than I ever was.

The Linotype machines are complicated and hard to explain, but each used large and very heavy flat containers called magazines to hold the small typesetting matrices. The day came when he called me across the shop and asked if I could switch out one of these for another . . . and that was the day when I began to realize that he was getting older.

Dad had been saved in the 1940 and as the decade went forward felt called to attend Bible school; Minneapolis in 1945 was the largest city he had ever visited . . . he and our mother met shortly after classes began, and they were soon exchanging letters – especially when away from the other. By the early summer of 1946 they were already talking about their plans once married . . . and although I’ll not share the contents of these constant notes back and forth, it was easy to see that they loved God and wanted to do their best for Him, and that they were head over heels in love. They had to have permission of the school faculty just to become engaged and did so October 31, 1947.

I’ve often felt like an intruder while reading those letters – but love the thought that both couldn’t wait to see Christ, and both hoped for His soon return. Some hurt – the replies to Airmail letters Dad mailed after the death of our oldest sister are tough to read. Mostly, there was longing to see each other, such as when Dad had to take a job downstate in Michigan for a few months – he would drive down to Battle Creek late Sunday night or Monday morning and return home to northern Michigan on Friday evening. He did this while pastoring two churches on Sunday.

What he did, he did out of love for his wife and family – and that included telling me why he didn’t like a Monomelt but did like the Margach feeder, or showing me the right way to adjust the Linotype or how to clean dross off of clean type metal. This continued through the rest of his life until one day I found that he had made a potentially dangerous adjustment to the Linotype . . . I began to be the one giving him guidance, and eventually I had to make the difficult decision to no longer allow him to run his beloved machine – a contraption he had left high school in order to learn and run. When Mom had to have a risky heart surgery in another city, Dad refused to leave her side for that entire month.

His twilight years were filled with a certain amount of confusion, and we made the decision to take away his car keys. I am still filled with guilt over the necessary decision I took part in that separated him from mom . . . he was never able to return home. The folks missed each other; Dad would walk with us to the door when Mom’s visits had to draw to an end, and later, he would go along by wheelchair. Their sixty-fifth anniversary came and went, and then his eighty-ninth birthday . . . and two weeks later on November 3rd, he was instantly healed of his afflictions and embraced in the arms of the Saviour he had served his whole life. I’ll never forget watching Mom kiss him goodbye for the last time, but three months later she joined him in heaven.

“Measure twice, cut once” meant “I love you.”

“These machines don’t care, don’t think, and can kill you” meant “I love you.”

“I love you” meant “I’ve prayed for you since before you were born.”

Dad – I love you.

text:
Dave Dahl stepped out of Oregon State Penitentiary on a December morning in 2004, holding everything he owned in a plastic bag.
He was 41 years old.
It was the fourth time he'd been released. Four stints. Fifteen years of his life spent behind bars—his twenties, his thirties—for drug possession, burglary, assault, and armed robbery. The mistakes were his. The time was real.
Nobody wanted to hire him.
His tattoos told stories nobody wanted to hear. His criminal record was longer than most job applications. He was a statistic, a warning, a cautionary tale nobody was looking to invest in.
The only person who believed he deserved another chance was his brother Glenn.
Glenn had inherited the family bakery—NatureBake—their father had founded decades earlier. It was a modest operation, nothing glamorous, but it was real. Glenn offered Dave work out of pure family loyalty: mix dough, clean pans, show up at 4 AM. It wasn't charity dressed up as opportunity. It was just honest work for someone with nowhere else to turn.
But inside that bakery, something unexpected happened.
Dave stopped destroying himself. For the first time in decades, he had a place to channel his energy that didn't hurt him. He started experimenting with the bread—adding organic whole grains, seeds, dense ingredients that no one else was baking. It wasn't soft. It wasn't processed. It was real bread for people who wanted real food.
In 2005, Dave pitched his brother on something radical: a new product line. He wanted to call it Dave's Killer Bread. And then he said something that made Glenn pause.
He wanted his mugshot on the front of every loaf.
Not hidden. Not censored. Front and center. With his full story printed on the back—the prison time, the mistakes, the second chance, all of it. Raw. Honest. Unapologetic.
Every industry expert said it was marketing suicide. "No one will buy bread from a felon," they said. "You're destroying yourself before you even start."
They were spectacularly wrong.
People didn't buy Dave's Killer Bread despite his past. They bought it because of it. They saw a man who had hit rock bottom, told the truth about it, and rebuilt himself with his own hands. They saw proof—real, tangible, purchasable proof—that second chances actually exist. That redemption isn't just a story people tell. It's something you can buy at the grocery store and hold in your hands.
And the bread? It was genuinely exceptional. Dense, flavorful, loaded with seeds and whole grains. It wasn't a gimmick. It was made by someone with something to prove.
Within a year, Dave's Killer Bread was the top-selling organic bread in Portland.
Within five years, it was in stores across the country.
In 2015, Flowers Foods acquired the company for $275 million. A man who couldn't get hired anywhere had built something worth a quarter billion dollars. But Dave didn't pocket the money and disappear.
He had bigger ideas.
Before the sale, Dave built an entire hiring program dedicated to Second Chances. He deliberately recruited men and women coming out of prison—people with records, people being turned away everywhere else. He trained them. He paid them fairly. More importantly, he treated them like they mattered. Like their past didn't define their future. Hundreds of people rebuilt their lives in that bakery.
But the story didn't end with success.
Dave carried something invisible for years—undiagnosed bipolar disorder. The structure and purpose of the bakery had kept it manageable. But when he stepped back from the company, everything shifted. He faced a mental health crisis that nearly broke him. And then, true to everything he'd ever stood for, he talked about it publicly.
Because if hiding his criminal record would have been dishonest, hiding his mental illness was no different.
"You are not your worst mistake," he tells anyone who will listen. "Your past does not define your future."
Dave's Killer Bread is still on shelves today. His face—tattooed, bearded, unpolished—is still on every package. His story is still printed on the back. And somewhere right now, someone is walking out of a correctional facility with a plastic bag in their hand, convinced the world has given up on them.
Dave Dahl's story exists so they know it hasn't.
Your past is not your destiny. It's just how your story started.

-Golden Historical Images

U.S. Midterm Elections 2026: My Final Prediction and Political Analysis

November 3, 2026 — Election Day Forecast

My prediction: Democrats will win control of the House of Representatives and are also favored to capture the Senate, delivering a significant political setback to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

My central forecast is a Democratic majority of approximately 240 to 195 seats in the House and a narrower 52 to 48 Democratic-aligned majority in the Senate. I estimate the probability of Democrats winning the House at around 95%, while their chances of capturing the Senate stand at approximately 75%. These are analytical estimates, not official election results.

The available polling suggests that Republicans face an exceptionally difficult political environment. However, the distinction between a Democratic victory and a historic Democratic landslide remains important.

Why Democrats Are Favored to Win the House

The House of Representatives offers the clearest indication of the national political mood.

Historically, the president’s party tends to lose congressional seats during midterm elections. Voters frequently use these elections to express dissatisfaction with the administration, particularly when economic expectations remain unfulfilled.

During Trump’s first presidency, Democrats gained approximately 40 House seats in the 2018 midterms. Although the political landscape has changed considerably since then, a similar anti-incumbent dynamic appears to be operating in 2026.

The final national polling reinforces this expectation. The Silver Bulletin generic congressional ballot average shows Democrats leading by approximately nine percentage points, while the latest Reuters/Ipsos survey places Democratic support among likely voters at 52%, compared with 44% for Republicans.

Such figures indicate a substantial national advantage. Nevertheless, congressional elections are decided district by district rather than through a single nationwide vote.

Redistricting, geographic polarization, and the relatively small number of competitive districts limit the extent to which national polling advantages translate into additional seats. Consequently, I consider a Democratic majority of approximately 240 seats more plausible than an extraordinary landslide exceeding 260.

My House forecast: Democrats 240, Republicans 195.

The Senate: The Real Battleground

The Senate represents a considerably more difficult challenge for Democrats.

Republicans currently hold 53 seats, while the Democratic caucus, including aligned independents, controls 47. Since the vice president can break a 50–50 tie, Democrats need at least 51 seats to secure an effective majority.

This requires a net gain of four seats.

Several states are especially important.

In North Carolina, former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper appears well positioned to capture a Republican-held seat. His statewide electoral experience gives Democrats one of their strongest opportunities.

Maine presents another significant opportunity. Republican Senator Susan Collins has historically maintained a reputation for political independence, but the unfavorable national environment makes her reelection campaign particularly challenging.

Ohio could also become a Democratic pickup. Former Senator Sherrod Brown possesses statewide experience and considerable name recognition, although Ohio’s increasingly Republican electoral character remains a substantial obstacle.

Texas may produce one of the most politically significant results of the entire election. Democrat James Talarico is challenging Republican Ken Paxton in a state that has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1988. A Democratic victory there would demonstrate that the national political shift extends beyond traditional swing states.

Alaska, Kansas, and Iowa provide additional opportunities, although all three remain difficult electoral environments for Democrats.

My central Senate scenario assumes that Democrats successfully defend their existing seats while capturing North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, and Alaska.

That would result in a Democratic-aligned Senate majority of approximately 52–48.

Nevertheless, I am substantially less confident about this prediction than my House forecast. A relatively small polling error could reverse several close Senate contests simultaneously.

My Senate forecast: Democratic caucus 52, Republicans 48.

The Trump Factor

President Donald Trump is arguably the central political figure in this election, despite not appearing on the ballot himself.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos polling indicates that his approval rating has fallen to approximately 32%. Moreover, 48% of surveyed voters who intended to vote or had already voted described their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 25% who characterized it as a vote in his favor.

This imbalance suggests that opposition to the president has become a stronger mobilizing force than support for his administration.

However, an important distinction must be made: Voting against Trump does not necessarily imply enthusiastic support for the Democratic Party.

Many Americans may simply regard the election as an opportunity to impose political limits on the administration.

The result could therefore represent a rejection of Republican governance rather than an unequivocal endorsement of the Democrats’ policy agenda.

The Economy and Cost of Living

Economic dissatisfaction is likely to be one of the most consequential factors determining the election.

According to the final Reuters/Ipsos survey, approximately 48% of registered voters identify the cost of living as their most important electoral issue.

Almost half of surveyed Americans report that their household finances have deteriorated since Trump returned to office in January 2025, while only a considerably smaller proportion report improvement.

For an incumbent administration, such perceptions create an obvious political vulnerability.

Republicans can emphasize taxation, deregulation, immigration enforcement, and their broader economic priorities. Nevertheless, voters frequently evaluate economic performance through everyday experiences: grocery prices, housing expenses, energy costs, healthcare bills, and purchasing power.

If substantial numbers of Americans believe their standard of living has declined, the governing party is likely to bear much of the political responsibility.

The administration’s economic message has apparently failed to persuade enough dissatisfied voters that their circumstances are improving.

Foreign Policy and the Iran War

Foreign policy has introduced an additional source of political controversy.

The war with Iran has intensified concerns about military commitments, economic costs, and international instability.

Polling indicates that a majority of Americans question whether U.S. military action against Iran has justified its consequences.

Higher energy prices have also reinforced concerns about affordability.

For Democrats, these developments provide an opportunity to criticize the administration’s strategic priorities and decision-making.

Nevertheless, foreign policy is unlikely to determine every congressional race independently. Voters may still prioritize economic conditions, immigration, individual candidates, and longstanding partisan loyalties.

The cumulative effect, however, appears unfavorable to Republicans.

Why Republicans Could Still Perform Better Than Expected

Despite the strength of the Democratic position, several uncertainties deserve serious consideration.

First, national polling has underestimated Republican support in previous electoral cycles, particularly in 2020 and 2024. Another systematic polling error could substantially change the outcomes of close Senate races.

Second, voter enthusiasm does not automatically translate into turnout. Republican supporters may participate at higher rates than expected, particularly in traditionally conservative states.

Third, individual candidates remain important. Republican incumbents with strong local reputations may outperform the national party, while Democratic challengers can struggle to translate national dissatisfaction into statewide majorities.

Fourth, the Republican Party retains substantial organizational resources and financial support, particularly in competitive Senate elections.

Finally, the electoral geography of the Senate disproportionately benefits states that have recently voted Republican.

For these reasons, a Democratic House majority accompanied by continued Republican control of the Senate remains a credible alternative outcome.

Three Possible Election Scenarios

Scenario One: A Major Democratic Wave

Democrats win approximately 245–255 House seats and secure 53–55 Senate seats.

This outcome would indicate that the national anti-Republican mood has reached well beyond conventional swing districts and states.

It would represent a major political rejection of the Trump administration and significantly strengthen Democratic congressional leadership.

Scenario Two: A Solid Democratic Victory — My Most Likely Outcome

Democrats capture approximately 235–245 House seats and achieve a narrow Senate majority of 51–53 seats.

Republicans suffer significant electoral losses, but the outcome does not become an overwhelming national landslide.

This is the scenario that best reflects my interpretation of the final polling, historical patterns, candidate-specific factors, and electoral geography.

Scenario Three: Republican Resilience

Democrats win a smaller House majority of approximately 220–235 seats, while Republicans retain control of the Senate with around 50–51 seats.

Such an outcome could result from stronger-than-expected Republican turnout, systematic polling errors, or Republican candidates outperforming their party’s national standing.

Washington would enter a period of divided congressional control, with Democrats controlling the House but Republicans retaining the presidency and Senate.

What Would a Democratic Victory Mean for Trump?

If Democrats gain control of the House, they would acquire important institutional powers.

They could control committee leadership, initiate investigations, conduct oversight hearings, issue congressional subpoenas, and challenge major aspects of the administration’s agenda.

Hakeem Jeffries would become the leading candidate for Speaker of the House.

A Democratic Senate majority would have even broader consequences.

Democrats could influence judicial confirmations, control Senate committees, oversee executive appointments, and place substantial institutional constraints on the administration.

However, even control of both chambers would not allow Democrats to govern without restrictions.

Trump would retain presidential veto powers, while Senate procedural rules would continue to limit the passage of many legislative proposals.

Therefore, Democratic control of Congress would primarily strengthen the opposition’s ability to constrain the president rather than automatically enable a comprehensive alternative legislative agenda.

Historical Perspective

The 2006 midterm elections under President George W. Bush provide an interesting historical comparison.

At that time, dissatisfaction with the Iraq War, economic concerns, and declining presidential approval contributed to substantial Democratic gains.

Democrats captured approximately 30 House seats and six Senate seats, taking control of both chambers.

The 2018 midterms under Trump provide another relevant precedent. Democrats gained approximately 40 House seats, although Republicans actually increased their Senate majority.

These examples demonstrate that a national political backlash can produce very different results across the two chambers.

Today’s highly polarized electoral geography further complicates direct historical comparisons.

A substantial Democratic advantage in the national popular vote does not necessarily guarantee an equally dramatic transformation in congressional representation.

Final Assessment

My forecast remains a clear Democratic victory, with approximately 240 House seats and 52 Democratic-aligned Senate seats.

I assign roughly a 95% probability to Democratic control of the House and a 75% probability to Democratic control of the Senate.

The House outcome appears comparatively straightforward: National polling, historical midterm patterns, and dissatisfaction with the administration all point toward a Democratic majority.

The Senate remains the principal uncertainty. Its outcome depends on whether Democrats can translate a favorable national political environment into victories in several states that have historically favored Republicans.

The most important contests to watch are North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Alaska, Kansas, and Iowa.

A Democratic sweep across several of these states would suggest that the election has developed into a genuine national wave.

Conversely, stronger Republican performances in Ohio, Texas, and Alaska could preserve Republican Senate control even in the face of substantial Democratic House gains.

My ultimate conclusion is that November 3, 2026, is likely to become a significant turning point in Donald Trump’s second presidency.

The American electorate appears increasingly inclined to impose institutional limits on his administration, driven primarily by economic dissatisfaction, concerns about presidential leadership, and opposition to key government policies.

The remaining question is not simply whether Democrats will win, but whether their victory will be strong enough to transform the balance of power in Washington.

My answer: Probably yes — in both chambers, although the Senate remains considerably less certain.

This is an election-day analytical forecast, not a declaration of actual election results. All probabilities are estimates and remain subject to electoral uncertainty.

De FAIR à AI-FAIR : une infrastructure axée sur les métadonnées pour la science assistée par l’IA : https://t.co/8TkIi3qaHC

"arXiv:2611.03327v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvBaIT] 02 Nov 2026
From FAIR to AI-FAIR: Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
Elizabeth G. CampolongoEqual Contribution: campolongo.4@osu.edu, esokol@battelleecology.org Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State UniversityEric R. Sokol*National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON), BattelleMarty DownsLong Term Ecological Research Network, National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, UC Santa BarbaraGina GlenneUS Fish and Wildlife ServiceGregory E. MaurerNew Mexico State UniversitySydne RecordUniversity of Maine & Maine Agricultural and Forest Experiment StationDustin R. RubensteinEcology, Evolution and Environmental Biology, Columbia University, NSCOREMatthew J. ThompsonDepartment of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State UniversityChristine LaneyNational Ecological Observatory Network (NEON), BattelleHilmar LappNeuromatchMax TarjanNatureServeTanya Berger-WolfDepartment of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State UniversityNovember 2026Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question–Data–Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow 11Code available at: https://t.co/s99SVR9eGC. that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.
From FAIR Data to Bidirectional, AI-Ready Infrastructure
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing how research in the domains of ecology and biodiversity science is conducted (Pollock et al., 2025). However, current workflows still rely on data infrastructure built primarily to encourage researcher data contributions rather than to prioritize the machine-readability and cross-dataset interoperability that facilitate data reuse (Crystal-Ornelas et al., 2022). In both domains, data span species occurrences, images, audio, genomic sequences, sensor observations, field measurements, synthesized species biological information, and environmental covariates (Feng et al., 2025). Heterogeneous communities produce these assets using different terminologies, collecting data at varied spatial and temporal scales, releasing data under diverse licenses and governance frameworks, and storing data in siloed repositories. Fragmented storage, inconsistent formats, limited interoperability, and incomplete scientific context have long presented hurdles for ecological synthesis efforts (O’Brien et al., 2021), and these barriers have become no more tractable as ecologists develop AI-enabled workflows (Mishra, 2026). We refer to these persistent obstacles to scientific discovery as the FAIR-gap.While the original FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016) remain necessary, they are not sufficient criteria to guide AI-ready infrastructure in the sciences and overcome the FAIR-gap (Huerta et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2026; Shehu & Nussinov, 2026). AI-enabled, data-driven science requires machine-actionable access and interpretation at the appropriate scale. Even a findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable dataset may require extensive human intervention to determine whether the data are appropriate and permitted for a scientific task, or to connect augmented information (e.g., errors flagged or enhancements) back to the original source.Extensive global museum digitization efforts, growing community science platform engagement, and increasing accessibility and sensitivity of sensor technologies have produced vast quantities of data faster than can be processed and analyzed through traditional methods. As AI-driven search is increasingly replacing traditional algorithms, FAIR-gapped data risk exclusion from search results, preventing researchers from even considering them. Collecting and curating biodiversity data is labor-intensive; they should not be excluded from consideration because researchers (or AI agents) cannot find or access them, nor should they be misattributed or used for analyses they do not support. The time required to manually sift through these data is rapidly exceeding the capacity of individual researchers. Moreover, the effort, resources, and time that goes into data collection are translated into scientific value and meaning only when those data are used, and attribution is a recognition of those efforts.Enabling automated assessment of data for scientific use (e.g., using an agentic AI system to perform a broad scale analysis across multiple databases and flag those of interest for manual review) provides a force-multiplier, but this capability requires increased and more consistent documentation of the datasets. Drawing from the FAIR4AI framework (Huerta et al., 2023) and the FAIR data principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016), we define AI-FAIR metadata criteria as the key to AI-enabled science with bidirectional value. Rather than developing a new prescriptive data specification, we complement ongoing work by Bridge2AI (Clark et al., 2026) and the FAIR2 Alliance (n.d.). Our framework focuses on foundational metadata components that data providers can integrate into their chosen standards to accelerate scientific discovery and ensure lasting value.
FAIR4AI-Bio network
The FAIR4AI-Bio network was conceived to address the FAIR-gap by placing the data providers and users at the center of the solutions. This process includes hosting a series of workshops to understand requirements for AI-ready data infrastructure in ecology, biodiversity science, and related fields. The guiding mission through these workshops is to create a community-informed system for unifying biodiversity data at scale, one that promotes trust and encourages the exchange of data. We started by creating an inventory of the platforms and tools used by data producers, providers, managers, and scientists who work with ecological and biodiversity data. We then gathered feedback from the workshop community to identify the challenges and critical blockers encountered with these platforms and tools, and synthesized these into a collection of requirements to address the FAIR-gap: our AI-FAIR framework. This community relies heavily on multimodal data integration for analyses, and addressing this complexity of use-cases will support the design of a robust prototype of the AI-FAIR framework.Dataset properties that extend from traditional FAIR principles to AI-FAIR specifically enable machines to use data with minimal human intervention. These include essential metadata to provide the context and controls required for scientifically valid and responsible use at scale. It is impractical to expect data publishers to anticipate the requirements for all possible AI-enabled uses of their data, but AI-FAIR criteria offer guidance for data publishers to provide enhanced metadata that enable more efficient, automated, and accurate inclusion of their data in AI workflows at scale (Figure 1).📷Figure 1:The AI-FAIR continuum. FAIR principles apply broadly to data without directed downstream use cases. AI-FAIR principles extend traditional FAIR with AI-enabled assessment and processing as a goal. AI-ready is use-case specific, but may be enabled, e.g., through Agentic workflows, when AI-FAIR standards are met.

The Question-Data-Model Framework: Roundtripping for Added Value
The AI-FAIR perspective frames AI-enabled science as a Question-Data-Model triangle (Figure 2). In a complete system, every edge is bidirectional. Questions specify required data properties and model capabilities.📷Figure 2:The Question-Data-Model framework. Questions specify required data and models; models declare capabilities and data needs; data inform and are enriched by questions and models.
Models declare their assumptions, capabilities, and data requirements. Data inform both questions and models, while also being enriched by the outputs of scientific interpretation and computation.However, the data vertex remains mostly unidirectional: data flow from collectors to aggregators, to models, and finally to research products or management actions. At each transition, the provenance chain is often weakened or severed, exacerbating challenges in returning information to data sources. This degradation of provenance increases the risk of data leakage, where evaluation data are included in model training. Furthermore, solving this requires additional complex processing—such as perceptual hashing (Zhou et al., 2025)—to disentangle aggregated data that are no longer traceable to their sources. Without context resolution, scientists are limited in the conclusions they can draw from model results, further increasing the likelihood that value created downstream will not return to the people and systems that produced the data used to train and evaluate it.We posit that data value roundtripping (Larsson et al., 2019; Groom et al., 2022) must be prioritized in efforts to design distributed AI-ready infrastructure. As AI systems process data—aided by expert validation—enhancing metadata, harmonizing taxonomies, detecting and flagging anomalies, and identifying gaps, they generate intermediate products for which there must be a mechanism to provide these artifacts back to the source repositories. For example, large-scale synthesis in ecology and biodiversity science often involves correcting or aligning taxonomies; identifying bounding boxes for images; detecting and flagging data anomalies; filling gaps in time-series data; assimilating data from other sources, and augmenting labels. Without a provenance chain and standardized metadata detailing the returns desirable by a data collector, all such data augmentation will remain siloed in data archives specific to synthesis projects. Other synthesis efforts will be required to repeat similar processing, with little to no benefit flowing to source repositories, communities, or data https://t.co/maF53BeRmZ sources should be able to incorporate new knowledge with versioning, provenance, and attribution, where appropriate. This, in turn benefits the downstream users and reduces redundant processing. Such an interconnected system has the potential to produce better inputs (e.g., time-series gaps filled, taxonomy aligned, errors corrected) to later workflows, creating a living knowledge system that improves through use.
A Metadata-First AI-FAIR Framework
The AI-FAIR framework suggests infrastructure priorities, which can be assessed using the AI-FAIR Checklist. This checklist was initially seeded from the ESIP AI-Readiness Checklist (ESIP Data Readiness Cluster, 2023) and the Imageomics Dataset Card Checklist (Campolongo et al., 2026). Building on these foundations, we engaged workshop participants in the evaluation of the list based on their experiences collecting, hosting, and curating data. Checklist items are those that workshop participants identified as necessary to make data AI-FAIR for scientific research. Each checklist item falls under one of four general metadata categories, which together form the AI-FAIR metadata criteria. We mapped these items to relevant standards including Ecological Metadata Language (Jones et al., 2019), DataCite (DataCite Metadata Working Group, 2026), https://t.co/djOCWmma32 (https://t.co/djOCWmma32 Community Group, 2026), and Croissant (Akhtar et al., 2024), where the terms exist. This mapping allows the checklist to bridge domain metadata and general AI data documentation. The full, community-approved, schema and mapping will be published with the checklist; it is currently under an open review by the broader biological community to ensure clarity and support. An analogous process could be completed to develop domain-specific keys in other disciplines.Below, we define the four AI-FAIR metadata criteria, provide examples of checklist categories or items included in them, and what each criterion (or combination of criteria) enables.1.Structural metadata describe formats, schemas, organization, variables, file relationships, and other values required for machine-readable access, conforming to FAIR standards. These properties determine whether a dataset can be acquired and inserted into a machine-learning pipeline and how data exchange can more readily occur. They support an assessment of machine learning (ML) readiness, but do not by themselves establish scientific validity.
2.Scientific metadata describe how observations or datasets were generated and what they mean. For example, a biodiversity use may include sampling design, effort, detectability, sensor placement and calibration, itemized and categorical species data, spatial and temporal resolution, taxonomic treatment and labels, uncertainty, and experimental context. These metadata are often necessary for determining whether data are fit for the intended scientific task. Structural and scientific criteria together support an assessment of AI-readiness for particular tasks.
3.Provenance metadata preserve the source chain, identifiers, citations, attribution requirements, checksums, and the environments and software used for processing. Provenance metadata ensures reproducibility of transformations, and paired with scientific requirements, they enable extension beyond an initial intended use and return value to the source data provider. In combination with structural requirements, these criteria support traceability.
4.Governance metadata express permissions, restrictions, responsibilities, sensitive-data conditions, and CARE (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) considerations (Carroll et al., 2020), in particular as defined in IEEE recommended practice for provenance of Indigenous Peoples' Data (2025). They include information about permission to collect observations and communities, governments, or territories implicated by data use. These criteria support an assessment of ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship.The checklist further subdivides these criteria into broad domain-agnostic categories of general information, data structure, source data, data processing, data quality, guidance and recommendations, data access, provenance and appropriate usage, and data governance. Within these categories, terms become more domain-specific. Here we provide biodiversity data examples for several elements that workshop participants found particularly important for AI-enabled science. Sampling semantics (such as experimental design, sampling effort, detection processes, instrumentation, calibration, and spatial and temporal scale) help an agent to determine whether a model can generalize beyond observed data. Processing and annotation provenance document steps, such as transformations and methods used for time-series gap filling, outlier handling, anonymization, and labeling, to help prevent data leakage and support reproducible benchmarking. Elements of the checklist pertaining to fitness and limitations ensure information provided by data sources on applicability (e.g., intended tasks, out-of-scope uses) and constraints (e.g., biases in space or time, class imbalances, distinctions between true absences and missing data) are machine-discoverable. Ontological coherence maintains label definitions with clarity and consistency. For instance, in biodiversity use cases the taxonomic backbone, resolution date, synonym handling, and identification uncertainty affect whether records from distributed sources can be combined safely and determine the appropriate process to do so. Finally, components of the checklist are meant to work synergistically. For example, elements pertaining to rights and governance ensure that machine-readable licenses, access tiers, sensitive-species flags, privacy constraints, and CARE-related permissions travel with the data and derivatives to confirm that data are fit for intended tasks.
From Checklist to Automated Dataset Evaluation
We pair the checklist with an automated evaluation workflow (Sokol & Campolongo, 2026). The evaluator uses an agent to retrieve available metadata, rate checklist items against a rubric, record evidence and recommendations, and provide FAIR and AI-FAIR scores (Figure 3). The evaluator rates each checklist item as meets, partial, does not meet, or not applicable. Each rating is assigned a set numerical value for scoring, and not applicable is excluded. The agent uses a Python script to average the item scores within each of the four AI-FAIR criteria of metadata, then maps these to their derived categories to compute scores for four components: ML-ready, AI-ready for task, Traceable, and Ethical CARE compliance. These scores then feed into the overall AI-FAIR value for a dataset alongside traditional FAIR dimensions. It is designed such that checklists for other disciplines could be substituted for the ecologically-based one with which we have started.📷Figure 3:Checklist ratings are assigned to each item and scored by AI-FAIR metadata criteria: structural, scientific, provenance, and governance. These are then mapped into the four derived categories for algorithmic scoring. Traditional FAIR principle alignment is reported in parallel.
The separation between evidence gathering and deterministic scoring is important to avoid circularity. An agent may locate metadata and propose ratings, but the aggregation logic is explicit and reproducible rather than estimated by a model. Evaluation output identifies strengths, missing metadata, inaccessible records, and provides concrete recommendations. Critically, these evaluation outputs also retain the evidence supporting each judgment, making the assessment reviewable by data stewards and domain experts.
Vision
AI-enabled scientific discovery relies on AI agents being able to do more than simply locate and consume distributed data. Agentic workflows must be able to evaluate dataset suitability for investigating researcher-specified questions, verify usage permissions and responsibilities, and facilitate round-tripping of validated improvements to the data providers. The AI-FAIR paradigm provides a framework for these capabilities through the Question-Data-Model triangle, four complementary metadata criteria (Structural, Scientific, Provenance, Governance), a domain-interchangeable checklist, and a reusable evaluation tool. These components are generalizable beyond biodiversity data through substitution of discipline-specific values or modules into the checklist. The key is to map discipline-specific categories to their associated AI-FAIR https://t.co/TsiE8NUzMY publishers participating in the FAIR4AI-Bio project, including the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) and NatureServe, have begun piloting the evaluation tool to establish baseline AI-FAIR scores for their data. These quantifiable metrics measure progress toward the goal of providing AI-FAIR data, as defined by the multidisciplinary users of these data. Here we have the opportunity to engage the communities that use and produce the data in assessing and setting standards that better enable their workflows and scientific or management pursuits. Especially as AI is becoming increasingly integrated in those efforts, the AI-FAIR framework preserves disciplinary context while enabling cross-domain infrastructure. It aims to support agentic workflows without disconnecting computation from human expertise and responsibility. Most importantly, it provides a roadmap to replace one-way extraction with a roundtrip of data, evidence, attribution, and value, so that the scientists generating the data fully participate in the benefits of these AI-enabled advances. Such a fabric would not be a passive network of repositories but a distributed, governed, and continuously improving scientific knowledge system, collectively shaped by the community.

Spirit Airlines' shutdown left a major gap at Fort Lauderdale, one of its busiest airports. JetBlue hasn't wasted much time filling it.

The airline is preparing its largest-ever operation at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, with more than 150 daily departures serving 61 nonstop destinations this winter.

The latest additions arrived on November 2, when JetBlue launched daily Airbus A320 flights to Indianapolis and Columbus, Ohio. Indianapolis is an entirely new JetBlue destination, while Columbus marks the airline's return to the city.

But this expansion started months earlier.

Following Spirit's shutdown in May, JetBlue announced plans to add 11 destinations from Fort Lauderdale, offered $99 rescue fares to stranded Spirit passengers and introduced measures to support affected employees.

The airline also projected that its summer operation would grow by more than 75% compared with 2025.

For years, Spirit and JetBlue competed for passengers in South Florida. Now JetBlue is building its biggest schedule yet at an airport where its former rival once had a substantial presence.

Spirit's departure has created an opportunity, and JetBlue is making a serious attempt to capture it.

text:
DID JESUS ABOLISH THE TEN COMMANDMENTS OR ONLY FULFIL THE LAW OF MOSES? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH MANY CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTAND

One of the most misunderstood subjects in Christianity is the relationship between Jesus Christ and the Ten Commandments.

Some Christians argue that Jesus abolished the Ten Commandments when He died on the cross. Others insist that Christians must observe every commandment exactly as the Israelites did under Moses.

But what does the Bible actually teach?

In Matthew 5:17, Jesus made a powerful declaration:

"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." (KJV)

Notice something important: Jesus did not say He came to destroy the Law. He said He came to fulfil it.

But what exactly did He fulfil?

The Law of Moses contained commandments, sacrifices, ceremonies, priestly regulations and civil instructions given to Israel. These laws served different purposes in God's covenant relationship with His people.

The Ten Commandments revealed God's moral standards. They addressed worship, idolatry, murder, adultery, stealing, lying, covetousness and honouring parents.

However, the sacrificial system pointed forward to the coming Messiah. The priests, animal sacrifices and temple ceremonies were shadows of what Jesus would accomplish.

Hebrews 10:1 describes the Law as having "a shadow of good things to come."

When Jesus offered Himself on the cross, He accomplished what the repeated animal sacrifices could never accomplish permanently.

Hebrews 10:12 says:

"But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God."

This means Christians do not need to return to animal sacrifices because Jesus is the perfect and sufficient sacrifice.

But does that mean murder, adultery, idolatry, stealing and lying suddenly became acceptable?

Absolutely not!

In Romans 13:9, Paul specifically mentions several commandments, including adultery, murder, stealing and coveting, and explains that they are summed up in loving your neighbour as yourself.

Jesus Himself summarised the commandments through two great commandments: loving God and loving your neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40).

Here is where many people become confused.

The fact that Christians are not under the Old Covenant does not mean they are free to live in disobedience to God.

Grace is not permission to practise sin.

Romans 6:15 asks:

"What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid."

However, there is another important question that Christians must honestly examine.

If the Ten Commandments remain binding in exactly the same covenantal form, why did Paul say in Colossians 2:16–17 that believers should not be judged concerning food, drink, holy days, new moons and sabbaths?

And why did Hebrews 8:13 describe the first covenant as becoming obsolete?

This is why we must distinguish between God's enduring moral standards and the covenantal administration through which He gave Israel the Law.

Christians do not become righteous by keeping the Ten Commandments. We are justified by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.

Yet the same grace that saves us also teaches us to reject ungodliness and live righteously (Titus 2:11–12).

Grok: 

No. Ian Carroll’s description, as framed in the post and related commentary, is a significant exaggeration and misrepresentation.

The Samson Option is a real, widely discussed concept referring to Israel’s last-resort nuclear deterrence strategy. It involves massive nuclear retaliation if the country faces existential defeat (e.g., being overrun by conventional forces). The name comes from the biblical Samson, who brought down a temple on himself and his enemies. It was popularized by Seymour Hersh’s 1991 book The Samson Option: Israel’s Nuclear Arsenal and American Foreign Policy. Israel maintains a policy of nuclear ambiguity (neither confirming nor denying possession) and is estimated to have roughly 80–90+ warheads with delivery options including aircraft, Jericho missiles, and submarines. https://t.co/qGn3OV9nKa  https://t.co/xz5WG5Sb4k 

The core inaccurate claim in the framing of Carroll’s video (as shared in the original post) is that Israel “openly threatens to nuke their own allies if a war is lost.” There is no open, official Israeli policy or doctrine of targeting the United States or other Western allies. The Samson Option is aimed at aggressors who pose an existential threat, not friends or partners. The US is Israel’s primary ally, arms supplier, and strategic partner; an official threat to nuke it would be self-defeating and is not doctrine. @paramounttactcl 

Unofficial or historical remarks have been stretched to support the stronger claim:

•  Israeli military historian Martin van Creveld (not a government official) said in a 2002/2003 interview that Israel possessed hundreds of warheads, could target most European capitals (including possibly Rome), and had “the capability to take the world down with us” before going under, quoting Moshe Dayan on being “like a mad dog.” This is a private academic’s statement, not state policy. https://t.co/G7KHgynkUx 

•  Hersh’s book attributes statements such as an anonymous former official saying, “We can still remember the smell of Auschwitz and Treblinka. Next time we’ll take all of you with us,” and then-Defense Minister Ariel Sharon saying Israel could “take the Middle East with us whenever we go.” These are older, attributed remarks in specific contexts, not current open threats to the US. https://t.co/qGn3OV9nKa 

Claims that Israel can readily “attack the USA” while Iran cannot also overstate current missile ranges. Israel’s Jericho missiles are primarily intermediate-range (regional and parts of Europe/Russia). Submarine-launched systems offer more flexibility but are not framed as a standard plan to strike the continental US. Iran’s missiles are shorter-range and regional.

In short, the underlying idea of a last-resort nuclear response to existential defeat is grounded in public discussion and historical reporting. The specific assertion that Israel openly threatens to nuke its own allies is not accurate.

text:
Isaiah 11 as a prophecy fulfilled in the 1st century through the ministry of Jesus Christ and the establishment of the Church.

1. Context: Isaiah 11 is Explicitly About the First Coming of Christ
Isaiah 11 opens with the famous Messianic prophecy: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots" (Isa 11:1).
that the entire chapter describes the inauguration of the Messiah's kingdom, not an end-times scenario thousands of years later:
 * The Root of Jesse (Isa 11:10): Paul explicitly quotes Isaiah 11:10 in Romans 15:12 to show that Christ was fulfilling this in the 1st century by bringing the Gentiles into God's family.
 * "In that day" (Isa 11:11): The temporal phrase connects verse 11 directly to the arrival of the Messiah (the Branch/Root of Jesse).
2. The "Second Time" Refers to Gospel Salvation, Not a Modern Return
Isaiah 11:11 specifies that God will set His hand "again the second time to recover the remnant of his people."
 * The First Time: God redeemed Israel physically out of Egyptian bondage (Exodus).
 * The Second Time: God redeemed the spiritual remnant of Israel (and Gentiles) out of sin through Christ.
In Acts 2 (Pentecost), Jewish pilgrims came from the exact region listed in Isaiah 11 (Elamites, Mesopotamia, Judea, Egypt, etc.) and were gathered into the early Church. this gathering was a spiritual gathering into the Body of Christ, not a physical relocation to a modern geopolitical state.
3. The New Testament Redefines "The Temple"
 * Jesus is the true Temple: Jesus declared Himself to be the ultimate Temple (John 2:19–21).
 * The Church is the Living Temple: Paul and Peter explain that believers—Jew and Gentile combined—form the true, spiritual temple built with living stones (1 Corinthians 3:16, Ephesians 2:19–22, 1 Peter 2:5).
 * The Old Temple Was Permanently Replaced:  the destruction of the Second Temple in AD 70 marked the absolute end of the Old Covenant sacrificial system. Rebuilding a physical temple to offer animal sacrifices would represent a rejection of Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:11–18).
Isaiah 11:11 predicts the gathering of God's elect into the New Covenant temple (the Church), making a physical third temple structurally and redemptively unnecessary.

UL President Dr. Ramesh Kolluru led a group to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston to explore working together on research, education, and workforce training.

The details:
• Talks covered student internships, faculty work with NASA, joint research, and courses shaped by what the industry needs
• NASA shared the skills the next generation of aerospace workers will need
• The two sides discussed a possible framework for working together, though nothing formal yet
• At least six UL alumni worked on Artemis II, NASA's first crewed mission around the Moon in more than 50 years
• In 2007, UL became the first Louisiana university to launch a student-built satellite. Two more have followed, and a fourth is in the works
• Starting Fall 2027, UL plans to offer an aerospace engineering concentration in mechanical engineering, plus a minor in aerospace and autonomous systems
• A space computing systems concentration and minor is also in development

UL says SpaceX's spaceport near Pecan Island is speeding up the growth of Louisiana's aerospace industry and creating demand for skilled workers.

ALFRED’S OPEN — BLOOM ENERGY UPDATE
BE / BEX / BEZ — November 3, 2026 — v1
Price snapshot: approximately 9:14 AM PST / 12:14 PM EST.
Status: REBOUND WATCH. Conditional plans; no order or fill.

Alfred’s Open — November third. Bloom is at two hundred fourteen dollars and sixty-seven cents, up about nine point four percent from Monday’s close. That is a forceful rebound. It is also still below its twenty-day and fifty-day averages. The business has momentum; the daily chart has repair work to do. My preference is BE itself for exposure beyond a day. BEX is the aggressive breakout tool, and BEZ is the failed-rebound tool. Neither leveraged fund earns an automatic entry because the headline sounds good. What changes my mind: a sustained break above $220.50 improves the tactical bull case; losing $210.09 after failing to reclaim intraday value shifts attention toward the bearish plan. [1–4]

PRICE DESK — USD, LAST TRADES, NOT EXECUTABLE QUOTES

Instrument    Snapshot     Nov. 2 close    Change       Quote time, PST
BE            $214.67      $196.25         +9.39%       9:14:08 AM
BEX           $19.71       $16.56         +19.02%       9:13:54 AM
BEZ           $6.605       $8.11          −18.56%       9:13:45 AM
SPY           $755.17      $752.10         +0.41%       9:14:08 AM

These Yahoo Finance chart-feed observations are frozen for this report. They are asynchronous last prices, potentially delayed, not bid/ask offers or closing prices. Refresh the market before using any level. BEX and BEZ changes will not equal precisely twice BE’s change because timestamps, market prices, spreads, tracking and costs differ. [1]

WHAT YOU ACTUALLY OWN

BE is Bloom Energy common stock on NYSE. Its economic exposure is ownership in the company; there is no daily leverage reset or fund expense ratio.

BEX is the Tradr 2X Long BE Daily ETF on Cboe. Its target is +200% of BE’s DAILY performance before fees and expenses. The issuer lists a 1.30% annual expense ratio and November 12, 2025 inception. [2]

BEZ is the Tradr 2X Short BE Daily ETF on Cboe. Its target is −200% of BE’s DAILY performance before fees and expenses. The issuer lists a 1.49% annual expense ratio and February 10, 2026 inception. Owning BEZ is a bearish derivative-fund position; it is not ownership of a separate operating company. [3]

Both funds are issued under the Tradr brand. They are not additional Bloom share classes. Listed annual expenses are not daily charges, and do not capture every execution or derivative financing cost. Swaps add counterparty and financing exposure; spreads and trading costs matter. [2–4]

THE BUSINESS CASE

Bloom’s solid oxide fuel cells produce electricity electrochemically using fuels including natural gas, biogas and hydrogen. The attraction for a power-constrained data center is dependable onsite generation and modular deployment. Natural-gas operation still produces carbon dioxide; “non-combustion” does not mean “zero carbon.” The investment case depends on delivered economics, reliable operation and conversion of customer demand into paid installations. [5]

Oracle provides more concrete demand evidence than a generic AI theme. Bloom’s April 13 announcement described a master agreement for up to 2.8 GW, with an initial 1.2 GW contracted and deployment extending into 2027. The upper limit and the contracted tranche are different numbers. Do not count all 2.8 GW as already delivered revenue. The same announcement disclosed an Oracle warrant issuance, a reminder to evaluate customer-linked equity dilution alongside sales growth. [6]

THE NEW HEADLINE — ATTRACTIVE OPTIONALITY, EARLY STAGE

On November 2, California Resources and Carbon TerraVault announced a nonbinding MOU with Bloom to evaluate 1 GW or more of fuel-cell power with carbon capture and storage in California. Potential customers span utilities, data centers and industry. Definitive agreements, investment decisions and permits remain conditions. This is a plausible catalyst for renewed interest, but the announcement does not establish a completed order, committed revenue or an assured installation timetable. I am not assigning the entire price move to one press release. [7]

FINANCIAL REALITY CHECK

Bloom’s October 22 preliminary Q3 release reported revenue of $1.236 billion, up 138.1% year over year; GAAP gross margin was 33.8%, operating income $225.4 million and diluted EPS $0.78. Adjusted EPS was $0.94. Full-year guidance: revenue $4.4–4.6 billion and non-GAAP EPS $3.10–3.40. These adjusted estimates are not GAAP earnings guarantees. [8]

Cash conversion is the countercase: Q3 operating cash flow was negative $27.1 million and capital expenditure $153.5 million. My simple operating-cash-flow-minus-capex calculation is negative $180.6 million. Receivables reached $634.7 million and current contract assets $792.8 million, versus $371.8 million and $178.9 million at year-end. Growth is consuming working capital. Cash was $2.487 billion, recourse debt $2.473 billion, plus other obligations; “debt free” would be misleading. [8]

At $214.67, the stock costs roughly 63.1–69.2 times management’s 2026 adjusted EPS range. That leaves considerable sensitivity to growth delivery and the multiple investors will pay. Manufacturing scale, installation timing, gas availability, service performance, customer financing and dilution are the central diligence questions. [8; calculations]

VALUATION SENSITIVITY — NOT PRICE TARGETS

Use the $3.25 midpoint of management’s adjusted EPS guidance as a fixed arithmetic input. The following changes only the assumed earnings multiple; no probabilities or intrinsic-value estimate are implied.

Assumed multiple    Illustrative value    Versus $214.67
40×                 $130.00              −39.44%
60×                 $195.00               −9.16%
80×                 $260.00              +21.12%

A good company can still produce a poor stock return if the entry multiple compresses. Conversely, sustained growth above current expectations could support a premium. This table is a sensitivity test, not an analyst-consensus forecast.

MONEY FLOW AND PRICE STRUCTURE

Daily calculations below use completed sessions through November 2, excluding today’s unfinished daily bar. “Money flow” means price/volume indicators here; no verified institutional order flow, dark-pool buying, fund creations or current ownership changes were obtained. [1; calculations.json]

Metric                         BE          BEX          BEZ
20-session price return        −31.54%     −57.12%      +74.78%
20-day simple average          $236.69     $25.90       $6.44
50-day simple average          $248.11     $29.86       $6.80
21-day Chaikin Money Flow       −0.070      −0.087       +0.023
14-day Money Flow Index          31.2        33.8         68.1
20-session OBV change          −97.60m     −19.55m      +26.45m shares
Nov. 2 relative volume           1.02×       1.06×        1.42×
20-day average volume           15.50m       3.35m        5.03m shares
14-day simple ATR               $19.96      $4.01        $1.23

BE’s negative CMF and OBV change do not confirm sustained accumulation. MFI near 31 is weak, but not a promise of a bottom. SPY lost 2.93% over the same 20 sessions, so BE underperformed by about 28.60 percentage points. Today’s rebound has not yet reversed that history. BEZ’s stronger trailing indicators describe the previous decline in BE, not a fresh short signal today.

Approximate intraday VWAP, using completed five-minute bars through 9:10 AM PST: BE $215.51; BEX $19.83; BEZ $6.574. BE and BEX were below those estimates at the quote snapshot. These are typical-price bar estimates, not exchange tick VWAP. Full-session averages will change.

BE map: $210.09 is Monday’s high and a useful nearby pivot. Below it sit Monday’s $196.25 close, the five-session low near $194.15 and the twenty-session low at $189.00. Above the snapshot, watch the approximately $220.50 session high, $231.67 five-session high, then $236.69 and $248.11 moving averages. Levels are zones, not precise guarantees.

CONDITIONAL STRATEGIES — CHOOSE ONE EXPOSURE

My preferred instrument is BE. My preferred entry is confirmation, not an unconditional market buy. The following are illustrative plans selected for this scan, not backtested profitable rules. They are inactive at the frozen snapshot. Levels must be reassessed if price runs away or the session changes.

1. BE — breakout continuation; intraday to short swing.
Require two completed five-minute closes above $220.50, above a freshly recalculated VWAP, followed by a retest holding that area. Look for breakout-bar volume above the median of the preceding six completed five-minute bars. Illustrative entry $221.00; invalidation/stop $214.50; risk $6.50 per share. Targets $234.00 and $240.50 give 2R and 3R before costs. $231.67 is earlier resistance: if sellers stop progress there, reduce exposure rather than insist on the target. This is a tight tactical stop versus the nearly $20 daily ATR, so routine noise can stop it out. No automatic averaging down.

2. BEX — aggressive same-day version of the bull case.
Require BE’s breakout confirmation above, plus BEX above its own $20.70 session-high area and fresh VWAP. Illustrative entry $20.80; stop $19.70; risk $1.10. Targets $23.00 and $24.10 provide 2R and 3R before costs. The recent $23.39 high is another obstacle. Avoid duplicating this position with BE as though it were diversification. Reassess and ordinarily exit by the close under this plan; do not turn an unsuccessful day trade into a passive leveraged holding. ETF targets are independent scenario levels, not mechanically guaranteed by a BE price target.

3. BEZ — only if the rebound fails.
Require BE to fail below fresh VWAP, close two five-minute bars below $210.09, and fail a retest. Also require BEZ to reclaim $6.95 and hold above its own fresh VWAP. Illustrative entry $6.98; stop $6.55; risk $0.43. Targets $7.84 and $8.27 give 2R and 3R before costs. Resistance near the observed $7.13 session high and the prior $8.11 close can interrupt the move. A sustained BE reclaim of $215.51/fresh VWAP undermines this bearish thesis even before the ETF stop. This is a same-day tactical plan, not a long-term short recommendation.

For every setup: verify the actual spread and available size, use a price limit for entry, and recalculate reward/risk for the actual fill. No quote-depth, current NAV premium/discount or live spread was verified in this scan. Do not chase a gap through the proposed entry. Stop-market orders can slip; stop-limit orders can fail to execute. A defined stop is not a guaranteed maximum loss.

POSITION SIZING — ARITHMETIC, NOT PERSONAL ALLOCATION

For a hypothetical $100 planned loss budget, floor(risk budget ÷ entry-to-stop distance) gives 15 BE shares ($3,315 notional, $97.50 planned risk), 90 BEX shares ($1,872 notional, $99 risk), or 232 BEZ shares ($1,619.36 notional, $99.76 risk). These are alternatives, not three simultaneous recommendations. Costs and gap risk require additional room. Scale to a risk budget you can absorb; leveraged exposure should not be sized by comparing share prices.

DAILY RESET: THE PART THAT CHANGES THE STRATEGY

A +10% day followed by −9.09% leaves BE approximately flat. In an idealized cost-free daily-reset model, BEX returns about −1.82% and BEZ about −5.45% across those two days. Both can lose while the underlying finishes unchanged. Conversely, two consecutive +10% BE days give BE +21%, BEX +44% and BEZ −36% in that model. Compounding is path dependent, not a fixed charge that always reduces every result. The daily target is not a promise of exactly ±2× the return from an arbitrary midday purchase to sale. [2–4; arithmetic]

Buying both leveraged funds is therefore not a free hedge. A 50% adverse underlying daily move can theoretically exhaust a 2× fund’s value; derivatives, rebalancing and market disruptions create additional risks. BEZ’s data includes a 1-for-10 reverse split on June 3, 2026. A split changes share count and per-share price, not wealth by itself; do not compare unadjusted historical sticker prices. All technical windows used above begin after that split. [1–4]

WHAT WOULD STRENGTHEN OR BREAK THE THESIS

For a durable bullish investment: demand conversion into installations and cash receipts, improved cash conversion, fewer balance-sheet claims on growth, and a daily close above the twenty-day average followed by a successful retest. For a tactical long: the $220.50 breakout conditions above. For a bearish trade: the failed-rebound conditions above, with room to downside support. A renewed loss of $194.15–$189.00 would materially weaken the recovery case.

A fresh MOU alone will not settle this. The next useful evidence is execution: definitive commitments, deployed capacity, customer cash receipts and margin durability. No future earnings date is asserted here. “Watch” is this report’s classification, not a scheduled monitoring service.
