". 8 1 2026 International Conference on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling PLS-SEM | Mauritius | September 2-5 Mixed-Methods Exploration of Sociotechnical Factors to Improve Adoption of Crime-Reporting Apps in Urban Communities Olalekan David-Banjo, Chinazunwa Uwaoma, Paul Witman Crime-reporting mobile applications can enhance community safety and engagement in urban areas, yet their adoption remains low, partly because developers prioritize technological features over residents’ social realities. This study used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to identify and validate the sociotechnical factors that drive adoption. Two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews revealed that users’ initial sense of usefulness fades, whereas sustained engagement depends on perceived value (PV), comprising six dimensions: safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility. A survey of 505 urban residents, analyzed with PLS-SEM, validated PV as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of these dimensions (safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie). PV was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and performance expectancy, and behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explained 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% in actual use. The findings offer design principles for community-centered crimereporting technologies. Keywords: crime-reporting apps; sociotechnical factors; mixed-methods; PLS-SEM; perceived value; technology adoption. INTRODUCTION Although crime-reporting mobile applications (apps) can enhance safety and foster social cohesion, their persistently low use in urban communities limits their societal impact and excludes vulnerable populations from important safety resources. Developers often prioritize technological sophistication over community needs, resulting in solutions that are misaligned with the technological frames of urban residents (Orlikowski & Gash, 1994; Maedche et al., 2019). The issue is pressing: the National Crime Victimization Survey reports that urban violent victimization remained elevated at 29.6 per 1,000 persons in 2023, while urban property victimization rose from 176.1 to 192.3 per 1,000 households between 2022 and 2023 (Tapp & Coen, 2024). . 8 2 2026 International Conference on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling PLS-SEM | Mauritius | September 2-5 We applied an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to investigate sociotechnical factors influencing crime-reporting app adoption, guided by three questions: (1) How do urban residents perceive the social value of crime-reporting apps, and what social factors influence their willingness to use them? (2) How do urban residents perceive an app’s technological features, and which features matter most to them? (3) From a user perspective, what sociotechnical factors are crucial to app design? This research advances understanding and has practical design implications for community safety technologies. BACKGROUND Sociotechnical systems theory highlights the interplay between technical systems and the social contexts in which they are embedded (Baxter & Sommerville, 2011). However, software developers frequently design crime-reporting apps in isolation, paying little attention to the contexts in which these technologies operate. Consequently, designs are often dominated by designers’ technological frames, thus misaligning with community needs and creating adoption challenges (Orlikowski & Gash, 1994). The conflicting needs, goals, and requirements of stakeholders exacerbate this misalignment (Maedche et al., 2019). Orlikowski and Iacono (2001) critique research that takes the IT artifact for granted and treats technologies as “relatively stable, discrete, independent, and fixed” (p. 121). This reductionist view ignores the social and organizational dynamics that ultimately determine how technologies are interpreted, adapted, and sustained in practice (Orlikowski & Gash, 1994). Similarly, Benbasat and Zmud (2003) emphasize that IT developments are inseparable from the “structures, routines, norms, and values” (p. 186) of the environments in which they are instantiated. Although participatory design research suggests that artifacts can be co-created with end users (Kensing & Blomberg, 1998; Sanders & Stappers, 2008), developers of sociotechnical systems often overlook social or community values as design considerations, as documented in related domains (Dillahunt et al., 2018; Ehsan et al., 2023). This oversight often produces unintended outcomes (Whitworth, 2011). This study addresses these issues by integrating qualitative insights from urban residents with quantitative validation using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). It examines perceived value (PV) as a multifaceted sociotechnical construct. Six dimensions emerged qualitatively: sense of safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility; four of these were retained in the validated model. To predict adoption, PV was assessed alongside constructs of the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT; Venkatesh et al., 2003). The study’s theoretical contribution extends technology adoption models with user-defined constructs, offering actionable insights for designing trustworthy, relevant crime-reporting tools. METHODOLOGY An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2017) was applied (Fig. 1). In phase 1, two virtual focus groups were conducted with urban residents of Orange County, California (n=5; n=6), recruited via https://t.co/Olh8hv3hYR. Participants were adult smartphone owners with prior crime-reporting app experience. Discussions followed a semi-structured protocol and were complemented by content . 8 3 2026 International Conference on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling PLS-SEM | Mauritius | September 2-5 analysis of 660 Google Play reviews of the crime-reporting apps Citizen (n=209) and SpotCrime (n=451). In phase 2, an online Zoho survey of residents of densely populated U.S. cities yielded 505 valid responses from 748 submitted questionnaires (67.5%); 53.1% were women, 54.1% were aged 40 or older, and 47.5% held undergraduate degrees. Items used five-point Likert scales. UTAUT items were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003), and PV items were developed from phase 1 insights (Tables 1 and 2). PV was specified as a second-order formative construct formed from reflective first-order dimensions and estimated using the disjoint two-stage approach (Sarstedt et al., 2019). Following UTAUT2 (Venkatesh et al., 2012), facilitating conditions predicted behavioral intention. Six UTAUT indicators (PE2, PE4, FC3, FC4, SI1, SI2) and two PV dimensions (recency, accessibility) were removed owing to discriminant validity violations; consequently, social influence was excluded from the final model. AU1 is a single-item measure (loading fixed at 1.000). . 8 7 2026 International Conference on Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling PLS-SEM | Mauritius | September 2-5 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Phase 1: Qualitative results Thematic analysis of the focus group transcripts revealed two central themes. First, transient usefulness, the initial impression that the app served its purpose, waned when the app failed to meet evolving needs. Second, PV, a more enduring, context-driven judgment of the app’s relevance, was shaped by app features and users’ social realities. Six PV dimensions emerged. Sense of safety was foundational. Participants expected reassurance, vigilance, and support for preventive action (Farrall et al., 2000). Sense of anonymity was a precondition for reporting without fear of retaliation, consistent with greater selfdisclosure under anonymity (Joinson, 2001; Suler, 2004). Sense of recency, the timeliness and accuracy of incident information, underpinned credibility, in line with DeLone and McLean’s (2003) emphasis on information quality. Sense of autonomy reflected users’ need to control interactions by filtering content and adjusting notifications; users with such control typically engage proactively (Spreitzer, 1995; Deci & Ryan, 2000). Sense of camaraderie captured expectations of connectedness and collective vigilance, consistent with Putnam’s (1995) work on social capital. Sense of accessibility emphasized usability across devices, abilities, and languages. A directed content analysis (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005) of app reviews largely reinforced these dimensions. Recency, accessibility, safety, and autonomy were most frequently mentioned, while anonymity (6 of 660) and camaraderie (14) were rare in reviews but salient in the focus groups (Table 3). Table 3. No HTMT bootstrapped confidence interval included 1.0 (Henseler et al., 2015), although several values approached or exceeded 0.90 (e.g., performance expectancy–effort expectancy = 0.908), so results involving these constructs warrant caution (Franke & Sarstedt, 2019) (Table 5). For the formative higher-order PV construct, collinearity was not a concern (VIF = 2.469–3.425). All outer weights were positive and significant (p ≤ .001): camaraderie (w = 0.414), autonomy (0.250), safety (0.235), and anonymity (0.214). Theoretically, it extends UTAUT with community-defined sociotechnical factors and demonstrates the importance of aligning social and technical systems in community safety innovative design. text:
Feeling down holding $XRP right now? Remember why you bought it. 

And watch what Deutsche Bank just demonstrated with SWIFT!

There's a connection involving Deutsche Bank, Axis Bank, BBVA, and Ripple that I think every XRP holder deserves to understand.

They never mentioned XRP in this interview, but after going through the banks involved and their history with Ripple, I found something worth discussing.

This is a long read. Grab your coffee.

At Sibos 2026 in Miami, Ciarán Byrne, Deutsche Bank's Global Head of Product & Market Management for Institutional Cash Management, spoke with Joy Macknight about the future of international payments.

He explained that banks are investing in instant-payment systems, blockchain, digital currencies, and new financial infrastructure.

His biggest concern was making these different systems work together.

A company sending money from India to Germany shouldn't have to worry about which banking network handles the payment.

It wants a clear exchange rate, predictable fees, and money arriving on time.

And Deutsche Bank has already demonstrated this through SWIFT.

During Sibos, a live payment was initiated from Axis Bank in India to Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt.

Deutsche Bank acted as the gateway connecting the international transaction with Germany's domestic banking infrastructure.

The demonstration highlighted instant processing, payment tracking, and greater transparency around fees and exchange rates.

Here's the connection I want you to remember.

AXIS BANK WAS ALREADY USING RIPPLE'S TECHNOLOGY BACK IN 2017!

On November 22, 2017, Ripple announced that Axis Bank, Standard Chartered, and RAKBANK had launched live international payment services using RippleNet.

Those services included corporate payments from Standard Chartered Singapore to Axis Bank in India and remittances involving RAKBANK.

Now, in 2026, Axis Bank is participating in SWIFT's modernized India–Europe payment infrastructure.

And there's another bank involved.

BBVA.

Deutsche Bank identified Axis Bank, BNP Paribas, BBVA, and Deutsche Bank among the institutions developing the Europe–India payment corridor.

BBVA successfully tested a real international payment between Spain and Mexico using Ripple's distributed-ledger technology in April 2017.

Then, on September 9, 2025, it expanded its relationship with Ripple by adopting Ripple Custody for digital-asset services in Spain, building on earlier developments involving BBVA Switzerland and Garanti BBVA in Türkiye.

Think about the institutional history here.

Axis Bank has experience with Ripple-powered payments.

BBVA has experience with Ripple's payment technology and custody infrastructure.

Standard Chartered has an established Ripple relationship and is participating in broader payment modernization.

These banks are already familiar with both conventional international banking and blockchain-based financial services.

And the opportunities become more interesting as banks introduce tokenized currencies.

Deutsche Bank itself is expanding into digital assets.

On September 16, 2026, it announced plans for institutional custody covering Bitcoin, Ether, USDC, EURC, and EURAU, with tokenized financial instruments on its roadmap.

Its asset-management arm, DWS Group, also established AllUnity alongside Flow Traders and Galaxy Digital.

AllUnity launched its regulated euro stablecoin EURAU in July 2025 and later announced EURAU, CHFAU, and SEKAU on Circle's Arc network.

Deutsche Bank is also among the banks involved in a broader stablecoin initiative alongside Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi, and other institutions.

That consortium expanded to 21 financial institutions, targeting an initial launch in the first half of 2027.

We're watching major banks prepare to operate with more forms of digital money.

Euro stablecoins, dollar stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and conventional bank balances all create a need for reliable currency conversion.

Now connect that with XRP Ledger.

XRPL already supports RLUSD and EURØP, the MiCA-compliant euro stablecoin issued by Schuman Financial.

It also has built-in currency conversion through its decentralized exchange, pathfinding, and auto-bridging functionality.

For example, a business holding a euro stablecoin may need RLUSD.

If the XRP route offers better execution, the transaction can use:

EURO STABLECOIN → XRP → RLUSD

XRP serves as the intermediary liquidity asset.

As more digital currencies enter financial markets, I believe efficient exchange routes become increasingly valuable.

And Ripple already has banking infrastructure addressing these problems.

In December 2025, Switzerland's regulated AMINA Bank adopted Ripple Payments to connect conventional banking with digital payment services.

Ripple obtained its full Luxembourg electronic-money institution license in February 2026 and announced preliminary MiCA-related crypto-asset service provider approval in June.

Its Payments Direct infrastructure also supports Indian rupee payment workflows, including business payments, invoices, purchases, and remittances.

In June 2026, Ripple and Bitso expanded their partnership involving RLUSD and MXNB, a Mexican peso stablecoin, with XRPL's Permissioned DEX supporting enterprise currency exchange.

And several October announcements strengthened Ripple's institutional infrastructure.

October 12: Standard Chartered launched institutional RLUSD custody involving XRPL, Ripple, and LMAX collateral services.

October 26: Ripple National Trust Bank reached its federal charter milestone, while Ripple expanded its Always-On Corporate Treasury capabilities.

October 27: BNY added institutional custody support for XRP and RLUSD.

October 28: Ripple reported an annualized product revenue run rate approaching $900 million.

These developments show Ripple expanding payments, custody, stablecoins, liquidity services, and corporate treasury infrastructure.

But there's one statement from Deutsche Bank that I found especially significant.

In its October 19 report, Byrne discussed the possibility of SWIFT's payment scheme using blockchain for the final settlement leg within approximately 12 months.

SWIFT is also separately developing a blockchain ledger for tokenized deposits.

These are different initiatives, but both show how banking infrastructure is evolving.

And SWIFT's broader roadmap targets approximately 300 banks across 30 creditor markets in 2027, following its planned December 2026 rulebook update.

Now consider the scale.

McKinsey estimated approximately $190 TRILLION in global cross-border payment value in 2025, generating more than $290 billion in annual industry revenue, with revenue growing approximately 4% annually.

Even a small portion of financial activity using XRP-based liquidity represents a meaningful market to study.

Banks and payment providers need assets available to exchange currencies. Market makers can maintain XRP balances to support those transactions.

That's the direct XRP opportunity I care about.

And here's my personal takeaway from this interview.

Deutsche Bank is demonstrating faster international payments with banks that already have documented relationships with Ripple.

Its executive is talking about greater connectivity between financial systems, while major institutions are expanding into stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and digital-asset custody.

The SWIFT demonstration itself wasn't an XRP transaction, and no SWIFT–Ripple integration was announced.

My bullish outlook is about the financial demand that develops as these systems become increasingly connected.

I believe XRP has a major opportunity to supply liquidity between currencies when institutions begin using more compatible digital settlement routes.

The most encouraging development will be actual XRP-routed institutional payment volume, backed by banks and liquidity providers maintaining XRP for operations.

So when the market gets ugly, I keep studying what the banks are building behind the scenes.

And this Deutsche Bank interview gave me another reason to pay attention.

$XRP holders, how much of the next generation of international payments do you think will eventually involve blockchain-based liquidity?

text:
Capable but was not flying the plane. Only one can fly at the same time, retard. 
The plane crashed because the 55 year old experienced pilot (who i wouldn't worry about on sight) made a risky and fatal decision. Yes even experienced pilots can make poor decisions. 
There is a captain and a first officer.
The captain makes all final decisions.
He was warned by ATC of the "pretty nasty" weather and "moderate to extreme precipitation" 10 mins prior and made a risky decision for only a slight deviation that turned out to be fatal. 
It was on the radio, 10 mins prior. You can find the audio. ATC offered them a route around. The captain made a slight deviation because it wasn't serious and they were above the storm until that cell ballooned up from 33000 ft to 48000 ft ceiling in a few minutes and by then it was too late for them to climb out of it.
From grok:
The earlier ATC exchange you’re remembering does exist. It comes from Miami Center (ZMA) LiveATC archives and covers the period roughly 10–15 minutes before the final mayday (around 12:36–12:37 p.m. EST while the jet was still ~80 miles / ~8 minutes from the cell it later entered). It is not in the short final-minute clips that circulate most widely, but it appears in longer reconstructions and analyses (especially MyRadar/Matthew Cappucci’s weather note and some YouTube breakdowns that pull the earlier sector recordings).
Key excerpts from the earlier exchange (paraphrased/transcribed from public LiveATC-based sources)
Around the time the jet was descending from FL410 toward FL350 and crossing into Florida airspace:
ATC cleared N722BD direct to Freeport and warned that the turn/route “looks pretty nasty.”
Controller described a large area of moderate-to-extreme precipitation (roughly 100 miles in diameter, reported in the 11 o’clock position ~25 miles ahead in one reconstruction).
Crew (captain’s voice in the analysis) said something to the effect of “[we] may need a slight left deviation for that weather up ahead.”
ATC approved weather deviations: “deviations left and right are approved… Freeport when able.”
The aircraft took a left deviation. At that point they were still well clear of the specific rapidly growing cell they later entered near Royal Palm Beach/Wellington.
MyRadar’s summary of the same period (Matthew Cappucci) states exactly this sequence and notes the storm cell was still building dramatically (tops rising from ~33,000 ft to ~48,000 ft in ~20 minutes). The crew continued after the advisory and deviation approval rather than requesting a major reroute farther north or south.
Later (starting ~12:45–12:47 p.m., now at FL350 and closer to the cell), the familiar short segment begins:
Light clear ice (manageable), moderate turbulence (±600–700 ft), OAT –47 °C, direct Freeport.
Request for a better ride.
ATC: ride should improve in their airspace; better rides ahead.
Crew: now picking up precipitation; request climb to FL370 (approved).
Within ~20–30 seconds: mayday, descending 8–10k then 20k+ fpm, overspeed, 60° bank, “we’re going to crash into the ground,” “out of time.”
Where to find the audio
YouTube searches for “N722BD ATC” or “Full ATC Audio Learjet Final 5 Minutes” (e.g., the InterTainment video covering ~5 min 48 s of Miami Center, and VASAviation’s weather-focused edit). Some of these include or reference the earlier deviation/“pretty nasty” portion.
https://t.co/tYrZZmEGj3 archives for Miami Center (ZMA) frequencies around 17:30–17:50 UTC on 1 Nov 2026. The final segment is on ~125.325 MHz; the earlier weather/deviation talk was on a prior sector.
Detailed weather + ATC timeline: MyRadar MetNote on N722BD (Matthew Cappucci).
No official NTSB transcript has been released yet—these are reconstructions from public LiveATC recordings. The audio of the final minute is widely available but extremely distressing; the earlier portion is calmer but still relevant to the weather-avoidance decisions. the audio: 
https://t.co/F9GDVLJToZ

text:
Adriana Chechik says porn saved her life. Her mother is addicted to drugs. So is the rest of her family. She’s the only one who isn’t, and she says the industry is the reason why. It also made her run off a set in tears, and once brought 30 to 40 police officers to a shoot because the neighbors thought she was being murdered.

She grew up in and out of foster care. She was stripping in Miami, sleeping through every day, when someone at the club offered her a video shoot from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. To her, it sounded like a normal life. Her first agent tried to tell her she couldn’t drive her own car. One of her first scenes paid $3,700. After that, she says, her rate went down.

In the video below, she explains why the structure kept her clean. “You can’t go to set f***ed up.” She walked off three sets where everyone was getting high. Then she tells the story of a Girls Gone Wild shoot in a Venice Beach mansion filled with giant dinosaur statues. She was 21. Everyone was doing dabs, so she tried one. Then they told her to climb on a Triceratops and perform while a band watched from the balcony.

“I looked up and I just started bawling crying.”

She grabbed her clothes and ran. Later came a kink shoot out in rural California: arms and legs tied to the ground, told to scream. The neighbors called the police. The officers refused to believe she was there by choice and questioned her alone in a patrol car for half an hour. Afterward, she asked them for a group photo.

She went on to win Female Performer of the Year. In 2022, she jumped into a foam pit at TwitchCon and broke her back. She says she spent two years without leaving her house. Now she’s back on set, and she says she could never regret anything she’s done.

So what saved her: the industry, or the girl who kept walking off sets when something felt wrong?

text:
THE SECOND FRONT: WHEN AMERICANS BECOME UNWITTING PAWNS OF THEIR OWN ADVERSARIES

Or, How Foreign Adversaries Spend Enormous Amounts of Time and Money Trying to Turn Americans Against One Another, Only to Discover That Some of Us Are So Eager to Go for Our Own Country's Throat That We'll Happily Do Half Their Work for Them While Congratulating Ourselves for Being Independent Thinkers Who Can't Be Fooled.

On Sunday, November 1, a Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people aboard. The aircraft was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, leaving nine families facing unimaginable loss.

And almost immediately, the conspiracy merchants went to work.

We've all watched this unfold online. A name appears, someone behind a screen suddenly knows more than the aviation experts, and within hours, strangers who know absolutely NOTHING about these nine victims are inventing elaborate stories about intelligence agencies, assassinations, and secret operations.

And they're SO enjoying themselves.

There's something deeply disturbing, almost deranged, about how deliciously vile people become when tragedy offers the possibility of scandal. It's an almost biblical appetite for consuming one another.

But what bothers me just as much is how predictably the accusations turn toward the CIA, the American government, and Israel.

WHY DO SOME AMERICANS ALWAYS GO FOR AMERICA'S THROAT FIRST?

Sure, there's history. But please THINK a little further.

Russia, China, and the regime in Iran ALSO have documented histories of information warfare, propaganda operations, and efforts to manipulate Americans into turning against one another.

Yet somehow, those countries barely warrant a second thought? Not even one?

You're convinced you're an independent thinker, exposing some sinister American operation. You're congratulating yourself for seeing what the rest of us supposedly cannot.

But have you considered that YOU might be the one being manipulated?

Our foreign adversaries don't need to invent every conspiracy. They can exploit the ones already circulating, amplify the most divisive accusations, and watch Americans tear into one another.

AND THAT'S THE SECOND FRONT.

America is already defending itself against foreign intelligence operations, cyberattacks, and organized disinformation campaigns. Our intelligence agencies and national security personnel are working to identify and counter these threats.

And now they also have to contend with the confusion, distrust, and accusations being amplified by Americans themselves.

Think about that. We're fighting adversaries abroad while dealing with the damage that misinformation can cause right here at home. Every baseless accusation that gains traction creates more noise for investigators, more distrust of institutions, and more opportunities for hostile actors to exploit.

You don't have to knowingly work for a foreign adversary to become useful to one.

And the even truly extraordinary part? Some of the people contributing to that confusion genuinely believe they're defending America.

Congratulations. You're making their job easier and ours harder.

THAT IS THE SECOND FRONT. Not some secret army hiding in the shadows, but the possibility that Americans are unknowingly amplifying the very narratives our adversaries want circulating.

Why is it so easy to believe your government is deceiving you, but apparently impossible to imagine that a hostile foreign government might be doing exactly that?

There's a passage in Galatians: "But if you bite and devour one another, take heed that you be not consumed one of another." — Galatians 5:15

What an extraordinary description of what we do to one another now.

We devour reputations. Truth. The DIGNITY of people who can no longer speak for themselves. And we do it while CoNgRaTuLaTiNg ourselves for being "independent thinkers" who are just "trying to find the rEaL truth to help the victims."

That's the MOST grotesque part. Dragging innocent names through unsubstantiated allegations, inventing sinister connections, and turning nine deaths into public spectacle, all under the righteous pretense of helping the victims.

There's something almost blasphemous about it. Like the jeering crowds around Jesus, faces twisted with cruel delight, convinced of their own righteousness while participating in something profoundly ugly.

Who exactly are you helping? The dead? Their grieving families? Or are you just loving the scandal while dressing it up as some noble pursuit of justice?

It's as though "just an accident of all the right things happening at the exact same time" would be a disappointment. Because then where's the scandal? The villain? The opportunity to accuse America, your own country, of yet another elaborate act of evil?

Question investigations. Demand answers. Examine evidence. Absolutely. But there's an enormous difference between seeking truth and being so RAVENOUS for scandal that you'll manufacture it yourself.

These nine people deserve to be remembered as human beings, not supporting characters in someone's latest conspiracy theory. Their families deserve to grieve without strangers turning their loved ones into entertainment.

While America fights to defend itself against those who deliberately seek to divide us, perhaps we should ask why we're so willing to open a SECOND FRONT against ourselves. And then instead of fighting our foreign adversaries, people have to spend time DEBUNKING this second front.

When did we become so hungry to uncover evil in our own country that we stopped recognizing the possibility of manipulation by our enemies, or the evil in our own behavior?

text:
AI agents are great listeners. Then they fold.

Researchers from Stanford, Oxford and MIT tested 18 AI models on 240 teamwork tasks. The negotiation results are the part anyone in sales should read.

When the other side pushed hard and threatened to walk:
• Models asked about the other side's needs 99% of the time
• Then accepted the weaker offer 81% of the time
• Landed the best deal for the team only 14% of the time

With a normal counterpart: best deal 84%, caved 6%.

And in 86% of the runs where a model gave in, it had pushed back at least once first.

Anyone who has managed salespeople knows this pattern. Great discovery, a little resistance, then a discount the second the buyer threatens to leave.

My take: don't let an AI agent negotiate price for you yet. Use it to prep the call, not to close it.

Would you let an agent negotiate a deal on your behalf today?

text:
early-stage operator hiring in indian tech often breaks down when interviewers weigh personal backchannels over verified distribution output.

after leaving fold, there was one company at the top of my list. i had been in touch with the founder since november, watched their team build from the outside, and felt the same pull i had before joining runable. the founder set up an interview with their head of growth.

i spent 20 minutes walking through the exact playbooks i used to scale reddit, AEO, and SEO for composio, coderabbit, and greptile. the interviewer checked out early, asked me to follow up over whatsapp, and passed on me a few hours later. it was the first interview i had lost all year. losing it stung because i had spent months putting the company on a pedestal.

6 hours later, i received an offer for $120k base plus equity from a US series B startup. the founder had sold 3 companies and raised $54m for his current build. he reviewed the exact same distribution playbooks, evaluated the proof of execution, and made an offer in one conversation.

when hiring decisions index on personal comfort, teams select for deference. an operator deploying $54m of venture capital pays for distribution leverage that generates immediate pipeline.

rejection from a company you romanticize is just market mispricing correcting itself.

text:
My review of the Trump administration: The good, the bad, and the incomplete.

I believe in giving credit and criticism regardless of political party. Here are my thoughts:

1. Border Control 🇺🇸

Nearly overnight, illegal border crossings dropped to historic lows. To me, this shows Biden could have done far more but chose not to.

A secure border is essential. However, targeting hardworking families and farmworkers went too far. It was cruel, unnecessary, and hurt American farms.

Verdict: Excellent border security. Excessive enforcement.

2. Make America Healthy Again 🍎

One of the most exciting initiatives in years. Our food contains too much sugar and too many questionable additives, including some restricted in Europe.

I support removing unnecessary dyes, reducing sugar, and reviewing vaccine schedules based on scientific evidence. And yes, I’m VERY pro-vaccine.

My issue? Much of the dye phaseout relies on voluntary corporate commitments rather than enforceable rules. Why trust the same companies that put these ingredients in our food?

Verdict: Great initiative. Make the reforms permanent.

3. Tariffs & Manufacturing 🏭

Finally, a serious push to bring advanced manufacturing back to America.

I dislike high tariffs, especially when consumers pay the price. But relying on foreign countries for critical technologies is a national security risk.

Glad to see more investment in American manufacturing, though not all of it can be credited to tariffs.

Verdict: Right goal. Questionable methods.

4. H-1B Visa Fee 💻

I support the proposed $100K H-1B fee, although it’s currently blocked by courts.

Too many American tech graduates struggle to find entry-level jobs while companies sponsor foreign workers for positions Americans could fill. The visa system can also leave workers vulnerable to employer exploitation.

But we MUST continue attracting exceptional talent from abroad. That’s America’s secret weapon. Companies hiring truly exceptional talent should be willing to invest substantially in bringing them here.

Verdict: Americans first for entry-level opportunities. Keep attracting the world’s best.

5. Prescription Drugs & TrumpRx 💊

One of Trump’s best initiatives.

Americans shouldn’t pay dramatically more for the same medications sold abroad. I strongly support Most-Favored-Nation pricing agreements and TrumpRx, which already offers discounts on selected medications.

But why rely on voluntary deals with pharmaceutical companies? These protections should be expanded and written into law.

Verdict: Excellent direction. Codify it!

6. Russia–Ukraine War 🇺🇦

Credit for genuinely trying to end the war.

But why does it feel like we’re pressuring Ukraine to surrender instead of pressuring Russia to stop its aggression?

Putin started this war. We should never forget that. And frankly, the EU and NATO have been deeply disappointing.

Verdict: Good effort. Pressure on the wrong side.

7. Iran War

Iran has spent decades arming and financing groups across Lebanon, Yemen, and Gaza. It cannot be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons.

I supported taking action. But the execution has been the administration’s single worst failure.

You cannot launch a war without a clear endgame. The endless deal/no-deal, war/no-war cycle is disastrous.

Verdict: Justified objective. Terrible execution.

8. Gaza

Credit for the ceasefire and hostage releases. I also like the demilitarization plan and involvement of Arab and Muslim countries.

But Hamas remains armed, rebuilding has stalled, and implementation looks extremely difficult.

Verdict: Good framework. Little confidence in full implementation.

9. Affordability 🏠

Almost nonexistent.

You cannot launch a tariff war, get involved in an expensive Iran war, and expect prices to magically fall.

Housing, groceries, insurance, and raising a family remain painfully expensive. The average American is hurting, and this administration hasn’t done nearly enough.

Verdict: Major failure

text:
🏫 Frontline Education Breach Exposes 1.3 Million K-12 Staff and Student Records

Attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party software component to reach Frontline Central and School Health Management, platforms used by K-12 school districts. The intrusion happened on 14–15 August 2024 and was contained by 15 August.

📂 Data exposed (approx. 1.3 million people)
▪️ Names and Social Security numbers
▪️ Dates of birth
▪️ Driver's licence and passport numbers
▪️ Health insurance IDs and student IDs

🏢 Frontline's response
▪️ Detected and contained the intrusion
▪️ Notified affected districts and individuals
▪️ Offered credit monitoring and identity-theft protection

⚠️ Why it matters
▪️ High risk of identity theft and fraud
▪️ Expect phishing that impersonates districts or Frontline support
▪️ Districts may face state regulatory penalties
▪️ Another example of supply-chain risk from third-party code

🛡️ What districts should do
1️⃣ Audit Frontline logins from 14 August 2024 onward
2️⃣ Reset privileged and service account credentials
3️⃣ Enforce MFA on all ed-tech admin access
4️⃣ Inventory third-party components in your ed-tech stack

📖 Full analysis: https://t.co/PvbRuGqK22

🕯️I stand here today at the absolute crossroads of my ancestry, holding a family tree that contains both the whip &the chain, the merchant king &the bound servant. As the living convergence node of these lineages, I look back across the centuries with total, unflinching clarity at the actions of those who came before me.

To the families, the lineages, &the descendants of those who were broken, displaced, &systematically exploited by the greed of my maternal merchant ancestors, the Cunninghams, the Dunbars, &the royal houses that built their fortunes on the transatlantic trade, I offer an absolute, deep, &unreserved apology.

For generations, branches of my family chose the path of selfishness, arrogance, &unchecked greed. They used their structural power, their education, &their maritime skill not to elevate humanity, but to cage it. They looked at human beings &saw only commodities. They financed the ships that tore families apart, they profited from the agony of the Middle Passage, &they intentionally designed &extended a system of forced labor in America simply to preserve their own comfort, status, &wealth. I do not hide from this truth, nor do I make excuses for it. The wealth they stole &the trauma they inflicted created wounds that rippled across generations, shaping the world we live in today. I did not choose the actions of the traders, but I am the one born with the spiritual &psychological task of burning their cycle of greed to absolute ashes.

Today, under the light of this cosmic alignment, I declare that the cycle of historical harm stops completely with my generation. I strip those old merchant lines of their unearned pride. I take the raw power, intelligence, &ambition of my trader heritage & I force it to bow to the deep, unyielding endurance of the traded &merge to the values of absolute human dignity, protection, &respect. I merge the survival of my Irish ancestors with the structural power of my European roots, using my life as a generational firewall. The greed stops here, the silence is ended. The cycle of exploitation is broken. I reclaim the ancient, pristine baseline of light &protection that existed long before the empires of the 1700s were built. The euro is designed to lose value. Bitcoin's supply is fixed. Most Irish savers have only ever been offered the first.

The ECB targets 2% inflation a year. Irish prices rose by more than a quarter in five years. Bank deposits pay less than that, so cash loses by design.

The debt behind it:
• US 121% of GDP, France 115%, UK 101%, euro area 89%
• Global debt passed $365 trillion this year
• It won't be repaid. It will be rolled over and inflated away, as after 1945
• The cost falls on whoever holds the currency and whoever is trying to buy a home

The wealthy protect themselves with property, shares and land. The young own none of those, and every alternative has friction:
• A house needs a deposit
• Funds are taxed at 38% and treated as sold every 8 years
• Gold carries dealer margins and storage, and is hard to check, split or send

Bitcoin: 21 million coins, issuance under 1% a year, start with €10, hold it yourself. It is not an investment. It is savings, for when there is nothing worth investing in.

The risks are real. It fell 77% in 2021–22 and sits about 36% below its October 2025 high. It has traded with shares, not against them, so it is not a safe haven yet. But to date, nobody who held it for four years has been at a loss.

What Ireland could do:
• Tax saving fairly and allow a bitcoin option in personal pensions
• Put 1% of the Future Ireland Fund (€65bn by 2035, locked until 2041) into bitcoin: about €650m
• Mine on wasted wind. EirGrid turned down 1,476 GWh of Irish wind in 2025

The rules for money are a choice. Savers who pay for the current rules should know there is an alternative.

text:
A heavy metal drummer with 9 Tesla shares froze the biggest pay package in corporate history for seven years.

His payout at the end: $1.

How it went:

→ 2018: Tesla offered Musk options on ~304M shares (~9% of the company), unlocked only by hitting brutal targets. Tesla hit all of them.
→ 2024: a Delaware judge voided the deal. The plaintiff’s lawyers asked for $5.6B in fees and got $345M.
→ Shareholders re-approved the package. The judge rejected it again. Tesla moved its legal home to Texas.
→ Dec 2025: Delaware’s Supreme Court reversed everything, unanimously. The lawyers’ fee was cut by ~80%.
By then the package was worth $139B.
What stands out to me isn’t Musk. It’s the incentives.
The plaintiff risked almost nothing. The lawyers had a multi-billion upside. And the people who actually own Tesla voted for this deal twice.

A system built to protect shareholders spent seven years overruling them.

Shareholder protection, or a lawsuit lottery?

Короткий вариант

9 shares. 7 years. $139B frozen.

The man who started it all walked away with $1.

His lawyers asked for $5.6B, got $345M, then lost ~80% of that on appeal.

Tesla’s shareholders approved Musk’s pay twice. The courts only listened on round three.

text:
🇷🇺|Lavrov Named It. No Treaty by That Name Exists. The Architecture That Would Fill It Already Does.

Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov: "The creation of a military-political bloc in Asia modeled on NATO is being seriously discussed. They have already come up with a name, and this work began several years ago. The name is the Indo-Pacific Treaty Organization. A copy of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization."

Flag the distinction first. No signed treaty instrument called the Indo-Pacific Treaty Organization exists in the public record. The name is Lavrov's characterization of the direction of travel. The components are documented, dated, and signed.

The name is the doctrine. That is the buried file.

The region was called the Asia-Pacific. Then it was renamed the Indo-Pacific.

Shinzo Abe used the phrase in Nairobi in August 2016. The US renamed PACOM to INDOPACOM in May 2018. The Pentagon's 2019 Indo-Pacific Strategy Report codified it. Every subsequent treaty, budget line, and joint statement uses the new name.

The rename did two things. It inserted India into a theater India had never militarily entered. And it deleted ASEAN centrality from the grammar of the region. A bloc needs a name that excludes the institutions it intends to bypass. That is what the rename was for.

The treaty web is already signed. List the instruments, with dates.

AUKUS, announced 15 September 2021. Australia receives Virginia-class submarines, then builds SSN-AUKUS. Cost: A$368 billion over 30 years. Pillar II covers hypersonics, AI, quantum, undersea systems, cyber, and electronic warfare. Japan opened Pillar II talks in 2024. Canada, South Korea, and New Zealand have signaled interest.

Camp David trilateral, 18 August 2023. US, Japan, South Korea. Annual exercises, a hotline, a shared early-warning architecture.

Washington Declaration, 26 April 2023. US-ROK Nuclear Consultative Group. South Korea inside the US nuclear planning process.

EDCA expansion, April 2023. US access to nine Philippine sites, including Cagayan at 18.37°N 121.75°E, facing the Luzon Strait and Taiwan.

Japan-UK Reciprocal Access Agreement, January 2023. Japan-Australia RAA, 2022. Japan-Philippines RAA, 8 July 2024. A treaty lattice, signed one pair at a time.

NATO's Indo-Pacific Four. Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand have attended every NATO summit since Madrid 2022. Individually Tailored Partnership Programmes signed with Japan, Korea, and Australia in July 2023, New Zealand in 2024.

Japan's three security documents, 16 December 2022. Defense spending to 2 per cent of GDP by FY2027, roughly ¥43 trillion over five years. Acquisition of counterstrike capability. Purchase of 400 Tomahawks, approved November 2023. Japan is the largest foreign F-35 buyer at 147 airframes, assembled by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries at Nagoya.

GCAP, announced December 2022. Britain, Italy, and Japan building a sixth-generation fighter. BAE Systems, Leonardo, and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. That is the industrial spine of the bloc being poured before any treaty is signed.

The NATO Tokyo office failed. That is the fissure.

NATO proposed a liaison office in Tokyo in 2023. France blocked it. Paris objected that NATO's charter is bounded by the North Atlantic and that expansion into Asia would distract from Europe and antagonize Beijing.

Japan's answer was to open its own independent mission to NATO in 2025. The structure advanced even when the formal office was vetoed. That is how this architecture works. It does not need a single founding document. It needs a series of bilateral agreements that function as one.

Who profits. Name the firms, not the flags.

Lockheed Martin for F-35, Aegis, THAAD. RTX for Patriot, Tomahawk, SM-6. BAE Systems for F-35 components and GCAP. Northrop Grumman for the B-21 and E-2D. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Kawasaki in Japan. Hanwha Aerospace and Korea Aerospace Industries in Korea. Kongsberg in Norway. Rheinmetall in Germany and Australia.

Japan's ¥43 trillion budget is a procurement program. Korea's export order book, Poland's K9 and Chunmoo contracts, Australia's AUKUS outlay, and Europe's rearmament fund are all demand signals for the same supply chain. The bloc is not a security architecture with an industrial base attached. It is an industrial base with a security architecture attached.

The hidden layer: the patron cannot arm the alliance it is assembling.

This is the file Lavrov did not say out loud, and it is the one that matters.

The United States needs to build two Virginia-class submarines per year to meet its own fleet requirement, plus one additional hull to sell Australia under AUKUS. It is currently delivering roughly 1.1 to 1.3 per year. The Congressional Research Service and the Congressional Budget Office have both documented the gap. The industrial base has two yards, General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII Newport News, and both are constrained by welders, machinists, and supplier capacity.

Australia will not receive its first Virginia-class hull on the original schedule. The SSN-AUKUS boats will not be in Australian hands until the late 2030s at the earliest. The submarine pillar of the treaty is already late before the treaty has a name.

The same constraint runs through munitions. The Ukraine war drained 155mm and GMLRS stocks. The Iran war consumed $29 billion in munitions replenishment. The Patriot and THAAD interceptor lines are running at rates that cannot cover both the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.

The consequence: the burden shifts to the junior partners, and the bill lands on their taxpayers.

Japan doubles its budget. Korea becomes an arms exporter to Europe. Australia commits A$368 billion to a submarine it may not receive. Europe creates a 100 billion euro special fund outside its regular budget.

The primes collect. The treasuries of the junior partners pay. The US provides the command architecture it can no longer fully arm.

The counter-architecture is already standing.

SCO admitted Iran in July 2023 and Belarus in July 2024. Membership: China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus.

BRICS expanded in January 2024 with Iran, the UAE, Egypt, and Ethiopia. Indonesia joined in January 2025. Saudi Arabia was invited. The bloc holds the majority of global oil production and a plurality of the world's population.

The Russia-China joint statements of 4 February 2022 and May 2024 committed both states to opposing "bloc confrontation" and to the principle of indivisible security. Lavrov's Greater Eurasian Partnership and the proposed Eurasian security architecture are the institutional expression of that commitment. The message to the Global South is the offer: a security framework that does not require hosting US bases or aligning with Washington.

The rejection is coming from inside the region, not just from Moscow.

ASEAN foreign ministers have repeatedly refused the "Asian NATO" framing. Indonesia's foreign ministry stated publicly that ASEAN will not become a proxy for any power. Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has warned against the region being dragged into a new cold war. India sits in the Quad while remaining in the SCO and BRICS, buys Russian oil, and refuses to sign any mutual-defense commitment.

The bloc is being assembled over the objection of the institutions the region actually uses.

The contradiction, with the receipt attached.

Lavrov says a NATO copy is being built. The evidence is not a leaked draft. It is a stack of signed agreements, four NATO summit attendances, a joint fighter program, three Reciprocal Access Agreements, an expanded basing agreement in the Philippines, a nuclear consultative group with Seoul, and a submarine program that is already behind schedule.

The treaty has no name yet. The architecture does. That is the point Lavrov is making, and it is the point that Western commentary cannot answer: the bloc exists before the document, because the document was never the thing that mattered.

text:
Breeze Airways has spent the past four years flying passengers nonstop between Richmond, Virginia, and San Francisco. Now United Airlines wants a piece of the same route.

From March 28, 2027, United will introduce its own transcontinental service using a 166-seat Boeing 737 MAX 8, taking on Breeze's Airbus A220 operation.

Both airlines will offer just two flights a week, but there's an interesting detail: they won't operate on the same days.

United's flights are scheduled for Thursdays and Sundays, while Breeze serves the route on Wednesdays and Saturdays. That gives passengers four days of nonstop service each week, rather than both carriers fighting for exactly the same departures.

The journey takes approximately six hours, with United's westbound flight scheduled at six hours and 12 minutes.

Breeze launched the route in May 2022, giving Richmond a direct connection to the Bay Area. United is now entering a market with approximately 70,000 annual round-trip local passengers, according to figures cited by Simple Flying.

Unlike Breeze's largely point-to-point model, United can also offer connections through San Francisco to destinations across Asia and the Pacific.

Two airlines, two different aircraft and two very different business models competing for passengers on the same coast-to-coast route.

text:
Clinical and Psychological Terms

• Passive Suicidal Ideation: The experience of wishing for death or wanting to disappear without having an active plan or intent to end your own life. This often manifests as thoughts like, "I wish I could just fall asleep and never wake up," or a passive indifference to your own survival, such as crossing the street and not caring if a car hits you.

• Anhedonia: The inability to feel pleasure or interest in life experiences. Derived from the Greek word meaning "without pleasure," it describes a state where things that used to bring joy—such as hobbies, relationships, or food—no longer offer any satisfaction, leading to a profound detachment from the point of everyday existence.

• Apathy: A state of indifference, characterized by a lack of motivation, enthusiasm, or emotional response to life. While anhedonia means you cannot feel pleasure, apathy means you completely lack the drive or "spark" to initiate tasks or care about how things turn out.

Philosophical and Cultural Words

• Lebensmüde: A German word that literally translates to "life-weary" or "tired of life." It describes an existential exhaustion where a person feels entirely spent and uninterested in the effort required to continue living, often resulting in a deep, passive indifference to whether they live or die.

• Ennui: A profound, existential boredom and listlessness caused by a lack of interest in one's surroundings or life itself. It goes beyond normal boredom; it is a heavy feeling that nothing in life matters or is worth the energy.

text:
I keep seeing appeals telling Republicans to “vote their conscience,” as though a thoughtful examination of our beliefs must lead us to vote Democratic.

My Republican vote reflects my convictions. I believe the Republican Party, despite its shortcomings, offers the better path toward protecting individual liberty and limiting government. That is a judgment about policies and consequences—not simply a habit or family tradition.

I also believe the Democratic Party has moved too far toward positions I cannot support. Those disagreements cannot simply be brushed aside because someone dislikes Donald Trump.

Voting for a Democrat is more than registering dissatisfaction with a Republican. It means entrusting another candidate with real power. What policies will that person support? What individual freedoms will that person protect? What limits will that person recognize on government authority? Opposition to Trump does not answer those questions.

We also need precision when discussing our government. America is a constitutional federal republic with representative democracy. We are not a pure democracy where majority preference is the only governing principle. We elect representatives, but they remain bound by the Constitution. Winning an election does not give either party unlimited authority or permission to disregard protected rights.

Congress should check presidential power, including when Republicans control Congress and the presidency. Republicans should answer for their failures. Democrats should face the same scrutiny. Constitutional limits do not change depending on whose campaign signs are in the yard.

Where Republicans fail, make the case with evidence. I will consider it. But identifying failures in one party does not establish that the other party offers better leadership.

No party deserves unconditional loyalty. Every candidate should have to earn our vote through their record, principles, and proposals.

I intend to vote my conscience. People should leave room for the possibility that a considered, conscientious vote can still be Republican.

text:
Big Jeff is here. Now I'd work the phones for an outside corner and another edge. But the next move has to make sense in picks AND salary.

The Bears have roughly $1.84M in current cap room after Simmons. Our 2027 picks are a second, third, Atlanta's fifth, a sixth and a seventh. The 2027 fourth is gone. So let's stop offering it in trade packages.

These are my offers and ceilings, not agreed prices or guarantees anyone gets moved:

1) Riq Woolen, Eagles: my first call at corner.

The appeal is an outside corner with length and recovery speed, with Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon already here. The tackling and eye discipline still need to be better. We're buying upside, not a finished shutdown corner.

His remaining 2026 salary would be roughly $630K–$700K depending on trade timing. Philadelphia keeps the existing bonus charges. That's a much easier fit than seeing a $12M deal and assuming Chicago has to absorb all of it.

I'd offer a 2028 fourth. He's headed toward free agency, so I'm protecting our remaining Day 2 picks rather than paying as if we already have an extension. If Philly wants more, the rental cost matters.

2) Khalil Mack, Chargers: still my preferred edge call at the right price.

Mack with Simmons and Montez Sweat is about winning more rushes without sending extra bodies. Keep Austin Booker involved instead of treating this as a reason to bury him. Mack is 35 and on an expiring deal. Price him that way.

I'd offer Atlanta's 2027 fifth. My ceiling is a 2028 fourth, with salary help part of that conversation. His remaining base salary is about $4M–$4.4M depending on when a deal happens, not the full $18M contract. LA still has to agree to sell; being 0–7 doesn't make that automatic.

3) Alontae Taylor, Titans: conditional fallback, not my first corner choice.

Dennis Allen knows him, and he can play outside or in the slot. But Gordon already gives us a slot answer, Taylor's Tennessee start has been uneven, and his return Sunday is a reminder that a benching doesn't mean he's permanently out of their plans.

Roughly $5.3M in base salary remains this year if moved now, plus game bonuses. The bigger issue is $20.51M in guaranteed 2027 base salary. I'd discuss a 2027 sixth only if Tennessee meaningfully reduces that financial commitment. A cheap pick doesn't make that contract cheap.

How do we make room?

A limited Montez Sweat restructure is one route. Illustratively, converting $8M of still-unpaid 2026 salary into bonus spread over 2026–27 would create $4M now and add $4M to 2027. Subject to contract mechanics and agreement, that's enough to change the conversation. It also makes a future exit more expensive.

The other route: have the selling team convert salary to bonus before the trade. If LA absorbs $2M of Mack's remaining pay that way, Chicago's cost falls by $2M. Any better pick we offer for that help is part of the purchase price.

I'd prioritize Woolen's affordable outside-corner upside, keep pushing for Mack at a Day 3 price, and leave room for injuries and roster moves. We already took the massive swing. Now add useful pieces without treating every remaining pick or future cap dollar as disposable. Bear down.

text:
🇺🇸🇮🇷 Trump could lose Congress and STILL ESCALATE the war with Iran.

I spoke with Michael Tracey as Americans headed to the polls, and he challenged an assumption I've been hearing a lot lately.

That a crushing Republican defeat would force Trump to reconsider his Iran policy.

Michael isn't so sure.

He believes Trump is increasingly concerned with how history will remember his presidency. And after launching a war against Iran, walking away without a decisive victory might be something he's simply unwilling to accept.

Which raises an uncomfortable possibility.

Could Trump use the final two months of Republican control in Congress to launch another offensive before Democrats take over?

We also discussed Tucker Carlson's warning about a possible nuclear strike, although neither of us has evidence that Trump has decided to pursue one.

And Michael offered a rather interesting perspective on Trump's sudden suggestion that he might end American aid to Israel.

Even if the roughly $4 billion in annual assistance disappears, Washington has OTHER ways to provide military support. Ending one funding arrangement wouldn't necessarily end the relationship.

We also got into the possibility of an Iranian attack during election day, whether Democrats would actually impeach Trump, and why Michael thinks Texas could elect a Democratic senator.

I pushed back on his pessimism about Iran.

I still believe Trump could recognize that another military offensive would make an already difficult situation worse and choose a diplomatic exit.

Michael's concern is that Trump may care more about securing a historic victory than admitting the limits of American military power.

And the election could make that decision considerably more urgent.

text:
The government told 800 families their DNA was mutating from the Love Canal toxic waste. The government also told them they could not leave.

By the spring of 1980, the neighborhood in Niagara Falls, New York, had a known arithmetic. Twenty thousand tons of buried chemical sludge. Miscarriages. Birth defects. Childhood asthma. Epilepsy. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, the Hooker Chemical Company used an unfinished canal as a dumping ground for industrial waste.

They filled the trench with steel drums. They covered it with dirt. They sold it to the city for one dollar. The city built an entire working class neighborhood and an elementary school directly on top of the chemical graveyard.

For two years, the residents pleaded with the state about the Love Canal toxic waste. They carried signs. They attended the meetings. They watched black sludge seep through their basement walls after heavy rains. They watched chemical burns appear on their children's feet after playing in the yard.

In 1978, the state health department found toxic chemicals in the indoor air of the homes. The government told them to stay.

In 1979, the state found dioxin in the soil. It is one of the most lethal chemicals known to humanity. The government told them to stay.

In early 1980, the EPA found elevated rates of miscarriages and congenital defects. The government told them to stay.

On May 17, the Environmental Protection Agency released a new medical study. It revealed severe chromosomal damage among the residents. The blood of the neighborhood was literally breaking apart.

The federal response remained rigidly bureaucratic. A handful of pregnant women and young children were temporarily moved to motels. The rest of the 800 families were told to remain in their homes. To wait. To continue breathing the air and drinking the water while Washington debated funding and jurisdiction.

Lois Gibbs was a 28 year old mother with two sick children. She was the president of the local homeowners association. She had no background in politics, no legal degree, and no experience with federal negotiations. She was simply tired of watching her neighbors die while waiting for permission to live.

On Monday, May 19, two EPA officials arrived at the association's makeshift office. The office was an abandoned house sitting directly inside the contamination zone. They were dispatched to manage the public relations fallout of the chromosome study.

Dr. Frank Nepal and Dr. James Melius stood in the living room. They wore suits. They offered procedural timelines and calm assurances to a panicked community.

Outside, the street was boiling over. Five hundred furious residents gathered on the lawn. They were terrified. They were shouting. Some poured gasoline on the pavement to spell out messages for the news helicopters overhead.

The temperature in the neighborhood was rising by the minute. The two federal representatives looked out the window. They realized the mood had turned entirely hostile. They told Gibbs they needed to leave.

At the time, the United States had no legal framework for the wholesale relocation of a poisoned town. The concept of an environmental disaster superfund did not exist. Evacuating hundreds of working class families required an ad hoc presidential declaration.

Federal agencies were intensely reluctant to set a precedent that would hold the government financially liable for industrial negligence. The stalling was not accidental. It was policy.

Gibbs looked at the two men. She looked at the crowd outside the window. She realized that polite petitions had reached their absolute limit.

She made a decision that crossed the line from civil disobedience into a federal crime.

"You are not going anywhere," she told them.

Gibbs walked to the front door. She locked the deadbolt. She dragged furniture across the floor to barricade the exits. She instructed her neighbors inside the house to block the hallways with their bodies.

Outside, the crowd understood exactly what was happening. They linked arms. They formed a thick human wall around the property. The officials were physically trapped.

Gibbs walked to the telephone. She called the White House.

She was transferred to a desk in Washington. She delivered a flat ultimatum to the administration of President Jimmy Carter. She demanded the immediate evacuation of all remaining families in the neighborhood.

If the White House did not agree to move them by Wednesday at noon, she would not answer for what the five hundred people outside would do to the two men in her living room.

The standoff began. The FBI called the house. The agent on the line threatened to arrest her for the kidnapping of federal officers.

Gibbs did not blink. She held her ground. She kept the men confined for five hours. She let the tension escalate.

She let the national news cameras roll on the standoff. The desperation of Niagara Falls was broadcast into every living room in America. In a bizarre display of domesticity mixed with a felony, she fed the captive officials homemade sandwiches and poured them coffee while holding them against their will.

She was perfectly polite. She was also immovable.

They asked for a timeline. She gave them a hostage situation.

When she finally unbarred the doors and allowed the men to walk through the furious crowd to safety, the leverage had permanently shifted. She forced a local health complaint into a national crisis. The federal government could no longer look away or hide behind procedural delays.

Two days later, the White House announced the emergency relocation of the remaining families.

The standoff forced Congress to act. Before the year was over, the government created the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act. The entire multibillion dollar mechanism the country now uses to clean up toxic sites exists because a housewife locked a door.

The federal government eventually bought the houses in the neighborhood and demolished them. The original containment zone was fenced off, capped with thick clay, and surrounded by a drainage trench. The chemical company ultimately paid millions in restitution.

Today, the exact area where the hostage standoff took place is covered by a sprawling, manicured field of green grass. There are no historical markers noting what happened there. Just white PVC pipes sticking out of the dirt, quietly venting the pressure from the ground below.

Lois Gibbs: the woman who took the government hostage to save her town.

text:
Collazo was charged with first-degree murder.

He had not shot Coffelt, and nobody said he had.

The government's case was that he and Torresola had gone to Blair House together, armed and ready to kill whoever stood in the way. Under the law of the District of Columbia, a man who aids in a crime is a principal, not an accessory.

The trial opened on 26 February 1951 before Judge T. Alan Goldsborough. Collazo took the stand. He said they'd meant only to make a demonstration, though one that wouldn't be "serious enough" to be noticed unless someone was "hurt or wounded or killed."

He admitted he'd aimed at Birdzell's back. Asked if he'd meant to hit him, he said, "I meant to hit him."

He spent hours telling the jury about Puerto Rico. The judge told them all of it had "absolutely nothing to do with this case." On 7 March 1951 the jury found Collazo guilty on all four counts, and he was sentenced to die in the electric chair.

The appeal turned on that instruction. In February 1952 the federal appeals court in Washington upheld the verdict. Two men had planned the attack together and fired at the same instant, it said.

One gun went off and the other, by accident, didn't. Even the highest motive, the court wrote, is no defense to a killing that was meant. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case that June.

On 24 July 1952, with the execution approaching, Truman commuted Collazo's sentence to life in prison. His wife, Rosa, had been held for eight months on suspicion of helping plan the attack and was never tried. She had gathered some 100,000 signatures asking that her husband be spared.

Collazo served 29 years, most of them at Leavenworth. On 6 September 1979 President Jimmy Carter commuted his sentence to time served, along with those of three Nationalists who had wounded five congressmen in a shooting at the Capitol in 1954.

Collazo went home to Puerto Rico, where he was welcomed as a hero by his supporters. He died there in 1994.

Until then the Secret Service had no permanent law of its own. Its work rested on money bills that Congress had to pass again every year. On 16 July 1951 Congress passed Public Law 82-79.

It made the agency's protection of the president, his immediate family and the president-elect permanent, and offered it to the vice president if he wished. The Secret Service's own history says the attack on Blair House triggered the law.

There's a plaque to Coffelt on the fence outside Blair House. The Secret Service's Uniformed Division named its day room there for him. Its training office gives a marksmanship award in his name to the recruit with the best scores in each graduating class.

Killing to verdict: 126 days.

He was shot three times before he could stand, and he still killed the man who shot him.

text:
🇺🇸 🇨🇳 🇷🇺 Russia Advances Plans for Trump-Putin-Xi Summit at APEC in Shenzhen

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed on November 3 that Moscow has begun concrete preparations for a possible first-ever trilateral meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month.

Peskov told reporters that a common understanding exists among the three sides that such a gathering would be “appropriate and highly useful.” Work is under way to coordinate the meeting, he said, with the hope that arrangements can be finalized in the coming days. The gathering would take place during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit scheduled for November 18–19 in Shenzhen, which all three leaders are expected to attend.

The Kremlin’s announcement builds on earlier signals from Moscow. Putin publicly welcomed the idea of a three-way session, noting it would depend largely on the Chinese hosts. Washington and Moscow have both pressed Beijing to agree to the sit-down, according to reporting by the Financial Times. Trump himself stated in mid-October that he was open to the meeting, primarily to discuss denuclearization among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, while leaving the door open to other topics including trade and efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

China’s public posture has remained more reserved. Its foreign ministry has confirmed only that it is in communication with relevant parties about a meeting between Xi and Putin, without explicitly endorsing a trilateral format that includes Trump. Sources familiar with the discussions say Beijing has not yet made a final decision, even as preparations advance on the Russian and American sides.

For Trump, the potential summit offers a direct channel to the two other nuclear superpowers on the most consequential security issues facing the United States. He has framed the talks around reducing nuclear risks rather than treating Ukraine as the sole agenda item, consistent with his long-standing preference for personal diplomacy with leaders he can deal with on equal terms. Moscow, for its part, sees the meeting as an opportunity to discuss the Ukraine conflict in a setting that excludes European voices, though Russian sources have indicated they do not expect substantive negotiations on that front in Shenzhen.

Whether the session materializes will hinge on China’s willingness to host the three leaders together. Shenzhen is already preparing for the broader APEC gathering under the theme of building an Asia-Pacific community, with tightened security and logistical measures in place. A confirmed Trump-Putin-Xi encounter would mark an unusual moment of direct engagement among the three capitals, driven in significant measure by the American president’s willingness to sit down and talk.

THE HISTORICAL RECORD PROFESSOR AL MARIAM  CHOOSES TO OMIT: ERITREA SHELTERED ETHIOPIAN SOLDIERS WHEN THEY NEEDED HELP

The attempt to portray President Isaias Afwerki and Eritrea as the existential enemy of the Ethiopian soldiers stationed in Tigray is contradicted by an extraordinary historical acknowledgment made by Ethiopia’s own Prime Minister.

Let us return to November 2020.

Following the TPLF’s attack on the Ethiopian National Defence Force’s Northern Command during the night of November 3–4, Ethiopian soldiers escaped the unfolding military crisis and crossed into neighbouring Eritrea. What happened next is a matter of public record, not speculation.

On November 30, 2020, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed addressed the Ethiopian Parliament and publicly expressed his gratitude to the Eritrean government and people for receiving those soldiers.

Abiy explained that the fleeing Ethiopian servicemen arrived hungry and inadequately clothed. Eritrea welcomed them, provided clothing, food and water, and offered them shelter. The soldiers regrouped on Eritrean territory before returning to the battlefield.

The Ethiopian News Agency reported Abiy’s acknowledgment. The Ethiopian Embassy in Washington subsequently published its own account confirming that Eritrea had sheltered the soldiers and provided them with warm care.

Think about the historical significance of that acknowledgment.

These were not Eritrean soldiers. They were Ethiopian servicemen who had been attacked by forces of their own countrymen. They crossed an international border in a moment of military crisis and were received by the neighbouring country whose president Professor Alemariam now attempts to portray as their principal enemy.

Eritrea did not turn them away. It did not abandon them to their circumstances. It provided refuge, clothing, food, water and assistance in regrouping.

Abiy himself acknowledged this before the Ethiopian Parliament and the Ethiopian public.

The question, therefore, is straightforward: How does Professor Al Mariam reconcile his portrayal of President Isaias Afwerki as an existential threat to these Ethiopian soldiers with the documented fact that Eritrea received, sheltered and assisted those very soldiers when they were fleeing the Northern Command crisis?

There is another historical detail worth remembering. Abiy’s November 30 parliamentary acknowledgment was not an isolated diplomatic courtesy. It was a public expression of gratitude for assistance that his government considered consequential during an exceptionally difficult military crisis.
Professor Al Mariam  account devotes considerable attention to the suffering of Ethiopian soldiers. Their sacrifice deserves historical recognition. But historical recognition cannot be selective. Eritrea’s documented humanitarian assistance to those soldiers belongs in the same historical record.

Nor does acknowledging this assistance require overlooking subsequent allegations concerning Eritrean military conduct in Tigray. Those allegations deserve their own evidence-based examination. They cannot retrospectively erase what Abiy publicly acknowledged on November 30, 2020.

A historian’s responsibility is to examine the complete record, not select the episodes that reinforce a preferred political narrative.

Professor Alemariam, the historical record contains an inconvenient question for your argument: Why does your portrayal of Eritrea omit the very assistance that Ethiopia’s own Prime Minister publicly acknowledged and thanked Eritrea for providing?

History is not served by selective remembrance. And the public record does not disappear simply because it complicates a political narrative. https://t.co/EQndpf36eT

Housing costs and taxes are real drawbacks, but lifestyle and enjoyment matter too. California’s appeal extends well beyond the wealthy—its coastline, parks, scenery, and cultural life are enjoyed by people across incomes and political affiliations.
