A very good respond to Marco Rubio State Secretary speech in Athens from a Greek writer, professor and researcher Dimitris Eleas 
I’m Greek. I Found Rubio’s Warning for the West Insulting
Dimitris EleasFacebookTwitterRedditBlueskyEmail
Since I was a little boy in Athens, I learned at school to cherish two words: integrity and parrhesia – the courage to speak frankly. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood at the Pnyx and presented ancient Greece as the birthplace of a civilization defined by excellence, ambition, duty and the pursuit of truth. Interesting. He also presented individualism and nationalism as fundamental characteristics of ancient Greek civilization. But that is a selective reading of a far more complex history.

What kind of West was Rubio talking about in Athens, standing before the Parthenon in all its marble splendor? What West was he wagging his finger at? Was it a West that has yet to learn that the heaviest price of war is always paid by the poor, their children, and the workers? Or perhaps a West where global wealth is concentrated in the hands of a tiny, privileged minority, while the masses struggle under economic hardship? Meanwhile, Rubio’s boss in the White House is estimated to be $2.7 billion wealthier than when he won the 2024 election. Rubio spoke of a West where, in his own home state of Florida, books are banned in public schools.

What kind of West did he represent when Donald Trump humiliated Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky –a leader whose country has suffered a brutal invasion by Russia– inside the Oval Office, while Rubio watched in silence? What kind of West is it when American foreign policy amounts to a revival of some of the darkest forms of imperialism in history? The ancient Greeks were hardly strangers to imperial ambition. But what does it say about the West’s claim to their legacy when the U.S. captures Nicolás Maduro and kills Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei? Where is the respect for sovereignty? Under Rubio, international law has been left in tatters. What kind of West is it when crushing sanctions are imposed on Cuba, punishing ordinary citizens, the poor and workers instead of the elites? What kind of West does Rubio lecture us about when the Trump administration targets immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for over two decades, own homes, and have children who serve in the American military or police force?

Rubio’s West is as close to the greatness of ancient Greece as Elon Musk is to Mars. Furthermore, ancient Greece does not belong exclusively to the modern West. Its ideas traveled far beyond its borders, and Greek thought was itself influenced by other cultures. History is far too complex to be reduced to a straight, convenient line stretching from ancient Athens to the White House.

It is a tragedy for modern Greece to offer its most sacred stage –the very ground where Theodoros Kolokotronis once spoke, the man Greeks revere as a liberator– to such an opportunist. America, a great nation in so many respects, is in dire need of leaders in the mold of Abraham Lincoln or Franklin D. Roosevelt, who embody the courage, knowledge, and integrity of the Founding Fathers. Instead, we are witnessing a political class that views democracy not as an active, daily responsibility, but as a historical trophy or tool to justify raw power.

Within the history of the West, democracy and civil liberties were never freely handed down by benevolent elites. They were won in the streets through the raised fists, strikes, and immense sacrifices by everyday people.

The real issue is not whether American politicians can admire ancient Greece. The issue is that Washington, D.C., uses those classical values to legitimize its global dominance, demanding that other nations respect an international “rules-based order” that the U.S. itself applies selectively. No nation has the right to pose as the ultimate guardian of democracy while simultaneously flouting the sovereign equality of states. The legacy of ancient Greece cannot be twisted into a shield for the doctrines of “America First” and “This Is Our Hemisphere.” (A worldview that treats the rest of the world as expendable.)

I support the West, and I firmly believe that if the West falls, the planet will be lost too. But to survive, the West must take the exact opposite path from the one championed by Rubio’s actions—not his spoken words. The fifth century BC belongs to all of humanity, not to the Greeks alone. It cannot become an excuse for 21st-century America’s failures. The departure of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, amid reports and allegations concerning her tenure, is another reminder of the gap between proclaimed ideals and political conduct. In Rubio’s West, integrity and parrhesia have become rare words. Hubris, by contrast, is everywhere.

🇺🇸 AMERICA IS VOTING. TRUMP'S BIGGEST PROBLEM IS HIS OWN PROMISES.

Voting has begun on the East Coast. According to University of Florida election data cited by The Guardian, more than 58 million early votes have already been cast — significantly more than during the 2022 midterm elections.

One of America's leading political analysts, Frank Luntz, recently offered a simple explanation for Trump's declining popularity: he promised too much.

Throughout 2024, Trump repeatedly assured Americans that he could solve practically every problem quickly and easily.

Wars would end on his first day in office. Foreign countries would pay tariffs, making Americans richer. The federal deficit would disappear, and the national debt would begin shrinking. Elon Musk would eliminate government waste. Prices would fall, wages would rise, and America would become great again almost overnight.

The gap between those promises and reality has become a central political problem for his administration.

Wars have continued. Tariffs have created economic controversy and additional costs for American businesses and consumers. Musk's government-efficiency initiative has faced criticism over its results. Federal debt remains enormous, and many households continue struggling with living costs.

Meanwhile, Americans see Trump pursuing expensive White House renovations, promoting symbolic renaming initiatives, complaining about the Nobel Peace Prize, and maintaining a relationship with Vladimir Putin that remains deeply controversial.

This is the political contradiction Frank Luntz identified: the greater the promises, the greater the disappointment when expectations are not met.

Trump made extraordinary promises. Now voters are judging his record.

And that is precisely what elections are for.

text:
FICTION WITH A PURPOSE.

What does writing books have to do with running for Congress?

More than you might think.

As an author, I've written stories about families, leadership, national security, military aviation, and the dangers of unchecked government power. These aren't just subjects I enjoy writing about. They're issues I've spent years thinking about, experiencing firsthand, and developing solutions for.

Joey America Series & The Green Vette

Strong Families. Logical Solutions. From educating our children to protecting family relationships, these stories connect with my CCTSPA Act and my commitment to education.

Dark Horizon & Ghost Tide Rising

Border security and the Title 40 FRES Amendment. Two separate issues with a common goal: giving those who protect our communities the tools and resources they need while spending taxpayer dollars responsibly.

DevilHog INBOUND

Military aviation, procurement, and the Aviation Versatility and Multi-Role Readiness Act. My experience as a Marine Corps pilot helped shape both the story and the legislative concept.

The Young Coach

Leadership isn't something you're born knowing. It's developed through mentorship, accountability, teamwork, and experience. And what better setting to explore that than Texas football?

Visa Officer: “Why do you want to travel to the United States?”
Applicant: “My elder brother has invited me to attend his wedding. He wants the whole family to be there.”

Visa Officer: “Your brother lives in America?”
Applicant: “Yes. He's been living there for almost fifteen years.”

Visa Officer: “And you've never visited him?”
Applicant: “No, sir. I've never had the opportunity.”

Visa Officer: “What does your brother do?”
Applicant: “He's an engineer. He works for a construction company in Texas.”

Visa Officer: “Who is sponsoring your trip?”
Applicant: “I'm paying for everything myself. I've been saving for this trip for almost two years.”
Visa Officer: “How long do you intend to stay?”
Applicant: “Three weeks. I have a business to return to.”

The officer looked through the applicant's documents before asking another question.
Visa Officer: “Your brother has offered you accommodation at his house?”
Applicant: “Yes, sir.”

Visa Officer: “I noticed something interesting. Your brother's invitation letter says this wedding is particularly important to him. Why?”
The applicant went quiet for a moment.
Applicant: “Because he almost didn't invite me.”
Visa Officer: “What do you mean?”

text:
Elon Musk lost a $56 billion pay package to a man who owned 9 Tesla shares. A judge voided the deal, then ordered Tesla to pay that man's lawyers $345 million, after they asked for $5.6 billion.

Then Delaware's Supreme Court gave it all back. By then the package was worth $139 billion. The man with 9 shares got $1.

In the video below, Musk walks on stage right after shareholders voted for his pay a second time: "Hot damn, I love you guys."

In 2018 Tesla's board offered Musk options on 304 million shares, about 9% of the company, if Tesla hit a set of huge targets. It hit every one.

Richard Tornetta, a former heavy metal drummer with 9 shares, sued that same year.

In January 2024 a Delaware judge struck the deal down and called it "unfathomable."

His lawyers asked for $5.6 billion in fees. The judge called that a windfall and gave them $345 million.

In June 2024 shareholders voted for the package again. In December the judge rejected it again.

Musk moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas.

On December 19, 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed it, unanimously. Throwing the deal out, it said, left Musk "uncompensated for his time and efforts over a period of six years." The lawyers' fee was cut by about 80%. Damages: $1.

Musk said he was "vindicated."

9 shares froze the biggest paycheck in history for 7 years. The final bill for the man who started it: $1.

Did the system protect shareholders, or did 9 shares nearly cost Musk $139 billion?

2/ This week’s newsletter has a common thread: stolen futures.

The namesake is in reference to my latest podcast episode, where I sat down with author David Z. Morris to talk about his book Stealing the Future: Sam Bankman-Fried, Elite Fraud, and the Cult of Techno-Utopia. Morris’ argument is that fraudulent and performative elitism steals the political and economic futures from democracy, as told through his case study on SBF and FTX.

I saw the same vibe when writing my recent essays as well. Data shows that the vast majority of active retail investors see sub-optimal outcomes. The featured chart above shows how only 35% of day traders have active trades after 1 year and that drops to 7% after 5 years. They have their financial futures stolen from them because of gaslighting and elite exploitation not dissimilar from Morris’ descriptions. The emergence of perpetual futures in traditional finance certainly could also play on a pun of “stolen futures”. These new instruments emerged in shady crypto from a formerly convicted criminal Arthur Hayes (pardoned by Trump). I explained the evolution from crypto to high FA-nance using Hayes’ own account which offered unique insight. I also wrote a short blurb in reaction to a neoliberal’s misunderstanding of the welfare state’s history. I use that 19th century history lesson to demonstrate how the current neoliberal agenda to dismantle the welfare (and developmental) state will also steal a more stable and prosperous future.

Finally, in my Furthermore section I catalogued some of the most insightful reads and listens. I spotlighted 3 pieces in economics, tech, and history. American economist Perry Mehrling unfortunately passed away this past month. His 2012 conference paper on the inherent hierarchy of money is worthwhile to read. Kyle Harrison’s recent essay McDonaldization of Venture Capital was a great breakdown of the current state of venture capital and how its evolving away from how we conventionally thought about it towards, for lack of a better term, slop. Then I review Stephen Meardon’s 2024 chapter on 19th century Henry C. Carey’s monetary theory and show how it has a lot of overlap with MMT. Each spotlighted piece reflects a potential stolen future. If Mehrling’s insights were more absorbed, would economics be better? If venture capital was not McDonaldizing, would tech be better? 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗢𝗳 𝗧𝗵𝗲 $𝟲.𝟯𝗕 𝗕𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗛𝗮𝗰𝗸, 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗔 𝗝𝗼𝗯 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗼 𝗘𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘆 𝗪𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘀
The biggest crypto theft in history started with a job interview.

A software engineer at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, had a profile on a job site. It mentioned they worked at Binance.

One day a message came in from a “Project Director” at another company. There was a role. Interested?

First came an interview with someone from HR. Then a second round, with the company’s CEO.

None of it was real. Not the HR person, not the CEO, not the company. On the other side were North Korean hackers, and they were about to take $6.3 billion.

Here’s how they did it, based on what Binance has now made public.

After the interviews, the “company” sent a take-home assignment. That’s normal in tech hiring. You download a small task, work on it, send it back.

The engineer downloaded it.

Hidden inside was a way into the laptop. From then on, the hackers could use that engineer’s work computer as if they were sitting at it.

But the laptop was just the front door. What they really wanted was Binance’s wallets.

In crypto, a wallet is where coins are kept. Whoever controls it can send those coins anywhere, and once they’re sent, there’s no bank to call and no “undo” button. Binance holds billions of dollars of its customers’ coins in its wallets. So the hackers went after the engineers who build and run them.

They already knew who those people were, because a second trap had been running at the same time.

The hackers ran an online ad pushing a fake version of Homebrew, a free tool developers use to install software on their computers. Another Binance engineer clicked the ad and installed the fake one. Binance caught it and removed it. Too late. The hackers had already learned that engineer’s role, and who else at Binance managed the wallets.

So now they had a laptop inside Binance and a list of names.

Next, they turned Binance’s own tools against it. Binance gives staff an internal AI tool for their work. From the hacked laptop, the attackers used it to take over two more engineers: one who runs the wallet systems day to day, and one who writes wallet software. Binance hasn’t said exactly how.

On one of those computers they found a “container deployment permission token.”

In plain English: big companies run their software inside sealed boxes called containers. A deployment token is a digital pass that lets you launch or change what runs in those boxes.

Binance says the attacker got into one of these containers, a working part of Binance’s own system, and from there sent out withdrawals Binance never approved.

That’s the part that should scare every company. They never stole the wallets’ private keys, the master passwords to crypto wallets. Binance says there’s no sign any key leaked. They didn’t need one. They got into Binance’s own machinery and had it send the money out.

On Thursday, October 29, they took over a series of Binance wallets and drained them.

$6.3 billion. More than four times the old record, the roughly $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in 2025, also blamed on North Korea.

Binance calls it a “monthslong scheme.” That means all of this happened before a single coin moved: a fake company, a fake HR person, a fake CEO doing a second-round interview, a fake download pushed through ads, and quietly mapping out who did what inside Binance.

Some of the money was saved. Part of what was taken was stablecoins, crypto tokens pegged 1:1 to the US dollar. Unlike Bitcoin, they’re issued by companies, and those companies can freeze them. Tether and Circle froze the stolen ones, and about $2.5 billion has been recovered.

Binance shut withdrawals for about 48 hours. It says it has refilled 98% of the stolen coins from its own reserves and that customer funds are safe.

Two details stay with me.

Binance has a policy that employees in roles that aren’t public-facing shouldn’t have LinkedIn profiles. It had already seen hackers targeting its staff on LinkedIn, and it says it stopped 57 North Korea-linked hacking attempts this year.

This one it didn’t stop.

And none of it needed a genius hack to get started. It needed a believable job offer and one engineer willing to do a take-home test.

text:
Can totally get to $50k+ fees as a solo headhunter. 

Here is the reality: 

Recruiting has an incredibly low barrier to entry. Have an email? A phone? Great, do that and pay a few $100 a month for sourcing software and you are in business.  

But let's get down to brass tacks. 

For a role to pay a $50k fee, the total comp needs to be at least $200k (assuming at least a normal 25% fee). 

In my experience, very hard for businesses that have <$10M revenue to have someone like that AND justify the fee to you (unless they are PE-backed and can make it an addback). 

A one-time $50k fee is just A LOT to them.  

So, you have to go after bigger businesses.  

Now, the problem is, you start going up against agencies (like me). They have teams and track records.

Venture into the world of businesses doing $50M+ and you are competing with the SHREK firms—(Spencer Stuart, Heidrick & Struggles, Russell Reynolds Associates, Egon Zehnder, and Korn Ferry). You can beat them, but have to have a real reason.  

Here are a few:

- You have real domain expertise.  

You know some obscure software or IT system and can be a real assessor of talent for people applying for roles that need that. 

- You have a narrow industry focus. 

I spoke with a PE fund that had a port co in waste management.  They told me they have a headhunter (and no idea if he is solo or not, but maybe) who is THE guy in the waste management world.  

He knows all the execs, where they are in their careers, and who is ready to move where.  

Hard to compete unless you have been in that industry and have a network and know-how. 

TAM on waste management in the US if you take out the top few firms is <$100 Billion. Small enough to be focused. 

(Also, no way this dude is not mobbed up. C'mon..in waste??!!) 

- You focus on a narrow set of roles, focused on industry. 

If you can be THE person who does CFOs for mid-size manufacturing firms, that's a real advantage.

Say "I do finance roles" and you might get some FP&A Manager positions

- You have real trust. 

See, recruiting is a professional service. And professional services are sold primarily on trust. 

Every new consulting firm wants to say they will do a better job than McKinsey, but no one ever got fired for hiring McKinsey.

Because it's a name that's trusted (by those who buy it).  

Unless you have already developed that trust with clients, hard to earn from the start.  

We actually got started as an events business, organizing networking events for veterans. That's how we built trust. And our CEO has 25 years in the recruiting world. 

---
Ok then, so then how do you develop your client base?  

1. Start with an existing one. Have people you can call from Day 1. Both candidates AND clients. 

2. You have to sell.  

This is hard. Because once you get a role to fill, you know have to run two different sales processes: 

- You have to run the process to find the candidate and get them to offer. 
- You have to keep selling to keep the top of funnel active so when a role is filled, you've got another one to go after.   

Everyone likes to say "Oh get a client that just keeps calling you back year after year" 

How often is that same manufacturing firm hiring a CFO? Maybe every 2-3 years.  So you need a wide client base.  

Now, if you go down market, say going after Data Center Project Managers, you might not make $50k/role, but you can get the volume to hit the gross discussed here. 

(Tech/finance are real exception here, but as a solo, need niche expertise).

In his homily, 85-year-old Father Martin Kelly recalled visiting Ciara at the hospice three weeks before her death to administer the Sacrament of the Sick.

After their conversation, Ciara insisted on going for a walk with him. When she noticed the elderly priest struggling, she offered to link arms with him and help him walk back to her room.

Father Kelly described it as one of the happiest moments of his life.

text:
══════════════ ❧ ════════════════

🎭 CULTURAL DEBUTS 🎭

══════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A CULTURAL TIME CAPSULE ⋆ NOVEMBER 3, 2026

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 8–10 MINUTES

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎵 Music ⋆ 📺 Television ⋆ 🎬 Film & Animation ⋆ 📚 Publishing & Literature ⋆ 🎭 Theatre ⋆ 📻 Radio ⋆ 🎮 Games & Other Cultural Firsts

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

“Every author, as far as he is great and at the same time original, has had the task of creating the taste by which he is to be enjoyed.” — William Wordsworth, Essay, Supplementary to the Preface, 1815.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎭 THE CURTAIN RISES. THE CLOCK TURNS BACK. THE MAGIC BEGINS!

“I see songwriting as having to do with experience, and the more you've experienced, the better it is.” — Mick Jagger, The Rolling Stone Interview: Jagger Remembers, December 14, 1995.

November 3 takes us on a journey through some extraordinary moments in entertainment history, where imagination, innovation, and a little bit of creative rebellion changed the cultural landscape.

In Japan, a monstrous creation emerged from the darkness, carrying the anxieties of a nation still haunted by the atomic age. Across the Pacific, an American Hollywood fantasy made an entirely new kind of journey, bringing millions of families together in front of their television sets.

Television was also finding its personality. A new morning program began welcoming America into its living rooms, an unconventional family arrangement introduced audiences to a future sitcom favorite, and a Queens cosmetics saleswoman walked into a wealthy Manhattan household and made herself right at home.

Music offered another collection of discoveries. A British rock band demonstrated that punk could grow beyond its original boundaries, while a Swedish pop phenomenon delivered an album whose polished melodies concealed some surprisingly personal emotions.

And somewhere between the familiar and the fantastical, an animated adventure invited viewers into a mysterious forest where getting lost might be the beginning of something wonderful.

Different eras, different creative visions, and different kinds of magic. Yet each reminds us that cultural history is not simply about what audiences experienced. It is also about the extraordinary ideas, risks, and decisions that made those experiences possible.

THE PAST IS CALLING. THE MEMORIES ARE ALIVE. LET US RELIVE THE MAGIC! ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎵 MUSIC

1978 — The Jam Release All Mod Cons 🎸

On November 3, 1978, British rock trio The Jam released their third studio album, All Mod Cons, through Polydor Records in the United Kingdom. Following the commercial disappointment of their previous album, This Is the Modern World, frontman Paul Weller faced considerable pressure to demonstrate that the group could develop beyond its energetic punk beginnings. The result was a remarkable creative breakthrough. Combining punk urgency with sophisticated melodies, sharp social observation, and influences drawn from British rock traditions, the album featured memorable songs including "Down in the Tube Station at Midnight," "English Rose," and "David Watts." It helped establish Weller as one of Britain's most compelling young songwriters and became a defining achievement of the mod-revival movement.

🧩 TRIVIA: The album's recording sessions took place at RAK and Eden Studios in London between July and August 1978. Producer Vic Coppersmith-Heaven and the band worked with a comparatively limited recording budget, making the finished album's clarity and musical sophistication particularly impressive.

🌀 OBSCURE: "David Watts" was actually a cover of a 1967 song by The Kinks. Weller transformed Ray Davies's original character study into a distinctly Jam interpretation.

💡 INSIGHT: Creative evolution does not require abandoning your identity. Sometimes the most important breakthrough comes from discovering how much more your original sound can accomplish.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Artistic growth begins when creators refuse to become prisoners of their own success.

·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  ·

1980 — ABBA Releases Super Trouper ✨

On November 3, 1980, ABBA released Super Trouper in Sweden, introducing the group's seventh studio album. By this stage, Benny Andersson, Björn Ulvaeus, Agnetha Fältskog, and Anni-Frid Lyngstad had become international superstars, but the record revealed a more reflective emotional dimension beneath their immaculate pop production. The album included the enormously successful title track, "Lay All Your Love on Me," and "The Winner Takes It All," a deeply personal song exploring the emotional aftermath of a failed relationship. Its themes were particularly poignant given the recent breakdown of Björn and Agnetha's marriage. Although Björn maintained that the song's story was fictional rather than a literal account of their relationship, he acknowledged that it drew upon the emotional experience of divorce. The album became an international success and ultimately topped the British charts, becoming the UK's bestselling album of 1980.

🧩 TRIVIA: The title track's lyrics describe the loneliness that can accompany life on the road, even when a performer is surrounded by thousands of cheering admirers. The song's central image is a powerful stage spotlight, a reminder that public adoration does not necessarily eliminate private loneliness.

🧐 CURIOSITY: The album's famous cover originally had a different photographic concept. When permission to photograph the group at London's Piccadilly Circus was refused, designer Rune Söderqvist arranged a circus-themed photo session at Europa Film Studios in Stockholm.

💡 INSIGHT: Some of pop music's most beautiful moments emerge when extraordinary commercial success meets very ordinary human vulnerability.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A perfect melody can make even the most complicated emotions impossible to forget.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📺 TELEVISION

1956 — The Wizard of Oz Makes Its Television Debut 🌪️

On November 3, 1956, American families experienced a remarkable television event when MGM's beloved 1939 motion picture The Wizard of Oz received its first nationwide television broadcast on CBS. An estimated 45 million viewers tuned in, bringing Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Man, and the Cowardly Lion into living rooms across the country. The broadcast represented an important moment in the relationship between Hollywood and television. A film that had originally reached audiences through theatrical exhibition was now becoming an event that entire families could experience together at home. Its subsequent television showings helped transform the movie into an enduring American tradition, introducing successive generations to one of cinema's most beloved fantasies.

🧩 TRIVIA: Although the 1956 broadcast was transmitted in color, relatively few American households owned color television sets. For most viewers, Dorothy's journey into Oz still unfolded on a black-and-white screen.

🏆 FIRST: This was the first television broadcast of The Wizard of Oz, not its theatrical premiere. Its enormous audience helped establish the annual television presentation as a major entertainment tradition.

💡 INSIGHT: Sometimes a familiar work discovers an entirely new audience when technology changes the way people experience it.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A great story never belongs exclusively to the generation that first discovers it.

·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  ·

1975 — Good Morning America Makes Its Debut ☀️

On November 3, 1975, ABC introduced Good Morning America, with David Hartman and Nancy Dussault serving as its original hosts. Broadcasting from ABC's headquarters in New York City, the program entered an increasingly competitive morning television market, offering viewers a mixture of news, interviews, entertainment, weather, and human-interest reporting. Its arrival represented an important development in American broadcast journalism, helping establish the modern morning-show format in which information and entertainment share the same screen. What began as a new television experiment would become one of America's most recognizable daily programs, celebrating its 50th anniversary in November 2025.

🧩 TRIVIA: Good Morning America replaced ABC's earlier morning program, AM America, which had struggled to establish itself against NBC's Today. The new program would go on to become one of the most recognizable morning broadcasts in American television.

💡 INSIGHT: Television succeeds when it becomes part of people's daily lives rather than simply another source of information.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most enduring broadcasts do more than deliver the news. They become part of the morning ritual.

·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  ·

1978 — Diff'rent Strokes Introduces an Unconventional Family 🏙️

On November 3, 1978, NBC premiered Diff'rent Strokes, introducing audiences to Arnold and Willis Jackson, two brothers from Harlem who are welcomed into the Manhattan household of wealthy widower Phillip Drummond. The premise offered a different perspective on the traditional American family sitcom, using the contrasting backgrounds of its characters to explore social class, race, privilege, and belonging. Conrad Bain played Drummond, while Gary Coleman and Todd Bridges portrayed the two brothers. Coleman quickly became the program's breakout star through Arnold's mischievous personality, sharp comic timing, and memorable one-liners. The series eventually ran for eight seasons across NBC and ABC, becoming one of the defining sitcoms of its generation.

🧩 TRIVIA: The show's success helped create another television institution. Charlotte Rae's character, housekeeper Edna Garrett, became the central character of the spin-off The Facts of Life, which premiered in 1979.

💡 INSIGHT: A successful comedy can entertain while quietly challenging audiences to reconsider their assumptions about family, opportunity, and social differences.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes the most meaningful television breakthroughs begin with an unconventional family.

·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  ·

1993 — The Nanny Arrives on CBS 👠

On November 3, 1993, CBS premiered The Nanny, introducing audiences to Fran Fine, a cosmetics saleswoman from Flushing, Queens, who unexpectedly finds herself employed as the nanny for the three children of wealthy Broadway producer Maxwell Sheffield. Fran Drescher starred as the unmistakable Fran, bringing her distinctive voice, exuberant personality, and unmistakable fashion sense to a character who quickly became a television favorite. The series combined romantic comedy, family entertainment, and cultural contrasts, with much of its humor arising from Fran's working-class background colliding with the sophisticated world of the Sheffield household. Created by Drescher and Peter Marc Jacobson, the sitcom ran for six seasons and became an international television success.

🧩 TRIVIA: The show's creators drew heavily on Fran Drescher's own upbringing in Queens and her experiences in the entertainment industry. Fran Fine's distinctive personality was rooted in a recognizable real-world background rather than being an entirely fictional invention.

💡 INSIGHT: An authentic character can become universally appealing when audiences recognize the humanity beneath the comedy.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Never underestimate the entertainment value of being unapologetically yourself.

·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  ·

2014 — Over the Garden Wall Opens the Door to the Unknown 🍂

On November 3, 2014, Cartoon Network premiered Over the Garden Wall, beginning a five-night presentation of its first animated miniseries. Created by Patrick McHale, the ten-episode fantasy follows two brothers, Wirt and Greg, who find themselves lost in a mysterious woodland known as the Unknown. Their journey introduces them to peculiar inhabitants, strange settlements, unsettling encounters, and a world that seems to operate according to its own mysterious rules. Featuring the voices of Elijah Wood, Collin Dean, and Melanie Lynskey, the series blended American folklore, vintage animation influences, dark humor, and haunting musical arrangements. Its unusual atmosphere and emotionally rich storytelling distinguished it from conventional children's animation and helped it develop a devoted following.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rather than being released as a conventional weekly television series, the ten episodes were presented in pairs over five consecutive evenings, beginning November 3 and concluding November 7.

🏆 FIRST: Over the Garden Wall was Cartoon Network's first animated miniseries, demonstrating the network's willingness to explore a longer-form storytelling format.

💡 INSIGHT: Animation has the freedom to explore emotions, mysteries, and philosophical ideas that are sometimes difficult to express through conventional storytelling.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most memorable journeys are not always about knowing where you are going. Sometimes they are about discovering what the journey reveals.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎬 FILM & ANIMATION

1954 — Godzilla (Gojira) Roars Into Japanese Cinemas 🦖

On November 3, 1954, Gojira received its nationwide theatrical release in Japan, introducing audiences across the country to a cinematic creature that would eventually become one of entertainment history's most recognizable monsters. Directed by Ishirō Honda, Gojira introduced a gigantic prehistoric creature awakened and transformed by the destructive consequences of nuclear testing. The film's spectacular destruction sequences were accompanied by a much darker underlying message. Japan was still living with the trauma of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, while the 1954 Castle Bravo hydrogen-bomb test and the contamination of the Japanese fishing vessel Daigo Fukuryū Maru had intensified public anxieties about nuclear weapons. Honda's monster therefore represented considerably more than a frightening cinematic attraction. Godzilla became an expression of technological terror, human responsibility, and the devastating consequences of scientific power. The film launched a franchise that would span generations and influence monster cinema around the world.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Godzilla suit weighed approximately 100 kilograms, making the actor's performance inside it physically demanding. Haruo Nakajima brought the creature to life through painstaking movements that helped establish the monster's unmistakable screen presence.

🌀 OBSCURE: Godzilla's famous roar was created by rubbing a leather glove coated with pine-tar resin across the strings of a double bass. The sound was recorded and manipulated, including changes in playback speed, producing one of cinema's most recognizable monster noises.

💡 INSIGHT: The most enduring cinematic monsters often represent something much more frightening than the creatures themselves: humanity's own fears, failures, and destructive ambitions.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A monster can become immortal when it gives a society a way to confront its deepest fears.

·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  · ·  ·  ·

1976 — Carrie Brings Stephen King's Horror to the Screen 🩸

November 3, 1976, marks the release date recorded by Stephen King's official website for the film adaptation of his debut novel, Carrie. Directed by Brian De Palma and starring Sissy Spacek in the title role, the film introduced audiences to a shy, socially isolated teenager whose emerging telekinetic abilities become intertwined with years of bullying, humiliation, and religious oppression. The story builds toward an unforgettable prom-night catastrophe, transforming an ordinary high-school ritual into a nightmare of supernatural revenge. Spacek's deeply unsettling performance, De Palma's distinctive visual direction, and the film's exploration of adolescent cruelty helped establish Carrie as a landmark of modern horror cinema. It also introduced a much wider audience to Stephen King's distinctive approach to supernatural storytelling.

🧩 TRIVIA: The famous sequence in which Carrie's house sinks into the ground used a half-scale exterior model built on an elevator mechanism. An originally planned shower of biblical proportions—rocks falling from the sky to bury the house—had to be abandoned because of technical problems with the conveyor system.

🧐 CURIOSITY: The theatrical-release history requires a little care. King's official website records November 3, while the American Film Institute documents the New York opening as November 16 and the Los Angeles opening as November 17. These dates describe different stages of the release history, rather than establishing a November 3 New York premiere.

💡 INSIGHT: Horror becomes especially powerful when the supernatural grows out of recognizable human experiences. In Carrie, the monster is not the only source of terror. The cruelty surrounding her is just as disturbing.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes the most frightening thing about a horror story is how much of it resembles real life.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

AND WHAT A SHOW IT HAS BEEN! 🎭

November 3 brought us a fascinating collection of cultural achievements, beginning with Godzilla's arrival in Japanese cinemas. Ishirō Honda's creation transformed nuclear anxieties into one of cinema's most enduring monsters, while Carrie demonstrated how supernatural horror could expose the very real cruelty of human behavior.

Television offered an equally remarkable collection of milestones. The Wizard of Oz found a second life before an enormous television audience, helping transform a Hollywood fantasy into a cherished family tradition. Good Morning America established a new kind of morning television, while Diff'rent Strokes and The Nanny demonstrated the enduring appeal of unconventional families and unforgettable personalities.

Animation took audiences in another direction. Over the Garden Wall showed that a relatively brief animated production could create an entire world of mystery, atmosphere, humor, and emotional depth.

Music provided its own evidence of creative evolution. The Jam's All Mod Cons demonstrated how punk could develop into sophisticated songwriting without losing its rebellious spirit. ABBA's Super Trouper revealed the emotional complexity beneath the group's polished pop perfection, reminding listeners that even the brightest musical productions can contain deeply personal stories.

These achievements may appear unrelated, but they share an important quality: the willingness to imagine something beyond what audiences had previously experienced.

Honda transformed a cultural fear into a cinematic legend. The creators of The Wizard of Oz discovered that a theatrical classic could become a shared television tradition. Fran Drescher turned an unmistakably personal personality into an international comedy favorite. The Jam expanded the possibilities of punk, while ABBA demonstrated how popular music could combine commercial brilliance with emotional honesty.

And perhaps that is the real magic of cultural history.

Creative achievements do not always reveal their importance on opening night, release day, or the first time a camera rolls. Sometimes their influence takes years to become apparent. Other times, a single broadcast or performance changes everything immediately.

The creators move on, the technology changes, and audiences grow older. Yet the characters, melodies, stories, and ideas remain.

November 3 reminds us that the greatest cultural creations don't simply entertain their own generation. They become part of every generation that follows.

THE YEARS MOVE ON. THE CREATIONS LIVE ON. THE MAGIC NEVER STOPS! ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🍬 CANDY

London, November 4, 1963.

The audience is dressed for royalty. The theater is packed, the atmosphere electric, and some of Britain's biggest entertainers are preparing to perform before the Queen Mother and Princess Margaret.

But one group of young musicians from Liverpool is about to deliver a performance that will become part of music history.

Before the evening is over, a cheeky remark about the cheaper seats and the more expensive ones will become legendary. The audience will erupt, television viewers across Britain will witness the spectacle, and Beatlemania will reach an entirely new level.

Four young men. One royal audience. And a moment that would become unforgettable.

Which legendary band delivered the performance, and what did John Lennon say that made the evening even more memorable? 😉

There's a little royal entertainment waiting in tomorrow's edition!

✈️ Lufthansa CEO Says TAP Acquisition Faces Limited Competition Concerns Ahead of EU Review

🇩🇪 Lufthansa Defends Acquisition: Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr says the German airline group's planned acquisition of up to 49.9% of TAP Air Portugal should face relatively limited competition concerns because the airlines operate largely complementary flight networks.

💶 $1.34 Billion Deal: Portugal selected Lufthansa's €1.2 billion offer for a stake of up to 49.9% in TAP on October 14, beating rival Air France KLM. Lufthansa has also proposed acquiring the government's remaining 50.1% stake through a combination of cash and shares.

🇪🇺 European Commission Review: The acquisition requires approval from European Union competition regulators in Brussels. Spohr acknowledged that regulators could demand concessions but said discussions about specific remedies would be premature.

🌎 Expansion Into Latin America: The acquisition would more than double Lufthansa's share of the Europe to Latin America aviation market, increasing it from approximately 9% to 20%. TAP's extensive connections to Brazil and Portuguese speaking African countries are central to the deal.

🛫 Lisbon Becomes Seventh Hub: Lufthansa plans to establish Lisbon as its seventh major aviation hub, strengthening international connections while expanding operations across Portugal, including Porto, Madeira, the Azores and the Algarve.

📈 Strategic Growth Opportunities: Lufthansa expects the acquisition to generate annual financial benefits of up to €450 million through operational efficiencies, improved connectivity and closer integration of airline services.

⚖️ Regulatory Approval Remains Critical: Although Lufthansa argues that limited route duplication should reduce antitrust obstacles, European regulators will independently examine whether the acquisition could weaken competition, particularly on routes connecting Europe with South America.

text:
THE CONTINENTAL CORNER | 3 NOVEMBER 2026
KAGAME’S RESCUERS TURN CRITICS: FROM INTERNATIONAL PROTECTION TO SANCTIONS—WHO IS NOW THE VICTIM, RESCUER OR PERSECUTOR?

When yesterday's international protectors become today's critics, the political drama changes. But does accountability amount to persecution, or has the relationship between power and protection finally reached a turning point?
By Noble Marara | Professional Critical Analysis & Political Satire

The Continental Corner examines President Paul Kagame's political journey through Stephen Karpman's Victim–Rescuer–Persecutor Drama Triangle, focusing on the changing relationships between Rwanda's leadership and its international supporters.
Kagame's early life involved displacement and refugee protection before his rise through Uganda's military structures and eventual leadership of Rwanda. His political career subsequently developed alongside substantial international diplomatic, military and development cooperation.

The more revealing question today is not how many times Kagame received assistance, but what happens when former supporters begin demanding accountability.

THE DRAMA TRIANGLE: VICTIM, RESCUER AND PERSECUTOR

Stephen Karpman's 1968 model identifies three roles that can perpetuate dysfunctional relationships:

The Victim: feels powerless, focuses on threats and may expect others to resolve problems.
The Rescuer: intervenes to solve problems, sometimes encouraging dependency instead of independence.

The Persecutor: uses blame, criticism or control, whether genuinely or as perceived by another participant.

The model illustrates how individuals can move between roles as relationships change. It is used here as a political analogy, not a psychological diagnosis of Kagame.

Counselling Directory+1📷

The Continental Corner applies this framework to Rwanda's international relationships.

For decades, Western governments supported Rwanda's reconstruction, security institutions and economic development following the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi.
However, international cooperation also attracted criticism where allegations of abuses by Rwandan forces received insufficient accountability.

The central irony is that a government can welcome external assistance while simultaneously objecting to external scrutiny.

WHEN THE INTERNATIONAL RESCUER BECOMES THE CHALLENGER

The political relationship becomes particularly interesting when examined through recent American sanctions.

On 2 March 2026, the United States sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force and four senior officials over alleged involvement in supporting the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

On 28 October 2026, Washington extended sanctions to Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, alleging their involvement in supporting M23 and related military operations.
U.S. Department of the Treasury+1📷

Rwanda denies supporting M23 and maintains that its security concerns, particularly those involving the FDLR, must be addressed.

Reuters+1📷

Here, The Continental Corner observes a striking reversal.
Yesterday, international support demonstrated diplomatic partnership. Today, sanctions demonstrate how quickly that partnership can become confrontation.

The former supporter is no longer simply offering assistance. It is demanding changes in conduct.

The satirical question becomes: has the rescuer turned into a persecutor, or is the rescuer finally acting as a challenger?
Those are not the same thing.

A persecutor seeks to dominate or punish. A constructive challenger demands responsibility and measurable change. Whether particular sanctions fulfil that constructive purpose must be judged by their evidence, proportionality and consequences.

THE POLITICAL DANGER OF PLAYING THE VICTIM

The Drama Triangle becomes particularly relevant when political leaders interpret international pressure as hostility rather than examining the conduct that prompted it.

Governments have legitimate reasons to defend sovereignty, challenge inaccurate allegations and oppose unfair international measures.

Nevertheless, sovereignty does not remove obligations under international law.

The Continental Corner asks whether relationships built on repeated international assistance can become politically uncomfortable when the same partners demand accountability.

There is considerable irony in welcoming international involvement when it provides financial assistance, diplomatic recognition and security cooperation, but questioning that involvement when it takes the form of sanctions.
Apparently, the international rescuer is welcome at the development conference but considerably less popular when arriving with an accountability report.

THE CREATOR: THE ROLE BEYOND VICTIMHOOD

The alternative Empowerment Dynamic replaces the Victim with the Creator, the Rescuer with the Coach, and the Persecutor with the Challenger.

The Creator focuses on outcomes, accepts responsibility and develops solutions rather than remaining trapped in blame.

The Empowerment Dynamic+1📷

Applied to international politics, the model raises three important questions.

First, can Rwanda's leadership respond to allegations through transparent investigations and constructive diplomatic engagement rather than treating every dispute as antagonism?
Second, can international partners replace inconsistent political protection with fair, evidence-based accountability?

Third, can regional governments address the security concerns of Rwanda and the DRC while protecting civilians from further violence?

The responsibility is not Rwanda's alone. International governments must also examine the consequences of their policies, including whether sanctions advance peace or impose additional burdens on ordinary citizens.
THE CONTINENTAL CORNER'S FINAL OBSERVATION

Kagame's political journey reflects decades of changing relationships with military allies, international institutions and Western governments.

The Drama Triangle offers a satirical lens through which to examine those changes, although it cannot establish any leader's private motivations.

The historical question concerns the assistance Rwanda received, the accountability demanded by its partners and the consequences of their changing policies.

Yesterday's rescuer may become today's critic. But criticism does not automatically make someone a persecutor, and receiving criticism does not automatically make a government a victim.

Perhaps the greatest lesson of the Empowerment Dynamic is that lasting independence requires moving beyond permanent dependence on rescuers and permanent conflict with challengers.

The Continental Corner therefore leaves one final question:
When international partners stop offering unconditional support and begin imposing sanctions, will the relationship remain trapped in the Victim–Rescuer–Persecutor Triangle, or can all parties move towards responsibility, transparency and constructive accountability?

Because political maturity is not measured by how many powerful friends a government has accumulated.

It is measured by whether that government can answer difficult questions even when those questions come from its former friends.

THE CONTINENTAL CORNER

By Noble Marara

text:
Washington, D.C. — President Trump announced Tuesday that the United States will stop sending Israel about $4 billion a year, after learning, roughly eight years into the current arrangement, that the country has its own money.

"They have become a very successful country," the president told "Fox & Friends" in a phone interview Tuesday morning, adding that "they don't need" it and that he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "made a deal months ago that we're stopping." Under a 2016 agreement, the U.S. sends Israel $3.8 billion a year through 2028. Netanyahu said in May that he wants to draw that figure down "to zero."

Aides described the discovery as the moment every parent eventually faces, when the grown kid you've been sending rent money to offers to pick up the check.

The realization prompted a review of America's own finances, which officials said went about as well as checking your balance at a gas station. The national debt stood at $40.5 trillion last week. "We were sending $3.8 billion a year out of an account that did not, at any point, have $3.8 billion in it," one Treasury official said. "That's not foreign policy. That's a guy buying a round for the whole bar on a card he knows is going to get declined."

Officials said the country has run for decades on the basic principle of being broke, which is that money isn't real until somebody asks for it back. The U.S. now pays about $2.9 billion a day in interest, a number one budget analyst said he tries not to look at directly, the way you don't open a letter from the IRS.

Asked whether Washington would ask for any of the money back, a senior official laughed for a long time. "You don't ask for it back," he said. "You stop answering the phone for a while and hope everybody forgets."

At press time Treasury officials had redirected the $4 billion toward interest on the debt, where it was expected to last until about Wednesday night.

text:
Some people really ARE above the law 😡 
The Wisconsin Elections Commission voted 5-1 to find probable cause that Elon Musk violated state election bribery law and referred the matter for prosecution. 

Why⁉️ Back in March 2025, the now-trillionaire offered two $1 million checks at an event limited to people who had voted, but he revised it within about 12 hours to say attendance required signing a petition and the recipients would serve as petition spokespeople. 

Special prosecutor Tim Gruenke ultimately declined charges, concluding he was “unlikely to persuade a jury to convict.”

Gruenke emphasized that "nobody was paid anything of value for voting or promising to vote" and treated the episode as a poorly worded offer that was corrected before money was distributed for voting. 

Musk spent at least $20 million supporting conservative Wisconsin Supreme Court candidate Brad Schimel, who lost to Susan Crawford in April 2025.

The prosecutor's decision closes the criminal inquiry without finding that Musk's initial wording was proper; it simply reflects his assessment that the evidence would not support a conviction.

LONG STORY SHORT: Musk did something wrong, but he’ll never be held responsible for it.

And the cycle continues…

🚨 🔥NEW SERIES ANNOUNCEMENT🔥🚨

💥Introducing 👇
DEEP DIVES 🌊

Everybody has a plan for the easy questions. Deep Dives is the show for the ones NOBODY wants to talk about — the "what if's" and "how-to's" that show up when times are questionable and the right action is NOT clear.

⁉️What if you wake up and nobody can tell you what's happening?

⁉️What if someone you love is hurt and help isn't coming?

⁉️What if the medicine runs out… the money stops working… you have fifteen minutes to leave?

🎯This series takes those questions head-on — raw and real, no sugar-coating — and walks each one through, step by step, until there's a decision you can actually stand on.

💥HOW EVERY EPISODE WORKS:

🔹 What it REALLY looks like — said plainly

🔹 The line you decide BEFORE it happens, so nobody has to invent it in a crisis

🔹 The actual words to say when the moment comes

🔹 One action you can take TONIGHT

🔹 And every episode closes with "The Way Forward" — the recap that pulls it all together

🎙️AT THE TABLE: a five-chair panel talking it through together — the Moderator, the Practical, the Steady Voice, the Provisioner, and a rotating specialist Guest Chair matched for each episode's topic.

🔥Facts come only from reliable official sources — https://t.co/Z3GVn6foOf, the National Weather Service, the CDC, and the American Red Cross — researched fresh for every episode. Where the show offers its own framework, it says so.

🎙️ EPISODE 1 IS HERE: "What If You Don't Know What's Happening?"
And the season ahead goes where it has to: fact vs. rumor when everyone's scared… stay or go… medicine running out… a loved one stranded or missing… the knock at the door… death, grief, and dignity… and the not-normal afterward.

💥16 episodes. Five arcs. The conversations that matter most are the ones nobody wants to have — so we're having them.

🫡🇺🇸Be Ready Before It Happens. 🇺🇸

Brought to you by Florida Flea 😎🌴🏴‍☠️

Follow along, share this with somebody you love, and pull up a chair. 🪑

text:
Yesterday, I spoke with two groups of people:

One group consisted of three strangers I met in the cafeteria; the other was a class of 13 students.

I told them specifically that 
I have been listening to Donald Trump speeches during  the last 30 days campaigning for candidates running for the House, the Senate, and local municipal offices.

For 30 consecutive days, I listened to 29 of Trump’s speeches—each lasting two hours.

I have a crystal-clear understanding of the origins and implementation of every single policy measure he has proposed.

Yet, these two groups…

Their attitude—filled with hatred and profound misunderstandings of Trump—left me absolutely speechless!

Beyond simply closing their ears and dismissing everything…

Ignoring how I heard Trump personally 
Over the 30 of his speeches 

And having followed Trump closely for the past 11 years—ever since 2015—

Every policy he promised has been fully implemented!

Not only did they refuse to accept what I said…

They went so far as to openly criticize Trump—accusing him of being greedy and self-serving, alleging that his family uses bribery, claiming he deploys troops to foreign nations, and asserting that he forcibly seized the President of Venezuela…

They even accused him of starting senseless wars, bombing Iran, and killing countless civilians… and so on, and so forth!

Listening to their baseless rebuttals, I nearly fainted.

It is a stark reality—a case of "Trump Derangement Syndrome" (TDS) that has spiraled completely out of control.

Continuing the argument would only have led to an unpleasant falling-out.

So, I left them with just one remark…

"Let’s wait and see what the election results reveal today."

Why did I wake up so early this morning to write about matters that have no direct bearing on my own country, Singapore?

Because I know, deep down, that in these U.S. midterm elections…

The Republican Party—in the House, the Senate, and at the local level—is headed for a landslide victory!

And why does that matter?

Because it concerns the future of the United States—its rise or fall—over the next 30, or even 100, years.

If the Republicans secure a majority in the White House, the Senate, the House, and local legislatures…

Then, after Trump leaves office in 2028, J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio could potentially carry the torch for another 16 years.

Trump might even live to see his own son, Barron Trump, become President.

I offer my prayers… I entrust it all to God

and I wait to see what unfolds.

Something truly wonderful is about to happen! 

November 26, 2004, 3:56 AM

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

THE FOOLE'S WEDDYNG V

There is no sensatioun upon earth more persuasive than the smell of a free cake in a hungrie cité.

Bològne awoke upon the Vigil of All Saints to a rumour of baking. It came in at the windowes before the bells, and the bells, being fewer that yeere, were the lesse able to compete. It rose from the ovens of the Hegemon, which had been lit upon the Tuesday and were not permitted to cool; it travelled along the alleys of the old quarters, where it found the broken houses and the empty chimneys and the persons who had been spared; and it entered them, as a rumour doth, by the nose, and did there what no proclamatioun had done in seven yeeres. It made them lyft their heades.

Forty thousand cakes had been baked. They were small and round, spiced with a little saffron, and marked upon the crust with a cross, according to the custom of the Vigil; and the Hegemon’s bakers, who had been instructed in the matter by the chamberlain, had added to the cross, in a manner never before permitted, a rysing sunne.

The poore of Bològne were thus to eat the arms of the Malvezzi, and to pray, in retourne, for the dead of the Malvezzi, upon the principle that a man who hath taken the sun from you may as well be thanked for the crust.

But the paper had been signed upon the Tuesday.

It had been drawn up, at the Egyptian’s instruction, by a notarie who was not asked whether he understood it, and who, being a prudent man, did not offer; and it was laid upon the table of the Hegemon’s private chamber, with a taper, a stick of wax, and the husband in the case, who could not read it. It was read to him, with some omissions, by the chamberlain. It was read to Herod not at all, the Hegemon having declared that he never examined the contents of a document that amused him.

The instrument ran as followeth:

Articles of Marriage between Violanté, called the Foole, and Zohra, called the Egyptian, made in the sight of God, the Hegemon, and a notarie.

I. That the said Zohra shall be struck from the Inventorie of the Hegemon’s curiosities, and entered in the Register of Persons, with a number.

II. That she shall keep her own name, whatsoever name the Church shall give her.

III. That she shall hold the keyes of her husband’s chamber, purse, and cupboard, and that he shall have the use of them upon her leave.

IV. That she shall be of the Lady’s household, with a chamber of her own, and shall not be put from it save at the Lady’s consent.

V. That the Hegemon’s laughter, which the said Violanté hath declared in the presence of witnesses to be his sole possessioun, shall stand surety for his keeping of the foregoing; and that, should he fayle, the said laughter shall be forfeit to the said Zohra, to be disposed of as she thinketh fit.

Violanté, hearing the fyfth article, had laughed until he fell off the bench. It seemed to him the finest joke that had ever been made in his hearing, and he had made it himself. He set his mark. The Hegemon, who had been told that the document contained a jest about his laughter, was so pleaused that he set his seal to it without enquirie.

It was the fyrst legally binding instrument in the history of Bològne to name the Hegemon’s laughter as collateral; and it was the fyrst, since the beginnyng of the One Way, in which the Hegemon’s signature had made a person safer.

He did not notice either distinctioun.

The bride was baptised at dawn, in a silver basin, by the chaplain, who had consulted the Fathers and found them silent. She was named Giovanna, which is to say, a name that the Church could enter in a register; and she answered to it in churches, and to Zohra in every other place, and the two names lay upon her, thenceforth, as a coat lyeth upon a coat.

The processioun began at noon.

It came down the One Way from the great market to the western arch, between the covered arcades and the new façades and the screens upon which the future avenue had been painted to hide the present one; and it was the grandest spectacle that Bològne had seen in her history, and, so far as the chroniclers could ascertain, the least attended by anyone who had not been told to be.

The poore were there, by thousands. They had been given cakes.

They ate them standing, in the streets, in the sun, with the grave and attentive manner of persons who have been hungrie for some tyme and are not yet sure of the etiquette. They ate them with their eyes upon the processioun, upon the horses and the banners and the musicians and the tumblers, and for the length of a cake they did not remember anything at all. It is the genius of a cake that it occupieth the mouth and the memory at once.

Among the crowd, by the foot of the arch, an old woman in a patched cloak stood with a cake in her hond, looking at it. She was the same old woman who, seven yeeres before, had asked her neighbour in a great hall whether the Hegemon meant to preserve the peace by fyrst taking away the roof above her head. Her house had since been taken down for a stonestore, and the stonestore had since been moved. She turned the cake over, and examined the sunne upon its crust.

“Is it a cake,” she said to her neighbour, “or a receipt?”

Her neighbour begged her to hold her tongue, and ate her own.

The Hegemon rode at the head, in a mantle of green and gold, upon a horse of such splendour that the horse seemed to be asking pardon for it; and about him, at every pillar and every window, stood the guaurds. They were doubled. They had been doubled for the Hegemon’s own safetie and tripled for the wedding’s, and the processioun, to a person of observatioun, resembled a festival conducted in a besieged fortress. It was observed that he laughed more loudlie than was his custom, and that he laughed a little before the jests.

Behind him came the bridegroom, in a coat of crimson and gold with sleeves that touched the ground, upon a mule decked in ribbons, which, being of a literall dispositioun, had been persuaded with some difficultie that it was to be married to nobody.

And behind the bridegroom, upon foot, between two maides of the Lady’s household, in a gown of deep blue lent from the Lady’s own presses, came the bride.

She walked slowly.

She did not look at the crowd, nor the arch, nor the Hegemon. She looked at the stones, the broad pale stones of the One Way, laid by men who had not been payd, and she walked upon them as a woman walketh upon a floor that she means to buy.

Upon her veil, at the left shoulder, there was a clasp in the shape of a lilie, of silver.

It had been put there by the Lady herself, upon the steps of the palays, that morning, without a word, and without the Hegemon’s knowledge; it was the clasp that Herod had ordered to be displayed whensoever the conversatioun turned to the prosperité of the House Malvezzi. Desiderata had taken it from her own veil, and set it upon the other’s, and stepped back.

It was a small gesture, and it was observed by no one. It is recorded here because no one else will record it.

The nuptial mass was said beneath the great arch, under the frieze of the Hegemon’s victories, before a congregation of five thousand and the figure of Civic Glory, who held, in her carved honds, a little model of the road, and who regarded the proceedings with a stone detachment that the bishop afterwaurd described as exemplarie.

Violanté had been coached.

He had been coached by the chaplain in the form of the vows, and by the young lordes in the spirit of them, and the two had not been reconciled. He knelt. He declared, in a voyce that carried to the third arcade, that he would love, honour, and keep the said Zohra as long as she kept him; that he would endow her with all his worldly goodes, being, he was given to understand, a bottle, a spoon, and a shawl; and that he would obey her in all things, in the manner of a man making a jest, the fyfth article of his own doctrine notwithstanding. The congregation laughed. The priest asked whether he was in earnest. He declared that he was always in earnest upon the matter of supper.

The bride made her vow in her own tongue.

It was the tongue of the counting-song, low, flat, and certain, and nobody in the arch understood a syllable; so that the priest, who was a man of resource, accepted it as Latin, and the congregation, who were instructed to be moved, were moved. It was afterwaurd reported in the poets’ accounts of the weddyng as an exquisite lament. It was, in the strict sense, the terms of the paper.

Herod gave her away.

It was a thing he did with great grace, taking her hond in his, in the sight of all, and placing it in the fool’s; and he held it a moment longer than courtesie required, as he had been wont to hold other people’s honds, and the bride did not withdraw hers. She looked at him with a perfect, attentive, courteous patience, and said, in Italian, “I thank my lord for the gyft.”

“ It cost me nothing,” said Herod, pleaused.

“So I have understood,” said the bride.

He did not hear it. He had alreadie tourned to the crowd.

By two o’clock there was a battle.

It was the fyrst of the spectacles, and it had been commissiouned, with great expense, from a company of players upon the meadow beyond Porta San Felice, in front of the foundation stone: The Overthrow of the Rebel Ferrabosco, or, Justice Triumphant. It was in five acts. The rebel was played by a tanner, in a beard of straw and a cap of rushes, upon a white mule, chalked; for it was a curious circumstaunce that the Hegemon’s own theatrical companie, in need of a rebel, had found that no one could imagine him upon any other horse.

He was defeated in the fyrst act by a company of the Hegemon’s guaurd, in the second by a general, in the third by an angel, and in the fourth by the unaided forces of nature; in the fyfth he was brought to the foot of the throne and forgiven, amid applause, and the white mule was led off, to be eaten.

A boy of seven, upon his father’s shoulders, in the front of the crowd, lifted his head at the end and said, clearly, to everyone who could hear him:

“But he never lost!”

His father, who had spent four yeeres learning to be quiet, put a cake in his mouth.

The banquet was held in the field of the new cité, upon trestles that stretched from the foundation stone to the line where the first street was to be, under a canopy of green and gold, with forty tables and four thousand guests, of whom some three hundred sat; and the Hegemon sat at the head, with his wyfe at his right hond, and the bridal couple at his left.

The envoys of the Guelphs and of the Ghibellines had both come. They sat at either end of the high table, a hundred feet apart, and had agreed upon exactly one point, which was that neither of them should sit lower than the other. Each had brought a gift: a gilded cup, from the same goldsmith, and each bowed to the other with a regard of the most perfect cordialitie, and lifted it, and drank.

“To the Hegemon,” said the Guelph.

“To the Hegemon,” said the Ghibelline. “And to his enemies.”

“Which?” said the Guelph.

The Ghibelline smiled.

Among the guests, near the door, there sat two couples of the poore. They had been married that autumn, in the parish of San Vitale, and had payd the Marriage Levy, a tenth of their portiouns, to the splendour of the occasioun. It was the Hegemon’s whim to invite them. They were placed at the lowest trestle and given a cake each, and a little wyne, and instructed to be happie.

They were happie.

They sat very straight, with their cakes before them untouched, the four of them, and looked at the high table, and at the golden cups, and at the roast peacockes, which were brought in with their tailes spread, and carved. And the younger wyfe, who was perhaps nineteen, laid her hond upon her husband’s sleeve and said something low, and he nodded, and it was not heard.

The poets sang the epithalamium.

It had been composed by five, in committee, with some difference of opinion about the metre, and was sung by a choir of twelve boyes with an accompaniment of recorders, upon a dais of green and gold, to the high table, in the manner of a song that is meant to be heard by persons who are not listening.
Ring out, ye belles, for the foole and his bryde; The hogge and the hawke on one hedge-rowe ryde: He bringeth a cappe and a borrowed shawle, She bringeth a paper, and keepeth it all.

Hey derrie, hey, for the weddyng cake, For the poore man’s soule and the great man’s sake! Eat while ye may, for the musique is sweete, And the reckonyng cometh after the meate.

The lorde gave the foole a palays, a purse, And leave to be wicked, which is better than worse; He gave him a wyfe at the pryce of a salt, And counted the bargayn, and found it no fault.

Hey derrie, hey, for the weddyng cake…

The preest sayeth, “Wilt thou?” The foole sayeth, “Aye!” The bryde sayeth nothyng, and noteth the daye; For a vowe that is spoken is blowen on the wynde, But a vowe that is written is wedded and signed.

Hey derrie, hey, for the weddyng cake…

They bake thee a cake for the soule that is gone, And a prayer for the lorde with the throte that is torne; But where is the bread for the quicke and the poore? There’s a cake for the grave, and a crust for the doore.

Hey derrie, hey, for the weddyng cake…

The lorde layeth stones in a field full of ayre, For a cité of marble where nobodie are; The foole layeth kysses where kysses are none, And both of them marvell that nothyng is done.

Hey derrie, hey, for the weddyng cake…

So drynk to the foole, and the bryde with her key, For the keyes of the house are the keyes to the fee; And whether the belle toll for weddyng or knell, The songe hath two meaninges, and one shall not tell.

The composers had intended it as a compliment.

It was heard, in the great hall of the Hegemon’s mind, as such; and the courtiers applauded, and the boyes bowed; and no one who had been taught by long experience to listen to the words of the Hegemon’s poets listened to these. But the song had been written to be sung twice. It was noted, by the end of the evening, that the kitchenne-women, bringing in the sweet, were humming the refrain; that the pages, carrying the wyne, had learned the fyfth verse; and that the poore at the lowest trestle, who had not been taught to listen, had listened, and heard what the composers had not known they had written.

It was a song that could be sung by two audiences, and meant a different thing to each.

By midnyght it was being sung in the old quarters. It was sung in the taverns beneath the broken houses, and in the barns of the contado, and in a cellar near the western gate, by a woman of forty who had learned it from a boy who had been given a cake. It was sung in the camp of the Green Court, by a carter who had been told it in a market. Not one verse of it was altered. Every verse had been changed.

The jester’s speech came after the sweet.

He rose upon his bench with a goblet of the Hegemon’s best, and the whole of the tables turned to him, as the sunflowers turn; and he gave, in a voyce already a little thick, the toast of the evenyng.

“My lordes, my ladyes, and my fellow-subjects of this great and well-fed Citie! It is the custom, upon the Vigil of All Saints, to remember the dead; and I have been given to understand that the Hegemon’s cousin, Messer Niccolò, hath been of late among them.”

A silence. He had not been told not to mention it. He had been told nothing at all.

“I am told,” said Violanté, “that it was the work of a Wodeman, who liveth in the Black Wode and drinketh the blood of lordes. I take comfort, my lord, that he hath no taste. I have drunk your lordship’s cellar, and it is mostly vinegar and debt.”

He laughed. The hall, after a pause in which a good many things were decided, laughed with him; and Herod, who had gone very white at the word, and who set down his cup with great care upon the board, laughed also, the longest and the loudest, with his hond upon his chest.

Desiderata, at his side, did not laugh.

She looked, with an attentioun that had no expressioun in it, at the figure of her husband laughing; and for a moment, which no one saw, she lifted her cup, and drank to the Wodeman, whoever he might be.

At nyghtfall the candles were lit.

It was the custom of the Vigil that the living should go out with lights to the churches, to the churchyardes, to the crossroads; to give to the dead who walk upon that nyght a little warmth, and to be reminded, by the dead, of the proportions of things. They went in thousands. They went along the One Way in long rivers of flame, with their cakes in their pockets and the sun upon the crust, and in the dark of the unfinished arcades, where the gardens had not been planted, they met the dead.

They were not frightened.

The dead of Bològne were a numerous companie that yeere: those who had died in the demolitions, and in the road-gangs, and in the debtors’ cells; those who had been taken from their beddes; those who had gone out in carts upon the Florence road and had not been heard of since. The living knew them. The living had, for the length of a cake, forgotten them. They remembered them now, in the dark, in the candlelight, in the smell of the saffron, and a number of persons were seen that nyght to weepe upon the One Way, who had not wept in seven yeeres, and could not have said for whom.

The children played at a game.

It was a game of the dark and of the hedges, in which one child was the Wodeman and the rest were the lost travellers, and the Wodeman, having caught one, asked him a question: what hast thou done? The traveller, if he were clever, answered, Nothing; and was freed. If he said, I do not know, he was kept. It spread through the old quarters that nyght, from the foot of the arch to the Porta San Felice, and was never afterwaurd forgotten.

The bridal couple were conducted to the apartment that had been prepared for them in the east wing of the palays, between the Lady’s chambers and the linen-room, by torchlight, with songs, and scattered nuts.

The bridegroom had been drinking since two in the afternoone.

He was put to bed, in his crimson coat and his bells, by two of the pages, with great ceremonie, and fell asleep before the door was shut, with his mouth open and one hond upon the shawl that he had never retourned. He snored. It was a vast, innocent, complacent snore, the sound of a man who has done the best day’s work of his life and been rewarded for it, and the walls of the east wing received it with the patience of walls.

The bride did not sleep.

She sat upon the edge of the bed in the borrowed gown, by a single taper, with the silver lily at her shoulder, and she took, from a place in her sleeve, a folded paper. It was the Articles of Marriage, sealed with the seal of the Hegemon. She unfolded it, and smoothed it upon her knee, and read it through, slowly, to the end.

She had learned her letters at nine, in a convent kitchen, in exchange for scouring the pots, and had told no one; for a woman who can read, in a palays, is a woman who is expected to be dishonest.

When she had finished she folded it agayn, and put it back.

She took the key of the chamber from her belt. It was the fyrst key she had ever owned. She turned it over in her fyngers, and looked at the sleeper, and at the door, and at the ceiling, where the roof-beams could be counted in the taperlyght.

There were eleven.

She counted them twice.

Then she rose, and drew the curtain, and looked out of the window at the One Way, where the candles of the living were still moving in the dark, in long, thin lines, among the unfinished arches. She watched them for a long tyme. They had been given cakes, and the cakes were eaten, and she knew, as clearlie as she knew the number of the beams, that in the morning the people who carried those candles would wake up hungrie.

And she knew, too, that someone would have to count them.
