what is his largest top 10 hot takes (negative)
Marques Brownlee’s most controversial, cynical, or generally critical "hot takes" over his career—opinions where he explicitly pushed against consumer trends or corporate hype cycles—focus on structural flaws in the industry.

Here are his top 10 most prominent negative or controversial tech hot takes:

1. Budget phones should be completely discontinued.
The Take: Marques argued that manufacturers should stop making new budget phones entirely. Instead, companies should just provide longer software support (5–7 years) for flagships, turning older premium phones into the "new" budget tier.

The Backlash: Critics labeled this an "out-of-touch" take, pointing out that a massive portion of the global population relies on immediate, ultra-affordable hardware and cannot wait three years for a flagship price to drop. [1]

2. Smartphone cameras are actively getting worse due to AI.
The Take: He has repeatedly argued that computational photography and aggressive AI processing have crossed a line. Instead of capturing a real moment, phones are heavily over-sharpening, smoothing, and artificially altering details (like color science or texture) to the point where the photos look synthetic and "unreal". [1, 2]
3. Hardware-first AI gadgets are fundamentally half-baked software apps.

The Take: During the peak hype of standalone AI hardware (like the Humane AI Pin or Rabbit R1), Marques maintained that these gadgets should not exist as standalone physical products. His take was that they are just unoptimized Android apps trapped inside overpriced, overheating, and battery-draining wearable shells. [1]

4. Customization options actually make consumer tech worse.
The Take: Despite being a dual-user who appreciates Android's utility, Marques has argued on his Waveform podcast that unrestricted user-defined customization lowers the aesthetic baseline of tech. He noted that giving users complete freedom over icon grids, colors, and layout configurations usually results in objectively messy, unpolished user interfaces. [1]
5. Small smartphones are completely dead, and consumers are to blame.
The Take: When fans begged for smaller devices (like the iPhone mini or small Asus Zenfones), Marques bluntly told his audience that small phones are dead because consumers didn't actually buy them. He took the stance that internet vocalism doesn't equal real-market sales data, proving consumers ultimately prefer large screens. [1]
6. Most people should completely skip first-generation foldables.
The Take: While many tech enthusiasts praise foldables as the absolute future, Marques consistently delivers a wet blanket take on them. Following the release of major hardware like the $2,000 iPhone Duo, he emphasized that foldables introduce too many basic regressions—worse cameras, poor selfie sensors, massive weight, and lack of app scaling—making them a massive waste of money for average consumers. [1, 2, 3]
7. Ecosystem lock-in has made Apple completely lazy.
The Take: He has called out iOS users for allowing Apple to stagnate. Because Apple’s "walled garden" (iMessage, ecosystem traps) successfully stops users from leaving, Marques argues Apple has no real incentive to innovate quickly. They hold back standard features (like fast-charging or baseline 120Hz displays) because they know their consumer base is too trapped to switch to Android to get them.
8. 5G was an overhyped marketing scam for the average person.
The Take: During the massive telecom push for millimeter-wave 5G, Marques dropped a video flatly stating "5G Sucks." He argued that the infrastructure was deeply impractical, drained smartphone batteries at catastrophic rates, and offered zero real-world utility over a standard, stable LTE connection for daily tasks. [1]
9. Touchscreens do not belong on traditional clamshell laptops.
The Take: For years, Marques resisted the idea of touchscreen laptops. Even when Apple relented and launched the touchscreen MacBook Pro, he called the final execution "sloppy and messy." His ongoing take is that until the operating system's architecture is fully rewritten for touch, slapping a touch panel on a traditional laptop screen is an ergonomic failure that introduces screen wobble and poor application scaling. [1]
10. Tech companies treat consumers like unpaid beta testers.
The Take: A recurring thesis in his reviews is his hatred of "ship now, fix via software later" culture. He heavily criticizes modern brands for launching physical products with missing core features, unoptimized software, or broken promises, forcing consumers to pay premium retail prices to essentially test unfinished tech.

4. Apple’s "Apple Intelligence" rollout was an anti-consumer marketing trick.

The Take: Marques heavily criticized Apple for launching phones and computers centered entirely around AI marketing, despite the actual software being months away from a stable release. He slammed this as a prime example of Apple selling an unfinished promise and using early buyers as unpaid beta testers.

The Take: For years, Marques argued that touchscreens didn't belong on clamshell laptops. He points out that the vast majority of people buying "Pro" hardware never touch a single professional workflow, while actual power users are left wanting more customizable software.

Would you like to look closer at his specific criticisms of the base-model iPhones, or explore his reviews on Apple's first foldable (the iPhone Duo)?

concise

Ecosystem Laziness: Argues Apple deliberately slows down hardware innovation because their "walled garden" (iMessage, lock-in) stops users from leaving anyway.

Malicious Product Tiering: Slams Apple for keeping ancient features (like slow 60Hz screens and slow data speeds) on expensive base-model iPhones just to force people to buy the "Pro" versions.

Touchscreen Macs are Sloppy: Called the touchscreen MacBook Pro an ergonomic failure and "sloppy" because macOS wasn't built for fingers.
Form Over Function: Faults Apple for letting aesthetics ruin usability, famously mocking the Magic Mouse charging from the bottom.

text:
This kebab shop’s chocolate pizza came with a £1 choice: go bigger or add cheese. 🍕

In October 2026, kebab-shop customer DaMonkfish was puzzling over a Nutella-pizza menu that offered cheese for £1 extra.

The plain ten-inch chocolate pizza was £5, and the twelve-inch version was £6.

Adding Smarties and marshmallow took those prices to £7 and £8, before the optional cheese.

The size upgrade deserves a closer look, because two extra inches across a pizza buy more than a thin strip along one edge.

The circle grows in both directions.

On the menu’s stated diameters, a round twelve-inch pizza has 44% more surface area than a round ten-inch one.

The plain version’s price rose by 20%, from £5 to £6, so the larger size cost less per square inch.

The £1 cheese option asks a different question: whether changing the combination would make the treat better.

DaMonkfish had initially been surprised by sweet pizzas themselves, then acknowledged that readers described eating them for years.

One recalled a pizza place offering Nutella on its own, with banana or with ricotta.

Another remembered trying a chocolate pizza with cheese and liking it more than expected.

Those accounts challenged the idea that chocolate on a pizza was automatically a terrible idea.

They did not settle what this shop’s version would taste like.

Some readers pictured a savoury pizza topping over Nutella and sweets, while others suggested cream cheese or ricotta.

The menu specified what the cheese cost, but not which cheese it was.

Some great insight from @10AJMcCarron on @TheUFL

Here's everything AJ McCarron says about the UFL on the Nov 3 Coach JB Show.

0:40:26, staff budget. "The league kind of sets this budget on you," so he has to work around it and reach out to coaches himself.

0:40:42, finding coaches. He says he knows plenty of coaches, but he has to find college analysts "willing to come in the off season" or guys who are retired.

0:41:05, contracts. "I don't set any contracts… they're a set pay by the league." Finding talent "ain't hard."

0:41:27, play calling. He didn't call plays in his first year as head coach. He says the main job then is clock management.

0:42:04, analytics. "I don't believe in the analytical side of it." He leans on veteran coaches on his staff instead.

0:46:00, 2026 timeline. After he was hired, he had two weeks to hire a staff, two more to get ready to draft 64 players, then two more before camp. He called it "extremely tough to do."

0:52:30, first-year staff. He hired guys he trusts, who "might not be the best coaches at their position," because he cared most about "not being backstabbed my first year." He didn't want "yes men."

0:53:27, camp. Setting up camp was the hardest part. He drew on his own two years playing in the XFL and UFL.

1:01:09, draft. It's November 18th, and the first two rounds air live. He has the 3rd pick in round 1 and the 2nd pick in round 2 (paraphrased, because the audio is muddy there).

1:01:27, draft plan. No early QB: "I gotta go O-line, D-line." At quarterback, "we got DTR."

1:01:45, DTR. He's surprised nobody "scooped up" DTR. They worked on his mental toughness. He thinks DTR "has a chance to be really, really good," and says staying healthy was "our biggest downfall last year."

1:02:45, roster. He kept most of his wideouts. They finished the year with 50 players and had to cut to 35 before the draft, so now they "got to work our way back up to 64."

1:03:02, staff openings. He offered a coach named Braden a job and hopes to hear back today. Another friend he's recruiting still hasn't called him back. He gives no last names or positions.

1:04:20, Siskey. "Siskey said he's gonna stay home. He ain't coming back this year." Then: "Love him to death, gonna miss him," and "Siskey always gonna be my guy." His business is doing well, and his youngest, Knox, is still at home. The audio is slightly unclear on "ain't," but the context supports it.

1:05:31, RB coach. His running backs coach also has to be his special teams coordinator. That rules out his friend "T-Rich," who never played special teams.
1:05:52, budget again. "If I had more money and I was able to hire more staff…" he'd bring in guys from winning programs, "but it makes it so tough."

text:
The rotor blades barely settled in Blacksburg before signs of James Franklin’s imminent departure first appeared. Yes, he loves helicopters and airports but more importantly, he loves money and himself the most. That’s why when Florida State fired Mike Norvell this past weekend, James Franklin’s time at Virginia Tech is coming to an end.

Say what you will and say the truth about Penn State football right now; Matt Campbell’s 1st season is not going well. And while that is true, what’s also true is that Franklin has Virginia Tech in a much better spot at 6-2 (3-1) than Penn State at 4-4 (1-3). In fact, if you take away the 2pt loss to Pitt and the 5 pt loss at Cal away, this team is 8-0 and most certainly ranked in the top 10. But you can’t take them away from Big Game James, because that’s his trademark. He gets you so close to feeling like your team is elite while never actually executing on the field to make your team elite. 

This strategy has worked for Franklin and as the old saying goes, “don’t hate the player, hate the game.” Florida State is desperate for national relevance again. They are falling behind not just Florida and Miami in state, but behind the likes of Pitt, Boston College, and every other school not named Georgia Tech in the ACC.

Franklin is a program builder seeking a higher level of prestige than what Virginia Tech can possibly offer. He wanted Florida State last year but couldn’t wait on Tallahassee so he settled for Blacksburg. Now, he has buyers remorse. Good for him, unlike a car, he can trade his job in for a more valuable one. 

So when Florida State announces James Franklin as their new Head Coach, don’t be mad at him for leaving Blacksburg. At least you can rest easy knowing he had a 45 minute car ride to the nearest airport on his way to Tallahassee.

text:
"The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds.

History is against Trump's Republicans: The sitting president's party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterm elections since World ‌War Two. Trump's approval rating is hovering near his all-time lows, dragged down by deep voter frustration over the war with Iran and the resulting rise in fuel prices.
There is little doubt this year's election is all about Trump, who is nearly two years into his second term. Trump himself has told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot," a message Democratic leaders have happily echoed.

In remarks that appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel, Trump said that he intended to stop $3.8 billion in promised annual funding to Israel after the ​end of this year, but it was unclear how he would do so, given a 2020 law mandating the funding levels.
The close US-Israel alliance has been a particular focus in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is running a closely watched campaign for Senate.
The ​president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, most in states he easily won in 2024. He also offered the novel inducement of a proposed $5,000 check to ⁠each US adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, which would have to approve the costly payout.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist.
But opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability, and disapprove of Trump's handling of the issue.

TRUMP DEPLOYS ELECTION MONITORS
Legal observers and ​Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge Tuesday's results if Republicans lose.

The US Justice Department said on Tuesday it was deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election ​Day monitoring effort in history.
Democrats have criticized the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of ‌the Senate's 100 ⁠seats, though most contests are not considered competitive. 

ELECTION DRAMA IN MICHIGAN, ALASKA, TEXAS
The Michigan Senate contest between El-Sayed, 42, and Rogers, 63, represents a high-profile test of whether Republicans' identity-based attacks – El-Sayed would be the nation's first Muslim senator — prove effective in a battleground state.

text:
$SWIM Q3 2026 earnings: Latham fiberglass pool sales surge, but rising overhead squeezes margins

Latham Group, the largest maker of in-ground residential swimming pools in North America, grew rapidly in fibreglass pools while its vinyl liner business slipped. Total revenue rose 13% from a year ago, and sales in the key Sand States jumped 21%, chief executive Sean Gadd said. Factory efficiency lifted gross margin, and the company narrowed its full-year outlook around the same middle target, leaving 13% fourth-quarter sales growth by our math.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago: +𝟖.𝟒% (total net sales $182.2M (+12.5%))
• Sand States sales growth: +𝟐𝟏.𝟏% (+16.6% over the first nine months)
• Gross margin: 𝟑𝟔.𝟕% (+1.3 percentage points from a year ago)
• Full-year sales and profit outlook: 𝐍𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 (middle of the range unchanged at $610M and $115M)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because third-quarter growth proved that summer pool demand was not just a one-time catch-up from wet spring weather. Factory margins recovered from second-quarter rush costs, and a debt refinancing to 2033 plus lower leverage cleared the way for a $100 million share buyback. One caution: heavy sales investments and acquisition payouts pushed overhead up 26%, causing standard operating margin to slip even as profit excluding one-offs rose.

The question now is whether higher marketing and sales overhead will pay off in 2027 without a rebound in U. S. housing and pool construction. Either the new Florida and Texas sales teams drive enough fiberglass volume to cover their cost, or overhead keeps eating into factory gains while vinyl liners lag. Management's initial 2027 outlook on the fourth-quarter call will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐒𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝟐𝟏% 𝐚𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬
"The Sand States remain a key growth market for Latham, which we believe has the potential to drive a step-change in companywide sales," chief executive Sean Gadd said. The Sand States are Florida, Texas, Arizona and California, where most U. S. swimming pools are built but where concrete pools still dominate. After giving only vague updates for two quarters, the pool maker reported that regional sales rose 21.1% from a year ago, lifting nine-month growth to 16.6%.

Gadd credited Florida and Texas for the pickup. Latham hosted community pool events in Florida neighborhoods and "partnered with a national homebuilder to offer Latham fiberglass pools as an option for its new home construction in Florida", installing its first pool in a model home. It also hired Todd Antonelli as chief commercial officer, "establishing the foundation for a world-class commercial organization" while adding field sales staff.

What to watch: whether the national homebuilder expands the Florida option to additional communities in 2027. A wider rollout would give the manufacturer recurring volume without having to win each backyard buyer one by one.

🟢 𝐅𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐏𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
Skeptics worried that second-quarter demand was just a one-time bounce after cold spring weather delayed early pool builds. Third-quarter results argued against that concern, as sales from businesses owned a year ago grew 8.4% even without the Freedom Pools acquisition in Australia and New Zealand. In-ground pool revenue led the quarter, and Gadd said fiberglass models are winning buyers "for their ease of installation, cost efficiency, durability, lifetime warranty, and low maintenance costs".

• In-ground pool sales: $92.4 million, up 22.6% from a year ago
• Underlying in-ground pool growth: up 13.9%, excluding Freedom Pools
• Target U. S. market share for fiberglass: about 25% of in-ground pools in 2026, up at least 1 percentage point

What to watch: fourth-quarter underlying sales growth. By our math, the full-year outlook points to 13.1% total sales growth in the fourth quarter, which will test demand against last year's warm-weather finish.

🟢 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐛𝐲 𝟏.𝟑 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬
In the second quarter, gross margin fell because factories scrambled to meet a sudden fiberglass order rush. Management promised to recover most of that $2.8 million cost in the second half as plants rebuilt stock. In the third quarter, cost of sales—the direct cost of making pools, liners and covers—fell by 1.3 percentage points of revenue to 63.3%, lifting gross margin to 36.7%.

Latham said the gain came from "reflecting greater plant absorption on higher volumes and the ongoing benefits from our lean manufacturing and value engineering initiatives". Ending inventory rose 23.3% from a year ago to $86.7 million by our math, showing that plants restocked as planned and absorbed fixed overhead despite raw material inflation.

What to watch: fourth-quarter gross margin. Holding above last year's 28.0% fourth-quarter level would confirm that factory efficiency and August liner price increases outran oil-linked resin costs.

concern eased — 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐚 $𝟏𝟎𝟎𝐌 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤
A standing concern was Latham's $75 million credit line maturing in February 2027 and its floating-rate debt. During the third quarter, the group completed a refinancing with a new $75 million credit line and a $300 million term loan "to extend maturities until 2033 and provide additional flexibility to advance our strategic priorities". The transaction triggered a one-time $5.0 million debt extinguishment loss, but net interest expense still fell 10.6% from a year ago to $5.4 million.

Strong summer cash generation cut net debt to 1.8 times trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and one-offs), beating the year-end target of below 2.0 times a quarter early. With the balance sheet settled, the board approved a three-year, $100 million share buyback program.

What to watch: actual share repurchases in the fourth quarter and the new interest rate on the 2033 term loan in the quarterly filing. Buying back shares during the slow winter season would lower the share count before peak 2027 earnings.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Gadd highlighted "achieving considerable operating leverage while investing to accelerate growth", pointing to an 18.1% jump in Adjusted EBITDA to $45.3 million. However, standard accounting tells a tighter story because selling, general and administrative expenses—sales, marketing and corporate overhead—jumped 25.5% from a year ago to $35.9 million.

• Overhead as a share of sales: 19.7%, up 2.0 percentage points from a year ago by our math
• Coverstar Central earn-out expense in overhead: $3.2 million in the quarter, $7.7 million year to date
• Operating margin: 13.0%, down 0.3 percentage points from 13.3% a year ago by our math

Because Latham adds back the Coverstar acquisition payouts and $1.5 million of restructuring charges to its preferred profit metric, Adjusted EBITDA margin rose 1.1 percentage points to 24.8% while standard operating margin slipped. Even stripping out the $3.2 million payout, overhead grew slightly faster than revenue by our math because of Sand States marketing and digital software spending.

What to watch: whether acquisition and integration add-backs drop in 2027 once the Coverstar Central payout period ends. Only a drop in reported overhead will let factory gains reach bottom-line operating profit.

🔴 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐨𝐥 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭
While fiberglass pools grew rapidly, Latham's vinyl liners business—which sells new and replacement liners for packaged pools—moved backward. Third-quarter liner revenue fell 4.9% from a year ago to $30.1 million by our math, after growing 6.0% in the second quarter. Gadd noted that the broader U. S. industry remains a "challenging market", as high borrowing costs keep overall new pool construction flat.

That weakness matters because vinyl liners make up 23% of nine-month revenue and carry steady replacement demand. At the same time, the narrowed full-year outlook leaves $113.0 million of total sales for the fourth quarter at the middle of the range, requiring 13.1% growth by our math against a year-ago quarter when warm weather extended the building season.

What to watch: fourth-quarter liner sales and management's 2027 U. S. pool starts outlook on the fourth-quarter call. Another drop in liners would mean homeowners are delaying even basic replacement maintenance.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟗.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Pool cover revenue rose 8.7% from a year ago, keeping a steady double-digit or near-double-digit pace after growing 10.0% in the second quarter and 6.0% in the first. Growth came from automatic safety covers—motorized covers that seal a pool at the flip of a switch—and cross-selling through acquired Coverstar dealers.

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒𝟐.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Operating cash flow of $48.8 million minus $6.1 million of capital spending produced $42.7 million of free cash flow by our math, down 5.5% from $45.2 million a year ago. Cash generation remained seasonal and high at 23.4% of sales, even as the manufacturer rebuilt inventory by $9.3 million over the first nine months.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟐.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Bottom-line profit rose 48.5% from $8.1 million a year ago, or to $0.10 per diluted share from $0.07, reversing a second-quarter drop. Profit grew despite a one-time $5.0 million debt refinancing loss because currency swings turned slightly positive and the effective tax rate fell to 19.7% from 47.9% a year ago.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: $𝟔𝟎𝟓–𝟔𝟏𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from $600–620 million
Unchanged at the middle of the range. Latham narrowed the band by $5 million on each side, keeping the $610 million midpoint and 11.7% full-year growth target after raising it by $15 million last quarter. By our math, that leaves $113.0 million for the fourth quarter, or 13.1% growth from a year ago against 12.5% in the third quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟏𝟏𝟐–𝟏𝟏𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from $110–120 million
Unchanged at the middle of the range. Management trimmed the top and bottom by $2 million, holding the $115 million midpoint (up 15.2% from 2025) after a $2.5 million raise in the second quarter. By our math, the plan leaves $13.0 million for the fourth quarter, up 23.7% from a year ago with an 11.5% margin.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: $𝟒𝟎–𝟒𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $40–45 million
Unchanged. The spending plan stays at a $42.5 million midpoint after being lowered from $42–48 million last quarter, and it includes the earlier purchase of four fiberglass factory sites. With $34.2 million spent across the first nine months, the outlook leaves about $8.3 million for the fourth quarter by our math.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐲𝐥 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝟓% 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
Liner revenue dropped 4.9% from a year ago to $30.1 million despite an August price increase. Did dealers buy ahead of the price hike in the second quarter, or are homeowners putting off replacement liners?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟑 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧?
Latham extended its $300 million term loan and $75 million credit line to 2033, booking a $5.0 million refinancing loss. What is the new interest spread, and did the company replace the interest rate hedge that expires in May 2027?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐨 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧-𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐝?
Performance payouts for the 2024 Coverstar Central acquisition cost $3.2 million in the third quarter and $7.7 million over nine months, weighing on operating profit. How much remains for the fourth quarter and 2027?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔?
Management previously targeted fiberglass to reach about 80% of Latham's in-ground pool revenue this year, up from 76.5% in 2025. The press release did not update that figure; where is it tracking after the third quarter?

text:
Glycerine, you’ve produced five separate rebuttals without disproving a single one of the five benefits you originally insisted didn’t exist.

Quite an achievement.

Let’s get something straight before we begin.

You are absolutely entitled to ask whether immigration benefits ordinary working people. You are entitled to question its effects on wages, housing, public services and living standards.

What you DON’T get to do is demand evidence, receive it, and then dismiss every documented benefit by declaring that immigrants caused the very problems they’re helping to address.

That’s not an argument. It’s a conclusion you’ve decided must be true regardless of the evidence.

1. THE NHS

Your response to 331,000 NHS staff reporting non-British nationalities is that Britain apparently functioned perfectly well before immigrants arrived.

Are you seriously unaware that the NHS has recruited overseas healthcare professionals since its foundation in 1948?

International recruitment isn’t some recent invention to accommodate immigration. It’s been part of British healthcare for generations.

And your suggestion that migrants bring untold diseases and overwhelm our health service?

Where’s your evidence?

The Health Foundation’s 2026 analysis found that migrants generally use NHS services LESS than UK-born residents and are more likely to work in the health service.

So the available evidence contradicts the simplistic picture you’re presenting.

You then accuse me of wanting millions of migrants to make myself feel virtuous.

No. I want healthcare services properly staffed, British workers properly trained and patients treated promptly.

And I don’t particularly care whether the qualified doctor treating someone was born in Birmingham, Belfast, Bangalore or Barbados.

2. SOCIAL CARE

Now this is where your reasoning becomes particularly ridiculous.

You suggest migrant care workers are somehow creating the very demand for elderly care they’re helping to meet.

Glycerine, Britain has an ageing population. We would have older adults requiring care even if immigration stopped tomorrow.

The King’s Fund reports that 47% of new care workers in 2025/26 were recruited internationally, while the sector still had approximately 65,000 vacancies.

Those workers provide care to people who need it, including elderly and disabled British citizens.

You claim they’re taking jobs from British workers.

Then why are there tens of thousands of unfilled positions?

Of course we should improve pay, conditions and domestic recruitment. Nobody is arguing otherwise.

But pretending migrant workers serve no useful purpose because Britain should theoretically have trained more domestic staff doesn’t solve today’s staffing shortages.

And your assertion that immigration suppresses wages?

Oxford University’s Migration Observatory found that the overall effects on UK-born workers’ wages are generally SMALL. Some lower-paid workers may experience modest negative effects, but that is nothing like the sweeping economic disaster you’ve described.

You have a legitimate argument for improving wages and working conditions.

What you don’t have is evidence that migrant workers are responsible for every failure of Britain’s labour market.

3. FOOD PRODUCTION

This one is particularly entertaining.

You claim migrant agricultural workers increase demand for food; therefore their contribution to producing it is somehow cancelled out.

Except you’ve overlooked something rather important.

Many seasonal agricultural workers come here temporarily, work for a few months and RETURN HOME.

They aren’t all permanently settling in Britain and adding generations of consumers to the population.

The seasonal worker visa specifically does not provide a route to permanent settlement.

Meanwhile, Defra reports that fewer than 5% of seasonal horticultural workers are British nationals.

So explain how British farmers would immediately replace the overwhelming majority of their seasonal workforce without consequences for production, costs or supply.

Simply declaring that immigrants created the problem doesn’t answer the question.

4. TAX REVENUE

Oh, this was magnificent.

I provided the Migration Advisory Committee’s estimate that a Skilled Worker main applicant contributes an average NET £689,000 to public finances over their lifetime.

Your response?

That Britain spends more than £689,000 in a single day on migrants.

Are you fucking serious?

You’ve just compared the estimated lifetime contribution of ONE individual with alleged daily expenditure on MILLIONS of people.

Those aren’t remotely comparable quantities.

It’s like arguing that one person’s annual income is worthless because the entire country spends more than that every afternoon.

And remember, £689,000 is the estimated NET contribution for that specific category of worker, after accounting for public expenditure.

It isn’t their gross salary or the total tax revenue from all immigration.

Different migrant groups have different fiscal outcomes. Some contribute more than they cost, while others impose net costs.

That’s precisely why serious researchers distinguish between migration categories instead of treating every immigrant as economically identical.

You might discover some interesting things if you actually examined the research.

5. BRITISH BUSINESSES

You asked how immigration benefits ordinary working people.

I showed you research identifying foreign-born founders among 54 of Britain’s 100 fastest-growing companies.

Businesses employ people, buy goods and services, pay taxes, and create economic opportunities.

Your response was to start talking about Somali businesses in America and Ilhan Omar.

What the fuck has that got to do with British economic research?

Nothing whatsoever.

You’ve completely ignored the evidence and introduced an unrelated American political reference.

Then you resort to some childish nonsense about my wife’s boyfriend.

Is this genuinely the intellectual standard of your economic analysis?

Apparently so.

NOW, YOUR WIDER ACCUSATIONS

You claim ordinary Britons are suffering because of immigration, that freedom of speech has disappeared, that crime is the inevitable result and that Britain cannot even afford a navy.

These are separate claims requiring separate evidence.

Some communities genuinely face housing shortages, overstretched services and economic insecurity.

Those concerns deserve proper examination.

But you cannot simply attribute every problem to immigration without demonstrating a causal relationship.

Nor can you assume that every crime involving a migrant proves immigration as a whole is harmful. That is not how statistics, economics or criminology work.

And accusing me of virtue signalling doesn’t make your economic claims any more accurate.

You repeatedly insist that immigrants create every problem, then dismiss their contributions because you’ve already assigned them responsibility for the problem in the first place.

It’s circular reasoning.

You have also managed to confuse migrant workers with asylum seekers, temporary workers with permanent residents, gross expenditure with net fiscal contributions, and individual economic effects with national totals.

And throughout all of this, you’ve repeatedly used demeaning language about people whose actual contributions you’ve barely attempted to examine.

Here’s the bottom line.

You demanded FIVE benefits.

I gave you FIVE documented examples.

You haven’t disproved them. You’ve offered personal insults, unrelated anecdotes, sweeping generalisations and repeated assertions that immigration must be harmful because you’ve decided it is.

I have never claimed immigration is free of costs or that every immigration policy benefits every British citizen.

But YOU claimed there were NO benefits.

That was an absolute claim.

And the evidence contradicts it.

So instead of another sprawling response telling me how wonderful your assumptions are, try something genuinely constructive.

Take ONE of the five examples.

Identify the specific factual claim you believe is incorrect.

Provide credible research demonstrating why.

And explain your reasoning without resorting to insults or irrelevant American political references.

Because writing more words doesn’t automatically make your argument more persuasive.

Especially when so many of those words are devoted to avoiding the evidence you demanded in the first place.

text:
**Job Title:** 

Senior Historical Selectivity Officer (Race & Empire Division)

**Salary:** Competitive appearance fees + residual column rates. Performance-related bonus for replies exceeding 500.

**Location:** Hybrid – television studios, radio booths, and anywhere a producer needs a “strong voice” at short notice.

**About the role**  
We are looking for a confident communicator to join our panel of professional opinion-havers. 

You will be responsible for presenting carefully curated slices of British history that maximise engagement while maintaining a consistent brand identity. 

The successful candidate will turn complex, multi-century topics into concise, high-temperature social media posts and studio contributions.

**Key responsibilities**  
- Identify moments of national pride (e.g. Royal Navy suppression of the slave trade) and reframe them as evidence of selective amnesia.  
- Ensure all historical commentary contains the words “millions,” “brutalised,” and at least one implication that the audience is insufficiently ashamed.  
- Generate measurable anger on social platforms; reply counts are a key performance indicator.  
- Appear on daytime television and radio to explain why certain politicians are “pathetic” and will never win the youth vote.  
- Maintain a steady pipeline of related columns for outlets that value clarity over completeness.

**Essential skills**  
- Ability to ignore inconvenient counter-examples (West Africa Squadron, 150,000 people freed, African participation in the trade) without hesitation.  
- Comfortable delivering the same core narrative across multiple platforms with only minor variations in wording.  
- Strong track record of converting controversy into further bookings.  
- Familiarity with the phrase “the younger generation will NEVER vote for…”

**Desirable**  
- Previous experience as a reality television contestant.  
- Willingness to describe any defence of British history as “race-baiting” while practising a more refined form of the same craft.

**What we offer**  
Regular paid media appearances, a loyal audience that either agrees with you or argues with you (both count), and the satisfaction of knowing every angry reply is, in some small way, helping to pay the mortgage.

Apply by sending three examples of selective framing and one screenshot of a post that made at least 200 people furious.

text:
The “Trojan horse” may not look like a conventional chip anymore.

It may look like a biosensor.

A biosensor is designed to detect biological information and convert it into a measurable signal.

Depending on the system, biosensors can be designed to monitor things like:

Electrical activity.

Chemical changes.

Temperature.

Pressure.

Movement.

Glucose.

Hormones.

Proteins.

Neural activity.

Muscle activity.

Other physiological signals.

Now take that basic concept and shrink it.

Technology that once required visible electronic components has been getting smaller for decades.

Today, researchers are developing microscale and nanoscale biosensors, injectable electronics, semiconductor nanowires, neural interfaces and wireless systems designed to interact directly with biological tissue.

That is where the discussion gets much bigger.

A biosensor doesn’t have to look like the traditional implant people imagine.

It may be microscopic.

It may be flexible.

It may be distributed across multiple locations.

It may be designed to sense biological activity.

It may communicate with an external system.

It may operate as part of a larger network.

And depending on the architecture, it may be capable of collecting information from the body and transmitting that information elsewhere.

UC Berkeley researchers developed “neural dust”, tiny, wireless, batteryless sensor systems designed to interface with nerves and muscles and communicate using ultrasound.

https://t.co/XWl3l9unb1

Nature Nanotechnology published research demonstrating syringe-injectable mesh electronics capable of integrating with biological tissue and recording neural activity.

https://t.co/33wEtHHRhd

DARPA’s N3 program pursued high-performance bidirectional brain-machine interfaces designed to both READ FROM and WRITE TO neural activity using optical, acoustic and electromagnetic approaches.

https://t.co/vqlqv3dXXa

And then there are Wireless Body Area Networks.

IEEE 802.15.6-2026 covers short-range wireless communication in the vicinity of, or inside, the human body.

https://t.co/r7P86gb85e

Think about what that means.

A biosensor is not just a tiny object.

It can be part of an information system.

A biosensor can detect something happening biologically.

That signal can be converted into data.

That data can potentially be transmitted to another device.

Multiple sensors can potentially function together.

A gateway can potentially move that information into a larger network.

Now add AI, cloud computing, neural interfaces and advanced wireless communication.

The question becomes much bigger than:

“Is there a chip?”

The better questions are:

Are there biosensors?

What are they sensing?

What biological information can they collect?

Can they communicate?

Can multiple biosensors operate together as a network?

Can they interact with the nervous system?

Can the same architecture that reads biological activity also be paired with systems designed to stimulate or influence biological activity?

Who receives the data?

Who controls the network?

And most importantly:

Did the person consent?

That's where the “Trojan horse” argument becomes serious.

The concern isn’t that every biosensor is dangerous.

Biosensors have legitimate medical, scientific and therapeutic applications.

The concern is what happens if a technology capable of sensing, communicating with or interfacing with the human body is ever introduced, deployed or used without informed consent.

That changes the entire conversation.

Medicine becomes surveillance.

Monitoring becomes data collection.

A therapeutic interface can potentially become a control interface.

And the person may not even know the system is there.

When people hear “nanoscale biosensor” and dismiss it as science fiction, they’re ignoring an entire field of bioelectronics that already exists.

Neural dust is real.

Injectable electronics are real.

Biosensors are real.

Wireless Body Area Networks are real.

Semiconductor nanowires are real.

Bidirectional brain-machine interfaces are real.

The question is what happens as these technologies converge and become smaller, more powerful and more connected.

Explore the research, patents, government records and technical documents: https://t.co/2PoblWjem7

The study discusses its findings alongside established research involving semiconductor nanowires, injectable mesh electronics, neural dust, biosensing, DARPA N3 and Wireless Body Area Networks.

Maybe we should be asking whether modern biosensing technology has already moved far beyond what most people picture when they hear that word.
How small can biosensors become?

text:
$BWXT KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM BWX TECHNOLOGIES’ 3Q26 EARNINGS CALL (11/02/26)

BWXT’s call supports a selective, rather than indiscriminate, positive view of the nuclear investment cycle. The strongest immediate read-through is to companies sharing its nuclear-services contracts, where management identified actual operating outperformance. The strongest longer-duration signals favor established reactor platforms, qualified component manufacturers, and enrichment capacity that resolves identifiable supply constraints. The negative implications concern the timing and economics of uncontracted reactor developments: financing availability does not settle construction-risk allocation, technology selection does not constitute a financed project, and different reactor designs create materially different supplier opportunities. These distinctions favor demonstrated capabilities and executable contracts over broad exposure to nuclear-themed valuations.

NUCLEAR SERVICES AND ENGINEERING

SHARED DOE CONTRACTS PROVIDE A DIRECT POSITIVE EARNINGS SIGNAL (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Amentum Holdings (AMTM: United States); Fluor Corporation (FLR: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for nuclear-services earnings, with potentially meaningful contributions within the relevant businesses but a more modest consolidated impact. This is the clearest near-term earnings read-through because the companies participate in the same operations identified by BWXT.

Supporting evidence: Geveden stated that technical services “once again boosted earnings in the quarter with outperformance on key programs, including Hanford and Savannah River.” Fitzgerald separately identified higher technical-services equity income as a contributor to government profitability.

Transmission mechanism: Amentum and Fluor participate alongside BWXT in Hanford Tank Waste Operations & Closure and Savannah River Mission Completion. Better execution, achievement of contractual performance objectives, and stronger incentive-fee outcomes at these shared ventures can support the partners’ attributable earnings. This is a direct contractual connection, not merely a favorable industry demand signal.

The important distinction is between project revenue and shareholder economics. The large headline contract ceilings are not guaranteed revenue, and neither partner receives the entire venture’s earnings. BWXT’s 22% government EBITDA growth also cannot be assigned entirely to these contracts because naval manufacturing productivity contributed substantially. Nevertheless, identified outperformance at shared operations provides a credible positive indicator for the partners’ nuclear-services results.

Timing and catalysts: Fluor’s November 6 results and Amentum’s November 24 results provide near-term tests of venture earnings, award fees, and cash distributions. These are more actionable catalysts than prospective commercial reactor announcements several years from operation.

Counterweight: Recognition periods, ownership interests, fee allocations, and distribution timing can differ between partners. Positive nuclear-services performance does not establish a consolidated earnings beat if other engineering or government programs underperform. Management’s acknowledgment that an unusually prolonged continuing resolution previously strained technical-services programs also argues against treating this revenue as immune to federal funding interruptions.

CANADIAN REFURBISHMENT OFFERS MORE VISIBLE ECONOMICS THAN SPECULATIVE REACTOR EXPORTS (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected companies: AtkinsRéalis Group (ATRL: Canada); Aecon Group (ARE: Canada).

Direction and magnitude: Positive, with meaningful multiyear implications for nuclear backlog execution and utilization. The incremental call signal is stronger for execution confidence than for undisclosed new awards.

Supporting evidence: BWXT reported 15% organic commercial revenue growth and completion of its Cambridge expansion, increasing that facility’s heavy-component capacity by approximately 50%. Management explicitly connected the expansion to its backlog of CANDU life extensions and SMR projects and reported completion slightly under budget and broadly on schedule.

Transmission mechanism: AtkinsRéalis supplies CANDU technology expertise, engineering, and project delivery; Aecon supplies construction and refurbishment capabilities. Their joint venture signed a C$1.7 billion, 3-year Pickering Unit 5 refurbishment contract in September. BWXT’s added capacity addresses a complementary part of the same industrial system: production of nuclear components needed to execute refurbishment programs.

More available component capacity can reduce schedule pressure and improve the ability to coordinate equipment deliveries with field execution. For AtkinsRéalis and Aecon, the value is improved conversion of awarded work into revenue and potentially fewer disruption costs. It is not ownership of BWXT’s manufacturing margin, nor entitlement to the entire refurbishment budget.

This opportunity also has a different fuel-risk profile from advanced reactors. Conventional CANDU technology uses natural uranium and does not depend on commercial HALEU availability. That makes the established refurbishment cycle less exposed to the fuel bottleneck BWXT identified for expanded TRISO production.

Timing and catalysts: AtkinsRéalis’ November 5 results provide a near-term opportunity to assess nuclear backlog and execution. Aecon already reported on October 29, including record backlog of approximately C$14.6 billion, so BWXT’s commentary is corroboration rather than a fresh prediction of that quarter’s outcome. The fundamental benefits extend through the refurbishment execution period.

Counterweight: Added BWXT capacity does not prove that every component requirement or construction bottleneck has been resolved. Labor, outage coordination, regulatory approvals, and contractor execution remain important. Potential CANDU deployment in Indiana should remain separate from the contracted Canadian opportunity: an evaluation of new reactors is not a construction award or an established export revenue stream.

REACTOR TECHNOLOGY AND CAPITAL EQUIPMENT

THE FIRST ORDER WAVE FAVORS BWRX-300, NOT EVERY NUCLEAR COMPONENT SUPPLIER EQUALLY (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: GE Vernova (GEV: United States); Curtiss-Wright Corporation (CW: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for GE Vernova’s nuclear platform and longer-term installed base. Negative for expectations that the earliest SMR awards automatically generate AP1000-sized reactor-coolant-pump opportunities for Curtiss-Wright. Near-term consolidated earnings effects are limited for both; order expectations and valuation narratives are more exposed.

Supporting evidence: Geveden stated, “the SMR opportunity is a bit ahead of the large reactor opportunity.” His expected sequence was Darlington units 2-4, followed by TVA-related BWRX-300 opportunities, with AP1000 opportunities following.

Transmission mechanism: GE Vernova Hitachi is the BWRX-300 technology provider. Additional deployments create opportunities for engineering, major-component procurement, project support, fuel, and subsequent lifecycle services. Progress toward repeat units also strengthens the platform’s reference-project advantage, potentially reducing engineering repetition and customer uncertainty.

The less obvious implication concerns Curtiss-Wright’s equipment content. Curtiss-Wright supplies the 4 reactor coolant pumps used by an AP1000. The BWRX-300 instead uses natural circulation through the reactor core, eliminating the equivalent pumped recirculation requirement. Consequently, a BWRX-300 award cannot be translated into Curtiss-Wright’s AP1000 coolant-pump content.

This does not imply that Curtiss-Wright has no opportunities in SMRs, instrumentation, valves, or other equipment. It establishes that supplier exposure must be mapped to the specific reactor design rather than inferred from the generic SMR label. Existing AP1000 work, naval programs, and aftermarket businesses are separate from this timing distinction.

Timing and catalysts: Curtiss-Wright reports November 4 and holds its call November 5. Platform-specific order commentary is the relevant near-term catalyst. For GE Vernova, Darlington follow-on procurement and firm U.S. BWRX-300 commitments through 1H27 are the more important milestones. The longer-duration benefit comes from repeat deployment and installed-base services, not an immediate step-change in group earnings.

Counterweight: BWXT’s sequence is a supplier’s expectation, not a binding customer procurement calendar. The referenced TVA reactor opportunity is not equivalent to a fully awarded fleet. AP1000 orders could also proceed in parallel.

U.S. MANUFACTURING EXPANSION DOES NOT EXCLUDE ESTABLISHED KOREAN SUPPLIERS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: Doosan Enerbility (034020: South Korea).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for medium- and long-term nuclear equipment opportunities; limited immediate earnings implication. The call argues against a simple thesis that BWXT’s U.S. expansion displaces foreign suppliers from prospective U.S. reactor construction.

Supporting evidence: Asked about Korean financing and equipment allocation, Geveden said BWXT expects to compete with “Doosan and IHI and all the usual suspects.” He added that “there’s actually still not that much capacity globally for these kind of components.”

Transmission mechanism: Doosan has established manufacturing capabilities in reactor vessels, steam generators, and heavy forgings, including AP1000-related equipment. Its current disclosures confirm continued large nuclear-forging awards and an AP1000 supply track record. If multiple reactor programs advance, qualified fabrication capacity and long manufacturing lead times can support order intake and factory utilization across several suppliers.

BWXT’s commentary is particularly useful because it comes from a prospective competitor. Management did not describe the U.S. market as reserved for domestic manufacturers or claim that its new plant would absorb all available demand. Korean participation in financing could influence commercial arrangements, but the call did not establish any guaranteed allocation to Doosan.

The principal benefit is volume and utilization, not necessarily unrestricted pricing power. BWXT explicitly acknowledged price pressure, and its commercial margin declined year over year despite strong revenue growth. Capacity scarcity therefore should not be converted automatically into an industry-wide margin expansion forecast.

Timing and catalysts: Supplier selection, funded long-lead procurement, and actual fabrication releases during 2027 are more meaningful than additional political investment announcements. Revenue realization would extend over multiple years.

Counterweight: BWXT’s Cambridge expansion, PCG capacity, and proposed U.S. facility will increase competing supply. That may constrain longer-term pricing even if the near-term market is not zero-sum. The magnitude of Doosan’s benefit remains dependent on awarded scope, not announced reactor counts.

NUCLEAR FUEL CYCLE

HALEU AVAILABILITY IS A REAL BOTTLENECK, SUPPORTING ENRICHMENT CAPABILITY RATHER THAN GENERIC URANIUM EXPOSURE (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: Centrus Energy (LEU: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for the strategic value of demonstrated domestic enrichment capability, potentially material over the longer term. The immediate EPS read-through is small because BWXT disclosed neither a Centrus supply award nor associated pricing.

Supporting evidence: BWXT said a larger TRISO facility requires both significant contracted demand and commercially available HALEU. Geveden stated, “we also need to see HALEU become available commercially.” The company also disclosed an initial 1 metric ton, multiyear TRISO agreement with Antares and potential expansion of its existing Lynchburg output.

Transmission mechanism: Additional advanced-reactor and TRISO demand cannot become sustained production without suitable enriched feedstock. Centrus has demonstrated HALEU production and signed a $900 million DOE enrichment-capacity contract. Its commercial expansion is therefore exposed to a specifically identified bottleneck, rather than merely to rising nuclear enthusiasm.

The economic opportunity is securing enrichment contracts, customer prepayments, utilization commitments, and returns on new capacity. It is not a direct read-through to mined uranium prices. TRISO fabrication and uranium enrichment are distinct activities, and the disclosed TRISO quantity cannot be translated mechanically into Centrus sales.

Centrus’ own latest quarterly disclosure reported approximately $3.0 billion of contingent LEU and HALEU sales commitments and a large-scale commercial HALEU agreement potentially including prepayments. Those disclosures support the transmission mechanism, but do not establish that BWXT or Antares is the unidentified customer. The first new expansion capacity was expected in 2029, placing much of the potential benefit beyond the next several quarters.

Timing and catalysts: Centrus reports November 4 and holds its call November 5. The actionable developments are conversion of contingent commitments, receipt of prepayments, operating arrangements for the existing cascade, and construction milestones. A new demand announcement without those developments would be less significant.

Counterweight: Scarcity does not guarantee immediate profitability. Centrus’ Technical Solutions segment recorded a gross loss in 2Q26, and its new capacity contract includes fixed-price obligations. BWXT’s pursuit of additional LEU and HALEU scope also argues against valuing Centrus as a perpetual monopoly. The positive conclusion concerns the value of established capability and customer commitments, not assured margins or exclusive access to future demand.

REACTOR DEVELOPMENT AND PROJECT FINANCE

WESTINGHOUSE EXPOSURE REQUIRES A CONTRACT-ECONOMICS DISCOUNT, NOT JUST A REACTOR-COUNT MULTIPLE (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: Cameco Corporation (CCJ: Canada).

Direction and magnitude: Negative for the certainty and timing of aggressive near-term Westinghouse new-build expectations, while leaving the longer-term opportunity intact. Potentially meaningful for the valuation of future growth, but limited evidence of an immediate reduction in established earnings.

Supporting evidence: Geveden identified allocation of construction risk as the principal barrier to reactor investment decisions: “I think it’s less about financing, it’s more about allocation of risk.” He also placed AP1000 opportunities behind the nearer BWRX-300 sequence and widened the practical U.S. order window from a possible year-end award to approximately 1H27.

Transmission mechanism: Cameco owns 49% of Westinghouse. Its exposure is therefore to Westinghouse’s attributable earnings and cash distributions from technology, engineering, equipment arrangements, fuel, and services. It is not a 49% claim on the gross construction budgets of announced reactor projects.

Unresolved responsibility for cost overruns can delay customer commitments, change contractual economics, or alter the pace of revenue and milestone payments. Government-supported financing improves the ability to fund projects, but does not by itself establish a bankable allocation of construction and completion risk. Earlier component procurement may proceed without the entire generating project reaching full commitment, so procurement activity and full-project certainty must also be separated.

Cameco had already reported on October 30, including C$143 million of attributable quarterly Westinghouse adjusted EBITDA. BWXT’s call is therefore a forward contracting signal, not a new predictor of Cameco’s already-reported quarter.

Timing and catalysts: Firm AP1000 commercial agreements, funded procurement packages, and disclosure of risk-sharing terms are the relevant catalysts through 1H27. The negative near-term implication is a higher hurdle for assuming a rapid new-build earnings step-up. The longer-term positive remains the creation of an expanded installed base requiring services and fuel.

Counterweight: This is not a negative read-through to all Westinghouse operations or to Cameco’s existing uranium contracts. Operating-reactor services and fuel demand are less dependent on new-project investment decisions. Additional qualified component capacity could also improve future execution economics.

DEVELOPMENT-STAGE NUCLEAR POWER SHOULD NOT BE VALUED LIKE CONTRACTED DATA-CENTER INFRASTRUCTURE (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: Fermi Inc., operating as Fermi America (FRMI: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Negative for aggressive valuation of the unfinanced nuclear portion of Project Matador. The effect could be substantial for that development option, but cannot be translated directly into a comparable reduction in total equity value because the nearer-term gas and customer infrastructure phases have different economics.

Supporting evidence: BWXT described risk allocation among hyperscalers, utilities, governments, and technology providers as the obstacle to new-build commitments. Geveden also distinguished the risk of manufacturing known components from the much broader risk of delivering a complete generating project.

Transmission mechanism: Fermi is developing an integrated power and computing campus that includes proposed AP1000 generation. Its nuclear economics depend on the alignment of reactor procurement, licensing, construction, financing, and customer demand. Progress on an individual component does not establish that the entire nuclear development has become financeable.

The appropriate implication is to maintain a substantial distinction between contracted near-term infrastructure and prospective nuclear cash flows. Delayed nuclear commissioning defers revenue while potentially increasing carrying costs and the duration of capital exposure. Illustratively, a 1-year delay reduces the present value of an otherwise unchanged future cash-flow stream by approximately 9% at a 10% discount rate, before additional interest or construction costs. This is a valuation sensitivity, not a forecast of a Fermi delay.

The counterevidence is important. Fermi’s August disclosure reported a binding 15-year TensorWave lease covering an initial 222 MW, additional liquidity, and a gas-generation partnership structured around contracted demand. Those developments mean that the nuclear financing challenge should not be used to characterize the entire campus as uncontracted or to infer failure of its initial power-delivery plan.

Timing and catalysts: The meaningful nuclear catalysts are fully specified construction arrangements, financing commitments, completion-risk allocation, and customer agreements matched to the nuclear delivery schedule. Licensing progress alone does not resolve those requirements. Near-term trading may react strongly to nuclear milestones, while the fundamental value depends on whether those milestones reduce financing and delivery risk.

Relationship qualification: BWXT did not disclose a Fermi award on this call. This read-through concerns shared project economics, not a lost or delayed BWXT contract, and does not establish new deterioration in Fermi’s company-specific negotiations.

POWER-GENERATION EQUIPMENT

NUCLEAR PROGRESS SUPPORTS A GAS-PLUS-NUCLEAR BUILDOUT RATHER THAN IMMEDIATE GAS DISPLACEMENT (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected company: GE Vernova (GEV: United States).

Direction and magnitude: Positive for the durability of gas-turbine and associated services demand alongside nuclear development. The broader mechanism is meaningful for GE Vernova’s Power business, although BWXT’s call itself does not establish an incremental turbine order or a near-term earnings revision.

Supporting evidence: BWXT expects initial U.S. reactor component awards around year-end or 1H27, while major investment decisions still require agreement on project risk. Management also emphasized the need to deliver reactors “more quickly and more reliably.” These are procurement and development milestones, not evidence of imminent nuclear electricity production.

Transmission mechanism: Customers needing firm power before new reactors enter service require an earlier generation solution. Gas equipment can therefore be procured ahead of nuclear construction, with subsequent service revenue as the turbines operate. Nuclear and gas equipment demand can coexist within the same customer project rather than representing mutually exclusive capital allocations.

GE Vernova’s disclosed Blue Energy project illustrates this mechanism directly. The planned Texas development combines approximately 1 GW from 2 GE Vernova gas turbines in 2030 with up to 1.5 GW from 5 BWRX-300 reactors beginning in 2032, subject to a 2027 final investment decision. The engineering relationship is established, but the planned fleet should not be treated as an unconditional equipment backlog addition.

This gives GE Vernova exposure to different stages of the same power-development cycle: earlier gas equipment and services, followed by nuclear engineering, reactor deployment, fuel, and lifecycle support. BWXT’s contracting timetable reinforces that sequencing.

Timing and catalysts: Near-term catalysts are project commitments, equipment reservations becoming firm contracts, and customer funding. Fundamental revenue and service benefits extend through the end of the decade and beyond.

Counterweight: The call does not support a specific increase in natural gas prices, pipeline utilization, or producer earnings. Those outcomes depend on plant location, actual commissioning, utilization, fuel procurement, and competing generation. The high-conviction conclusion is equipment complementarity and sequencing, not an immediate commodity-demand shock.

CROSS-PORTFOLIO CONCLUSION

The most actionable near-term signals are the shared-contract earnings implications for Amentum and Fluor and the execution confirmation for AtkinsRéalis ahead of their reporting dates. The most important platform distinction favors GE Vernova’s BWRX-300 opportunity without automatically transferring AP1000 pump content to Curtiss-Wright. Longer-duration positives support qualified heavy-component capacity and demonstrated enrichment capability. The clearest negatives apply to front-loaded assumptions about uncontracted AP1000 earnings and the valuation of development-stage nuclear generation before construction risk and financing are fully allocated.

text:
On This Day: Paisley Park Shares a Limited-Time Prince Exhibit at Mall of America
Sender: Paisley Park (@PaisleyPark)
Date: November 3, 2016
Time: 22:50:45 GMT (4:50 PM CST)
Subject: #Prince: The #Artist, The #Icon, The #Legend. Experience for a limited time at @mallofamerica
Link:
On November 3, 2016—six months after Prince’s death—Paisley Park posted a promotional call inviting fans to the free, temporary exhibit Prince: The Artist, The Icon, The Legend at Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota. 
Located on Level 3 East and open through November 14 during regular mall hours, the compact display drew from the Paisley Park archives. It featured never-before-shown items including the hand-painted blue cloud suit from the “Raspberry Beret” video, the jacket and guitar from the 2007 Super Bowl halftime show, the cane from the Grammys, awards such as the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame trophy and an American Music Award, early Purple Rain storyboards, and other costumes and memorabilia. Giant photos and concert footage lined the walls; photography was prohibited to protect the collection. 
The post, which included four photos and hashtags #MPLS and #PaisleyPark, underscored the short window for Minnesotans and visitors to encounter these pieces of Prince’s history in a public setting while Paisley Park itself was still navigating its transition to a museum. It offered an accessible way to celebrate the artist, icon, and legend in the place he called home.

DID YOU KNOW??

Pretending to be Batman can dramatically increase a person's focus, self-control, and perseverance through a psychological phenomenon known as the "Batman Effect"!

​First documented by researchers at the University of Minnesota and the University of Pennsylvania, the strategy works through a technique called self-distancing.

When children or adults adopt the persona of a competent, hard-working character, they mentally step back from their own immediate frustration and anxiety, allowing executive function and impulse control to operate at peak levels. Let me explain 👇🏾👇🏾 

1. How Self-Distancing Works in the Brain​:

A. The 10-Minute Boredom Test: In the landmark 2016 study, 4- and 6-year-old children were assigned a tedious, repetitive task on a computer for 10 minutes while being offered the option to take breaks to play a fun video game.

Children who pretended to be Batman (dressed in a cape and asking themselves "Is Batman working hard?") spent significantly more time staying focused on the task than children who thought about themselves in the first person ("Am I working hard?").

2. ​Adult Application & Beyoncé's "Sasha Fierce": The psychological mechanism isn't just for kids. Many top athletes, performers, and public speakers use the exact same strategy by creating alter egos to overcome performance anxiety, most famously Beyoncé, who adopted the persona "Sasha Fierce" to step onto stage with heightened confidence.

3. ​The Subway Altruism Experiment: In a 2025 study in Italy, researchers tested a real-world variation of the effect. When a person dressed as Batman entered a crowded subway car, the percentage of commuters who offered their seat to a pregnant woman nearly doubled (from 38% to 67%).

The visual presence of a superhero disrupted people's "autopilot" mode and primed them toward prosocial, helpful behavior, wierd! 🤌🏾 😂 

SUMMARILY! 
​Whether it helps a child push through difficult homework or prompts subway commuters to perform acts of kindness, the "Batman Effect" proves that taking a mental step outside yourself and channeling a heroic identity gives your brain the focus and resilience needed to succeed.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

Minnesota is ten wins, three losses and three overtime losses, with a plus-sixteen goal differential. Philadelphia is four, eight and four, at minus-nineteen. Minnesota also has unresolved availability concerns around an already depleted roster. ELECTION NEWS: WHY NOT TAKE THE DOJ UP ON ITS LOVELY OFFER? MINNESOTA COUNTY REJECTS POLL MONITORS
Hennepin County denied a U.S. Department of Justice request to put federal election monitors inside Minneapolis-area polling places Tuesday, keeping them outside the 100-foot boundary set by Minnesota law, the county attorney's office said. Ramsey County also said no.

The monitors are DOJ lawyers in plain clothes, with no badges or guns, who may interview voters on the way out, Secretary of State Steve Simon said. He said they followed all the rules during the August primary.

"Our office is committed to ensuring free, safe, and fair elections," County Attorney Mary Moriarty said.

By turning the monitors away, Moriarty has taken responsibility for a well-run election, and every polling place in America has issues of one sort or another.

TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 2026
MEN'S DIVISION I | POINT SPREADS ONLY
The college basketball season is underway, and today's 19 Division I matchups feature several significant differences between public betting tickets, the money being wagered and sportsbook line movement.
The biggest question isn't which favorites attract the most bets. It's whether the betting dollars and changing point spreads support or contradict that public enthusiasm.
TOP CONTRARIAN SIGNALS

WOFFORD +25.5 AT TENNESSEE
6:00 PM ET

PUBLIC CONSENSUS: 87% TENNESSEE!

Only 13% of tracked tickets support Wofford, but those bets account for 34% of the money.

Tennessee attracts 87% of tickets but only 66% of the handle.
An additional sportsbook sample shows 79% of tickets on Tennessee, while a separate Las Vegas market reports 83% of spread dollars backing Wofford.

OPENING: Tennessee -27.5.
CURRENT: Tennessee approximately -25 to -25.5.

BETTING IMPLICATION:

This is one of today's more compelling corroborated contrarian situations.

The overwhelming ticket majority supports Tennessee, but significant money is reaching Wofford, and the line has moved approximately two points toward the underdog.

The movement supports the contrarian interpretation, although the betting splits are not uniform across sportsbooks.
SOUTH DAKOTA STATE +11.5 AT KANSAS STATE
8:00 PM ET

PUBLIC CONSENSUS: 68% KANSAS STATE.

MONEY CONSENSUS: 60% SOUTH DAKOTA STATE!

Only 32% of tickets support the Jackrabbits, but they account for 60% of the tracked handle.

That's a 28-percentage-point difference between ticket share and money share.

OPENING: Kansas State -11.5.
CURRENT: Kansas State -10.5 to -11.5.
BETTING IMPLICATION:

A meaningful Pros vs. Joes discrepancy favors South Dakota State.

The money concentration is significant, although independent sportsbook readings are not uniformly as strong.

The modest line movement provides some supporting evidence, but this is not a confirmed marketwide sharp-money consensus.

7:00 PM ET

CURRENT: Georgia Tech -13.5 to -14.5.

BETTING IMPLICATION:

The public prefers Georgia Tech, but meaningful betting dollars favor Hampton in multiple sportsbook samples.

The market has also offered slightly smaller Georgia Tech spreads than the opener.
This is a reasonably corroborated contrarian money signal, although the price movement remains modest. Action Network

text:
Flames legend Jarome Iginla battling health issues

https://t.co/7JuLA25LGT
-

By Eric Francis - Sportsnet
-

For years, Jarome Iginla played through just about everything hockey could throw at him.

Broken bones, bruises, bumps, slashes, playoff wars and the relentless punishment of more than 1,600 NHL games. Nothing seemed capable of keeping one of the toughest competitors in Calgary Flames history down for long.

Now, the Hockey Hall of Famer is facing a battle far removed from the rink.

“Unfortunately I have been battling some health issues,” said the 49-year-old from his home in Lake Country, B.C.

“Some neurological issues. I’m not entirely sure what it is, it may be from metal toxins from reaction to the cobalt hip.”

Iginla underwent hip replacement surgery a few years ago after a career spent absorbing the physical toll of professional hockey. Complications followed, along with medications that have affected his energy, weight and speech.

There are concerns that the cobalt-chromium components used in some artificial hip implants can release metal ions and debris through wear or corrosion, potentially causing complications as they enter the bloodstream.

He also had high mercury levels in his body and is working to get that down, while trying to determine if the cause is related to the cobalt poisoning.

Iginla has spent well over a year getting tests and consulting with medical professionals in an ongoing effort to get answers about what is happening and how best to treat it.

“I need more time to figure it all out, but I’m still hopeful that I will recover fully,” he said.

“Things are slowly getting under control, thanks be to God.”

That's the encouraging part. The rest remains a work in progress.

The news will undoubtedly hit Flames fans hard, particularly those who remember the force of nature Iginla was during his 16 seasons in Calgary as the face of the franchise.

A powerful right winger with a wicked shot, an imposing frame and a rare combination of skill, toughness and leadership, Iginla became the standard against which Flames players were measured.

He remains the club's all-time leader in games played, goals and points, finishing his Calgary career with 525 goals and 1,095 points in 1,219 games, before moving on to Pittsburgh, Boston, Colorado and L.A.

His finest moment in a Flames uniform came during the unforgettable 2004 playoff run, when he helped drag a team that few expected to contend all the way to Game 7 of the Stanley Cup Final. The Flames ultimately fell one game short against Tampa Bay, but Iginla's performance that spring cemented his place in Calgary hockey folklore.

He was a two-time 50-goal scorer, a six-time NHL All-Star and a two-time Olympic gold medallist with Canada, including the iconic 2010 Vancouver Games, when he assisted Sidney Crosby's golden goal.

His international résumé also includes a World Championship, World Cup of Hockey title and World Junior Championship. He won two Memorial Cups with the Kamloops Blazers before becoming the 11th-overall selection in the 1995 NHL Draft. He was inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 2020.

Since retiring in 2018, Iginla has largely stayed out of the spotlight, devoting much of his time to coaching and supporting his children as they pursued their own hockey careers.

Two of his children, Tij and Jade, have turned professional, while his youngest son Joe was selected by the Flames this summer, creating another connection between the family and the organization Jarome helped define.

Iginla returned to the Flames in an official capacity in 2023, when he was named special advisor to general manager Craig Conroy. His role has included occasional trips to Calgary to watch the team and offer guidance.

He has never been one to chase the cameras, preferring to let his work and his family life take priority.

That relative privacy has made recent glimpses of Iginla all the more noticeable.

A video featuring Jarome and Joe filmed ahead of this summer's NHL Draft surfaced recently, prompting concern among fans, with some struck by Iginla's noticeably slimmer appearance and a voice that sounded different from the one they remembered.

The reaction speaks to the affection Calgary still has for its former captain.

Only Lanny McDonald can rival Iginla's standing among Flames fans. His impact went well beyond the numbers, built on years of carrying the club, playing through pain and representing the city with a combination of pride and humility.

For now, Iginla is asking for time as doctors work to determine exactly what is wrong.

“Still working through it, but I’m hopeful,” added the Edmonton native.

After everything he gave the game, Flames fans everywhere will be hoping he can summon that same determination for the most important fight of his life.
